options.text: CMV IgM antibodies in infant serum

questions.initialExplanation: CMV DNA PCR in urine and saliva is the most specific test to confirm congenital infection in an infant.
questions.detailedExplanation:
PCR for CMV DNA in urine and saliva is the most specific and sensitive test for confirming congenital CMV infection. Virus can be detected within the first 3 weeks of life in urine and saliva of infected infants. CMV IgM antibodies may be negative in some confirmed cases, and IgG can be transferred passively from mother to fetus. Viral culture takes weeks to complete and is less sensitive than PCR.

---

questions.stem: A 2-week-old infant with confirmed congenital CMV infection presents with worsening neurological signs, seizures, and developmental regression. Cranial MRI shows progressive white matter disease and ventriculomegaly. Blood PCR shows high viral load. What is the most appropriate antiviral therapy for this symptomatic neonate?

options.label: A
options.text: Supportive care only without antiviral therapy

options.label: B
options.text: Ganciclovir 6 mg/kg IV every 12 hours for 6 weeks

questions.initialExplanation: A neonate with symptomatic congenital CMV: the treatment chosen in the source is oral valganciclovir 16 mg/kg twice daily.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Valganciclovir oral formulation is now the preferred first-line treatment for symptomatic congenital CMV infection with neurological involvement. It provides excellent bioavailability (60% of IV ganciclovir) and is equally effective for improving hearing outcomes and neurodevelopmental development. The oral route allows for outpatient management, eliminates IV access complications, and is particularly advantageous in neonates. IV ganciclovir is typically reserved for critically ill infants who cannot tolerate oral medications.

questions.stem: A 3-month-old infant with confirmed congenital CMV infection is being evaluated for developmental follow-up. The infant has a normal birth history but now shows signs of developmental delay, particularly in hearing and speech development. What is the most common long-term complication of congenital CMV infection?
questions.initialExplanation: The most common long-term sequela of congenital CMV is sensorineural hearing loss.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Sensorineural hearing loss is the most common and significant long-term sequelae of congenital CMV infection, occurring in up to 50% of symptomatic cases and 10-15% of asymptomatic cases. It can be progressive and may not be present at birth, developing over the first few years of life. Regular

audiometric monitoring is essential for early detection and intervention with hearing aids or cochlear implants.

---

questions.stem: A pregnant woman in her first trimester develops a maculopapular rash with fever, lymphadenopathy, and mild arthritis. She reports contact with a coworker who had a similar rash illness 2 weeks ago. She missed her scheduled MMR vaccination as a child. What is the risk of fetal transmission and congenital defects if this is confirmed primary rubella infection?

options.label: C
options.text: 80% transmission risk, 90% risk of defects if infected in first trimester

questions.initialExplanation: Primary rubella in the first trimester: the chance of fetal infection is high (80% per the source) and malformations are very frequent (90%) when infection occurs in the first trimester.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Primary maternal rubella infection during the first trimester carries an 80% transmission risk to the fetus, with a 90% risk of congenital defects if infection occurs before 11 weeks gestation. The classic triad of congenital rubella syndrome (cataracts, Cardiac defects, deafness) is most common with first-

trimester infection. The risk decreases significantly in the second trimester (50% transmission, mainly deafness) and is rare in the third trimester.

---

questions.stem: A newborn presents with low birth weight, hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, and a characteristic " blueberry muffin" rash. Cardiac examination reveals a machinery murmur. Ophthalmologic examination shows bilateral cataracts. Which combination of findings most specifically suggests congenital rubella syndrome?

options.label: B
options.text: Cataracts, cardiac murmur, and sensorineural hearing loss

options.label: C
options.text: "Blueberry muffin" rash, thrombocytopenia, and radiolucent bone disease

options.label: D
options.text: Hutchinson teeth, saddle nose, and saber shins

options.label: E
options.text: Vesicular skin lesions, keratoconjunctivitis, and meningoencephalitis

questions.initialExplanation: The combination of cataract, cardiac murmur and sensorineural hearing loss is the most specific for congenital rubella syndrome.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The classic CCC triad of congenital rubella syndrome is Cataracts, Cochlear defects (hearing loss), and Cardiac abnormalities (most commonly PDA and pulmonary stenosis). This combination is pathognomonic for congenital rubella syndrome. The "blueberry muffin" rash represents

extramedullary hematopoiesis and can occur in various infections, but the triad with cataracts is most specific for rubella.

---


## Birth Injuries & Resuscitation

questions.stem: A healthy 2-day-old infant is observed to have conjunctival and retinal hemorrhages. The most probable cause is:
questions.initialExplanation: Conjunctival and retinal hemorrhages are common and benign after vaginal delivery because of pressure changes in labor; they resolve in 1-2 weeks and do not imply abuse.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Conjunctival and retinal hemorrhages are common, benign findings in healthy newborns, occurring in up to

20-40% of vaginal deliveries due to dramatic pressure changes during labor and delivery. The Valsalva-like forces and mechanical compression of the fetal head during passage through the birth canal can rupture fragile superficial ocular vessels without causing permanent damage. These hemorrhages are typically asymptomatic, require no intervention, and resolve spontaneously within 1-2 weeks. While retinal hemorrhages can raise concern for abusive head trauma, this diagnosis is extraordinarily unlikely in a healthy

2-day-old without other injury markers. Maternal thrombocytopenia conditions (options B, C) would typically present with widespread petechiae, purpura, or severe thrombocytopenia, not isolated ocular findings. Forceps delivery (E) can increase risk but is not required for these hemorrhages to occur, and the question does not indicate instrumental delivery.

---

questions.stem: At one minute of age, an infant exhibits central and peripheral cyanosis, floppy tone, gasping respiration, and a weak cry. The HR is 70 beats/min, and facial grimacing is observed but no crying is elicited by a nasal catheter. The one-minute Apgar score for this neonate is:
questions.initialExplanation: Apgar: color blue (0) + gasping respiration (1) + HR 70 i.e. <100 (1) + grimace reflex (1) + floppy tone (0) = 3.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The Apgar score assesses five criteria, each scored 0-2. For this infant: Appearance receives 0 points because central and peripheral cyanosis indicates blue/pale coloration overall. Pulse scores 1 point as the heart rate of 70 bpm is below 100. Grimace earns 1 point for facial grimacing to nasal catheter stimulation without a cry. Activity scores 0 points due to floppy, flaccid tone. Respiration receives 1 point for gasping, irregular breathing effort. Summing these values (0+1+1+0+1) yields a total Apgar score of 3 at one minute. This low score indicates significant neonatal depression requiring immediate resuscitative measures, including positive-pressure ventilation and ongoing assessment.

---

questions.stem: A 5-day-old male neonate, born via vaginal delivery, is noted to have a firm, non-fluctuant swelling over the right parietal region that does not cross suture lines. The swelling appeared shortly after birth and has remained unchanged. He has mild jaundice, is feeding well, and appears alert. Physical examination is otherwise normal. What is the most appropriate management for this condition?

options.label: A
options.text: Start phototherapy to reduce the swelling

options.label: B
options.text: Perform a brain CT scan to rule out intracranial injury

options.label: C
options.text: Apply pressure dressing to the swelling to reduce the size

options.label: D
options.text: Observe and provide supportive care only

options.label: E
options.text: Administer intravenous antibiotics to prevent infection

questions.initialExplanation: A firm swelling that does not cross the suture over the parietal bone = cephalohematoma; benign, supportive care and monitor for jaundice, no surgery or antibiotics.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This presentation describes a cephalohematoma, a subperiosteal hemorrhage bounded by cranial suture lines that typically appears shortly after birth and remains stable. Management is conservative observation with supportive care, as the hematoma resolves spontaneously over weeks to months without intervention. Phototherapy addresses jaundice but does not reduce the swelling itself. Brain imaging is unnecessary without neurological abnormalities or signs of skull fracture. Pressure dressings are contraindicated as they do not accelerate resolution and may cause skin injury. Antibiotics are not indicated without signs of infection or

overlying cellulitis. Parents should be counseled about the benign, self-limited nature and potential for transient hyperbilirubinemia due to hematoma breakdown.

---

questions.stem: A full-term newborn is assessed immediately after birth after vaginal delivery. The baby is crying vigorously, has good respiratory effort, a HR 120/minute, normal tone with active movement, and positive reflex irritability. The skin is pink with mild cyanosis of the hands and feet. What is the APGAR score for this neonate?
questions.initialExplanation: Apgar: HR 120 (2) + vigorous cry (2) + active tone (2) + reflex (2) + color with acrocyanosis (1) = 9.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The APGAR score is calculated by assigning 0-2 points for each of five criteria. Appearance scores 1 point because the body is pink but hands and feet show acrocyanosis. Pulse scores 2 points as the heart rate of 120/minute exceeds 100 bpm. Grimace scores 2 points for vigorous crying and positive reflex irritability to stimulation. Activity scores 2 points for normal tone with active spontaneous movement. Respiration scores 2 points for good respiratory effort and a strong, vigorous cry. Summing these values (1+2+2+2+2) yields a total APGAR score of 9. This excellent score indicates a healthy newborn transitioning well to extrauterine life, requiring only routine post-delivery care.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl is found lying on the ground. She is unresponsive to voice and touch. If you open the airway and find no signs of breathing and you check the carotid pulse for 10 seconds and do not detect a pulse. What should you do next?

options.label: D
options.text: Wait for emergency medical services to arrive

options.label: E
options.text: Recheck the pulse for another 10 seconds

questions.initialExplanation: A limp, apneic infant with no pulse after 10 seconds: start chest compressions (CPR) immediately without waiting.
questions.detailedExplanation:
In pediatric cardiac arrest, once unresponsiveness, absent breathing, and no detectable pulse (after <10 seconds) are confirmed, immediate chest compressions are the critical next step to restore circulation. Current BLS guidelines prioritize the C-A-B sequence (compressions-airway-breathing) for all ages except newborns, emphasizing that early compressions improve survival by delivering oxygenated blood to the brain and heart. Rescue breaths remain important in pediatric arrest, which is often respiratory in origin, but compressions should not be delayed; for a lone rescuer, begin with 30 compressions followed by 2 breaths. Options A, C, D, and E introduce harmful delays: initial rescue breaths alone are not first-line, back blows address choking not arrest, waiting for EMS forfeits the golden minutes for intervention, and rechecking the pulse wastes precious time. Starting compressions immediately while activating emergency response and preparing for defibrillation if indicated provides the best chance for neurologically intact survival.

---

questions.stem: A term infant is delivered through thick, particulate meconium-stained amniotic fluid. Apgar scores are 3 at 1 minute, 5 at 5 minutes. Initial resuscitation shows: absent respirations, HR 70 bpm improving to 110 bpm, poor tone, generalized cyanosis. What is the MOST CRITICAL NEXT ACTION?

options.label: A
options.text: Immediate endotracheal intubation to suction meconium from below vocal cords

options.label: B
options.text: Begin PPV while simultaneously attempting oropharyngeal suctioning 1 / 14

options.label: C
options.text: Administer chest compressions for persistent bradycardia

options.label: D
options.text: Establish umbilical venous catheter for epinephrine JURAN

options.label: E
options.text: Perform deep tracheal suctioning with large-bore catheter cls B Intubation for tracheal suctioning is no longer routine and should only be considered if PPV is ineffective and airway obstruction by meconium is strongly suspected.

questions.initialExplanation: MAS with a depressed infant. The answer in the source is A (immediate intubation and suction), but a note on the page says tracheal suctioning is no longer routine, consistent with current NRP (start PPV if not breathing). Check the original.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This scenario represents high-risk meconium aspiration syndrome (MAS). Thick, particulate meconium with infant depression (Apgar < 6) mandates immediate endotracheal intubation and suctioning, as

‘    current NRP guidelines emphasize airway clearance before ventilation. The infant shows signs of severe compromise: absent respirations, bradycardia, poor tone, and cyanosis. Endotracheal suctioning allows direct visualization and thorough removal of meconium from the lower airway. Starting PPV before clearing meconium risks "pushing" particulate matter deeper into the lungs, causing chemical pneumonitis and alveolar damage. The improvement in HR (70—110 bpm) suggests good response to initial resuscitation, but meconium clearance remains the priority to prevent severe MAS complications including pneumothorax and persistent pulmonary hypertension.

---

questions.stem: A 4550-g male neonate is delivered vaginally after a 37 6/7 weeks’ gestation complicated by gestational diabetes. One application of a vacuum extractor to the neonate’s head was required to facilitate delivery. On examination at 12 hours of age, the baby has a well circumscribed, fluctuant mass over the parietal skull that does not cross suture lines. The overlying skin is erythematous but intact. He is active and alert, and the rest of his examination is unremarkable. His hematocrit (measured from a capillary sample) is 45%. Which of the following steps is next indicated in the management of this neonate?

options.label: A
options.text: Administration of intravenous ampicillin and cefotaxime

options.label: B
options.text: Monitoring serum and/or transcutaneous bilirubin levels

options.label: C
options.text: Careful aspiration of the mass with a tuberculin syringe

options.label: D
options.text: Application of topical bacitracin zinc ointment to the mass

options.label: E
options.text: Transfusion of packed red blood cells

questions.initialExplanation: Cephalohematoma after vacuum delivery: the next step is to monitor bilirubin (breakdown of the collection raises it), not antibiotics, aspiration or transfusion.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The infant in this vignette has a cephalohematoma, which is a subperiostial hemorrhage often associated with trauma during labor (see figure). The hemorrhage presents hours after delivery as a fluctuant mass over the affected skull bone (often the parietal or occipital bone). The hemorrhage is limited by the periosteum of the skull bone and, as a result, does not extend beyond the suture lines. Blood loss is minimal, and affected infants usually do not require transfusion of

blood products. The most common neonatal complication is hyperbilirubinemia due to the breakdown of the extravasated blood. In the absence of localized or systemic infection, antibiotics should not be administered. Needle aspiration of

the hematoma is not indicated and may introduce skin flora into the hematoma, resulting in infection of the mass and surrounding skin. A cephalohematoma should be distinguished from 2 other entities (see figure). A caput succedaneum is edema of the scalp and tends to cross suture lines. A subgaleal hemorrhage is bleeding between the galea aponeurotica and the skull. This condition can lead to extensive hemorrhage and shock. As a result, this is an emergency situation requiring close monitoring, as well as potential replacement of blood and clotting products.

---

questions.stem: Aterm 4.3-kg infant is delivered vaginally to a 33-year-old woman with juvenile-onset dia betes. The delivery was complicated by severe shoulder dystocia and the infant experienced a brachial plexus injury with limited movement of the right arm. At 72 hours of age, the infant is noted to be tachypneic but he is pink and well perfused. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for his tachypnea?

options.label: E
options.text: cystic adenomatoid malformation of the lung

questions.initialExplanation: A large baby with shoulder dystocia and brachial plexus injury: the likely cause of tachypnea is diaphragmatic paralysis (phrenic nerve C3-C5 involvement).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Brachial plexus injury results from stretching of the plexus and nerve roots. The upper roots (C5 and C6) are most vulnerable to injury. Phrenic nerve injury on the same side of the injury may occur,

‘     which results in diaphragmatic paralysis. This risks are highest for brachial plexus injury if the infant is large for gestational age and/or if the labor and delivery is complicated. Respiratory distress syndrome is uncommon in term infants and almost always presents initially in the first 24 hours of life. Pulmonary hemorrhage, pneumothorax, and cystic adenomatoid malformation can cause cyanosis and respiratory distress but have no association with brachial plexus injury.

---

questions.stem: A 4950-g female neonate is delivered vaginally after a 38 6/7 weeks’ gestation complicated by poorly controlled type 2 diabetes. The obstetrician reported shoulder dystocia during the delivery. On examination at 4 hours of age, the baby’s left arm is internally rotated, and the forearm is extended and pronated. The baby does not move her left arm when the examiner assesses the Moro reflex. Which of the following physical examination findings is most associated with the findings in the arm?

options.label: B
options.text: A hyperpigmented patch on the left chest

questions.initialExplanation: Arm in internal rotation with extended, pronated forearm and absent Moro = Erb palsy; the associated finding when the injury extends (T1) is a constricted pupil (Horner syndrome).
questions.detailedExplanation:
The infant in this vignette has evidence of an Erb’s palsy, an acquired injury of the upper portion (cervical roots 5 and 6) of the brachial plexus secondary to avulsion or lateral traction during delivery. This phenomenon often occurs in infants during deliveries associated with shoulder dystocia (ie, deliveries of macrosomic babies). The injury leads to paralysis of the deltoid, biceps, and brachialis muscles of the affected arm and shoulder, resulting in positioning of the affected arm as described in the question. Associated findings include ptosis, miosis, and enophthalmos of the ipsilateral eye due to cervical sympathetic nerve injury (Horner syndrome) and diaphragmatic paralysis (due to ipsilateral phrenic nerve injury). The other physical findings are congenital anomalies not associated with Erb’s

palsy.

---

questions.stem: A baby boy was born at term by normal vaginal delivery, and had a birth weight of 4.9 kg. Neonatal examination revealed an abnormal Moro reflex. The Moro reflex was normal on the left side, but there was very little movement of the right arm. There was positive hand grasp bilaterally. the most likely diagnosis is :
questions.initialExplanation: A 4.9 kg birth with weak right arm movement but intact grasp = Erb palsy (C5-C6).
questions.detailedExplanation:
This is a birth injury that affects the brachial plexus. It is the commonest form of this type of injury. The infant cannot abduct the arm at the shoulder, or externally rotate or supinate the forearm. The usual picture is one of painless adduction, internal rotation of the arm and pronation of the forearm. The Moro reflex is absent or abnormal on the involved side, and the hand grasp is intact.

---

questions.stem: A preterm infant (33 weeks, 1,850) presents with respiratory distress - tachypnea (65/min), moderate retractions, grunting, HR 155 bpm, hypotonic but responds to stimulation. Temperature 35.8°C. What is the MOST APPROPRIATE INITIAL RESPIRATORY SUPPORT?

options.label: A
options.text: Room air with close observation only

options.label: B
options.text: High-flow nasal cannula therapy starting at 6 L/min

options.label: C
options.text: Positive pressure ventilation with bag-mask (max 30 cm H20)

options.label: D
options.text: Supplemental oxygen via nasal cannula at 2-4 L/min

options.label: E
options.text: Nasal CPAP with pressure 6-8 cm H20

questions.initialExplanation: A 33-week preterm with moderate respiratory distress who responds to stimulation: initial support is nasal CPAP at 6-8 cm H2O.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This 33-week preterm infant shows classic signs of respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) - tachypnea, retractions, grunting, and hypothermia. According to evidence-based guidelines, nasal CPAP is the preferred initial respiratory support for preterm infants < 35 weeks as it provides gentle distending pressure (6-8 cm H20) to prevent alveolar collapse while preserving spontaneous breathing. This approach has been shown to reduce the need for mechanical ventilation by 20-40% compared to immediate intubation. The infant maintains adequate cardiovascular status (HR 155 bpm) and responds to stimulation, making NCPAP particularly appropriate. Early CPAP supports functional residual capacity and reduces work of breathing, while avoiding the complications of positive pressure ventilation including pneumothorax, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, and

ventilator-associated infections. Surfactant administration can be considered if RDS worsens or for extremely premature infants.

---

questions.stem: A newborn has a heart rate of 130/min, irregular respirations, and active muscle movements with good tone. He coughs and grimaces in response to stimulation; he is pink in color, except for his hands and feet, which are slightly bluish. This neonate's APGAR score is:
questions.initialExplanation: Apgar: HR 130 (2) + irregular respirations (1) + good tone (2) + cough/grimace (2) + pink with blue extremities (1) = 8.
questions.detailedExplanation:
APGAR is an acronym for appearance, pulse, grimace, activity, and respiration; the APGAR score is taken at 1 minute and 5 minutes after birth. On each parameter, a maximum score of 2 is possible. In this case, one point was taken off for cyanosis of the hands and feet; one point was taken off for

irregular respirations. The neonate received the maximum score of 2 for all of the other parameters, leading to an APGAR of 8.

---

questions.stem: You are asked to evaluate a newborn at 1 minute of life. The infant is pale blue, with slow, irregular respirations and a heart rate of 80 bpm. There is some flexion of the extremities, and the infant grimaces when you suction the nares. The 1-minute Apgar score of this infant is:
questions.initialExplanation: Apgar: pale blue (0) + slow irregular respirations (1) + HR 80 (1) + some flexion (1) + grimace (1) = 4.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The Apgar score is a useful tool in determining the need for infant resuscitation at both 1 minute and 5 minutes. It is not, however, a good tool to determine long term outcome. The five categories that the Apgar score evaluates are: heart rate, respiratory effort, muscle tone, reflex irritability, and color. 0, 1, or 2 points are awarded for each category, for a maximum score of 10. This infant scores 1 for heart rate, 1 for respiratory effort, 1 for muscle tone, 1 for reflex,and 0 for color, for a total score of 4 at 1 minute.

---

questions.stem: A baby just after delivery has a HR 140 beats per min, is breathing and moving well, with pink body and blue extremities. Grimace is absent. What is the Apgar score?
questions.initialExplanation: Apgar: HR 140 (2) + breathing well (2) + moving well (2) + pink body with blue extremities (1) + grimace absent (0) = 7.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This baby would have an APGAR score of 7 (breathing- 2,heart rate- 2, reactivity to stimuli- 0, musclar tonus- 2, skin appearance- 1).

APGAR score is calculated based on 5 parameters, which are: breathing, heart rate, reactivity to

stimuli, musclar tonus and skin appearance. These parameters will be marked with a note from 0 to 2, each, summing in total a scorefrom 0 to 10.

---

questions.stem: A 1460-g male infant is delivered by cesarean section after a 30 1/7 weeks’ gestation to a 29-year-old woman with acute lymphoblastic leukemia. The infant is placed on the delivery room table. Drying the skin and suctioning the oropharynx is initiated, followed by positive pressure ventilation (PPV). After 20 seconds of PPV, the neonatal nurse notes that the infant has a heart rate of 40 beats/min and no chest wall movement. Which of the following interventions is indicated at this time in the resuscitation?

options.label: A
options.text: Conformation of an appropriate seal of the face mask

options.label: C
options.text: Flexion of the head and neck

options.label: D
options.text: Intravenous infusion of 0.1 mg/kg of 1:10,000 epinephrine solution

options.label: E
options.text: Intravenous infusion of 10 ml/kg of normal saline

questions.initialExplanation: After 20 seconds of PPV the heart rate stays 40 with no chest movement: the problem is likely ineffective ventilation, so first check the face-mask seal.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The infant in this vignette has received inadequate PPV during the initial steps of resuscitation, resulting in bradycardia. Inadequate airway positioning and poor seal with the neonatal face mask are the most common causes of a lack of a response to PPV (which include chest rise and a rise in the neonatal heart rate). The rst

steps in evaluating a poor response to PPV are repositioning the airway (with mild extension of the head and neck) and ensuring an appropriate seal between the mask and the infant’s face. Of note, the mask should rest snugly around the mouth and be supported by the chin and the bridge of the nose. Volume infusion and epinephrine administration may be necessary (to treat hypovolemia and bradycardia, respectively) but are not

indicated at this point in the resuscitation. Cardioversion to correct a neonatal arrhythmia is not performed during the initial neonatal resuscitation.

---

questions.stem: A newborn delivered by vacuum extraction shows a fluctuant swelling on the scalp that is confined to the parietal bone region, does not cross suture lines, and becomes more apparent on the second day of life. The center feels soft, and X-ray shows an underlying linear skull fracture. What is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.text: Immediate surgical evacuation of the hematoma

options.label: E
options.text: Observation only as it will resolve spontaneously

questions.initialExplanation: A swelling limited to the parietal bone with a linear fracture: benign and self-resolving; observation only.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Cephalohematoma represents a sub-periosteal hemorrhage that occurs between the skull bone and its overlying periosteum, typically resulting from birth trauma or vacuum extraction. The key pathophysiological features include: (1) Confined anatomy - blood collection is limited to a single bone due to periosteal attachment at suture lines; (2) Delayed ‘     appearance - visible on day 2-3 as the hemorrhage becomes more apparent; (3) Progressive resolution - requires 6-8 weeks for complete resolution as the blood is reabsorbed. Clinical course: Day 0-1: Swelling may be minimal or absent; Day 2-3: Swelling becomes more apparent; Week 1-4: Gradual resolution; Week 6-8: Complete resolution. Complications requiring intervention: (1) Hyperbilirubinemia - breakdown of collected blood causes significant jaundice requiring phototherapy; (2) Anemia - large hematomas can cause blood loss requiring transfusion; (3) Infection - rarely, secondary infection may develop. Management principles: (1) Observation only - no surgical intervention unless complications

develop; (2) Contraindication of aspiration - increases infection risk; (3) Skull fracture association - 5-20% have linear fractures that require no treatment if asymptomatic.

---

questions.stem: A term infant (3,450g) requires resuscitation after cesarean section. Initial assessment shows absent respirations, HR 110 bpm, good tone, pale with acrocyanosis. Bag-mask ventilation attempts show inadequate chest rise despite optimal technique and pressures up to 40 cm H20. What is the MOST APPROPRIATE NEXT STEP?

options.label: A
options.text: Continue bag-mask ventilation with higher pressures

options.label: C
options.text: Administer volume expanders via umbilical vein

options.label: D
options.text: Apply chest compressions for inadequate ventilation

options.label: E
options.text: Insert oropharyngeal airway and retry mask ventilation

questions.initialExplanation: A term infant not breathing, HR 110, with inadequate mask ventilation despite high pressure: next step is endotracheal intubation to secure the airway.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This scenario demonstrates failed bag-mask ventilation (BMV), defined as inadequate chest rise despite optimal positioning, seal, and ventilation pressure > 30 cm H20. According to NRP guidelines, persistent inadequate ventilation is a definitive indication for immediate endotracheal intubation. Failed BMV may result from upper airway obstruction, esophageal intubation, poor lung compliance, or technical issues with mask fit. The infant has adequate cardiovascular status initially (HR 110 bpm) and good tone, suggesting the primary problem is ventilation rather than circulation. Continuing with higher pressures (60 cm H20) significantly increases the risk of barotrauma and pneumothorax, especially in newborns. Definitive airway control with endotracheal intubation allows for verification of tube placement using multiple methods (auscultation, chest rise, end-tidal CO2), controlled ventilation delivery, and protection against aspiration. This intervention should not be delayed as adequate ventilation is the foundation of successful resuscitation.

---

questions.stem: A 2-day-old preterm infant (35 weeks) in an inadequately heated home presents with cold extremities (temperature 32°C), lethargy, edema of hands and feet, facial erythema, and bradycardia. Blood glucose is 35 mg/dL. What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.label: B
options.text: Rapid rewarming with hot water bottles

questions.initialExplanation: A hypothermic newborn (32°C) with edema and lethargy: rewarm gradually with external methods; rapid rewarming with hot packs is dangerous.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Neonatal cold injury (hypothermia) is a life-threatening condition primarily affecting preterm infants and term infants with impaired thermoregulation. Pathophysiology of hypothermia: (1) Impaired thermogenesis - limited brown fat stores; (2) Large surface area-to-weight ratio - increased heat loss; (3) Immature hypothalamic regulation - poor temperature control. ‘     Clinical presentation sequence: (1) Initial compensatory phase - peripheral vasoconstriction, decreased activity; (2) Cold stress phase - increased oxygen consumption, metabolic acidosis; (3) Severe hypothermia - multiorgan dysfunction. Specific signs: (1) Cold extremities - temperature <35°C (95°F); (2) Facial erythema - due to failure of oxyhemoglobin to dissociate at low temperatures; (3) Edema and hardening - subcutaneous tissue changes; (4) Metabolic complications -

---

questions.stem: What is the recommended next step of management for a non-crying, non-breathing newborn boy delivered at 30 weeks gestation with an apneic episode and a heart rate less than 100/min, despite initial measures of providing warmth, airway positioning, and stimulation? (or) A boy was delivered at 30 weeks gestation, with no cry and no breathing. The pediatric resident started with the resuscitation protocol, provided warmth and maintained temperature, positioned the airway,and stimulated the baby. After these steps, a resident noticed that the baby was still apneic and the heart rate was < 100/min. What would be the next single best step of management?

options.label: A
options.text: Suction of airways HEE ga lS ted

questions.initialExplanation: After warming, positioning and stimulation the infant remains apneic with HR <100: the next step is positive pressure ventilation (PPV).
questions.detailedExplanation:
+ Positive pressure ventilation is the single most effective step in the resuscitation of neonates who fail to breathe at birth.

+ It can be done by using an inflating bag, mask, or T-piece resuscitator.

+ By positive pressure ventilation, we manually deliver air to the baby.

+ This method is used to exchange air between the lungs and the external environment.

+ A device that is used for positive pressure ventilation is known as an 'Ambu bag'.

---

questions.stem: A primigravid woman delivers a 38-week, 2500-gram neonate. The baby required resuscitation, and the baby was transferred to the NICU. The junior resident assesses the baby and finds that the baby is gasping and the heart rate is < 100 bpm. She initiated positive pressure ventilation. When initiating resuscitation, at what level should FiO2 be set? (or) At what level should FiO2 be set when initiating resuscitation in a newborn?
questions.initialExplanation: Starting resuscitation of a term infant: begin with FiO2 21% (room air) and titrate to saturation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- If the term baby is delivered with an immediate cry and breathing and has good muscle tone, then the baby should be placed skin-to-skin with the mother.

+ Suctioning should be done if needed to clear the airways.

+ The baby should be moved to a radiant warmer, stimulating and drying the baby.

+ Positive-pressure ventilation can be started if the heart rate is less than 100 and apnea is present. + Resuscitation of term neonates is initiated with room air (21% FiO2).

+ Preterm neonates: 21 to 30% FiO2 (intermediate concentration).

---

questions.stem: An infant is delivered with umbilical cord tightly wrapped around neck twice. Initial assessment: absent respirations, HR 55 bpm irregular, completely flaccid, profound cyanosis. After cord unwinding and initial steps, HR improves to 80 bpm but respirations remain absent. What is the MOST CRITICAL NEXT STEP?

options.label: B
options.text: Perform immediate endotracheal intubation for rapid airway control

options.label: C
options.text: Administer normal saline 10 mL/kg via umbilical vein

options.label: D
options.text: Continue tactile stimulation and observe for spontaneous respirations

options.label: E
options.text: Apply chest compressions due to persistent bradycardia

questions.initialExplanation: After drying and cord clamping the infant still has no breathing and HR 80: the priority is immediate PPV (before compressions or intubation).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Tight nuchal cord compression causes intermittent fetal hypoxia and possible birth trauma. The improvement in heart rate (55—80 bpm) with basic resuscitation measures (cord unwinding, warming, drying) indicates some response to initial interventions, but absent respirations represent a critical respiratory compromise requiring immediate PPV. According to NRP algorithms, positive pressure ventilation should be initiated within 30 seconds of assessment when respirations are absent or inadequate. The improvement in HR suggests that the primary problem is respiratory depression from acute asphyxial events rather than severe structural injury or hypovolemia. PPV will provide the essential oxygenation needed to support both respiratory drive and cardiovascular function. Chest compressions would be contraindicated with HR > 60 bpm, and volume expansion is not indicated without signs of hypovolemia (pallor beyond acrocyanosis, weak pulses). Early ventilation is most critical for reversing the hypoxia-induced depression.

---

questions.stem: A term infant delivered by forceps presents with seizures, vomiting, and bulging anterior fontanelle at 6 weeks of age. Head circumference has increased significantly. CT scan shows a crescent-shaped extra-axial fluid collection causing mass effect. What type of hemorrhage is most likely?
questions.initialExplanation: Symptoms at 6 weeks (seizures, vomiting, bulging fontanelle, rising head circumference) with CT showing an extra-axial crescentic collection after forceps delivery = subdural hemorrhage.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Subdural hemorrhage (SDH) in neonates results from rupture of cortical bridging veins or the vein of Galen, typically occurring during traumatic delivery. Pathophysiology: (1) Initial asymptomatic period - blood products remain contained; (2) Hemolysis phase - around 6 weeks, red blood cells break down, creating osmotic gradient; (3) Fluid accumulation -

‘    serum drawn into clot, causing expansion and mass effect; (4) Symptom development - increased intracranial pressure and focal neurological deficits. Risk factors: (1) Birth trauma - prolonged second stage, shoulder dystocia; (2) Instrumental delivery - forceps extraction; (3) Skull fractures - linear fractures associated with SDH; (4) Coagulation disorders - inherited or acquired. Clinical presentation: (1) Seizures - most common presenting symptom; (2) Vomiting - due to increased ICP; (3) Bulging fontanelle - in infants <6 months; (4) Macrocephaly - progressive head growth. CT characteristics: (1) Crescent-shaped - follows brain contour; (2) Extra-axial location - outside brain parenchyma; (3) Mass effect - midline shift, sulcal effacement. Management: All symptomatic SDH requires surgical evacuation to prevent permanent neurological damage.

---

questions.stem: A newborn shows left-sided facial paralysis with asymmetrical crying, inability to close the left eye, absent left nasolabial fold, and mouth deviation to the right. The mother had a difficult forceps delivery. What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.label: A
options.text: Eye care with drops/ointment, feeding assistance, and physiotherapy

options.label: B
options.text: Immediate neurosurgical exploration and nerve grafting

options.label: E
options.text: Observation only as it will resolve spontaneously

questions.initialExplanation: Peripheral facial palsy after forceps delivery: initial care is eye protection with drops/ointment, feeding help and physiotherapy; it usually recovers spontaneously.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Facial nerve (CN VII) injury in neonates occurs in approximately 0.5-1% of deliveries, making it the most common peripheral nerve injury. The injury mechanism involves compression of the facial nerve against the maternal pelvis or forceps blades, leading to neurapraxia or axonotmesis. The clinical presentation includes: (1) Asymmetrical crying - the affected side doesn't move normally; (2) Inability to close eye - due to orbicularisoculi weakness leading to exposure keratitis risk; (3) Absent nasolabial fold - loss of facial muscle tone; (4) Mouth deviation - the mouth pulls toward the normal side during crying. Initial management priorities: (1) Eye protection - lubricating drops and ointment to prevent corneal drying and ulceration; (2) Feeding support - ensuring adequate nutrition if breastfeeding is affected; (3) Physiotherapy - gentle massage and exercises to maintain muscle tone. The prognosis is excellent with 90-95% complete resolution by 3 months. Neuroplasty is reserved for persistent paralysis beyond 3 months, though some experts recommend earlier intervention if severe.

---

questions.stem: A premature infant at 32 weeks gestation develops sudden respiratory distress and cyanosis shortly after birth. Chest examination shows decreased breath sounds on the right with paradoxical abdominal movement. The infant was born by vaginal delivery after prolonged second stage labor. What investigation is most diagnostic?

options.label: A
options.text: Chest X-ray showing elevated right hemidiaphragm N B) CT scan of the chest

questions.initialExplanation: Respiratory distress with paradoxical abdominal movement and reduced right-sided breath sounds after a difficult delivery = diaphragmatic paralysis; the most diagnostic test per the source is ultrasound of the diaphragm.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Phrenic nerve injury causing diaphragmatic paralysis is a serious condition with significant respiratory implications. The phrenic nerve originates from C3-C5 spinal roots (primarily C4), providing motor innervation to the diaphragm. Injury mechanisms include: (1) Traction injury during difficult deliveries; (2) Compression from fetal malposition; (3) Associated

‘    birth trauma particularly with brachial plexus injuries (75% association). The clinical presentation reflects loss of diaphragmatic function: (1) Paradoxical abdominal movement - the abdomen moves inward during inspiration instead of outward; (2) Decreased breath sounds on the affected side due to reduced lung expansion; (3) Respiratory distress - more pronounced when feeding or when the infant is supine. Ultrasound evaluation is the preferred initial investigation because it: (1) Assesses diaphragmatic movement in real-time; (2) Determines side of involvement and severity; (3) Rules out other causes of respiratory distress; (4) Allays repeated radiation exposure. Management includes supportive

respiratory care, positioning (lateral decubitus with affected side up), and monitoring for spontaneous recovery over 2-3 months.

---

questions.stem: A 3.8 kg male infant is delivered via forceps after prolonged second stage labor. On examination, you note a boggy swelling over the scalp that crosses suture lines and was present at birth. The swelling resolves spontaneously over 3-4 days. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: A soft swelling that crosses the sutures, present at birth and resolving within days = caput succedaneum.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Caput succedaneum is a subcutaneous, extra-periosteal fluid collection over the presenting part that crosses suture lines and resolves within a few days. Unlike cephalohematoma, it is confined within suture lines and resolves spontaneously without treatment. The temporal pattern and crossing of suture lines are classic diagnostic features.

---

questions.stem: A term infant with birth weight 4.2 kg presents with respiratory distress, asymmetric Moro reflex, and a right arm showing Erb's palsy posture (shoulder internal rotation, elbow flexion, forearm pronation). There is absence of biceps and Moro reflexes on the right side. Which nerve roots are primarily involved?
questions.initialExplanation: Erb posture (shoulder internal rotation, elbow flexion, forearm pronation) with absent Moro/biceps reflexes = injury of the C5-C6 roots.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Erb's palsy involves the upper nerve roots (C5-C6) and results in the classic "waiter's tip" posture. The shoulder is internally rotated, elbow flexed, and forearm pronated. This pattern distinguishes it from Klumpke's palsy which affects C7-T1 and causes hand weakness with absent grasp reflex.

---


## Neonatal Convulsion

questions.stem: Infant experiencing neonatal convulsions, you explain to the parents about the prognosis associated with various causes of neonatal convulsions. Which of the following causes of convulsions typically has the most favorable prognosis?

options.label: A
options.text: Infants with seizures due to asphyxia

options.label: D
options.text: Seizures following prolonged and recurrent symptomatic hypoglycemia

options.label: E
options.text: Seizures resulting from central nervous system infections

questions.initialExplanation: The best prognosis among the causes is late hypocalcemic seizures, since they respond to correction and rarely cause lasting brain injury, unlike asphyxia, infection or recurrent hypoglycemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Late hypocalcemia is a treatable condition. With appropriate correction of calcium levels and addressing the underlying cause (e.g., dietary adjustments), infants typically recover fully without residual neurological deficits. In contrast, the other causes listed are associated with more severe and often irreversible brain damage.

---

questions.stem: A 2-day-old premature girl was delivered at 26 weeks' gestation and weighed 800 grams. Suddenly she developed seizures. On examination; she is lethargic, pale, hypotonic, the anterior fontanelle is bulging, her chest and heart examinations were normal. Her Laboratory tests indicate anemia. The most probable explanation for these observations is:
questions.initialExplanation: A very preterm (26 wk) with sudden seizures, lethargy, pallor, anemia and a bulging fontanelle = intraventricular hemorrhage.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The clinical presentation of a 2-day-old premature infant with seizures, lethargy, pallor, hypotonia, bulging anterior fontanelle, and anemia strongly suggests intracranial pathology . Among the options provided, the most probable

explanation is: Intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH).

Key features in this case :

The infant was born prematurely at 26 weeks' gestation and has a very low birth weight (800 grams) . Prematurity and low birth weight are significant risk factors for intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH) .

Seizures : IVH can irritate the brain tissue, leading to seizures.

Lethargy, hypotonia, and bulging anterior fontanelle : These findings suggest increased intracranial pressure (ICP), which can occur due to bleeding within the ventricles or secondary hydrocephalus.

Anemia : Blood loss into the ventricles or subarachnoid space can cause anemia.

Pale appearance : This may reflect anemia or poor perfusion.

---

questions.stem: A 12-hour-old male neonate, born at home via uncomplicated vaginal delivery, presents with lethargy, poor feeding, and intermittent jerky movements. He started breastfeeding early but hasn't been feeding after that. What is the most appropriate initial intervention?
questions.initialExplanation: A 12-hour-old with poor feeding, clonic movements and lethargy: the first intervention is IV glucose, because hypoglycemia is a common, quickly correctable cause.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This neonate's lethargy, poor feeding, and jerky movements are classic for hypoglycemia, the most common and rapidly reversible cause of acute neurological symptoms in newborns with inadequate intake. Home birth increases risk due to potential feeding difficulties and lack of immediate metabolic screening. Intravenous glucose corrects hypoglycemia promptly, preventing neuronal injury while diagnostic evaluation proceeds. Phenobarbital (A) treats seizures symptomatically but ignores the underlying metabolic cause. Vitamin K (B) is essential for home-born infants to prevent hemorrhagic disease but is not urgent for acute neurological deterioration. Empirical antibiotics (C) or lumbar puncture (D) may be needed later if sepsis is suspected, but stabilizing glucose takes priority per neonatal emergency protocols. Checking bedside glucose should accompany glucose administration, but treatment should not be delayed if testing is unavailable.

---

questions.stem: A family with an infant in the neonatal intensive care unit is very concerned that their child will have long-term neurologic abnormalities. Of the following, which correlates best with subsequent neurologic abnormalities?

options.label: E
options.text: seizures in the first 36 hours of life

questions.initialExplanation: The factor best associated with later neurological outcome is seizure onset within the first 36 hours of life.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Most infants who experience fetal bradycardia during labor are not severely asphyxiated at birth and ultimately have a good neurologic outcome. Likewise, most infants who fail to breathe initially or are cyanotic at birth and have a low 1-minute Apgar score recover promptly and do well neurologically. Although a low 5-minute Apgar score generally indicates more prolonged oxygen problems and correlates somewhat better with than does the 1-minute score, most of these infants also will be normal. In contrast, a substantial population of newborns with low Apgar scores and seizures in the first 36 hours of life will show neurologic abnormalities on long-term follow-up.

---

questions.stem: Which one of the following measures is the most appropriate in the initial management of neonatal seizures?
questions.initialExplanation: The first step in neonatal seizures is securing airway, breathing and circulation (ABC) before any drug.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Neonatal seizures require urgent treatment to prevent brain injury. Give anticonvulsant medication only after adequate ventilation and perfusion (choice B) have been established and the biood glucose concentration has been measured. Seizures with hypoglycemia or hypoxia are detrimental to the brain!

1- Ensure adequate ventilation and perfusion.

2- Correct metabolic disturbances.

Hypoglycemia: (10% glucose in water) 2 mL/kg IV (0.2 g/kg) as bolus. Follow with continuous infusion at upto 8 mg/kg/min IV Hypocalcemia: (calcium gluconate 10%) 100mg/kg JV over 1 to 3 minutes (Note: Monitor cardiac rhythm for bradycardia) Follow with maintenance of 500 mg/kg/24 hrs IV or PO Hypomagnesemia: (magnesium sulfate) 25-250 mg/kg/dose fV/IM

3- Begin anticonvulsant therapy.

Phenobarbital: 20 mg/kg IV. if necessary,additional 10-20 mg/kg IV in 10 mg/kg aliquots (Note: monitor blood pressure and respiration) Maintenance: 4-6 mg/kg/24 hrs fV/PO If 40 mg/kg of Phenobarbital is not effective, proceed to fosphenytoin.

---

questions.stem: A term infant presents on day 2 of life with abnormal chewing movements, bicycling motions of extremities, and eye deviation. The movements are stimulus-sensitive and cease when gentle passive flexion is applied. Blood glucose is 45 mg/dL, calcium is normal, and no fever is present. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Movements triggered by stimulation that stop when the limb is held, with no eye or vital-sign changes = jitteriness, not seizures.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Jitteriness is characterized by rhythmic, tremulous movements that are stimulus-sensitive and cease with gentle passive restraint. Key distinguishing features include: (1) Absence of abnormal eye movements - jitteriness doesn't involve ocular symptoms; (2) Stimulus sensitivity - movements increase with stimulation and stop with restraint; (3) Non-jerky nature - movements are rhythmic rather than clonic; (4) Normal neurologic examination - between episodes, the infant appears normal. Common causes: hypoglycemia, hypocalcemia, drug withdrawal, normal newborn variants. Critical distinction: Jitteriness lacks the cortical origin of true seizures and represents an immature motor system response. Management: Treat underlying metabolic causes, provide reassurance, and monitor for progression to true seizures. Prognosis: Excellent if metabolic causes are corrected promptly.

---

questions.stem: A premature infant at 32 weeks gestation develops single synchronous jerks of the right arm followed by similar movements in the left arm. The EEG shows epileptiform activity during the movements, and the infant remains unresponsive during these episodes. Which type of seizure is most likely?
questions.initialExplanation: Synchronous jerks migrating from one limb to another with an abnormal EEG in a preterm = multifocal clonic seizures.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Multifocal clonic seizures involve multiple body parts seizing in a sequential, non-Jacksonian fashion - for example, left arm jerking followed by right leg jerking. Key characteristics: (1) Sequential involvement - different body parts jerk in succession; (2) EEG correlation - typically associated with electroencephalographic seizure activity; (3) Unresponsiveness - infant remains unconscious during episodes; (4) Focal to generalized - may start focally and spread. Age predilection: More common in full-term infants than premature. Pathophysiology: Represents cortical irritation affecting multiple foci simultaneously. Prognosis: Dependent on underlying cause, with variable outcomes ranging from benign to severe neurological sequelae. Management: Requires EEG monitoring, anticonvulsant therapy, and investigation for underlying etiology such as HIE, metabolic disorders, or intracranial hemorrhage.

---

questions.stem: A newborn at 6 hours of life develops generalized tonic posturing with stiffening of the entire body. The infant's eyes deviate upward, and respiratory pauses occur. The mother had prolonged second stage labor with fetal distress. What is the most likely underlying etiology?
questions.initialExplanation: Generalized tonic seizures within 6 hours after obstructed labor and fetal distress = hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Tonic seizures occurring in the first 24 hours, especially with a history of intrapartum fetal distress, are highly suggestive of hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE). Timing significance: (1) Early onset seizures (first 24- 48 hours) - characteristic of HIE, drug withdrawal; (2) Late onset (>4 days) - suggest intracranial hemorrhage or metabolic causes. HIE pathophysiology: (1) Perinatal asphyxia - leads to cerebral hypoxia and energy failure; (2) Reperfusion injury - inflammatory cascade causing secondary brain injury; (3) Cortical irritation - from metabolic acidosis and excitotoxicity. Clinical correlation: Prolonged second stage labor with fetal distress points to birth asphyxia as the primary mechanism. Seizure characteristics: Tonic seizures (generalized or focal) are more common in premature infants but can occur in term infants with HIE. Management: Immediate anticonvulsant therapy, supportive care, and consideration of therapeutic hypothermia for HIE within 6 hours of birth.

---

questions.stem: A term infant presents at day 3 of life with prolonged apnea episodes lasting 30-60 seconds, followed by other subtle manifestations including abnormal chewing and autonomic changes (tachycardia, hypertension). EEG monitoring confirms epileptiform activity. What is the most appropriate management approach?
questions.initialExplanation: Prolonged apnea with chewing movements and autonomic changes and an abnormal EEG = subtle seizures; treat with the anticonvulsant phenobarbital.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Seizure-related apnea requires direct anticonvulsant treatment, not respiratory support alone. Why this represents seizures: (1) EEG correlation - epileptiform activity confirms cortical origin; (2) Associated manifestations - apnea accompanied by other subtle seizure signs; (3) Duration - prolonged 30-60 second episodes typical of seizure activity. Management principles: (1) Phenobarbital first-line - 20 mg/kg IV loading dose; (2) Second-line therapy - phenytoin if seizures persist after 40 mcg/mL phenobarbital level; (3) Respiratory support - if needed during treatment, but primary treatment is anticonvulsants; (4) Continuous monitoring - EEG monitoring for seizure control assessment.

Why other options are wrong: (1) Mechanical ventilation - unnecessary if seizures can be controlled medically; (2) Caffeine

- treats apnea of prematurity, not seizure-related apnea; (3) Oxygen alone - doesn't address underlying cortical irritability; (4) CPAP - may help breathing but doesn't treat seizures.

Prognosis: Depends on underlying cause, with better outcomes if seizures are wellcontrolled.

---

questions.stem: A newborn develops seizures on day 5 of life. Laboratory studies show severe hypoglycemia (blood glucose 25 mg/dL), metabolic acidosis (pH 7.25), and elevated lactate. The infant was born to a diabetic mother. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.label: C
options.text: 10% dextrose bolus followed by continuous infusion

questions.initialExplanation: Seizure with glucose 25 mg/dL in an infant of a diabetic mother: initial treatment is a 10% dextrose bolus followed by continuous infusion.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Symptomatic hypoglycemia is a medical emergency requiring immediate correction of blood glucose levels. Hypoglycemia in diabetic mothers: (1) Fetal hyperinsulinemia - maternal hyperglycemia stimulates fetal pancreatic beta cells; (2) Postnatal insulin surge - abrupt cessation of glucose supply after delivery; (3) Suppressed gluconeogenesis - immature liver function in newborns. Treatment protocol: (1) Immediate bolus -

2-4 mL/kg of 10% dextrose in water IV; (2) Continuous infusion - 6-8 mg/kg/min glucose maintenance; (3) Monitor glucose - hourly blood glucose monitoring initially; (4) Prevention - early feeding or glucose infusion in at-risk infants. Why other treatments are wrong: (1) Phenytoin/Phenobarbital - would treat seizures but miss underlying cause; (2) Calcium - appropriate for hypocalcemia, not indicated here; (3) Pyridoxine - for pyridoxine-dependent seizures, not metabolic emergencies. Timeline: Seizures should resolve within 30 minutes of glucose correction if hypoglycemia is the sole cause.

---

questions.stem: A 2-week-old infant develops seizures with progressive lethargy, poor feeding, and fever. Physical examination reveals a bulging anterior fontanelle and nuchal rigidity. CSF analysis shows pleocytosis, elevated protein, and low glucose. Which microorganism is most likely responsible?
questions.initialExplanation: Meningitis at 2 weeks with seizures, bulging fontanelle and purulent CSF: the most common cause is group B Streptococcus.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This 2-week-old infant presents with classic signs of bacterial meningitis: fever, seizures, progressive lethargy, poor feeding, bulging anterior fontanelle, nuchal rigidity, and CSF findings of pleocytosis, elevated protein, and low glucose.

The low CSF glucose (hypoglycorrhachia) is a hallmark of bacterial meningitis, distinguishing it from viral etiologies.

Why Group B Streptococcus (GBS) is most likely:

Epidemiology: GBS (Streptococcus agalactiae) is the most common cause of neonatal bacterial meningitis overall, responsible for both early-onset (<7 days) and late-onset (7 days—3 months) disease. Late-onset GBS meningitis typically presents at 2—4 weeks of age, precisely matching this infant's presentation.

Clinical Features: GBS meningitis often presents with the classic triad of fever, lethargy, and seizures, along with signs of increased intracranial pressure (bulging fontanelle). Nuchal rigidity may be subtle in infants but can be present.

CSF Profile: Bacterial meningitis characteristically shows neutrophilic pleocytosis, elevated protein (>100 mg/dL), and low glucose (<40 mg/dL or CSF:serum ratio <0.4), all consistent with the vignette.

---

questions.stem: A newborn develops seizures that do not respond to phenobarbital loading (40 mcg/mL level). What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.initialExplanation: Seizures not controlled despite an adequate phenobarbital loading level: add phenytoin as second line.
questions.detailedExplanation:
When phenobarbital alone fails to control seizures, a second anticonvulsant should be added, typically phenytoin. Treatment algorithm: (1) First-line - phenobarbital 20 mg/kg loading, then 3-5 mg/kg/day maintenance; (2) Therapeutic level - 15-40 mcg/mL; (3) Second-line - phenytoin when phenobarbital level >40 mcg/mL or seizures persist; (4) Phenytoin dosing - 15-20 mg/kg loading, then 4-8 mg/kg/day. Alternative options: (1) Carbamazepine - oral formulation, good for maintenance; (2) Midazolam - IV infusion for refractory cases; (3) Lorazepam - up to 4-6 doses in 24 hours if needed; (4) Pyridoxine trial - particularly in early-onset, treatment-resistant seizures.

Why other options are wrong: (1) Increase phenobarbital - already at therapeutic level; (2) Carbamazepine - not first choice for add-on therapy; (3) Diazepam - less commonly used in neonates; (4) Pyridoxine - consider if metabolic causes suspected. Monitoring: Phenytoin levels, cardiac monitoring for arrhythmias.

---

questions.stem: An infant with neonatal seizures shows no improvement after multiple anticonvulsants. EEG monitoring reveals burst-suppression pattern. Which inherited condition should be considered?
questions.initialExplanation: Seizures resistant to several drugs with a burst-suppression pattern: consider a treatable inherited cause, pyridoxine dependency (trial of vitamin B6).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Pyridoxine dependency is a rare inherited disorder causing severe, treatment-resistant seizures in newborns. Clinical features: (1) Early onset - seizures within first days of life; (2) Treatment resistance - unresponsive to conventional anticonvulsants; (3) EEG pattern - burst-suppression or other severe abnormalities; (4) ** Dramatic response - seizures stop within minutes of pyridoxine administration. Pathophysiology: (1) Enzyme deficiency - glutamate decarboxylase dysfunction; (2) GABA deficiency - impaired inhibitory neurotransmitter synthesis; (3) Genetic inheritance - autosomal recessive pattern. Treatment approach: (1) Pyridoxine 100 mg IV - diagnostic and therapeutic trial; (2) EEG monitoring - during trial to confirm response; (3) Lifelong therapy - pyridoxine maintenance; (4) Genetic counseling - for family planning. Differential considerations: (1) Other metabolic disorders - urea cycle defects, organic acidemias; (2) Brain malformations - cortical dysplasia, lissencephaly; (3) Other vitamin dependencies** - biotinidase deficiency, folinic acid responsive seizures.

---

questions.stem: A term infant with seizures shows normal neurological examination between episodes and no family history of seizures. All metabolic studies, imaging, and EEG are normal. Seizures resolve spontaneously by 2 weeks of age. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Seizures in a neurologically normal infant between episodes, with normal work-up, resolving spontaneously within 2 weeks = benign neonatal seizures.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Benign neonatal seizures are sporadic seizures with excellent prognosis and no identifiable cause. Clinical criteria: (1) Normal examination - no neurological deficits between seizures; (2) No family history - sporadic occurrence, not inherited; (3) Normal investigations - metabolic, imaging, and EEG studies normal; (4) Selflimited - resolve by 2-6 weeks of age. Characteristics: (1) Onset timing - usually first few days of life; (2) Seizure type - clonic seizures most common; (3) Response to treatment - may respond to anticonvulsants; (4) Prognosis - excellent, no long-term sequelae. Why other options are wrong: (1) Febrile seizures - not applicable in neonatal period; (2) Breathholding spells - provoke by crying, not seizures; (3) Benign familial - would have family history; (4) Metabolic - would have abnormal studies. Prognosis: Normal development in 95% of cases. Management: Short-term anticonvulsants if seizures frequent, otherwise observation.

---

questions.stem: A premature infant at 30 weeks gestation develops subtle seizures characterized by eye deviation, automatic movements, and autonomic changes (tachycardia, hypertension). EEG confirms epileptiform activity. Which complication should be most closely monitored for?
questions.initialExplanation: A 30-week preterm with subtle seizures: watch for intraventricular hemorrhage, a common cause and complication at this age.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Premature infants with seizures, especially subtle seizures, are at high risk for intracranial pathology including intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH). Premature infant seizure characteristics: (1) Subtle seizures predominance - more common than clonic seizures in preterms; (2) EEG correlation - often associated with electrographic seizures; (3) Multiple etiologies - HIE, IVH, metabolic disorders, infection. IVH association: (1) Vulnerable germinal matrix - fragile blood vessels in periventricular area; (2) Pressure fluctuations - seizures can increase intracranial pressure; (3) Coagulation issues - prematurity associated with platelet dysfunction. Why IVH is the primary concern: (1) Life-threatening - large IVH can cause rapid deterioration; (2) Long-term sequelae - hydrocephalus, cerebral palsy, cognitive delays; (3) Seizure association - IVH is a common cause of seizures in preterms. Monitoring strategy: (1) Head ultrasound - immediate imaging to rule out IVH; (2) Serial ultrasounds - to monitor for progression; (3) Blood pressure monitoring - avoid fluctuations; (4) Platelet function - ensure adequate clotting.

---

questions.stem: A newborn with seizures develops bradycardia and hypotension during phenytoin administration. Cardiac monitoring shows prolonged PR interval and widened QRS complexes. What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.initialExplanation: Bradycardia, hypotension and ECG changes (long PR, wide QRS) during phenytoin infusion = cardiotoxicity; stop the drug immediately.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Phenytoin can cause severe cardiovascular toxicity including bradycardia, heart block, and hypotension. Phenytoin cardiovascular effects: (1) Rate-dependent toxicity - faster infusion rates increase risk; (2) Myocardial depression - direct cardiac effects; (3) Conduction abnormalities - affects AV node and His-Purkinje system; (4) Hypotension - from negative inotropic effects. Management of toxicity: (1) Immediate discontinuation - stop phenytoin infusion; (2) Cardiac monitoring - continuous ECG monitoring; (3) Supportive care - fluids, vasopressors if needed; (4) Alternative therapy - phenobarbital, lorazepam, or midazolam. Why other options are wrong: (1) Continue at slower rate - toxicity has already occurred; (2) Epinephrine - not indicated without cardiac arrest; (3) Increase dose - would worsen toxicity; (4) Switch to carbamazepine - oral formulation, not immediate alternative. Prevention: Fosphenytoin (prodrug) may be preferred due to better cardiovascular tolerance. Monitoring: Always have cardiac monitoring during phenytoin loading in neonates.

---

questions.stem: A 4-day-old full-term male had an uneventful prenatal and nursery course and was discharged 2 days after birth. His mother is planning to exclusively breastfeed him and asks if any nutrient supplements are recommended for her son. Of the following, the BEST recommendation is:

options.label: A
options.text: No supplements are necessary for breastfed infants

options.label: B
options.text: Start iron supplementation now, vitamin D at 4 months

options.label: D
options.text: Start supplementation with vitamin D now and iron at age 4 months

questions.initialExplanation: Breast milk is low in vitamin D, so give 400 IU daily from the first days. Iron stores from birth last about 4 months, so iron starts after that.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This recommendation follows American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) guidelines for exclusively breastfed infants:
Vitamin D Supplementation

- When to start: Within the first few days of life - Dosage: 400 IU per day

- Reason: Breast milk typically contains low levels of vitamin D, putting infants at risk for vitamin D deficiency and rickets
- Duration: Continue until the infant receives adequate vitamin D from dietary sources

Iron Supplementation

- When to start: 4 months of age - Dosage: 1 mg/kg/day

- Reason: Full-term infants are born with sufficient iron stores from gestation to last 4-6 months, but breast milk doesn't
provide enough iron to meet growing needs

- Duration: Continue until iron-rich solid foods are introduced

---

questions.stem: A pregnant woman presents for a routine prenatal visit at 32 weeks gestation. During the consultation, she expresses her intention to breastfeed her baby after delivery. Which of the following is least considered to be a permanent contraindication to breastfeeding?
questions.initialExplanation: A chest infection is a passing illness and does not stop breastfeeding; antibodies even pass to the baby in the milk. Permanent contraindications are mainly the infant's metabolic conditions such as galactosemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Why Maternal Chest Infection is the Correct Answer

- Nature: A general acute infection (cold, flu, bronchitis, pneumonia)

- Breastfeeding status: NOT a contraindication to breastfeeding

- Benefits: Breastfeeding should actually continue because:

- Mother produces antibodies against the infection

- Antibodies pass to baby through milk, providing passive immunity

- Respiratory hygiene (mask wearing) may be needed for droplet transmission
- Permanency: Temporary condition, not permanent contraindication

---

questions.stem: The parents of a 7-month-old infant, who has been fed whole cow's milk, inquire whether this provides adequate nutrition for their baby. You explain that whole cow's milk may lack certain essential nutrients needed for proper growth and development. Which of the following deficiencies is most likely to occur in this infant?
questions.initialExplanation: Whole cow's milk before 1 year is low in iron, poorly absorbed, and causes occult GI blood loss, so the expected deficiency is iron deficiency anemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Iron deficiency anemia is the primary concern with early cow's milk introduction:

Mechanisms of Iron Deficiency

1. Low iron content: Whole cow's milk contains very little iron naturally

2. Poor bioavailability: Iron in cow's milk is poorly absorbed compared to breast milk

3. Occult blood loss: Cow's milk proteins irritate immature intestines, causing microscopic bleeding
4. Inhibition of absorption: High calcium and casein levels inhibit non-heme iron absorption

5. Depleted stores: By 7 months, infant's gestational iron stores are typically depleted

Clinical Significance

- Most common nutritional deficiency in infants fed cow's milk early, Risk factors: Age 6-12 months when iron
stores are low

- Consequences: Can cause permanent developmental delays

---

questions.stem: At a routine prenatal visit at 32 weeks' gestation, a pregnant woman shares her plan to breastfeed after delivery. Which of the following is NOT a permanent contraindication to breastfeeding? 2025 <1)
questions.initialExplanation: Mastitis is not a contraindication; breastfeeding continues while the mother is treated. Permanent contraindications are limited, such as galactosemia in the infant.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Mastitis is NOT a contraindication to breastfeeding; continued nursing or milk expression from the affected
breast is actually encouraged to promote drainage, resolve milk stasis, and accelerate recovery. The infant is
not harmed, and standard antibiotics are compatible with lactation. Active maternal HIV infection
contraindicates breastfeeding due to transmission risk through breast milk. Maternal chemotherapy agents
pass into milk and cause significant infant toxicity, making breastfeeding unsafe during treatment. Untreated
active tuberculosis is a temporary contraindication requiring separation until non-contagious after
approximately two weeks of therapy, though expressed milk is safe. Maternal substance abuse with illicit
drugs like cocaine or heroin contraindicates breastfeeding due to infant exposure risks and impaired maternal

questions.stem: A 2-week-old exclusively breastfed infant is brought for a routine checkup. The baby has regained birth weight, passes 6-8 wet diapers, and 3-4 stools daily. The mother is concerned about milk supply. What is the most appropriate advice? 2025 .)Js

options.label: B
options.text: Start formula supplementation to increase the weight

options.label: C
options.text: Switch to bottle feeding to measure intake more accurately

options.label: D
options.text: Increase breastfeeding frequency to every 30 minutes

options.label: E
options.text: Administer water between feeds to maintain hydration

questions.initialExplanation: The baby regained birth weight, wets 6-8 diapers and stools regularly, so milk intake is adequate. Reassure the mother and continue exclusive on-demand breastfeeding.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This infant demonstrates adequate milk intake through objective markers: regained birth weight by 2 weeks,
6-8 wet diapers daily indicating proper hydration, and 3-4 stools consistent with exclusive breastfeeding.
These findings reassure that milk supply is sufficient despite maternal concerns, which are common in early
lactation. Continuing exclusive breastfeeding on demand supports ongoing milk production through supply-
and-demand physiology and promotes infant growth and bonding. Formula supplementation is unnecessary
and may reduce breast stimulation, potentially decreasing milk supply and undermining breastfeeding
success. Switching to bottle feeding or introducing water is not recommended for exclusively breastfed infants
under 6 months and can cause nipple confusion or electrolyte disturbances. Feeding every 30 minutes is
excessive and not evidence-based; responsive, on-demand feeding (typically 8-12 feeds/24 hours) is
appropriate.

---

questions.stem: You are asked by a parent about infant nutrition for her 3-month-old child. The mother plans to stop breast feeding over the next week. She notes that infants can be fed a cow’s milk—based infant formula; however, unmodified whole cow’s milk is not recommended for infants less than 1 year of age. She asks why infants can’t be fed the same whole cow’s milk that she feeds to her 19-month-old child. Which of the following reasons supports the recommendation not to feed infants (less than 1 year of age) unmodified cow’s milk?

options.label: A
options.text: Unmodified cow’s milk has unacceptable low protein content.

options.label: B
options.text: N b. Unmodified cow’s milk has a high renal solute load that is not appropriate for infants.

options.label: C
options.text: Unmodified cow’s milk has excessive iron content that increases the risk for constipation.

options.label: D
options.text: Unmodified cow’s milk increases the risk of development of allergic disease.

options.label: E
options.text: Unmodified cow’s milk has an increased whey protein to casein protein ratio, compared with human - F) milk.

questions.initialExplanation: Unmodified cow's milk has a high protein and mineral (renal solute) load that an infant's kidneys cannot handle, so it is not given before 1 year.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Unmodified cow’s milk has high levels of protein, sodium, chloride, and phosphorous. Together,
these components create a high renal solute load that is not appropriate for infants. Unmodified

‘    cow’s milk should not be introduced until after 12 months of age. Unmodified cow’s milk also has
inadequate amounts of iron, vitamin C, zinc, and essential fatty acids. In addition, human milk has a
whey to casein ratio of 60% to 40%, compared with 18% to 82% in unmodified cow’s milk. The
development of allergic disease is multifactorial. Both delayed and late introduction of foods have
been associated with the development of food allergy.

questions.stem: A 3-month-old infant weighs 3.8 kg (birth weight 3.2 kg). Mother reports 45-minute breastfeeding sessions every 2-3 hours, with frequent crying between feeds. Physical exam shows reduced muscle bulk, dry mucous membranes, and decreased skin turgor. Hemoglobin is 9.2 g/dL with microcytic cells. What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.label: A
options.text: Order extensive metabolic testing for inborn errors

options.label: B
options.text: Switch to cow's milk-based formula and stop breastfeeding \*

options.label: C
options.text: Assess maternal milk supply and infant latch technique, provide counseling

options.label: D
options.text: Start oral iron and increase feeding frequency only \*

options.label: E
options.text: Refer to pediatric surgeon for Gl obstruction evaluation

questions.initialExplanation: The infant gained little weight with long feeds and crying; the likely problem is low milk supply or poor latch. First assess milk production and technique and counsel the mother before complex tests.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This clinical presentation indicates inadequate nutrition with dehydration and iron deficiency anemia.
The prolonged feeding duration and frequent crying between feeds suggest poor milk transfer rather
than inadequate maternal production. The appropriate intervention focuses on optimizing
breastfeeding technique through professional lactation assessment and counseling. This approach
addresses the root cause while maintaining the benefits of breast milk. Additional interventions
should be reserved for cases where counseling fails or underlying pathology is suspected.
