questions.stem: An 11-month-old boy presented with watery bowel motions for 10 days increasing in severity. He is bottle fed with some complementary diet. His systemic examination is normal apart from abdominal distention and excoriation of perianal skin. What investigation you highly prefer for this infant?
questions.initialExplanation: Chronic watery diarrhea with perianal skin breakdown and a distended abdomen in an infant suggests zinc deficiency (acrodermatitis-like), so check serum zinc.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The 11-month-old infant presents with:

- Watery diarrhea for 10 days, increasing in severity

- Abdominal distention

- Excoriation of perianal skin

- Bottle-fed with complementary diet

- Normal systemic examination otherwise

Why Serum Zinc Level is the Answer

- Serum zinc level (option d) is the preferred investigation for suspected zinc deficiency or acrodermatitis
enteropathica, which can present with: Persistent diarrhea, Periorificial rash (which may present as perianal
excoriation), Abdominal distention, Failure to thrive

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old girl has stunted growth. The mother reports that she has been experiencing chronic, frequent, foul-smelling, pale stools accompanied by abdominal distension. A provisional diagnosis of celiac disease was made. Select the most TRUE statement:

options.label: A
options.text: It is an autosomal dominant inherited disorder

options.label: B
options.text: It is an autoimmune disorder associated with type 1 diabetes mellitus

options.label: C
options.text: It is caused by antibodies that damage the colonic mucosa

options.label: D
options.text: It is due to a deficiency in pancreatic exocrine enzyme function

options.label: E
options.text: Improvement of symptoms after removing gluten from diet can confirm the diagnosis

questions.initialExplanation: Celiac disease is an autoimmune disorder associated with type 1 diabetes and other autoimmune syndromes.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Celiac disease is indeed an autoimmune disorder with strong associations to other autoimmune conditions, particularly:
- Autoimmune Association

- Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus: Most significant association

- Prevalence: 3-10% of Type 1 diabetic patients have celiac disease

- General population: Much lower prevalence

- Other associations: Autoimmune thyroiditis, Addison's disease, Sjogren's syndrome
Pathophysiology

- Autoimmune mechanism: Gluten ingestion triggers immune response

- Target organ: Small intestine (duodenum and jejunum)

- Damage pattern: Villous atrophy and crypt hyperplasia

- HLA associations: HLA-DQ2 and HLA-DQS8 alleles

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old girl presented with recurrent abdominal pain, bloating, and foul-smelling diarrhea. These symptoms exacerbate after consuming foods such as bread and pasta. Her pediatrician suspected her to have a celiac disease. Which of the following would be the most appropriate choice?

options.label: A
options.text: Testing serum antibodies for tissue transglutaminase (tTG-IgA)

options.label: B
options.text: Performing upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with duodenal biopsy

options.label: D
options.text: Examining stool for fecal fat content

questions.initialExplanation: Clinical suspicion of celiac, once serology is positive, is confirmed by duodenal biopsy via upper GI endoscopy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with duodenal biopsy is the gold standard for definitive celiac disease diagnosis:

Diagnostic Hierarchy

1. Screening: tTG-IgA serological testing (first-line)

2. confirmation: Upper Gl endoscopy with duodenal biopsy (gold standard)

3. Pathological correlation: Histological evidence of villous atrophy

Biopsy Advantages

- Direct visualization: Allows assessment of duodenal mucosa

- Histological confirmation: Shows characteristic changes: Villous atrophy, Crypt hyperplasia, Increased intraepithelial
lymphocytes

- Definitive diagnosis: Cannot be made on serology alone

- Excludes other conditions: Differentiates from other malabsorptive disorders

---

questions.stem: A 10-month-old infant presents with 2 weeks of persistent watery, frothy diarrhea and abdominal bloating, following recovery from febrile gastroenteritis. Symptoms worsen with milk or formula and are accompanied by abdominal fullness and perianal redness. The infant is active, afebrile, with no vomiting, blood in stool, or weight loss. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Chronic frothy diarrhea in an active, well-growing infant after gastroenteritis = secondary lactose intolerance.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This presentation is classic for secondary lactose intolerance following viral gastroenteritis:
Key Pathophysiology

- Post-infectious onset: Symptoms began after febrile gastroenteritis

- Viral damage: Rotavirus and other viruses damage intestinal brush border

- Lactase deficiency: Enzyme located at tips of villi, most susceptible to damage
- Temporary condition: Usually resolves as intestine heals (weeks to months)
Characteristic Symptoms

- Worsens with milk/formula: Contains lactose, undigested in lactase deficiency
- Watery, frothy diarrhea:

- Watery: Undigested lactose draws water via osmosis

- Frothy: Bacterial fermentation produces gas

- Perianal redness: Acidic stools from lactic acid production irritate skin

- Abdominal bloating: Gas production from fermentation

- No blood or mucus: Distinguishes from inflammatory conditions

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl presents with a 6-week history of frequent, watery, pale, bulky stools, poor intake, and progressive weight loss despite a normal diet. She appears pale, has abdominal distension, and shows failure to thrive. What is the most likely diagnosis? 2025 ¢.)Js
questions.initialExplanation: Weeks of watery diarrhea with pallor, abdominal distension and failure to thrive in a child weaned onto gluten = celiac disease.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This presentation is classic for celiac disease: chronic watery, pale, bulky stools (steatorrhea) due to fat
malabsorption, abdominal distension, failure to thrive, pallor from iron deficiency anemia, and poor appetite
despite a normal diet. Symptoms typically emerge after gluten introduction and worsen with ongoing
exposure. Cow's milk protein intolerance usually presents in infancy with blood/mucus in stool and eczema.
Inflammatory bowel disease typically includes bloody diarrhea, fever, or extraintestinal manifestations.
Lactose intolerance causes osmotic diarrhea triggered by dairy without failure to thrive or steatorrhea.
Toddler's diarrhea features loose stools but normal growth and appetite. Confirmatory testing includes tissue
transglutaminase IgA antibodies and duodenal biopsy showing villous atrophy. Management involves strict
gluten-free diet, which leads to symptom resolution and catch-up growth.

---

questions.stem: A 5 yr old in your practice underwent screening for celiac disease because his mother was recently diagnosed with this condition. His screening test is positive, however he is asymptomatic. Intestinal biopsy is negative. How would you classify this patient, and what are your recommendations to the mother?

options.label: A
options.text: A- The child has potential celiac disease and should be monitored for the development of future symptoms; a

options.label: C
options.text: B- The child does not have celiac disease and requires no further testing or dietary intervention

options.label: D
options.text: C- The child has latent celiac disease and should start a gluten-free diet

options.label: E
options.text: D- The child has celiac disease and should undergo testing for associated autoimmune diseases - F) E- The child has silent celiac disease and should initiate gluten-free diet

questions.initialExplanation: Positive celiac serology but negative biopsy = potential celiac disease; monitor, and do not start a strict diet unless symptoms or damage develop.
questions.detailedExplanation:
gluten-free diet is not mandatory

Potential celiac disease is defined when patients are identified by positive screening studies but without documented
celiac disease on small bowel biopsy. It is important to follow these patients because they can develop established celiac
disease in the future (see Table 330-6). There is a consensus that all celiac disease patients should be treated with a
gluten-free diet regardless of the presence of symptoms. However, whereas it is relatively easy to assess the health
improvement after treatment of celiac disease in patients with clinical symptoms of the disease, it proves difficult in
persons with asymptomatic celiac disease. The nutritional risks, particularly osteopenia, are those mainly feared for
subjects who have silent celiac disease and continue on a gluten-containing diet. Little is known about the health risks in
untreated patients with minor enteropathy, which may be clinically silent. There are no guidelines concerning the need for
a gluten-free diet in subjects with "potential" celiac disease (patients with positive celiac disease—associated serology but
without enteropathy).

---

questions.stem: A 14-month-old infant is referred to the pediatric gastroenterology clinic by the family physician with a 6-month history of chronic, non-bloody diarrhea. The parents report 4-5 large, pale, greasy, and foul-smelling stools daily, often described as "floats in the toilet." Despite adequate caloric intake and normal appetite, the infant demonstrates poor weight gain with current weight and height measurements below the third percentile for age. Physical examination reveals marked abdominal distension, particularly in the upper quadrants, with visible peristalsis. Proximal muscle wasting is evident with increased wrinkling of the skin over the hip girdle region. The infant was exclusively breastfed for 6 months, with gradual introduction of gluten-containing cereals beginning at 8 months of age. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.initialExplanation: Malabsorption symptoms and growth delay after introducing gluten-containing cereals = celiac disease.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This presentation is classic for celiac disease. The onset after gluten introduction (typically 6-18 months),
chronic diarrhea with pale, foul-smelling stools, failure to thrive, and abdominal distension are characteristic
features. Proximal muscle wasting and growth parameters below the third percentile are also typical. The
timeline fits with gluten introduction and disease development. Toddler's diarrhea occurs in older children and
doesn't cause failure to thrive; cow's milk protein allergy usually presents earlier; lactose intolerance typically
causes watery, explosive diarrhea immediately after feeding; post-infectious malabsorption usually follows
acute gastroenteritis.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old child presents with 3-month history of chronic watery diarrhea refractory to multiple dietary modifications. Child passes 3-4 loose stools daily with visible mucus and undigested vegetable matter. Despite diarrhea, maintains normal growth at 50th percentile with excellent appetite. Symptoms worsen after fruit juice, improve with increased fiber. What is most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Chronic diarrhea in an active, well-growing child that worsens with juice and improves with fiber = toddler's diarrhea (chronic nonspecific diarrhea).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Toddler's diarrhea (chronic non-specific diarrhea of childhood) typically affects children above 2 years
of age and is characterized by normal growth and development despite chronic diarrhea. The
presence of mucus and undigested food particles, along with rapid transit time, are typical features.
The condition is benign and self-limiting. Other options would typically present with failure to thrive,
malnutrition, or abnormal laboratory findings. Celiac disease and inflammatory bowel disease cause
growth impairment; giardiasis and lactose intolerance would have specific stool characteristics and
symptoms.

---

questions.stem: A 10-month-old infant presents with persistent diarrhea 2 months after rotavirus gastroenteritis requiring hospitalization. Infant develops explosive watery diarrhea within 1-2 hours after consuming any dairy products, with bloating and flatulence. Stool analysis shows pH 4.6 and strongly positive reducing substances. What is most appropriate management and expected duration?
questions.initialExplanation: Persistent diarrhea after gastroenteritis with stool pH 4.6 and positive reducing substances = lactose intolerance, treated with a lactose-free diet for 4-6 weeks.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This is secondary lactose intolerance following rotavirus infection. The timing of symptoms after
lactose ingestion, acidic stool pH <5.5, and positive reducing substances confirm carbohydrate
malabsorption. Secondary lactose intolerance from viral gastroenteritis typically resolves within 4-6
weeks as lactase enzymes regenerate. Treatment involves temporary lactose restriction during this
period. Gluten-free diet is for celiac disease; antibiotics are not indicated; probiotics may help but
dietary modification is primary; IV hydration is unnecessary in mild cases.

---

questions.stem: A 16-month-old child with chronic diarrhea and failure to thrive undergoes celiac evaluation. Serology shows elevated anti-tTG IgA (>100 U/mL) and positive antiendomysial antibodies. Duodenal biopsy reveals total villous atrophy with increased intraepithelial lymphocytes. HLA typing positive for DQ2/DQ8. What is definitive treatment and monitoring strategy?
questions.initialExplanation: Biopsy-proven celiac with HLA DQ2/DQ8: the definitive treatment is a lifelong gluten-free diet with follow-up.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Celiac disease is definitively diagnosed by the combination of positive serology (anti-tTG and anti-
endomysial antibodies), characteristic duodenal biopsy findings, and HLA typing showing DQ2/DQ8.
The definitive treatment is lifelong gluten-free diet, avoiding wheat, rye, and barley. This leads to
clinical improvement, normalization of serology, and histological recovery. Corticosteroids and
immunosuppressants are not first-line treatments; surgery is rarely needed; nutritional
supplementation is supportive but doesn't address the underlying cause.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child with chronic diarrhea and failure to thrive unresponsive to gluten-free and lactose- free diets. Physical examination shows digital clubbing and peripheral edema. Laboratory reveals severe hypoproteinemia, iron deficiency anemia, and prolonged prothrombin time. Child has recurrent pneumonia with Pseudomonas aeruginosa. What investigation is most helpful?
questions.initialExplanation: Failure to thrive, fatty diarrhea and Pseudomonas lung infections suggest cystic fibrosis; the test is the sweat chloride test.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This presentation suggests cystic fibrosis: chronic diarrhea with failure to thrive, clubbing,
hypoproteinemia, and recurrent respiratory infections. Cystic fibrosis is caused by defective chloride
transport affecting multiple organ systems, including pancreas (leading to malabsorption and chronic
diarrhea) and lungs. Sweat chloride test is the gold standard diagnostic test, showing elevated
chloride levels (>60 mEq/L confirms diagnosis). Other tests: Anti-tTG is for celiac disease; stool
culture for infections; colonoscopy for inflammatory conditions; breath hydrogen for carbohydrate
malabsorption.

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old child develops chronic watery diarrhea 4 weeks after rotavirus gastroenteritis requiring hospitalization. Child has lost 1.5 kg with signs of malnutrition. Stool shows reducing substances and fat droplets, cultures negative. Diarrhea persists despite conservative management. What pathophysiological mechanism is most likely responsible?
questions.initialExplanation: Persistent watery diarrhea after rotavirus despite conservative care: villous damage causes post-infectious malabsorption.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Post-infectious malabsorption syndrome (PIMS) or post-enteritis syndrome occurs after acute
gastroenteritis and involves multiple factors: prolonged small intestinal mucosal injury, ineffective
villous repair, persistent infection, malabsorption of carbohydrates and fats, and increased
absorption of foreign proteins. This creates a vicious cycle of mucosal injury and malabsorption.
The timing (4 weeks), weight loss, and persistent symptoms despite negative cultures are typical.
Secondary lactose intolerance is part of this broader syndrome but doesn't explain all the findings.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child with celiac disease on gluten-free diet presents for routine monitoring. Parents report strict adherence but admit occasional inadvertent school exposure. Child shows clinical improvement with normalized growth. However, recent school performance declined and child appears irritable. What laboratory parameter best monitors compliance, and what additional assessments are needed?
questions.initialExplanation: Adherence to a gluten-free diet is monitored by anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies, which fall with compliance.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Anti-tissue transglutaminase (tTG) antibodies are the most sensitive and specific serological markers
for celiac disease and are excellent for monitoring dietary compliance. Levels should decrease and
normalize within 6 months of strict gluten withdrawal. Persistent elevation suggests continued gluten
exposure or poor compliance. CBC may improve but is not specific for compliance; serum albumin
may normalize but takes longer; iron studies improve with resolution of malabsorption but aren't
specific; liver function is usually normal in uncomplicated celiac disease.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child with chronic diarrhea and failure to thrive undergoes duodenal biopsy showing subtotal villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes. Celiac serology (anti-tTG IgA and anti-endomysial) negative with normal total IgA. Child has sibling with selective IgA deficiency. What additional investigation is helpful and what differential diagnoses should be considered?

options.label: E
options.text: Genetic testing for familial villous atrophy

questions.initialExplanation: With selective IgA deficiency, celiac serology can be falsely negative, so HLA typing for DQ2/DQ8 helps strongly exclude disease if negative.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Negative celiac serology with positive biopsy findings could indicate celiac disease in the setting of
IgA deficiency (since tTG and endomysial antibodies are IgA-based) or could represent other
conditions like familial villous atrophy. HLA typing for DQ2/DQ8 is helpful because the absence of
these alleles essentially rules out celiac disease, while their presence supports the diagnosis. If
negative, other causes of villous atrophy should be considered. Repeat serology would be less
informative; elimination diet may help but doesn't provide diagnostic confirmation; electron
microscopy isn't standard; genetic testing for familial villous atrophy is not routinely available.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old child with well-controlled celiac disease presents to emergency department with acute severe watery diarrhea and vomiting. Parents report accidental gluten exposure at birthday party. Physical examination shows hypovolemic shock with tachycardia (HR 140), hypotension (BP 85/50), poor capillary refill. Laboratory shows severe hypokalemia (K+ 2.1), metabolic acidosis, and acute kidney injury. What complication is occurring and what is emergency management?
questions.initialExplanation: Celiac crisis is a rare emergency with severe diarrhea, dehydration, acidosis and renal failure; it needs IV resuscitation, steroids and appropriate nutrition.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Celiac crisis is a severe, potentially life-threatening complication of celiac disease characterized by
acute onset of severe diarrhea, vomiting, dehydration, and shock with severe hypokalemia. It can be

‘    triggered by gluten exposure in patients with known celiac disease. This represents an acute
exacerbation of the underlying condition. Management requires immediate rehydration, electrolyte
correction, and strict gluten avoidance. Gl infection could occur but the context suggests gluten
exposure; medication side effects are unlikely; IBD wouldn't present this acutely; lactose intolerance
wouldn't cause this severity of presentation.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child with chronic diarrhea has stool examination showing Giardia lamblia cysts and trophozoites on multiple samples. Child attends large daycare and swims frequently in community pools. Presents with 2-month history of intermittent cramping, bloating, and loose stools unresponsive to dietary modifications. CBC shows mild eosinophilia. What is appropriate treatment and preventive measures?
questions.initialExplanation: Chronic diarrhea with cysts/trophozoites in stool (Giardia) is treated with metronidazole 50 mg/kg/day for 5-7 days plus hygiene measures.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Giardiasis is effectively treated with metronidazole 50 mg/kg/day in three divided doses for 5-7 days.
Alternative treatments include tinidazole (for children >3 years) or nitazoxanide. Giardia infection is
common in daycare settings due to fecal-oral transmission. Treatment eliminates the parasite and
resolves symptoms. amoxicillin is not effective against Giardia; steroids have no role; gluten-free and
lactosefree diets are not indicated for giardiasis.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child with previously normal growth presents with 2-month history of chronic diarrhea unresponsive to empirical lactose elimination and probiotics. Physical examination shows well-nourished child with normal weight/height at 50th percentile. Parents report diarrhea occurs during daytime with mucus and undigested vegetable matter. Symptoms worsen after apple juice, improve with increased fiber. What is appropriate management and dietary counseling?
questions.initialExplanation: Toddler's diarrhea needs no drugs or tests; reassure parents and give dietary advice (less juice, more fat and fiber).
questions.detailedExplanation:
This presentation is classic for toddler's diarrhea (chronic non-specific diarrhea of childhood). Key
features include: age >2 years, normal growth and development, benign course, stools containing
mucus and undigested food, and no failure to thrive. The condition is self-limiting and requires no
extensive investigation or treatment. Reassurance and dietary counseling (avoiding excessive fruit
juice, ensuring adequate fiber) are appropriate. Extensive investigations, endoscopy, elimination
diets, and probiotics are unnecessary in this typical presentation.

---

questions.stem: A 12-month-old infant with chronic diarrhea and failure to thrive undergoes celiac serology testing. Anti-tTG IgA antibodies negative, but total serum IgA markedly reduced (<5 mg/dL). No recurrent infections or immunodeficiency signs. IgG and IgM levels normal. Infant's older sibling has selective IgA deficiency and celiac disease. What does this suggest about celiac serology interpretation ?

options.label: B
options.text: Serology cannot rule out celiac disease

options.label: C
options.text: The infant has selective IgA deficiency

options.label: D
options.text: The test is unreliable and should be repeated

questions.initialExplanation: With selective IgA deficiency, celiac IgA tests may be negative despite disease, so serology alone does not exclude celiac.
questions.detailedExplanation:
In patients with selective IgA deficiency, celiac-specific antibodies (anti-tTG and antiendomysial)
cannot be measured as they are IgA-based. Therefore, negative serology does not exclude celiac
disease in IgA-deficient patients. In such cases, alternative testing approaches are needed: IgG-
based serology (anti-deamidated gliadin peptide antibodies) or duodenal biopsy without prior
serology. The finding suggests selective IgA deficiency which is associated with increased risk of
celiac disease, but doesn't definitively diagnose or exclude it. The infant does not have combined
immunodeficiency based on this information alone.

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old child with chronic diarrhea undergoes duodenal biopsy showing increased intraepithelial lymphocytes (>30/100) but preserved villous architecture with normal villus-to-crypt ratio. Stool examination negative for reducing substances, occult blood, and pathogenic bacteria. CBC reveals mild eosinophilia (8%). Child has history of exposure to untreated well water, frequent camping, and plays in contaminated streams. Recent episodes of diarrhea associated with cramping and bloating that resolve spontaneously. What is most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Cramps and bloating that resolve spontaneously with villous changes on biopsy = giardiasis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Increased intraepithelial lymphocytes with preserved villous architecture is characteristic of giardiasis.
Giardia lamblia infection typically causes inflammation of the small intestinal mucosa without causing
villous atrophy. The parasite attaches to the brush border of intestinal epithelial cells and causes
malabsorption and diarrhea. Other conditions: early celiac disease would show some degree of
villous atrophy; toddler's diarrhea typically shows normal histology; cow's milk protein allergy can
cause various histological changes but not typically isolated intraepithelial lymphocytosis; IBD affects
primarily the colon.

---

questions.stem: A 12-year-old adolescent presents with a 6-month history of chronic diarrhea, abdominal pain, and weight loss of 8 kg. Physical examination reveals oral ulcers, perianal fissures, and a palpable mass in the right lower quadrant. Laboratory findings show elevated inflammatory markers (ESR 65 mm/hr, CRP 12 mg/L) and iron deficiency anemia. The child has a history of recurrent aphthous ulcers and joint pain. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Teen with chronic diarrhea, anemia, mouth ulcers and joint pain = Crohn's disease.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Crohn's disease presents with chronic diarrhea, abdominal pain, weight loss, and extraintestinal
manifestations including oral ulcers, perianal disease, and arthritis. The presence of a palpable
mass suggests terminal ileal involvement. Inflammatory markers are elevated, distinguishing it from
functional disorders. Perianal fissures and oral ulcers are characteristic of Crohn's disease rather
than ulcerative colitis.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old child presents with chronic diarrhea, abdominal distension, and foulsmelling stools that contain undigested food particles. The child has normal growth and development. Laboratory investigations show elevated stool fat content but normal celiac serology and normal pancreatic function tests. Breath hydrogen test is positive after lactose challenge. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: A positive hydrogen breath test after a lactose load = lactose intolerance.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The positive hydrogen breath test after a lactose challenge is the diagnostic hallmark of lactose
intolerance. In primary lactase non-persistence, lactase enzyme activity naturally declines after age 3
-5 years. Undigested lactose reaches the colon, where bacterial fermentation produces hydrogen gas
(detected on breath testing), short-chain fatty acids, and osmotic fluid shifts, causing abdominal
distension, flatulence, foul-smelling stools, and diarrhea. Normal growth and development strongly
support a specific enzyme deficiency rather than a diffuse malabsorptive or inflammatory disorder.

---

questions.stem: An 18-month-old girl presented with a 6 month history of diarrhea, abdominal distension, failure to thrive, irritability, and decreased appetite. Of the following, the MOST likely diagnosis is :
questions.initialExplanation:
Chronic diarrhea with abdominal distension, failure to thrive, irritability and poor appetite in a young child = celiac disease.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl presents with a 6-week history of frequent, watery, pale, bulky stools, poor intake, and progressive weight loss despite a normal diet. She appears pale, has abdominal distension, and shows failure to thrive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Weeks of watery diarrhea with pallor, abdominal distension and failure to thrive = celiac disease (repeat of Question 5).
questions.detailedExplanation:
This presentation is classic for celiac disease in a young child:
Characteristic Clinical Features

- Age (8 years): Typical presentation age after gluten introduction

- Pale, bulky, watery stools: Classic steatorrhea from fat malabsorption

- Abdominal distension: "Celiac potbelly" from gas and fluid accumulation
- Failure to thrive: Inability to absorb nutrients leading to growth halt

- Pallor: Iron-deficiency anemia (common in celiac due to duodenal damage)
- 6-week duration: Consistent with chronic malabsorptive condition
Pathophysiology

- Gluten exposure: Autoimmune reaction damages small intestinal villi

- Malabsorption: Fat, iron, and other nutrients poorly absorbed

- Fatty stools: Unabsorbed fats create pale, bulky, floating stools

- Growth failure: Chronic malnutrition despite adequate diet

Persistent && Chronic dia A

---

## Malnutrition & Failure to Thrive

> Question numbers not present in the source file for this topic: 5.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old male is brought to the clinic, weighing 55% of his ideal body weight and without edema. Which of the following statements about this condition is least accepted?

options.label: A
options.text: The diagnosis in this case is likely marasmus

options.label: B
options.text: Extreme wasting is a characteristic feature

options.label: D
options.text: The child's abdomen is typically protruded

options.label: E
options.text: Irritability is a common symptom associated with this condition

questions.initialExplanation: A child at 55% of ideal weight without edema = marasmus. The abdomen is usually shrunken, not protuberant; a swollen belly is a feature of kwashiorkor.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This case describes a child with severe malnutrition based on:

- Weight < 60% of expected (55% of ideal body weight)

- No edema present

- This presentation is classic for Marasmus (distinguished from Kwashiorkor by the absence of edema).

Why Option (d) is the "Least Accepted" (Incorrect) Statement

The child's abdomen is typically protruded is FALSE for marasmus:

- Protruded abdomen ("pot belly") is characteristic of Kwashiorkor

- Caused by: Hepatomegaly (fatty liver) and fluid retention/edema

- In Marasmus: Abdomen is typically shrunken, flat, or even concave due to extreme wasting of abdominal
muscles and loss of visceral fat

---

questions.stem: A 15-month-old boy presents with a 2-week history of diarrhea, poor feeding, and leg swelling. On admission, he is lethargic, has bilateral edema, temperature 35.5°C, and capillary glucose of 48 mg/dL. He is refusing to eat. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.label: A
options.text: Administer 5 mL/kg of 10% dextrose via nasogastric tube

options.label: B
options.text: Begin treatment with high-protein F-100 therapeutic milk

options.label: C
options.text: Begin oral antibiotics for suspected infection

options.label: E
options.text: Begin IV fluid bolus with isotonic saline

questions.initialExplanation: A child with low glucose (48 mg/dL) refusing feeds: the priority is to treat hypoglycemia immediately with 10% glucose via NG tube if unable to drink.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This case presents with severe acute malnutrition showing classic signs of Kwashiorkor:
Clinical Features of Kwashiorkor

- Bilateral edema: Pathognomonic for kwashiorkor

- Diarrhea and poor feeding: Common in SAM

- Lethargy: Sign of severe illness                                               Correct Dosage and Route

- Hypothermia (35.5°C): Life-threatening complication                         10% dextrose 5 mL/kg: Standard WHO protocol for

- Hypoglycemia (48 mg/dL): Below 54 mg/dL threshold for SAM               hypoglycemic SAM patients

Why IV Glucose via NG Tube is the Correct Answer                            Nasogastric route: When IV access unavailable or difficult
WHO Guidelines for Hypoglycemia in SAM                                      Rapid absorption: Can reverse hypoglycemia quickly

- Critical emergency: Hypoglycemia can cause immediate death

- Lethargic child: Requires glucose administration

- IV access may be difficult: NG tube route is acceptable alternative

- Immediate life-saving intervention: Takes precedence over all other treatments

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old child is brought to the clinic due to poor growth and lethargy. On examination, the child weighs 50% of the expected weight for age, has a distended abdomen, bilateral pitting edema, hypopigmented hair with alternating dark and light bands, and patchy skin lesions with desquamation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Edema with hair and skin changes (dark/light bands and peeling) and severe wasting = marasmic-kwashiorkor.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This case represents a combination of severe protein-energy malnutrition types:

Mixed Malnutrition Features

Marasmus Component (Severe Wasting):

- Weight 50% of expected: Severe wasting (<60% = marasmus threshold)
- Poor growth: Chronic calorie deficiency

- Muscle and fat wasting: "Skin and bones" appearance

Kwashiorkor Component (Edema & Specific Signs):

- Bilateral pitting edema: Distinguishing feature of kwashiorkor
- Distended abdomen: Hepatomegaly (fatty liver) or ascites

- Hair changes: "Flag sign" - alternating dark and light bands

- Skin lesions: "Flaky paint dermatosis" with desquamation

Zn SR TN FR TN    SI, SN, SR SN SEEN FN SN

---

questions.stem: The body of the malnourished child may have compensated for micronutrient deficiencies with lower metabolic and growth rates, and refeeding may unmask these deficiencies. Refeeding syndrome is characterized by : dehydration
questions.initialExplanation: Refeeding syndrome occurs when rich feeding starts after malnutrition, with low potassium, phosphate and magnesium; the main one here is hypokalemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Nutritional rehabilitation can be complicated by refeeding syndrome, which is characterized by fluid
retention, hypophosphatemia, hypomagnesemia, and hypokalemia. Careful monitoring of laboratory
values and clinical status with severe malnutrition is essential.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl presents with 6 weeks of worsening peripheral edema and behavioral changes. She was weaned from breastfeeding when her brother was born 8 months ago. Current weight: 11.5 kg (25th percentile weight-for-age, > 97th percentile weight-forheight due to edema). Examination reveals bilateral pitting edema to mid-shin, moon face, enlarged tender liver, and sparse hypopigmented hair with "flag sign." She is apathetic with poor appetite. Serum albumin: 18 g/L. What dietary intervention is most appropriate during initial stabilization?

options.label: B
options.text: Breast milk re-initiation with protein supplements

options.label: D
options.text: Low-protein, high-carbohydrate diet with careful electrolyte monitoring

questions.initialExplanation: In kwashiorkor with severe hypoalbuminemia, feed cautiously: low protein and high carbohydrate with electrolyte monitoring during stabilization.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child presents with classic kwashiorkor: protein deficiency with relatively adequate energy intake,
evidenced by the edema (due to hypoalbuminemia), moon face, enlarged liver, hair changes including the "flag
sign," and apathetic behavior. The "flag sign" represents a pale band across the hair corresponding to the
period of malnutrition, providing historical evidence of the nutritional insult.

The pathophysiology involves protein deficiency leading to decreased oncotic pressure, causing edema, and
impaired synthesis of various proteins including digestive enzymes and transport proteins. The liver becomes
enlarged due to fatty infiltration as the body attempts to compensate for the protein deficiency.

During initial stabilization (days 1-7), severely malnourished patients cannot tolerate normal amounts of
protein, fat, and sodium due to compromised hepatic and renal function. A low-protein, high-carbohydrate diet
(1.5-2 g/kg/day protein initially) prevents overwhelming the compromised organs while providing adequate
energy. Gradual protein increase occurs during the rehabilitation phase.

---

questions.stem: A 16-month-old boy with severe malnutrition presents hypothermic (axillary 34.8°C) and hypoglycemic (glucose 2.1 mmol/L). He appears lethargic with weak cry and poor perfusion. Weight: 5.8 kg with both wasting and pitting edema. Heart rate: 120 bpm with muffled heart sounds. What is the most appropriate immediate intervention sequence?
questions.initialExplanation: Order of emergency care in SAM: treat hypoglycemia first, then warm the child (hypothermia), then feed, then antibiotics.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child is in immediate life-threatening danger from hypothermia and hypoglycemia. Hypoglycemia (glucose <3 mmol/L)
can cause seizures, brain damage, and death, making it the highest priority intervention. The hypothermia (axillary
<35.0°C) combined with poor perfusion suggests severe compromise requiring immediate warming.

The pathophysiology involves depleted energy stores and impaired thermoregulation in severe malnutrition. Hypoglycemia
occurs because the body cannot maintain glucose homeostasis due to depleted glycogen stores and impaired
gluconeogenesis. The poor perfusion and lethargy indicate cardiovascular compromise.

Intervention sequence rationale:

1. Glucose first: IV dextrose immediately prevents neurological damage and death

2. Warming second: External warming with blankets, warm environment, or incubator care
3. Feeding third: Once stable, gradual enteral feeding begins

4. Antibiotics fourth: Empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics for suspected sepsis

---

questions.stem: A 20-month-old child presents with features of both marasmus and kwashiorkor. Weight: 6.8 kg (weight-for-height: 45% of median) with severe upper body wasting but bilateral pitting edema of lower extremities. Food insecurity began 4 months ago. Liver enlarged to 5 cm below costal margin with signs of vitamin deficiencies including angular stomatitis. What is the expected mortality rate for this condition?
questions.initialExplanation: Mixed marasmic-kwashiorkor with vitamin deficiencies is the most dangerous form, with mortality over 40%.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has marasmic-kwashiorkor, the most severe form of proteinenergy malnutrition (PEM), combining the wasting

of marasmus with the edema and metabolic complications of kwashiorkor. The mortality rate exceeds 40% in

resourcelimited settings, making it the deadliest form of PEM. The pathophysiology involves severe protein and energy
‘     deficiency leading to multiple organ dysfunction. The combination of muscle wasting (from energy deficiency) and edema

(from protein deficiency) indicates severe compromise of multiple body systems. The presence of vitamin deficiencies

(angular stomatitis suggesting B-vitamin deficiency) compounds the problem.

Why the high mortality:

1. Multiple organ involvement: Heart, liver, kidney, and immune system all compromised

2. Increased infection risk: Severe immunodeficiency from protein deficiency

3. Metabolic instability: Electrolyte imbalances, hypoglycemia, hypothermia

4. Delayed presentation: Often presents late when multiple complications have developed

5. Treatment complexity: Requires careful management to avoid refeeding syndrome

---

questions.stem: A 12-month-old infant with marasmus shows recovery signs after 8 days: temperature 36.8°C, weight gain 12 g/kg/day for 3 consecutive days, alert and responsive, accepting feeds well, no vomiting or diarrhea. Laboratory shows improving electrolytes. Which treatment phase should be initiated next?

options.label: A
options.text: Begin rehabilitation phase with increased caloric density

options.label: C
options.text: Start follow-up phase with outpatient monitoring

questions.initialExplanation: After stabilization (electrolytes stable, appetite returning) move to the rehabilitation phase with increased calories.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has met the WHO criteria for transitioning from initial stabilization to rehabilitation phase.
The recovery criteria include: stable temperature (36.5-37.5°C), weight gain >5g/kg/day for 3
successive days, improved mental status, good appetite, and absence of gastrointestinal symptoms.
The rehabilitation phase (weeks 2-6) represents the period of rapid catch-up growth. During this
phase, nutritional rehabilitation becomes more aggressive with increased caloric density and protein
content to facilitate rapid weight gain and restoration of body composition.

---

questions.stem: A 15-month-old child with severe kwashiorkor develops cardiac arrhythmias, muscle weakness, and confusion 4 days after starting nutritional rehabilitation. Laboratory: K+ 2.1 mmol/L, PO4 0.3 mmol/L, Mg 0.4 mmol/L, glucose 12.3 mmol/L. ECG shows flattened T waves and U waves. What is the most critical immediate intervention?

options.label: E
options.text: Correct electrolyte imbalances with IV supplementation

questions.initialExplanation: Flattened T waves and U waves with low K, Mg and phosphate = an electrolyte disturbance threatening the heart, so the priority is IV replacement.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This represents classic refeeding syndrome (RFS), a life-threatening complication of nutritional rehabilitation. The electrolyte
abnormalities (severe hypophosphatemia, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia) and cardiac manifestations (arrhythmias, ECG changes)
indicate severe RFS requiring immediate intervention. Pathophysiology of RFS: When malnourished patients begin receiving nutrition,
insulin secretion increases dramatically in response to glucose. This drives phosphate, potassium, and magnesium into cells, causing
severe intracellular shifts. The resulting hypophosphatemia (<0.5 mmol/L) is particularly dangerous as it affects:

- Cardiac function: Arrhythmias, heart failure - Respiratory function: Respiratory muscle weakness, ventilatory failure

- Neurological function: Confusion, seizures, coma - Hematological function: Hemolysis, thrombocytopenia

Intervention sequence:

1. IV electrolyte replacement: Aggressive supplementation of PO4, K+, and Mg2+
2. Cardiac monitoring: Continuous ECG monitoring for arrhythmias

3. Reduce feeding rate: Decrease but don't stop nutrition completely

4. Supportive care: Oxygen, ventilatory support if needed

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy with failure to thrive shows: weight-for-age <5th percentile, height-forage <5th percentile, weight-for-height <5th percentile. Examination reveals multiple bruises in various healing stages, unwashed skin, untreated impetigo, and dirty uncut fingernails. Developmental assessment shows significant delays. Weight improved from 8.5 kg to 9.2 kg since foster placement 6 weeks ago. What intervention is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Mandatory reporting for suspected child abuse

options.label: B
options.text: Continued pediatric monitoring with social services support

questions.initialExplanation: Weight gain after placing the child in a caring environment indicates an environmental/social cause of FTT, so medical follow-up continues with social service support.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child demonstrates classic psychosocial failure to thrive (FTT) with signs of neglect and improvement since foster
placement. The combination of physical findings (bruises, poor hygiene, untreated skin conditions) with developmental
delays and improvement in nutritional status after placement change strongly suggests environmental rather than organic
causes.

The improvement in weight from 8.5 kg to 9.2 kg over 6 weeks demonstrates that the current environment is conducive to
recovery. This validates the decision to continue current care while providing comprehensive support services.

Key indicators of psychosocial FTT:

- Physical signs of neglect: Unwashed skin, untreated impetigo, dirty nails

- Bruises in various stages: Suggesting ongoing trauma or neglect

- Developmental delays: Secondary to lack of stimulation and interaction

- Improvement with placement change: Strong evidence for environmental etiology

- Lack of organic findings: Normal physical examination beyond neglect signs

---

questions.stem: A 4-month-old infant with severe malnutrition develops septic shock during initial stabilization. Current status: temperature 35.2°C, BP 65/35 mmHg, HR 160 bpm, capillary refill >3 seconds. Receiving therapeutic feeds for 2 days. What antibiotic regimen is most appropriate?
questions.initialExplanation: Septic shock in a malnourished child needs broad-spectrum IV antibiotics immediately with careful shock management.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This infant has developed septic shock, evidenced by hypotension, tachycardia, prolonged capillary refill, and hypothermia.
In severe malnutrition, sepsis is the leading cause of death, often presenting atypically without fever due to compromised
immune function.

Pathophysiology: Malnourished children have severely impaired immune function due to protein deficiency, lymphopenia,
and impaired antibody production. They are particularly susceptible to gram-negative bacteria from the gastrointestinal
tract, as well as opportunistic infections. Hypothermia instead of fever is a classic sign of severe sepsis in malnutrition.

Why broad-spectrum IV antibiotics:

1. Coverage spectrum: Must cover gram-positive, gram-negative, and anaerobicorganisms
2. Route: IV essential for septic shock with poor perfusion

3. Timing: Early antibiotic therapy crucial for survival in septic shock

---

questions.stem: An 18-month-old child presents with severe wasting and no edema. Weight: 7.2 kg, length 72 cm (weight-for-length <3rd percentile). Has "old man's face" appearance with prominent ribs and "pot belly" from weak abdominal muscles. Appetite preserved, alert and irritable. Liver not enlarged, minimal skin changes. This represents which classification?
questions.initialExplanation: Severe wasting without edema in an alert, irritable child = marasmus.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child demonstrates classic marasmus, the most common form of severe acute malnutrition. The key distinguishing features are:
severe wasting with preserved appetite and mental status, absence of edema, normal liver size, and minimal skin/hair changes.
Marasmus pathophysiology: Results from prolonged severe restriction of all nutrients (energy, protein, and micronutrients). The body
adapts by:

- Metabolic adaptation: Reduced basal metabolic rate to conserve energy

- Muscle wasting: Protein catabolism to provide amino acids for essential functions

- Fat depletion: Loss of subcutaneous fat for energy

- Preserved organ function: Vital organs relatively preserved until late stages

Clinical features:

- "Old man's face": Loss of buccal fat pads and facial subcutaneous tissue, - "Pot belly": Abdominal muscle wasting with relatively
preserved abdominal girth, - Preserved appetite: Unlike kwashiorkor, appetite is usually maintained or increased

- Alert behavior: Mental status preserved, may be irritable from hunger, - Normal organ size: Liver not enlarged, distinguishing from
kwashiorkor

---

questions.stem: During rehabilitation phase, a 14-month-old child with marasmus is not achieving expected weight gain despite adequate caloric intake (160 kcal/kg/day). Mother reports 3-4 loose stools daily with undigested food particles. What factor most likely explains poor weight gain?

options.label: E
options.text: Intestinal mucosal atrophy and enzyme deficiency

questions.initialExplanation: Poor weight gain during rehabilitation with loose stool and undigested food means atrophic gut mucosa and enzyme deficiency.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has intestinal malabsorption secondary to malnutrition-induced mucosal damage. The loose stools with
undigested food particles indicate incomplete digestion and absorption, explaining why adequate caloric intake fails to
produce expected weight gain.

Pathophysiology of malnutrition-induced malabsorption:

- Mucosal atrophy: Prolonged malnutrition causes villous atrophy and reduced absorptive surface

- Enzyme deficiency: Reduced production of pancreatic enzymes and brush border enzymes

- Bacterial overgrowth: Impaired gut flora balance due to reduced secretory IgA

- Increased intestinal permeability: Allowing bacterial translocation and inflammation

Evidence for malabsorption:

- Undigested food particles: Suggests pancreatic insufficiency and enzyme deficiency

- Loose stools: May indicate fat malabsorption (steatorrhea) or rapid transit

- Persistent symptoms: Despite adequate caloric intake in rehabilitation phase

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old with kwashiorkor develops extensive skin changes: hyperpigmented, desquamating patches primarily affecting lower extremities, buttocks, and perineum. Affected areas resemble partial- thickness burns with some epithelial loss. What is the most appropriate skin management strategy?

options.label: B
options.text: Gentle cleansing with emollients and careful monitoring

questions.initialExplanation: The fragile skin of kwashiorkor is managed with gentle cleaning and emollients with monitoring, not treated as severe burns.
questions.detailedExplanation:
These skin changes are characteristic of kwashiorkor, resulting from protein deficiency affecting skin
integrity, healing, and barrier function. The hyperpigmentation, desquamation, and ulceration
represent impaired epidermal regeneration and increased susceptibility to minor trauma.
Pathophysiology of kwashiorkor skin changes:

- Protein deficiency: Affects collagen synthesis and skin repair mechanisms

- Impaired wound healing: Due to reduced protein for cellular repair

- Increased fragility: Skin becomes thin and easily damaged

- Secondary infection risk: Compromised barrier function allows bacterial/fungal invasion

---

questions.stem: A 2.5-year-old child presents with weight-for-age <3rd percentile, height-for-age <3rd percentile, but weight-for-height >50th percentile. Parents report he is healthy with normal appetite and activity. Birth history and developmental milestones normal. What interpretation is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: Constitutional short stature with normal nutrition

options.label: B
options.text: Organic failure to thrive due to malabsorption \*

options.label: D
options.text: Constitutional short stature with normal nutrition

questions.initialExplanation: A child eating actively with normal development and proportionally low weight and height = constitutional short stature with normal nutrition.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This pattern represents constitutional short stature, a normal variant where height and weight are
proportionally reduced but weight-for-height ratio is preserved. The child is well-nourished but
genetically programmed to be smaller than average.

Characteristics of constitutional short stature:

- Proportional reduction: Both height and weight reduced equally

- Preserved weight-for-height ratio: Indicates adequate nutrition for body size

- Normal development: No delays in milestones

- Healthy appearance: Good appetite, activity level, and general health

- Family history: Often has family members with similar growth patterns

---

questions.stem: A 14-month-old with marasmus displays "pot belly" appearance with abdominal distension despite severe generalized wasting. Mother reports normal formed stools with no abdominal pain. What is the underlying mechanism for this finding?

options.label: B
options.text: Abdominal muscle wasting with weak abdominal wall

questions.initialExplanation: Distended abdomen with normal stool and no pain in marasmus is due to weak abdominal wall muscles after wasting (pot belly).
questions.detailedExplanation:
The "pot belly" in marasmus results from selective wasting of abdominal wall muscles while intra-abdominal contents
remain relatively preserved, creating a disproportionate abdominal appearance.

Pathophysiology of "pot belly" in marasmus:

- Selective muscle wasting: Abdominal muscles are among the last to waste in the progressive muscle catabolism
- Preserved abdominal contents: Organs and fat deposits maintain relative volume

- Weak abdominal wall: Cannot maintain normal abdominal tone and contour

- Normal bowel function: Absent malabsorption, parasites, or obstruction

Anatomical explanation:

- Rectus abdominis: Wastes but less dramatically than other muscle groups

- Internal obliques and transversus: Significant wasting creates flaccid abdominal wall

- Preserved visceral fat: Intra-abdominal fat deposits may be relatively preserved

- Gas pattern: Normal bowel gas pattern without obstruction

---

questions.stem: A 15-month-old infant presents with failure to thrive. Growth measurements show crossing down 2 major percentile lines for weight over 3 months, while height remains on 25th percentile. Birth weight was 4.2 kg (>97th percentile). What does this growth pattern most likely represent? Chronic disease process
questions.initialExplanation: A fall in the growth curve from a high percentile (birth weight >97th) to the 25th is constitutional catch-down growth, which is normal.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This represents constitutional catch-down growth, a normal physiological process where infants who are large at birth
gradually descend to their genetic growth centiles. The pattern of preserved height with declining weight centiles is
characteristic.

Constitutional catch-down growth mechanism:

- Genetic programming: Each child has a predetermined growth centile based on genetics

- Large birth weight: 4.2 kg at >97th percentile indicates above-average genetic potential

- Catch-down process: Gradual descent to genetic centiles over first 2-3 years

- Height preservation: Linear growth continues along genetic lines

Timeline and pattern:

- Early phase: Weight crosses down, height remains stable, - Duration: Usually complete by 2-3 years of age, - Final
outcome: Child settles on genetically appropriate growth curve, - No pathology: This is normal physiological adaptation

---

questions.stem: A 14-month-old child with severe malnutrition is evaluated for readiness to transition from inpatient to outpatient care. Current status: weight gain 15 g/kg/day for 5 consecutive days, temperature 36.7°C, alert and playful, accepting feeds well, no vomiting or diarrhea, no edema. Mother trained in food preparation and hygiene. What additional criterion must be met before discharge?
questions.initialExplanation: Before discharge of an SAM child, clinical stability for an extra 48 hours is required in addition to the other criteria.
questions.detailedExplanation:
According to WHO guidelines, children must demonstrate 48 hours of stable clinical condition before discharge from inpatient care. This includes
maintaining weight gain, normal temperature, good appetite, and absence of complications. Laboratory values alone are not discharge criteria.
WHO discharge criteria:

1. Stable clinical condition: 48 hours of consistent improvement

2. Weight gain: Sustained weight gain for multiple consecutive days

3. Normal temperature: Stable thermoregulation

4. Good appetite: Accepting adequate feeds

5. No complications: Absence of vomiting, diarrhea, edema

6. Family readiness: Mother trained in care and feeding

Why 48-hour requirement:

- Stability assessment: Ensures consistent improvement, not temporary response

- Complication monitoring: Allows detection of delayed complications

- Feeding tolerance: Confirms sustained tolerance to nutritional rehabilitation

- Family preparation: Time for adequate training and preparation

---

questions.stem: A 22-month-old boy in a rural region of sub-Saharan Africa presents with lethargy, bilateral pitting edema up to the knees, and sparse, discolored hair with alternating pale and dark bands. He was weaned abruptly at 12 months onto a maize-based diet with minimal protein. On exam, he weighs <3rd percentile, has a “flaky paint” skin rash over the buttocks, apathy, hepatomegaly, and a serum albumin of 1.8 g/dL. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.label: D
options.text: Iron deficiency anemia with failure to thrive

options.label: E
options.text: Congestive heart failure secondary to anemia

questions.initialExplanation: Edema, rash, hepatomegaly and very low albumin (1.8) in a child in a food-deficient area = kwashiorkor.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Kwashiorkor is characterized by protein deficiency with relatively adequate caloric intake, leading to
edema, hypoalbuminemia, apathy, skin changes (“flaky paint” dermatosis), hair changes (flag sign),
and hepatomegaly due to fatty liver. Marasmus lacks edema and presents with severe wasting and
preserved alertness. Marasmic-kwashiorkor combines features of both (severe wasting + edema), but
this child’s weight is moderately low (not <60% expected), and wasting is masked by edema—classic
for kwashiorkor. Cardiac or iron-deficiency causes do not explain the dermatosis, hair changes, or
hypoalbuminemia.

---

questions.stem: A 10-month-old infant is brought to a clinic in a drought-affected area. The mother reports the child has not gained weight in 4 months and appears “skin and bones.” He is irritable but alert, with extreme muscle wasting, loss of subcutaneous fat (including buccal fat pads), and a “wizened” facial appearance. There is no edema. He eagerly accepts food when offered. Vital signs are stable, and labs show normal serum albumin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Severe wasting without edema, normal albumin and ravenous appetite = nutritional marasmus.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Marasmus results from severe deficiency of both calories and protein, causing extreme wasting, loss
of subcutaneous fat, “old man” facies, and preserved appetite and alertness. The absence of edema
and normal albumin distinguish it from kwashiorkor. Cystic fibrosis and hypothyroidism cause failure
to thrive but with additional systemic features (e.g., steatorrhea, delayed reflexes). Rickets presents

with skeletal deformities, not global wasting.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child presents with severe wasting of the arms and trunk, bilateral pitting edema of the legs, apathy, and skin ulceration over the buttocks. Weight is 50% of expected for age. Serum albumin is 1.6 g/dL. Which classification best describes this child’s condition?.

options.label: E
options.text: Secondary failure to thrive due to IBD

questions.initialExplanation: Wasted arms and trunk with edema and albumin 1.6 = marasmic-kwashiorkor.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has marasmic-kwashiorkor, the most severe form of protein-energy malnutrition (PEM), combining features of
both marasmus and kwashiorkor. According to FAQ, this diagnosis requires:

- Weight-for-height <60% of expected (here, 50%)

- Presence of edema (bilateral pitting)

- Additional kwashiorkor signs: skin ulceration (“flaky paint”), apathy, hypoalbuminemia

- Severe wasting in upper body (arms/trunk), while lower limbs may appear less wasted due to edema

This hybrid form carries the highest mortality risk (>20% even in hospital settings). Option B (pure kwashiorkor) typically
shows weight 60-80% of expected with edema but less profound wasting. Option A is incorrect because marasmus alone
lacks edema. IBD (E) would present with bloody diarrhea, growth failure, and abdominal pain—not classic PEM dermatosis
or hypoalbuminemia without inflammation markers. The Waterlow classification, which assesses wasting (weight-for-
height) and stunting (height-for-age) independently, would classify this as severe wasting + edema, confirming marasmic-
kwashiorkor.

---

questions.stem: A 14-month-old boy in a refugee camp is diagnosed with severe acute malnutrition. On day 2 of hospitalization, he develops tachycardia, tachypnea, hypophosphatemia, and hypokalemia shortly after initiation of high-calorie milk feeds. What is the most likely underlying mechanism?

options.label: E
options.text: Sepsis-induced metabolic acidosis Refeeding syndrome Diarrheal dehydration Acute heart failure Adrenal insufficiency

questions.initialExplanation: Low K and phosphate and shortness of breath after starting a high-calorie milk = refeeding syndrome.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Refeeding syndrome is a life-threatening complication that occurs when aggressive carbohydrate
feeding is initiated too rapidly in severely malnourished children. the pathophysiology involves:

Sudden glucose load — insulin surge — cellular uptake of phosphate, potassium, and magnesium
Resulting in hypophosphatemia, hypokalemia, and hypomagnesemia

- This causes high-output cardiac failure: tachycardia, tachypnea, hepatomegaly, and peripheral
edema

- Onset typically occurs 24-48 hours after refeeding begins

---

questions.stem: A 6-month-old exclusively breastfed infant presents with weight below the 5th percentile, height at the 40th percentile, and no edema. The mother reports insufficient milk supply and inability to afford formula. Physical exam shows mild muscle wasting but no skin or hair changes. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: C
options.text: Evaluate for inborn errors of metabolism

options.label: E
options.text: Educate on appropriate complementary feeding and support lactation

questions.initialExplanation: A breastfed infant with low weight and mild muscle wasting is managed with education on complementary foods and breastfeeding support.
questions.detailedExplanation:
At 6 months of age, WHO and standard pediatric guidelines recommend the introduction of nutrient-dense
complementary foods alongside continued breastfeeding. This infant has mild undernutrition (low weight-for-
age but preserved height and no signs of severe acute malnutrition such as edema, apathy, or skin changes),
so inpatient therapeutic feeding is not indicated. The priority is nutritional counseling: support breastfeeding,
introduce iron- and protein-rich complementary foods (e.g., fortified porridge, legumes, mashed vegetables),
and address maternal concerns. F-75 (B) is reserved for severe acute malnutrition with complications during
the stabilization phase. RUTF (D) is used in uncomplicated severe malnutrition in outpatient settings. IV
albumin (A) is ineffective and not recommended in protein-energy malnutrition, as edema results from
metabolic and inflammatory factors, not just low albumin. Inborn errors (C) typically present with vomiting,
lethargy, metabolic acidosis, or neurological regression—not isolated mild undernutrition.

---

questions.stem: A 24-month-old child presents with bilateral pitting edema, apathy, and a serum albumin of 1.7 g/dL. His diet for the past 6 months has consisted almost entirely of maize porridge. He has sparse hair with alternating pale and dark bands and skin lesions over the buttocks resembling “peeling paint.” Which biochemical abnormality is most central to the pathophysiology of his condition?
questions.initialExplanation: Edema in kwashiorkor is mainly due to hypoalbuminemia (low plasma oncotic pressure).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Hypoalbuminemia is the key biochemical feature driving edema in protein-deficient states. With
albumin below 2.8 g/dL, plasma oncotic pressure falls, allowing fluid to leak into the interstitial space
and causing pitting edema. This child’s maize-based diet provides calories but lacks sufficient high-
quality protein, leading to impaired hepatic albumin synthesis. While liver enzymes may be mildly
elevated due to fatty infiltration, and electrolyte imbalances can occur, none are as directly causative
of the clinical syndrome as hypoalbuminemia. This pattern—edema, apathy, flag sign, and
dermatosis —is classic for kwashiorkor.

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old with marasmic-kwashiorkor develops tachypnea, tachycardia, and rapid hepatomegaly on the second day of hospitalization after starting high-calorie milk feeds. He has no fever and clear lung fields on auscultation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Tachycardia and tachypnea after a high-calorie milk without fever or pneumonia = refeeding syndrome.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Refeeding syndrome typically manifests 24-48 hours after initiating aggressive nutritional support in
severely malnourished children. The sudden influx of carbohydrates triggers insulin release, which
drives phosphate, potassium, and magnesium into cells, leading to hypophosphatemia, hypokalemia,
and fluid retention. This results in high-output cardiac failure with tachycardia, tachypnea,
hepatomegaly, and peripheral edema. The absence of fever, focal infection signs, or abnormal lung
sounds makes infectious or cardiac causes less likely. Management requires slowing the feeding rate
and correcting electrolyte abnormalities promptly.

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy with kwashiorkor has sparse, brittle hair with alternating pale and dark horizontal bands. His diet has consisted almost entirely of cassava for the past 4 months. He is apathetic, with bilateral pitting edema and skin lesions over his thighs. Which hair finding is most specific to his diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Red/pale hair with alternating color bands is called the flag sign and is typical of kwashiorkor.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The flag sign—characterized by alternating pale and dark bands across the hair shaft—is a classic
feature of kwashiorkor, reflecting periods of protein deficiency alternating with transient nutritional
improvement during hair growth. This sign is highly specific to protein-energy malnutrition with a
kwashiorkor phenotype. Alopecia areata and scarring alopecia involve patchy or permanent hair loss,
not banding. Premature graying and telogen effluvium occur in other systemic illnesses but lack the
distinctive banding pattern. Normal hair is typically preserved in marasmus, further distinguishing it
from kwashiorkor.

---

questions.stem: A 20-month-old child presents with extreme muscle wasting, loss of subcutaneous fat, and a “‘wizened” facial appearance. He is irritable but alert, with no edema, and eagerly accepts food when offered. Which feature most reliably distinguishes this condition from kwashiorkor?
questions.initialExplanation: The key difference between marasmus and kwashiorkor is the absence of edema.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The presence or absence of edema is the key distinguishing feature between marasmus and
kwashiorkor. This child has classic marasmus: severe wasting, preserved appetite, alertness, and no
edema. In contrast, kwashiorkor always includes bilateral pitting edema, along with apathy, skin
changes, and hair abnormalities. While both conditions can cause weight loss, anemia, and diarrhea,
only edema is diagnostic for kwashiorkor. Age of onset may overlap, and degree of weight loss
varies; thus, edema remains the most reliable differentiator.

---

questions.stem: A 1-year-old with marasmic-kwashiorkor dies on day 5 of hospitalization despite appropriate care. Autopsy reveals no acute infection. Which of the following is the most common direct cause of death during the first week of treatment in severe malnutrition?
questions.initialExplanation: The commonest cause of death in the first week of treating severe malnutrition is hypoglycemia (also hypothermia and sepsis).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Hypoglycemia is one of the four direct causes of death in severe malnutrition, particularly during the
first week of hospitalization. It results from depleted glycogen stores and impaired gluconeogenesis,
and is often triggered by fasting (e.g., overnight). It may present as lethargy, seizures, or sudden
death, especially in marasmus or marasmic-kwashiorkor. While refeeding syndrome (A) and
electrolyte imbalances (C) are also life-threatening, hypoglycemia is the most frequent acute
metabolic emergency. Myocardial infarction and pulmonary embolism are exceedingly rare in this
population. Early recognition and prophylactic feeding every 2-3 hours are critical to prevention.

---

questions.stem: A 7-month-old has weight-for-age below —2 standard deviations, height-for-age above -1 standard deviation, and weight-for-height below -2 standard deviations. There is no edema. Which description best characterizes his nutritional status?
questions.initialExplanation: Weight-for-age and height-for-age below -2 SD without edema = underweight and wasting.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Underweight = low weight-for-age

Wasting = low weight-for-height (acute malnutrition)

Stunting = low height-for-age (chronic malnutrition)

This child has low weight-for-age and low weight-for-height, but normal height-for-age, indicating
recent-onset acute malnutrition without chronic growth failure. This pattern is typical of inadequate
recent intake, such as from poor feeding practices or illness. Marasmic-kwashiorkor (D) requires
edema, which is absent. Overnutrition (E) and isolated stunting (A) are not supported. The
combination of underweight and wasting signals a need for urgent nutritional intervention.

---

questions.stem: A 7-month-old boy presents with progressive lethargy over 3 days. His mother reports he was born at term but has never regained birth weight. He is exclusively fed diluted evaporated milk. On exam, weight is 4.1 kg (<3rd percentile), length is 62 cm (10th percentile), and there is no edema. He has dry skin, sparse hair, and mild muscle wasting. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin 8.2 g/dL, albumin 3.6 g/dL, and normal electrolytes. What is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?

options.label: E
options.text: Serum thyroxine and TSH - F) moowy

questions.initialExplanation: Weakness and tiredness with mild anemia and normal albumin first calls for a thorough dietary and social history.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This infant has failure to thrive due to primary malnutrition from an inadequate, inappropriate diet
(diluted evaporated milk lacks protein, iron, and essential fatty acids). His normal albumin and
absence of edema rule out kwashiorkor; the preserved length suggests recent-onset undernutrition.
While anemia is present, the first priority is confirming the etiology through detailed dietary and
caregiver assessment—including feeding practices, food security, caregiver mental health, and
potential neglect. Secondary causes (e.g., CF, hypothyroidism) are less likely without specific red
flags (steatorrhea, constipation, neurologic delay). Jumping to diagnostics (A, B, D, E) before
thorough history is inefficient and misses the most probable cause.

---

questions.stem: A 22-month-old girl from a drought-affected region presents with bilateral lower-limb edema, apathy, and a serum albumin of 1.9 g/dL. She develops sudden onset of confusion and tachypnea on day 3 of F- 75 feeding. Vital signs: HR 160 bpm, RR 48/min, BP 80/50 mmHg. Lungs are clear. Serum phosphate is 0.8 mmol/L (low), potassium 2.6 mmol/L (low). What is the most likely cause of her acute decompensation?
questions.initialExplanation: Falling phosphate and potassium after starting feeds in a malnourished child = refeeding syndrome.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child with kwashiorkor developed acute cardiopulmonary decompensation 72 hours after
initiating F-75, with hypophosphatemia, hypokalemia, tachycardia, and tachypnea—classic signs of
refeeding syndrome. Despite using F-75 (a low-osmolarity formula), overly rapid advancement or
inadequate monitoring can still trigger it. The clear lungs and absence of fever argue against
pneumonia (A) or malaria (D). Hypophosphatemia impairs ATP production, leading to diaphragmatic
weakness, cardiac dysfunction, and altered mental status. Immediate actions include slowing feeds,
IV phosphate/potassium replacement, and cardiac monitoring. This is not lactic acidosis (E), which
would present with shock and metabolic acidosis, not isolated electrolyte shifts.

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old with severe acute malnutrition is admitted. On day 2, he develops watery diarrhea, tachycardia (HR 150), and hepatomegaly. He is on F-75 at 100 mL/kg/day. Labs: Na* 130, K* 2.8, PO.%" 0.7 mmol/L. He has no fever or abdominal tenderness. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.label: A
options.text: Stop all feeds and start IV rehydration

options.label: B
options.text: Continue F-75 and add standard ORS

options.label: D
options.text: Slow feeding rate and correct phosphate/potassium

options.label: E
options.text: Start metronidazole for presumed C. difficile - F) moowy

questions.initialExplanation: With refeeding syndrome, slow the feeding rate and correct phosphate and potassium.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child shows early signs of refeeding syndrome: diarrhea, tachycardia, hepatomegaly, and severe
hypophosphatemia/hypokalemia—occurring 48 hours after starting F-75. Although F-75 is low-
calorie, overly aggressive volume or frequency can still trigger metabolic shifts. Feeds should not be
stopped (A), as this worsens catabolism. Standard ORS (B) contains too much sodium and worsens
fluid retention. Lactose intolerance (C) causes osmotic diarrhea but not electrolyte shifts or
hepatomegaly. C. difficile (E) is unlikely without antibiotic exposure or bloody stools. The correct

action is to reduce feed volume, monitor vitals closely, and replace phosphate and potassium
cautiously.

---

questions.stem: A 5-month-old girl is brought for “not growing.” Birth weight was 2.8 kg; current weight is 4.0 kg (<8rd percentile), length 60 cm (25th percentile). She is exclusively breastfed, but her mother reports “low milk supply” and frequent crying during feeds. No vomiting, diarrhea, or fever. Exam shows mild muscle wasting, no edema, and normal skin/hair. Which diagnostic step is most likely to reveal the underlying cause?

options.label: C
options.text: Observed feeding session with lactation support

questions.initialExplanation: An infant girl not growing with low weight: observing a feeding session with breastfeeding support reveals the cause (latch/supply).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Failure to thrive in a young breastfed infant is most often due to inadequate milk transfer, not
maternal malnutrition or infant disease. An observed feeding assesses latch, suckling efficiency,

‘    maternal positioning, and milk transfer—key factors missed in history alone. Maternal prolactin (A) is
rarely useful; prealbumin (B) is unreliable in acute illness; ultrasound (D) and newborn screen (E) are
low-yield without red flags. Non-organic FTT from feeding difficulties is the leading cause in this age
group. Lactation support often resolves the issue without extensive testing.

---

questions.stem: A 9-month-old boy presents with progressive weight loss over 2 months. He was exclusively breastfed until 6 months, then switched to rice water and tea due to family belief that “solid food causes colic.” He is irritable, with profound muscle wasting, absent subcutaneous fat, and a “wizened” face. There is no edema. His mother reports he cries during feeds but calms when offered food. Which dietary misconception most likely contributed to his condition?

options.label: B
options.text: Dilution of formula to save cost \*

options.label: E
options.text: Belief that breast milk alone suffices beyond 6 months Use of herbal teas as hydration Delayed introduction of complementary foods Preference for carbohydrate-rich gruels Avoidance of animal-source protein

questions.initialExplanation: A common misconception: delaying complementary foods beyond 6 months leads to malnutrition.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Exclusive breastfeeding is recommended only for the first 6 months. After this, complementary
feeding is essential to meet increasing caloric and protein demands. This child’s diet of rice water
and tea provides negligible protein and calories, leading to marasmus. While animal-source protein
(E) is ideal, even plant-based complementary foods (e.g., legumes, fortified cereals) would prevent
severe wasting. The core error is the complete absence of complementary feeding after 6 months,
not the type of food avoided. Herbal teas (B) may displace nutrient intake but are not the primary
cause. Breast milk alone (A) is appropriate up to 6 months, not beyond.

---

questions.stem: A 24-month-old child with marasmic-kwashiorkor develops sudden lethargy and seizures on day 4 of hospitalization. Bedside glucose is 48 mg/dL. He received F-75 at 2 a.m. but refused the 5 a.m. feed. His temperature is 34.9°C. What is the most appropriate immediate intervention? Nc

options.label: A
options.text: IV 10% dextrose 5 mL/kg followed by 50 mL of F-75 via NG tube

questions.initialExplanation: Low glucose and low temperature (34.9): give IV dextrose 10% 5 mL/kg then F-75 via NG.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has hypoglycemia (glucose <54 mg/dL), a direct cause of death in severe malnutrition,
often occurring during overnight fasting. Because he is lethargic, oral or IM routes are unsafe or
ineffective. IV dextrose is mandatory for altered mental status. After correction, immediate feeding
(even via NG tube) is critical to prevent recurrence —malnourished children lack glycogen stores and
cannot maintain euglycemia without frequent carbohydrate intake. Glucagon (B) fails due to absent
glycogen. Hydrocortisone (D) and saline (E) do not address hypoglycemia. The coexisting mild
hypothermia does not change glucose management priority.

---

questions.stem: A 4-month-old exclusively breastfed infant presents with weight at the 10th percentile, length at the 50th percentile, and normal development. The mother is anxious about “poor milk supply” but reports 6 wet diapers/day and audible swallowing during feeds. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: C
options.text: Reassure and schedule weight check in 2 weeks

questions.initialExplanation: An infant feeding well (6 diapers and audible swallowing) with weight within limits: reassure parents and recheck after two weeks.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This infant is growing appropriately (weight at 10th percentile is normal), with adequate hydration (6
wet diapers/day) and effective breastfeeding (audible swallowing). Maternal perception of low milk
supply is common but often inaccurate. In the absence of red flags (failure to regain birth weight by
2 weeks, <4 wet diapers/day, lethargy), no intervention is needed. Formula supplementation (A) can
reduce milk supply and is unnecessary. Prolactin testing (B) is rarely useful. Iron (E) is not indicated
before 6 months in term infants. Renal ultrasound (D) has no indication. Reassurance and close
follow-up are standard.

Mainu | Failure to rive AA
