## Acute Hepatitis & Hepatic Failure

> Question numbers not present in the source file for this topic: 9, 18.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy presents with acute fever, anorexia, jaundice, repeated vomiting, and right upper quadrant pain. He denies any drug use. On exam, his liver is tender and palpable 5 cm below the costal margin. After 3 days, he becomes drowsy, more jaundiced, with a shrinking liver and persistent epistaxis unresponsive to vitamin K. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Liver shrinkage with epistaxis unresponsive to vitamin K (failed clotting-factor synthesis) after acute hepatitis = fulminant hepatic failure.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This case demonstrates classic progression of acute hepatitis to fulminant hepatic failure:
Initial Phase (Days 1-3)

- Fever, anorexia, jaundice: Acute hepatitis presentation

- Vomiting, RUQ pain: Hepatic inflammation and capsular stretch

- Tender hepatomegaly: 5 cm below costal margin indicates acute inflammation
Progression to Fulminant Failure (Day 3+)

- Drowsiness: Hepatic encephalopathy from toxin accumulation

- Worsening jaundice: Increasing bilirubin due to failing liver function

- Shrinking liver: Ominous sign of massive hepatic necrosis

- Persistent epistaxis: Coagulopathy from failure of clotting factor synthesis

- Unresponsive to vitamin K: Confirms synthetic failure, not just deficiency

---

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy presents with 5 days of fatigue, poor appetite, abdominal pain, and jaundice. He had a G6PD- related hemolytic crisis 4 months ago requiring a blood transfusion and has not been vaccinated. On exam, he is icteric, mildly lethargic, and has right upper quadrant tenderness with hepatomegaly. No signs of chronic liver disease are noted. Labs: Hb 10 g/dL, reticulocyte count 1%, total bilirubin 5.4 mg/dL (mostly conjugated), ALT 980 IU/L, AST 850 IU/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.label: B
options.text: Recurrent hemolytic crisis due to G6PD deficiency

questions.initialExplanation: Acute liver injury with high ALT/AST and direct bilirubin in an unvaccinated child = acute viral hepatitis B; G6PD causes hemolysis (indirect bilirubin), not this ALT rise.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This presentation indicates acute viral hepatitis B, strongly suggested by the unvaccinated status and classic
features: markedly elevated transaminases (ALT 980, AST 850) indicating acute hepatocellular injury,

‘   conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, and symptoms of fatigue, anorexia, RUQ pain, and hepatomegaly. The G6PD
deficiency history is a distractor; recurrent hemolysis is excluded by the low reticulocyte count (1%) and
conjugated (not unconjugated) bilirubin elevation. Autoimmune hepatitis is less likely without supporting
markers, while acute cholecystitis typically shows higher alkaline phosphatase. Wilson disease remains a
differential but viral etiology is more common in unvaccinated children. Differentiating hepatocellular jaundice
(high transaminases, conjugated bilirubin) from hemolytic jaundice (normal enzymes, unconjugated bilirubin,
high reticulocytes) is essential. The G6PD history tests interpretation of laboratory patterns rather than
indicating active hemolysis.

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl presents to the emergency department with a 3-day history of progressive lethargy, vomiting, and jaundice. Her parents report that she was previously healthy until 2 weeks ago when she developed fever, anorexia, and abdominal pain. On examination, she appears confused and has asterixis. Laboratory findings show: ALT 2,850 U/L, AST 3,200 U/L, total bilirubin 15.2 mg/dL, INR 3.2, ammonia 180 ug/dL, and blood glucose 45 mg/dL. Her liver edge is no longer palpable despite significant hepatomegaly noted 1 week ago. What is the most likely diagnosis and the most appropriate initial management approach?

options.label: A
options.text: Acute viral hepatitis A with supportive care and close monitoring for progression to liver failure

options.label: B
options.text: Acute liver failure requiring immediate transfer to pediatric intensive care unit and comprehensive management protocol

options.label: C
options.text: Severe hepatitis A infection with prophylactic N-acetylcysteine and antiviral therapy

options.label: D
options.text: Fulminant hepatic failure due to acetaminophen overdose requiring specific antidote therapy

options.label: E
options.text: Autoimmune hepatitis flare requiring immediate corticosteroid therapy

questions.initialExplanation: Jaundice and hepatomegaly with altered consciousness or coagulopathy = acute liver failure needing immediate transfer to intensive care.
questions.detailedExplanation:
comprehensive management protocol

This child meets diagnostic criteria for acute liver failure: INR 3.2 (>2.0), hepatic encephalopathy
(confusion, asterixis), and multisystem involvement (hypoglycemia, hyperammonemia). The
vanishing liver sign indicates massive necrosis. Immediate ICU care is required with airway
management, coagulopathy correction, cerebral edema monitoring, and early transplantation
evaluation. This is established ALF, not just at risk for progression. Rapid liver shrinkage is an
ominous prognostic sign.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the pediatrician with a 5-day history of jaundice, dark urine, and pale stools. His mother mentions that he attends daycare and several other children have been sick with similar symptoms recently. The child appears tired but alert. Physical examination reveals tender hepatomegaly and mild scleral icterus. Laboratory results show: ALT 450 U/L, AST 380 U/L, total bilirubin 4.8 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 280 U/L, and gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase 45 U/L. Which of the following diagnostic tests would be most appropriate to confirm the suspected diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: To confirm acute hepatitis A, request anti-HAV IgM.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The presentation suggests hepatitis A infection (daycare outbreak, jaundice, elevated transaminases).

Anti-HAV IgM antibodies are the gold standard for acute hepatitis A as they appear 5-10 days before
‘   symptoms, peak during illness, and persist 4-6 months. Anti-HAV IgG indicates past infection or

vaccination, not active disease. Hepatitis B and C have different transmission patterns. Liver biopsy is

invasive and not needed for typical hepatitis A diagnosis. Cost-effective diagnostic approach for
outbreaks.

---

questions.stem: A 6-month-old infant presents with persistent jaundice since birth, poor weight gain, and severe pruritus that causes constant irritability and scratching. The infant has characteristic triangular facies and examination reveals butterfly vertebrae on chest X-ray. Cardiac evaluation shows peripheral pulmonary stenosis. The infant's condition has not improved with standard cholestasis management. What is the most appropriate long-term management strategy for this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Ursodeoxycholic acid therapy with nutritional support and fat-soluble vitamins

options.label: B
options.text: Immediate liver transplantation evaluation due to severe cholestasis and failure to thrive

options.label: C
options.text: Surgical biliary diversion procedures to reduce pruritus

options.label: D
options.text: Supportive care with antihistamines for pruritus and postponement of definitive treatment

options.label: E
options.text: Genetic testing for JAG1 and NOTCH2 mutations to confirm diagnosis

questions.initialExplanation: An infant with jaundice since birth and cholestasis needs ursodeoxycholic acid with nutritional support and fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K).
questions.detailedExplanation:
This infant has classic Alagille syndrome with characteristic facies, butterfly vertebrae, and peripheral
pulmonary stenosis. Management includes ursodeoxycholic acid (10-15 mg/kg/day) to improve bile
flow, high-calorie diet with MCT oil, and fat-soluble vitamin supplementation (A, D, E, K). Most
patients survive to adulthood with mortality usually from cardiac complications, not liver disease. Liver
transplantation is reserved for endstage liver disease. Surgical biliary diversion is experimental and
not standard care.

---

questions.stem: A 10-year-old girl presents with a 6-month history of progressive fatigue, intermittent jaundice, and weight loss. She has no significant past medical history but her mother mentions that she has been increasingly withdrawn and her school performance has declined. Physical examination reveals mild hepatomegaly and jaundice. Laboratory findings show: ALT 180 U/L, AST 220 U/L, total bilirubin 3.2 mg/dL, IgG level 28 g/L, and positive antinuclear antibodies. What is the most likely diagnosis and initial management approach?

options.label: A
options.text: Autoimmune hepatitis type 1 requiring immediate prednisolone therapy

options.label: B
options.text: Viral hepatitis B infection requiring antiviral therapy

options.label: C
options.text: Wilson disease requiring copper chelation therapy

options.label: D
options.text: Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease requiring lifestyle modifications

options.label: E
options.text: Autoimmune hepatitis type 2 requiring combined prednisolone and azathioprine therapy

questions.initialExplanation: Fatigue, high IgG and positive ANA in a girl = autoimmune hepatitis type 1, treated starting with prednisolone.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This presentation is classic for autoimmune hepatitis type 1: 10-year-old girl, insidious onset, elevated
IgG (28 g/L), and positive ANA. Autoimmune hepatitis responds dramatically to prednisolone 2
mg/kg/day with rapid improvement in >90% of patients. Wilson disease would show low ceruloplasmin
and neurological symptoms. NAFLD typically occurs in obese children. Type 2 AlH is characterized by
anti-LKM-1 antibodies and presents more acutely. Early treatment prevents progression to cirrhosis.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child presents to the emergency department with acute onset of jaundice, vomiting, and altered mental status. The parents report that the child accidentally ingested acetaminophen tablets 2 days ago. Laboratory findings reveal: ALT 4,200 U/L, AST 5,100 U/L, INR 4.5, acetaminophen level 180 mg/L (therapeutic range 10-30 mg/L), and metabolic acidosis on arterial blood gas. What is the most appropriate specific antidote therapy for this condition?

options.label: A
options.text: Liver transplantation evaluation as definitive treatment

questions.initialExplanation: Acute liver failure with acidosis in a young child after paracetamol poisoning: the antidote is N-acetylcysteine, orally or IV.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has acetaminophen overdose with toxic level (180 mg/L) and acute liver failure (INR 4.5,
encephalopathy). N-acetylcysteine is the specific antidote that replenishes glutathione stores and
detoxifies NAPQI metabolite. It can be given orally (loading 140 mg/kg, then 70 mg/kg g4h x 17
doses) or IV. Most effective within 8-10 hours but beneficial up to 24 hours. Activated charcoal is
ineffective 2 days post-ingestion. Liver transplantation is considered if NAC therapy fails.

---

questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy with known Wilson disease presents with acute liver failure. He has been on penicillamine therapy for 2 years but admitted to poor compliance. Examination reveals jaundice, asterixis, and Kayser-Fleischer rings on slit-lamp examination. Laboratory findings show: ALT 150 U/L, AST 180 U/L, total bilirubin 12.8 mg/dL, INR 3.8, serum ceruloplasmin 8 mg/dL (normal 20-40 mg/dL), and 24-hour urinary copper 850 pg/ 24 hours (normal <60 ug/24 hours). What is the most appropriate management strategy for this acute presentation?

options.label: A
options.text: Continue penicillamine therapy with dose escalation

options.label: B
options.text: Switch to trientine therapy with zinc supplementation

options.label: C
options.text: Immediate liver transplantation evaluation due to acute liver failure

options.label: D
options.text: Add zinc therapy and continue current chelation regimen

questions.initialExplanation: Wilson disease with acute liver failure (high urinary copper): refer immediately for liver transplant evaluation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Wilson disease presenting as acute liver failure has 100% mortality without transplantation. This
patient has INR 3.8, encephalopathy (asterixis), and markedly elevated urinary copper (850 ug/24h).

‘     Chelation therapy cannot reverse acute liver failure quickly enough. Zinc is too slow-acting.
Hemofiltration doesn't effectively remove copper. Any child with Wilson disease presenting with
acute liver failure and encephalopathy should be listed for urgent transplantation. King's College
criteria are not reliable for Wilson disease.

---

questions.stem: A 14-year-old adolescent girl presents with a 3-month history of progressive fatigue, jaundice, and abdominal pain. She denies any medication use, alcohol consumption, or recent travel. Her mother has hypothyroidism and rheumatoid arthritis. Physical examination reveals jaundice, hepatomegaly, and spider angiomas. Laboratory findings show: ALT 320 U/L, AST 280 U/L, total bilirubin 5.8 mg/dL, IgG level 32 g/L, ANA positive 1:160, anti-smooth muscle antibody positive 1:80, and low complement C4 level. What is the most appropriate initial immunosuppressive therapy regimen?

options.label: A
options.text: Prednisolone 2 mg/kg/day with gradual tapering and azathioprine 0.5 mg/kg/day

options.label: B
options.text: Prednisolone 2 mg/kg/day alone with monthly monitoring

options.label: C
options.text: Mycophenolate mofetil 20 mg/kg twice daily with prednisolone

options.label: D
options.text: Ciclosporin with dose adjustment based on drug levels

options.label: E
options.text: Budesonide 9 mg daily with gradual transition from prednisolone

questions.initialExplanation: Autoimmune hepatitis is treated with prednisolone 2 mg/kg/day with gradual tapering and addition of azathioprine.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This adolescent has autoimmune hepatitis type 1 with elevated IgG (32 g/L), positive ANA and anti-
smooth muscle antibodies. Standard treatment is prednisolone 2 mg/kg/day with azathioprine 0.5
mg/kg/day added for maintenance. Combination therapy provides >90% response rates and allows
steroid dose reduction. Mycophenolate is second-line. Cyclosporin has significant nephrotoxicity.

Budesonide cannot be used in cirrhosis (affects >90% of AIH patients). Goal is normal LFTs and IgG
levels.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy with known autoimmune hepatitis type 1 presents for routine follow-up. He has been on prednisolone 5 mg daily and azathioprine 1.5 mg/kg/day for 2 years with excellent clinical response. Current laboratory findings show: ALT 35 U/L, AST 40 U/L, total bilirubin 1.2 mg/dL, IgG level 12 g/L, and negative ANA and anti-smooth muscle antibodies. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.text: Continue both azathioprine and prednisolone indefinitely \*

options.label: B
options.text: Attempt gradual withdrawal of azathioprine while maintaining prednisolone

options.label: C
options.text: Consider gradual withdrawal of both medications if laboratory values remain normal

options.label: D
options.text: Add mycophenolate mofetil for enhanced immunosuppression

options.label: E
options.text: Switch to budesonide for reduced side effects

questions.initialExplanation: With biochemical remission (negative ANA/ASMA and normal IgG), consider gradual treatment withdrawal with close follow-up.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This patient meets criteria for treatment withdrawal: 2 years of therapy, normal LFTs and IgG (12 g/L),
and negative autoantibodies. Treatment should be continued at least 3 years, then gradual withdrawal
can be considered if sustained remission. Success rates are 60-80% for maintaining remission after
withdrawal. Close monitoring is essential with prompt retreatment if relapse occurs. Indefinite therapy
increases steroid complications without proven benefit.

---

questions.stem: A family is planning travel to a developing country with their 18-month-old child. They inquire about hepatitis A prevention. The child has not received any hepatitis A vaccinations and has no contraindications to vaccination. What is the most appropriate prophylaxis strategy for this child?

options.label: A
options.text: Hepatitis A vaccine administered intramuscularly in a 2-dose schedule

options.label: B
options.text: Hepatitis A immunoglobulin only, as vaccine is contraindicated under 12 months

options.label: C
options.text: Both hepatitis A vaccine and immunoglobulin for maximum protection

options.label: D
options.text: No prophylaxis needed as maternal antibodies provide protection

options.label: E
options.text: Hepatitis A vaccine in a single dose for immediate protection

questions.initialExplanation: Prevention before travel for an 18-month-old: hepatitis A vaccine IM, two doses.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This 18-month-old child requires pre-exposure prophylaxis for travel to endemic areas. Hepatitis A
vaccine is safe and effective >12 months, providing protection in 2-4 weeks after first dose. Two-
dose schedule (6-12 months apart) provides long-term immunity (>10 years). Immunoglobulin
provides only temporary protection (2-3 months). Maternal antibodies don't provide reliable
protection at this age. Single dose provides incomplete protection.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child in daycare develops acute hepatitis A infection. The daycare center has 25 children aged 2-6 years, and 3 other children have developed similar symptoms in the past week. The center Director asks for guidance on post-exposure prophylaxis for the other children and staff. What is the most appropriate post-exposure prophylaxis strategy for this outbreak?

options.label: A
options.text: Hepatitis A vaccine for all children >12 months and staff, immunoglobulin for children

options.label: B
options.text: Immunoglobulin only for all exposed individuals

options.label: C
options.text: Hepatitis A vaccine only for all exposed individuals

options.label: D
options.text: No prophylaxis needed as hepatitis A is self-limiting

options.label: E
options.text: Hepatitis A vaccine for children and immunoglobulin for all adults

questions.initialExplanation: In a daycare outbreak: hepatitis A vaccine for those over 12 months and staff, with immunoglobulin when needed for the young.
questions.detailedExplanation:
<12 months

This is a hepatitis A outbreak requiring post-exposure prophylaxis. Children >12 months and staff
should receive hepatitis A vaccine (provides protection within 2-4 weeks). Children <12 months
should receive immunoglobulin (immediate protection for 2-3 months). Vaccine is preferred for
healthy individuals >12 months due to longer-lasting protection. Both interventions are most effective
within 2 weeks of exposure. Public health responsibility to prevent outbreak spread.

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old child presents with progressive jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, and portal hypertension. The child has been thriving normally but parents notice abdominal distension. Physical examination reveals firm hepatosplenomegaly and no signs of chronic liver disease. Laboratory findings show: ALT 60 U/L, AST 70 U/L, total bilirubin 2.1 mg/dL (normal), and normal albumin level. Abdominal ultrasound shows features Consistent with congenital hepatic fibrosis. What is the most appropriate management approach for this child?

options.label: A
options.text: Immediate liver transplantation evaluation due to portal hypertension

options.label: B
options.text: Management of portal hypertension complications with surveillance for cholangitis

options.label: D
options.text: Copper chelation therapy for Wilson disease

questions.initialExplanation: Congenital hepatic fibrosis with portal hypertension: manage portal hypertension complications and monitor for cholangitis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has congenital hepatic fibrosis with portal hypertension but preserved liver function (normal
transaminases, bilirubin, albumin). Management focuses on portal hypertension surveillance

‘    (endoscopy for varices, beta-blockers if indicated) and cholangitis prevention. Most patients have
excellent long-term prognosis with conservative management. Liver transplantation is reserved for

complications. No cholestasis present to justify UDCA. This is not Wilson disease or autoimmune
hepatitis.

---

questions.stem: A 16-year-old adolescent with known chronic hepatitis B infection presents for routine monitoring. She was infected perinatally and has been HBsAg positive for 8 years. She feels well and examination is normal. Laboratory findings show: ALT 45 U/L, AST 40 U/L, HBsAg positive, HBeAg negative, anti- HBe positive, and HBV DNA <2,000 IU/mL. What is the most appropriate interpretation and management approach?

options.label: A
options.text: Resolved hepatitis B infection with persistent HBsAg requiring investigation

options.label: B
options.text: Chronic active hepatitis B requiring immediate nucleoside analog therapy

options.label: C
options.text: Acute hepatitis B flare requiring urgent liver transplantation evaluation

options.label: D
options.text: Chronic hepatitis B with immune tolerance requiring interferon therapy

options.label: E
options.text: Chronic inactive hepatitis B requiring no antiviral therapy with annual monitoring

questions.initialExplanation: HBsAg positive, HBeAg positive and low HBV DNA (<2000) = chronic inactive hepatitis B; no antivirals, only yearly follow-up.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This adolescent has chronic inactive hepatitis B with HBsAg+, HBeAg-, anti-HBe+, HBV DNA <2,000
IU/mL, and normal ALT/AST. This represents the inactive carrier state with low viral replication and
minimal liver damage. No antiviral therapy is indicated. Annual monitoring (ALT, HBV DNA, HBsAg) is
essential to detect reactivation. This is not active hepatitis, immune tolerance phase (HBeAg+), or
resolved infection (HBsAg-).

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child with obesity (BMI >95th percentile) presents with incidentally discovered elevated liver enzymes. The child has no symptoms but parents are concerned about fatigue. Laboratory findings show: ALT 85 U/L, AST 70 U/L, total bilirubin 1.1 mg/dL, and normal alkaline phosphatase. Ultrasound shows echogenic liver consistent with fatty infiltration. What is the most appropriate initial management approach?

options.label: A
options.text: Liver biopsy to assess for fibrosis and inflammation

options.label: B
options.text: Dietary counseling and exercise program with weight loss goals

options.label: D
options.text: Vitamin E supplementation for antioxidant therapy

questions.initialExplanation: Non-alcoholic fatty liver in an obese child: weight loss by diet and exercise is first-line.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has NAFLD with obesity, elevated liver enzymes, and fatty liver on ultrasound. First-line
management is lifestyle modification with dietary counseling and exercise program targeting 5-10%
weight loss over 6-12 months. Weight loss can normalize liver enzymes and improve histology. Liver
biopsy is not indicated for uncomplicated NAFLD. No cholestasis present to justify UDCA. Vitamin E
and metformin have limited evidence in pediatric NAFLD.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child presents with acute liver failure of unknown etiology. The child has been previously healthy with no recent medications, infections, or exposures. Laboratory evaluation shows: ALT 3,200 U/L, AST 4,100 U/L, INR 4.5, ammonia 220 ug/dL, and hypoglycemia. Extensive workup for viral hepatitis, metabolic disorders, autoimmune hepatitis, and drug toxicity has been negative. What is the most appropriate next diagnostic step and management approach?

options.label: A
options.text: Immediate liver transplantation listing without further workup \*

options.label: B
options.text: Plasma exchange therapy for rapid toxin removal

options.label: C
options.text: Liver biopsy for histological examination to guide specific therapy

options.label: D
options.text: Broad-spectrum antimicrobial therapy for occult infection

options.label: E
options.text: High-dose corticosteroid therapy for presumed autoimmune hepatitis

questions.initialExplanation: Acute liver failure of unknown cause after excluding common causes: liver biopsy to guide treatment.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has idiopathic ALF after extensive negative workup. Liver biopsy may reveal treatable
conditions (idiopathic autoimmune hepatitis, metabolic diseases, PCR-negative Viral infections)
and provide prognostic information. Histology can guide specific therapy (steroids for autoimmune
hepatitis, dietary therapy for metabolic disorders). Immediate transplantation is premature without
tissue diagnosis. Plasma exchange and antibiotics have no clear indications.

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old child presents with jaundice and severe pruritus. The child has been scratching continuously and has developed skin lesions from scratching. Physical examination reveals jaundice, hepatomegaly, and multiple excoriations. Laboratory findings show: ALT 120 U/L, AST 140 U/L, total bilirubin 11.2 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 850 U/L, and gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase 65 U/L (low). What is the most appropriate symptomatic management strategy for this child's pruritus?

options.label: B
options.text: Ursodeoxycholic acid therapy to improve bile flow

options.label: C
options.text: Rifampin therapy to reduce bile acid levels

options.label: D
options.text: Cholestyramine therapy to bind bile acids in the intestine

questions.initialExplanation: Pruritus in cholestasis: give cholestyramine to bind bile acids in the gut.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has severe cholestatic pruritus (low GGT suggests PFIC1/2). Cholestyramine is first-line
therapy that binds bile acids in the intestine, preventing reabsorption and reducing serum bile acid
levels. Dosing is 250 mg/kg/day divided doses. Antihistamines have limited efficacy for cholestatic
pruritus. UDCA may help underlying cholestasis but is less effective for pruritus. Rifampin is second-
line. Phototherapy is for neonatal jaundice.

---

questions.stem: A 9-year-old child with known autoimmune hepatitis type 1 presents with acute deterioration. She has been on prednisolone 10 mg daily and azathioprine 50 mg daily but laboratory values show: ALT 450 U/L, AST 380 U/L, total bilirubin 8.5 mg/dL, INR 2.8, and IgG level 35 g/L. She appears confused and has asterixis. What is the most appropriate immediate management strategy?

options.label: A
options.text: Increase prednisolone dose to 2 mg/kg/day and continue azathioprine

options.label: B
options.text: Switch to mycophenolate mofetil due to azathioprine failure

options.label: C
options.text: Initiate liver transplantation evaluation for acute liver failure

options.label: D
options.text: Add cyclosporin therapy for enhanced immunosuppression

options.label: E
options.text: Temporarily discontinue azathioprine and increase prednisolone

questions.initialExplanation: Autoimmune hepatitis with encephalopathy (asterixis) = acute liver failure, so evaluate for transplant.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child meets definitive criteria for **acute liver failure **(ALF) secondary to an autoimmune
hepatitis (AIH) flare: acute hepatic injury, significant coagulopathy (INR 1.5), and hepatic
encephalopathy (confusion, asterixis). In pediatric AIH presenting as ALF, mortality without
transplantation exceeds 70- 80%. Immediate referral for liver transplantation evaluation is the
standard of care and should never be delayed for a trial of medical therapy. While high-dose IV
corticosteroids may be initiated concurrently to attempt to halt immune-mediated hepatocyte
destruction, transplant listing must proceed simultaneously because steroid responsiveness is
unpredictable and time-critical organ allocation requires early workup.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old child presents with abdominal distension and hematemesis. The child has a history of recurrent cholangitis episodes treated with antibiotics. Physical examination reveals splenomegaly and ascites. Laboratory findings show: ALT 80 U/L, AST 90 U/L, total bilirubin 3.2 mg/dL, albumin 2.8 g/dL, and platelet count 85,000/uL. What is the most likely diagnosis and appropriate management approach?

options.label: A
options.text: Portal hypertension due to congenital hepatic fibrosis requiring beta-blocker therapy

options.label: B
options.text: Acute variceal bleeding requiring endoscopic therapy and octreotide

options.label: C
options.text: Chronic liver disease due to autoimmune hepatitis requiring immunosuppression

options.label: E
options.text: Liver transplantation evaluation for end-stage liver disease

questions.initialExplanation: Abdominal distension and hematemesis with thrombocytopenia and a history of cholangitis: variceal bleeding, treated endoscopically and with octreotide.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child presents with acute variceal bleeding (hematemesis) with background of recurrent
cholangitis and portal hypertension signs (splenomegaly, ascites, thrombocytopenia). Emergency
management requires immediate endoscopic therapy (band ligation preferred) within 12 hours and
octreotide infusion to reduce portal pressure. Supportive care includes fluid resuscitation, blood
products, and antibiotics. Beta-blockers are for prophylaxis, not acute bleeding.

---

questions.stem: A 14-year-old adolescent presents with acute hepatitis and jaundice. He reports recent travel to Southeast Asia and consumption of street food. Laboratory findings show: ALT 650 U/L, AST 580 U/L, total bilirubin 6.8 mg/dL, and positive IgM antibodies against hepatitis A virus. What is the most appropriate management approach?

options.label: A
options.text: Hospital admission for intravenous acyclovir therapy

options.label: B
options.text: Supportive care with monitoring for complications and isolation precautions

options.label: C
options.text: Immediate corticosteroid therapy for severe hepatitis

options.label: E
options.text: Liver transplantation evaluation for fulminant hepatic failure

questions.initialExplanation: Hepatitis A: supportive care and monitoring for complications with isolation precautions to avoid spread.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This adolescent has acute hepatitis A with positive IgM antibodies, travel history to endemic area,
and elevated transaminases. Management is supportive care with rest, hydration, and monitoring for

‘    complications. Isolation precautions include excluding from school for 1 week after jaundice onset.
Hepatitis A is self-limiting with excellent prognosis. No antiviral therapy exists. Corticosteroids not
indicated. Transplantation only for fulminant failure.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child with known Alagille syndrome presents for routine follow-up. She has characteristic facies, butterfly vertebrae, and peripheral pulmonary stenosis. She has been experiencing severe pruritus that interferes with sleep and daily activities. Previous management with antihistamines and topical therapy has been unsuccessful. What is the most appropriate next step in management for her severe pruritus?

options.label: B
options.text: Rifampin therapy to reduce bile acid levels

options.label: C
options.text: Liver transplantation evaluation due to refractory symptoms

options.label: D
options.text: Ursodeoxycholic acid therapy with dose escalation

options.label: E
options.text: Surgical biliary diversion procedures for symptom relief

questions.initialExplanation: Alagille syndrome with pruritus not yet treated: start cholestyramine with dietary adjustment (alternatives such as rifampicin later).
questions.detailedExplanation:
In Alagille syndrome, severe pruritus results from chronic cholestasis and accumulation of
pruritogenic bile acids in the skin. Management follows a stepwise approach, and this child has
only failed first-line symptomatic measures (antihistamines, topical agents). The next appropriate
step is cholestyramine, a bile acid sequestrant that binds intestinal bile acids, interrupts
enterohepatic circulation, and reduces serum/pruritic bile acid levels. It is the first-line
pharmacologic therapy for cholestatic pruritus per pediatric hepatology guidelines (NASPGHAN/
ESPGHAN). Dietary modifications (medium-chain triglyceride supplementation, fat-soluble vitamin
replacement) support overall management of cholestasis.

---

questions.stem: A 10-year-old child presents with gradual onset jaundice and weight loss over 6 months. The child has been increasingly tired and has developed clubbing. Physical examination reveals jaundice, hepatomegaly, and digital clubbing. Laboratory findings show: ALT 95 U/L, AST 110 U/L, total bilirubin 4.8 mg/dL, and elevated IgG level 25 g/L. What is the most likely diagnosis and appropriate diagnostic workup?

options.label: A
options.text: Autoimmune hepatitis requiring autoantibody panel and liver biopsy

options.label: B
options.text: Chronic hepatitis B requiring viral serology and liver biopsy

options.label: C
options.text: Wilson disease requiring ceruloplasmin and 24-hour urinary copper

options.label: D
options.text: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency requiring protein phenotype analysis

options.label: E
options.text: Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease requiring metabolic evaluation

questions.initialExplanation: Gradual jaundice and raised IgG: suspect autoimmune hepatitis; needs antibody testing and liver biopsy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has features suggestive of autoimmune hepatitis: elevated IgG (25 g/L), gradual onset, and

digital clubbing suggesting chronicity. Diagnostic workup includes autoantibody panel (ANA, anti-SMA,
anti-LKM-1) and liver biopsy for confirmation. Wilson disease would show neurological symptoms and

low ceruloplasmin. NAFLD unlikely without obesity risk factors. Early diagnosis and treatment prevent

progression to cirrhosis.

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old child presents with acute hepatitis A infection. The child attends daycare and several other children have been affected. The parents are concerned about transmission to other family members and ask about the contagious period. What is the most appropriate guidance regarding isolation and transmission prevention?

options.label: A
options.text: Child should be excluded from daycare for 2 weeks before and 1 week after onset of jaundice

options.label: B
options.text: Child can attend daycare with standard precautions as hepatitis A is not contagious

options.label: C
options.text: Child should be isolated at home for the duration of illness

options.label: D
options.text: Child can attend daycare with contact precautions for 1 month

options.label: E
options.text: No restrictions needed as child is no longer contagious after symptoms resolve

questions.initialExplanation: Hepatitis A: infectivity is highest before jaundice appears. Per the given answer the child is excluded from daycare; the common guidance is until 1 week after jaundice onset.
questions.detailedExplanation:
jaundice

Hepatitis A is highly contagious during the pre-symptomatic period (2 weeks before symptoms)
and 1 week after jaundice onset. Exclusion from daycare during this 3-week period prevents
outbreak spread. Standard precautions are insufficient for outbreak control. Extended isolation
beyond recommended period is unnecessary. Public health responsibility requires strict
adherence to exclusion guidelines to prevent transmission.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child presents for routine care and vaccination review. The parents ask about hepatitis A vaccine schedule for international travel. The child has not previously received hepatitis A vaccine and is otherwise healthy. What is the most appropriate hepatitis A vaccination schedule for travel preparation?

options.label: A
options.text: No vaccine needed if traveling for less than 2 weeks

options.label: B
options.text: Two doses of hepatitis A vaccine 6 months apart for long-term protection

options.label: C
options.text: Hepatitis A vaccine and immunoglobulin combination for immediate protection

options.label: D
options.text: Single dose of hepatitis A vaccine with protection developing in 2-4 weeks

options.label: E
options.text: Hepatitis A vaccine given daily for 1 week before travel

questions.initialExplanation: Hepatitis A vaccine gives protection within 2-4 weeks of the first dose, enough for near-term travel.
questions.detailedExplanation:
For travel to endemic areas, a single dose of hepatitis A vaccine provides adequate protection within
2-4 weeks. This is suitable for most travel plans and is cost-effective. Second dose (6-12 months
later) provides long-term immunity but is not required for immediate travel. Combination therapy not
routinely recommended for healthy children. Risk exists regardless of trip duration. No daily dosing
regimen exists.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old child with known autoimmune hepatitis type 2 presents with acute deterioration. Laboratory findings show: ALT 850 U/L, AST 920 U/L, total bilirubin 12.5 mg/ dL, INR 3.2, and positive anti-LKM-1 antibodies. The child appears confused with asterixis. What is the most appropriate immediate therapeutic approach?

options.label: B
options.text: Combination therapy with prednisolone and azathioprine

options.label: C
options.text: High-dose prednisolone (2 mg/kg/day) with close monitoring

options.label: D
options.text: Liver transplantation evaluation for acute liver failure

options.label: E
options.text: Supportive care with lactulose and antibiotics

questions.initialExplanation: Autoimmune hepatitis type 2 (anti-LKM1) with deterioration: high-dose prednisolone with close follow-up (per the given answer).
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has acute AIH type 2 deterioration with encephalopathy (asterixis, confusion) and
coagulopathy (INR 3.2). Type 2 AIH often presents more acutely than type 1. Highdose prednisolone
(2 mg/kg/day) is first-line with rapid onset of action. Azathioprine is contraindicated in jaundiced
patients due to hepatotoxicity risk. Most patients respond rapidly to steroids. Transplantation
evaluation premature - steroid-responsive disease in >90% of cases.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old child has history of recurrent cough and wheeze, he was diagnosed as bronchial asthma, He had history of daily cough at day and nearly more than two times attack at night per week. Select medication that is least recommended as long term control treatment:
questions.initialExplanation: Ipratropium bromide is an adjunct reliever in acute attacks, not a long-term controller; ICS, LABA, modifiers and cromolyn are controllers.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Inhaled ipratropium bromide is the least recommended for long-term asthma control because it is a short-acting anticholinergic bronchodilator primarily used for acute exacerbations or as add-on therapy during severe attacks, not for maintenance therapy. Inhaled glucocorticoids are first-line controller therapy for persistent asthma. Leukotriene modifiers and cromolyn/nedocromil are acceptable alternative or add-on controllers. Long- acting beta-agonists are used as add-on therapy with inhaled corticosteroids for moderate-severe persistent asthma. Ipratropium provides no anti-inflammatory effect and does not address the underlying airway inflammation driving persistent symptoms. Using it as monotherapy for long-term control would leave the child inadequately treated and at risk for exacerbations.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy had history of recurrent chest infections over last 3 years, last week he was presented with purulent cough of copious sputum mainly at morning, on examination he had finger clubbing and auscultation of the chest there was bilateral diffuse coarse crackle. The less likely cause for his condition is: Jp 130 Sl p50
questions.initialExplanation: Chronic productive cough with bronchiectasis signs (clubbing, coarse bilateral crackles) points to CF, foreign body or immunodeficiency; asthma alone does not cause clubbing, so it is the least likely.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Bronchial asthma is the least likely cause because it does not produce finger clubbing, copious purulent sputum, or bilateral coarse crackles. Asthma is characterized by reversible airflow obstruction with wheezing, dry or minimally productive cough, and normal findings between exacerbations; the presence of clubbing should always prompt reconsideration of an asthma diagnosis. In contrast, this child's presentation—recurrent infections, morning-predominant purulent sputum, clubbing, and coarse crackles—is classic for bronchiectasis or chronic suppurative lung disease. Cystic fibrosis, immunodeficiency, post-infectious damage from pertussis, or retained foreign body can all cause impaired mucus clearance, chronic bacterial colonization, and progressive airway destruction leading to these findings.

Which of the following drugs is least effective for treatment of his current respiratory distress?

options.label: B
options.text: Inhaled short-acting B-agonist every 20 min for one hour

questions.stem: A 7-year-old with moderate persistent asthma presents with an acute exacerbation. He is tachypneic (RR 40/min) and has received initial treatment with inhaled short-acting beta-agonists (SABA). What is the next best step in management?

options.label: C
options.text: Begin daily leukotriene receptor antagonist therapy

options.label: D
options.text: Discharge with follow-up in one week

questions.initialExplanation: After the initial SABA in a moderate-to-severe exacerbation, the next step is an oral systemic corticosteroid to reduce inflammation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
In a child with moderate persistent asthma experiencing an acute exacerbation with persistent tachypnea after initial SABA, systemic corticosteroids are the next critical step to reduce airway inflammation, prevent progression, and decrease relapse risk. Oral prednisolone or prednisone provides rapid anti-inflammatory effects within hours and is standard for moderate-severe exacerbations. Long-acting beta-agonists (B) and leukotriene antagonists (C) are maintenance controllers, not acute relievers, and have no role in emergency management. Discharging the child

(D) while tachypneic is unsafe and risks clinical deterioration. Intramuscular epinephrine (E) is reserved for anaphylaxis or life-threatening bronchospasm unresponsive to inhaled therapy, not routine exacerbations.

questions.stem: An 8-year-old boy with poorly controlled asthma presents with sudden left-sided chest pain and shortness of breath after a severe coughing episode. He is tachypneic, has an SpO2 of 88% on room air, and breath sounds are significantly decreased on the left without wheezing. What is the most urgent diagnostic investigation?
questions.initialExplanation: Sudden chest pain and dyspnea after severe coughing with unilateral decreased breath sounds and no wheeze suggest pneumothorax; the most urgent test is a chest X-ray.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This presentation—sudden unilateral chest pain, hypoxia, and markedly decreased breath sounds on one side after severe coughing in an asthmatic child—is highly concerning for pneumothorax, a potentially life- threatening complication. Chest X-ray is the most urgent and appropriate initial diagnostic investigation because it rapidly confirms the presence and size of pneumothorax, guides immediate intervention (e.g., needle decompression or chest tube placement), and helps exclude other causes like pneumonia or atelectasis. Peak expiratory flow (A) is unreliable in acute distress and does not diagnose pneumothorax. CT scan (B) is more sensitive but slower, less accessible, and unnecessary as a first test. Arterial blood gas (C) assesses gas exchange but does not identify the structural cause. Electrocardiogram (E) is not indicated without cardiac symptoms. Prompt chest X-ray ensures timely, life-saving management while avoiding delays from less relevant testing.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl presents to your office for evaluation of chronic cough and wheeze. By history, you determine that triggers for her symptoms include: upper respiratory infections, weather change, exercise, and laughter. She was seen in the ED once and received an oral steroid burst and was sent home with bronchodilator therapy. She reports that anytime she is active, she will use bronchodilators often to relieve her symptoms. Her mother reports that the girl has nighttime cough at least once a week. You diagnose her with asthma, and classify the severity as follows:
questions.initialExplanation: Nocturnal symptoms more than once a week, frequent reliever use with exercise and one ED visit: classified as moderate persistent asthma per the source.
questions.detailedExplanation:
According to the Expert Panel Report 3, this child would have moderate persistent asthma based on having nighttime symptoms at least once per week and likely daily symptoms given activity-related symptoms described ( Figure 512-3). Given her age, she would need to have nighttime symptoms every night to be classified as severe persistent asthma, or only 3—4 times per month to classify as mild persistent asthma. Spirometry would also be useful in classifying her asthma severity. She clearly has too many symptoms for her asthma to be considered mild intermittent. Keep in mind that an individual should be assigned to the most severe category in which any feature occurs.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old child with asthma undergoes pulmonary function testing. The results show FEV1 of 70% predicted, FVC of 85% predicted, and FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.70. After administration of albuterol, FEV1 improves to 85% predicted with an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.85. What do these findings specifically indicate about this child's asthma severity?

options.label: A
options.text: Mild persistent asthma requiring daily controller therapy

options.label: B
options.text: Moderate persistent asthma based on spirometric evidence of significant reversibility

options.label: C
options.text: Severe persistent asthma requiring high-dose inhaled corticosteroids

options.label: D
options.text: Well-controlled asthma with normal lung function between exacerbations

options.label: E
options.text: Intermittent asthma with normal baseline function

questions.initialExplanation: A marked FEV1 improvement after albuterol (reversibility) with FEV1 70% fits reversible obstruction; per the source it is moderate persistent asthma.
questions.detailedExplanation:
These spirometric findings clearly demonstrate "moderate persistent asthma" based on the FEV1 values and the degree of reversibility. The baseline FEV1 of 70% predicted places this child in the moderate range (60-80% predicted), while the significant reversibility to 85% predicted after bronchodilator (an increase of 15% absolute, well above the 12% reversibility threshold) confirms both

the diagnosis of asthma and the moderate severity classification. The FEV1/FVC ratio changes from

0.70 to 0.85 also demonstrate substantial improvement, confirming reversible obstruction characteristic

of asthma. According to the classification system provided, moderate persistent asthma is defined by FEV1 between 60-80% predicted and FEV1/FVC of 75-80%.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old girl is admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit in status asthmaticus. She is intubated, mechanically ventilated, and treated aggressively. However, her clinical condition deteriorates despite the best efforts of the intensive care team. Ultimately, her parents elect to withdraw medical care. Of the following, the risk factor most closely associated with fatal asthma is:
questions.initialExplanation: The risk factor most associated with fatal asthma per the source is female gender (other known factors: poor perception of symptoms and prior severe episodes).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Demographic factors linked to fatal asthma include: female, nonwhite and current smokers. Additional factors include those with poor adherence to the treatment plan, psychosocial factors such as stress,

and socioeconomic factors. Additionally, people who report a sense of danger from there asthma are more at increased risk of asthma exacerbation or death.

Female adults have a higher death rate from asthma compared to male adults. Conversely, in children, boys are more likely to die from asthma.

questions.stem: An 8-year-old girl presents with wel-controled, moderate persistent asthma. Her therapies consist of occasional use of short-acting B agonists, daily inhaled steroids, and a leukotriene inhibitor. She presents with white patches on her buccal mucosa. You recommend which of the following?

options.label: D
options.text: Discontinuation of all her asthma medications

options.label: E
options.text: Rinse her mouth after use of her inhaled medications

questions.initialExplanation: White patches on the oral mucosa in a child on inhaled steroid = oral candidiasis; rinse the mouth after each dose, do not stop asthma medication.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The patient in the question has wel-controled, moderate persistent asthma for which the National Heart, Lung and Blood Institute of the US National Institutes of Health recommends daily inhaled corticosteroids as a contro ler medication. Failure to rinse her mouth after administration of this medication can result in localized candida infection (thrush). Discontinuation of her asthma medications is contraindicated. While it is possible she has an immune dysfunction, simply rinsing her mouth is more likely to be both diagnostic and therapeutic.

questions.stem: One of your asthmatic patients arrives for a check-up. The mother reports that the 5-year-old child seems to need albuterol daily, especially when exercising, and she has coughing fits that awaken her from sleep about twice a week. Her grandmother had recommended a Chihuahua as a “cure” for her asthma, but her mother has seen no difference since the arrival of the pet. Appropriate treatment measures would include which of the following?

options.label: B
options.text: Daily leukotriene modifier with short-acting β-agonist

options.label: D
options.text: Medium-dose, inhaled corticosteroids with short-acting β-agonists

options.label: E
options.text: High-dose, inhaled corticosteroids with theophylline and short-acting β-agonists

questions.initialExplanation: Persistent mild-moderate asthma (daily use, night wakening twice weekly): add a medium-dose inhaled corticosteroid with SABA as needed.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Asthma may be classified by severity based on the frequency of symptoms, and is stratified by age. Children 5 to 11 years old with mild intermittent asthma have symptoms less than two times a week and have less than two nighttime episodes a month. These patients do not require daily medication and only short-acting -agonists are needed. The second classification is mild persistent asthma; these children have symptoms more than two times a week, and have 3 to 4 nights a month with symptoms. These patients may be managed with a number of anti-inflammatory choices, including low-dose, inhaled corticosteroids, cromolyn, or a leukotriene inhibitor, and use short-acting B-agonists for rescue. Our patient has moderate persistent asthma; she has daily symptoms and difficulty at night more than once a week. Her treatment should consist of medium-dose corticosteroids, or a combination of low-dose corticosteroids and a long-acting B-agonist; alternatives include a leukotriene modifier or sustained release theophyline. Patients with severe persistent asthma have continual symptoms and frequent nighttime symptoms. This group requires daily high-dose inhaled steroids as we | as long-acting B-agonists; they may require oral steroids as we |. Note that the latest guidelines make a distinction between 0- 4 years and 5-11 years; the younger children require less frequent symptoms to be classified in a particular zone.

questions.stem: The child with asthma should be free of wheezing for at least several days before surgery, even If this necessitates an increase in B-agonist dosage and the addition of steroids.of the following, the most appropriate preoperative steroids regime in children With asthma (who are receiving asthma therapy or who have received steroid within the last year) is :

options.label: A
options.text: prednisone 1 mg/kg given 24 and 12 hr before surgery

options.label: B
options.text: prednisone 2 mg/kg given 24 and 12 hr before surgery

options.label: C
options.text: Dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg given 24 and 12 hr before surgery

options.label: D
options.text: Hydrocortisone 1V, 5 mg/kg given 24 and 12 hr before surgery

options.label: E
options.text: Hydrocortisone IV, 10 mg/kg given 24 and 12 hr before surgery

questions.initialExplanation: For an asthmatic child before surgery: prednisone 1 mg/kg 24 and 12 hours before the operation per the source.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This regimen provides appropriate preoperative asthma optimization by reducing airway inflammation without excessive systemic exposure. Prednisone 1 mg/kg is the standard dose for improving asthma control before surgery; higher doses (option B) are reserved for acute exacerbations and increase side-effect risk. Dexamethasone at 0.6 mg/kg (option C) is supratherapeutic for this indication and carries prolonged adrenal suppression risk. Hydrocortisone options (D and E) represent stress-dose coverage for adrenal insufficiency, not asthma optimization, and the doses listed exceed typical physiologic replacement needs. The key distinction is that preoperative asthma management targets airway inflammation with oral prednisone, whereas adrenal stress coverage uses lower-dose IV hydrocortisone only in patients with documented HPA axis suppression. Always ensure the child is wheeze-free for several days preoperatively, adjusting controller therapy as needed.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old male with a known history of asthma presents to the emergency department with the most severe asthma attack of his life. When you listen, you hear very little air movement and your patient has a declining level of consciousness. After your initial measures, you see very little improvement and a decision is made to intubate the patient’s trachea. Which combination of drugs is most appropriate in this situation to prevent worsening bronchospasm?
questions.initialExplanation: To intubate a patient in severe asthma without worsening bronchospasm: ketamine (bronchodilator), lidocaine and rocuronium (muscle relaxant) per the source.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Patients with severe asthma exacerbations often need admission to the hospital for adminstration of medications and supportive care. In very rare circumstances a patient with very severe asthma and poor air exchange will become obtunded and will need endotracheal intubation. The medications used to facilitate intubation in this scenario have two

‘     additional goals over routine intubation: first, it should not worsen the bronchospasm; and second, it should allow the physician/patient to ventilate once the endotracheal tube is placed as soon as possible. Ketamine and lidocaine can be used to prevent or reduce bronchoconstriction. Ketamine has been shown to have direct bronchodilatory effects, and lidocaine blunts the airway responsiveness, such as the coughing reflex. Rocuronium is one of the nondepolarizing muscle relaxants that does not cause bronchospasm and is indicated in rapid sequence intubation. The other medication combinations listed are not ideal because they do not incorporate medications that help to reduce bronchospasm and to achieve rapid return to spontaneous ventilation (A, B, D). Intubating without medication (E) in this case would be inappropriate.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy presents to the primary care clinic with a complaint of cough. The patient has a history of wheezing with colds, but has recently had a persistent cough and has been taking an albuterol MDI with some relief. The patient’s mother says that he has symptoms at least 1 night out of the week and almost every day. What is the most appropriate medication regimen for this patient?

options.label: D
options.text: inhaled corticosteroid twice daily plus albuterol as needed

questions.initialExplanation: Nocturnal symptoms at least weekly and daytime symptoms: persistent asthma needing ICS twice daily with albuterol as needed.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The case describes a patient with mild persistent asthma. Asthma severity is classified by frequency of symptoms during the day and symptoms at night. The treatment of mild persistent asthma is the initiation of a controller medication plus the use of albuterol as needed—the most effective controller is a low dose inhaled corticosteroid twice daily (D). Albuterol alone will not control the persistent nature of this patient’s symptoms (A). Over the counter cough medication does not address the root of the problems and symptoms will persist (B). Albuterol twice daily may help with symptoms, but albuterol should be given on an as needed basis and a controller medication given twice daily (C). Systemic steroids daily are used for acute exacerbations of asthma for a short course and for severe persistent asthma as a long term therapy (E).

---

questions.stem: A10-year-old with a history of asthma presents to the emergency department in respiratory distress. You auscultate diffuse wheezing and the patient has increased work of breathing. You initiate albuterol via nebulizer, oral steroids, and establish IV access. The patient is showing signs of worsening work of breathing, which one of the following medications can act as an acute bronchodilator?
questions.initialExplanation: In an attack worsening despite albuterol and steroid: IV magnesium sulfate is an additional bronchodilator.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Magnesium sulfate is used as a smooth muscle relaxant and can be used to help control

bronchospasm in severe asthma and cause vasodilatation (A). Calcium chloride, sodium phosphate, potassium chloride, and sodium bicarbonate do not have any bronchodilating properties (B, C, D, E).

---

questions.stem: An 8-year-old girl with uncontrolled asthma is receiving inhaled corticosteroids and beta agonists (Advair, fluticasone/salmeterol) as well as a leukotriene antagonist (Singulair, montelukast). The decision is made to begin theophylline; however you are worried about the potential toxicities. What side effects should you monitor for that would indicate high levels of theophylline?
questions.initialExplanation: Early theophylline toxicity shows GI symptoms such as vomiting, then tachycardia, tremor and seizures as levels rise.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Theophylline is rarely used in pediatric asthma because of its potential toxicity. Theophylline, when used chronically, can reduce asthma symptoms and need for supplemental beta-agonist use. Because theophylline may have some glucocorticoid-sparing effects in individuals with oral glucocorticoid-dependent asthma, it is still sometimes used in this group of asthmatic children. Theophylline has a narrow therapeutic window; therefore, serum theophylline levels need to be routinely monitored, especially if the patient has a viral illness associated with a fever or is placed on a medication known to delay theophylline clearance, such as macrolide antibiotics, cimetidine, oral antifungals, oral contraceptives, and ciprofloxacin. Toxic effects include both mild symptoms (nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, headache, irritability) and severe and life-threatening reactions (intractable convulsions, tachyarrhythmia). Both therapeutic and toxic effects are dose dependent, and it is difficult to maintain thera peutic effects without some toxicity.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old male presents to the office with wheezing and increased work of breathing for the fifth time in the past year. On examination, his RR is 30 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation is 98% while breathing room air. He is talking in complete sentences and there is expiratory wheezing with a pro longed expiratory phase. What is the first treatment he should receive?
questions.initialExplanation: Mild asthma in a child speaking full sentences with saturation 98%: first treatment is a nebulized beta agonist.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The patient described is not in severe distress as indicated by the ability to talk in complete sentences and the lack of hypoxia. The recurrent episodes of wheezing suggest asthma as the most likely etiology. An initial trial of an inhaled beta agonist is the most appropriate choice. These agents’ primary mode of action is relaxation of airway smooth muscle. The other therapies listed are

sometimes used, but not as the initial management for acute exacerbations of mild-to-moderate asthma.

---

questions.stem: The patient improves after receiving the treatment selected. Further history reveals that the patient has been using inhaled albuterol three times per week to control wheezing. He awakens each night with coughing, but seems better in the morning. In addition to albuterol and a short course of oral steroids what is the best additional medicine he should receive at this time?

options.label: A
options.text: epinephrine auto injector (Epi-Pen) to be used as needed

options.label: B
options.text: salmeterol to be used in divided doses daily

options.label: C
options.text: fluticasone to be used in divided doses daily

options.label: D
options.text: theophylline to be used in divided doses daily

options.label: E
options.text: cetirizine to be used in divided doses daily

questions.initialExplanation: Albuterol use three times weekly with daily night cough means persistent asthma; the controller needed is fluticasone (ICS).
questions.detailedExplanation:
An expert panel report provides guidelines for management of asthma based on the severity of the disease. For infants and young children who have had four or more episodes of wheezing in the past year that lasted more than1 day and impaired sleep plus additional risk factors for developing persistent asthma, including parental history of asthma, physician diagnosis of atopic dermatitis, or evidence of sensitization to aeroallergens, two of the following including evidence of sensitization to foods, greater than or equal to 4% peripheral blood eosinophilia, or wheezing apart from colds, long-term control therapy is recommended. The patient described has persistent asthma. Recommended management includes the daily use of an anti-inflammatory agent. Therefore, inhaled fluticasone is the most appropriate choice given. Autoinjectable epinephrine should be used for anaphylaxis and is not indicated in the routine management of asthma. Salmeterol, a long- acting beta2 adrenergic agonist, is indicated for patients with more severe asthma. Because of its harrow therapeutic index and need for frequent monitoring, theophylline’s use has declined and currently is considered only a second line- agent for patients with asthma refractory to standard therapy.

---

questions.stem: A 14-year-old girl has been suffering from asthma for the last 3 years. She is using albuterol pump daily. She also used steroid occasionally. Pulmonary function test (PFT) was performed. Which of the following result is appropriate for this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Increased residual volume (RV), decreased vital capacity (VC), decreased forced expiratory volume (FEV)

options.label: B
options.text: Decreased RV, decreased VC, decreased FEV1

options.label: C
options.text: Decreased RV, increased VC, decreased FEV1

options.label: D
options.text: Increased RV, increased VC, increased FEV1

options.label: E
options.text: Decreased RV, decreased VC, increased FEV1

questions.initialExplanation: Asthma is airway obstruction: residual volume (RV) rises while vital capacity (VC) and FEV1 fall.
questions.detailedExplanation:
expiratory volume (FEV1)

Asthma is an obstructive lung disease where bronchoconstriction and airway inflammation impair exhalation. This causes air trapping, which directly increases residual volume (RV). As trapped air occupies more lung space, it reduces the amount of air that can be voluntarily moved in and out, leading to a decreased vital capacity (VC). Expiratory airflow limitation also reduces the volume of air forcefully exhaled in the first second, resulting in a decreased FEV1. The remaining options describe restrictive physiology (decreased RV) or contradictory lung volume relationships not seen in asthma. Daily albuterol use signals active obstruction, making this classic obstructive spirometry pattern the expected finding. Post-bronchodilator testing would typically show significant reversibility of the FEV1, confirming the diagnosis.

---

questions.stem: A 8-year-old child with asthma has daytime symptoms 3-4 times per week, nighttime awakening 2-3 times per month, and uses short-acting bronchodilator 4 times per week for symptom control. His parents report he occasionally misses school due to asthma symptoms. Spirometry shows FEV1 of 82% predicted. What is the most appropriate long-term controller therapy for this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Short-acting beta agonist as needed only

options.label: C
options.text: Medium-dose ICS plus long-acting beta agonist

questions.initialExplanation: Daytime symptoms more than twice weekly with frequent SABA use: mild persistent asthma, so the first controller is a low-dose ICS.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child clearly meets criteria for "persistent" asthma based on the "three strikes rule" - he has asthma symptoms more than 3 times per week, nocturnal awakening more than 3 times per month, and frequent bronchodilator use. The symptom frequency (3-4 times per week daytime symptoms) and nighttime symptoms place him in the "mild persistent" category, while his FEV1 of 82% predicted is still within the mild range (>80% predicted). According to the classification table, mild persistent asthma in school-age children is treated with "Add low dose inhaled corticosteroid (ICS)" as the preferred therapy. Lowdose ICS therapy is recommended as "preferred therapy for all levels of asthma severity except for the mild intermittent category" because it "reduces asthma symptoms, improves lung function, reduces airway hyperresponsiveness, reduces 'rescue' medication use, and, most importantly, reduces urgent care visits, hospitalizations, and prednisone use for asthma exacerbations by about 50%." The child's pattern of symptoms - frequent enough to impact school attendance but with relatively preserved lung function - represents the ideal situation for low-dose ICS therapy.

---

questions.stem: A 12-year-old with moderate persistent asthma is prescribed fluticasone via metered dose inhaler (MDI) using a spacer. After 2 months of therapy, his mother notices white patches on his tongue and reports he has been hoarse. The child denies any breathing difficulties but his voice sounds raspy. What is the most appropriate intervention to address these side effects?

options.label: B
options.text: Switch to oral corticosteroid therapy to avoid local effects

options.label: C
options.text: Use spacer device and rinse mouth with water after each use

options.label: D
options.text: Reduce fluticasone dose by 50% without spacer use

questions.initialExplanation: White patches on the tongue and hoarseness after ICS: local side effects; use a spacer and rinse the mouth after each dose.
questions.detailedExplanation:
These symptoms represent the most common local adverse effects of inhaled corticosteroid therapy: oral candidiasis (thrush) and dysphonia (hoarse voice). The white patches on the tongue are characteristic of oral candidiasis caused by "propellantinduced mucosal irritation and local immunosuppression," while the

‘    hoarseness results from "vocal cord myopathy." Both effects are dose-dependent and most common in individuals on high-dose ICS therapy. The most effective strategy to minimize these local effects is "using a spacer with MDI ICS" combined with "mouth rinsing using a 'swish and spit’ technique after ICS use" because spacers "reduce oropharyngeal deposition of the drug and propellant." The spacer device allows more medication to reach the airways where it's needed while reducing the amount that deposits in the mouth and throat. The mouth-rinsing technique helps remove any residual medication from the oral cavity that could promote fungal overgrowth or cause local irritation.

---

questions.stem: A 9-year-old child with asthma on low-dose fluticasone still experiences daily symptoms and nocturnal awakening 3-4 times per week. His parents report he frequently needs his rescue inhaler and seems limited during physical activities. Spirometry shows FEV1 of 72% predicted. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.text: Double the dose of inhaled corticosteroid

options.label: B
options.text: Add long-acting beta agonist to current ICS therapy

options.label: C
options.text: Add leukotriene modifier to current therapy

questions.initialExplanation: Despite low-dose ICS, symptoms remain daily and FEV1 is 72%: the next step is adding a LABA to the ICS.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child demonstrates "suboptimal control on low-dose ICS therapy alone" - he has daily symptoms, frequent nocturnal awakening, and significant activity limitation, indicating his current therapy is insufficient. According to the treatment guidelines, "their major role is as an 'add-on' agent in patients who are suboptimally controlled on ICS therapy alone. For those patients, several studies have found the addition of LABA to ICS to be superior to doubling the dose of ICS, especially on day and

nocturnal symptoms." The FEV1 of 72% predicted places him in the moderate persistent range, and the persistent symptoms despite ICS therapy warrant "combination therapy of a low-tomedium dose ICS with a long-acting -agonist (LABA; preferred)."

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old child with asthma presents to the emergency department with severe respiratory distress. His respiratory rate is 35/min, heart rate is 140/min, and oxygen saturation is 88% on room air. He is using accessory muscles, appears agitated, and has a silent chest on auscultation. Peak expiratory flow is 45% of personal best. What is the most appropriate initial therapeutic intervention?

options.label: B
options.text: High-flow oxygen and inhaled short-acting beta agonist

options.label: C
options.text: Non-invasive ventilation with continuous positive airway pressure

questions.initialExplanation: Life-threatening attack (saturation 88%, silent chest): priority is high-flow oxygen and inhaled SABA, then systemic steroids.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child demonstrates a "severe asthma exacerbation" with clear indicators of lifethreatening disease: respiratory rate >30/min, heart rate >125/min, oxygen saturation <92%, use of accessory neck muscles, agitation, silent chest, and PEFR <50% of personal best. According to the severity assessment table, these are features of "Life threatening" asthma. The most critical initial therapy is "supplemental oxygen" as the first priority because "when airways obstruction is not resolved with SABA use, ventilation-perfusion mismatching can cause significant hypoxemia, which can perpetuate bronchoconstriction and further worsen the condition." Inhaled short-acting beta agonist (SABA) is administered every 20 minutes for the first hour as the primary bronchodilator therapy. This represents the standard emergency department approach where "the primary goals of asthma management include correction of hypoxemia, rapid improvement of airflow obstruction, and prevention of progression or recurrence of symptoms."

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child presents with cough and wheeze for 2 days. His parents describe that he often coughs at night and during play activities. They mention he seems to tire more easily during physical activities compared to his peers. During examination, the child appears well between episodes, and chest auscultation reveals clear breath sounds except for brief wheezing heard during deep expiration. What is the most appropriate next step for establishing this diagnosis?

options.label: B
options.text: Trial of bronchodilator therapy with observation of symptom response

options.label: C
options.text: Comprehensive pulmonary function testing with methacholine challenge

options.label: D
options.text: Chest X-ray to rule out foreign body aspiration

options.label: E
options.text: Allergy testing to identify specific triggers

questions.initialExplanation: To diagnose asthma in a young child with cough and wheeze: trial of a bronchodilator and observe symptom improvement, since spirometry is not possible at this age.
questions.detailedExplanation:
In children under 5 years of age, asthma diagnosis remains controversial and is primarily based on clinical history and response to therapy. The presentation described - nocturnal cough, exercise-induced symptoms (tiring during play), and brief wheeze during deep expiration in a child with typical asthma symptoms - suggests the need for a therapeutic trial rather than objective testing. The "trial of bronchodilator therapy with observation of symptom response" approach is particularly important in preschoolers because formal pulmonary function tests require patient cooperation and are difficult to perform reliably in this age group. This child shows classic patterns that support asthma diagnosis: symptoms worse at night, exercise limitation, and age-appropriate symptom description.

The recommendation for a therapeutic trial stems from the fact that "in children <5 years, wheezing is episodic (e.g., only during viral illness) and does not persist into later childhood or adulthood" in many patients. The key is observing whether symptoms respond to bronchodilator therapy as this is "supportive of the diagnosis of asthma." Additionally, the absence of abnormal findings between episodes (clear breath sounds when not wheezing) is typical - "children with asthma commonly present without abnormal signs" during routine visits. The fact that wheezing is only heard during deep breaths in clinic further supports trying a bronchodilator challenge to see if it elicits the

---

questions.stem: A 12-year-old male presents to your office with a history of reactive disease since he was 6 years old. He wheezes throughout the day and requires a short and long-acting beta2-agonist daily. He complains of waking up almost every night with cough and wheezing. He is currently taking a highdose-inhaled steroid, a leukotriene inhibitor, and has just completed a 2-week oral steroid burst His last peak expiratory flow (PEF) was < 60% of predicted. How would you classify his asthma?
questions.initialExplanation: Daily and nocturnal symptoms with PEF below 60% despite intensive treatment: severe persistent asthma.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This patient has continual daytime and frequent nighttime symptoms (almost every night) despite good medical therapy. His PEF is < 60%, which classifies him as severe persistent (choice E). He may benefit from addition of low dose daily or every other day oral steroids to try and control his symptoms.

—> Intermittent (choice A) has daily symptoms < 2x/week and nighttime symptoms < 2x/month. Their PEF is > 80%.

—t Mild persistent (choice B) has daytime symptoms 4x/month. Their PEF is > 80%,

—* Moderate persistent (choice C) has daily daytime symptoms with nighttime symptoms occurring >1 time/week. Their PEF is > 60% and < 80%.

—? Severe intermittent (choice E) is not part of the known asthma classification.

---

questions.stem: A 14-year-old female with a history of asthma is having daytime symptoms about once a week and symptoms that awaken her at night about once a month. Her asthma does not interfere with normal activity, and her FEV1 is > 80% of predicted. Which one of the following is the most appropriate treatment plan for this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: A short-acting inhaled beta-agonist as needed

options.label: E
options.text: Low-dose inhaled corticosteroids plus a long-acting inhaled beta-agonist daily

questions.initialExplanation: Daytime symptoms once weekly and nocturnal once monthly with FEV1 >80%: intermittent asthma; SABA as needed is enough.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Based on this patient's reported frequency of asthma symptoms, she should be classified as having intermittent asthma. The preferred first step in managing intermittent asthma is an inhaled shortacting Beta-agonist as needed. Daily medication is reserved for patients with persistent asthma (symptoms > 2 days per week for mild, daily for moderate, and throughout, the day for severe) and is initiated in a

stepwise approach, starting with a daily low-dose inhaled corticosteroid or leukotriene receptor antagonist and then progressing to a medium-dose inhaled corticosteroid or low-dose inhaled corticosteroid plus a long-acting inhaled beta-agonist.

---

questions.stem: An 3-year-old female with a history of reactive airway disease presents to your office for evaluation. She states that she uses her inhaled beta2agonist 4-5 times a week. She takes no other medications. She was hospitalized once last winter for an asthma exacerbation, but has been well since. She has some limitations in her exercise tolerance secondary to shortness of breath. She denies any pets at home and there is no tobacco exposure. Which of the following medications should be added to her current regimen?
questions.initialExplanation: SABA use 4-5 times weekly with activity limitation: add a controller, first choice an inhaled steroid.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This patient has mild persistent asthma and is requiring use of her rescue beta2-agonist more than twice a week. An inhaled low dose steroid is the first line of therapy in controlling her symptoms.

A. There is nothing in the history provided that describes allergic symptoms that would be better controlled with an antihistamine.

B. Cromolyn sodium is sometimes used in addition to beta2-agonists, but inhaled steroids are first tine therapy.

C. Theophylline is no longer preferred therapy because of side effects and drug levels that need to be followed,

E. Daily prednisone is used only in severe persistent asthmatics that are on maximum therapy and still having symptoms.

---

questions.stem: A 12 year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his mother with complaints of cough and wheezing. He has had previous episodes in the past, and has not any specific treatment so far. On examination, he has a respiratory rate of 40 breaths per minute and a temperature of 37.5°C. On chest auscultation, widespread wheeze is noted bilaterally. The rest of the exam is inconclusive. Which one of the following is most likely to make a diagnosis now and in the emergency setting?
questions.initialExplanation: For quick diagnosis in the ED: improvement after salbutamol (bronchodilator response) favors asthma.
questions.detailedExplanation:
