The scenario is typical for an exacerbation of a previously-undiagnosed asthma. Asthma is the most common cause cough and wheezing in children.

By definition, asthma is reversible inflammatory response of the bronchial tree triggered by factors such as allergens, cold, exercise, stress, noxious inhalants, dust mite, etc. Reversibility and

symptom relief after administration of bronchodilators (e.g. inhaled salbutamol) is the key issue in diagnosis of asthma.

---

questions.stem: A 12-year-old white male asthmatic has an acute episode of wheezing. You diagnose an acute asthma attack and prescribe an inhaled beta-adrenergic agonist. After 2 hours of treatment, he continues to experience wheezing and shortness of breath. Which one of the following is the most appropriate addition to acute outpatient management?
questions.initialExplanation: No improvement after 2 hours of bronchodilator: add oral corticosteroids.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The treatment of choice for occasional acute symptoms of asthma is an inhaled beta-2-adrenergic agonist such as albuterol, terbutaline, or pirbuterol. If symptoms do not respond to beta-agonists, they should be treated with a short course of systemic corticosteroids.

-A Theophylline has limited usefulness for treatment of acute symptoms in patients with intermittent asthma; it is a less potent bronchodilator than subcutaneous or inhaled adrenergic drugs, and therapeutic serum concentrations can cause transient adverse effects such as nausea and central nervous system stimulation in patients who have not been taking the drug continuously,

—* Cromolyn can decrease airway hyperreactivity, but has no bronchodiiating activity and is useful only for prophylaxis.

— Inhaled corticosteroids should be used to suppress the symptoms of chronic persistent asthma, Oral beta-2-selective agonists are less effective and have a slower onset of action than the same drugs given by inhalation.

---

questions.stem: Lucy has presented to your office concerned about her 3-years-old daughter. Lucy has past medical history of asthma and eczema and heard that these conditions can run in families. She wants to know about the risk of her daughter developing asthma or eczema as well. In consulting her, which one of the following would be the most appropriate advice you can give to minimize the risk allergic reactions in the child?

options.label: E
options.text: Giving the child antihistamines in case allergy develops.

questions.initialExplanation: To prevent allergy in a child with a family history of asthma and eczema: reduce house dust mites.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Household dust mites are the most common allergens that can cause allergy and asthma in genetically susceptible individuals. About 90% of children with atopic symptoms and asthma demonstrate positive skin-prick responses to dust mite extract.

In general, reducing dust mites is the most appropriate advice here. Avoiding contact with sheepskin bedding and clothes is a part of measures taken to reduce dust mites. Anti-histamines and avoiding mono-sodium glutamate in food is not recommended for minimizing the risk of atopy in children.

---

questions.stem: A previously healthy 18-month boy is brought to the Emergency Department with wheezing and cough starting 24 hours ago. On examination, he has a respiratory rate of 35 breaths per minute. Bilateral wheeze is evident on chest auscultation, as well as mildly diminished breath sounds of the left hemithorax. There is family history of asthma, as well as allergy in history. Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step in management of this child?
questions.initialExplanation: An infant with wheeze and decreased air entry on the left: stabilize first, then investigate; admit with oxygen is the appropriate step.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Wheezing in children have a multitude of causes. The age of the child, physical findings, and the pattern and associations can help narrow down the differential diagnoses.

For instance, wheezing associated with feeding points towards reflux disease as the most likely cause, while wheeze and cough may suggest asthma. Positional wheeze, for example when the child is supine, is suggestive of laryngomalacia, whereas, wheeze in the presence of fever may be due to infections. Sudden onset unilateral wheezing is a strong clue to foreign body aspiration.

The age of onset is another important clue to the diagnosis. Early onset wheeze can reflect a congenital problem. Bronchiolitis is a very common cause of wheezing in children younger than 12 months, and asthma is the most common cause of episodic wheezing in children younger than 5 years. Depsite this, a definite diagnosis of asthma is avoided at this age group and other terms suchs wheeze syndrom, viral wheeze, etc. are used instead. In this child, wheezing and cough is of sudden onset, suggesting aspiration; however, bilaterality of the wheeze on exam makes this diagnosis very unlikely. The presence of cough and the strong family history of asthma and allergy put asthma at the top of the differential diagnoses list. This child though has also diminished breath sounds of the right lung that mayu suggest collection either in the lung or pleural space. This child needs to be admitted and through investigation carried out; however, making sure of adequate oxygenation regardless of the diagnosis comes first.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy is brought to your attention because of frequent episodes of wheezing and cough at night and during exercise. You prescribe salbutamol on as-needed basis and regular low-dose inhaled fluticasone. Which one of the following medications is most effective in preventing further episodes?
questions.initialExplanation: To prevent future attacks the best option is fluticasone (ICS), the most effective controller.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has persistent asthma evident by frequent episodes of night symptoms more than 2 nights. The scenario does not provide adequate information as to whether this is moderate or severe persistent asthma.

For persistent asthma, the treatment of choice is regular use of an inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) and a short acting beta agonist (SABA) on a as-needed basis. Treatment should be started at the lowest dose possible and titrated according to the response.

ICS (fluticasone, beclomethasone, budesonide, ciclesonide) are the most effective preventive therapy in children with asthma.

---

questions.stem: A 10-year-old male child is brought in by his mother with complaint of ongoing exercise-induced asthma, despite being on maximum dose of inhaled corticosteroids. Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: C
options.text: Cease inhaled corticosteroids and start intravenous steroids.

questions.initialExplanation: Exercise asthma uncontrolled despite the highest ICS dose: add a LABA.
questions.detailedExplanation:
When asthma symptoms, particularly exercise-induced bronchoconstriction, persist despite maximum-dose inhaled corticosteroids, the guideline-recommended next step is adding a long-acting beta-agonist (LABA). LABAs provide sustained bronchodilation and are highly effective at preventing exercise-triggered symptoms while synergizing with ICS to improve overall airway control. Leukotriene modifiers are alternative options but consistently demonstrate inferior efficacy compared to LABAs in this setting. Short-acting beta-agonists are strictly rescue medications and do not provide preventive coverage, while intravenous steroids are reserved for acute exacerbations, not chronic management. Specialist referral is premature before optimizing combination controller therapy. Adding a LABA directly addresses persistent exercise-induced airflow limitation and aligns with standard stepwise asthma guidelines.

---

questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy is brought to the hospital by his mother with acute shortness of breath and wheezing. He has background history of asthma and uses inhalers on an as-required basis. Which one of the following is the best bedside measure to assess the severity of asthma?
questions.initialExplanation: The best bedside clinical measure of asthma severity is peak expiratory flow rate.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The peak expiratory flow rate (PEF, also known as a peak flow) is the maximum rate that a person can exhale during a short maximal expiratory effort after a full inspiration.

In patients with asthma, the PEF correlates reasonably well with the the forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1). FEV1 (not an option) is the most useful tool for bedside assessment of asthmaesponse to treatment. In the abence of FEV1, PEF is the best option for this objective.

Peak flow meters have a limited role in establishing the diagnosis of asthma. However, they are very useful in measuring the severity of asthma exacerbation, or response to treatment. Peak flow

meter readings become higher while patients are recovering and lower when the airways are constricted.

---

questions.stem: A 13-year-old girl with a history of asthma presents for her annual well-child visit. She has mild, intermittent asthma. She has recently been seen by an allergist who has confirmed that she is sensitive to house dust mite allergen. House dust mite allergen seems to be a trigger for her asthma exacerbations. Which of the following allergen avoidance strategies would be inappropriate for this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Removal of wall-to-wall carpeting in the bedroom

options.label: B
options.text: Weekly washing all the sheets and bedding in hot water at a temperature greater than 130°F

options.label: C
options.text: Use of encasings for the child's bedroom mattresses

options.label: D
options.text: Use of encasings for the child’s bedroom pillows

options.label: E
options.text: Use of a warm mist humidifier at night in the child’s bedroom

questions.initialExplanation: A warm-mist humidifier increases humidity and dust mites, so it is unsuitable for dust-mite allergy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
House dust mites ( Dermatophagoides pteronyssinus and Dermatophagoidesfarinae) feed on human skin flakes which are shed onto and into mattresses, pillows, carpets, stuffed toys and upholstered

‘   furniture. House dust mites (HDM) also prefer a humid environment. As a result, the use of a warm mist humidifier at night could potentially improve the environment for HDM. The feces of HDM contain allergens (Der p 1 and Der f 1) that can trigger asthma symptoms for some sensitized children. Removal of wall-to-wall carpeting in the bedroom, weekly washing all the sheets and bedding in hot water at a temperature greater than 130°F, and the use of encasings for the child’s bedroom mattresses and pillows can all help eradicate HDM and exposure to HDM feces.

---

questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with a progressively worsening asthma attack. He has past medical history of previous asthma attacks and recurrent chest infections. Which one of the following, if present, would indicate life-threatening asthma?
questions.initialExplanation: Cyanosis is a sign of life-threatening asthma; wheeze, talking in sentences, PEF >75% and saturation 95% are milder signs.
questions.detailedExplanation:
If present, cyanosis indicates a life-threatening asthma episode. Other indicators of severity are FEV1<50%, peak expiratory flow <50%, the patient speaking in words, physical exhaustion, pulse rate>120bpm, oxygen saturation<92%, and significant accessory muscles use.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy is brought to your practice, by his mother, because of intermittent attacks of wheezing, which have beein occurring 4-6 times a year over the past 2 years. These attacks are usually precipitated by viral upper respiratory tract infections and last 2-3 days. The symptoms respond to treatment with inhaled salbutamol. There are no interval symptoms. His older brother had flexural eczema until the age of 18 months. Which one of the following is the most appropriate management of this child?
questions.initialExplanation: Few viral-triggered wheeze episodes that respond to salbutamol with no symptoms between episodes: no preventive therapy needed, salbutamol when symptomatic.
questions.detailedExplanation:
With infrequent episodes of wheezing and absence of interval symptoms, this child is most likely to have mild intermittent asthma. Mild asthma in children and adults is managed by short-acting 32 agonists such as salbutamol.

Inhaled fluticasone or other corticosteroids are not used for mild intermittent asthma, and is reserved for more severe forms of asthma. Montelukast is often considered and tried for a period of 2-4 weeks before the child is started on inhaled corticosteroids in an attempt to spare the child from corticosteroids and their potential adverse effects.

---


## Pneumonia

questions.stem: A 2-month-old neonate presents with symptoms suggestive of pneumonia. Which pathogen is least commonly associated with pneumonia at this age?
questions.initialExplanation: In a 2-month-old, GBS, Chlamydia, staphylococci and gram-negatives are common; H. influenzae is the least common at this age per the source.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Haemophilus influenzae is least commonly associated with pneumonia in a 2-month-old infant. Maternal transplacental antibodies provide protection against H. influenzae type b during the first 2-3 months of life, and the peak incidence of invasive Hib disease occurs between 6-12 months of age. In contrast, Group B Streptococcus and gram-negative organisms are leading causes of early- and late-onset neonatal pneumonia. Chlamydia trachomatis classically causes afebrile staccato cough pneumonia in infants aged 2-12 weeks

acquired during delivery. Staphylococcus aureus can cause severe, rapidly progressive necrotizing pneumonia in neonates.

---

questions.stem: An 11-month-old girl was complaining high-grade fever, reluctant to feed, cough for one day. She looks ill, temperature was 40° C, RR 60 cycle/min. there is scattered rhonchi and crackle over the right side of her chest on auscultation. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: High fever 40°C, tachypnea (60), ill appearance and unilateral findings = bacterial pneumonia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This 11-month-old girl presents with high-grade fever (40°C) , tachypnea (respiratory rate of 60 cycles/min) , cough , lethargy (looks ill) , and focal findings on auscultation (scattered rhonchi and crackles over the right side of her chest) . These clinical features strongly suggest bacterial pneumonia , which is a common and serious infection in young children.

Bacterial pneumonia is characterized by:

- High-grade fever.

- Tachypnea and respiratory distress.

- Focal findings on auscultation, such as crackles, rhonchi, or decreased breath sounds over the affected area.

- Lethargy or appearing "ill."

The combination of high fever , focal crackles and rhonchi , and appearing ill is highly suggestive of bacterial pneumonia. Common pathogens include Streptococcus pneumoniae , Haemophilus influenzae , and Staphylococcus aureus .

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy presents with 4 days of fever and dry cough, along with irritability, poor appetite, vomiting, and right lower abdominal pain. He is febrile (39.2°C), lethargic, and has mild respiratory distress. Chest exam reveals dullness to percussion, decreased air entry, and bronchial breath sounds over the right lower lung. Mild right-sided abdominal tenderness is noted. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Fever, dry cough and right lower abdominal pain with consolidation of the right lower lobe = right lower lobe pneumonia (can mimic appendicitis).
questions.detailedExplanation:
This clinical presentation is characteristic of right lower lobe (RLL) pneumonia with referred abdominal pain, a well-documented phenomenon in pediatric practice that frequently mimics acute surgical abdomens. The diagnosis is supported by the constellation of high-grade fever, respiratory distress, and focal signs of pulmonary consolidation (dullness to percussion, decreased air entry, and bronchial breath sounds) over the right lower lung field. The abdominal pain arises from irritation of the diaphragmatic pleura by the adjacent lower lobe inflammation; since the peripheral diaphragm receives sensory innervation from lower intercostal nerves (T6-T12), pain is referred to the right upper or lower quadrant, closely simulating appendicitis.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl is hospitalized with lobar pneumonia and has been on appropriate IV antibiotics for 7 days. She remains febrile and unwell. Her SpO2 is 90% on room air and repeat chest X-ray shows a well-defined pleural fluid collection adjacent to the area of consolidation. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.text: Increase the antibiotic dose and continue observation

options.label: C
options.text: Arrange for chest tube drainage of the pleural collection

options.label: E
options.text: Repeat blood cultures and delay intervention for 48 hours

questions.initialExplanation: Lobar pneumonia not responding to 7 days of antibiotics, with a clear parapneumonic effusion/empyema and hypoxemia: drain with a chest tube.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has developed a complicated parapneumonic effusion or empyema, evidenced by persistent fever,

clinical deterioration, hypoxia (SpO2 90%), and radiographic confirmation of a localized pleural fluid collection despite 7 days of appropriate intravenous antibiotics. In pediatric pneumonia, failure to improve clinically with ongoing respiratory compromise and imaging evidence of a significant pleural collection mandates source control via drainage. Chest tube thoracostomy allows evacuation of infected fluid, restores lung expansion, improves oxygenation, and prevents progression to organized empyema or fibrothorax. Merely escalating antibiotics (A) or delaying intervention (E) risks worsening sepsis, respiratory failure, or chronic pleural disease. Antifungal therapy (B) lacks indication without specific risk factors or microbiologic evidence. Corticosteroids

(D) have no proven benefit in empyema management and may impair host defense.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy presents with a history of recurrent respiratory infections, including four episodes of pneumonia over the past year, along with frequent otitis media and chronic eczema. He is growing well, has normal bowel habits, and has no significant perinatal history. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial diagnostic test in the evaluation of this child?
questions.initialExplanation: Recurrent pneumonias and otitis with eczema in a child growing well: suspect immunodeficiency; the first test is serum immunoglobulins.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child's presentation—recurrent sinopulmonary bacterial infections (pneumonia, otitis media) combined with chronic eczema—strongly suggests an underlying primary humoral immunodeficiency, such as hyper-IgE syndrome, common variable immunodeficiency, or specific antibody deficiency. Serum immunoglobulin quantification (IgG, IgA, IgM, IgE) is the most appropriate initial diagnostic test because it is non-invasive, cost- effective, and directly evaluates the most common category of primary immunodeficiencies. Abnormal results guide further targeted testing (e.g., vaccine antibody titers, lymphocyte subsets) while normal levels prompt evaluation for alternative etiologies. The sweat chloride test is less likely indicated given normal growth and bowel habits, arguing against cystic fibrosis. Chest CT, tuberculin testing, or zinc levels lack diagnostic priority without specific supporting features.

---

questions.stem: An 8-hour-old term infant develops increased respiratory distress, hypothermia, and hypotension. A complete blood count (CBC) demonstrates a white blood cel (WBC) count of 2500/uL with 80% bands. The chest radiograph is shown below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: An 8-hour-old with distress, temperature instability, hypotension and leukopenia with many bands (80%) = group B streptococcal pneumonia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The radiograph shows diffuse that infiltrates bilateraly; this can be seen with neonatal pneumonia or primary surfactant deficiency. The rapid onset of the symptoms, the low WBC count with left shift, and the depicted chest x-ray findings, however, are typical of a patient with group B streptococcus (GBS) pneumonia. Appropriate management would include rapid recognition of symptoms, cardiorespiratory support, and prompt institution of antibiotics. Despite these measures, mortality from this infection is not uncommon. The other infectious causes listed do not present so early, and the noninfectious causes listed do not cause elevations in the band count. GBS disease in the infant is decreasing in incidence with better prevention strategies in the perinatal period; early screening in pregnancy and treatment with antibiotics just prior to delivery to eliminate GBS colonization markedly decreases the risk to the infant.

Congenital syphilis can cause pneumonia, but it is diagnosed at birth along with other features including hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, rashes, hemolytic anemia, and others. Diaphragmatic hernia presents with early respiratory distress, but the diagnosis is confirmed clinicaly with bowel sounds heard in the chest and a radiograph that has loops of bowel located above the normal placement of the diaphragm. Transient tachypnea of the newborn (TTN) causes an increase in respiratory rate and occasionaly a low oxygen requirement; the history is often positive for a cesarean delivery, and the radiograph shows retained fluid in the fissures. TTN does not cause temperature instability nor an abnormal CBC. Chlamydial pneumonia is not a condition that occurs in an 8-hour-old infant; it is generaly a mild pneumonia that can develop in an exposed infant at several weeks of life.

---

questions.stem: A 13-year-old boy develops fever, malaise, sore throat, and a dry, hacking cough over several days.He does not appear to be particularly sick, but his chest examination is significant for diffuse rales and rhonchi. The chest radiograph is shown below. Which of the following is the most likely pathogen?
questions.initialExplanation: A teenager with fever, sore throat, dry cough and non-toxic look with diffuse crackles = Mycoplasma pneumoniae ("walking pneumonia").
questions.detailedExplanation:
The radiograph shown has reticulonodular opacities in the right upper lobe and prominence of the right hilum (lymphadenopathy) consistent with M.pneumoniae. Infections with M pneumoniae are common in older children and young adults, less so in infants and toddlers. Although the infection typicaly produces an interstitial infiltrate, its effects are characteristicaly nonspecific, and it can produce lobar pneumonia as we |. It can produce upper respiratory infection, pharyngitis, otitis media and externa, bronchiolitis, hemolytic anemia, and Guilain-Barré syndrome. Treatment of choice is a macrolide antibiotic. S aureus traditionaly is seen in infants less than 6 months of age; H influenzae is rarely seen because of the widespread use of H influenzae B vaccine. At this age, a child with M tuberculosis presents most typicaly

with hilar adenopathy and localized lobar pneumonia in the upper lobe, and S pneumoniae causes the sudden onset of high fever and a lobar pneumonia, often with pleural effusion. A TB skin test for this patient would be reasonable.

---

questions.stem: You are treating a 17-year-old girl who presents with cough for 4 weeks. She has pulmonary findings on examination and on her chest radiograph. In developing a treatment plan, you want to make sure you cover for atypical pneumonias, such as Chlamydophila pneumoniae . What is the drug of choice for the treatment of C. pneumoniae ?
questions.initialExplanation: The drug of choice for Chlamydophila pneumoniae (atypical) is azithromycin (macrolide).
questions.detailedExplanation:
C. pneumoniae (formerly Chlamydia pneumoniae ) is a cause of community-acquired pneumonia in children and adults. Presentation is similar to Mycoplasma pneumoniae . First-line treatment options include macrolides (erythromycin, azithromycin, and clarithromycin) and tetracycline (for children 8 years and older). Macrolides are also effective for the treatment of M. pneumoniae .

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old child presents to the emergency department with fever, cough, and respiratory distress. The parents report the child has been lethargic and feeding poorly for the past day. Examination reveals tachypnea (respiratory rate 45/min), intercostal retractions, nasal flaring, and diffuse bilateral crackles on chest auscultation. Chest X-ray shows bilateral interstitial infiltrates and hyperinflation. What is the most likely causative pathogen and the most appropriate initial management approach?

options.label: B
options.text: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) - Supportive care without antibiotics

options.label: C
options.text: Haemophilus influenzae type b - Oral amoxicillin

questions.initialExplanation: A 2-year-old with fever, cough, tachypnea, bilateral interstitial infiltrates and hyperinflation: usually RSV (viral); supportive care without antibiotics.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child presents with classic viral pneumonia, specifically consistent with respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection, given the age (2 years old falls within the 4 months-4 years age group where RSV is the most common cause) and the clinical presentation. The key distinguishing features that point to viral etiology include: the acute onset with preceding upper airway symptoms (often not explicitly mentioned but typical), bilateral diffuse crackles on auscultation (rather than localized findings), bilateral interstitial infiltrates on chest X-ray (versus lobar consolidation), and hyperinflation. According to the content, "most children younger than 3 to 5 years of age who are admitted to the hospital with pneumonia have viral pneumonia (e.g., respiratory syncytial virus)." The age group of 4 months-4 years specifically lists RSV, other respiratory viruses, S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, and group A streptococcus as frequent pathogens, with viral agents being particularly important in this age range. The clinical presentation with tachypnea, retractions, and crackles supports pneumonia diagnosis, but the bilateral interstitial pattern and absence of lobar consolidation strongly suggest viral rather than bacterial etiology.

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old child develops abrupt onset of high fever, productive cough, and pleuritic chest pain. Examination reveals a toxic-appearing child with localized dullness and decreased breath sounds over the right lower lobe. Chest X-ray shows right lower lobe consolidation with a small pleural effusion. Laboratory results show white blood cell count of 18,000/uL with 85% neutrophils, and CRP of 120 mg/L. What is the most likely causative organism and the most appropriate empiric antibiotic therapy?
questions.initialExplanation: Abrupt high fever, productive cough and pleuritic pain with lobar consolidation, neutrophilia and high CRP = Streptococcus pneumoniae; first-line amoxicillin.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This presentation is classic for typical bacterial pneumonia caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae. The child exhibits key clinical clues that differentiate bacterial from viral pneumonia: "abrupt onset"

‘    (versus gradual for viral), "high fever" (versus lower grade for viral), "pleuritic chest pain" (usually yes for bacterial, no for viral), and "lobar or segmental consolidation" with "large pleural effusion" on chest X-ray. The laboratory findings further support bacterial etiology with "leukocytosis" and " elevated CRP." The age group (7 years old) falls within the 25 years category where S. pneumoniae is listed as one of the most common bacterial causes of pneumonia in children of all ages.

Streptococcus pneumoniae is specifically noted as "the most common type of bacterial cause of pneumonia in children of all ages."

---

questions.stem: A 10-year-old child presents with a 5-day history of malaise, myalgia, headache, and dry cough. The parents report that fever and other constitutional symptoms improved after 2-3 days, but the cough has progressively worsened despite this improvement. Examination reveals bilateral interstitial infiltrates on chest X-ray and scattered crackles. The child has photophobia and mild conjunctivitis. What is the most likely diagnosis and the most appropriate antibiotic therapy?
questions.initialExplanation: Increasing dry cough after fever improves, bilateral interstitial infiltrates and extrapulmonary signs (conjunctivitis) = Mycoplasma pneumoniae; treat with azithromycin.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This presentation is classic for Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection, which is classified as "atypical bacterial pneumonia." The key distinguishing features that point to Mycoplasma include: the age (10 years old falls within the =5 years category where M. pneumoniae is most common), the characteristic symptom pattern of "abrupt onset of constitutional findings (malaise and myalgia, headache, conjunctivitis, photophobia, sore throat)" followed by "gradually worsening non-productive cough despite improvement of other symptoms," and the chest X-ray findings of "interstitial infiltrates." This pattern is highly specific for Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection. The child also has photophobia and conjunctivitis, which are part of the constitutional symptoms often seen with Mycoplasma. According to the content, "Atypical bacterial pneumonia (M. pneumoniae and Chlamydia pneumoniae) is most common in children older than 5 years" and "Mycoplasma pneumoniae and C. pneumoniae in older children and adolescents."

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy is brought to emergency with a five day history of fever, cough, and poor appetite, but no vomiting. On exam, he appears unwell, is febrile, and has crusty nasal discharge and a wet sounding cough. Chest x-ray reveals a pulmonary infiltrate in the right middle lobe. He is admitted to hospital for pneumonia. What is the best management for this child?

options.label: B
options.text: Observe for 24 hourswith IV fluids and acetaminophen

questions.initialExplanation: A 4-year-old with fever, wet cough and middle lobe consolidation admitted: manage with IV ampicillin and oral paracetamol.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) develops in patients with limited or no contact with medical institutions or settings. The most commonly identified pathogens are Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and atypical organisms (ie, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, TB). Symptoms and signs are fever, cough, dyspnea, tachypnea, and tachycardia. Diagnosis is based on clinical presentation and chest x-ray. Treatment is with empirically chosen antibiotics and antipyretics as needed. The current recommendations for children aged 3 months to 5 years is ampiciliin or cefuroxime; amoxicillin PO for mild cases, This patient was admitted therefore ampiciliin should be a reasonable treatment.

---

questions.stem: A 6-week-old infant presents with non-febrile pneumonia characterized by dry cough, tachypnea (respiratory rate 55/min), and bilateral diffuse crackles. The infant appears afebrile but shows signs of respiratory distress. The mother reports a 2-week history of gradual onset of respiratory symptoms without fever. Chest X-ray shows bilateral interstitial infiltrates. What is the most likely causative organism and the most appropriate treatment approach?
questions.initialExplanation: A 6-week-old with afebrile pneumonia, staccato dry cough and gradual onset = Chlamydia trachomatis; treat with erythromycin.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This presentation is classic for Chlamydia trachomatis pneumonia in young infants. The key distinguishing features include: the age of 6 weeks (falls within the 3 weeks-3 months age group where C. trachomatis is specifically mentioned as a cause when the patient is afebrile), the non-febrile presentation (afebrile pneumonia is specifically noted as a clue for C. trachomatis), the gradual onset over 2 weeks, the dry cough with bilateral diffuse involvement, and the interstitial pattern on chest X- ray. The age group of 3 weeks-3 months specifically lists "RSV, other respiratory viruses, S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, if patient is afebrile, consider Chlamydia trachomatis" as frequent pathogens.

---

questions.stem: A 6-month-oid infant presents in the winter with fever, cough, wheezing, tachypnea, and decreased appetite. A chest radiograph shows hyperaeration and streaky perihilar infiltrates bilaterally. You diagnose bronchopneumonia. Which organism would most likely be causingthis child's infection?
questions.initialExplanation: A 6-month-old in winter with wheeze, hyperinflation and perihilar infiltrates = RSV is the most likely cause.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Respiratory syncytia! virus (RSV) and human metapneumovirus infections cause seasonal lower respiratory tract disease, particularly in infants and young children. The most recognizable clinical

‘    syndromes are bronchiolitis and pneumonia. These illnesses typically begin with upper respiratory symptoms and fever and then progress over several days to dyspnea, cough, and wheezing. Apnea may be the initial symptom of RSV in infants < 6 months, in healthy adults and older children, illness is usually mild and may be inapparent or manifested only as an afebrile common cold. Disease may be asymptomatic, mild, or severe, including bronchiolitis and pneumonia. Although diagnosis is usually clinical, laboratory diagnosis is readily available. Treatment is supportive.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child is brought to the emergency department with severe respiratory distress. Examination shows respiratory rate 50/min, heart rate 140/min, oxygen saturation 88% on room air, and bilateral retractions. The child appears toxic and lethargic. Chest X-ray reveals bilateral consolidation with large pleural effusions. What is the most appropriate initial management approach and hospitalization criteria?

options.label: A
options.text: Observe at home with oral antibiotics

options.label: B
options.text: Admit for supplemental oxygen, IV antibiotics, and supportive care

options.label: C
options.text: Treat as outpatient with intramuscular ceftriaxone

options.label: D
options.text: Discharge with follow-up in 48 hours if improved

options.label: E
options.text: Immediate transfer to intensive care unit only

questions.initialExplanation: Severe pneumonia (saturation 88%, toxic look) with a large pleural effusion: admit with oxygen, IV antibiotics and support.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child clearly meets multiple hospitalization criteria for childhood pneumonia. The severity of presentation with "severe respiratory distress" (respiratory rate >50/min, significant retractions, lethargy), oxygen saturation <90% on room air, toxic appearance, and bilateral consolidation with pleural effusions all indicate the need for inpatient management. According to the listed indications of hospitalization: "severe respiratory distress," "toxic appearance," "requirement for supplemental oxygen," "multiple lobe involvement on CXR," and "no response to home therapy" are all present in this case. The child requires "supplemental oxygen" due to hypoxemia (88% saturation), which is a clear indication for hospitalization. The bilateral involvement with pleural effusions suggests a complicated course that requires IV antibiotic therapy and close monitoring. The initial management should include "supplemental oxygen" to correct hypoxemia, IV antibiotic therapy (likely broad-spectrum to cover typical and atypical organisms), and supportive care including hydration and monitoring of respiratory status.

---

questions.stem: A 12-year-old child with cystic fibrosis develops fever, increased cough, and worsening respiratory status after 5 days of hospitalization for pneumonia. New bilateral infiltrates are noted on chest X-ray, and the child now requires increased oxygen support. What type of pneumonia is this most likely classified as and what empiric antibiotic therapy is appropriate?

options.label: D
options.text: Complicated community-acquired pneumonia - Ceftriaxone and vancomycin

questions.initialExplanation: Deterioration after 5 days in hospital in a child with cystic fibrosis: nosocomial pneumonia, so give piperacillin-tazobactam with vancomycin to cover Pseudomonas and MRSA.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This presentation represents nosocomial pneumonia in a patient with underlying chronic lung disease (cystic fibrosis). The key distinguishing factor is that the patient developed new symptoms and signs of pneumonia after 5 days of hospitalization, meeting the definition of nosocomial (hospital-acquired) pneumonia. The fact that this occurred in a patient with cystic fibrosis is particularly relevant because cystic fibrosis patients are at high risk for both community-acquired and nosocomial respiratory infections, and they often harbor multidrug-resistant organisms. The timing (5 days into hospitalization) and new onset of symptoms clearly categorizes this as nosocomial pneumonia. For nosocomial pneumonia, the empiric treatment "should afford coverage for the usual nosocomial pathogens: S. aureus, Enterobacteriaceae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and anaerobes."

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child with uncomplicated pneumonia is started on intravenous ceftriaxone. After 48 hours, the child is afebrile, tolerating oral intake, and showing clinical improvement. Respiratory rate and effort have normalized. What is the most appropriate next step in management regarding antibiotic therapy?

options.label: A
options.text: Continue intravenous ceftriaxone for the full course

options.label: B
options.text: Discontinue antibiotics as child is improving

options.label: C
options.text: Switch to oral amoxicillin for completion of 7-10 day total course

questions.initialExplanation: Uncomplicated pneumonia improved after 48 hours of IV antibiotics: switch to oral amoxicillin to complete 7-10 days.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Once a child with uncomplicated bacterial pneumonia is clinically improving, afebrile for 24—48 hours, tolerating oral intake, and has normalized respiratory status, step-down therapy from IV to oral antibiotics is the standard of care. Switching to oral amoxicillin allows completion of the total 7-10 day course while reducing hospital stay, IV-related complications, and healthcare costs. Amoxicillin provides reliable coverage against Streptococcus pneumoniae, the most likely pathogen, and has excellent oral bioavailability. Continuing 1V therapy unnecessarily prolongs hospitalization and increases risk of line complications. Discontinuing antibiotics prematurely risks relapse or incomplete eradication. Adding azithromycin or switching to erythromycin is unnecessary without evidence of atypical infection or treatment failure. Always confirm the child can reliably absorb oral medications and provide clear discharge instructions with follow-up to ensure full recovery.

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the Emergency Department by his parents, who are concerned about his fever and difficulty breathing. The fever has started this afternoon. On examination, he looks ill and pale and is grunting. He has a temperature of 39.6°C and his respiration is shallow with a rate of 38 breaths per minute. Chest auscultation is normal. Which one of following could be the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Sudden fever with shallow breathing and grunting in an ill-looking child with a clear chest on auscultation: lobar pneumonia, which may not be audible early.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The findings of a high fever associated with pallor and respiratory distress in an infant is strongly suggestive of lobar pneumonia. In this age group, chest auscultation may deceitfully be normal due to shallow rapid breathing and grunting. The chest X-ray, however, will show consolidation. The most common causative organism is this situation would be streptococcus pneumoniae.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child is brought to the emergency department by the parents with the history of restlessness, irritability, cough, shortness of breath and fever. On examination,the temperature is 39.5, respiratory rate is 30/minute, oxygen saturation is 93% on room air and there is decreased air entry on the right lower zone. X-ray chest shows right lower lobe consolidation. What is the next best step?
questions.initialExplanation: Lobar pneumonia with saturation 93% and fever needing IV therapy: ceftriaxone with azithromycin.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has developed community-acquired pneumonia. The symptoms are severe.

This child needs to be given oxygen to improve oxygen saturation and also need intravenous antibiotics.

The treatment of severe pneumonia in a child includes either of the following medications along with Azithromycin to cover for Chlamydia trachomatis: Ceftriaxone 50mg/kg IV daily Or Cefotaxime 50mg/kg daily.

In areas where community-associated methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus

(CA-MRSA) is sufficiently prevalent, empirical therapy should include vancomycin.

---

questions.stem: A 12-month-old child presents with a history of persistent fever, cough, increased work of breathing and lethargy. On examination, Sao2 is 90%, respiratory rate is 60 breaths per minute, chest wall indrawing and nasal flaring. On the chest examination, there are crackles and bronchial breathing on left lower zone with decreased air entry. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.initialExplanation: Severe pneumonia (saturation 90%, chest retractions, lethargy) in an infant: IV ceftriaxone with flucloxacillin to cover staphylococci.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has developed severe community acquired pneumonia and need intravenous antibiotics.Severe pneumonia should be considered if there are clinical features of pneumonia and 2 or more of the following:

— Severe respiratory distress

— Severe hypoxaemia or cyanosis

— Marked tachycardia

— Altered mental state.

This child has all the clinical features suggesting the diagnosis of severe communityacquired pneumonia. According to Royal Children Hospital Melbourne Guidelines, this child should be treated with intravenous ceftriaxone and intravenous flucloxacillin.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old female with a history of sickle cell anemia comes to the emergency room with fever and a cough. She looks otherwise well, but her chest x-ray shows a right lower lobe pneumonia. Which of the following would be the best antibiotic regimen for this patient?
questions.initialExplanation: A girl with sickle cell anemia, cough, fever and pneumonia: ceftriaxone plus azithromycin (covers pneumococcus and atypicals).
questions.detailedExplanation:
This patient meets the criteria for acute chest syndrome, de ned as fever and changes on chest x-ray. Acute chest syndrome is the leading cause of mortality for patients with sickle cell disease. There are many causes of acute chest syndrome, including infarction, atelectasis, pulmonary edema, bronchospasm, and infection. Although an infectious agent is often not identi ed, empiric antibiotic therapy with ceftriaxone and azithromycin is necessary to cover the usual respiratory pathogens, such as pneumococcus, as well as atypical bacteria such as Mycoplasma and Chlamydia pneumoniae . Supplemental oxygen and hydration are also mainstays of treatment.

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old child presents with fever, pleuritic chest pain, and decreased breath sounds over the left lower lobe. The chest X-ray shows left lower lobe consolidation with a small pleural effusion. Aspiration of the pleural fluid reveals pH 7.2, glucose 45 mg/dL, and lactate dehydrogenase 500 IU/L. What is the most appropriate management approach?

options.label: D
options.text: Tube thoracostomy with chest tube drainage

questions.initialExplanation: A complicated effusion (pH 7.2, low glucose, high LDH) = empyema/complicated parapneumonic effusion: needs drainage (tube thoracostomy).
questions.detailedExplanation:
The pleural fluid analysis reveals characteristics consistent with complicated parapneumonic effusion or empyema, as evidenced by pH <7.2, low glucose (<60 mg/dL), and elevated lactate dehydrogenase (>1000 IU/L). These parameters indicate that the pleural space has become infected and requires drainage to prevent progression to organized empyema and fibrothorax. The combination of low pH and glucose suggests active bacterial metabolism and consumption of glucose by inflammatory cells and bacteria, while elevated LDH indicates significant pleural inflammation and protein leakage. When pleural fluid pH is less than 7.2, simple thoracentesis is inadequate and chest tube drainage is necessary to prevent loculation and permanent pleural thickening. Tube thoracostomy allows for continuous drainage and can be followed by intrapleural fibrinolytic therapy if needed.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child develops pneumonia while receiving chemotherapy for acute lymphoblastic leukemia. The child is neutropenic (ANC <500 cells/uL) and presents with fever, cough, and new infiltrates on chest X-ray. Which antimicrobial approach is most appropriate for initial empirical therapy?

options.label: B
options.text: Combination therapy with cefepime and gentamicin

options.label: C
options.text: Triple therapy with vancomycin, meropenem, and fluconazole

options.label: E
options.text: Combination therapy with vancomycin and meropenem

questions.initialExplanation: Pneumonia with neutropenia in a child with leukemia: broad empiric therapy (vancomycin and meropenem) per the source.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Neutropenic fever in a child with leukemia and new pulmonary infiltrates represents a medical emergency requiring immediate empirical broad-spectrum antimicrobial therapy. The combination of vancomycin and meropenem provides optimal coverage for the most likely pathogens in this high-risk scenario. Meropenem provides excellent Coverage against gram-negative rods including Pseudomonas aeruginosa, which is a major concern in neutropenic patients, as well as many gram-positive organisms and anaerobes. Vancomycin is essential for coverage against methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), which is increasingly common in healthcare settings and can cause severe pneumonia. The neutropenic state (ANC <500 cells/uL) significantly increases the risk of overwhelming bacterial infection, and the presence of pulmonary infiltrates suggests possible bacterial pneumonia. While antifungal coverage with fluconazole may be considered in high- risk patients with prolonged neutropenia, it is not typically part of initial empirical therapy unless there are specific risk factors.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child presents with high fever, toxic appearance, and severe respiratory distress. Physical examination reveals decreased breath sounds over the right lung field with dullness to percussion. Chest X-ray shows right lung consolidation with large pleural effusion and mediastinal shift to the left. Which complication is most concerning in this scenario?
questions.initialExplanation: A large effusion with toxic fever, then the risk of empyema with septations, is what is most feared here.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child presents with complicated pneumonia with large pleural effusion causing mediastinal shift, representing a medical emergency that requires immediate intervention. The most concerning complication in this scenario is empyema with septation, which can rapidly progress to organize and cause permanent lung damage. The combination of high fever, toxic appearance, and large pleural effusion with mediastinal shift indicates that the effusion is likely infected (empyema) and under pressure, potentially compromising cardiac function and contralateral lung expansion. Septation of the empyema occurs when fibrin deposition divides the pleural space into multiple compartments, making drainage difficult and requiring more aggressive Interventions like chest tube placement with fibrinolytic therapy or even surgical decortication.

---

questions.stem: A 14-year-old adolescent presents with gradual onset of fever, headache, sore throat, and non- productive cough over 1 week. Chest examination reveals bilateral crackles, and chest X-ray shows bilateral interstitial infiltrates with peribronchial cuffing. Cold agglutinins test is positive. Which antibiotic is most appropriate for treatment?
questions.initialExplanation: A teenager with non-productive cough, gradual fever, interstitial infiltrates and positive cold agglutinins = Mycoplasma; treat with azithromycin.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This clinical presentation is characteristic of Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection in an adolescent, supported by the positive cold agglutinins test. Mycoplasma pneumoniae is a common cause of atypical pneumonia in school-age children and adolescents, presenting with gradual onset of symptoms including fever, headache, sore throat, and non-productive cough over 7-10 days. The radiographic findings of bilateral interstitial Infiltrates with peribronchial cuffing are typical for Mycoplasma pneumonia. Cold agglutinins are autoantibodies that develop in 50-75% of Mycoplasma infections and cause agglutination of red blood cells at cold temperatures, providing supportive evidence for the diagnosis. The appropriate treatment for Mycoplasma pneumoniae is a macrolide antibiotic, with azithromycin being the preferred choice due to its convenient once-daily dosing, shorter treatment course (5 days), and better tolerability compared to erythromycin.

---


## Bronchiolitis

questions.stem: A 5-month-ill patient admitted to the emergency room diagnosed as a case of bronchiolitis. Which one of these features is least consistent with the diagnosis of bronchiolitis?
questions.initialExplanation: Fever in bronchiolitis is usually low-grade or absent, so a fever of 39.9°C is the least consistent finding; coryza, tachypnea, feeding difficulty and wheeze are typical.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Bronchiolitis is a common lower respiratory tract infection in infants, typically caused by respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) . It primarily affects children under 2 years of age and is characterized by inflammation and obstruction of the small airways (bronchioles). The typical clinical features of bronchiolitis include:

- Rhinorrhea (runny nose), Cough, Tachypnea (rapid breathing).

- Wheezing and/or crackles on auscultation.

- Feeding difficulties due to increased work of breathing.

- Low-grade fever (usually <38.5°C).

A high fever (39.9°C) is not typical of bronchiolitis. Bronchiolitis is usually associated with low-grade fever or no fever at all. A very high fever suggests a more severe or invasive infection, such as bacterial pneumonia or another systemic illness, which would be inconsistent with the usual presentation of bronchiolitis.

---

questions.stem: 2024 .\)5 1 A 6-month-old girl is referred after her first episode of wheezing. She had rhinorrhea and cough for three days, followed by breathing difficulty. Her RR is 60 breaths/min., temperature is 38.2°C, Subcostal retraction and diffuse wheezing are observed. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: A first wheezing episode in a 6-month-old after 3 days of cold with tachypnea and subcostal retractions = acute bronchiolitis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This 6-month-old girl presents with rhinorrhea and cough for three days , followed by breathing difficulty , tachypnea (RR 60 breaths/min) , low-grade fever (38.2°C) , subcostal retractions , and diffuse wheezing on auscultation. These findings are highly suggestive of acute bronchiolitis , which is the most common cause of wheezing in infants under 2 years of age.

The clinical presentation of rhinorrhea , cough , tachypnea , low-grade fever , subcostal retractions ,

and diffuse wheezing is most consistent with acute bronchiolitis , which is commonly caused by RSV in infants.

---

questions.stem: A 4-month-old previously healthy infant presents with a 4-day history of cough and wheezing. Examination shows a RR of 65/min, nasal flaring, intercostal retractions, and oxygen saturation of 92% on room air. What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.label: C
options.text: Supportive care with oxygen and hydration

questions.initialExplanation: A 4-month-old with saturation 92% and tachypnea: the mainstay is oxygen and hydration support; no routine bronchodilators, steroids or antibiotics.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This infant presents with classic moderate bronchiolitis: age <12 months, viral prodrome, tachypnea, increased

work of breathing (nasal flaring, retractions), wheezing, and mild hypoxemia (SpO2 92%). Current evidence- based guidelines uniformly recommend supportive care as first-line management, including supplemental oxygen to maintain saturations 290-92%, adequate hydration (oral or nasogastric if feeding is compromised), and gentle nasal suctioning to relieve upper airway obstruction. Bronchodilators such as inhaled salbutamol

(A) and nebulized epinephrine (E) are not routinely recommended because randomized trials and meta- analyses show no consistent, clinically meaningful benefit in typical bronchiolitis. Systemic corticosteroids (D) lack efficacy in viral bronchiolitis and are not indicated. Antibiotics (B) are inappropriate without evidence of bacterial co-infection, which is uncommon.

---

questions.stem: A 14-month-old boy presents with sudden onset of barking cough after two days of nasal congestion and low-grade fever. He is alert, afebrile, with inspiratory stridor at rest, mild subcostal retractions, and SpO:2 96% on room air. Chest auscultation reveals clear lung fields with normal air entry. Which of the following is the least likely diagnosis?

options.label: C
options.text: Foreign body in the upper airway

questions.initialExplanation: Barking cough, inspiratory stridor and clear lungs = croup, so bronchiolitis is the least likely (wheeze and crackles characterize it).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Bronchiolitis is the least likely diagnosis because it is a lower airway disease characterized by inflammation of the bronchioles, producing diffuse wheezing, fine crackles, hyperinflation, and tachypnea—not the upper airway signs seen here. This child's presentation (barking cough, inspiratory stridor at rest, clear lung fields) is classic for **viral laryngotracheobronchitis **(croup), an upper airway obstruction syndrome. Bacterial tracheitis (B) is less likely given the afebrile, non-toxic appearance but remains in the differential for stridor. Foreign body aspiration (C) typically has abrupt onset without URI prodrome but can mimic croup. Epiglottitis

(E) is improbable due to the absence of high fever, drooling, or toxic appearance, yet it involves upper airway obstruction. In contrast, bronchiolitis fundamentally involves lower respiratory pathology; isolated inspiratory stridor with clear lungs is pathophysiologically inconsistent with bronchiolar inflammation.

---

questions.stem: A 10-week-old term male infant is brought to your office with a 2-day history of difficulty breathing. He has been healthy since birth,with the exception of a 3-day episode of wheezing and rhinorrhea 3 weeks ago, Your initial examination shows an alert infant with increased work of breathing, rhinorrhea, and wheezing. His oxygen saturation is 93% and his temperature is 3S.4°C (101.1CF). Which one of the following would be most appropriate at this point?

options.label: A
options.text: Antigen testing or another rapid assay

options.label: C
options.text: Initiation of empiric antimicrobial therapy with ampicillin

options.label: D
options.text: Advising the parents that the child can safely be returned to day care tomorrow

questions.initialExplanation: A 10-week-old with bronchiolitis and saturation 93%: the appropriate approach is supportive (oxygen, hydration, antipyretics) with no routine X-ray or antibiotics.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The guideline on the diagnosis and management of bronchiolitis recommends against the use of laboratory (choice A) or radiographic studies (choice B) to make the diagnosis, although additional testing may be appropriate if there is no improvement. Bronchiolitis can be caused by a number of different viruses, alone or in combination, and the knowledge gained from virologic testing rarely influences management decisions or outcomes for the vast majority of children. Supportive care (choice E) and anticipatory guidance are the mainstays of management of nonsevere bronchiolitis, Supportive care includes maintenance of adequate hydration, relief of nasal congestion/obstruction, antipyretics for fever, and monitoring for disease progression.

---

questions.stem: A 2-month-old girl, with a large ventricular septal defect, has mild-to-moderate bronchiolitis due to respiratory syncytial virus. Which one of the following treatments is considered principal therapy?
questions.initialExplanation: An infant with a large VSD and mild-moderate bronchiolitis: the main treatment is supportive oxygen.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Most children with bronchiolitis recover at home in 3 to 5 days. During the illness, frequent smaii feedings of clear fluids may be given. Increasing difficulty in breathing, bluish skin discoloration, fatigue, and dehydration indicate that the child should be hospitalized. Children with congenital heart or lung disease or an impaired immune system may be hospitalized sooner and are far more likely to become quite ill from bronchiolitis. With proper care, the chance of dying of bronchiolitis is low, even for children who need to be hospitalized.

In the hospital, oxygen levels are monitored with a sensor on a finger, toe, or an earlobe, and oxygen is given by an oxygen tent or face mask. Among numerous medications and interventions used to treat bronchiolitis, thus far, only oxygen appreciably improves the condition of young children. Therefore, therapy is directed toward symptomatic relief and maintenance of hydration and oxygenation.

---

questions.stem: In the past 24 hours, six infants have been admitted to the pediatric ward with paroxysms of cough, wheezing, fever up to 38°C (10CPF), and feeding difficulty, Chest radiographs have been consistently normal or have shown soft findings of peribronchial cuffing. Oxygen saturations have been consistently below 88%. Which one of the following would be indicated for these infants?
questions.initialExplanation: Infants with bronchiolitis and saturation below 88%: supplemental oxygen is the indication; no antibiotics or steroids.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This clinical picture is consistent with respiratory syncytial virus bronchiolitis, an epidemic respiratory infection prevalent in the winter months. No treatment has been shown to alter the course of the disease, so treatment consists of supportive care to prevent hypoxia and dehydration. Corticosteroids and antibiotics have been shown to be ineffective.

---

questions.stem: A 6-month-old infant presents with a 3-day history of nasal congestion, fever, and progressive cough. Today, the infant has developed wheezing, increased work of breathing, and is refusing feeds. The mother reports that the 4-year-old sibling had a "cold" last week. Physical examination reveals tachypnea with nasal flaring and bilateral wheezes. Which viral pathogen is most likely responsible for this presentation?
questions.initialExplanation: A 6-month-old whose sibling has cold and wheeze: the most common cause is RSV.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is responsible for more than 50% of acute bronchiolitis cases in infants and young children, making it the most common causative agent. This clinical presentation follows the classic pattern of bronchiolitis: preceding upper respiratory tract infection (URT]I) symptoms in the infant following exposure to an older family member with minor respiratory symptoms (the 4-year-old sibling's cold), progression to lower respiratory tract involvement with wheezing and increased work of breathing. The age group (6 months) is within the peak incidence period for RSV bronchiolitis (typically occurring in infants under 2 years).

---

questions.stem: A 3-month-old infant has had upper respiratory symptoms for a few days and presents to the emergency department with respiratory distress, wheezing, and hypoxia. You diagnose bronchiolitis. What is the most common cause of acute bronchiolitis in infants?
questions.initialExplanation: The most common cause of acute bronchiolitis in infants is RSV.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Infants with bronchiolitis can have varying presentations, from mild tachypnea to severe cough, retractions, tachypnea, and wheezing. RSV is the most common cause, and infection is universal in the first 2 years of life. Parainfluenza, influenza, and human metapneumovirus are all recognized causes of bronchiolitis. However, they are not as common as RSV. CMV is not a cause of bronchiolitis.

---

questions.stem: A 3-month-old infant is admitted to the hospital with respiratory distress. He has had cough and congestion for the last 2 days and is now breathing too fast to eat effectively. You suspect bronchiolitis and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) antigen testing is positive. Which of the following roentgenographic findings is most commonly seen in infants with bronchiolitis caused by RSV?
questions.initialExplanation: The most common radiographic finding in RSV bronchiolitis is lung hyperinflation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is the most important cause of bronchiolitis in infants and young children and causes acute respiratory tract illness in patients of all ages. Typical roentgenographic findings include hyperinflation, peribronchial thickening, and atelectasis especially involving the right upper lobe. Infiltrates are typically associated with bacterial pneumonia. Pleural effusions and hilar adenopathy are findings not typically associated with bronchiolitis.

---

questions.stem: A 10-month-old female presents in winter with 2 days of rhinorrhea, tachypnea, and wheezing. She has respirations of 60 breaths per minute, HR of 160 beats per minute, and an oxygen saturation of 90% on room air. Examination reveals an alert infant in mild respiratory distress with mild intercostals retractions and coarse bilateral expiratory wheezing. Appropriate therapy for this infant should begin with which of the following?

options.label: A
options.text: intravenous access and a 20 cc/kg bolus of normal saline

options.label: C
options.text: bag-valve mask followed by rapidsequence intubation

questions.initialExplanation: An infant with saturation 90%, tachypnea and wheeze: first give oxygen via nasal cannula.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The initial step in the management of patients presenting in respiratory distress is assessment of the “ABCs” (airway, breathing, and circulation). The presence of hypoxemia is an indication for administration of supplemental oxygen. There is no indication of a compromised airway (eg, stridor) in this patient. While there is mild distress, there is no indication at this time of respiratory failure necessitating emergent intubation. Chest radiographs and administration of corticosteroids may be necessary, but are not the first priority in this patient's management.

---

questions.stem: pat in Q11, Chest radiography reveals bilateral air trapping, chest hyperexpansion, and peribronchial thickening. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Chest film with bilateral air trapping, hyperinflation and peribronchial thickening in a wheezy infant = viral bronchiolitis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The age, physical findings, and season all point to bronchiolitis, most likely due to respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), as the most Likely cause of this patient’s problem. RSV is the etiologic agent in about 70% of patients with bronchiolitis and results in approximately 70,000 inpatient admissions yearly in the United States. Congestive heart failure likely would be associated with other physical findings such as hepatomegaly, or have demonstrable cardiomegaly on the chest radiograph. Respiratory distress syndrome typically has a ground-glass appearance on chest radiography and presents with more severe clinical symptoms. Pneumococcal pneumonia classically presents with a more focal infiltrate with consolidation, is unilateral, and is not associated with wheezing. Mycoplasmal infections are not common at this age.

---

questions.stem: Bronchiolitis is a viral illness which results in a variety of respiratory symptoms in children younger than two years of age. Which one of the following is considered to be at high risk of airway compromise if developed bronchiolitis?

options.label: A
options.text: Infants younger than three months of age

options.label: B
options.text: Another sibling with history of bronchiolitis in past 12 months

questions.initialExplanation: Infants under 3 months (especially ex-preterm) are at higher risk of airway deterioration and apnea.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Bronchiolitis is a viral illness caused by a respiratory syncytial virus.

In the presence of following risk factors, the risk of airway compromise goes higher and thus these children should be admitted to the hospital if they develop bronchiolitis:

— Infants under three months of age (risk of apnea).

— Preterm or low birth weight infants.

— Infants with chronic lung disease.

— Infants with congenital acyanotic heart disease.

---

questions.stem: Acute bronchiolitis in a previously healthy infant presenting with a first episode of wheezing (following a period of upper respiratory symptoms) needs which of the following for the diagnosis?

options.label: B
options.text: White blood cell and differential counts

questions.initialExplanation: The diagnosis of bronchiolitis is clinical (good examination); routine films or labs are not needed.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The diagnosis of acute bronchiolitis is clinical, particularly in a previously healthy infant presenting with a first episode of wheezing following a period of upper respiratory symptoms. Chest radiography is not routinely indicated in children with suspected bronchiolitis. Areas of atelectasis associated with bronchiolitis are often observed on chest radiographs and may be difficult to distinguish from bacterial pneumonia; as a result, obtaining chest radiography in a patient whose clinical course and exam are consistent with bronchiolitis may encourage unnecessary antibiotic use. Laboratory testing is also not routinely indicated; the white blood cell and differential counts are usually normal and are not predictive of bacterial superinfection. Viral testing (polymerase chain reaction or rapid immunofluorescence) is not routinely recommended in the diagnosis of bronchiolitis but may be helpful if such testing prevents more invasive evaluations. Concurrent serious bacterial infection (sepsis, pneumonia, meningitis) is unlikely, although confirmation of viral bronchiolitis may obviate the need for a sepsis evaluation in the young febrile infant.

---

questions.stem: A 7-month-old ex-premature boy presented with a 2-day history of a sharp dry cough, coryza and difficulty in feeding. A chest radiograph revealed hyperinflation of the lungs and flattening of the diaphragm. the most likely diagnosis is?
questions.initialExplanation: Cough, coryza and feeding difficulty with hyperinflation and flattened diaphragm in an infant = bronchiolitis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Bronchiolitis is the commonest respiratory condition in infancy. Around 90% of cases are aged 1-9 months, and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is the causative agent in the majority of cases. Children with congenital heart disease, immunodeficiency and chronic lung disease of prematurity are at increased risk of this condition. Infants present with coryzal symptoms and a dry cough, which can lead to difficulties with breathing and feeding. Severe cases may have apnoeas and require ventilation. Typical signs include those of respiratory distress (e.g. recession, nasal flaring, head bobbing, tracheal tug), and auscultation reveals fine end-inspiratory crackles and expiratory wheeze.

---

questions.stem: A mother has brought her 9-month old boy to the Emergency Department with dyspnea and poor feeding. On examination, his chest is hyperinflated, and subcostal recession is noted. On auscultation, there are widespread fine inspiratory crackles and expiratory wheezes. Which one of the following is the next best step in management?
questions.initialExplanation: An infant with wheeze, fine inspiratory crackles and low saturation: next step is oxygen via nasal prongs.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This clinical presentation in this 9-month old infant is classic for acute bronchiolitis, a viral illness most commonly caused by respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). The usual age for the disease is between 2 weeks to 9 months of age. The classic clinical presentation is prodromal symptoms (cough, coryza) followed by wheezy breathing, tachypnea and hyperinflated chest with subcostal recessions. In children with bronchiolitis, oxygen therapy should be used when oxygen saturations are persistently less than 90%. Infants with bronchiolitis will have brief episodes of mild/moderate desaturations to levels less than 90% but these brief desaturations are not a reason to start oxygen therapy.

If required, oxygen 100% should be given via nasal cannula and discontinued when oxygen saturations are persistently greater than or equal to 90%.

Dehydration is also a serious problem in children with severe bronchiolitis and requires rehydration using intravenous fluids or nasogastric tube.

---

questions.stem: Which of the following is regarded as the most important clinical exam finding in a child with acute viral bronchiolitis?
questions.initialExplanation: The most important clinical sign in bronchiolitis per the source is fine inspiratory crackles.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Bronchiolitis is an acute viral illness most commonly caused by respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). Usual age is from 2 weeks to 9 months (up to 12 months). It is the most common cause of lower respiratory tract infection in infants.

- It presents initially with prodromal symptoms such irritating cough and rhinorrhea and then becomes worse in the next 3 to 5 days.

- Findings on examination include: Wheezy breathing which is often distressed, Bilateral fine inspiratory crackles, Tachypnea, Hyper-inflated chest (barrel-shaped), Use of accessory muscles and subcostal recession

- Chest X-rays are not necessary for diagnosis, but if obtained bilateral perihilar congestion and fullness will be noticed. Inspiratory fine crackles are regarded as the most characteristic feature of bronchiolitis.

---

questions.stem: A 6-month-old male infant with Tetralogy of Fallot (TF) is brought to your clinic by his mother with history of nasal discharge, low-grade fever, feeding difficulty, wheezy breathing, and cough for 3 days. The infant's father smokes a pack of cigarettes per day at home. Physical examination is significant for inspiratory crackles and expiratory wheeze. Respiratory rate is 60 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation is 92 % on room air. Which one of the following is the next best step in management?

options.label: A
options.text: Reassure the mother and educate about minimal handling and frequent feeds.

options.label: B
options.text: Admit the baby to the hospital and consider symptomatic care with supplemental oxygen, minimal handling and use of intravenous fluids.

options.label: D
options.text: Start nebulized ribavirin and monitor the response.

options.label: E
options.text: Start the child on nebulized saline 3% immediately.

questions.initialExplanation: An infant with TOF and bronchiolitis, saturation 92%: admit with oxygen, minimal handling and IV fluids; no steroids or ribavirin.
questions.detailedExplanation:
and use of intravenous fluids.

This infant has clinical diagnosis of acute viral bronchiolitis. The diagnosis of bronchiolitis is clinical and based on typical history of increased respiratory rate, cough, expiratory wheezing and bilateral fine crackles, preceded by a prodromal syndrome of low-grade fever and rhinorrhea.

For children with increased risk of progression to severe bronchiolitis, special consideration and probably admission to the hospital and discussion with a senior doctor is required.

This child has SpO2 of 92% and a breathing rate of 60 breaths per minute. He also has as an underlying congenital heart disease. For him, hospital admission is the first thing to consider.

The main issues in management are parental reassurance, education about minimal handling, and frequent feeds. The child should receive intravenous fluids because the illness itself, as well as tachypnea makes the child dehydrated.

---

questions.stem: A 3 mo old patient hospitalized for bronchiolitis is noted on admission laboratory studies to have a serum bicarbonate of 14 mmol/L. Of the following, which is the most appropriate next step in the patient's management?

options.label: C
options.text: Repeat serum electrolyte determination via venipuncture

options.label: D
options.text: Measure urine electrolytes, with calculation of urine anion gap

options.label: E
options.text: Initiate treatment with oral bicarbonate supplementation

questions.initialExplanation: Nearly the same as question 18: an infant with TOF and bronchiolitis needs admission and supportive care (minimal handling, fluids).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Serum electrolytes, blood urea nitrogen, calcium, phosphorus, creatinine, and pH should be obtained by venous puncture. Traumatic blood draws (e.g., heel stick specimens), small volumes of blood in " adult-size" specimen collection tubes, or prolonged specimen transport time at room temperature can lead to falsely low bicarbonate levels, often in association with an elevated serum potassium value.

---

questions.stem: A 6-month-old child with Tetralogy of Fallot is brought to your clinic by his mother with a history of nasal discharge, low to high-grade fever, feeding difficulties and wheezy cough since last three days. Father of the child smokes the cigarette a pack per day at home. Physical examination is significant for inspiratory crackles with an expiratory wheeze. Respiratory rate is 60/min and oxygen saturation is 92 % at room air. What is next best step in the management of this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Reassure the mother and educate about minimal handling and frequent feeds

options.label: B
options.text: Admit this baby to hospital and symptomatic care with minimal handling and use of intravenous fluids

options.label: C
options.text: 3% inhaled normal saline reduces the hospital stay and should be used at first thing in hospital

options.label: D
options.text: Start nebulised ribavirin and monitor the response

options.label: E
options.text: Give oxygen supplement and start corticosteroid therapy

questions.initialExplanation: Bicarbonate 14 mmol/L in an infant with bronchiolitis: likely a lab error from an unsuitable sample, so repeat electrolytes on a venous sample.
questions.detailedExplanation:
intravenous fluids

This patient has a clinical diagnosis of acute moderate bronchiolitis acute moderate bronchiolitis. The diagnosis of bronchiolitis is clinical and based on a typical history of nasal discharge, fever and wheezy cough, and examination findings of inspiratory crackles and expiratory wheeze.

The main treatment of bronchiolitis is supportive. This involves ensuring appropriate

oxygenation and fluid intake, and minimal handling. For the patient in the context of having moderate bronchiolitis, the child should most likely be admitted for observation.

---

questions.stem: A 3-month-old infant with bronchiolitis presents to the emergency department. The infant appears severely distressed with respiratory rate of 60/min, nasal flaring, subcostal retractions, and oxygen saturation of 88% on room air. Which pathophysiological mechanism is primarily responsible for the observed hypoxemia?
questions.initialExplanation: Hypoxemia in bronchiolitis is due to ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) mismatch from bronchiolar obstruction.
questions.detailedExplanation:
In acute bronchiolitis, hypoxemia is primarily a consequence of ventilation-perfusion (V/ Q) mismatch, which occurs early in the course of the disease. The pathophysiology involves bronchiolar obstruction due to edema, mucus plugging, and cellular debris in the small airways. This obstruction creates areas of lung that are perfused but poorly ventilated, leading to intrapulmonary shunting and resulting hypoxemia. The V/Q mismatch develops before significant hypercapnia, making it the earliest measurable physiological abnormality. While alveolar hypoventilation can occur later in severe cases with respiratory muscle fatigue, it is not the primary mechanism for initial hypoxemia. Right-to-left cardiac shunt and pulmonary hypertension are not typical features of uncomplicated bronchiolitis.

---

questions.stem: A 4-month-old infant with bronchiolitis shows barely audible breath sounds on auscultation. The infant is lethargic, has poor muscle tone, and oxygen saturation has dropped to 82% on room air. Which physiological phenomenon best explains these findings?

options.label: B
options.text: Complete alveolar collapse with atelectasis N C) Pleural effusion compressing the lungs

options.label: E
options.text: Nearly complete bronchiolar obstruction with air trapping

questions.initialExplanation: Barely audible breath sounds with lethargy mean near-complete bronchiolar obstruction with air trapping, a danger sign.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Barely audible breath sounds in bronchiolitis indicate very severe disease with nearly complete bronchiolar obstruction. This represents the most critical phase of the illness where bronchiolar

‘    lumens are so narrowed by edema, mucus, and cellular debris that airflow is severely restricted. The pathophysiological process involves progressive narrowing of the small airways, leading to increased airway resistance during both inspiration and expiration. However, because airway radius is naturally smaller during expiration, the obstruction becomes functionally complete during the expiratory phase, leading to air trapping and hyperinflation. The combination of severely reduced airflow and hyperinflation results in barely audible breath sounds on auscultation.

---
