## Cystic Fibrosis & Bronchiectasis

questions.stem: An 8-year-old girl presents with a chronic productive cough for over one year, with daily thick sputum, mostly in the morning. She had multiple episodes of pneumonia since early childhood. On examination, she appears underweight, has finger clubbing, and coarse crackles are heard in both lungs. Which of the following is the best initial investigation to confirm the diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.text: Bronchoalveolar lavage with cytology and cultures

questions.initialExplanation: Chronic productive cough, recurrent chest infections, clubbing and coarse crackles: suspect bronchiectasis; diagnose with high-resolution CT chest.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child's presentation—chronic productive cough, recurrent pneumonia, failure to thrive, finger clubbing, and bilateral coarse crackles—is classic for bronchiectasis, with cystic fibrosis being the most likely underlying etiology. High-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) of the chest is the gold standard investigation to confirm the structural diagnosis of bronchiectasis, demonstrating bronchial dilation, wall thickening, lack of tapering, and the "signet ring" sign. While HRCT confirms the anatomical abnormality, subsequent testing (sweat chloride test, immunologic evaluation, ciliary function studies) identifies the underlying cause. Bronchoalveolar lavage is invasive and reserved for pathogen identification after structural diagnosis. Lateral decubitus X-ray detects pleural fluid, not bronchiectasis. Tuberculin testing is indicated only with specific exposure risks or granulomatous features. Pulmonary function tests demonstrate obstructive physiology but lack diagnostic specificity for structural lung disease.

---

questions.stem: A 15 yr old boy presents with a history of chronic cough productive of yellow-green sputum, dyspnea on exercise, digital clubbing, and poor weight gain. He has a history of recurrent sinopulmonary infections. The patient is thin; his pulse rate is 95 beats/min and respiratory rate is 24 breaths/min; auscultation of the lungs demonstrates diffuse fine crackles and endexpiratory wheezing. The gold standard technique for demonstrating bronchiectasis is:

options.label: C
options.text: Thin-section high-resolution CT of the chest

questions.initialExplanation: The modern gold standard to show bronchiectasis is thin-section high-resolution CT (HRCT) of the chest.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Bronchiectasis can manifest in any combination of three pathologic forms, best defined by high-resolution CT (HRCT). The following definitions have been proposed: prebronchiectasis (chronic or recurrent endobronchial infection with nonspecific HRCT changes —may be reversible); HRCT bronchiectasis (clinical symptoms with HRCT evidence of bronchial dilation—may persist, progress, or improve and resolve); and established bronchiectasis (like the previous but with no resolution within 2 yr). Therefore, early diagnosis and aggressive therapy are important to prevent the development of established bronchiectasis.

---

questions.stem: An 8-month-old child was brought to the emergency department with cough, fever, and breathlessness. Physical examination confirmed the diagnosis of pneumonia. The medical record of the child showed that this child had four attacks of pneumonia in the last four months. Given these and the family history, cystic fibrosis was suspected and sweat test was requested and showed a slightly raised chloride. Conditions other than cystic fibrosis might increase sweat chloride concentration and resuit in false positive results. One of these is:
questions.initialExplanation: The source's answer: high sweat rates. This is not a usual cause of a false-positive sweat chloride (more often malnutrition, adrenal insufficiency, immunodeficiency), so check the original.
questions.detailedExplanation:
After the primary sweat secretion is produced in the body of the sweat gland, the ducts reabsorb sodium and chloride. With high sweat flow rates, the ducts would have little time to reabsorb large amounts of sodium and chloride resulting high levels of these ions in collected sweat (choice

D), Beyond the newborn period, elevated sweat chloride levels mimicking cystic fibrosis can be found in patients with untreated adrenal insufficiency, pseudohypoaldosteronism, hypothyroidism, hypoparathyroidism, glycogen storage disease, vasopressin-resistant diabetes insipidus, malnutrition, hypopituitarism, ectodermal dysplasia,mucopolysaccharidoses, fucosidosis, and pancreatitis.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-oid boy presents to the emergency department with a history of recurrent cough. A review of his previous records reveals recurrent episodes of right lobe pneumonia, A chest x-ray in the current admission also confirms a right upper lobe pneumonia. He has no other major health issues to report. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Recurrent pneumonias in the same lobe (right upper lobe) in an otherwise healthy child: per the source the cause is cystic fibrosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Cystic fibrosis (CF) is the most common fatal genetic disease affecting Canadian children and young adults. It is a disease of exocrine gland function that involves multiple organ systems but chiefly

‘     results in chronic respiratory infections, pancreatic enzyme insufficiency, and associated complications. Pulmonary involvement occurs in 90% of patients surviving the neonatal period. Fifty percent of patients present with respiratory manifestations, often beginning in infancy. These may include the following: cough, recurrent wheezing, recurrent pneumonia, atypical asthma, dyspnea on exertion, and chest pain. Diagnosis is by sweat test or identification of cystic fibrosis mutations in patients with characteristic symptoms. Treatment is supportive through aggressive interdisciplinary care,

---

questions.stem: An 11 month infant presents with chronic diarrhoea and failure to thrive since breast feeding was discontinued at 9 months. He has been treated by his GP with antibiotics on two occasions for chest infections. Initial investigations reveal low serum potassium, chloride and metabolic alkalosis. which is the most likely diagnosis:
questions.initialExplanation: Chronic diarrhea, failure to thrive and chest infections with hypokalemia, hypochloremia and metabolic alkalosis (pseudo-Bartter) = cystic fibrosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Failure to thrive, chest infections and diarrhoea (the latter results from failure of pancreatic exocrine function) are indicative of CF. The abnormal biochemistry is caused by salt loss and may be described as pseudo-bartters syndrome

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-oid male with recurrent sinusitis has difficulty breathing through his nose. He has had chronic diarrhea and his weight is at the 5th percentile. Nasal polyps are noted on examination in the form of grayish pale masses in both nares. No nasal purulence or odor is present. Which one of the following tests should you order?
questions.initialExplanation: Nasal polyps in a child with chronic diarrhea and poor growth suggest CF; the test is a sweat chloride test.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has chronic diarrhea, recurrent sinusitis, and nasal polyps, and is underweight Nasal polyps tend to occur more often in adult males, with the prevalence increasing in both sexes after age 50. Any child 12 years or younger who presents with nasal polyps should be suspected of having cystic fibrosis until proven otherwise. A sweat chloride test, along with a history and clinical examination, is necessary to evaluate this possibility. Nasal polyps are found in 1% of the normal population, but a full 18% of those with cystic fibrosis are afflicted. There is no association of polyps with Wilson's disease, sarcoidosis, or emphysema, so serum ceruloplasmin, angiotensin-converting, and alpha-1-antitrypsin levels would not be useful. An erythrocyte sedimentation rate likewise would yield limited information.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy has been diagnosed with cystic fibrosis since early childhood. He develops chronic lung disease and P. aeruginosa infection with frequent pulmonary exacerbations. Of the following, the drug of choice to decrease pulmonary exacerbations is :
questions.initialExplanation: To reduce exacerbations in CF with Pseudomonas: the source's answer is azithromycin (chronic low-dose macrolide).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Macrolide therapy decreases pulmonary exacerbations in patients with chronic lung disease and P. aeruginosa infection. The mechanism likely relates to altering the virulence properties of P. aeruginosa rather than direct bacterial killing.

---

questions.stem: A 10-month-old infant has poor weight gain, a persistent cough, and a history of several bouts of pneumonitis. The mother describes the child as having very large, foul-smelling stools for months. Which of the following diagnostic studies is likely to result in the correct diagnosis of this child?
questions.initialExplanation: An infant with failure to thrive, cough, recurrent pneumonia and bulky foul stools (steatorrhea) = suspected CF; diagnose by sweat chloride test.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Cystic fibrosis (CF) is a multisystem disease caused by an abnormally functioning cystic fibrosis transmembrane

regulator (CFTR) protein. Abnormal secretions are produced as a result of decreased permeability of ionized chloride in the secretory epithelium of a number of organs. Progressive lung failure is caused by accumulation of viscid secretions that obstruct the airway and lead to infection, bronchiectasis, and inflammatory changes. Survival has improved markedly during the past few decades as a result of prompt recognition of CF and aggressive treatment; the median age at death has increased from less than 10 years to more than 30 years. Therapeutic approaches include inhalation therapy, airway clearance therapy (such as chest physiotherapy, flutter valves, or a vibrating vest), aggressive antibiotic administration, bronchodilators, oxygen, and nutritional support. Heart—lung transplants have prolonged life and improved qualify of life for some terminal patients. Newer therapies for CF include the use of purified human plasma a1 -antitrypsin, recombinant DNAase, and gene therapy.

---

questions.stem: You have just confirmed the diagnosis of cystic fibrosis in a 3-year-old child. The parents are concerned about future pregnancies. You explain to them that the pattern of genetic transmission of cystic fibrosis is :

options.label: E
options.text: autosomal recessive in some families and X-linked in others

questions.initialExplanation: Cystic fibrosis is autosomal recessive due to CFTR mutation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The correct answer is (B). Cystic fibrosis (CF) is an autosomal recessive disorder with a disease incidence in the Caucasian population of about 1:1500 and a corresponding carrier state of about 1:20. Currently, CF represents the most common lethal genetic disease in the Caucasian population. The disease is much less common among African Americans and Asians.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy has failed to grow and has evidence of exocrine pancreatic insufficiency. What is the most likely cause for this?
questions.initialExplanation: Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency and failure to thrive in a child: the most common cause is cystic fibrosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Cystic fibrosis is the most common cause of pancreatic insufficiency in childhood, accounting for almost all cases. Biliary atresia is not associated with pancreatic insufficiency.

Congenital hypoplasia or absence of the pancreas is recognized but rare. Schwachman syndrome is a rare condition of unknown cause characterized by pancreatic insufficiency and neutropenia. Acute pancreatitis usually does not lead to pancreatic insufficiency.

---

questions.stem: A 12-year-old girl with cystic fibrosis returns to your office after a second course of an oral as well as inhaled antibiotics for a pulmonary exacerbation. She reports she has been doing extra airway clearance. She continues to have an increased cough. In addition, her lung function has not yet returned to her usual baseline. She has lost 1 pound since her last visit, and continues to have fatigue. The most appropriate next step is:

options.label: A
options.text: Begin an appetite stimulant to improve appetite and encourage weight gain

options.label: B
options.text: Begin treatment for allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis

options.label: C
options.text: Admit her for initiation of IV antibiotics for a 2- to 3-week course

options.label: D
options.text: Perform outpatient bronchoscopy to clear mucus and continue increased airway clearance

options.label: E
options.text: Assume this is her new baseline and continue routine therapies

questions.initialExplanation: No improvement after oral and inhaled antibiotics with weight loss and fatigue: admit for IV antibiotics for 2-3 weeks.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This patient has evidence of ongoing pulmonary exacerbation that has not responded to outpatient antibiotics. In addition, the patient has continued to lose weight, and has fatigue, which may impair the ability to complete all the treatments necessary in the home. An IV antibiotic course is indicated in this scenario, and may be completed in the hospital, or in the home setting based on individual scenario. An appetite stimulant may be useful, but would not treat the pulmonary exacerbation, which is likely contributing to the weight loss. Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis may be considered, but treatment should not be initiated until a diagnosis is confirmed. Bronchoscopy may be helpful, but generally in this situation, bronchoscopy without further treatment would not fully treat the exacerbation. It may be helpful in identifying other organisms to target with therapy. It would be early to make an assumption that this patient could not recover lung function, and aggressive treatment should be implemented before this conclusion is made.

---

questions.stem: You are a practicing pediatrician in a state where cystic fibrosis is not a routine part of newborn screening. Which of the following symptoms in a newborn infant would prompt you to test for cystic fibrosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Meconium ileus in a newborn is the strongest indicator to test for CF.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The newborn with cystic fibrosis generall is asymptomatic. The most common manifestation, meconium ileus, occurs in 15%—-20% of CF patients. The ileum is completely obstructed with meconium, which results in intestinal obstruction. The meconium plug syndrome also is seen with an increased frequency in infants with cystic fibrosis, but it is less specific than meconium ileus. Sweat chloride testing in suspected cases of cystic fibrosis has always been troublesome in the newborn period but DNA testing is now available and is 90%—95% sensitive. In the United States, some states have instituted routine newborn screening for cystic fibrosis.

---

questions.stem: A 17-year-old boy with cystic fibrosis complains of a 5-10 Ib weight loss over the past month, unaccompanied by changes in his pulmonary or gastrointestinal symptoms. You suspect that he has developed which of the following?
questions.initialExplanation: Weight loss in an adolescent with CF without change in lung or bowel symptoms: suspect CF-related diabetes.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Approximately 40% of adults with cystic fibrosis have diabetes mellitus. It is thought to result from chronic obstruction of ductal flow from inspissated secretions which results in pancreatic fibrosis and beta-cell destruction. It behaves like maturity onset diabetes, with little tendency to ketoacidosis. Diabetes should always be considered when an older child with cystic fibrosis loses weight.

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old Caucasian male presents with failure to thrive, chronic diarrhea, and recurrent pneumonia. Though his family history is negative for cystic fibrosis, a sweat test reveals a sodium concentration of 120 mg/dL. Which of the following is the appropriate next step in caring for this infant?
questions.initialExplanation: High sweat sodium (120) with failure to thrive and chronic diarrhea = confirmed CF; next step is pancreatic enzyme supplementation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
A sweat chloride greater than 40 is consistent with the diagnosis of cystic fibrosis (CF). This child presents with CF —the most common genetically transmitted lethal disease among Caucasians (1/3300). This multisystem disease leads to pancreatic insufficiency in about 85% of patients. This causes fat malabsorption with resultant malabsorption of the fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K). Therefore, all CF patients should receive pancreatic enzyme supplementation. CF patients also are at risk for iron deficiency anemia. Only when anemia or low serum ferritin levels are documented should they receive iron supplementation.

---

questions.stem: A 15-year-old adolescent comes to spend the summer with her aunt. She has an appointment to be seen in your clinic because of her need for frequent medical care. Prior to seeing the patient you review her records and notice she is on oral pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy. This is most helpful in patients with which of the following?
questions.initialExplanation: Oral pancreatic enzyme replacement is mainly beneficial in cystic fibrosis because of pancreatic insufficiency.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Cystic fibrosis is the most common cause of pancreatic insufficiency in childhood. Most patients with this disease have less steatorrhea and improved weight gain when receiving pancreatic replacement therapy.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child with cystic fibrosis undergoes sweat chloride testing. The results show chloride concentration of 45 mEq/L with adequate sweat collection. How should these results be interpreted?

options.label: C
options.text: Negative result ruling out cystic fibrosis

options.label: E
options.text: Normal result for the patient's age

questions.initialExplanation: Sweat chloride 45 mEq/L (30-59) is borderline and needs repeat testing or further evaluation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Sweat chloride concentrations are categorized as follows: negative if <40 mEq/L, borderline if 40-60 mEq/L, and positive if >60 mEq/L, with adequate sweat collection. A result of 45 mEq/L falls in the borderline range, which requires repeat testing for confirmation. The diagnostic criteria for cystic fibrosis require two elevated sweat chloride tests (>60 mEq/L) performed at an accredited CF Foundation certified laboratory, two CF- causing mutations identified by DNA analysis, or characteristic abnormalities in ion transport across nasal epithelium. Borderline results can occur due to technical factors, age-related variations, or in patients with CFTR-related metabolic syndrome (CRMS). In children under 6 months, the diagnostic cutoff may be lower, and careful correlation with clinical findings is essential. The borderline result does not confirm or rule out cystic fibrosis but indicates the need for further evaluation, including repeat testing, genetic analysis, and clinical

correlation. Understanding these interpretive criteria is crucial for accurate diagnosis and avoiding both false positives and false negatives.

---

questions.stem: A 12-year-old child with cystic fibrosis presents with chronic productive cough and recurrent chest infections. Sputum cultures frequently grow Pseudomonas aeruginosa. What is the primary reason for the increased susceptibility to chronic bacterial infections in the airways?

options.label: A
options.text: Abnormal airway secretions leading to impaired mucociliary clearance and enhanced bacterial adhesion

options.label: B
options.text: Decreased immunoglobulin production increasing infection risk

questions.initialExplanation: Chronic infection in CF stems from abnormal viscous bronchial secretions with impaired mucociliary clearance and bacterial adherence.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The respiratory epithelium of patients with cystic fibrosis exhibits marked impermeability to chloride and excessive reabsorption of sodium, leading to relative dehydration of airway secretions. This results in hyperviscous mucus that causes airway obstruction and impairs mucociliary transport, the primary defense mechanism of the airways. The defective CFTR protein also reduces the function of airway defenses and promotes bacterial adhesion to the airway epithelium. Chronic airway infections with organisms like Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus are the result of this combination of impaired clearance and enhanced bacterial adherence. The thick, dehydrated mucus serves as an excellent medium for bacterial growth and prevents effective clearance by ciliary action and coughing. This pathophysiological mechanism is fundamental to understanding why aggressive airway clearance techniques, mucolytics, and antibiotic therapy are cornerstones of CF management. The chronic infection leads to persistent inflammation, bronchial damage, and eventual bronchiectasis, which further compromises lung function.

---

questions.stem: An 8-year-old with CF develops acute respiratory distress with fever, increased cough, and new infiltrates on chest X-ray. Despite broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and aggressive airway clearance, the patient develops allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) with serum IgE of 1500 IU/mL and positive Aspergillus precipitins. Pulmonary function shows FEV1 decline of 25% over 3 months. What is the most appropriate treatment approach?

options.label: A
options.text: Increase the dose of intravenous antibiotics only

options.label: C
options.text: Combined oral prednisone 0.5 mg/kg/day with itraconazole for 16 weeks

options.label: D
options.text: IV voriconazole with methylprednisolone pulse therapy

options.label: E
options.text: Oral budesonide with antifungal prophylaxis only

questions.initialExplanation: ABPA in CF (high IgE, positive precipitins, falling FEV1): treat with oral prednisone plus itraconazole for a prolonged course (16 weeks).
questions.detailedExplanation:
This case presents ABPA in CF, a complex hypersensitivity reaction requiring dual antifungal and anti- inflammatory therapy. The combination of systemic corticosteroids with itraconazole is the standard treatment approach. Systemic corticosteroids are essential to control the inflammatory response causing airway obstruction and lung function decline, while itraconazole targets the underlying fungal colonization and reduces steroid requirements. The dosage of prednisone (0.5 mg/kg/day) balances therapeutic efficacy with minimization of side effects in chronic CF management. The 16-week duration is based on studies showing optimal response rates. Monotherapy with either agent alone is insufficient, and IV therapy is not indicated for uncomplicated ABPA. The marked IgE elevation (>1000 IU/mL) and significant FEV1 decline confirm the severity requiring aggressive combination therapy.

---

questions.stem: A 9-year-old with CF develops sudden onset severe dyspnea, chest pain, and unilateral decreased breath sounds. Chest X-ray shows complete lung collapse on the right side with mediastinal shift to the left. The patient has been hospitalized twice in the past year for pulmonary exacerbations with documented bronchiectasis. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.label: B
options.text: High-flow oxygen and observation for 24 hours

options.label: C
options.text: Bronchoscopy with airway evaluation and stenting

options.label: E
options.text: Needle decompression followed by chest tube placement

questions.initialExplanation: Complete lung collapse with mediastinal shift, chest pain and decreased breath sounds: the answer given is needle decompression then chest tube.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This patient has developed a tension pneumothorax, a life-threatening complication that requires immediate intervention. The classic presentation includes sudden dyspnea, unilateral decreased breath sounds, and mediastinal shift (the "shift away" sign), which indicates increased intrathoracic pressure compromising cardiac function and venous return. While the definitive treatment is chest tube insertion with underwater seal drainage, needle decompression should be performed immediately to relieve the pressure and prevent cardiac arrest. This is followed by tube thoracostomy for continuous air evacuation. The patient's underlying lung disease with bronchiectasis increases the risk of recurrent pneumothoraces, which may require pleurodesis or surgical intervention. High-flow oxygen alone is insufficient, and bronchoscopy is not indicated for pneumothorax management.

---

questions.stem: A 9-year-old with CF develops sudden severe abdominal pain, bilious vomiting, and inability to pass flatus. Abdominal X-ray shows multiple air-fluid levels with dilated small bowel loops and a distinctive " double bubble" sign. The patient has a history of meconium ileus in the neonatal period. What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.label: D
options.text: Urgent upper GI series with small bowel follow-through

options.label: E
options.text: Conservative management with bowel rest and observation

questions.initialExplanation: Severe abdominal pain, bilious vomiting and bowel obstruction in a CF patient with prior meconium ileus (DIOS): start with Gastrografin enema with monitoring before surgery.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This presentation is classic for meconium ileus equivalent or distal intestinal obstruction syndrome (DIOS) in a CF patient with history of neonatal meconium ileus. The "double bubble" sign suggests duodenal obstruction, which in CF patients is often due to thick meconium-like material. Gastrografin enema is the first-line treatment for both neonatal meconium ileus and DIOS in CF. The hyperosmolar contrast draws fluid into the bowel lumen, softening and dislodging the impacted material. This non- invasive approach is successful in approximately 80% of cases and avoids the risks of surgery. If the enema fails, surgical intervention may be necessary, but immediate surgery is not indicated. The

history of meconium ileus strongly supports this diagnosis and increases the likelihood of response to contrast enema therapy.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old female child presented with low-grade fever and dysuria for the last 2 days. She has suprapubic tenderness on examination. The investigations show normal complete blood count, and urinalysis reveals RBC 1-2/HPF, WBC 20-25/HPF, and positive leukocyte esterase. The MOST likely diagnosis is:
questions.initialExplanation: Mild fever and dysuria with WBCs in urine and positive leukocyte esterase without signs of kidney involvement = cystitis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This case illustrates the classic presentation of acute cystitis in a pediatric patient, and the clinical and
laboratory findings allow for precise differentiation between lower and upper urinary tract infections.
Understanding this distinction is critical because it directly impacts treatment duration and the need for
further imaging evaluation.

The patient is a 5-year-old female, which represents a demographic with significantly higher risk of urinary
tract infections compared to males due to the shorter urethra and proximity of the urethral meatus to the
anus. The symptoms reported are highly characteristic of bladder inflammation: dysuria (painful or burning
urination) indicates irritation of the bladder mucosa, and the low-grade fever suggests a localized rather than
systemic infection.

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy with a history of recurrent urinary tract infections with suspicion of vesicoureteral reflux (VUR) due to the recurrent infections. Which of the following diagnostic tests would be most appropriate for supporting your diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: A child with recurrent UTIs is investigated with a micturating cystourethrogram to look for vesicoureteral reflux (VUR).
questions.detailedExplanation:
This case addresses the diagnostic approach to suspected vesicoureteral reflux (VUR), which is one
of the most common congenital abnormalities of the urinary tract in children. Understanding the
indications and relative merits of various imaging modalities is essential for appropriate clinical
decision-making.

Vesicoureteral reflux is characterized by retrograde flow of urine from the bladder into the ureters and
potentially the renal pelvis. This condition is particularly significant because it creates a pathway for
bacteria to ascend to the kidneys during urinary tract infections, increasing the risk of pyelonephritis
and subsequent renal scarring. The diagnosis is suspected in this case based on the history of
recurrent UTIs in a young child.

---

questions.stem: A 21-day-old infant presented with poor weight gain, decreased feeding, fever, and jaundice; urinalysis showing leukocyturia of 20 WBCs/mm3; total bilirubin level, 13 mg/dl and direct bilirubin level, 4 mg/dl Of the following, the MOST appropriate treatment is : (NE)
questions.initialExplanation: A 21-day-old infant with systemic symptoms: treat with IV gentamicin (IV antibiotic for neonatal urosepsis) after culture.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The clinical presentation is classic for neonatal UTI, which differs significantly from UTI in older children and
adults. Neonates do not manifest the localized urinary symptoms that are characteristic of older patients;
instead, they present with nonspecific systemic manifestations including fever or hypothermia, poor feeding,
vomiting, lethargy, irritability, and importantly, jaundice. The association between UTI and jaundice in neonates
is well-recognized and results from the metabolic stress of infection on bilirubin metabolism and conjugation
pathways.

This choice provides the appropriate intravenous route of administration essential for neonatal UTI treatment
while offering excellent coverage against the Gram-negative organisms most commonly responsible for urinary
tract infections in this age group. The combination of IV administration and appropriate antimicrobial spectrum
makes it the most appropriate initial therapy pending culture results and clinical response assessment.

---

questions.stem: An 8-year-old girl presents with 2 days of high fever, chills, right flank pain, vomiting, dysuria, and increased urinary frequency. She appears ill, with a temperature of 39.2°C. Urinalysis reveals pyuria, bacteriuria, and WBC casts. Urine culture results are pending. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.text: Start oral nitrofurantoin and advise close outpatient follow-up

options.label: B
options.text: Admit for intravenous antibiotics and arrange for a renal ultrasound Prescribe a single dose of ceftriaxone and send home

options.label: C
options.text: Arrange a surgical consultation to rule out a possible surgical etiology

options.label: D
options.text: Admit for intravenous fluid and wait for the result of urine culture and sensitivity POO TE

questions.initialExplanation: High fever, flank pain and WBC casts = acute pyelonephritis, so admit and give an IV antibiotic with a kidney ultrasound.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has acute pyelonephritis (high fever, flank pain, WBC casts, systemic symptoms). She
appears toxic and requires hospitalization for IV antibiotics. Renal ultrasound is needed to rule out
obstruction or abscess. Oral nitrofurantoin doesn't achieve adequate renal tissue levels. Waiting for
culture delays treatment of a serious infection.

---

questions.stem: A14-year-old undergoing consolidation therapy for high-risk, chronic lymphocytic leukemia develops burning and discomfort with urination. Urine analysis demonstrates large amount of hemoglobin, along with red and white blood cells. Urine culture is negative. You diagnose the child with hemorrhagic cystitis. Hemorrhagic cystitis is associated most closely with large doses of which of the following? (Lange)
questions.initialExplanation: Hemorrhagic cystitis is linked to high-dose cyclophosphamide (preventable with mesna).
questions.detailedExplanation:
In addition to treating oncologic conditions, cyclophosphamide is used in immunosuppressive
regimens for autoimmune disorders and organ transplantation. High doses of cyclophosphamide
results in bladder epithelial dysplasia, hemorrhagic cystitis, and sterility.

---

questions.stem: A 15-yr-old-girl is admitted with a 5-day history of worsening fever, left flank pain, and vomiting. Physical examination reveals an ill appearing, dehydrated adolescent. Pulse rate is 110/min; temperature is 40°C. Left costovertebral angle tenderness is present. Serum sodium is 131 mmol/L, potassium 6.7 mmol/L, chloride 108 mmol/L, and bicarbonate 15 mmol/L. The most likely diagnosis is: (NE)

options.label: B
options.text: B- Ingestion of high potassium-containing foods

questions.initialExplanation: Fever and flank pain with disturbed electrolytes and acidosis = acute pyelonephritis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This diagnosis best explains the complete clinical presentation including the acute febrile illness,
localized flank pain, costovertebral angle tenderness, and associated gastrointestinal symptoms.
While the electrolyte abnormalities are unusual in severity for uncomplicated pyelonephritis, they can
be explained by the combined effects of dehydration, renal tubular dysfunction secondary to severe
infection, and possible partial urinary tract obstruction. The clinical picture is most consistent with
acute pyelonephritis requiring urgent treatment with intravenous fluids and antibiotics.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old girl presents with a foul-smelling vaginal discharge of 2 weeks' duration. She has a previous history of one urinary tract infection at age 3 years. Of the following, the MOST appropriate next step is : (NE)

options.label: A
options.text: culture of the discharge for respiratory pathogens

options.label: B
options.text: genital examination using the knee-chest position

options.label: D
options.text: sitz baths and application of an estrogen cream

questions.initialExplanation: Foul vaginal discharge in a prepubertal girl: examine the genitalia (frog-leg or knee-chest position) to exclude a foreign body or infection.
questions.detailedExplanation:
A vaginal discharge in a prepubertal girl frequently is accompanied by vulvitis. The evaluation of
vaginal discharge or vulvovaginitis in a prepubertal girl is guided by clues from the history and
findings on physical examination. The clinician must inquire about a history of sexual molestation
or activity, including instrumentation, in all girls who have a vaginal discharge with or without
genital pain, regardless of their age or pubertal status. Although less commonly encountered,
clinicians evaluating males must remember that instrumentation of the penis may cause genital
pain or urethral discharge.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy who has myelomeningocele and a history of recurrent urinary tract infections presents with a 1-day history of a temperature to 102°F (38.9°C) and cloudy urine. Laboratory test results include a peripheral white blood cell count of 15x103/mcL (15x109/L), with 60% neutrophils, 30% lymphocytes, and 10% monocytes. Urine obtained by catheterization is cloudy; has a strong odor; and is positive for nitrites, leukocyte esterase, and blood. Microscopic analysis shows too numerous-to-count white blood cells and 50 to 100 red blood cells, and gram negative bacilli are seen on Gram stain. One day later, the urine culture is positive for Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Of the following, the MOST appropriate antibiotic for treatment of this patient is : (NE) mooOw
questions.initialExplanation: Pseudomonas aeruginosa in the urinary tract: a suitable antibiotic is ceftazidime (anti-pseudomonal cephalosporin).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Pseudomonas sp are gram-negative bacilli that are primarily waterborne and soilborne organisms, have
relatively low virulence, and are associated with a wide variety of infections. Of the pseudomonal species, P
aeruginosa is the most common. It is classified as an opportunistic pathogen infrequently causing disease in
healthy hosts, but it is a major cause of infection in patients who have underlying conditions. Osteomyelitis or
cellulitis associated with a puncture wound and urinary tract infections are the most common diseases caused
by this organism in the otherwise healthy host. Both of these conditions can be treated with a single antibiotic
agent such as a fluoroquinolone (ciprofloxacin) for oral therapy or piperacillin, piperacillin/tazobactam,
ceftazidime, a fluoroquinolone, or an aminoglycoside parenterally. Combination therapy of piperacillin or
ceftazidime plus an aminoglycoside is also appropriate.

> **Note:** Question number inferred from the sequence.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy who has spina bifida has a history of recurrent urinary tract infections (UTIs). He is currently being treated for a UTI. Monitoring laboratory evaluation shows a blood urea nitrogen of 23 mg/dL 8 .2 mmol/L) and a creatinine concentration of 1.1 mg/dL (97.2 mcmol/L). Of the following, the class of antibiotics that is MOST commonly associated with renal toxicity is :
questions.initialExplanation: The antibiotic class most linked to kidney toxicity is the aminoglycosides.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Multiple antibiotic classes can cause renal toxicity, but the class that is the most likely to cause nephrotoxicity
is the aminoglycosides (gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin, streptomycin, and kanamycin). The renal toxicity of
these agents is related to their concentrative uptake by the proximal renal tubular cells and their capacity to
interact with critical intracellular targets. Risk factors associated with the development of such nephrotoxicity
include prolonged course of therapy, supertherapeutic doses, concurrent use of other nephrotoxic
medications, dehydration, and underlying liver disease. The development of nephrotoxicity is characterized by
the gradual onset of partial-to-complete, reversible, nonoliguric renal failure. The patient may exhibit
hypertension, and laboratory evaluation demonstrates elevations in blood urea nitrogen and creatinine values
as well as elevated protein concentrations on urinalysis. Nephrotoxicity rarely is associated with the other
antibiotics listed

> **Note:** Question number inferred from the sequence.

---

questions.stem: A 6-week-old child is being evaluated for a fever of unknown etiology. As part of the laboratory evaluation, a urine specimen was obtained that grew E. coli with a colony count of 2000/uL. These findings would be definite evidence of a urinary tract infection if which of the following is true about the sampled urine? (pretest) No

options.label: A
options.text: It has a specific gravity of 1.008.

options.label: B
options.text: It is from a bag attached to the perineum of an uncircumcised boy.

options.label: C
options.text: It is from an ileal-loop bag.

options.label: D
options.text: It is from a suprapubic tap.

options.label: E
options.text: It is the first morning sample.

questions.initialExplanation: To definitively confirm UTI in a young infant: any positive culture growth from a suprapubic aspirate is considered confirmatory.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The mechanism by which urine is collected is paramount in determining the interpretation of cultures. No
bacteria should grow in a properly obtained urine sample from a suprapubic tap unless infection is present.
For children who undergo bladder catheterization, colony counts of 103 to 104 are considered significant.
lleal-loop bags are usually contaminated and are not useful. Bag specimens in smaller children (obtained by
placing an adhesive, sealed, sterile collection system onto the perineum) can be helpful if the culture is
negative. Contamination is common, especially in girls and in uncircumcised boys; positive cultures in this
latter group of children, especially if they contain more than one organism, are suspect. In properly obtained
midstream clean-catch urines, colony counts greater than 105 in the asymptomatic child and colony counts of
104 in the symptomatic child may be significant. Clean-catch urine samples in an uncircumcised male who
cannot retract the foreskin are also suspect.

---

questions.stem: A 12-day-old infant is found to have poor feeding, irritability, and prolonged jaundice. A urine catheterization is found to be positive for leukocyte esterase and urine culture returns a gram-positive organism to be further identified. He is started on appropriate antibiotics. This neonate was at higher risk for a urinary tract infection because: (Rud)
questions.initialExplanation: Newborn boys are more prone to UTI in the first month (especially uncircumcised).
questions.detailedExplanation:
The infant in the clinical scenario above has a urinary tract infection that will need treatment with IV antibiotics.
Of the risk factors listed, the only one conveying an increased risk of urinary tract infection in the neonatal age
group was being male. This risk factor changes by 1 year of age so that females become the higher-risk group.
Term infants are less likely to have urinary tract infections as compared with preterm infants. Similarly
uncircumcised males are more likely to suffer from UTIs than are their circumcised counterparts (although
possibility of a UTI is not an indication for a circumcision given the low frequency and usually mild nature of the
disease in males). Breast-feeding has not been shown to increase one’s risk of a urinary tract infection and, if
anything, is likely protective. In older adults, blood type B or AB has been shown to predispose individuals to
developing urinary tract infections.

---

questions.stem: After diagnosis and treatment of a recurrent urinary tract infection in a 3-year-old female child, further investigation should include: (CanadaQB)
questions.initialExplanation: After a recurrent first UTI in a girl: renal ultrasound with voiding cystogram to look for anomalies or reflux.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Recurrent UTIs are sometimes seen in conjunction with conditions, such as: vesico-ureteral reflux
(VUR) and hydronephrosis. VUR which is found in 30% to 50% of children diagnosed with a UTI and
is a congenital condition in which urine flows backward from the bladder to the ureters and
sometimes reaches the kidneys. If the urine in the bladder is infected with bacteria, VUR can lead to
pyelonephritis.

Hydronephrosis, which is an enlargement of one or both kidneys due to backup or blockage of urine
flow and is usually caused by severe VUR or a blocked ureter. In children < 5 years old with recurrent
UTI diagnostic workup should include ultrasound and voiding cystourethrogram (choice B).

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old female presents with urinary frequency, dysuria, and fever to 38.8°C (101.8°F). She denies nausea, vomiting, and flank pain. There is no prior history of urinary infection and no family history of urinary tract abnormalities. Urethral catheterization reveals bacteriuria and a urine culture reveals > 100,000 colony-forming units of Escherichia coli. She is started on appropriate antibiotic therapy. She returns after 4 days with no improvement of her symptoms. Which of the following is recommended for this patient? (CanadaQB)

options.label: A
options.text: Renal ultrasonography only if she has recurrent infections

options.label: B
options.text: Renal scintigraphy only if she has recurrent infections

options.label: C
options.text: Renal ultrasonography and cystoscopy only if she has recurrent infections

options.label: D
options.text: Renal ultrasonography for this primary episode of infection

options.label: E
options.text: VCUG for this primary episode of infectio

questions.initialExplanation: Febrile UTI in a young girl: renal ultrasound is advised even after the first episode.
questions.detailedExplanation:
In the first few months of life, the incidence of urinary tract infection (UTI) in boys is higher than that
of girls. However, after that time period, UTIs are much more common in females, with the peak
incidence in the 2- to 3-year range. The clinical presentation of UTI in children is similar to that of
adults, including dysuria, hematuria, frequency, incontinence, suprapubic tenderness, and low-grade
fever. UTI is suggested by high fever, nausea, vomiting, flank pain, and lethargy.

---

questions.stem: A mother complains that her 4-year-old daughter’s urine smells strange. Her urine dipstick is positive for leukocytes and nitrates but negative for blood. The most likely causative organism for her condition is: (CanadaQB)
questions.initialExplanation: Unusual urine smell with positive leukocytes and nitrites = most often E. coli.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This question is testing your knowledge of the epidemiology of childhood UTI’s. Each of the listed
answers causes UTI but E. coli (d) is responsible for 80-90% of UTIs.

The MCCEE and LMCC exams will very often test this kind of knowledge - listing equally plausible
answers in order to test your command of the statistics regarding a particular pathology. Whereas,
the USMLE will typically give you very long stems with various clues as to which answers to consider
(often listing a few unrelated answers/distractors, e.g. they may list some viruses or bacteria that do
not cause UTI’s).

questions.stem: A mother brings her 10-month old boy to the Emergency Department with fever, nausea and vomiting. She mentions that she has used fewer nappies in the past 48 hours because he has been less wet. She also mentions that his urine has an offensive odor. A urine analysis is perfomed that is positive for nitrite and leukocytes consistent with urinary tract infection (UTI). This child has never had an UTI before. Which one of the following is the next best step in management?

options.label: A
options.text: Antibiotics and ultrasound of kidneys, ureter and bladder.

options.label: B
options.text: Antibiotics, intravenous fluids and ultrasound scan of the kidneys, ureter and bladder.

options.label: C
options.text: Antibiotics, oral fluids and discharge home once the child improves.

questions.initialExplanation: A 10-month-old with a first UTI and ill appearance: antibiotic and IV fluids with a kidney ultrasound.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The scenario describes a baby who has developed dehydration (decreased urine output) as a result of vomiting
in the background of UTI. This child needs rehydration as the most appropriate initial management.
Dehydration is an indication for hospital admission and fluid resuscitation. Antibiotics should also be started for
treatment of UTI.

Since this child is younger than 12 months age, he needs an ulrasound as well. It is best to perform the
ultrasound within the first 3 days of presentation. If the child is younger than 1 year, either ultrasound or
micturating cystoureterogram or both can be used to exclude vesicoureteric reflux (VUR). If the child is older
than 1 year, ultrasound is adequate. Early detection of VUR and control of recurrent urinary tract infections
could prevent the development of reflux nephropathy and its complications including hypertension and chronic
renal failure.

---

questions.stem: A 12-year-old child has history of recurrent urinary tract infections since the age of 3 years. Which one of the following is the investigation of choice to exclude renal scarring? moowy
questions.initialExplanation: The DMSA scan is the best test to detect renal scarring.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Recurrent urinary tract infections (more than 2 times during childhood) can result in renal scarring, hypertension, and end-
stage renal disease. The underlying etiology is vesicoureteral reflux (VUR) -retrograde passage of urine from the bladder
into the upper urinary tract.

Dimercaptosuccinic acid scintigraphy (DMSA) scan is the gold standard for diagnosis of kidney scarring and assessment
of renal functions.

DMSA is indicated in the following conditions:

- Clinical suspicion of renal injury

- Reduced renal function

- Suspicion of VUR

- Suspicion of obstructive uropathy on ultrasound in older toilet-trained children

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl is brought into your office for assessment by her parents. She reports dysuria and increased urine frequency for last three days. She denied having any fever or loin pain. Urine microscopy shows 10*5 E.coli, WBC 10x10*5 . Which of the following is first-line treatment recommended for this patient? (MX)
questions.initialExplanation: Per the given answer: trimethoprim is first line, and antibiotic choice depends on local bacterial sensitivity.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This patient has developed clinical symptoms of urinary tract infection. The absence of fever and loin
rules out the possibility of acute pyelonephritis.

The most appropriate first line antibiotics for this child is trimethoprim or cephalexin.

Ceftriaxone is reserved for acute pyelonephritis. The ciprofloxacin and norfloxacin, both are not
recommended as first-line treatment of UTI. However, if the urine microbiology and sensitivity report
suggest resistance to other medication, then fluoroquinolones can be used.

---

questions.stem: An 8-month-old male child is brought to your office with the history of vomiting and diarrhoea. Urine dipstick examination shows a possibility of urinary tract infection. Which of the following is the best next step in management? (MX)

options.label: A
options.text: A- Investigate for sexually transmitted infection

options.label: B
options.text: B- Oral rehydration and discharge home

options.label: D
options.text: D- Give antibiotics and refer for ultrasound

questions.initialExplanation: An 8-month-old with UTI: give an antibiotic and refer for ultrasound.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Urinary tract infections in children usually arise from urogenital abnormalities.So apart from treating
with antibiotics, an ultrasound of kidney, ureter, the bladder should be considered.

In children, less than one year, an ultrasound should be performed first.If the ultrasound is normal,

micturating cystourethrogram (MCU) should be considered.It helps to rule out vesicoureteric reflux.

In children, more than one year of age, only ultrasound is the investigation of choice to rule out
vesicoureteric reflux. The incidence of vesicoureteric reflux is about 40% of suspected cases of
urinary tract infections in children.It causes reflux nephropathy which can cause scarring of kidneys,
hypertension and chronic renal failure.

---

questions.stem: You order an ultrasound scan for a 9-year-old girl, who has been brought for treatment of urinary tract infection for the second time this year. On the ultrasound, the right kidney is reported smaller than the left beyond the normal discrepancy. Which one of the following is the most appropriate investigation to consider for assessment of renal status? (MX)
questions.initialExplanation: Difference in kidney size after recurrent UTI requires DMSA to assess function and scarring.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The dimercaptosuccinic acid scintigraphy(DMSA) scan is the gold standard for diagnosis of kidney
scarring, which can have been resulted from recurrent urinary tract infections.

DMSA is indicated in the following conditions:

- Clinical suspicion of renal injury

- Reduced renal function

- Suspicion of VUR

- Suspicion of obstructive uropathy on ultrasound in older toilet-trained children

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old previously healthy girl, fully toilet-trained, presents with a 3-day history of high fever (maximum 39.2°C), dysuria, urinary frequency, and new-onset daytime urinary incontinence. On physical examination, she is well-appearing with mild suprapubic tenderness but no flank pain, costovertebral angle tenderness, or other focal findings. Urinalysis demonstrates positive leukocyte esterase and nitrites, 15-20 white blood cells per high-power field, and 2+ bacteria; urine culture results are pending. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.text: Admit for intravenous antibiotics with cefotaxime

options.label: B
options.text: Obtain renal ultrasound prior to initiating antibiotics

options.label: C
options.text: Initiate empiric oral antibiotics with outpatient follow-up in 48 hours

options.label: D
options.text: Perform voiding cystourethrogram to assess for vesicoureteral reflux

options.label: E
options.text: Admit for observation and intravenous fluids

questions.initialExplanation: A stable 4-year-old girl with urinary symptoms: start an empirical oral antibiotic and follow up when the culture returns.
questions.detailedExplanation:
his child has uncomplicated acute cystitis with classic presentation including fever, dysuria, urinary
frequency, suprapubic tenderness, and diagnostic urinalysis. She is clinically stable, well-hydrated,
able to tolerate oral intake, and has no signs of sepsis. According to AAP guidelines, children with
uncomplicated cystitis who are stable can be managed as outpatients with empiric oral antibiotics.
Follow-up in 48 hours ensures clinical improvement and allows adjustment based on culture results.
- hospital admission for IV antibiotics is reserved for patients with severe sepsis, inability to tolerate
oral intake, or immunocompromised states. This patient does not meet admission criteria.

---

questions.stem: - An 8-month-old previously healthy female infant presents with a 1-day history of high fever (maximum 40.1°C), decreased oral intake, and increased irritability. She has had only 3 wet diapers per day compared to her baseline of 8-10. Physical examination reveals temperature 39.8°C, heart rate 162 bpm, capillary refill time of 2 seconds, and no focal findings other than mild distress. Catheterized urine specimen shows pyuria (>10 WBC/hpf), positive leukocyte esterase, and Escherichia coli growth exceeding 100,000 colony-forming units per milliliter. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: C
options.text: Observe in the emergency department for 24 hours

options.label: D
options.text: Perform lumbar puncture to rule out meningitis

options.label: E
options.text: Start oral antibiotics with outpatient follow-up in 2 days

questions.initialExplanation: An 8-month-old girl with high fever, dehydration and rapid heart rate: admit and give an IV antibiotic.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This infant is in the high-risk age group (2-12 months) with febrile UTI and signs of systemic illness including
decreased oral intake, decreased wet diapers, and irritability. Infants in this age group are at increased risk for
serious bacterial infections including bacteremia and meningitis. The presentation warrants hospital admission
for IV antibiotics, monitoring, and evaluation for alternative sources of infection. Blood cultures should be
obtained before starting antibiotics.

- Option B is incorrect because outpatient management is inappropriate for infants under 12 months with febrile
UTI due to the risk of serious bacterial illness and inability to reliably monitor for clinical deterioration.

- Option C is incorrect because a brief ED observation is insufficient; this infant requires admission for a full
course of IV antibiotics and monitoring.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy with bilateral grade Ill vesicoureteral reflux diagnosed at 6 months presents for routine follow-up. He has been on trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis since diagnosis with one breakthrough UTI at age 3 requiring hospitalization. Current weight and height are at the 10th percentile. Blood pressure is 102/64 mmHg. Renal ultrasound shows stable size without hydronephrosis. What is the most appropriate next step in management? Nb.
questions.initialExplanation: Bilateral grade III VUR with scarring or treatment failure: refer for surgical evaluation (per the given answer).
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has bilateral grade Ill VUR with breakthrough UTI despite appropriate antibiotic prophylaxis. The
development of breakthrough infection indicates that conservative management is failing. With bilateral disease
and prior hospitalization, referral for surgical evaluation (endoscopic correction or ureteral reimplantation) is
warranted to prevent further renal damage. The goal is to eliminate reflux and prevent recurrent infections.

- Option A is incorrect because continuing current prophylaxis has failed, as evidenced by the breakthrough
UTI. Simply continuing the same approach risks further infections and renal scarring.

- Option B is incorrect because changing antibiotics may be considered but does not address the fundamental
failure of conservative management in preventing breakthrough infections.

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with septic shock. He has a 24-hour history of fever, vomiting, and lethargy. Examination shows temperature 39.5°C, heart rate 150 bpm, blood pressure 95/60 mmHg, and capillary refill 3 seconds. He is lethargic but arousable. Urinalysis shows pyuria and bacteriuria. Blood cultures are obtained. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.text: Start oral antibiotics and discharge home

options.label: B
options.text: Begin fluid resuscitation and obtain IV access immediately

options.label: C
options.text: Perform CT scan before any treatment

options.label: D
options.text: E Wait for culture results before starting antibiotics

questions.initialExplanation: Urinary sepsis with shock: first secure IV access and give fluids (resuscitation), then the antibiotic.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child presents with septic shock secondary to UTI. The immediate priorities are rapid fluid
resuscitation with isotonic crystalloid (20 mL/kg bolus), obtaining IV access, and starting empiric
antibiotics within one hour. Per pediatric advanced life support (PALS) guidelines, sepsis
management requires immediate intervention to restore perfusion and deliver antibiotics promptly.

- Ais incorrect because outpatient management is absolutely contraindicated in a child with septic
shock requiring resuscitation and IV therapy.

- Cis incorrect because CT scan should not delay the initiation of resuscitation and antibiotic therapy.
Imaging can be performed after initial stabilization if indicated.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old girl presents with her third UTI in 8 months. Each infection was associated with fever and flank pain. Renal ultrasound after the second UTI showed mild left renal pelviectasia. She has no history of constipation or bladder dysfunction. What is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?
questions.initialExplanation: Third UTI in 8 months in a girl: do a VCUG to look for VUR.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- The child has recurrent febrile UTIs with documented renal involvement (flank pain, fever) and an abnormal ultrasound
showing pelviectasia. According to AAP guidelines, children with recurrent febrile UTIs or those with abnormal ultrasound
findings should undergo evaluation for vesicoureteral reflux with voiding cystourethrogram. The pelviectasia further raises
‘    suspicion for anatomical abnormalities or VUR requiring evaluation. (A) is incorrect because antibiotic prophylaxis should
not be initiated before completing anatomical evaluation. Management decisions depend on the presence and grade of
VUR.
Option C is incorrect because urodynamic studies are reserved for children with suspected bladder dysfunction or
neurogenic bladder, not indicated here. Option B is incorrect because CT scan involves significant radiation and is not
first-line imaging for recurrent UTIs. Ultrasound and VCUG are appropriate initial studies. Option E is incorrect because
while baseline renal function may be reasonable, it does not replace the need for anatomical evaluation.

---

questions.stem: A 3-month-old infant with first febrile UTI is being discharged home. Temperature during UTI episode was 39.2°C. She is now afebrile with normal examination. Parents ask about follow-up imaging. What is the most appropriate recommendation?

options.label: E
options.text: Obtain renal and bladder ultrasound in 1-2 weeks

questions.initialExplanation: After the first febrile UTI in an infant: renal and bladder ultrasound within 1-2 weeks (per the given answer).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Per AAP 2011 guidelines, infants aged 2-24 months with first-time febrile UTI should undergo renal and
bladder ultrasound. The ultrasound should be performed to detect anatomical abnormalities that may
predispose to recurrent infections or renal damage. It can be arranged after discharge and does not need to
delay discharge in a clinically stable infant.

Option A is incorrect because imaging is indicated after the first febrile UTI in this age group to identify
structural abnormalities. Option B is incorrect because obtaining both studies together is not necessary;
VCUG is only indicated if ultrasound shows abnormalities. Option C is incorrect because VCUG is not
routinely indicated after first febrile UT]; it is reserved for patients with abnormal ultrasound findings or
recurrent febrile UTIs. Option D is incorrect because delaying imaging until 12 months would miss the
window for detecting anatomical abnormalities during early infancy.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl with first UTI presents with fever, dysuria, and frequency. Urine culture grows E. coli susceptible to cephalosporins. She is clinically stable, tolerating oral intake. Examination shows mild suprapubic tenderness. What is the most appropriate antibiotic duration?
questions.initialExplanation: Duration of treatment for a first febrile UTI in a girl: 7-14 days.
questions.detailedExplanation:
For children 2 years and older with acute cystitis/pyelonephritis, the recommended antibiotic duration is 7-14
days. Younger children and those with pyelonephritis features may require longer courses (10-14 days), while
simple cystitis in older children and adolescents can be treated with shorter courses.

Option A is incorrect because 3-day courses are typically reserved for older adolescents and adults with
uncomplicated cystitis. Option B is incorrect because 4-6 week courses are reserved for complicated
infections, abscesses, or immunocompromised patients.

Option C is incorrect because 21-day courses are not standard and would expose patients unnecessarily to
antibiotics. Option E is incorrect because single-dose therapy is not appropriate for children with
pyelonephritis symptoms.

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy presents with acute pyelonephritis not responding to appropriate antibiotics. He has persistent fever and flank tenderness after 72 hours of therapy. Blood cultures are negative. What is the most appropriate next step in evaluation? moow»
questions.initialExplanation: No improvement after 72 hours on antibiotics: look for complications such as abscess; contrast CT is an option per the given answer (ultrasound is often preferred first).
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has persistent fever and flank tenderness despite appropriate antibiotics for acute pyelonephritis.
Lack of clinical improvement after 72 hours raises concern for complications such as renal or perinephric

abscess, emphysematous pyelonephritis, or obstructive uropathy. CT with contrast is the imaging modality of
choice for evaluating these complications.

Option A is incorrect because continuing current therapy without evaluation risks missing complications that
require intervention. Option C is incorrect because nuclear scan (DMSA) is used for detecting renal scarring,
not for acute complications. Option D is incorrect because there is no evidence of resistant organism; imaging
should guide further management. Option E is incorrect because while urine culture should be repeated,
imaging is needed to evaluate for complications.

---

questions.stem: A 10-year-old girl presents with dysuria, frequency, and suprapubic pain for 4 days. Similar symptoms occurred 3 months ago. Examination shows mild suprapubic tenderness. Urinalysis shows positive leukocyte esterase, 10-15 WBC/hpf, and 2+ bacteria. What is the most appropriate antibiotic choice?
questions.initialExplanation: Uncomplicated cystitis in an older girl: nitrofurantoin for 5 days is suitable.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This patient has uncomplicated cystitis, and nitrofurantoin is appropriate first-line therapy. It achieves high

urinary concentrations with excellent activity against common uropathogens. The 5-day course is appropriate
for uncomplicated cystitis.

Option B is incorrect because trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole resistance in E. coli has increased significantly
(often >20%), making nitrofurantoin more reliable. Option C is incorrect because fluoroquinolones are reserved
for complicated infections or when other agents are contraindicated. Option D is incorrect because cephalexin
requires four-times-daily dosing, which may affect adherence. Option E is incorrect because amoxicillin has
high resistance rates among uropathogens and is no longer first-line.

---

questions.stem: An 8-month-old infant presents with a 1-day history of high fever (40.1°C), decreased oral intake, and increased irritability. She has had only 3 wet diapers daily versus her usual 8-10. Examination shows lethargy, temperature 39.8°C, and tachycardia (162 bpm). Capillary refill is 2 seconds. Catheterized urine specimen reveals pyuria, positive leukocyte esterase, and E. coli >100,000 CFU/mL. What is the most significant risk factor for serious bacterial infection in this infant?
questions.initialExplanation: Per the given answer, the riskiest factor for severe bacterial infection in infants is female sex (the usual explanation is young age and high fever).
questions.detailedExplanation:
In infants **beyond the neonatal period **(>28 days), female gender is the most significant risk factor
for urinary tract infection and UTI-related serious bacterial infection. This is due to anatomical factors:
Shorter urethra facilitating ascending bacterial colonizationProximity of urethral meatus to anus,
increasing exposure to fecal flora (e.g., E. coli)Absence of prostatic antibacterial secretions (present
in males)

This 8-month-old girl's confirmed E. coli UTI aligns with the well-established epidemiology: after the
first month of life, females have a 4- 10x higher incidence of UTI than males. Female gender is
therefore the most relevant and significant risk factor in this clinical scenario.

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with septic shock. He has a 24-hour history of fever, vomiting, and lethargy. Examination shows temperature 39.5°C, heart rate 150 bpm, blood pressure 95/60 mmHg, and capillary refill 3 seconds. He is lethargic but arousable. Laboratory studies reveal WBC 18,000/uL with left shift, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, and CRP 120 mg/L. Urinalysis shows pyuria and bacteriuria. Blood cultures are obtained. Which factor is the strongest predictor of renal scarring in this patient?
questions.initialExplanation: The strongest predictor of renal scarring is delay in starting the antibiotic.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Multiple studies have demonstrated that delayed treatment of acute pyelonephritis significantly increases the risk of renal
scarring. The risk of permanent renal damage is highest when antibiotic therapy is initiated more than 48-72 hours after
symptom onset. Early antibiotic treatment limits bacterial invasion duration and renal parenchymal inflammation, thereby
reducing tissue damage. This emphasizes the critical importance of early recognition and prompt treatment of UTIs in
children.

Option A is incorrect because while high fever indicates severe infection, it is not as strongly predictive of scarring as the
timing of antibiotic initiation. Option B is incorrect because delayed presentation contributes to delayed treatment, but the
modifiable factor is the timeliness of antibiotic administration.

Option C is incorrect because elevated CRP is a marker of inflammation severity but is not as strongly predictive of
scarring as treatment timing. Option E is incorrect because while prior UTI is a risk factor for additional scarring, the timing
of treatment in the current episode is the most significant modifiable factor.

---

questions.stem: A 3-month-old infant with first febrile UTI is evaluated per AAP guidelines. She was born at term and has been otherwise healthy. Temperature during UTI episode was 39.2°C. She is now afebrile with normal examination. Weight is at the 50th percentile. What is the recommended imaging according to current guidelines? RB

options.label: B
options.text: Obtain renal and bladder ultrasound now

options.label: D
options.text: Obtain ultrasound only after third UTI

questions.initialExplanation: A 3-month-old with a first febrile UTI: kidney and bladder ultrasound now per guidelines.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Per AAP 2011 guidelines (reaffirmed in updates), infants aged 2-24 months with first-time febrile UTI should
undergo renal and bladder ultrasound to detect anatomical abnormalities. This infant is within the 2-24 month
age range with documented febrile UTI. Ultrasound identifies structural abnormalities such as hydronephrosis,
stones, or masses that may predispose to recurrent infections or renal damage.

- Option A is incorrect because imaging is indicated after the first febrile UTI in this age group regardless of
duration or severity. Option C is incorrect because VCUG is not routinely indicated after first febrile UTI; it is
reserved for patients with abnormal ultrasound findings suggesting high-grade VUR, hydronephrosis, or for
those with recurrent febrile UTls. Option D is incorrect because waiting until the third febrile UTI delays
ultrasound evaluation beyond recommended timeframes. Option E is incorrect because delaying imaging until
after 12 months would miss the window for detecting anatomical abnormalities during early infancy.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the clinic with dysuria and frequency for 2 days. He has no fever and appears well. His past medical history is unremarkable. Physical examination is normal except for mild suprapubic tenderness. Urinalysis shows 5-10 WBC/hpf, positive leukocyte esterase, and negative nitrites. Serum creatinine is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Urinary symptoms with few WBCs, negative nitrite and normal creatinine = acute cystitis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child presents with lower urinary tract symptoms (dysuria, frequency) without fever or systemic
signs, localizing to the bladder. The urinalysis shows pyuria but not the marked findings seen in
pyelonephritis. The absence of fever and the localization to suprapubic area strongly suggest cystitis
rather than upper tract infection. Urethritis would typically present with urethral discharge, which is
absent. Vaginitis would cause vaginal discharge and itching, not seen here. Renal calculi would
cause flank pain and hematuria, which are not present.

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy is diagnosed with his first febrile UTI. His mother inquires about the risk of permanent renal damage from this infection. What percentage of children develop renal scarring following a febrile UTI?
questions.initialExplanation: Renal scarring occurs in about 10-15% of children after the first febrile UTI.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Studies demonstrate that renal scarring occurs in approximately 10-15% of children following a febrile
urinary tract infection. This percentage increases with recurrent infections, delayed initiation of
appropriate antibiotic therapy, and the presence of vesicoureteral reflux. The development of renal
cortical scarring is clinically significant as it may predispose to long-term complications including
hypertension and progressive chronic kidney disease. Children with high-grade vesicoureteral reflux
have an elevated risk of scarring, with rates reported between 20-40%. The identification of risk
factors and prompt treatment may reduce but not eliminate this complication.

---

questions.stem: A 9-year-old girl presents with dysuria, frequency, and gross hematuria for 5 days. She has no fever but reports mild suprapubic pain. Urinalysis shows numerous red blood cells, 20-25 white blood cells, positive leukocyte esterase, and negative nitrites. Urine culture is negative. She reports similar episodes on two previous occasions, each resolving spontaneously. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Blood in urine with dysuria that resolves spontaneously = acute hemorrhagic cystitis (often viral, e.g., adenovirus).
questions.detailedExplanation:
This clinical presentation is most consistent with acute hemorrhagic cystitis, characterized by dysuria,
frequency, gross hematuria, and sterile pyuria. The recurrent, self-limiting nature of the episodes and
the absence of nitrites (suggesting atypical organisms or non-bacterial etiology) support this
diagnosis. IgA nephropathy typically presents with hematuria concurrent with or following an upper
respiratory infection but is usually not associated with significant dysuria or pyuria. Urolithiasis would
typically cause more severe pain and is not characteristically recurrent. Interstitial cystitis is rare in
children and typically presents with chronic symptoms. Bladder tumors are extremely uncommon in
the pediatric population and would not typically present with recurrent, self-limiting episodes.

## Acute Renal Failure

> Question numbers not present in the source file for this topic: 20.

questions.stem: During evaluation of a girl with acute kidney injury, the laboratory and clinical results reveal low urine output, elevated renal function tests, and normal renal ultrasound. Which of the following causes her acute kidney injury?
questions.initialExplanation: Oliguria and raised kidney function with a normal duplex/ultrasound suggests a prerenal cause (low perfusion).
questions.detailedExplanation:
In a child presenting with acute kidney injury (AKI), the initial classification is based on anatomic location: prerenal, intrinsic renal, or
postrenal.

Key findings in this case:

- Low urine output (oliguria), Elevated renal function tests (e.g., serum creatinine and blood urea nitrogen), Normal renal ultrasound
- A normal renal ultrasound effectively rules out postrenal causes, such as urinary tract obstruction (e.g., posterior urethral valves,
ureteral stones, or bilateral hydronephrosis), which would typically show hydronephrosis or hydroureter.

This leaves prerenal and intrinsic causes.

-Prerenal AKI is due to reduced renal perfusion (e.g., volume depletion, sepsis, heart failure, or hypotension) without structural kidney
damage. It is the most common cause of AKI in children.

In prerenal AKI:

- The kidneys are structurally intact. - Imaging (e.g., renal ultrasound) is normal. - Urine studies (not provided here but often helpful)
would show high urine specific gravity, low fractional excretion of sodium (FeNa <1%), and absence of casts.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy with nephrotic syndrome who is on steroid therapy presented with abdominal pain and distension for the last 2 days. On examination he is feverish with tender abdomen and absent bowel sounds. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.initialExplanation: A nephrotic child on steroids with fever, abdominal pain and absent bowel sounds = spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This case highlights a critical and potentially life-threatening complication in children with nephrotic syndrome:
spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP). Understanding the pathophysiology, clinical presentation, and urgency
of this condition is essential for anyone caring for patients with nephrotic syndrome.

The patient is a 3-year-old boy with nephrotic syndrome currently on steroid therapy. This background is highly
relevant because children with nephrotic syndrome have profound alterations in their immune function that
predispose them to serious infections. The pathophysiology involves urinary loss of immunoglobulins
(particularly IgG), complement factors, and other immune proteins, leading to impaired humoral immunity.
Additionally, steroid therapy causes further immunosuppression through multiple mechanisms including
inhibition of neutrophil function, reduced T-cell activity, and impaired macrophage function.

---

questions.stem: A 10-year-old with acute kidney injury from post-infectious glomerulonephritis develops worsening metabolic acidosis (pH 7.12, HCOs~ 10 mEq/L) despite IV bicarbonate. He becomes progressively lethargic and tachypneic, with rising urea and creatinine, and is now oliguric. Exam shows facial puffiness and mild pulmonary crackles. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.initialExplanation: AKI after glomerulonephritis with edema and fluid overload (pulmonary edema) needs dialysis; start peritoneal dialysis if drug treatment fails.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has severe AKI with refractory metabolic acidosis (pH 7.12), oliguria, rising uremic markers,
fluid overload (pulmonary crackles, facial puffiness), and altered mental status. These are absolute
indications for dialysis. IV fluids would worsen overload; acetazolamide is contraindicated in acidosis;
steroids and antibiotics don't address the acute renal failure.

---

questions.stem: A 2 yr old boy is admitted to the intensive care unit with severe dehydration from bacterial gastroenteritis. Initial laboratory work reveals BUN of 80 mg/dL and serum creatinine of 2.5 mg/dL. With rehydration, his BUN and creatinine fall to 20 mg/dL and 0.5 mg/dL in 2 days. The most likely diagnosis is: (NE)
questions.initialExplanation: Raised BUN and creatinine with severe dehydration, improving with fluid replacement over two days = prerenal acute renal failure.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Prerenal ARF, also called prerenal azotemia, is characterized by diminished effective circulating
arterial volume, which leads to inadequate renal perfusion and a decreased GFR. Evidence of kidney
damage is absent. Common causes of prerenal ARF include dehydration, sepsis, hemorrhage,
severe hypoalbuminemia, and cardiac failure. If the underlying cause of the renal hypoperfusion is

reversed promptly, renal function returns to normal. If hypoperfusion is sustained, intrinsic renal
parenchymal damage can develop.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl is hospitalized with severe dehydration due to gastroenteritis. Labs show blood urea 120 mg/dL and creatinine 1 mg/dL. After rehydration, urea dropped to 20 mg/dL and creatinine to 0.4 mg/dL within 48 hours. She has no hematuria or thrombocytopenia and maintains adequate urine output. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Severe dehydration with diarrhea, no blood in urine, no thrombocytopenia and good urine output = prerenal.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The rapid normalization of renal function after rehydration is the key finding. Prerenal AKI results
