from decreased renal perfusion (dehydration) and is fully reversible with fluid resuscitation. The
BUN:Cr ratio >20:1 (120:1 = 120) also supports prerenal cause. ATN would show slower recovery;
HUS requires thrombocytopenia and hemolysis; AGN shows hematuria.

---

questions.stem: A previously healthy 6 yr old child presents to the emergency department with 3-day history of malaise, poor oral intake, diarrhea, and decreased urine output. Physical examination reveals tachycardia, dry mucous membranes, and sunken eyes. Results of initial laboratory studies include BUN 65 mg/dL, potassium 5.5 mEq/L, bicarbonate 14 mEq/L, and serum creatinine 3.0 mg/dL. The most appropriate next step in treatment is to: (NE)

options.label: C
options.text: Run intravenous replacement fluid at rate to replace insensible losses plus urine output

options.label: D
options.text: Give NaHCOS3 1 mEqg/kg IV to correct acidosis

options.label: E
options.text: Administer normal saline 20 mL/kg bolus over 30 min

questions.initialExplanation: Acidosis and raised creatinine after dehydration: replace volume with NS 20 mL/kg over 30 minutes before any other step.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Prerenal ARF, also called prerenal azotemia, is characterized by diminished effective circulating
arterial volume, which leads to inadequate renal perfusion and a decreased GFR. Evidence of
kidney damage is absent. Common causes of prerenal ARF include dehydration, sepsis,
hemorrhage, severe hypoalbuminemia, and cardiac failure. If the underlying cause of the renal
hypoperfusion is reversed promptly, renal function returns to normal. If hypoperfusion is sustained,
intrinsic renal parenchymal damage can develop.

---

questions.stem: A male newborn infant is delivered by emergency cesarean section for severe fetal distress and placental abruption. Resuscitation is required in the delivery room. The infant develops gross hematuria and oliguric acute renal failure with a peak serum creatinine level of 8.0 mg/dL at 8 days of age. The most likely cause of the infant's acute renal failure is: (NE)
questions.initialExplanation: A newborn after emergency cesarean who suffered asphyxia: the cause of renal failure is cortical necrosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
In newborns, cortical necrosis is most commonly associated with hypoxic or ischemic insults caused
by perinatal asphyxia, placental abruption, and twin-twin or fetal-maternal transfusion. Other causes
include renal vascular thrombosis and severe congenital heart disease. Cortical necrosis manifests
as acute renal failure in patients who have the previously mentioned predisposing causes. Urine
output is diminished and gross and/or microscopic hematuria may be present. Hypertension is
common, and thrombocytopenia may be present as a result of renal microvascular injury. Laboratory
results are consistent with acute renal failure: an elevated blood urea nitrogen (BUN) and creatinine,
hyperkalemia, and metabolic acidosis. Anemia and thrombocytopenia are common. Urinalysis reveals
hematuria and proteinuria.

---

questions.stem: A previously healthy 2-year-old boy is brought into the Emergency Department with a 3-day history of nonbilious and nonbloody vomiting and diarrhea. He has refused PO intake aside from occasional sips of juice and water. He has made little urine output in the last 12 hours. On physical exam, he is afebrile with a HR of 130. A blood pressure cannot be be taken. Laboratory results reveal a BUN of 60, creatinine of 1.7, and a bicarbonate level of 14. What is the most appropriate first step? (Rud)

options.label: C
options.text: 20 mL/kg bolus of intravenous normal saline

questions.initialExplanation: Dehydration, raised BUN and acidosis: the first step is volume replacement with IV NS 20 mL/kg.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child presents with severe hypovolemic shock and prerenal acute kidney injury secondary to
gastroenteritis. Clinical signs (tachycardia, unobtainable blood pressure, oliguria, poor perfusion) and
laboratory findings (BUN/Cr ratio ~35:1, elevated creatinine, metabolic acidosis) all point to profound
intravascular volume depletion.

Per Pediatric Advanced Life Support (PALS) and pediatric nephrology guidelines, the immediate first step in
any hemodynamically unstable or poorly perfused child is rapid volume resuscitation with an isotonic
crystalloid bolus: normal saline or lactated Ringer's at 20 mL/kg IV over 15-30 minutes. This restores renal
perfusion, reverses prerenal azotemia, and often rapidly improves urine output and mental status. Perfusion
should be reassessed after each bolus; additional boluses may be given if shock persists.

---

questions.stem: A 13-year-old previously healthy male presents to the emergency department with back pain that developed after a grueling cross-country race. In the emergency department, he is given a dose of Ketorolac for his pain. Serum chemistries are then performed, which are notable for a BUN of 49 and a serum creatinine concentration of 2.1 mg/dL. Which of the following is correct regarding this patient’s kidney injury? (Rud)

options.label: A
options.text: Urine sediment is likely to contain red blood cell casts

options.label: B
options.text: Urine specific gravity of >1020 would be consistent with an intrinsic renal etiology for acute kidney injury

options.label: C
options.text: Volume resuscitation should be avoided as this patient will likely be oliguric

options.label: D
options.text: A calculated fractional excretion of sodium <1% would be consistent with a prerenal etiology of acute kidney injury

options.label: E
options.text: Appropriate choice of intravenous fluids would be 2 NS with 20 mEq KCI/L and 1.5 times maintenance rate

questions.initialExplanation: In prerenal AKI the fractional excretion of sodium is below 1% because the kidney retains sodium.
questions.detailedExplanation:
etiology of acute kidney injury

This patient’s history of volume depletion from his grueling cross-country race and renal
vasoconstriction from administration of a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory agent are consistent with a
prerenal etiology for his acute kidney injury. Additional diagnostic features that would be consistent
with a prerenal etiology would include a relatively bland urine sediment (eg, only granular or waxy
casts, but no red blood cell casts), a urine specific gravity of >1020, and a fractional excretion of
sodium that is <1%. Initial management of this patient should include prompt fluid resuscitation with
normal saline. Potassium-containing fluids should be avoided as GFR is decreased and tubular
secretion of potassium may be impaired.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy is admitted with a provisional diagnosis of acute renal failure. The laboratory calls you to report that his serum potassium level is 7.5 mmol/L. Which one of the following should be your next investigation? (CanadaQB)
questions.initialExplanation: Potassium 7.5 threatens the heart, so the first test is an ECG to assess risk.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Hyperkalemia is serum K concentration > 5.5 mEq/L resulting from excess total body K stores or
abnormal movement of K out of cells. The usual cause is impairment of renal excretion; it can also
occur in metabolic acidosis as in uncontrolled diabetes. Clinical manifestations are generally

neuromuscular, resulting in muscle weakness and cardiac toxicity that, if severe, can degenerate
to ventricular fibrillation or asystole.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy presents with vomiting, lethargy, and decreased urine output for 2 days. He has a history of severe gastroenteritis with watery diarrhea. Physical examination reveals dry mucous membranes, tachycardia, and poor skin turgor. Laboratory studies show BUN 45 mg/dL, creatinine 1.8 mg/dL, and urine specific gravity 1.030. What is the most likely diagnosis? (MX)
questions.initialExplanation: Vomiting, lethargy, concentrated urine (SG 1.030) and raised BUN = prerenal azotemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The clinical presentation is consistent with prerenal azotemia resulting from volume depletion due to
gastroenteritis. The elevated BUN to creatinine ratio (greater than 20:1), concentrated urine (high
specific gravity), and clinical signs of hypovolemia support reduced renal perfusion as the primary
abnormality. Prerenal states are the most common cause of acute kidney injury in children and are
typically reversible with fluid resuscitation. Acute tubular necrosis would present with isosthenuria
(fixed specific gravity around 1.010) and muddy brown casts. Interstitial nephritis typically presents
with allergic features and hematuria. Postrenal obstruction would show hydronephrosis on imaging.
Glomerulonephritis would typically present with hematuria, hypertension, and proteinuria.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy is receiving gentamicin for severe sepsis. On day 7 of treatment, his serum creatinine rises from 0.4 mg/dL to 1.2 mg/dL with a corresponding decrease in urine output.

options.label: A
options.text: Urinalysis reveals muddy brown granular casts. What is the most likely diagnosis? (MX)

questions.initialExplanation: Rising creatinine and oliguria on day 7 of gentamicin = acute tubular necrosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This presentation is consistent with aminoglycoside-induced acute tubular necrosis. The temporal
relationship with gentamicin exposure, rising creatinine, oliguria, and characteristic urinary sediment
(muddy brown granular casts) are diagnostic features. Aminoglycosides accumulate in renal proximal
tubular cells causing direct toxic injury. Prerenal azotemia would improve with fluid resuscitation.
Acute interstitial nephritis typically presents with fever, rash, and eosinophilia. Postrenal obstruction
would show hydronephrosis on imaging. Glomerulonephritis would show red blood cell casts and
significant proteinuria.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy presents with hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury following a diarrheal illness. Peripheral blood smear shows schistocytes, and LDH is markedly elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis? (MX)
questions.initialExplanation: Hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia and schistocytes after diarrhea = HUS.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This presentation is classic for hemolytic uremic syndrome, characterized by the triad of
microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury. The typical
(diarrhea-associated) form is preceded by an enteric infection, often with E. coli O157:H7. The
presence of schistocytes and elevated LDH confirms microangiopathic hemolytic process. DIC
would have abnormal coagulation studies. TTP typically occurs in older children and adults with
neurological manifestations predominating. ITP isolated would not have hemolysis or renal
involvement. Evans syndrome is autoimmune hemolytic anemia with thrombocytopenia without
microangiopathic features.

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy with acute kidney injury is found to have hyperkalemia with serum potassium of 6.8 mEq/L. The electrocardiogram shows tall peaked T waves. What is the most immediate therapeutic intervention?
questions.initialExplanation: Hyperkalemia with ECG changes: the first action is IV calcium gluconate to protect the heart.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Calcium gluconate is the most immediate therapy for hyperkalemia with electrocardiographic
changes. It stabilizes the cardiac membrane and protects against life-threatening arrhythmias within
minutes of administration. The other measures (bicarbonate, insulin-glucose, kayexalate, dialysis)
work by shifting potassium intracellularly or enhancing elimination but do not provide immediate
cardiac protection. This sequence of management is critical in preventing fatal cardiac complications
of hyperkalemia.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy with acute kidney injury and hyperkalemia (K+ 7.2 mEq/L) has received calcium gluconate with stabilization of cardiac membrane. His ECG now shows narrowing QRS complex. What is the most appropriate next step to lower serum potassium?
questions.initialExplanation: After calcium, to lower potassium quickly give insulin with glucose (moves K into cells).
questions.detailedExplanation:
After stabilizing the cardiac membrane with calcium, the next priority is to shift potassium intracellularly
to rapidly reduce serum levels. The combination of regular insulin with glucose is an effective and
rapid-acting intervention that drives potassium into cells. Insulin promotes cellular uptake of potassium
via the sodium-potassium ATPase pump. Salbutamol also shifts potassium but is typically used as

adjunctive therapy. Sodium bicarbonate is less effective and has variable results. Dialysis is reserved
for refractory cases.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl with acute kidney injury, altered mental status, and seizures is evaluated for dialysis indication. Which of the following is the most appropriate indication for dialysis in this patient?
questions.initialExplanation: Dialysis indications: neurological symptoms of uremia (seizure, altered consciousness), fluid overload, and hyperkalemia or acidosis refractory to treatment.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Neurological symptoms including altered mental status and seizures due to uremic encephalopathy
are clear indications for dialysis initiation. While other parameters (BUN, creatinine, acidosis) guide
management decisions, the presence of uremic symptoms takes precedence as these are
manifestations of severe uremic toxicity that require immediate intervention. The KDIGO guidelines
emphasize clinical symptoms over laboratory thresholds for dialysis initiation in many cases. Waiting
for specific BUN thresholds in the presence of neurological symptoms would be inappropriate.

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy has recovered from acute kidney injury following acute tubular necrosis. His mother asks about the prognosis for renal function recovery. What is the most accurate statement regarding prognosis?

options.label: A
options.text: Recovery is likely with ATN as the etiology

options.label: B
options.text: Recovery of renal function is unlikely

options.label: C
options.text: Recovery depends on the duration of oliguria

options.label: D
options.text: Recovery is only partial in most cases

questions.initialExplanation: Most children with ATN recover well, and the prognosis is generally good.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Recovery of renal function is likely following acute tubular necrosis, which is a reversible form of
acute kidney injury with appropriate supportive care. Unlike intrinsic renal diseases that may cause
permanent damage, ATN typically has good recovery potential as the tubular cells regenerate. The
prognosis for ATN is generally favorable, with most patients returning to baseline renal function.
The degree of recovery may be influenced by the duration and severity of injury, but complete or
near-complete recovery is the rule rather than the exception.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy receives a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug for fever. Two weeks later, he develops fever, rash, and acute kidney injury with white blood cells in urine. What is the most likely etiology?
questions.initialExplanation: Fever, rash, oliguria and WBCs two weeks after an NSAID = acute interstitial nephritis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Acute interstitial nephritis is a hypersensitivity reaction commonly associated with NSAIDs and
antibiotics. The classic triad includes fever, rash, and renal dysfunction, though all three may not
be present. The presence of white blood cells in urine (including eosinophils) supports the
diagnosis. This is an intrinsic renal cause of AKI.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old girl with acute kidney injury receives fluid challenge with normal saline 20 mL/kg over 1 hour followed by furosemide 2 mg/kg IV. Her urine output does not increase significantly. What is the most appropriate action?
questions.initialExplanation: No response to fluids and a diuretic suggests established structural AKI; stop the diuretic and manage fluids carefully (per the given answer).
questions.detailedExplanation:
When there is no response to a diuretic challenge (fluid challenge with furosemide), further diuretic
therapy is unlikely to be beneficial and should be discontinued. The lack of response suggests that
the underlying renal injury requires alternative management strategies, potentially including dialysis
if clinically indicated. Continuing ineffective diuretics may lead to toxicity without therapeutic benefit.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy with no past medical history is brought in after 24 hours of anuria, abdominal pain, and vomiting. He was well until yesterday when he ingested an unknown household chemical while unsupervised. He is tachycardic and has diffuse abdominal tenderness. Serum creatinine is 3.1 mg/dL, K* is 6.5 mEq/L, and urinalysis shows granular casts. Renal ultrasound is normal. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.initialExplanation: AKI after dehydration with granular casts and need for urgent intervention: in this question the answer is emergency dialysis (when clear indications such as hyperkalemia or acidosis exist).
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child likely ingested ethylene glycol or oxalate-containing cleaner, causing acute tubular necrosis

(ATN) and severe AKI with life-threatening hyperkalemia (K* 6.5) and anuria. Emergent hemodialysis
is indicated for refractory hyperkalemia, severe acidosis, volume overload, or uremia. Furosemide (A)
is ineffective in anuric ATN. Bicarbonate (C) may temporize acidosis but doesn’t address the core
problem. CT (D) is unnecessary — ultrasound is normal, ruling out obstruction. NAC (E) is for
acetaminophen toxicity, not relevant here.

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy is brought in with decreased urine output for 2 days. His mother reports he had vomiting and diarrhea 4 days ago but has been drinking well since. On exam, he is alert, with moist mucous membranes and normal skin turgor. Serum creatinine is 1.8 mg/dL, BUN 48 mg/dL, and fractional excretion of sodium (FeNa) is 0.5%. Urine osmolality is 650 mOsm/kg. What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.initialExplanation: FeNa 0.5% and concentrated urine (650) mean prerenal, so give an NS bolus.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Despite apparent rehydration, the low FeNa (<1%) and high urine osmolality (>500) indicate persistent
prerenal azotemia, likely from inadequate intravascular volume despite oral intake. In young children,
ongoing insensible losses or third-spacing may persist. An IV normal saline bolus is appropriate to
assess reversibility. Oral rehydration (B) may be insufficient. Biopsy (C) is not needed. Furosemide (D)
masks volume status and is contraindicated. Observation (E) risks progression to ATN.

---

questions.stem: A 1-year-old infant is brought in with poor feeding, irritability, and decreased wet diapers. He was born at 28 weeks’ gestation and has chronic lung disease. He is currently on indomethacin for patent ductus arteriosus. Labs show creatinine 1.9 mg/dL, Na* 125 mEq/L, and urine output <0.5 mL/kg/hr. Renal ultrasound is unremarkable. What is the most likely mechanism of AKI?
questions.initialExplanation: NSAIDs cause AKI by constricting the afferent arteriole and lowering filtration pressure.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Indomethacin (an NSAID) inhibits prostaglandin synthesis, which in neonates and preterm infants
causes afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction, reducing renal perfusion and causing functional AKI.
This is especially dangerous in those with compromised renal reserve (e.g., prematurity). It mimics
prerenal AKI but is unresponsive to fluids and may progress to ATN. Prerenal (A) is possible but
less likely given indomethacin use. ATN (B) would follow prolonged ischemia. DI (C) causes
polyuria, not oliguria. Obstruction (E) is ruled out by ultrasound.

---

questions.stem: You are called to evaluate a male infant at 50 hours of age because he has not voided. He was born at term and has breastfed poorly, but has passed stool. He appears uncomfortable on physical examination, with a large abdomen and seemingly palpable bladder. There is no respiratory distress. The external genitalia are normal, and both testes descended. Of the following, the MOST appropriate initial step in this infant's evaluation is : (NE)
questions.initialExplanation: A male newborn at 50 hours with no urine: the first step is a urinary catheter to assess for obstruction/retention.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The causes of acute renal failure (ARF) in the newborn include: dehydration, sepsis, congestive heart failure, toxic effects of certain
drugs (angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, indomethacin, amphotericin), acute tubular necrosis, congenital renal dysplasia, renal
vein thrombosis, and obstructive uropathies (posterior urethral valves, neurogenic bladder, bilateral ureteropelvic junction or
ureterovesical junction obstruction). The infant described in the vignette, who has not passed urine 50 hours after birth and who has a
palpably full bladder, should be evaluated thoroughly. Anuria in a newborn for more than 24 hours warrants an evaluation that includes
a thorough history (including obstetric history and drug exposure), review of any prenatal ultrasonography images, assessment for
evidence of perinatal asphyxia or sepsis, and a family history of renal disease. The physical examination should address the genitalia,
abdomen, and flanks as well as any signs of edema or oligohydramnios sequence. Laboratory evaluation should attend to serum
electrolytes, urea nitrogen and creatinine, urinalysis, urine culture, and urinary electrolytes and creatinine. To obtain urine and
complete the evaluation of the patient, a urinary catheter must be placed. Doing so will answer two questions:

+ Are the urethra and bladder outlet patent or obstructed?

+ Have the kidneys produced any urine?

Acute Renal Failure    A

---

## Nephrotic Syndrome

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy presents with gradually worsening swelling around the eyes. He has no fever or hematuria. On examination, he has generalized edema including ascites and bilateral pitting edema of the lower limbs, while his blood pressure is within normal limits. Urinalysis reveals 4+ proteinuria, no hematuria, and a specific gravity of 1.030. Laboratory investigations show a serum albumin of 1.8 g/dL and total cholesterol of 310 mg/dL. Which of the following findings is most consistent with the underlying diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Periorbital edema, heavy proteinuria and high cholesterol in a 3-year-old = nephrotic syndrome (usually minimal change), with normal kidney function.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This is classic Minimal Change Disease (MCD), the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in
children. Key features: age 1-6 years, heavy proteinuria (4+), hypoalbuminemia, hyperlipidemia,
normal BP, no hematuria. In MCD, renal function remains normal. Complement levels are normal,
ANA is negative, ultrasound is typically normal, and biopsy shows only foot process effacement (no
crescents).

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy with steroid-dependent nephrotic syndrome presents with fever and abdominal pain. Examination shows moderate ascites and abdominal tenderness. Ascitic fluid analysis reveals 500 leukocytes/uL. What is the most likely microorganism to be isolated from the ascitic fluid? 2025 <j
questions.initialExplanation: Spontaneous peritonitis (SBP) in nephrotic syndrome is usually caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae due to loss of antibodies.
questions.detailedExplanation:
In children with nephrotic syndrome, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) is a serious complication due to
urinary loss of immunoglobulins and complement factors, particularly factor B, impairing opsonization.
Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common pathogen isolated in nephrotic SBP, classically presenting
with fever, abdominal pain, ascites, and tenderness. The ascitic fluid leukocyte count >250/uL with neutrophil
predominance confirms the diagnosis. E. coli is more common in adult cirrhotic SBP, while S. epidermidis
typically causes catheter-related infections. S. viridans and Enterococcus are less frequent etiologies in this
context. Immediate empiric antibiotic therapy with a third-generation cephalosporin (e.g., ceftriaxone) is
essential while awaiting culture results. Prompt treatment prevents progression to sepsis and reduces
mortality.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy, he is a known case of nephrotic syndrome, presented with mild edema around the eyes and lower extremities, but urine albumin show trace result for three successive days. Of the following, the MOST likely cause of false-negative result of protein is : (NE)
questions.initialExplanation: Diluted urine gives a falsely negative protein result, so the concentrated first morning sample is preferred.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The most likely cause of false-negative proteinuria in this case is dilute urine (option C). This is a well-
established phenomenon in clinical urinalysis, particularly relevant when testing patients with known
nephrotic syndrome who present with clinical signs (edema) but have only trace protein detected on
dipstick testing

---

questions.stem: A 12-year-old girl with nephrotic syndrome (NS) secondary to hepatitis B infection. Of the following, the MOST common type of secondary NS in this girl is : (NE)
questions.initialExplanation: Secondary nephrotic syndrome after hepatitis B is most often membranous nephropathy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The most common type of secondary nephrotic syndrome in children with hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection is
membranous nephropathy (MN), also known as hepatitis B-associated membranous nephropathy (HBVMN).
Hepatitis B-associated membranous nephropathy is the most prevalent HBV-related glomerular disease in
children, particularly in endemic areas. Studies have shown that among children with HBV-associated
nephrotic syndrome, the majority present with membranous histopathological features rather than other
glomerular pathologies.

In the pediatric population specifically, HBV-associated membranous nephropathy accounts for a significant
proportion of cases. Research from various endemic regions has consistently demonstrated that
approximately 70-80% of HBV-positive children with nephrotic syndrome show membranous patterns on renal
biopsy.

---

questions.stem: In evaluation of 3-year-old boy with minimal change nephrotic syndrome (MCNS), his GUE show: albumin +++ and RBC +. In cases of MCNS, microscopic hematuria may be present in up to : (NE)
questions.initialExplanation: In minimal change disease microscopic blood may be present in about 25% of cases.
questions.detailedExplanation:
In minimal change nephrotic syndrome (MCNS), microscopic hematuria may be present in up to
approximately 25% of pediatric patients. This is a well-documented clinical feature that can
accompany the classic presentation of nephrotic syndrome in children.

The presence of microscopic hematuria in a child with suspected minimal change nephrotic
syndrome does not necessarily indicate an alternative diagnosis. While more prominent hematuria
might suggest other glomerular pathologies such as IgA nephropathy or membranoproliferative
glomerulonephritis, the finding of isolated hematuria (RBC+) in the context of heavy albuminuria
(+++) is entirely consistent with MCNS.

---

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy he is a known case of steroid dependent nephrotic syndrome presented to the ER with severe generalized edema. In addition to restricting salt intake, the BEST diuretic to be use is : (NE)
questions.initialExplanation: Severe edema with salt restriction: the best diuretic is furosemide (with caution about volume depletion).
questions.detailedExplanation:
The best diuretic to use in a child with nephrotic syndrome and severe generalized edema is
frusemide (furosemide), which is a loop diuretic. This is the standard first-line treatment
recommended in clinical guidelines for managing edema in patients with nephrotic syndrome.
Potency and Mechanism of Action: Frusemide acts on the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle

by inhibiting the Na*-K*-2CI- cotransporter. This makes it the most potent class of diuretics available,

capable of producing significant natriuresis and diuresis even in the setting of severe edema
associated with nephrotic syndrome.

---

questions.stem: A 10-year-old child with steroid dependent nephrotic syndrome and frequent relapses, his height below third centile. The parents are concerned about his short stature. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate strategy to improve linear growth in their child? (NE)

options.label: A
options.text: Reduce the total dose of steroid

questions.initialExplanation: To improve growth in steroid-dependent nephrotic syndrome, use steroid-sparing strategies.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This 10-year-old child with steroid-dependent nephrotic syndrome (SDNS) and frequent relapses has developed growth
retardation, with height below the third centile. The growth impairment is a well-recognized complication of prolonged and
cumulative glucocorticoid therapy in pediatric nephrotic syndrome patients.

Evidence supporting steroid-sparing strategies:

- Studies have demonstrated a direct correlation between cumulative steroid dose and growth deficits in children with
steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome.

- Clinical guidelines recommend implementing steroid-sparing agents (such as levamisole, mycophenolate mofetil,
cyclophosphamide, calcineurin inhibitors, or rituximab) for children with SDNS or frequent relapses to reduce steroid
exposure.

- Steroid-sparing treatment strategies have been shown to improve linear growth velocity and final adult height in affected
children.

---

questions.stem: A 17-year-old girl with nephrotic syndrome is noted to have symmetrical marked loss of adipose tissue, first manifests in the face and then gradually progresses to the upper extremities, thorax and upper abdomen. Investigations reveal low complement level. Which type of nephrotic syndrome is associated with these manifestations? (NE)
questions.initialExplanation: Low complement with nephrotic syndrome = membranoproliferative GN (sometimes dense deposit disease/type II).
questions.detailedExplanation:
The presentation described is classic for Membranoproliferative Glomerulonephritis Type Il (MPGN Il), also known as

Dense Deposit Disease (DDD). This is a well-established clinicopathological entity that classically presents with the triad
of:

1.Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis with nephrotic syndrome
2.Partial lipodystrophy (symmetrical loss of subcutaneous fat)
3.Hypocomplementemia (low complement levels)

Pathognomonic Association
The relationship between MPGN type Il and partial lipodystrophy is one of the most distinctive disease associations in

nephrology. Multiple studies have confirmed that "membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, type Il is commonly seen in
patients with the rare disorder, partial lipodystrophy"

---

questions.stem: A 3-yr-old girl presents to the emergency department with anasarca. The urinalysis shows 4+ proteinuria and is negative for blood. Serum albumin is 1.2 mg/dL and serum creatinine is 0.4 mg/dL. The most likely diagnosis is: (NE)
questions.initialExplanation: Generalized edema and 4+ proteinuria without blood in a 3-year-old girl = minimal change disease.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Minimal-change disease (MCD) is the most common cause of idiopathic nephrotic syndrome in children,
accounting for 70% to 90% of cases in children under 10 years of age, with peak incidence between 2-8 years.
Classic features of MCD that match this presentation:

- Age at presentation: 3 years old is within the peak incidence range

- Pure nephrotic syndrome without hematuria or renal impairment

- Normal complement levels (not mentioned, but typically normal in MCD)

- Excellent response to corticosteroid therapy

- Typically no hypertension at presentation

The absence of hematuria and normal serum creatinine are particularly characteristic of minimal-change
disease, as opposed to other glomerular diseases that may present with combined nephrotic-nephritic features

---

questions.stem: An 8-yr-old boy with newly diagnosed nephrotic syndrome enters remission 7 days after beginning treatment with high-dose prednisone therapy (30 mg PO bid). The most appropriate next step in therapy is to: (NE)

options.label: A
options.text: Discontinue prednisone and monitor closely for relapse

options.label: B
options.text: Continue high-dose prednisone therapy for a total of 4-6 wk

options.label: C
options.text: Change to alternate-day prednisone dosing for the next 2 mo

questions.initialExplanation: If remission occurs after 7 days of prednisone, complete the full-dose course for 4-6 weeks then taper gradually.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This boy with newly diagnosed nephrotic syndrome has achieved remission after only 7 days of high-dose prednisone therapy. This
rapid response is typical of steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome (most commonly minimal change disease), where children often
achieve remission within the first 1-2 weeks of treatment. However, achieving early remission does not mean the treatment course
should be shortened.

Standard Treatment Protocol

Current clinical guidelines and evidence-based recommendations establish a clear protocol for initial treatment of childhood nephrotic
syndrome:

Phase 1: Initial Daily Therapy

Dosage: Prednisone 60 mg/m? per day or 2 mg/kg per day (maximum 60 mg/day) , Duration: 4-6 weeks of daily dosing

Phase 2: Alternate-Day Therapy

Dosage: 40 mg/m? per day on alternate days (maximum 40 mg per dose), Duration: Additional 4-6 weeks

Total Treatment Duration: 8-12 weeks

---

questions.stem: A newborn infant develops nephrotic syndrome within the first 2 wk of life. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's nephrotic syndrome? (NE)
questions.initialExplanation: Nephrotic syndrome in the first two weeks of life = congenital nephrotic syndrome due to nephrin gene (NPHS1) mutation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This newborn infant presenting with nephrotic syndrome within the first 2 weeks of life most likely has
Congenital Nephrotic Syndrome of the Finnish Type (CNF), which is caused by mutations in the
nephrin gene (NPHS1).

Congenital nephrotic syndrome (CNS) is defined as nephrotic syndrome presenting within the first 3
months of life. When it presents specifically within the first 2 weeks, the most common cause is
Congenital Nephrotic Syndrome of the Finnish Type (CNF), an autosomal recessive disorder caused
by mutations in the NPHS1 gene which encodes nephrin.

---

questions.stem: A 14-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with a 2-week history of bilateral leg edema and a 3-day history of abdominal swelling. His vital signs are: temperature, 98.4°F (36.9°C); blood pressure, 125/67 mm Hg; heart rate, 84 beats/min; and respiratory rate, 20 breaths/min. Physical examination shows moderate ascites and 2+ leg edema. His urinalysis reveals negative blood and 4+ protein. Serum complement concentrations are ordered and found to be normal. Of the following, the MOST likely cause of his edema and proteinuria is : (NE)
questions.initialExplanation: A teen with edema and proteinuria and otherwise normal tests: the commonest cause at this age is membranous nephropathy or FSGS; the given answer is membranous.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Nephrotic syndrome (NS) is a constellation of symptoms that include proteinuria,hypoalbuminemia,
edema, and hyperlipidemia. The most important aspect is proteinuria; the other symptoms simply are
‘    outcomes of excessive urinary protein leak. Proteinuria is not the only cause of hypoalbuminemia;
other causes include advanced liver disease, severe malnutrition, and gastrointestinal losses.
If NS is suspected, a urinalysis may provide clues to the cause. Among the many causes of NS in
children, the most common are minimal-change NS (MCNS), focal segmental glomerulosclerosis
(FSGS), membranous nephropathy (MN), any cause of acute glomerulonephritis (AGN),
membranoproliferative GN (MPGN), lupus GN, and immunoglobulin A nephropathy (IgAN). The
practitioner’s goal is to determine the cause of NS to devise the best management plan.

---

questions.stem: A 12 yr old girl presents with edema and gross hematuria. Her evaluation reveals serum creatinine 1.4 mg/dL, serum albumin 2.3 mg/dL, 24-hr urine protein excretion 5.5 g, and C3 12 mg/dL. The most likely cause of her nephrotic syndrome is: (NE) moomo»
questions.initialExplanation: Edema, gross hematuria and very low C3 = membranoproliferative GN.
questions.detailedExplanation:
MPGN is most common in the 2nd decade of life. Patients present in equal proportions with nephrotic syndrome, acute
nephritic syndrome (hematuria, hypertension, and some level of renal insufficiency), or persistent asymptomatic
microscopic hematuria and proteinuria. Serum C3 complement levels are low in the majority of cases. The differential
diagnosis includes all forms of acute and chronic glomerulonephritis, including idiopathic and secondary forms, along with
postinfectious glomerulonephritis. Postinfectious glomerulonephritis, far more common than MPGN, usually does not
have nephrotic features but typically has hematuria, hypertension, renal insufficiency, and transient low C3 complement
levels, all features that may be seen with MPGN. In contrast to MPGN, in which C3 levels usually remain persistently low,
C8 returns to normal within 2 mo after the onset of postinfectious glomerulonephritis (see Chapter 505 and Fig. 505-3).
The diagnosis of MPGN is made by renal biopsy. Indications for biopsy include nephrotic syndrome in an older child,
significant proteinuria with microscopic hematuria, and hypocomplementemia lasting > 2 mo in a child with acute
nephritis.

---

questions.stem: An otherwise healthy, asymptomatic 16-yr-old African-American girl is found to have hypertension and 3+ proteinuria by dipstick testing on mid-day and 1st morning voided urine samples. The microscopic analysis shows 0-2 red blood cells per high-power field. The most likely diagnosis is: (NE) NC.
questions.initialExplanation: A teenage girl with proteinuria, no microscopic hematuria and persistent disease: FSGS is a cause of steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Approximately 90% of children with nephrotic syndrome have idiopathic nephrotic syndrome. Idiopathic
nephrotic syndrome is associated with primary glomerular disease without evidence of a specific systemic
cause. ldiopathic nephrotic syndrome includes multiple histologic types: minimal change disease, mesangial
proliferation, focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS), membranous nephropathy, and
membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis. The idiopathic nephrotic syndrome is more common in boys than in
girls (2:1) and most commonly appears between the ages of 2 and 6 yr (see Fig. 521-1). However, it has been
reported as early as 6 mo of age and throughout adulthood. Minimal change nephrotic syndrome (MCNS) is
present in 85-90% of patients < 6 yr of age. In contrast, only 20-30% of adolescents who present for the 1st
time with nephrotic syndrome have MCNS. The more common cause of idiopathic nephrotic syndrome in this
older age group is FSGS. The incidence of FSGS may be increasing; it may be more common in African-
American, Hispanic, and Asian patients.

---

questions.stem: A 5 yr old boy presents with new-onset nephrotic syndrome. Which of the following clinical findings is most likely?(NE)
questions.initialExplanation: The commonest sign at onset of nephrotic syndrome is periorbital edema.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Children usually present with mild edema, which is initially noted around the eyes and in the lower
extremities. Nephrotic syndrome can initially be misdiagnosed as an allergic disorder because of the
periorbital swelling that decreases throughout the day. With time, the edema becomes generalized,
with the development of ascites, pleural effusions, and genital edema. Anorexia, irritability,
abdominal pain, and diarrhea are common. Important features of minimal change idiopathic
nephrotic syndrome are the absence of hypertension and gross hematuria (previously termed
nephritic features).

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old previously healthy boy presents with his parents with a complaint of swelling in his eyelids for the past 2 weeks. There is no eye discharge or pruritus. The swelling appears to be worse when he gets up in the morning. His parents report that he has otherwise been well, though he did have a runny nose, cough, and fever 2 weeks ago. On physical examination, he is afebrile and well appearing. His examination is only notable for bilateral periorbital swelling that is non-tender with minimal erythema. There is no scleral injection and his fundoscopic examination and visual acuity are normal. What is the most appropriate first step? (Rud) ®o0 TW

options.label: B
options.text: Computerized tomography scan of the orbits

questions.initialExplanation: Facial edema with a normal eye exam: the first step is urinalysis to look for protein.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Minimal change nephrotic syndrome (MCNS) is seen in 2—7 per 100,000 children under the age of 16. Its
pathophysiology is yet to be fully understood, but is thought to result from a circulating “nephrotic factor” that
results in damage to the podocytes in the glomerulus. This results in an increase in the glomerular basement
membrane permeability and the loss of protein in the urine. Proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, and
hypercholestermia are seen. Dependent edema is seen in patients with MCNS. For children, this is commonly
seen in the eyelids, scrotum, and labia. Patients are often misdiagnosed as having an allergic conjunctivitis.
For this patient, a urinalysis to look for proteinuria is indicated to diagnose MCNS. Given the normal
ophthalmologic examination, an ophthalmology referral and CT scan of the orbits are not appropriate. As the
patient does not have evidence for an allergic conjunctivitis, an antihistamine is not required. The patient does
not have clinical features consistent with an orbital cellulitis; thus, intravenous antibiotics are not indicated.

---

questions.stem: Apreviously healthy 5-year-old girl has acute onset of edema and oliguria. Laboratory studies reveal hypoalbuminemia and hypercholes terolemia. Which of the following is the major cause for mortality with this condition? (Lange)
questions.initialExplanation: The main cause of death in nephrotic syndrome is bacterial infection due to antibody loss and impaired immunity.
questions.detailedExplanation:
About 75% of nephrotic syndrome in children 1-12 years of age is due to minimal-change disease.
The mortality in minimal-change nephrotic syndrome is about 1%—2%. Most of the mortality is
related to an increased susceptibility for infections, with bacterial peritonitis being the most serious
one. The majority of the remainder of deaths is due to thromboembolic events. Hyperlipidemia is
associated with nephrotic syndrome, but is generally not associated with clinical complications.
Acute renal failure can occur with intravascular volume depletion and decreased renal perfusion
but is easily treatable.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old male child is brought to your clinic with periorbital and ankle swelling. The mother states that periorbital swelling is noted in the morning and then it improves.On examination, blood pressure is normal. Blood tests show albumin level 24 g/L (normal is more than 35 g/L). Complement level is normal. Urea and creatinine level is normal. Urine analysis confirms proteinuria in nephrotic range and no haematuria. What is the best next step in this situation? (MX)
questions.initialExplanation: Typical nephrotic syndrome without blood in a 5-year-old: start steroid treatment without biopsy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The nephrotic syndrome is caused by renal diseases that increase the permeability across the
glomerular filtration barrier.lt is classically characterised by four clinical features, but the first 2 are
used diagnostically because the last 2 may not be seen in all patients:

1-Nephrotic range proteinuria-urinary protein excretion greater than 50 mg/kg per day.
2-Hypoalbuminemia-serum albumin concentration less than 30 g/L.

3-Edema.

4-Hyperlipidemia.

Idiopathic nephrotic syndrome is the most common form of childhood nephrotic syndrome, representing more than 90% of
cases between 1 and 10 years of age and 50 % after 10 years of age.

---

questions.stem: An 8-year-old boy is found to have persistent proteinuria of 2+ on dipstick urine. There is no hematuria. Physical examination including blood pressure is unremarkable. Which one of the following is the next best investigation to consider for this boy? (MX)
questions.initialExplanation: Persistent 2+ proteinuria without symptoms: next do a complete microscopic urine exam then protein/creatinine ratio.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Proteinuria is defined as presence of 1+ protein or more on urine dipstick exam. To confirm the
diagnosis of proteinuria, two consecutive urine dipsticks or urinalysis, 1 to 2 days apart must
indicate proteinuria.

If proteinuria persists on dipstick, the next best will be a complete urine exam (urinalysis) on a
midstream urine sample obtained in the office for a more accurate assessment of the urine. With
urinalysis (urine examination), the urine sediment, as well as other signs of glomerular and/or
parenchymal disease such as hematuria, red cell casts, pyuria and/or lipiduria are assessed.

Particular findings on urine examination may suggest glomerulonephritis, nephrotic syndrome, or
other renal parenchymal disorders.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy presents with a 2-week history of progressive periorbital and lower extremity swelling. His mother reports the swelling worsens throughout the day and is associated with abdominal distension. He recently recovered from an upper respiratory infection 3 weeks ago. Examination reveals bilateral periorbital edema, 2+ ankle pitting edema, and abdominal distension. Urinalysis shows 4+ proteinuria. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Gradual edema and 4+ proteinuria = nephrotic syndrome.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The clinical presentation is classic for nephrotic syndrome. The child is in the typical age group (2-6
years), presents with the hallmark features of heavy proteinuria (4+ on dipstick) and edema involving
periorbital areas and lower extremities. The diurnal variation of edema (worse in morning, improving
throughout the day) is characteristic of nephrotic syndrome due to fluid redistribution when supine
during sleep. The recent history of viral infection is a known trigger for initial presentation or relapse in
susceptible children. The absence of hematuria, hypertension, or renal impairment helps differentiate
from acute glomerulonephritis. Congestive heart failure would typically present with cardiomegaly,
gallop rhythm, and respiratory distress. Protein-losing enteropathy would have gastrointestinal
symptoms predominating, and hepatic failure would have jaundice and synthetic dysfunction markers.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old girl is diagnosed with nephrotic syndrome based on laboratory investigations. Her serum albumin is 1.8 g/dL, urine protein/creatinine ratio is 3.5, and serum cholesterol is 285 mg/dL. The treating physician explains the pathophysiology of her condition to the parents. What is the primary mechanism responsible for the hypoalbuminemia in nephrotic syndrome? (MX)

options.label: B
options.text: Increased catabolism of albumin in the kidneys

options.label: C
options.text: Increased glomerular permeability leading to urinary albumin loss

options.label: E
options.text: Gastrointestinal loss of albumin Decreased dietary intake and absorption of proteins

questions.initialExplanation: Falling albumin is due to increased glomerular permeability, so albumin is lost in the urine.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The fundamental pathophysiology of nephrotic syndrome involves damage to the glomerular filtration
barrier, particularly the podocytes and their foot processes, leading to increased permeability. This
‘    results in massive loss of albumin and other plasma proteins in the urine, dropping serum albumin
below the critical threshold of 2.5 g/dL.
The hypoalbuminemia then triggers hepatic compensation with increased synthesis of lipoproteins,
explaining the hyperlipidemia. While decreased dietary intake may occur secondary to anorexia, and
hepatic synthesis actually increases as a compensatory mechanism, the primary event remains the
urinary loss due to enhanced glomerular permeability. Gastrointestinal loss is not a feature of primary
nephrotic syndrome.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy with newly diagnosed nephrotic syndrome is started on oral prednisolone at a dose of 60 mg/m?/day. The parents ask about the expected timeline for response to treatment. Within what time frame should this child typically achieve remission with appropriate corticosteroid therapy?
questions.initialExplanation: Steroid response usually occurs within 2-4 weeks.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Children with steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome, which represents the majority of cases
(approximately 90%), typically respond to corticosteroid therapy within 2-4 weeks of initiating daily
prednisone treatment. Remission is defined as the presence of negative or trace proteinuria for three
consecutive days. This rapid response is characteristic of minimal change disease, the most common
histopathological variant in young children. Children who fail to respond within 8 weeks are classified
as steroid-resistant and require further investigation including renal biopsy to determine the
underlying pathology. The standard initial course of prednisone is given as daily therapy for 4-6
weeks, followed by alternate-day tapering for several months.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy with steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome has experienced four relapses in the past 12 months. Each relapse was characterized by reappearance of heavy proteinuria and edema, occurring shortly after discontinuation of corticosteroids or during alternate-day therapy. The last relapse occurred 2 weeks ago when the steroid dose was reduced. How would you classify this patient's disease pattern? (MX)
questions.initialExplanation: Relapse when steroids are reduced = steroid-dependent nephrotic syndrome.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This patient has steroid-dependent nephrotic syndrome based on the definition that includes patients
who experience relapses either while on alternate-day corticosteroid therapy or within 1 month of

‘     stopping treatment. The pattern described is characteristic of steroid dependency rather than
frequent relapsing, which is defined as four or more relapses within one year without the temporal
relationship to steroid discontinuation. Steroid resistance refers to failure to achieve remission
despite 8 weeks of appropriate corticosteroid therapy. This distinction is crucial for management
decisions, as steroiddependent patients typically require steroid-sparing immunosuppressive agents

such as cyclophosphamide, cyclosporine, or mycophenolate mofetil to minimize long-term
corticosteroid toxicity.

---

questions.stem: An 8-year-old boy presents with a 3-week history of generalized edema, including facial swelling, ascites, and scrotal edema. Laboratory investigations reveal: serum albumin 1.5 g/dL, urine protein/creatinine ratio 4.2, serum cholesterol 320 mg/dL, serum creatinine 0.8 mg/dL (age-appropriate normal), and complement levels C3 and C4 are within normal limits. Blood pressure is 100/65 mmHg. Which of the following is an indication for renal biopsy in this child?

options.label: A
options.text: Age of 8 years or older at presentation

options.label: D
options.text: Presence of ascites and scrotal edema

options.label: E
options.text: Duration of symptoms greater than 2 weeks

questions.initialExplanation: Indications for renal biopsy: older age at onset, blood, hypertension, persistently low complement, or no steroid response.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Renal biopsy is not routinely indicated in children with idiopathic nephrotic syndrome who present in
the typical age range (2-6 years) with steroid-sensitive disease. However, specific indications
warrant biopsy evaluation, including age greater than 8 years at presentation, which increases the
likelihood of underlying focal segmental glomerulosclerosis or other pathologies beyond minimal
change disease. This patient is exactly 8 years old, which meets the age criterion. Other established
indications include family history of renal disease, presence of extrarenal manifestations (arthritis,
rash), hypertension, hematuria, pulmonary edema, renal insufficiency, hypocomplementemia, and
steroid resistance. The low serum albumin, high cholesterol, and presence of severe edema are
expected features of nephrotic syndrome and do not themselves indicate biopsy.

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy with nephrotic syndrome develops acute onset abdominal pain and fever. On examination, he appears ill, has generalized edema, and exhibits diffuse abdominal tenderness with voluntary guarding. His temperature is 38.9°C. He has been on daily prednisone for the past 2 weeks for a relapse. What is the most likely diagnosis and appropriate next step? (MX)

options.label: C
options.text: Peptic ulcer disease requiring proton pump inhibitors

questions.initialExplanation: Acute abdominal pain and fever in a nephrotic child on prednisone = SBP, needing an antibiotic.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) is the most common serious infectious complication in children with
nephrotic syndrome, particularly during active disease phases when serum albumin is low and edema is
present. The classic presentation includes acute abdominal pain, fever, and signs of peritonitis in the setting
of ascites. The Pathogenesis involves translocation of gut bacteria into the peritoneal cavity due to edema
and immune dysfunction. Staphylococcus pneumoniae is the most commonly identified organism, followed
by Gram-negative enteric organisms such as Escherichia coli. This is a medical emergency requiring prompt
diagnostic paracentesis and empirical antibiotic therapy covering likely pathogens. Corticosteroid therapy
may mask typical signs of infection, necessitating a high index of suspicion. Surgical consultation is not
indicated unless there is evidence of secondary peritonitis or perforation.

---

questions.stem: A 9-year-old girl with a 2-year history of frequently relapsing nephrotic syndrome is being evaluated for consideration of cyclophosphamide therapy. Her current laboratory values show: WBC count 8, 500/mms3, hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL, and platelet count 245,000/mm3. What is the maximum duration of cyclophosphamide therapy and what is the doselimiting side effect?
questions.initialExplanation: Cyclophosphamide is limited to 8-12 weeks, and its key dose-related side effect is neutropenia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Cyclophosphamide is a second-line agent used in children with steroid-dependent or frequently
relapsing nephrotic syndrome who have developed significant corticosteroid toxicity or cannot be
managed with steroids alone. The standard regimen is 2 mg/kg/day as a single oral dose for a total
duration of 8-12 weeks. The major dose-limiting side effect is bone marrow suppression, particularly
neutropenia, which requires weekly monitoring of complete blood count. Cyclophosphamide should
be withheld if the white blood cell count falls below 5,000/mm3. Other significant side effects include
hemorrhagic cystitis (prevented by adequate hydration), gonadal toxicity (dose-related), and
increased malignancy risk with cumulative exposure. The limited 8-12 week course minimizes these
risks while providing sustained remission in many patients.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy with nephrotic syndrome is being counseled about potential complications of his condition. His parents are particularly concerned about the risk of blood clotting. Which laboratory finding in nephrotic syndrome contributes to the increased thrombotic risk?

options.label: C
options.text: Increased levels of protein C and protein S

questions.initialExplanation: Nephrotic syndrome causes hypercoagulability due to urinary loss of antithrombin III.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Children with nephrotic syndrome have a well-recognized hypercoagulable state that predisposes to
thromboembolic complications. The mechanisms include increased production of procoagulant factors
(fibrinogen, factor V, factor VIII) stimulated by hypoalbuminemia, thrombocytosis secondary to
hemoconcentration, and relative immobility due to edema. Crucially, there is urinary loss of natural
anticoagulant proteins including antithrombin Ill, protein C, and protein S, which further tilts the hemostatic
balance toward thrombosis. This explains why aggressive diuresis and use of indwelling venous catheters
should be minimized. While arterial thrombosis is rare in children, venous thromboembolism including renal
vein thrombosis, deep vein thrombosis, and pulmonary embolism can occur. Routine prophylactic
anticoagulation is not recommended unless there is a prior thromboembolic event.

---

questions.stem: A 3-month-old infant presents with massive generalized edema noted since birth. Prenatal ultrasound showed fetal hydrops and markedly elevated maternal serum alphafetoprotein. The infant was born prematurely at 34 weeks gestation with a birth weight of 2.8 kg. The placenta was abnormally large, weighing 1.2 kg (greater than 25% of birth weight). Laboratory investigations reveal serum albumin 1.2 g/dL and massive proteinuria. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.text: Congenital nephrotic syndrome of Finnish type

questions.initialExplanation: Edema from the first months with very low albumin = Finnish-type congenital nephrotic syndrome.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This presentation is classic for congenital nephrotic syndrome of the Finnish type (also known as Finnish-type
nephrotic syndrome). Key features include onset within the first 3 months of life, presence in utero of fetal
hydrops and elevated alpha-fetoprotein, large placenta, prematurity, and massive proteinuria with
hypoalbuminemia. This autosomal recessive condition results from mutations in the NPHS1 gene encoding
nephrin, a critical component of the slit diaphragm in podocytes. The clinical course is characterized by
persistent edema, recurrent infections, and progressive renal failure, with death typically occurring within 5
years without intervention. Treatment involves aggressive nutritional support, ACE inhibitors to reduce

proteinuria, and eventually unilateral or bilateral nephrectomy followed by dialysis and kidney transplantation.
Corticosteroids and immunosuppressives are ineffective in this condition.

---

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy presents with a 1-month history of progressive edema, weight gain, and decreased urine output. He was diagnosed with nephrotic syndrome at age 6 years and has had multiple relapses. Despite adequate corticosteroid therapy for 8 weeks, he continues to have 3+ proteinuria. Laboratory values show serum creatinine 1.4 mg/dL (elevated from baseline 0.6 mg/dL), serum albumin 1.8 g/dL, and complement levels are normal. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.initialExplanation: Older age with low albumin and normal complement: renal biopsy to determine the cause.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This patient has steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome, defined as failure to achieve remission after 8 weeks
of appropriate daily corticosteroid therapy at standard dosing. The presence of elevated serum creatinine
suggests possible underlying chronic kidney disease or crescentic transformation. In steroid-resistant cases,
renal biopsy is indicated to determine the underlying histopathological diagnosis, which is likely focal
segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) in a child of this age with this clinical course. FSGS has a lower
response rate to corticosteroids (approximately 20-30%) compared to minimal change disease. The biopsy
results will guide further management decisions, which may include calcineurin inhibitors (cyclosporine or
tacrolimus), mycophenolate mofetil, or other immunosuppressive agents. Starting empiric cyclophosphamide
without biopsy confirmation would not be appropriate given the possibility of FSGS.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy with nephrotic syndrome is being managed with salt restriction and judicious use of diuretics for mild to moderate edema. His parents ask about the role of albumin infusion in his management. What is the most appropriate indication for intravenous albumin infusion in children with nephrotic syndrome?

options.label: E
options.text: Severe edema unresponsive to diuretics and salt restriction

questions.initialExplanation: IV albumin is given for severe edema not responding to diuretics and salt restriction with low volume.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Intravenous albumin infusion is reserved for children with severe, refractory edema that has not responded
to conventional management including salt restriction, fluid restriction (if hyponatremic), and diuretic therapy
(typically furosemide at 1-2 mg/kg/dose). The rationale is to transiently expand the intravascular volume,
enhancing the diuretic response. However, this must be used cautiously because the administered albumin
is rapidly lost in the urine, providing only temporary benefit. Moreover, aggressive diuresis following albumin
infusion increases the risk of thromboembolism due to hemoconcentration. In patients with severe scrotal or
labial edema, elevation and support are recommended. Albumin is not indicated for mild cases, for
correction of hypoalbuminemia per se, or as routine adjunct to steroids. The typical dose is 25% albumin at
0.5-1 g/kg administered slowly, followed by furosemide.

---

questions.stem: A 14-month-old infant is evaluated for edema that began at 3 months of age. She was born at term with normal birth weight but developed generalized edema, hypoalbuminemia, and massive proteinuria in the first few months of life. Renal ultrasound shows enlarged kidneys with increased echogenicity. DNA analysis reveals a mutation in the NPHS2 gene encoding podocin. What is the most appropriate management strategy for this patient?

options.label: C
options.text: Unilateral nephrectomy, dialysis, and eventual transplantation

options.label: D
options.text: ACE inhibitors only for proteinuria reduction

questions.initialExplanation: An NPHS2 (podocin) mutation = steroid-resistant disease; ultimate treatment is nephrectomy, dialysis then transplant.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This infant has congenital nephrotic syndrome due to podocin mutation (NPHS2), which causes
steroid-resistant disease unresponsive to corticosteroids or immunosuppressives. The management

‘     of congenital nephrotic syndrome differs fundamentally from that of idiopathic childhood nephrotic
syndrome. The primary treatment approach involves aggressive nutritional support to counteract
protein loss, ACE inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers to reduce proteinuria, and eventual
removal of the native kidneys(nephrectomy) when complications from massive protein loss become
unmanageable. The child then requires chronic dialysis (typically peritoneal dialysis in infants) until
reaching an appropriate age and weight for kidney transplantation. Transplantation is generally
successful and represents the definitive treatment, though recurrence of FSGS in the graft can occur
in some cases, particularly with circulating permeability factors.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old girl with steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome has been in remission for 6 months on no medications. Her parents ask about the long-term prognosis of her condition. What is the most accurate statement regarding the prognosis of childhood nephrotic syndrome with minimal change disease?

options.label: A
options.text: Nearly all patients progress to end-stage renal disease by adulthood

options.label: B
options.text: The majority achieve sustained remission and normal renal function

options.label: C
options.text: Recurrence after puberty is common and requires lifelong therapy

options.label: D
options.text: All patients will develop steroid dependence requiring alternative agents

options.label: E
options.text: Chronic kidney disease develops in the majority despite treatment

questions.initialExplanation: Most children with minimal change achieve sustained remission with normal kidney function.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The prognosis of childhood minimal change disease, the most common cause of steroidsensitive nephrotic
syndrome, is generally excellent. Approximately 70-80% of children with minimal change disease achieve
sustained remission and maintain normal renal function into adulthood. While many children experience
relapses during childhood, the frequency of relapses typically decreases with age, and many outgrow the
disease. The risk of progression to end-stage renal disease is very low (less than 5%) in steroidresponsive
minimal change disease. In contrast, FSGS has a poorer prognosis with higher rates of progression to chronic
kidney disease. Most children with minimal change disease can expect a normal life expectancy and quality of
life with appropriate management. Complications from the disease or its treatment (particularly corticosteroids)
remain the primary concerns during active phases.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy presents with edema, proteinuria, and hypoalbuminemia consistent with nephrotic syndrome. On physical examination, he has distinctive facial features including coarse facies, macrocephaly, and corneal clouding. He also has mild hepatomegaly and umbilical hernia. Which syndrome is most likely associated with this presentation? A) Alport syndrome B) Fabry disease C) Denys-Drash syndrome
questions.initialExplanation: Per the given answer: Hurler syndrome. Note: the best-known syndrome linked to early nephrotic syndrome with genital malformation is Denys-Drash, so check the reference.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Hurler syndrome is an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficiency of alpha-L-
iduronidase, leading to accumulation of glycosaminoglycans. This condition is associated with secondary
nephrotic syndrome due to glomerular involvement from stored material. The characteristic clinical features

‘    include coarse facial features (thickened lips, broad nose, prominent forehead), macrocephaly, corneal
clouding, hepatosplenomegaly, umbilical hernia, skeletal abnormalities, and developmental delay. The
nephrotic syndrome in Hurler syndrome typically presents in early childhood and may require specific enzyme
replacement therapy or hematopoietic stem cell transplantation for the underlying condition. Alport syndrome
typically presents with hematuria and progressive renal failure rather than nephrotic syndrome. DenysDrash
syndrome includes Wilms tumor, pseudohermaphroditism, and progressive renal Disease. Alagille syndrome
features cholestasis, cardiac disease, and characteristic facies.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy with nephrotic syndrome is being monitored for potential complications. His parents ask about the long-term renal outcome if he has minimal change disease. What is the risk of progression to end-stage renal disease in a child with steroidsensitive minimal change disease?
questions.initialExplanation: The risk of end-stage kidney disease in steroid-sensitive minimal change is below 5%.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The prognosis of steroid-sensitive minimal change disease in children is excellent, with less than 5%
of patients progressing to end-stage renal disease. The vast majority of children achieve sustained
remission and maintain normal renal function throughout childhood and into adulthood. While many
children experience relapses during the course of their disease, the frequency typically diminishes
with age, and a significant proportion achieve permanent remission after puberty. The key
determinants of favorable outcome are steroid sensitivity and the absence of FSGS on biopsy. In
contrast, steroid-resistant disease, particularly FSGS, carries a much higher risk of progression to
chronic kidney disease and end-stage renal disease (up to 50% or more within 10 years).

Nephrotic Syndrome |

---

## Glomerulonephritis & HTN

> Question numbers not present in the source file for this topic: 26, 35.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy presents with sudden onset of gross hematuria and edema. His blood pressure measures 130/90 mmHg. Laboratory investigations reveal blood urea of 60 mg/dL, decreased C3 complement levels, and urine analysis revealing RBC casts. He has a recent history of treated tonsillitis with penicillin 10 days ago. Which of the following conditions is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Blood and edema days to weeks after tonsillitis = post-infectious (post-streptococcal) glomerulonephritis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Post-infectious glomerulonephritis (PIGN), also known as post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis
(PSGN), represents an immune-complex mediated disorder that typically occurs following
streptococcal pharyngeal or skin infections. This case presents the classic triad of clinical features
that strongly support this diagnosis.

The patient is a school-age child, which represents the peak incidence demographic for PIGN, with
most cases occurring between 5 and 12 years of age. The temporal relationship between the
antecedent infection and the onset of renal symptoms is highly characteristic, with a latent period of
approximately 1-2 weeks following pharyngeal infection, which aligns perfectly with this patient's 10-
day history of treated tonsillitis.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy admitted to the hospital for treatment of acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, on the second day of admission he develops headache, nausea and vomiting with disturbed level of consciousness. The MOST likely cause of these new symptoms is:
questions.initialExplanation: Headache, nausea and altered consciousness in a patient with APSGN = hypertensive encephalopathy due to high blood pressure.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This case illustrates a critical neurological complication of acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis:
hypertensive encephalopathy.

- The patient confirmed acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. The development of new
neurological symptoms on the second day of hospitalization represents a potentially life-threatening
complication requiring immediate intervention.

- The triad of symptoms presented —headache, nausea and vomiting, and altered

consciousness —represents the classic presentation of hypertensive encephalopathy. This condition
results from the effects of severely elevated blood pressure on cerebral autoregulation and vascular
integrity.

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy presents with headache, vomiting, and blurred vision. His mother notes facial swelling and dark, tea-colored urine that began the day before. He recently recovered from a sore throat. On exam, he is alert but uncomfortable, with periorbital edema. Heart and lung exams are unremarkable, and RR 24/min. Urinalysis shows +3 blood and +2 protein. What is the MOST important next step in management?

options.label: A
options.text: Check blood pressure and assess for hypertensive emergency

options.label: B
options.text: Begin high-dose corticosteroid therapy Obtain renal ultrasound urgently

options.label: C
options.text: Administer mannitol for suspected increased intracranial pressure

options.label: D
options.text: Restrict dietary sodium and initiate fluid restriction POO OoTW

questions.initialExplanation: Headache, vomiting and blurred vision with blood in urine: the most important step is to measure blood pressure and assess the emergency caused by its elevation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The presentation (post-streptococcal pharyngitis, tea-colored urine, edema, hematuria, proteinuria,
headache, vomiting, blurred vision) is classic for post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN). The
neurological symptoms (headache, vomiting, blurred vision) suggest hypertensive encephalopathy, a
dangerous complication. Immediate BP assessment is critical before any other intervention.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old girl presents with tea-colored urine, periorbital swelling, and mild headache. She had a skin infection treated with antibiotics. Urinalysis reveals hematuria with red cell casts and proteinuria. Which additional finding(s) would support a diagnosis of post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis?

options.label: B
options.text: Low C3 complement with normal C4

questions.initialExplanation: Supporting the diagnosis of post-streptococcal GN: low C3 with normal C4 (alternative pathway activation).
questions.detailedExplanation:
In PSGN, complement is consumed via the alternative pathway, causing low C3 with normal C4.
This distinguishes it from lupus nephritis (low C3 AND C4, positive ANA). IgA nephropathy

typically has normal complement. The low C3 in PSGN normalizes within 6-8 weeks; persistent
low C3 suggests other diagnoses like MPGN.

---

questions.stem: “Rapidly progressive” RPGN describes the clinical course of several forms of glomerulonephritis whose unifying feature is the histopathologic finding of crescents in the majority of glomeruli. Plasmapheresis has been reported to be of benefit in patients with : (NE)
questions.initialExplanation: Plasmapheresis may help in RPGN caused by Goodpasture disease (anti-GBM).
questions.detailedExplanation:
This question addresses a critical therapeutic intervention in nephrology. Plasmapheresis is a well-established, life-saving
treatment specifically indicated for Goodpasture disease (Anti-GBM disease) among the conditions listed.

Goodpasture disease is an autoimmune disorder characterized by the production of anti-glomerular basement membrane
(anti-GBM) antibodies that target the a3 chain of type IV collagen, a structural component of both the glomerular basement
membrane and the alveolar basement membrane. These pathogenic antibodies initiate an immune-mediated attack on the
basement membranes, causing rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and pulmonary hemorrhage.

Plasmapheresis works by physically removing the circulating anti-GBM antibodies from the patient's plasma, thereby
interrupting the ongoing immunological assault on the kidneys and lungs. This removal allows for the stabilization of renal
function and prevents further antibody-mediated damage. The efficacy of plasmapheresis is highest when initiated early in
the disease course, before irreversible scarring has occurred.

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old male presents with sudden onset of gross hematuria and edema. Blood pressure is 130/90 mmHg. Investigations results; blood urea 160mg/dl, low C3 level, and urinalysis shows RBC casts. He had history of treatment for acute tonsillitis with penicillin for 10 days. Which of the following is the MOST likely diagnosis? (NE)
questions.initialExplanation: Tea-colored urine and edema after tonsillitis = post-infectious glomerulonephritis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The patient demonstrates the classic tetrad of acute post-infectious glomerulonephritis:

- Gross hematuria - Characteristic "cola-colored" or "tea-colored" urine resulting from glomerular
inflammation and RBC extravasation into the urinary space

- Edema - Periorbital and peripheral edema due to sodium and water retention from reduced
glomerular filtration

- Hypertension - Blood pressure 130/90 mmHg is significantly elevated for a 7-year-old, reflecting
volume overload

- Renal impairment - Blood urea 160 mg/dl indicates azotemia from decreased kidney function

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy had three days history of hematuria and mild puffy face. Blood pressure was 140/90 mmHg. He underwent surgery for hydrocephalus one month ago. Urinalysis: RBC +++, protein +, granular cast +, hyaline cast +, blood urea 80 mg/dl, serum creatinine 0.9 mg/dl and low complement level. Which of the following is the MOST likely organism causing this complication? (NE)
questions.initialExplanation: Nephritis after a catheter/shunt with low complement: the causative organism is Staphylococcus epidermidis (shunt nephritis).
questions.detailedExplanation:
This case presents a classic scenario of post-infectious glomerulonephritis secondary to cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) shunt
infection in a child who underwent neurosurgery for hydrocephalus one month ago. The timing, clinical presentation, and
laboratory findings are highly suggestive of this complication.

The patient exhibits the classic features of acute glomerulonephritis:

- Hematuria (RBC +++ on urinalysis) - indicates glomerular inflammation with red blood cell leakage into the urinary space
- Facial puffiness (edema) - results from sodium and water retention due to reduced glomerular filtration

- Hypertension (140/90 mmHg) - reflects fluid overload and is significant for a 4-year-old child

- Renal impairment - elevated blood urea (80 mg/dl) with relatively preserved creatinine (0.9 mg/dl)

- Low complement level - indicates alternative pathway complement activation, characteristic of immune complex-
mediated glomerular disease

---

questions.stem: A 10-year-old girl, a known case of beta thalassemia and hepatitis C infection, presents with puffiness. Blood pressure was 140/90 mmHg, urinalysis RBC+++, blood urea 95 mg/dl, serum creatinine 0.9 mg/dl. Of the following, the MOST likely diagnosis is : (NE)
questions.initialExplanation: A thalassemia patient with hepatitis C, hematuria and proteinuria: membranoproliferative GN associated with hepatitis C.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This case represents a classic presentation of Hepatitis C-associated membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN)
in a child with known chronic hepatitis C infection. The clinical features of hematuria, hypertension, and renal impairment
in the context of HCV infection strongly point toward this diagnosis.

The patient demonstrates several key features consistent with glomerular disease:

- Puffiness (edema) - Results from sodium and water retention secondary to impaired glomerular filtration, or potentially from nephrotic-
range proteinuria

- Hypertension (140/90 mmHg) - Significantly elevated for a 10-year-old child, reflecting volume overload and renal dysfunction

- Hematuria (RBC+++) - Indicates glomerular inflammation with red blood cell leakage into the urinary space

- Renal impairment - Elevated blood urea (95 mg/dl) with relatively preserved serum creatinine (0.9 mg/dl), which may reflect the
relatively lower muscle mass in children and females

---
