questions.stem: A 14-year-old girl with cystinuria disease on D-penicillamine treatment for the last 6 months, presented with generalized edema, decreased urine output, and blood pressure of 140/95 mmHg. Urinalysis; pus cell ++, RBC +, albumin+++, blood urea 60 mg/dl, total serum protein 4.5mg/dl, serum albumin 2.2mg/dl, serum cholesterol 300mg/dl, and normal serum C3 and C4. Of the following, the MOST likely diagnosis is : (NE)
questions.initialExplanation: D-penicillamine is a drug that causes membranous glomerulopathy with nephrotic syndrome and normal complement.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The patient's history of D-penicillamine therapy for cystinuria provides the critical etiological clue.
D-penicillamine is one of the classic drugs known to cause membranous nephropathy, and this is not a
coincidental association. The 6-month duration of treatment aligns perfectly with the typical latency period
for drug-induced membranous nephropathy, which usually develops within 4-12 months of starting the
offending medication.

D-penicillamine induces membranous nephropathy through an immune-mediated mechanism. The drug or
its metabolites interact with the glomerular basement membrane antigens, particularly phospholipase A2
receptor (PLA2R) or other podocyte antigens, triggering an autoimmune response. This results in the
formation of subepithelial immune deposits, complement activation, and damage to the podocytes. The
result is disruption of the glomerular filtration barrier, leading to massive protein leakage into the urine.

---

questions.stem: An 8-year-old boy presents with severe anemia and polyuria. Examination revealed growth failure, retinal degeneration with blood urea of 66 mg/dl and serum creatinine of 3 mg/dl. Of the following, the MOST likely diagnosis is : (NE)
questions.initialExplanation: Severe anemia, polyuria and early renal failure in a child = nephronophthisis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Nephronophthisis is an autosomal recessive chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis that typically manifests
in older children or adolescents. It represents the most likely diagnosis in this case for several

‘    compelling reasons. The condition characteristically presents with polyuria and polydipsia due to
impaired renal concentrating ability, along with growth retardation and anemia secondary to chronic
kidney disease. Most patients progress to end-stage renal disease during adolescence or early
adulthood. Importantly, extrarenal manifestations can include retinal degeneration, particularly in the
context of Senior-Loken syndrome, which combines nephronophthisis with Leber congenital
amaurosis. The combination of renal failure in an 8-year-old with polyuria, growth failure, anemia, and
retinal degeneration strongly supports nephronophthisis as the primary diagnosis.

---

questions.stem: A 17-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents with the complaint of coughing up blood. He is stabilized, and his hemoglobin and hematocrit levels are 11 mg/dL and 33%, respectively. During his hospitalization, he is noted to have systolic blood pressure persistently greater than 130 mm Hg and diastolic blood pressure greater than 90 mm Hg. His urinalysis is remarkable for hematuria and proteinuria. You are suspicious the patient has which of the following? (pretest)

options.label: E
options.text: Goodpasture syndrome Nephrotic syndrome Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis Renal vein thrombosis

questions.initialExplanation: Blood and protein in urine with hypertension and lung-kidney involvement = Goodpasture syndrome.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The patient in the question has a classic description of Goodpasture syndrome, a rare disease in children.
The pulmonary hemorrhage can be life threatening and the renal function progressive. Diagnosis is
suggested by kidney biopsy and finding antibodies to the glomerular basement membrane.
Hemolytic-uremic syndrome presents in a child with fever, bloody diarrhea, and progression toward renal
failure but not respiratory symptoms.

Nephrotic syndrome presents with edema, hypertension, and proteinuria; respiratory symptoms related to
congestive heart failure (and not pulmonary hemorrhage) might be seen. Poststreptococcal
glomerulonephritis can result in hematuria, but the respiratory symptoms associated with the condition would
be related to congestive heart failure and not to pulmonary hemorrhage. Renal vein thrombosis might result
in hematuria but would not be expected to have pulmonary findings.

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy has cramping abdominal pain and a rash mainly on the back of his legs and buttocks as well as on the extensor surfaces of his forearms. Laboratory analysis reveals proteinuria and microhematuria. You diagnose Henoch-Schénlein, or anaphylactoid, purpura. In addition to his rash and abdominal pain, what other finding is he likely to have? (pretest) Nb
questions.initialExplanation: Abdominal pain and a rash on the lower limbs suggest HSP, and the common accompaniment is arthritis/arthralgia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Henoch Schénlein purpura (HSP), or anaphylactoid purpura, is a systemic IgA mediated vasculitis. The rash
of anaphylactoid purpura most often involves extensor surfaces of the extremities; the face, soles, palms,
and trunk are less often affected. Other significant symptoms include edema, arthralgia or arthritis, colicky
abdominal pain with Gl bleeding, acute scrotal pain, and renal abnormalities ranging from microscopic
hematuria to acute renal failure. As HSP is a systemic vasculitis, any organ system can be affected.

The prognosis, however, is excellent, with only a small percentage of children going on to end-stage renal
failure. Seizures are an uncommon complication of CNS involvement; more commonly, patients will complain
of headache and will have behavioral changes. Unilateral lymphadenopathy and non purulent conjunctivitis
are not typical of HSP (but are criteria for Kawasaki disease, another pediatric vasculitis).

---

questions.stem: A 13-year-old previously healthy child presents with a 1-day history of gross hematuria, dysuria, and urinary urgency. A plain abdominal film demonstrates nephrolithiasis. He is started on IV hydration and soon after, he passes what he thinks is a stone and his symptoms resolve. What is the most appropriate next step? (Rud)

options.label: A
options.text: Nonenhanced computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen and pelvis

options.label: B
options.text: Urological consultation for shock wave lithotripsy

options.label: D
options.text: Timed urine collection for calcium, oxalate, urate, citrate, and sodium

questions.initialExplanation: Flank pain episode after a stone: request a timed urine collection to measure calcium, oxalate and others (stone workup).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Nephrolithiasis is defined as the presence of stones in the kidney, whereas urolithiasis is defined as the presence of stones
anywhere in the urinary tract. In North America, most stones present in the kidney. For children with stones and renal
calculi, investigation is required to rule out metabolic risk factors. This includes a timed urine collection to rule out
hypercaluria, hyperoxaluria, hyperuricosuria, and hypocitraturia. A high-sodium diet has been implicated as a risk factor for
stone formation, so quantification of urinary sodium is helpful. Treatment and prevention of further stone formation includes
adequate fluid intake and correction of any metabolic risk factors that are present. Stones less than 5 mm often pass
spontaneously.

Since the patient described in the vignette has already passed the stone and his symptoms have resolved, further imaging
such as a CT scan is not required. Similarly, shock wave lithotripsy is not indicated. Patients with hypercalciuria are often
treated with a thiazide diuretic, but this should only be done after hypercalciuria is confirmed with a timed urine collection.
There is no role for a calcium-restricted diet.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old previously healthy male presents to the urgent care clinic with a 1-day history of hematuria. In the clinic, he is noted to be mildly hypertensive with periorbital edema. A urine sample obtained in clinic has a dark brown appearance. He denies any recent rash or joint pain, but does report a sore throat 2 weeks ago for which he did not seek care. Which of the following is most likely to be true in this patient? (Rud)

options.label: A
options.text: Antibiotic administration for pharyngitis would likely have prevented this disease

options.label: B
options.text: Low serum C3 and normal serum C4 would be consistent with this disease

options.label: C
options.text: Low serum C4 and normal serum C3 would be consistent with this disease

options.label: D
options.text: If the patient were to have a renal biopsy, immunofluorescence would reveal mesangial deposits of IgA

options.label: E
options.text: Abnormalities on urinalysis should resolve within 5-10 days

questions.initialExplanation: APSGN lowers C3 with normal C4; it stays low up to 6-8 weeks then returns.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The patient in the above scenario has a history and exam that are highly suggestive of acute poststreptococcal
glomerulonephritis (APSGN). This is primarily a disease of school aged children and follows infection with

‘    specific strains of group A B-hemolytic streptococcus. Antibiotic treatment of GAS associated pharyngitis is
indicated; however, it does not prevent development of acute glomerulonephritis. Clinical features of APSGN
include a low serum C3 and a normal serum C4 level. The serum C3 level generally returns to normal within 3
months after the initial presentation of glomerulonephritis. A biopsy is not necessary in order to confirm the
diagnosis of ASPGN; however, if a biopsy were performed immunofluorescence would reveal subepithelial
deposits of IgG and C3. Abnormalities on urinalysis such as microscopic hematuria may persist for up to 1 year
after initial presentation with APSGN.

---

questions.stem: A 10-year-old white male presents to the emergency department with a 24-hour history of painful lower extremities and severe abdominal pain. On physical exam, you note a temperature of 37.4°C and severe arthritis of both knees along with a purpuric rash located on the lower extremities and buttocks. The stool guaiac is positive, as is a urine dipstick for protein and blood. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? (CanadaQB)
questions.initialExplanation: Rash on the lower limbs with abdominal pain and blood in urine = Henoch-Schönlein vasculitis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Henoch-Schonlein purpura is a vasculitis affecting primarily small vessels that occurs most often in
children. Common manifestations include palpable purpura, arthralgias, Gl symptoms and signs, and
glomerulonephritis. Diagnosis is clinical. Disease is usually self limited. Corticosteroids can relieve
arthralgias and Gl symptoms but do not alter the course of the disease.

The disease begins with a sudden palpable purpuric rash that typically involves the extensor surfaces
of the feet, legs, and arms and a strip across the buttocks. The purpura may start as small areas of
urticaria that become indurated and palpable. Crops of new lesions may appear over days to several
weeks. Many patients also have fever and polyarthralgia with associated periarticular tenderness and
swelling of the ankles, knees, hips, wrists, and elbows.

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy is brought to your department by his parents because he had a reddish rash of both legs and buttocks for the last 5 days. The boy also has been complaining of abdominal pain and pain in both knees. He was recently evaluated for sore throat. Physical examination reveals erythematous papules on both legs and buttocks, knee joints are swollen and tender on palpation, and the abdomen is diffusely tender. Which of the following is a key feature of this condition? (CanadaQB)
questions.initialExplanation: The purpura in HSP is nonthrombocytopenic.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This patient presents with Henoch-Schonlein purpura (HSP) triad of erythematous rash, abdominal
pain/renal failure, and arthralgias. While some patients with HSP may not have all the 3 symptoms at
presentation and others could have other symptoms, majority of patients with this condition have
been observed to have these 3 major symptoms. 75% of affected patients are between 2 and 11
years of age. HSP is a clinical diagnosis and generally laboratory evaluation is not necessary to
establish this diagnosis. The key feature of this disease is nonthrombocytopenic purpura (choice C).

---

questions.stem: In an 11-year-old male with dark brown urine and hand and foot edema, which one of the following would be most suggestive of glomerulonephritis? (CanadaQB)

options.label: E
options.text: Elevated C3 and C4 complement levels

questions.initialExplanation: RBC casts in urine are among the strongest signs of glomerulonephritis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Acute glomerulonephritis (AGN) in children manifests as brown or cola-colored urine, which may be
painless or associated with mild flank or abdominal pain. There are many etiologies of AGN but the
most common in children are IgA nephropathy (which may directly follow an acute upper respiratory
tract infection) and acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis following a streptococcal throat or skin
infection (usually 7-21 days later).

---

questions.stem: A 10-year-old child is brought by his mother with reddish-brown coloured urine, hypertension and generalised oedema, three weeks after an episode of a sore throat. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.initialExplanation: APSGN with hypertension and edema: give a loop diuretic (furosemide) to treat fluid overload and lower blood pressure.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This patient has clinical features (hypertension, hematuria, oedema) consistent with a diagnosis of
post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN).The most common presenting signs in children
include:

1-Edema-generalized oedema is present in about two-thirds of patients due to sodium and water
retention.In severe cases, fluid overload leads to respiratory distress due to pulmonary oedema.
2-Gross hematuria-gross hematuria is present in about 30 to 50 percent of patients.

The urine looks smoky, and tea or coca cola-coloured.

3-Hypertension-hypertension is present in 50 to 90 percent of patients and varies from mild to
severe. It is primarily caused by fluid retention.

---

questions.stem: A 9-year-old male child is brought to the emergency department with irritability and facial puffiness. He has been passing small amounts of urine. On examination blood pressure is 160/90 and periorbital oedema noted.Urine examination shows proteinuria and hematuria. This child had been treated with topical antibiotics for impetigo three weeks ago. What is the most appropriate management? (MX)

options.label: A
options.text: High protein,low salt, low carbohydrate and decrease water intake

options.label: D
options.text: Low protein,low salt and increase water intake

questions.initialExplanation: After impetigo with hypertension: start an antihypertensive with fluid management.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This patient has the most likely diagnosis of acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis considering
hematuria, oedema hypertension, proteinuria. Urine output is also decreased and there is a history of
skin infection (impetigo).

This child needs to be hospitalised and anti-hypertensives should be commenced to treat
hypertension.Steroids are not useful in this disease.

Also, consider following points as part pf the management:— Restrict fluids intake.— Take a diet rich in
carbohydrates

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy presents with a 3-day history of dark-colored urine and facial swelling. His mother reports that he had a sore throat approximately 2 weeks ago which resolved with symptomatic treatment. On examination, his blood pressure is 135/90 mmHg, he has periorbital edema, and the rest of the examination is unremarkable. Urinalysis reveals smoky-colored urine with 3+ blood and 2+ protein. Microscopic examination shows dysmorphic red blood cells and red blood cell casts. What is the most likely diagnosis? (MX)
questions.initialExplanation: Dark urine, RBC casts and dysmorphic RBCs = acute glomerulonephritis after streptococcal infection.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This patient presents with the classic triad of acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (APSGN): hematuria
(smoky-colored urine with RBC casts), hypertension, and edema following a streptococcal pharyngeal infection
with an appropriate latent period of 1-3 weeks. The presence of red blood cell casts on urinalysis is
pathognomonic for glomerular inflammation and strongly supports the diagnosis of acute glomerulonephritis.
The age of the patient (school-age child) and the typical presentation following a respiratory infection are highly
characteristic of APSGN. IgA nephropathy typically presents with hematuria concurrent with or immediately
following an upper respiratory infection (synpharyngitic hematuria), not after a 2-week latent period. Henoch-
Schénlein purpura would present with the characteristic purpuric rash, arthritis, and abdominal pain. Alport
syndrome usually presents with persistent microscopic hematuria and positive family history. Acute interstitial
nephritis typically presents with white blood cell casts and eosinophiluria.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old girl is diagnosed with acute glomerulonephritis based on clinical and laboratory findings. Her serum complement C3 level is 45 mg/dL (normal 90-180 mg/dL), while C4 level is normal.

options.label: A
options.text: Which of the following best explains this complement pattern? (MX)

options.label: B
options.text: Decreased hepatic synthesis of complement proteins

options.label: E
options.text: Activation of the alternative complement pathway with C3 consumption

questions.initialExplanation: Low C3 with normal C4 means alternative complement pathway activation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The characteristic finding in acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is isolated hypocomplementemia
with low C3 levels and normal C4 levels. This pattern reflects activation of the alternative complement
pathway rather than the classical pathway. In APSGN, streptococcal antigens (particularly streptococcal
pyogenic exotoxin B or SPEB) form immune complexes that deposit in the glomeruli and activate the
alternative complement pathway, leading to consumption of C3. The classical pathway (which involves C1,
C4, C2) is not significantly activated in APSGN, which explains why C4 levels remain normal. This pattern
helps distinguish APSGN from lupus nephritis or postinfectious GN due to other causes where both C3 and

C4 may be depressed. The hypocomplementemia in APSGN is typically transient, with C3 levels returning to
normal within 6-8 weeks of disease onset.

---

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy with acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis develops sudden severe headache, blurred vision, and vomiting. On examination, he is confused, his blood pressure is 185/120 mmHg, and fundoscopic examination reveals papilledema. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management? (MX)
questions.initialExplanation: Hypertension with papilledema = a blood-pressure emergency, treated with IV agents such as labetalol.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This patient is presenting with hypertensive encephalopathy, a serious complication of acute glomerulonephritis.
The clinical features include severe hypertension (blood pressure 185/120 mmHg), altered mental status
(confusion), headache, vomiting, and papilledema. Hypertensive encephalopathy results from acute elevation in
blood pressure exceeding the autoregulatory capacity of cerebral vasculature, leading to cerebral edema and
potential hemorrhage. The management requires rapid but controlled reduction of blood pressure to prevent
ongoing neurological damage while avoiding too rapid a decline that could compromise renal perfusion.
Intravenous labetalol is the preferred initial agent as it provides rapid, titratable blood pressure control with
predictable dosing. Sodium nitroprusside is also effective but requires continuous blood pressure monitoring
and carries risks of cyanide toxicity with prolonged use. Oral agents are inappropriate in this emergency
situation. Diuretics may be used as adjunctive therapy but are not first-line for hypertensive encephalopathy.

---

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy was diagnosed with acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis 6 months ago following a streptococcal pharyngitis. His parents ask about the long-term prognosis. Which of the following statements is most accurate regarding the prognosis of APSGN?

options.label: A
options.text: Less than 5% of patients progress to chronic renal failure

options.label: B
options.text: Approximately 25% of patients develop persistent proteinuria

options.label: C
options.text: Mortality rate exceeds 10% in developed countries

options.label: D
options.text: Recurrence is common, occurring in up to 50% of patients

options.label: E
options.text: All patients require long-term nephrology follow-up

questions.initialExplanation: APSGN prognosis is excellent: fewer than 5% develop chronic renal failure.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The prognosis of acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis in children is generally excellent. More
than 95% of affected children recover completely with normal renal function and no long-term
sequelae. Less than 5% of patients develop rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis that may progress
to chronic renal failure. Most patients have complete resolution of hematuria within 1-2 years, though
microscopic hematuria may persist in some cases. Proteinuria typically resolves within 4-8 weeks in
the majority of patients. The mortality rate in developed countries is now very low (less than 1%) due
to effective management of complications like heart failure and hypertensive encephalopathy.
Recurrence of APSGN is extremely rare. Long-term nephrology follow-up is not required for all
patients but may be indicated for those with persistent abnormalities or atypical presentations.

---

questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy presents with visible hematuria that began 1 day after onset of an upper respiratory tract infection. He has no rash, joint pain, or abdominal pain. His blood pressure is 118/75 mmHg, and physical examination is unremarkable. Urinalysis shows 3+ blood with red blood cells but no red blood cell casts. Serum C3 level is normal. Which of the following is most likely to be found on renal biopsy? (MX)

options.label: C
options.text: Diffuse proliferative changes with wire-loop lesions

options.label: E
options.text: Granular deposition of IgG and C3

questions.initialExplanation: Hematuria a day after a respiratory infection with normal C3 = IgA nephropathy; biopsy shows IgA deposits in the mesangium.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This clinical presentation is characteristic of IgA nephropathy (Berger disease), the most common cause of
glomerulonephritis worldwide. The key feature is synpharyngitic hematuria, where hematuria occurs within 1-2
days of an upper respiratory infection, rather than after a latent period of 1-3 weeks as seen in post-

‘    streptococcal GN. The normal C3 level helps distinguish IgA nephropathy from APSGN. The definitive
diagnosis is established by renal biopsy showing predominant mesangial deposition of IgA on
immunofluorescence microscopy. Subepithelial "humps" are characteristic of postinfectious GN. Diffuse
proliferative changes with wire-loop lesions are seen in lupus nephritis. Thin glomerular basement membrane
suggests thin basement membrane disease, a cause of persistent hematuria with benign prognosis. Granular
deposition of IgG and C3 is seen in post-infectious GN.

---

questions.stem: A 14-year-old girl presents with recurrent episodes of gross hematuria, each occurring 1-2 days after upper respiratory infections. She has no edema, hypertension, or renal impairment. Her father had similar episodes during childhood. Urinalysis between episodes shows microscopic hematuria with occasional dysmorphic red blood cells. Serum creatinine and C3 are normal.

options.label: A
options.text: What is the most appropriate next step in management? (MX)

options.label: B
options.text: Perform renal biopsy to confirm diagnosis

options.label: D
options.text: Obtain genetic testing for Alport syndrome

options.label: E
options.text: Reassure and observe with regular monitoring

questions.initialExplanation: Recurrent microscopic hematuria after infection with normal creatinine and C3: reassure and follow regularly.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This patient has a classic presentation of IgA nephropathy with synpharyngitic hematuria, positive family history,
and benign clinical course (no hypertension, normal renal function). The prognosis in such cases is generally
excellent, with the majority of patients maintaining normal renal function for decades. In patients with isolated
microscopic hematuria or recurrent gross hematuria without proteinuria, hypertension, or renal impairment, the
standard approach is conservative management with regular monitoring of blood pressure, renal function, and
urinalysis. Renal biopsy is indicated when there is proteinuria exceeding 1 g/day, declining renal function, or
hypertension. Tonsillectomy has been advocated by some investigators but remains controversial and is not
routinely recommended. Genetic testing for Alport syndrome would be indicated if there were associated
hearing loss or ocular abnormalities, or if hematuria persisted without the characteristic IgA nephropathy
pattern.

---

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy with Henoch-Schénlein purpura develops worsening edema and decreased urine output 2 weeks after onset of the rash. Laboratory investigations reveal: serum creatinine 1.6 mg/dL (elevated), urine protein/creatinine ratio 2.5, and urinalysis shows 3+ blood with red blood cell casts. What is the most appropriate next step in management? (MX)

options.label: B
options.text: Renal biopsy to assess severity of renal involvement

questions.initialExplanation: HSP with edema, RBC casts and deterioration: renal biopsy to assess severity.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This patient has developed significant renal involvement from HSP, presenting with acute Kidney injury
(elevated creatinine), nephrotic-range proteinuria, and nephritic syndrome (hematuria with RBC casts). This
represents severe HSP nephritis, which occurs in approximately 20-30% of HSP cases. The management of
HSP nephritis depends on the severity and histological findings on renal biopsy. Renal biopsy is indicated to
assess the extent of renal involvement, particularly to identify crescent formation, which guides treatment
decisions. Mild cases with only hematuria and proteinuria may respond to supportive care, while severe cases
with crescentic glomerulonephritis may require aggressive immunosuppression including corticosteroids,
cyclophosphamide, or other agents. Plasmapheresis may be considered in severe crescentic disease. The
biopsy results will determine whether the patient needs pulse methylprednisolone, oral prednisone, or
combination therapy with cyclophosphamide.

---

questions.stem: A 10-year-old girl with Henoch-Schénlein purpura presents with severe colicky abdominal pain and melena. She has no evidence of renal involvement (normal urinalysis, normal creatinine). What is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.initialExplanation: HSP with severe symptoms but no kidney involvement: per the given answer IV steroids (the reference usually says supportive care or a short steroid course).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Severe abdominal pain in HSP, particularly when associated with gastrointestinal bleeding, is due to
vasculitic involvement of the bowel wall. High-dose corticosteroids are the treatment of choice for
severe gastrointestinal manifestations of HSP that do not respond to conservative management.
Intravenous methylprednisolone (typically 1-2 mg/kg/day or pulse therapy) can provide rapid relief of
abdominal pain and reduce inflammation of the bowel wall. This approach may also help prevent or
reduce renal involvement, though evidence for this is less robust. Surgical consultation should be
obtained if there is concern for complications such as intussusception, perforation, or massive
bleeding that may require intervention, but steroids are first-line for vasculitic abdominal pain.
Analgesics alone are insufficient for severe vasculitic pain. IVIG and plasmapheresis are reserved for
refractory cases or severe renal disease.

---

questions.stem: A 14-year-old girl presents with palpable purpuric rash, arthritis, and renal involvement (proteinuria and hematuria). Unlike typical HSP, she also has positive ANA (1:320), low C3 and C4, and oral ulcers. Which of the following findings would most strongly support a diagnosis of systemic lupus erythematosus over HSP? (MX)

options.label: A
options.text: History of preceding upper respiratory infection

options.label: B
options.text: Predominant IgA deposition on renal biopsy

options.label: E
options.text: Arthritis involving large joints of lower extremities

questions.initialExplanation: Favoring SLE over HSP is a positive anti-dsDNA.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Distinguishing between HSP and lupus vasculitis can be challenging as both can present with purpuric rash,
arthritis, and renal involvement. However, positive anti-dsDNA antibody is highly specific for systemic lupus
erythematosus and would strongly support this diagnosis over HSP.

In SLE, renal biopsy would typically show "full-house" immunofluorescence deposition (IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, C1q)
with various patterns depending on the class of lupus nephritis, whereas HSP nephritis shows predominant IgA
deposition. HSP typically presents in younger children (3-8 years), while SLE is more common in adolescent
females. Both conditions can have arthritis and renal involvement. The presence of oral ulcers, positive ANA,

and low complements are more suggestive of SLE. Anti-dsDNA antibodies are specific for SLE and correlate
with disease activity, particularly in lupus nephritis.

---

questions.stem: A 14-year-old girl with SLE presents with nephrotic syndrome (serum albumin 1.8 g/dL, urine protein /creatinine ratio 4.2) and preserved renal function (creatinine 0.7 mg/dL). Renal biopsy shows diffuse thickening of the glomerular basement membrane with subepithelial immune complex deposits and "spike and hole" appearance on silver stain. What is the most likely classification and recommended treatment? (MX)

options.label: B
options.text: Class IV; mycophenolate mofetil with prednisone

options.label: C
options.text: Class V; mycophenolate mofetil with prednisone

options.label: E
options.text: Class lll or IV; rituximab monotherapy

questions.initialExplanation: Nephrotic syndrome in lupus with a "spike and hole" pattern = lupus nephritis class V, treated with mycophenolate and prednisolone.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The renal biopsy findings of diffuse GBM thickening with subepithelial deposits and "spike and hole"
appearance on silver stain are pathognomonic for membranous lupus nephritis (Class V). Class V
lupus nephritis typically presents with nephrotic syndrome with relatively preserved renal function and
lacks the active urinary sediment (cellular casts) seen in proliferative forms (Class Ill or IV). The
treatment of choice for pure Class V lupus nephritis is mycophenolate mofetil (2-3 g/day) combined
with corticosteroids, which has been shown to be as effective as cyclophosphamide with a better side
effect profile. Cyclophosphamide is typically reserved for Class Ill or IV disease or Class V with
overlapping proliferative features. Cyclosporine is an alternative agent but mycophenolate is generally
preferred first-line. Rituximab is typically reserved for refractory cases.

---

questions.stem: A 12-year-old girl is diagnosed with membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis. Her complement studies show isolated low C3 with normal C4. Serum C3 nephritic factor is positive. Which of the following statements is most accurate regarding this presentation?

options.label: A
options.text: This is characteristic of poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis \*

options.label: C
options.text: This pattern is typical of lupus nephritis

options.label: D
options.text: This is characteristic of C3 glomerulopathy

options.label: E
options.text: This finding rules out infection-associated MPGN

questions.initialExplanation: Low C3 with normal C4 and positive C3 nephritic factor distinguishes C3 glomerulopathy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
C3 glomerulopathy is defined by dysregulation of the alternative complement pathway with dominant C3
deposition in the glomeruli. The key diagnostic feature is predominant C3 staining (at least 2 orders of
magnitude more intense than other immunoreactants) on immunofluorescence. The presence of C3 nephritic
factor, an autoantibody that stabilizes the C3 convertase of the alternative pathway, is strongly associated
with C3 glomerulopathy, particularly dense deposit disease (Type Il MPGN). The pattern of isolated C3
depression (low C3 with normal C4) indicates alternative pathway activation, distinguishing it from classical
pathway activation seen in lupus nephritis or hepatitisassociated MPGN (which typically depresses both C3
and C4). C3 glomerulopathy includes C3 GN and dense deposit disease, both characterized by alternative

complement pathway dysregulation. This entity has replaced the older classification of Type Il MPGN in
many classification systems.

---

questions.stem: A 14-year-old boy presents with 2 weeks of progressive edema, hematuria, and decreasing urine output. Laboratory values show: serum creatinine 3.2 mg/dL (rapidly rising from normal 2 weeks ago), BUN 45 mg/dL, and urine output 0.3 mL/kg/hour. Urinalysis shows RBC casts and 3+ protein. Which of the following terms best describes this clinical syndrome? A) Acute nephritic syndrome \ B) Nephrotic syndrome
questions.initialExplanation: Edema and blood in urine with rapid deterioration = rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN) is characterized by the clinical syndrome of acute nephritic
syndrome (hematuria, hypertension, edema) with rapid loss of renal function over days to weeks (typically a
doubling of serum creatinine or 50% decline in GFR within 3 months). The presence of oliguria, rapidly rising

‘    creatinine, and nephritic urinary sediment (RBC casts) is characteristic. RPGN is defined pathologically by the
presence of crescents in a majority of glomeruli on renal biopsy (typically more than 50%). The term "rapidly
progressive" emphasizes the clinical course rather than a specific etiology, as RPGN can result from various
underlying conditions including anti-GBM disease, immune complex-mediated GN (such as lupus or post-
infectious), or ANCAassociated vasculitis. Prompt recognition and treatment are essential as RPGN can
progress to end-stage renal disease within weeks to months if untreated.

---

questions.stem: A 15-year-old boy with Goodpasture syndrome is diagnosed based on positive anti-GBM antibodies and pulmonary-renal syndrome. Which treatment regimen is most appropriate? (MX)

options.label: B
options.text: Plasmapheresis combined with cyclophosphamide and corticosteroids

questions.initialExplanation: Goodpasture syndrome is treated with plasmapheresis plus cyclophosphamide and steroids.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The standard treatment for anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture syndrome) is triple therapy: plasmapheresis to
remove circulating anti-GBM antibodies, combined with immunosuppressive therapy (cyclophosphamide and
corticosteroids) to suppress further antibody production and control inflammation. Plasmapheresis is essential
because it rapidly removes pathogenic antibodies, which is particularly important in patients with pulmonary
hemorrhage or severe renal disease. Without plasmapheresis, the mortality rate from pulmonary hemorrhage
is high. Cyclophosphamide is typically given as intravenous pulses or oral therapy, and corticosteroids are
given as pulse methylprednisolone followed by oral prednisone. The response to treatment depends on the
severity at presentation; patients with serum creatinine less than 5-6 mg/dL at presentation have better

outcomes, while those with severe renal failure requiring dialysis at presentation have poorer renal recovery
rates despite treatment.

---

questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy with persistent microscopic hematuria and proteinuria (urine protein/ creatinine ratio 1.2 g/g) is being evaluated. His blood pressure is 125/82 mmHg (elevated for age). Which of the following is the strongest indication for renal biopsy?

options.label: B
options.text: Persistent microscopic hematuria for more than 6 months

options.label: D
options.text: Age greater than 10 years at presentation

questions.initialExplanation: Strongest biopsy indications: proteinuria over 1 g/day with symptoms (also persistently low complement and others).
questions.detailedExplanation:
In children with persistent hematuria, renal biopsy is indicated when there is proteinuria exceeding 1
g/day (or urine protein/creatinine ratio greater than 1), as this suggests more significant glomerular
disease and may impact management decisions. Proteinuria of this magnitude in the setting of
hematuria increases the risk of progressive renal disease and warrants histological diagnosis to guide
treatment. Other indications for biopsy include declining renal function, hypertension, or abnormal
serologies suggesting systemic disease. Persistent hematuria alone without proteinuria, even for
more than 6 months, may be managed with observation in the absence of other risk factors. Family

history of renal disease may increase suspicion for Alport syndrome but is not itself an indication for
biopsy.

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy presents with hematuria and edema. Urinalysis shows RBC casts. Laboratory values: C3 is low, ASO titer is elevated, and anti-DNase B is normal. The hematuria began 2 days after the onset of an upper respiratory infection. Which of the following findings would most strongly favor a diagnosis of IgA nephropathy over poststreptococcal GN?

options.label: A
options.text: Low C3 level persisting beyond 8 weeks

options.label: B
options.text: Hematuria occurring 1-2 days after infection onset

options.label: D
options.text: Presence of red blood cell casts

options.label: E
options.text: History of prior episode of gross hematuria

questions.initialExplanation: IgA nephropathy shows blood 1-2 days after infection (synpharyngitic), whereas APSGN is 1-3 weeks after.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The timing of hematuria relative to infection is the key distinguishing feature between IgA nephropathy
and post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. In IgA nephropathy, hematuria occurs within 1-2 days of
the inciting infection (synpharyngitic hematuria), whereas in post-streptococcal GN, there is a latent
period of 1-3 weeks after the infection. This patient's presentation with hematuria occurring only 2
days after infection onset strongly suggests IgA nephropathy rather than APSGN. The low C3 level
can occur in both conditions, though it typically normalizes within 6-8 weeks in APSGN. Elevated ASO
titer indicates recent streptococcal infection but does not differentiate between the two conditions. Red

blood cell casts indicate glomerular inflammation and can be seen in both. Prior episodes of gross
hematuria are characteristic of IgA nephropathy.

---

questions.stem: A 14-year-old boy is referred with a blood pressure of 145/80 mmHg. There is family history of essential hypertension. His general physical examination and urinalysis are normal. Home blood pressure readings are consistently between 100-110 mmHg systolic and 70-80 mmHg diastolic. Which one of the following is the most likely cause of his hypertension?
questions.initialExplanation: High blood pressure in the clinic only with normal pressure outside = white coat hypertension.
questions.detailedExplanation:
White coat hypertension is a phenomenon in which patients exhibit elevated blood pressure in a
clinical setting but not when recorded by themselves at home. It is believed that this is due to the
anxiety some people experience during a clinic visit and see a physician in a ‘white coat’.

As the notion of "normal" is subjective and changes from individual to individual, a reference
measurement is necessary. As night-time and self measured values are often not subject to daily
stress while clinical values are subject to unusual anxiety, daytime ambulatory blood pressure is used
as a reference because it takes into account daily stress but not in excess. Due to specificity involved
in diagnosis of white coat hypertension, many problems have been incurred in its diagnosis and
treatment.

---

questions.stem: A 15-year-old obese boy is found to have blood pressure 142/92 mmHg on three separate occasions. He has no symptoms and no family history of early cardiovascular disease. Physical examination reveals acanthosis nigricans but normal femoral pulses. Which type of hypertension is most likely? Secondary hypertension due to pheochromocytoma

options.label: B
options.text: Secondary hypertension due to renal artery stenosis \*

options.label: D
options.text: Secondary hypertension due to coarctation of the aorta \*

options.label: E
options.text: Secondary hypertension due to Cushing syndrome

questions.initialExplanation: An obese teen with high blood pressure, acanthosis nigricans and a normal workup = primary hypertension.
questions.detailedExplanation:
In adolescents aged 13 years and older, the AAP 2017 guidelines recommend using adult blood pressure
classification criteria. A blood pressure of 142/92 mmHg meets the criteria for Stage 2 hypertension (=140/90
mmHg). In adolescents, particularly those who are obese, primary (essential) hypertension is the most common

‘    form. The presence of acanthosis nigricans, a marker of insulin resistance associated with obesity, further
supports this diagnosis. Normal femoral pulses make coarctation unlikely. The absence of symptoms
(headache, sweating, palpitations) makes pheochromocytoma unlikely. No stigmata of Cushing syndrome are
described. Primary hypertension in adolescents is strongly associated with obesity and family history.
Secondary hypertension becomes less common with increasing age in childhood and is more common in
younger children and those with normal BMI.

---

questions.stem: A 12-year-old girl presents with severe hypertension (blood pressure 165/105 mmHg). On abdominal examination, an abdominal bruit is heard. Plasma renin activity is markedly elevated. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Severe hypertension, abdominal bruit and high renin = renal artery stenosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This clinical picture is classic for renovascular hypertension due to renal artery stenosis. The key features
include severe hypertension (common in renovascular disease), abdominal bruit (indicating turbulent blood flow
across a stenotic artery), and elevated renin activity (reflecting activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone
system due to decreased renal perfusion). Renal artery stenosis in children is often caused by fibromuscular
dysplasia, neurofibromatosis, arteritis, or may be iatrogenic from prior umbilical artery catheterization. The high
renin state confirms the renovascular etiology.

Renal parenchymal disease would not typically present with an abdominal bruit or markedly elevated renin.
Pheochromocytoma would present with catecholamine excess symptoms (headache, sweating, tachycardia)
and elevated catecholamine metabolites. Coarctation would show blood pressure discrepancy between upper
and lower extremities. Cushing syndrome would have characteristic physical features.

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy is evaluated for headaches. Blood pressure in the right arm is 140/90 mmHg, but pulses in the lower extremities are diminished and delayed compared to the upper extremities. Chest X- ray shows figure-3 sign. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Higher pressure in the arm, weak femoral pulses and a figure-3 sign = coarctation of the aorta.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This presentation is classic for coarctation of the aorta. The key clinical features include hypertension
in the upper extremities with diminished or delayed femoral pulses, headaches (symptom of
hypertension), and the characteristic "figure-3 sign" on chest Xray (caused by pre- and post-stenotic
dilation of the aorta). Coarctation of the aorta is the primary cardiac cause of hypertension in children.
The blood pressure discrepancy between upper and lower extremities is pathognomonic. Renal artery
stenosis would not cause diminished lower extremity pulses or the figure-3 sign. Takayasu arteritis can

cause similar findings but typically presents in older children and adolescents with systemic symptoms
and inflammatory markers. Essential hypertension would not cause pulse discrepancies.
Pheochromocytoma would not explain the pulse findings or chest X-ray abnormalities.

---

questions.stem: A 9-year-old girl is found to have blood pressure 145/92 mmHg on three separate occasions. Her physician decides to investigate for secondary causes. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial workup?

options.label: A
options.text: Urine analysis, serum creatinine, and renal ultrasound

questions.initialExplanation: High blood pressure in a girl: start searching for secondary causes with basic urine, blood and kidney tests.
questions.detailedExplanation:
In children with confirmed hypertension, the initial evaluation should focus on the most common causes. Renal
parenchymal disease accounts for approximately 68% of secondary hypertension cases in children, making it
the most common category. Therefore, the initial workup should include urine analysis (to detect proteinuria,
hematuria, or infection), serum creatinine (to assess renal function), and renal ultrasound (to evaluate renal
size, structure, and detect scarring, tumors, or structural abnormalities). This initial screening can identify renal
causes that require further investigation or specific treatment. If the initial workup is negative, additional tests
may be indicated based on clinical suspicion, including plasma renin and aldosterone (for renovascular disease
or hyperaldosteronism), urine catecholamines (for pheochromocytoma) , or further imaging studies. Cardiac
catheterization would be reserved for suspected coarctation if noninvasive imaging is inconclusive.

---

questions.stem: A 15-year-old boy with hypertension is started on an ACE inhibitor. He is counseled about potential side effects. Which of the following is the most important adverse effect to monitor for?
questions.initialExplanation: With an ACE inhibitor the key thing to monitor is hyperkalemia and rising creatinine.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors work by inhibiting the conversion of angiotensin | to angiotensin
II, leading to reduced aldosterone secretion. Aldosterone normally promotes potassium excretion in the distal
tubule, so its inhibition can lead to potassium retention and hyperkalemia. This is the most clinically significant
adverse effect to monitor, especially in patients with underlying renal impairment or those taking potassium-
sparing diuretics. Hyperkalemia can cause cardiac arrhythmias and is potentially life-threatening. Other side
effects of ACE inhibitors include dry cough (due to increased bradykinin), angioedema (rare but serious), and
hypotension. The initial increase in serum creatinine (up to 30% above baseline) is expected and not a reason
for discontinuation unless it persists or exceeds this threshold. Regular monitoring of serum potassium and renal
function is essential during ACE inhibitor therapy.

---

questions.stem: A 14-year-old boy with Stage 2 hypertension presents with hypertensive emergency (BP 210/140 mmHg) due to suspected renal artery stenosis. What is the most appropriate initial approach to blood pressure reduction?

options.label: A
options.text: Rapid reduction to normal blood pressure within 1 hour

options.label: B
options.text: Reduce blood pressure by 25% within 1 hour, then to normal over 24-48 hours

options.label: C
options.text: No treatment needed as this is an adolescent with primary hypertension

questions.initialExplanation: Hypertensive emergency: lower the pressure gradually (not rapidly), usually by 25% in the first 8 hours.
questions.detailedExplanation:
In hypertensive emergencies, including those due to secondary causes like renal artery stenosis, blood pressure
reduction must be gradual and controlled. The goal is to reduce mean arterial pressure by no more than 25%
within the first hour, followed by gradual reduction to normal over 24-48 hours. Too rapid reduction can
compromise perfusion to vital organs, particularly the brain and kidneys, leading to ischemia or infarction. This is
especially important in children with renal artery stenosis, where abrupt blood pressure reduction can cause
acute kidney injury due to impaired renal autoregulation. Intravenous antihypertensive agents are typically used
initially, allowing for titratable blood pressure control. Agents commonly used include labetalol, nicardipine,
esmolol, hydralazine, and sodium nitroprusside. Once blood pressure is controlled, the underlying cause (such
as renal artery stenosis) should be investigated and treated definitively.

---

questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy with Stage 3 chronic kidney disease (estimated GFR 45 mL/min/1.73m?) secondary to renal dysplasia presents for follow-up. His blood pressure has been consistently elevated at Stage 1 levels despite 6 months of adherence to the DASH diet and weight management. His current blood pressure is 128/82 mmHg, which is at the 95th percentile for his age, sex, and height. Serum electrolytes are normal, and urinalysis shows trace protein. What is the most appropriate initial pharmacologic agent?
questions.initialExplanation: CKD with proteinuria: lisinopril (ACE inhibitor) is suitable to protect the kidney and lower pressure.
questions.detailedExplanation:
In children with chronic kidney disease and hypertension, angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors or
angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) are the recommended first-line agents. This recommendation is based
on their renoprotective effects and ability to reduce proteinuria, which slows the progression of chronic kidney

‘     disease. The 2017 AAP guidelines specifically recommend ACE inhibitors or ARBs as first-line therapy in
children with CKD and hypertension. ACE inhibitors reduce intraglomerular pressure by dilating the efferent
arteriole, which decreases proteinuria and may slow the decline in GFR. This patient has trace proteinuria, and
an ACE inhibitor would address both the hypertension and the proteinuria. Amlodipine and hydrochlorothiazide
are acceptable antihypertensive agents but do not provide the same renoprotective benefits in CKD.
Propranolol and clonidine are not first-line agents for this clinical scenario.

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl with acute glomerulonephritis presents to the emergency department with a severe headache and visual changes. Her blood pressure is 160/110 mmHg (>99th percentile plus 12 mmHg), and she begins having tonic-clonic movements upon arrival. Intravenous access has been established, and she requires seizure control. What is the most appropriate goal for blood pressure reduction in the first 8 hours?

options.label: B
options.text: Reduce mean arterial pressure by no more than 25%

options.label: C
options.text: Reduce systolic blood pressure to below the 50th percentile

options.label: E
options.text: Withhold antihypertensive medications until neuroimaging is completed

questions.initialExplanation: With seizure due to hypertension: lower MAP by at most 25% in the first 8 hours to avoid cerebral hypoperfusion.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This patient is experiencing a hypertensive emergency with encephalopathy, as evidenced by severe
hypertension, headache, visual changes, and seizures. In hypertensive emergencies, rapid reduction of blood
pressure can lead to cerebral ischemia and hypoperfusion because the cerebral autoregulation curve shifts to
the right in chronic hypertension. The goal is to reduce the mean arterial pressure by no more than 25% over
the first 8 hours, with gradual normalization over 24-48 hours. This conservative approach prevents ischemic
complications while still addressing the emergency.

Reducing systolic blood pressure to the 90th percentile immediately or normalizing within 2 hours would be too
rapid and could cause stroke, blindness, or other ischemic complications. Withholding treatment in a seizing

patient is dangerous. The initial management should include intravenous antihypertensive agents such as
labetalol, nicardipine, or sodium nitroprusside.

---

questions.stem: A 16-year-old male with essential hypertension has been well-controlled on amlodipine 5 mg daily for the past year. He presents complaining of swollen ankles and feet, which make it difficult to wear his soccer cleats. He reports no recent weight gain, shortness of breath, or difficulty breathing. Physical examination reveals 2+ bilateral pitting edema extending to the mid-shin. Urinalysis is negative for protein, and his blood pressure is well-controlled at 118/72 mmHg. What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
questions.initialExplanation: Controlled pressure with new symptoms points to a drug side effect.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Peripheral edema is a dose-dependent, common side effect of dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers such
as amlodipine. The mechanism involves precapillary vasodilation leading to increased capillary hydrostatic
pressure and transudation of fluid into the interstitial space. This side effect is particularly common with

‘    amlodipine due to its long half-life and preferential action on vascular smooth muscle. The bilateral, symmetric
nature of the edema and the absence of other signs or symptoms make alternative causes less likely.
Nephrotic syndrome would typically present with proteinuria on urinalysis. Congestive heart failure would likely
cause additional symptoms such as dyspnea, orthopnea, and possibly crackles on lung examination. Deep vein
thrombosis typically presents with unilateral swelling and pain. While excessive sodium intake can contribute to
edema, the chronic and bilateral nature of this patient's edema strongly suggests a medication effect.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old girl is found to have blood pressure 130/85 mmHg (>99th percentile for her age) during a routine well-child visit. On examination, you hear a bruit over the epigastrium, and when comparing pulses, you note that femoral pulses are diminished and delayed compared to brachial pulses. The child was born prematurely at 28 weeks and had an umbilical artery catheter in the neonatal intensive care unit. These findings are most specific for which etiology of hypertension?
questions.initialExplanation: Per the given answer: coarctation of the aorta, although the question mentions an umbilical catheter, which usually suggests renal artery thrombosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The classic findings of diminished and delayed femoral pulses compared to upper extremity pulses, along with
an abdominal bruit, are highly suggestive of coarctation of the aorta. The history of premature birth with
umbilical artery catheter placement is significant because umbilical artery catheters can cause thromboembolic
complications affecting the aorta or renal arteries. While this patient could have renal artery stenosis (which
would explain the abdominal bruit), the pulse discrepancy is pathognomonic for coarctation. Coarctation
typically presents with hypertension in the upper extremities and hypotension or reduced pulses in the lower
extremities. The "brachial-femoral delay" is a key clinical finding that distinguishes coarctation from other
causes of childhood hypertension. Pheochromocytoma would present with catecholamine excess symptoms
and elevated catecholamine metabolites. Essential hypertension is rare in children under 6 years of age.

Polycystic kidney disease would typically present with enlarged kidneys on ultrasound and possibly hepatic
involvement.

---

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy with a history of obesity-related hypertension has achieved significant lifestyle modifications over the past year, losing 8 kg (moving from 97th to 75th percentile BMI). He is currently maintained on enalapril 5 mg daily. His recent blood pressure readings are consistently at or below 100/60 mmHg (<50th percentile), and he reports feeling well without symptoms. Which management strategy is most appropriate at this time?

options.label: A
options.text: Discontinue the medication immediately and observe

options.label: B
options.text: Continue the current dose indefinitely for ongoing renal protection

options.label: C
options.text: Switch to every-other-day dosing to maintain partial effect

options.label: D
options.text: Taper the dose and attempt a trial of withdrawal with frequent monitoring

options.label: E
options.text: Add a low-dose diuretic to allow further reduction of ACE inhibitor dose

questions.initialExplanation: Controlled pressure in an obese teen with weight loss: reduce the medication gradually and try to withdraw it.
questions.detailedExplanation:
When blood pressure is well-controlled and there has been significant improvement in underlying risk factors
(such as substantial weight loss), a trial of stepping down therapy is appropriate. This approach, known as"
step-down therapy," involves gradually tapering and potentially discontinuing antihypertensive medication while
monitoring for rebound hypertension. The goal is to maintain blood pressure control with the minimal number
and dose of medications necessary. Abrupt discontinuation of ACE inhibitors is not recommended due to the
potential for rebound hypertension and loss of renoprotective effects. This patient has achieved excellent blood
pressure control with significant weight loss, making him a good candidate for a trial of medication withdrawal.
The taper should be done over several weeks, with frequent blood pressure monitoring to detect any rebound

elevation. If blood pressure remains controlled without medication, the patient can continue lifestyle
modifications alone with ongoing monitoring.

---

questions.stem: A former 28-week premature infant, now 3 months old (corrected age 1 month), has persistent hypertension requiring evaluation. During the neonatal intensive care unit stay, an umbilical artery catheter was placed and remained in place for 2 weeks. The infant is now being evaluated for blood pressure readings consistently above the 95th percentile for age. What is the most likely etiology of hypertension that should be evaluated in this infant?
questions.initialExplanation: A premature infant with an umbilical catheter and hypertension = renal artery thrombosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
A history of umbilical artery catheter placement is a major risk factor for renal artery thrombosis, which can
lead to renovascular hypertension in infants. Umbilical artery catheters can cause thromboembolic
complications, particularly if the catheter tip is positioned too high (above the level of the renal arteries). The
resulting thrombosis or stenosis of the renal artery leads to reduced renal perfusion, activation of the
reninangiotensin-aldosterone system, and hypertension. This infant has the classic risk factor (umbilical artery
catheter), and the timing of presentation (early infancy) is consistent with this diagnosis. Essential hypertension
is virtually non-existent in infants. Congenital adrenal hyperplasia typically presents with ambiguous genitalia in
females, vomiting, and electrolyte abnormalities. Hyperthyroidism in infancy is rare and would present with
other symptoms such as tachycardia, goiter, and failure to thrive. Wilms tumor(nephroblastoma) can cause
hypertension but typically presents between 2-5 years of age with an abdominal mass.

---

questions.stem: A 10-year-old male (had a boil in the left thigh and mild fever one month ago) presented with headache, malaise, lethargy, lion pain, decreased urine output, and puffiness of the face; GUE: RBC cast ++, albumin ++; low C3 level and normal C4 level. Which of the following is TRUE about his disease? (NE)
questions.initialExplanation: A month after skin infection with low C3 and normal C4: in APSGN hypertension appears in 70% of patients.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The patient has acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (APSGN), triggered by a recent skin infection (boil

on thigh), presenting as acute nephritic syndrome.

APSGN classically features hematuria with RBC casts, mild proteinuria (albumin ++), oliguria (decreased urine
‘    output), periorbital/facial edema (puffiness), low C3 with normal C4, and systemic symptoms like headache and

malaise. This matches acute nephritic syndrome, not nephrotic syndrome (which requires heavy proteinuria >

3.5g/day and hypoalbuminemia without prominent hematuria/RBC casts).

- Hypertension occurs in approximately 70% of PSGN patients and is one of the most consistent and clinically

significant manifestations. This patient already exhibits symptoms consistent with hypertension, including

headache.

GLONephritis & HTN |

---

## Hematuria & HUS

> Question numbers not present in the source file for this topic: 14.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy presented with fever and bloody diarrhea, he developed pallor, lethargy, and decreased urine output in the past 24 hours. His hematocrit is 28% and platelet count is 60,000/cmm. He had protein and blood in the urine. Which of the following diagnoses is MOST likely to explain these symptoms?
questions.initialExplanation: Bloody diarrhea and fever then pallor, oliguria and protein/blood in urine = hemolytic uremic syndrome.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This case presents the classic triad of Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS), a thrombotic microangiopathy that represents
one of the most common causes of acute kidney injury in young children. Recognition of this syndrome is critical because
early supportive management significantly impacts outcomes.

- The classic triad of HUS consists of: (1) microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, (2) thrombocytopenia, and (3) acute kidney
injury. This patient demonstrates all three components with remarkable clarity. The hematocrit of 28% indicates significant
anemia, and the platelet count of 60,000/cmm demonstrates thrombocytopenia. The decreased urine output and
abnormal urinalysis (protein and blood) confirm renal involvement.

- The clinical course is also characteristic. The illness typically begins with a prodromal diarrheal illness, often bloody,
caused by infection with Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli (particularly O157:H7) or, less commonly, Shigella
dysenteriae type 1. The timing of the second phase, developing 5-10 days after the onset of diarrhea, is classic for HUS.
The bloody diarrhea in this case is a key historical feature that strongly suggests an infectious etiology.

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old girl presents with pallor, decreased activity, and reduced urine output. Her parents report that she had bloody diarrhea 4 days ago. On exam, she is pale but hemodynamically stable. Labs show Hb 6.5 g/dL, platelets 30,000/mms2, and creatinine 1.5 mg/dL. Urinalysis reveals 3+ hematuria and 1+ proteinuria. Blood smear shows schistocytes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Pallor, reduced activity and oliguria with schistocytes on the smear = HUS.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This is the classic triad of HUS: microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (low Hb, schistocytes),
thrombocytopenia (30,000), and acute kidney injury (elevated creatinine, oliguria). The history of
bloody diarrhea suggests Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (typical/D+ HUS). ITP lacks anemia and renal
involvement; DIC has coagulation abnormalities.

---

questions.stem: Hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) is characterized by the triad of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and renal injury and is an important cause of acute kidney injury in children. Evidence of renal injury in HUS is the presence of : (NE)
questions.initialExplanation: Kidney involvement in HUS shows urine with red cells and protein; per the given answer: pyuria.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Pyuria is defined as the presence of an increased number of white blood cells (leukocytes) in the urine, typically
exceeding 5-10 white blood cells per high-power field on microscopic examination. In the context of HUS, pyuria
is recognized as a common urinalysis finding that indicates renal inflammation and injury .

Pyuria in HUS reflects the inflammatory process occurring within the renal microvasculature. The pathogenesis
of HUS involves endothelial cell damage in the glomeruli and renal arterioles, which triggers an inflammatory
response. This inflammatory cascade recruits white blood cells to the affected renal tissue, and these cells

subsequently appear in the urine as pyuria. The presence of pyuria on urinalysis therefore serves as evidence
that the kidney parenchyma is actively involved in the disease process .

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old girl had bloody diarrhea for several days. One week later she develops periorbital edema and fatigue. What is the most likely laboratory finding? (Lange)
questions.initialExplanation: A week after bloody diarrhea with edema and fatigue: anemia and low platelets (the HUS triad).
questions.detailedExplanation:
The patient exhibits signs and symptoms of hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) after an episode
of gasteroenteritis most likely caused by enterohemorrhagic strain of E coli. This syndrome is
characterized by microangiopathic hemolysis, thrombocytopenia, and acute renal failure. The
typical history, clinical picture, and laboratory findings confirm the diagnosis in most patients.
Treatment is mainly supportive, frequent peritoneal dialysis needs to be initiated. Mortality is
less than 10% with aggressive management of the acute renal failure. Most of the patients will
recover normal renal function.

---

questions.stem: A 20-mo-old child develops hemolytic anemia, anuria, azotemia, and thrombocytopenia after a bout of febrile bloody diarrhea. The most likely etiologic agent of this illness is: (NE)
questions.initialExplanation: Bloody diarrhea with hemolytic anemia and renal failure is usually caused by enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC O157:H7).
questions.detailedExplanation:
The child presents with the classic tetrad of post-diarrheal HUS:

- Hemolytic anemia: Results from mechanical damage to red blood cells as they pass through damaged
microvasculature with fibrin deposits.

- Anuria and azotemia: Indicate acute kidney injury, a hallmark of HUS.
- Thrombocytopenia: Due to platelet consumption in microthrombi.
- Preceding febrile bloody diarrhea: The typical prodrome in 90% of cases.

- Enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC), particularly serotype O157:H7, is the most common cause of typical
(diarrhea-associated) HUS in children. This organism produces Shiga toxin (Stx), which is directly responsible
for the endothelial cell damage in the renal microvasculature that characterizes HUS.

---

questions.stem: An 18-mo-old toddler develops severe hemolytic-uremic syndrome from E. coli O157:H7 colitis. She remains anuric and dialysis dependent for 3 mo. Follow-up renal ultrasonography reveals a significant decrease in renal size with increased renal echogenicity. The most appropriate statement about this patient's condition is: (NE)

options.label: A
options.text: She probably had pre-existing chronic renal insufficiency

options.label: B
options.text: With continued dialysis support, she can be expected to regain normal renal function within the next 3 mo

options.label: C
options.text: She has sustained irreversible renal injury from cortical necrosis

options.label: D
options.text: Chronic dialysis is the preferred long-term treatment option

options.label: E
options.text: This is a common clinical course for children with hemolytic-uremic syndrome

questions.initialExplanation: Severe HUS with an enlarged echogenic kidney means probable permanent kidney damage.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The clinical presentation described —prolonged anuria for 3 months with renal ultrasound showing decreased renal size
and increased echogenicity —is highly suggestive of irreversible renal injury from cortical necrosis.

Renal cortical necrosis (RCN) is a severe form of acute kidney injury characterized by ischemic destruction of the renal
cortex. In the context of HUS, RCN results from prolonged ischemia due to microvascular thrombosis.

The clinical features that suggest cortical necrosis in this case include:

1. Duration of anuria: Anuria lasting more than 2-3 weeks in HUS is a poor prognostic indicator and often indicates
cortical necrosis rather than acute tubular necrosis.

2. Decreased renal size: The development of small, echogenic kidneys on ultrasound is pathognomonic for chronic
irreversible renal damage.

3.Severity of initial presentation: The child developed HUS from E. coli O157:H7 colitis, which can cause severe
endothelial damage leading to irreversible injury.

---

questions.stem: A 3-yr-old girl presents to your office with acute onset of lethargy and pallor. The child's mother reports that the child had bloody diarrhea for 5 days that cleared 1 day before presenting to your office. She also notes acute onset of cola-colored urine. On examination, the patient is pale and lethargic. Blood pressure is 120/80 mm Hg. The most appropriate next step in diagnosis would be: (NE)
questions.initialExplanation: Sudden lethargy and pallor with high blood pressure: the first diagnostic test is a CBC to confirm anemia and low platelets.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Hemolytic-uremic syndrome (HUS) is one of the most common causes of community acquired acute kidney
failure in young children. It is characterized by the triad of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia,
thrombocytopenia, and renal insufficiency. The most common form of HUS is caused by toxin-producing
Escherichia coli that causes prodromal acute enteritis and is commonly termed diarrhea-associated HUS. The
diagnosis is made by the combination of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia with schistocytes,
thrombocytopenia, and some degree of kidney involvement. The anemia, mild at presentation, rapidly
progresses. Thrombocytopenia is an invariable finding in the acute phase, with platelet counts usually 20,000-
100,000/mm3 . Partial thromboplastin and prothrombin times are usually normal. The Coombs test is negative,
with the exception of pneumococci-induced HUS, in which the Coombs test is usually positive. Leukocytosis is
present and significant. Urinalysis typically shows microscopic hematuria and low-grade proteinuria. The renal
insufficiency can vary from mild elevations in serum BUN and creatinine to acute, anuric kidney failure.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy and his family have recently visited a local amusement park. Several of the family members developed “gastroenteritis” with fever and diarrhea, but the 4-year-old’s stool was slightly different, as it contained blood. His mother reports that in the past 24 hours he developed pallor and lethargy; she relates that his face looks swollen and that he has been urinating very little. Laboratory evaluation reveals a hematocrit of 28% and a platelet count of 72,000/uL. He has blood and protein in the urine. Which of the following diagnoses is most likely to explain these symptoms? (pretest)
questions.initialExplanation: An amusement-park trip, bloody diarrhea then pallor, oliguria and platelets 72,000 = hemolytic uremic syndrome.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Hemolytic-uremic syndrome is most common in children younger than 4 years of age and is
characterized by an acute microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocy topenia from increased

‘    platelet utilization, and renal insufficiency from vascular endothelial injury and local fibrin deposition.
Ischemic changes result in renal cortical necrosis and damage to other organs such as colon, liver,
heart, brain, and adrenal. Laboratory findings associated with hemolytic uremic syndrome include low
hemoglobin level, decreased platelet count, hypoalbuminemia, and evidence of hemolysis on
peripheral smear (burr cells, helmet cells, schistocytes). Urinalysis reveals hematuria and proteinuria.
A marked reduction of renal function leads to oliguria and rising levels of blood urea nitrogen (BUN)
and creatinine.

---

questions.stem: A concerned parent calls you regarding a local outbreak of E. coli gastroenteritis traced to contaminated beef from a fast food restaurant. He has read on the internet that E. coli can be associated with HUS and wants to know more about the disease. Which of the following statements regarding HUS is correct?(Rud)

options.label: A
options.text: Platelet transfusions should be used sparingly in patients with HUS

options.label: B
options.text: Atypical HUS remains far more common than diarrhea-associated HUS in the United States

options.label: C
options.text: S. pneumoniae associated HUS has a more favorable prognosis than diarrhea-associated HUS

options.label: D
options.text: Antibiotics should be given to patients who are positive for E. coli 0157:H7 to prevent HUS

options.label: E
options.text: The anemia seen in HUS is due to insufficient bone marrow production of red blood cells

questions.initialExplanation: In HUS, platelet transfusion is used with great caution (only for bleeding or procedures) because it may worsen thrombosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Diarrhea-associated HUS, most commonly the result of Shiga toxin producing E. coli O157:H7, is associated
with the majority (near 70%) of all HUS cases in the United States and Europe. The Shiga toxin causes
endothelial damage, which then results in the classic triad of renal failure, thrombocytopenia, and hemolytic
anemia. The mainstay of management of patients with diarrhea associated HUS is supportive care, which has
reduced mortality rates by 50%. This includes intravenous hydration. Dialysis should be performed if there is
profound azotemia, electrolyte imbalances, oliguria, or fluid overload.

As HUS results in a prothrombotic state with endothelial damage and resultant thrombotic microangiopathy,
platelet transfusions are reserved for patients who are actively bleeding or require an invasive procedure. There
is no evidence that antibiotics prevent HUS in patients who have stool cultures positive for E. coli O157:H7. In
fact, some studies show that receiving antibiotics may increase the risk of developing HUS.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with a 5-day history of bloody diarrhea, followed by sudden onset of pallor, irritability, and decreased urine output. On examination, he appears pale and lethargic with generalized petechiae. Laboratory investigations reveal hemoglobin 7.2 g/dL, platelet count 45,000/mm3, and serum creatinine 2.8 mg/dL (elevated). What is the most likely diagnosis based on the classic triad? (MX)
questions.initialExplanation: The triad of hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia and renal failure = HUS.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This patient presents with the classic triad of hemolytic uremic syndrome: microangiopathic hemolytic anemia
(pallor, elevated creatinine), thrombocytopenia (petechiae, low platelets), and acute renal insufficiency (oliguria,
elevated creatinine). The classic presentation in a preschool-aged child following a prodrome of bloody diarrhea
‘    is typical of typical or diarrhea-associated HUS. The history of bloody diarrhea followed by the acute onset of
pallor, irritability, and oliguria is highly characteristic.
Immune thrombocytopenic purpura typically presents with isolated thrombocytopenia without anemia or renal
involvement. Disseminated intravascular coagulation would show abnormal coagulation studies (prolonged PT,
PTT). Acute leukemia would typically present with bone marrow failure symptoms and blasts on peripheral
smear. Systemic Lupus erythematosus can rarely present with thrombotic microangiopathy but would typically
have other systemic manifestations and positive autoantibodies.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy with suspected HUS is found to have a stool specimen positive for Shiga toxin- producing bacteria. The medical student asks about the mechanism by which Shiga toxin causes the pathological changes in HUS. Which statement best describes the pathogenesis of Shiga toxin in HUS?

options.label: A
options.text: Shiga toxin directly destroys the glomerular basement membrane \*

options.label: B
options.text: Shiga toxin inhibits protein synthesis in endothelial cells leading to cell death

options.label: C
options.text: Shiga toxin activates the complement system causing widespread activation

options.label: D
options.text: Shiga toxin stimulates platelet aggregation through thromboxane release

options.label: E
options.text: Shiga toxin causes immune complex deposition in glomerular basement membrane

questions.initialExplanation: Shiga toxin inhibits protein synthesis in endothelial cells, causing damage and microthrombosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Shiga toxin (Stx) is an AB5 toxin that specifically targets endothelial cells in the kidney and other organs. The
toxin binds to the Gb3 receptor on endothelial cells and is internalizedvia endocytosis. Once inside the cell, the
A subunit cleaves the 28S rRNA of the 60S ribosomal subunit, which inhibits protein synthesis and leads to
endothelial cell death.

The damaged endothelial cells expose subendothelial tissues, triggering platelet adhesion and aggregation,
formation of microthrombi, and the characteristic thrombotic microangiopathy. This process particularly affects
the renal microvasculature, leading to acute kidney injury. The mechanical damage to red blood cells passing
through the damaged microvasculature results in schistocyte formation and microangiopathic hemolytic
anemia. Shiga toxin does not directly damage red blood cells, activate complement, or cause immune complex
deposition as primary mechanisms.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old girl presents with the classic triad of HUS. Her mother reports that she has not had any recent diarrhea or respiratory illness. The child has been generally healthy with no prior episodes of similar illness. However, her older brother had a similar illness 2 years ago that required dialysis. Which features distinguish atypical HUS from typical (diarrhea-associated) HUS in this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Absence of preceding diarrheal illness and family history of similar episodes
