The four abnormalities include right ventricular outflow obstruction, VSD, dextroposition of the aorta, and right ventricular hypertrophy; the cyanosis presents in infants and in young children. Mitral valve prolapse occurs with the billowing into the atria of one or both mitral valve leaflets at the end of systole. It is a congenital abnormality that frequently manifests only during adolescence or later. It is more common in girls than in boys and seems to be inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion. On clinical examination, an apical murmur is

noted late in systole, which can be preceded by a midsystolic click. The diagnosis is confirmed with an echocardiogram that shows prolapse of the mitral leaflets during mid to late systole.

---

questions.stem: A 13-year-old girl presents with chest pain after strenuous exercise; with completely normal physical examination, assessed by family doctor who order an ECG, chest X-ray and echocardiography; all shows normal results apart from accidental finding of tiny PDA. Of the following, the BEST advice is to:

options.label: A
options.text: go forward for Holter monitoring assessment

options.label: B
options.text: refer to pediatric cardiologist for closure of PDA

options.label: D
options.text: describe simple analgesia and reassurance about cardiac lesion

options.label: E
options.text: ensure regular follow-up for cardiac lesion on 6-monthly bases

questions.initialExplanation: A very small incidental PDA with otherwise normal findings: reassure the parents with simple analgesia for chest pain; no treatment needed.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The pain follow strenuous exercise in a healthy adolescent is usually muscular in origin. A silent PDA is a tiny defect that cannot be heard by auscultation and is only detected by other means such as

echocardiography. Life expectancy is always normal in this population and the risk for endocarditis is extremely low.

---

questions.stem: You are caring for a now 5-day-old infant born after 28 weeks of gestation. On physical examination you note bounding pulses and a harsh “washing machine” murmur. The patient has also had an increasing oxygen requirement. You order an echocardiogram and diagnose a patent ductus arteriosus. Which of the following therapies may correct this problem?
questions.initialExplanation: Indomethacin (a COX inhibitor) is used to close a PDA in a preterm; prostaglandin keeps the duct open.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Apatent ductus arteriosus is a common abnormality seen in premature infants secondary to hypoxia, acidosis, and increased pulmonary pressure from significant lung disease. The ductus arteriosus should close within the first 2-3 days of life, when this does not occur properly the patient can exhibit signs of pulmonary edema and heart failure. One medical option for assisting the ductus to close is the initiation of indomethacin.indomethacin inhibits prostaglandin synthesis and allows the ductus to close. Repeat courses may be needed. If this is ineffective, surgical correction may be needed. A dopamine infusion would be needed if the patient were hypotensive, and is not appropriate in this case (A). Administration of 100% oxygen may cause a lowering of the pulmonary vascular resistance and cause more pulmonary blood flow, worsening pulmonary edema (B). A prostaglandin infusion is used to keep a ductus arteriosus open in the case of cyanotic heart disease (D). Corticosteroids have no role in the closure of a patent ductus arteriosus (E).

---

questions.stem: You are explaining the effectiveness of supportive measures in spontaneous closure of PDA in extremely preterm infants to a junior colleague. Which of the followings represent the MOST appropriate answer?

options.label: A
options.text: Most of the infants eventually will needs cyclooxygenase inhibitors

options.label: B
options.text: About half of them will be cured

options.label: C
options.text: Most of them will be cured

options.label: D
options.text: Surgical intervention is high in those who treated by this way

options.label: E
options.text: It is no longer considered as an option for treatment

questions.initialExplanation: The answer in the source: most PDAs in very preterm infants close with supportive care and waiting (most of them will be cured).
questions.detailedExplanation:
By the time of discharge in the majority of extremely preterm infants (>90%), the PDA will close spontaneously. Spontaneous ductal closure may be facilitated by general supportive measures, including early (<7 days of age) avoidance of excessive fluid administration and judicious use of diuretics to manage pulmonary edema. Pharmacologic and surgical ductal closure may be indicated in the premature infant with a moderate to large, hemodynamically significant PDA when there is a delay in clinical improvement or deterioration.

---

questions.stem: An 18-day-old, ex-preterm baby (30 wks of gestation), his current weight 1.44 kg, had weaned from nasal CPAP, and on increasing feeding protocol. The staff nurse reported an increase need for nasal O2, increase work of breathing, and decrease urine output < 1ml/kg/hr. By examination, you have noticed bounding pulse and hepatomegaly. Of the following, the MOST appropriate action is to :

options.label: B
options.text: order renal function and monitor urine output

questions.initialExplanation: A preterm with increasing oxygen need, falling urine output, bounding pulses and hepatomegaly (heart failure from PDA): the answer given in the source is diuretics.
questions.detailedExplanation:
All the above mentioned actions are true, but evidently the baby has developed pulmonary edema and deterioration of renal function from undiagnosed PDA and consequent cardiac volume overload. The first action is to administer diuretics and order fluid restriction, meanwhile waiting for an echocardiography and renal function results. Starting cyclooxygenase (COX) inhibitors (indomethacin or ibuprofen) is a later on decision depending on progress and case response to supportive treatment.

---

questions.stem: The mother of a 4-month-old is concerned because he is taking longer to finish feeds, sweats when he sucks, and breathes more quickly when he nurses. He has not gained much weight in the last month. He has little subcutaneous tissue, is tachypneic without retractions, has hepatomegaly, and diffusely diminished pulses. You hear a murmur on his examination. Which lesion is NOT likely to cause this clinical picture of failure to thrive and congestive heart failure?
questions.initialExplanation: A secundum ASD does not usually cause heart failure or failure to thrive in infancy, whereas a large PDA, large VSD, truncus and AV canal do.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This patient is presenting with heart failure. Infants and young children present with poor feeding, failure to thrive, respiratory distress, diaphoresis, and pallor. Patients with a large PDA, large VSD, truncus arteriosus, and complete common AV canal all develop high pressure/high volume left to right shunts after the pulmonary vascular resistance drops. This subsequently causes an increase in pulmonary blood flow relative to systemic blood flow (increased Qp:Qs), which results in pulmonary over-circulation and symptoms of congestive heart failure symptoms. These patients may also have decreased systemic blood flow. Even large atrial septal defects will not cause such an increase in pulmonary blood flow and they seldom cause congestive heart failure at this age.

---

questions.stem: During a 10-year-old’s well-child visit, you hear a loud first heart sound and a widely split second heart sound that does not vary with respiration. He has a RV lift and a soft systolic flow murmur at the LUSB. Pulses are normal. He is a good soccer player and has been healthy. What lesion is most likely to explain these findings?
questions.initialExplanation: A soft flow murmur at the upper left border with right ventricular heave and a wide fixed split S2 = atrial septal defect.
questions.detailedExplanation:
An ASD shunt increases the volume of flow across the pulmonic valve, causing the fixed split S2 and the flow murmur in the main pulmonary artery. Most children with an ASD are asymptomatic and the lesion is detected on routine examinations. There is minimal pressure difference between the atria, so the murmur is due to increased flow volume across the pulmonic valve. Aortic stenosis, pulmonic valve stenosis, and VSD murmurs generally are detected early in infancy/childhood due to increased pressure gradients. The pulses and blood pressure are normal, so aortic coarctation is unlikely.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old girl with asymptomatic small ASD secundum, echocardiography shows no dilatation of cardiac chambers. Family concerned about the timing of closure of the defect. What is the MOST appropriate answer?

options.label: A
options.text: The best time for closure is now

options.label: B
options.text: We need to watch the girl closely anticipating the complications

options.label: C
options.text: We need not to worry as it is a small defect and closure is not indicated

options.label: D
options.text: The closure is needed before school entry even it is small to prevent Eisenmenger syndrome

options.label: E
options.text: We can wait till adolescent period when her weight will be good enough to bear operation

questions.initialExplanation: A small secundum ASD without chamber enlargement does not need closure per the source (may close spontaneously or be left).
questions.detailedExplanation:
In patients with small secundum ASDs and minimal left-to-right shunts without RV enlargement, the consensus is that closure is not required. Infants with small to moderate-sized ASDs can be watched closely, since these defects will often grow smaller in the 1st yr of life. Transcatheter device or surgical closure is advised for all symptomatic patients, as well as for asymptomatic patients with Qp:Qs ratio of at least 2 : 1 and those with RV enlargement. The timing for elective closure is usually after the 1st yr of life and before entry into school.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl diagnosed as a case of large ASD secundum, not fit for transcatheter closure and need surgery. Echocardiography shows right atrial and right ventricular dilatation. Family shows no much interest in repairing the defect as they see their child has no much symptoms; they want to postponed it till adulthood. What is your BEST advice for the family?

options.label: A
options.text: It is better to be done as early as possible

options.label: B
options.text: There is good chance for spontaneous closure; so | would agree to wait till adulthood

options.label: C
options.text: We can wait as long as she is well and having normal growth parameters

options.label: D
options.text: We can do appointment echocardiography every 3 months for close follow-up

options.label: E
options.text: The best period for closure is just before adolescence

questions.initialExplanation: A large ASD with right ventricular and right atrial enlargement: closure is best done early to prevent pulmonary hypertension and right heart failure.
questions.detailedExplanation:
For large defects, repair is preferred during early childhood because surgical mortality and morbidity are significantly greater in adulthood; the longterm risk of arrhythmia caused by chronic atrial dilation is also greater after ASD repair in adults.

---

questions.stem: A 3-month-old infant presents with failure to thrive, profuse sweating during feeds, and recurrent respiratory infections. Physical examination reveals a harsh holosystolic murmur best heard at the left lower sternal border, a palpable thrill, parasternal lift, and displaced apical impulse. Echocardiography shows a 1.2 cm membranous VSD with Qp:Qs ratio of 2.5:1 and estimated right ventricular pressure of 85% of systemic pressure. Which of the following represents the MOST critical factor determining long- term prognosis in this case?

options.label: A
options.text: Size of the VSD and degree of pulmonary vascular resistance

options.label: B
options.text: Patient's age at presentation and weight gain pattern

options.label: D
options.text: Effectiveness of medical heart failure management

questions.initialExplanation: The most important prognostic factor in VSD is the size of the defect and the degree of pulmonary vascular resistance (Eisenmenger if it rises).
questions.detailedExplanation:
The long-term prognosis in large VSD is primarily determined by the size of the defect and the degree of pulmonary vascular resistance. When the Qp:Qs ratio exceeds 2:1 and pulmonary vascular resistance begins to rise, there's risk of progression to Eisenmenger syndrome, which is irreversible. The 1.2 cm membranous VSD with Qp:Qs ratio of 2.5:1 and RV pressure at 85% of systemic suggests a non-restrictive VSD with significant pulmonary hypertension development. This represents a critical window for intervention before irreversible pulmonary vascular changes occur. The age (3 months) and symptoms are typical for large VSD presentation, but the defining prognostic factor is the hemodynamic impact on pulmonary circulation rather than just clinical presentation timing.

---

questions.stem: A 6-month-old infant with a known small muscular VSD is brought for routine follow-up. The murmur is now barely audible, and echocardiography shows the VSD has decreased from 0.3 cm to 0.1 cm with minimal shunting. However, the infant has developed newonset stridor during feeding and occasional cyanosis with crying. Echocardiography reveals the development of progressive infundibular pulmonary stenosis with a gradient of 45 mmHg. This represents which of the following complications?

options.label: A
options.text: Spontaneous VSD closure with development of secondary complications

options.label: B
options.text: Natural protective mechanism against pulmonary overcirculation

options.label: E
options.text: Progression of VSD to atrioventricular septal defect

questions.initialExplanation: Gradual development of infundibular pulmonary stenosis with a small VSD is considered, per the source, a natural protective mechanism against excess pulmonary flow.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This scenario represents a natural protective mechanism where infundibular pulmonary stenosis develops as the body's adaptive response to prevent pulmonary overcirculation. Approximately 5-10% of patients with large VSDs develop acquired infundibular stenosis, which creates a partial right ventricular outflow tract obstruction. This stenosis actually protects the pulmonary circulation from excessive blood flow and helps prevent the development of severe pulmonary hypertension. The gradient of 45 mmHg is significant enough to create a right-to-left shunt component, explaining the cyanosis and stridor. This phenomenon is more common in certain populations and represents a natural correction attempt by the cardiovascular system, though surgical intervention may still be required depending on symptoms and progression.

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old child with a large perimembranous VSD presents with new-onset exertional dyspnea, fatigue, and decreased exercise tolerance. Physical examination reveals a soft systolic murmur (previously harsh), decreased pulmonary component of S2, and paradoxical pulse. Chest X-ray shows decreased pulmonary vascular markings compared to previous studies. Echocardiography demonstrates RV pressure equal to systemic pressure with bidirectional shunting. Which diagnosis represents the most concerning complication?

options.label: A
options.text: Congestive heart failure with cardiac cachexia The ug I. . . e decreased pulmonary component of S2 (P2) is the critical

options.label: B
options.text: Atrial septal defect development with volume overload discriminator:

options.label: C
options.text: Development of aortic regurgitation from septal aneurysm In Eisenmender syndrome, pulmonary artery pressuro is systemic

options.label: D
options.text: Infundibular pulmonary stenosis with obstruction In infundibular (subvalvular), the obstruction is below the

options.label: E
options.text: Progressive pulmonary vascular disease (Eisenmenger syndrome) pumonary valve. Right ventricular pressure is systemic, but pulmonary artery pressure is lower — P2 is soft or decreased.

questions.initialExplanation: A large VSD with a soft P2, decreased pulmonary vascularity on film and bidirectional shunt = Eisenmenger syndrome (progressive pulmonary vascular disease).
questions.detailedExplanation:
The clinical picture represents Eisenmenger syndrome, the most serious complication of large VSDs. The progression from high-pitched harsh murmur to soft murmur indicates decreased left-to-right shunting, while bidirectional shunting on echo with RV pressure equal to systemic pressure confirms the development of pulmonary vascular disease. The decreased pulmonary vascular markings on chest X-ray represent the pathological changes of pulmonary vascular remodeling. Once Eisenmenger syndrome develops (typically 10% of large VSD patients), it's irreversible and represents a contraindication to Surgical repair. The paradoxical pulse results from right ventricular volume overload. This complication typically develops in the first or second decade without intervention, making early surgical repair crucial for prevention.

---

questions.stem: A 4-month-old infant with a known large VSD is brought for emergency evaluation due to acute onset of respiratory distress, poor feeding, and lethargy over the past 12 hours. Temperature is 38.5°C, respiratory rate 70/min, and oxygen saturation 88% on room air. Examination reveals bilateral crackles, hepatomegaly, and a soft systolic murmur. White blood cell count is 15,000/uL with left shift. Chest X-ray shows bilateral infiltrates and cardiomegaly. Which complication represents the MOST LIKELY diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.text: Bacterial pneumonia secondary to viral upper respiratory infection

options.label: B
options.text: Acute left ventricular failure due to rapid progression of VSD

options.label: C
options.text: Congestive heart failure precipitated by intercurrent iliness

questions.initialExplanation: An infant with a large VSD, fever, distress, desaturation, congestion and hepatomegaly: most likely congestive heart failure precipitated by an intercurrent illness (infection).
questions.detailedExplanation:
The clinical presentation is classic for congestive heart failure precipitated by an intercurrent illness in a patient with a large VSD. The acute deterioration over 12 hours with fever, elevated white count, and bilateral infiltrates suggests a viral illness that has pushed the already-compromised cardiovascular system into overt failure. Large VSDs with elevated pulmonary blood flow create a state of chronic volume overload and increased cardiac work. When an intercurrent illness increases metabolic demands and can cause fever-induced tachycardia, this can precipitate acute decompensation. The bilateral crackles and hepatomegaly confirm heart failure, while the soft murmur suggests decreased shunt velocity. This represents one of the most common Complications of large VSDs and requires urgent medical management to stabilize the patient.

---

questions.stem: A 5-month-old infant presents with fever, irritability, poor feeding, and a new harsh holosystolic murmur. Blood cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus. Echocardiography shows a large vegetation on the ventricular septum adjacent to a previously undiagnosed 0.8 cm VSD. Which complication represents the MOST SERIOUS immediate concern in this case?

options.label: A
options.text: Systemic embolization to brain or kidneys

options.label: D
options.text: Acute heart failure from valve destruction

questions.initialExplanation: Infective endocarditis with S. aureus and a large vegetation: the most feared complication is systemic embolization to the brain or kidney.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Systemic embolization represents the most serious immediate concern in infective endocarditis with a VSD vegetation. Large vegetations (size not specified) on the ventricular septum carry a high risk of embolization to systemic circulation, particularly the brain, kidneys, and spleen. The Staphylococcal species is particularly aggressive and can cause rapid vegetation growth. Embolic events can cause stroke, renal infarction, or splenic abscesses, which may be life-threatening. While heart failure and arrhythmias are complications, embolization risk is immediate and requires urgent surgical consultation. The 0.8 cm VSD size is significant enough to allow adequate vegetation formation, and the location on the septum increases embolic potential compared to other locations.

---

questions.stem: A preterm infant born at 28 weeks gestation presents on day 5 of life with increasing oxygen requirements, apnea spells, and poor feeding tolerance. Physical examination reveals bounding peripheral pulses, wide pulse pressure, and a continuous machinery murmur best heard at the left infraclavicular area. Chest X-ray shows increasing pulmonary edema and cardiomegaly. Which factor represents the MOST CRITICAL determinant of treatment approach in this case?

options.label: A
options.text: Birth weight and gestational age at presentation A Co

options.label: B
options.text: Size of the ductus arteriosus and shunt magnitude Fo oication for Closure": Option Bs the correct

options.label: C
options.text: Presence of associated cardiac anomalies For "Indication for Surgery vs. Medicine": Option D

options.label: D
options.text: Response to medical management with indomethacin Bor ro a Aooroacht (Broadly): Option B is

options.label: E
options.text: Maternal history of diabetes or rubella infection generally preferred because it encompasses the decision to intervene at all, which is the most critical safety step.

questions.initialExplanation: The source's answer is D (response to indomethacin), but a page note says duct size and shunt size (B) matter most; check the original.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The response to medical management with indomethacin represents the most critical determinant of treatment approach in this preterm infant with PDA. Indomethacin effectiveness in closing the ductus arteriosus depends on the infant's gestational age, renal function, and degree of maturation of the ductal tissue. Preterm infants born before 30 weeks have a much higher success rate with indomethacin (60-80%) compared to more mature preterm infants. The response to the first course of indomethacin often predicts the need for subsequent courses or surgical intervention. Additionally, indomethacin can cause renal dysfunction, gastrointestinal complications, and affect cerebral blood flow, requiring careful monitoring. The decision to proceed to surgical ligation depends heavily on whether medical closure can be achieved safely and effectively.

---

questions.stem: A term infant born at 40 weeks gestation presents at 6 weeks of age with poor weight gain, sweating during feeds, and respiratory distress. Examination reveals bounding pulses, wide pulse pressure (80/30 mmHg), and a continuous machinery murmur. Echocardiography shows a large PDA (4 mm) with Qp:Qs ratio of 3:1 and left ventricular dilation. Which pathophysiological mechanism BEST explains the maternal risk factors that led to this presentation?

options.label: A
options.text: Maternal rubella infection during first trimester

options.label: B
options.text: Prostaglandin E1 exposure during perinatal period

options.label: C
options.text: Genetic predisposition to connective tissue disorders

options.label: D
options.text: Maternal diabetes with abnormal fetal circulation

questions.initialExplanation: Maternal rubella in pregnancy is associated with PDA (and peripheral pulmonary stenosis) in the newborn per the source.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Maternal rubella infection during the first trimester represents the most likely pathophysiological mechanism leading to PDA in this term infant. Congenital rubella syndrome is classically associated with PDA as the most common cardiac manifestation, occurring in up to 50% of cases. The rubella virus causes inflammation and damage to the developing ductus arteriosus, preventing normal structural and functional closure. The presentation at 6 weeks with large PDA and significant hemodynamic consequences Is typical for rubella-associated PDA, which tends to be larger and more clinically significant than idiopathic PDA. The maternal history of first-trimester viral illness would be

key to establishing this diagnosis, and the infant may have other manifestations of congenital rubella syndrome including cataracts, hearing loss, and intellectual disability.

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old child with a known PDA presents with recurrent episodes of chest pain, exercise intolerance, and syncope. Physical examination reveals a continuous murmur that is now softer, decreased peripheral pulses, and clubbing of the fingers and toes. Echocardiography shows a large PDA with bidirectional shunting, RV pressure equal to systemic pressure, and tricuspid regurgitation. Which complication represents the MOST SERIOUS long-term consequence in this case?

options.label: D
options.text: Cor pulmonale and right heart failure

questions.initialExplanation: A PDA child with a bidirectional shunt and Eisenmenger symptoms; the source's answer A (progressive LV dysfunction) differs from the expected finding (Eisenmenger/cyanosis), so check the original.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The development of Eisenmenger syndrome represents the most serious long-term consequence in this case. The progression from continuous murmur to softer murmur, decreased pulses, and eventual clubbing indicates reversal of shunting and irreversible pulmonary vascular disease. Once Eisenmenger syndrome develops, the PDA becomes inoperable, and the patient faces progressive deterioration from chronic hypoxemia, right heart failure, and complications of polycythemia. The bidirectional shunting allows paradoxical emboli to bypass pulmonary circulation, increasing stroke risk. The chronic hypoxemia leads to secondary erythrocytosis, hyperviscosity, and increased risk of thrombosis. Additionally, patients with Eisenmenger syndrome face significant mortality risks from arrhythmias, bleeding complications, and sudden cardiac death. Early closure of hemodynamically significant PDAs is crucial to prevent this irreversible complication.

---

questions.stem: A newborn presents with cyanosis, poor feeding, and respiratory distress within the first 24 hours of life. Physical examination reveals diminished femoral pulses, differential cyanosis (upper body pink, lower body cyanotic), and a continuous murmur heard best in the back. Echocardiography shows interrupted aortic arch with PDA providing the only source of lower extremity blood flow. Which therapeutic intervention represents the MOST appropriate initial management?
questions.initialExplanation: Interrupted aortic arch with a PDA supplying the lower body: start prostaglandin E1 to keep the duct open.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Prostaglandin E1 infusion represents the most appropriate initial management for this newborn with interrupted aortic arch and PDA-dependent systemic circulation. Interrupted aortic arch is a ductal- dependent lesion where the PDA provides the only source of blood flow to the lower body and abdominal organs. Without prostaglandin maintenance of ductal patency, the infant will develop shock and organ failure as the ductus closes naturally. Prostaglandin E1 (alprostadil) keeps the ductus arteriosus open, maintaining systemic blood flow to the lower extremities while the infant is stabilized for surgical repair. Oxygen therapy would be contraindicated as it promotes ductal closure. Surgical repair cannot be performed emergently due to the need for preoperative stabilization and planning. This represents a ductal-dependent systemic circulation where prostaglandin infusion is lifesaving.

---

questions.stem: A 6-month-old infant with PDA presents with new-onset seizures, motor regression, and developmental delay. Physical examination reveals cyanosis, digital clubbing, and a continuous murmur. Echocardiography shows bidirectional shunting with RV pressure equal to systemic pressure. Brain MRI reveals multiple small infarcts. Which complication represents the MOST LIKELY explanation for the neurological symptoms?

options.label: B
options.text: Paradoxical emboli through PDA causing cerebral infarcts

questions.initialExplanation: Multiple cerebral infarcts in a PDA child with bidirectional shunt: the likely cause is paradoxical embolism across the duct.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Paradoxical emboli through the PDA represents the most likely explanation for the neurological symptoms in this case with established Eisenmenger physiology. The bidirectional shunting allows

’    embolic material from the systemic venous circulation to bypass the pulmonary filter and enter systemic arterial circulation, including the cerebral arteries. The brain MRI showing multiple small infarcts in a patient with cyanotic heart disease and bidirectional shunting is classic for paradoxical emboli. The cyanosis and clubbing confirm chronic right-to-left shunting. These emboli can be small pieces of thrombus, fat, air, or other material that would normally be filtered by the pulmonary circulation. The neurological symptoms represent the most common manifestation of paradoxical embolization in patients with Eisenmenger physiology and right-to-left shunting.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old child presents with exercise intolerance and mild dyspnea on exertion. Physical examination reveals fixed splitting of the second heart sound, a systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border, and a short mid-diastolic murmur at the left lower sternal border. Echocardiography shows a large secundum ASD (2.2 cm) with Qp:Qs ratio of 2.5:1 and right ventricular enlargement. Which factor represents the MOST important determinant of optimal timing for intervention?

options.label: B
options.text: Size of the defect and degree of shunting

options.label: D
options.text: Family history of congenital heart disease

questions.initialExplanation: The timing of intervention in a large ASD is determined by defect size, the degree of shunt (Qp:Qs) and right ventricular enlargement.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The size of the defect and degree of shunting represents the most important determinant of optimal timing for intervention in this child with ASD. The large 2.2 cm secundum ASD with Qp:Qs ratio of

2.5:1 indicates significant hemodynamic burden requiring intervention. According to current guidelines, ASDs with Qp:Qs ratio 21.5:1 should be closed, regardless of symptoms, to prevent long- term complications. The size (2.2 cm) is substantial and unlikely to close spontaneously. Early closure (before school age) is recommended to prevent complications such as pulmonary hypertension, arrhythmias, and right heart failure that can develop in the third to fourth decade. While symptoms are important, the hemodynamic burden (Qp:Qs 2.5:1) is the primary indication for closure in children, making timing crucial to prevent irreversible changes.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child with a large secundum ASD presents for elective closure. However, during cardiac catheterization, the patient develops severe pulmonary vasospasm with acute elevation of pulmonary artery pressure to systemic levels and development of hypoxemia. Which therapeutic intervention represents the MOST appropriate immediate management?

options.label: A
options.text: Immediate surgical closure of the defect

options.label: C
options.text: Prostaglandin E1 infusion to maintain ductal patency

options.label: E
options.text: Oxygen therapy and nitric oxide inhalation

questions.initialExplanation: Acute pulmonary vasospasm during catheterization with hypoxemia: immediate oxygen and inhaled nitric oxide.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Oxygen therapy and nitric oxide inhalation represents the most appropriate immediate management for acute pulmonary vasospasm during cardiac catheterization. The acute elevation of pulmonary

’     artery pressure to systemic levels indicates a pulmonary hypertensive crisis, which can be life- threatening. Nitric oxide is a selective pulmonary vasodilator that can rapidly reduce pulmonary vascular resistance without causing systemic hypotension. Oxygen therapy also promotes pulmonary vasodilation and improves oxygenation. Immediate closure of the ASD during a hypertensive crisis would be contraindicated as it could precipitate acute right heart failure. Prostaglandin E1 would worsen the situation by promoting ductal patency and potentially increasing pulmonary blood flow.

This complication requires immediate pulmonary vasodilation and stabilization before any definitive intervention can be considered.

---


## RHD & Infective Endocarditis

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child with a repaired cyanotic heart disease and a prosthetic valve presents with an acute onset of unexplained fever, malaise, and recent weight loss. Exam shows tachycardia, splenomegaly, and a new heart murmur. What is the gold standard for diagnosis in this setting?
questions.initialExplanation: A child with a prosthetic valve, fever, splenomegaly and a new murmur: suspect infective endocarditis; the diagnostic standard is blood cultures.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Blood cultures are the gold standard for diagnosing infective endocarditis, as they definitively identify the causative pathogen and guide targeted antimicrobial therapy. This child's presentation—fever, malaise, weight loss, new murmur, splenomegaly, and high-risk cardiac history (prosthetic valve) —is classic for infective endocarditis. Obtaining multiple sets

‘    of blood cultures (typically three from separate venipuncture sites) before initiating antibiotics maximizes diagnostic yield and is a major criterion in the modified Duke diagnostic criteria. Chest X-ray, complete blood count, electrocardiogram, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate may provide supportive evidence (e.g., cardiomegaly, leukocytosis, conduction abnormalities, or elevated inflammatory markers) but lack specificity and cannot confirm the diagnosis or identify the organism. In prosthetic valve endocarditis, common pathogens include Staphylococcus aureus, coagulase-negative staphylococci, and streptococci; culture results direct appropriate prolonged intravenous antibiotic therapy and surgical consultation if needed.

---

questions.stem: Antibiotic therapy can be helpful for prevention of rheumatic fever if initiated up to how many hours/days following onset of symptoms of Group-A streptococcal throat infection?
questions.initialExplanation: Primary prevention of rheumatic fever is possible by giving antibiotics within 9 days of the onset of streptococcal pharyngitis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Rheumatic fever is a nonsuppurative, acute inflammatory complication of group A streptococcal infection, causing combinations of arthritis, carditis, subcutaneous nodules, erythema marginatum, and chorea. Diagnosis is based on applying the Jones criteria to information from history, examination, and laboratory testing. Rheumatic fever can be prevented in a case of strep pharyngitis by giving penicillin. Even when started as late as 9 days after the onset of pharyngitis, penicillin effectively prevents primary attacks of acute rheumatic fever.

---

questions.stem: A 8-year-old child presents with acute rheumatic fever manifesting as polyarthritis and subcutaneous nodules. Laboratory studies show elevated ASO titer (1:400), normal ESR, and normal CRP. The child has no cardiac involvement on physical examination and echocardiography. Which therapeutic approach represents the MOST appropriate management?
questions.initialExplanation: Arthritis and subcutaneous nodules without carditis: treat with high-dose aspirin only per the source (plus secondary penicillin prophylaxis later).
questions.detailedExplanation:
High-dose aspirin therapy alone represents the most appropriate management for this child with acute rheumatic fever limited to polyarthritis and subcutaneous nodules without cardiac involvement. Arthritis in rheumatic fever is highly responsive to NSAIDs, particularly aspirin, and typically shows dramatic improvement within 24-48 hours. The absence of carditis means corticosteroids are not indicated. Subcutaneous nodules don't require specific anti-inflammatory treatment beyond what's needed for arthritis. While antibiotic therapy for GAS eradication is essential, it doesn't address the acute inflammatory joint symptoms. Low-dose aspirin would be insufficient for controlling the inflammatory arthritis. Supportive care alone would not provide adequate symptom relief. The dramatic response to NSAIDs is both therapeutic and diagnostic - lack of response after 2- 3 days should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis.

---

questions.stem: A 12-year-old child presents with migratory polyarthritis affecting the knees, ankles, and wrists for the past 5 days. Physical examination reveals a new onset holosystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the left axilla, subcutaneous nodules over the elbows, and laboratory studies showing elevated ASO titer (1:800), ESR 85 mm/hr, and CRP 45 mg/L. ECG demonstrates first-degree AV block with PR interval of 0.24 seconds. The child's mother reports a recent sore throat treated with antibiotics for only 3 days. Which additional finding would be MOST critical for establishing the diagnosis of rheumatic fever?

options.label: B
options.text: History of incomplete antibiotic treatment for GAS pharyngitis

questions.initialExplanation: To diagnose rheumatic fever evidence of recent streptococcal infection (ASO or anti-DNase B) is required; here the answer is a raised anti-DNase B.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Elevated antistreptococcal DNAse B titer represents the most critical additional finding for establishing Rheumatic fever diagnosis. While the ASO titer is elevated (1:800), showing a single elevated antibody titer may not definitively confirm recent GAS infection, especially since the child received incomplete antibiotic treatment. The antistreptococcal DNAse B titer is particularly important because it remains elevated longer than ASO titers and can detect recent infections that ASO might miss. In cases where only one streptococcal antibody is elevated, confirmation with a second antibody test strengthens the diagnosis. The clinical presentation already shows evidence of recent GAS pharyngitis (incomplete treatment), but laboratory confirmation through multiple elevated antibodies provides the definitive evidence required for rheumatic fever diagnosis according to revised Jones criteria.

---

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy, the star pitcher for the Salt Lake City Little League baseball team, had a sore throat about 2 weeks ago but did not tell anyone because he was afraid he would miss the play-offs. Since several children have been diagnosed with rheumatic fever in the area, his mother is worried that he may be at risk as well. You tell her that several criteria must be met to make the diagnosis but the most common finding is which of the following?
questions.initialExplanation: The most common major criterion in rheumatic fever is migratory polyarthritis, then carditis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The diagnosis of rheumatic fever can be difficult because no single clinical manifestation or laboratory test is confirmatory. However, an accurate diagnosis must be made since treatment of the acute problems promptly and effectively is required and long-term antibiotic prophylaxis to prevent recurrences must be instituted. To assist in diagnosis, the American Heart Association identified a set of major and minor standards relating to the manifestations of the disease, called the Jones criteria (modified), and recommends these criteria be applied in the diagnosis of every patient with possible rheumatic fever. The major criteria are carditis, polyarthritis, erythema marginatum, chorea, and subcutaneous nodules. The minor criteria are arthralgia (joint pain with no objective findings); fever; history of rheumatic fever; increased erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), positive C-reactive protein; or leukocytosis; and prolonged PR intervals on ECG. To make the diagnosis of rheumatic fever, the following criteria should be met: two major manifestations, or one major and two minor manifestations plus strong evidence of a preceding group A B-hemolytic streptococcal infection (culture, rapid antigen- antibody rise, or elevation) or scarlet fever. The presence of Sydenham chorea is an exception in that, by itself, it is enough to make the diagnosis of rheumatic fever. Of the major criteria, polyarthritis is the most common finding (75%), followed by carditis (50-60%), chorea (10-15%), erythema marginatum (<3%), and subcutaneous nodules (£1%).

---

questions.stem: A patient comes to your office for a hospital follow-up. You had sent him to the hospital 3 weeks earlier for persistent fevers but no other symptoms; he was diagnosed with endocarditis and is currently being treated appropriately. Advice to this family should now include which of the following?

options.label: A
options.text: Restrict the child from all strenuous activities.

options.label: B
options.text: Give the child a no-salt-added diet.

options.label: C
options.text: Provide the child with antibiotic prophylaxis for dental procedures.

options.label: D
options.text: Test all family members in the home with repeated blood cultures.

options.label: E
options.text: Avoid allowing the child to get upset or agitated.

questions.initialExplanation: After treating endocarditis: advise antibiotic prophylaxis before dental procedures because the risk of infection remains high.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The American Heart Association updates the guidelines for the use of prophylactic antibiotics regularly. Among those patients currently recommended to receive antibiotic prophylactic treatment are patients for whom any heart infection would result in the highest incidence of adverse outcome: previous history of endocarditis, prosthetic valve or material for repair, heart transplant patients, and severe or partially repaired congenital heart defects (2007 AHA guideline revision). Activity is not usually limited unless there is extensive destruction of heart muscle or the conducting system leading to failure. Minimizing salt intake is generally a good idea, but not any more so in an individual who has endocarditis. Bed rest should be instituted only in the case of heart failure. Family members are not typically at risk.

---

questions.stem: A five-month-old child with unrepaired tetralogy of Fallot presents to the clinic with 2 weeks of intermittent low-grade fever, malaise, weight loss, and irritability with movement. His parents have been watching for “tet spells” but have noted no cyanosis. A workup performed at a freestanding clinic the prior day revealed a normal white count, but a blood culture grew Kingella kingae. The next step in management should be:

options.label: A
options.text: Repeat the blood culture and reassure the parents that the child has a viral illness and that the organism in the blood culture is a typical skin contaminant

options.label: B
options.text: Increase the caloric density of his formula to help with weight gain and follow-up next week

options.label: C
options.text: Arrange an evaluation by his cardiologist next week

options.label: D
options.text: Initiate oral clindamycin therapy and follow-up in two days

options.label: E
options.text: Admit directly to the hospital, get two more blood cultures, and start vancomycin

questions.initialExplanation: An infant with unrepaired TOF, low-grade fever and a positive culture (Kingella): admit with additional cultures and start vancomycin (IV therapy) for suspected endocarditis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Infective endocarditis may present as fulminant disease with shock and overwhelming sepsis, but the subacute form presents with more subtle findings, including low grade fever, weight loss, lethargy, sleep disturbances, arthralgias, and myalgias. The much discussed Osler nodes (small tender nodules in the tips of fingers and toes), Janeway lesions (nontender hemorrhagic lesions on the hands and feet), and splinter hemorrhages (dark lines under nails) are uncommon findings. Children at the greatest risk of endocarditis are those with unrepaired cyanotic heart disease, those with prosthetic material from a repair, or those with a prior history of infectious endocarditis.

In children, endocarditis is typically caused by streptococcus organisms in the viridans group and Staphylococcus aureus. Other potential pathogens include coagulase negative staphylococcus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and the HACEK organisms including Haemophilus sp, Actinobacillus actinomycetemcomitans, Cardiobacterium hominis, Eikenella corrodens, and Kingella species. Diagnosis may be confirmed with serial positive blood cultures and echocardiogram findings of vegetations and myocardial abscesses. Treatment is an appropriate antibiotic for 4 to 8 weeks. Surgical intervention is reserved for patients with valvular obstruction, congestive heart failure (CHF), or abscess; persistent bacteremia may also result in surgery.

---

questions.stem: A previously healthy 8-year-old boy has a 3-week history of low-grade fever of unknown source, fatigue, weight loss, myalgia, and headaches. On repeated examinations during this time, he is found to have developed a heart murmur, petechiae, and mild splenomegaly. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the diagnosis of this child’s condition?

options.label: B
options.text: Serial measurement of platelet count and initiation of aspirin therapy

options.label: E
options.text: Chest radiograph and placement of a purified protein derivative (PPD)

questions.initialExplanation: Fever of unknown origin for weeks with a new murmur, petechiae and splenomegaly: next step is an echocardiogram to look for endocarditis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The presentation of infective endocarditis can be quite variable, ranging from prolonged fever with few other symptoms to an acute and severe course with early toxicity. A high index of suspicion is necessary to make the diagnosis quickly. Identification of the causative organism (frequently Streptococcus sp or Staphy-lococcus sp) through multiple blood cultures is imperative for appropriate treatment. Echocardiography may identify valvular vegetations and can be predictive of impending embolic events, but a negative echocardiogram does not rule out endocarditis. Treatment usually consists of 4 to 6 weeks of appropriate antimicrobial therapy. Bed rest should be instituted only for heart failure. Antimicrobial prophylaxis prior to and after dental cleaning is indicated. Antistreptolysin antibody testing might be useful to help confirm the diagnosis of rheumatic fever; this child has none of the major criteria. Serial measurement of platelet count and initiation of aspirin would be appropriate for Kawasaki disease, but the child in the question is older than typical for Kawasaki disease (80% will present under the age of 5 years) and the history is not consistent with the diagnosis. Scarlet fever (rapid streptococcal test) is typically self-limited and would not be consistent with the 3- week time course. Tuberculosis can cause prolonged lowgrade fever, but cardiac involvement is unusual, consisting of pericarditis; thus a friction rub would be the typical examination finding.

---

questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy has migratory arthritis with red, warm, and swollen joints. He has serologic evidence of recent group A streptococcal infection. Arthritis in this condition is characterized by which of the following?

options.label: D
options.text: seen only in patients with concurrent carditis

options.label: E
options.text: involves large and small joints equally

questions.initialExplanation: Arthritis in rheumatic fever is painful and migratory and heals without deformity.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The arthritis of acute rheumatic fever is a painful acute migratory polyarthritis. Although any joint can be involved, it is primarily the large joints of the extremities that are affected in most cases. Pain and swelling in one joint subsides as another joint becomes symptomatic. Eventually, all joints heal without deformity or other permanent sequelae. Fever and arthritis usually occur concomitantly but may occur in the presence or absence of carditis.

---

questions.stem: A 12-year-old child with a surgically corrected pulmonary shunt is to undergo an invasive dental procedure. Which of the following antibiotics would be most appropriate for prophylaxis against bacterial endocarditis?
questions.initialExplanation: A patient with a surgical shunt before a dental procedure: prophylaxis with amoxicillin.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Although many organisms can cause endocarditis following a dental procedure, Streptococcus viridans remains the most common. Penicillin is highly effective, with a longer half-life, and is the drug of choice. For those allergic to penicillins or amoxicillin against this organism, but amoxicillin, the use of cephalexin or another first-generation oral cephalosporin, clindamycin, or a macrolide such as azithromycin, or clarithromycin is recommended.

---

questions.stem: A previously healthy 10-year-old girl has a 4-week history of low-grade fever, malaise, decreased appetite, weight loss, myalgia, and headaches. On examination, she has a new diastolic murmur, petechiae, and a palpable spleen tip. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Chronic low-grade fever, weight loss, a new diastolic murmur, petechiae and splenomegaly = infective endocarditis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
IE is an infection of the endocardium, typically involving the cardiac valves. The presentation of endocarditis can be variable. Presentation can be slow onset, or subacute, with intermittent fevers and few other symptoms. Other cases may present with fever, fulminant symptoms of heart failure, and embolic complications. IE can occur in children with or without underlying cardiac disease. The diagnosis is primarily dependent on clinical features (see Table 490-1 for Revised Duke Clinical Diagnostic Criteria). Importantly, identifying the causative organism through multiple blood cultures is imperative before starting an antibiotic. Treatment usually lasts for 4-6 weeks. Echocardiography is a secondary diagnostic modality; it can identify the valve involved and the potential risk of embolic events.

Tuberculosis can present with intermittent fevers and a pericardial friction rub, but generally does not directly involve the heart or the valves. Kawasaki disease has a 4- to 5-day course of high fever, irritability, conjunctivitis, and rash. Rheumatic fever can present with carditis; however, this presentation does not fit the major or minor criteria of ARF. Scarlet fever has a more self-limited course (<1 week) and is associated with pharyngitis and a rash.

---

questions.stem: A 10-year-old child presents with fever, migratory polyarthritis affecting large joints, and a new heart murmur 3 weeks after an untreated streptococcal pharyngitis. Which pathophysiological mechanism best explains the development of acute rheumatic fever?

options.label: A
options.text: Autoimmune destruction of synovial joints due to bacterial endotoxins

options.label: B
options.text: Type Ill hypersensitivity reaction with immune complex deposition in tissues

options.label: C
options.text: Direct bacterial invasion of cardiac tissue by group A streptococcus

options.label: D
options.text: Type II hypersensitivity reaction with molecular mimicry between streptococcal M protein and myocardial antigens

options.label: E
options.text: Type | hypersensitivity reaction with IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation

questions.initialExplanation: Mechanism of rheumatic fever: a hypersensitivity reaction (per the source) through molecular mimicry between streptococcal M protein and heart tissue.
questions.detailedExplanation:
and myocardial antigens

The most accepted mechanism for acute rheumatic fever involves molecular mimicry where antibodies developed against streptococcal M protein crossreact with human proteins (most commonly myosins) due to structural similarities. This leads to a type Il hypersensitivity reaction causing acute inflammatory sequela. Group A B-hemolytic streptococcal pharyngitis without antibiotic treatment triggers this immune response, typically occurring 2-4 weeks after the initial infection. The cross-reaction affects nerve and myocardial proteins, leading to the characteristic clinical manifestations.

---

questions.stem: A 10-year-old child with acute rheumatic fever has erythematous rash characterized by centrifugally expanding pink rings with well-defined outer borders and central clearing. The rash is painless, nonpruritic, and affects the trunk and limbs while sparing the face. What is this characteristic rash called and what is its diagnostic significance?

options.label: A
options.text: Erythema migrans - characteristic of Lyme disease

options.label: B
options.text: Erythema nodosum - minor Jones criterion associated with streptococcal infections

options.label: C
options.text: Erythema marginatum - a major Jones criterion in acute rheumatic fever

options.label: D
options.text: Scarlet fever rash - diffuse erythroderma with sandpaper texture

options.label: E
options.text: Drug hypersensitivity reaction - temporal relationship to NSAID therapy

questions.initialExplanation: A pink, centrifugally spreading, non-itchy, non-painful ring rash sparing the face = erythema marginatum, a major Jones criterion for rheumatic fever.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Erythema marginatum is a characteristic rash of acute rheumatic fever, described as centrifugally expanding pink or light red rash with well-defined outer borders and central clearing. It is painless

’    and nonpruritic, affecting the trunk and limbs while sparing the face, and may rapidly appear and disappear at different locations. This finding represents one of the five major Jones criteria for acute rheumatic fever diagnosis. The presence of erythema marginatum along with other major criteria strengthens the diagnostic confidence significantly.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old girl develops acute rheumatic fever manifested by fever, arthritis and carditis. Chest radiography shows cardiomegaly with pulmonary edema. She is on oral amoxicillin treatment. Of the following, the MOST appropriate initial treatment for this girl is:
questions.initialExplanation: Rheumatic fever with carditis, cardiomegaly and heart failure (severe carditis): the initial treatment per the source is oral prednisolone (steroid).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Patients with typical migratory polyarthritis and those with carditis without cardiomegaly or congestive heart failure should be treated with oral salicylates. Patients with carditis and more than minimal cardiomegaly and/or congestive heart failure should receive corticosteroids.

---

questions.stem: A previously healthy 7 yr old girl has a 3-wk history of fever, myalgias, and a positive blood culture for Staphylococcus aureus. The past medical history is negative including a normal camp physical examination 6 mo ago, which did not reveal any heart murmur. She now has a harsh murmur on your exam. After repeating a blood culture, the next step in her evaluation should be:
questions.initialExplanation: S. aureus in the blood with a new murmur: the next step is an echocardiogram to look for vegetations.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Early manifestations of infective endocarditis are usually mild, especially when viridans group streptococci are the infecting organisms. Prolonged fever without other manifestations (except, occasionally, weight loss) that persists for as long as several months may be the only symptom. Alternatively, the onset may be acute and severe, with high, intermittent fever and prostration. Usually, the onset and course vary between these two extremes. The symptoms are often nonspecific and consist of low-grade fever with afternoon elevations, fatigue, myalgia, arthralgia, headache, and, at times, chills, nausea, and vomiting. New or changing heart murmurs are common, particularly with associated heart failure. Splenomegaly and petechiae are relatively common. The critical information for appropriate treatment of infective endocarditis is obtained from blood cultures. In 90% of cases of endocarditis, the causative agent is recovered from the 1st 2 blood cultures. The combination of transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography enhances the ability to diagnose endocarditis. The Duke criteria help in the diagnosis of endocarditis. Major criteria include (1) positive blood cultures (2 separate cultures for a usual pathogen, 2 or more for less typical pathogens) and (2) evidence of endocarditis on echocardiography (intracardiac mass on a valve or other site, regurgitant flow near a prosthesis, abscess, partial dehiscence of prosthetic valves, or new valve regurgitant flow).

---

questions.stem: A 14-year-old adolescent with acute rheumatic fever undergoes ECG examination. Which cardiac conduction abnormality is most commonly associated with acute rheumatic carditis?

options.label: B
options.text: Second-degree AV block (Mobitz type | or Il)

questions.initialExplanation: The most common conduction disturbance in rheumatic carditis is PR prolongation (first-degree AV block).
questions.detailedExplanation:
First-degree atrioventricular block, characterized by a prolonged PR interval on ECG, is the most common conduction abnormality in acute rheumatic carditis. This finding represents a minor Jones criterion for acute rheumatic fever diagnosis. The conduction delay results from inflammation affecting the AV node and His-Purkinje system due to the autoimmune process. Unlike pericarditis associated with other etiologies, pericardial tamponade and constrictive pericarditis rarely occur in rheumatic fever, but conduction abnormalities are common and may precede clinical carditis manifestations.

---

questions.stem: A 8-year-old child with acute rheumatic fever develops severe pancarditis with signs of congestive heart failure. Initial treatment with NSAIDs has been insufficient, and the patient shows worsening cardiac function. Which additional treatment is most appropriate for this clinical scenario?

options.label: B
options.text: Increased NSAID dosing with combination therapy

questions.initialExplanation: Heart failure with pancarditis not improving on NSAIDs: add a systemic steroid (prednisone).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Systemic corticosteroids, particularly prednisone, are indicated for moderate-to-severe carditis in acute rheumatic fever when NSAIDs alone are insufficient. The combination of corticosteroid therapy with NSAIDs provides better control of the inflammatory process in severe carditis cases. Corticosteroids work by suppressing the autoimmune inflammatory response that causes cardiac tissue damage. While cardiac glycosides like digoxin may be used for heart failure management in established rheumatic heart disease, they do not address the underlying inflammatory process in acute rheumatic carditis.

---

questions.stem: A 13-year-old adolescent presents with acute onset of chest pain, fever, and dyspnea. Physical examination reveals a pericardial friction rub, muffled heart sounds, and pulsus paradoxus of 15 mmHg. Echocardiography shows moderate pericardial effusion without tamponade physiology. ECG demonstrates diffuse ST-segment elevation. Laboratory studies show elevated ASO titer, ESR 90 mm/hr, and CRP 60 mg/L. Which therapeutic approach represents the MOST appropriate initial management?
questions.initialExplanation: Pericarditis from rheumatic fever without tamponade: treat with NSAIDs and monitor; no tap or surgery.
questions.detailedExplanation:
NSAIDs alone with close monitoring represents the most appropriate initial management for acute rheumatic pericarditis. Unlike pericarditis from other causes, rheumatic pericarditis rarely causes tamponade or constrictive complications. The pericardial effusion is moderate without hemodynamic compromise, and the pulsus paradoxus of 15 mmHg is not severe enough to indicate tamponade. NSAIDs (particularly high-dose aspirin or naproxen) are first-line therapy for rheumatic pericarditis and arthritis. Corticosteroids are reserved for severe carditis with heart failure or when NSAIDs are ineffective. Pericardiocentesis or surgical intervention is not indicated without evidence of tamponade or progressive effusion. Antibiotic therapy for GAS eradication should be administered but doesn't address the acute inflammatory pericardial process. The goal is to control

inflammation while avoiding unnecessary invasive procedures in a condition that typically responds well to NSAIDs.

---

questions.stem: A 14-year-old adolescent with a history of intravenous drug use presents with acute onset fever, chills, and new cardiac murmur. Physical examination reveals petechiae, Janeway lesions, and Osler nodes. Echocardiography shows large vegetations on the tricuspid valve. Which organism is most likely responsible for this clinical presentation?
questions.initialExplanation: An IV drug user with tricuspid valve vegetations and Janeway and Osler signs: the most likely organism is Staphylococcus aureus.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause of infective endocarditis in intravenous drug users and typically presents with an acute, severe course. Staphylococcal IE often affects the tricuspid valve

’    in IV drug users, causing septic pulmonary emboli. The organism's ability to cause rapid tissue destruction leads to large vegetations and severe valvular destruction. The acute presentation with systemic signs (fever, chills) and peripheral manifestations (petechiae, Janeway lesions, Osler nodes) is characteristic of S. aureus IE. The tricuspid valve involvement in IV drug users reflects the direct passage of organisms to the right side of the heart.

---

questions.stem: A 15-year-old adolescent with unrepaired congenital heart disease presents with subacute bacterial endocarditis. Which factor most significantly increases the risk of developing infective endocarditis in children with congenital heart disease?

options.label: A
options.text: Turbulent blood flow across cardiac defects

options.label: C
options.text: Presence of associated syndromes (e.g., Down syndrome)

questions.initialExplanation: The main risk factor for endocarditis in congenital heart disease is turbulent flow across the defects.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Turbulent blood flow across cardiac defects is the primary factor increasing IE risk in children with congenital heart disease. This turbulent flow damages the endocardium and creates a favorable environment for bacterial colonization and vegetation formation. Defects with high-velocity flow (like VSD, PDA, tetralogy of Fallot) carry higher IE risk than low-flow defects. The hemodynamic consequences, rather than the anatomical size or associated syndromes, determine the infectious

risk. Understanding this principle helps in appropriate antibiotic prophylaxis recommendations for dental procedures.

---

questions.stem: A 12-year-old child presents with fever, polyarthritis, and a new cardiac murmur. The history reveals recent streptococcal pharyngitis. Initial investigations show elevated ASO titers and mild mitral regurgitation on echocardiography. Which finding would most strongly support a diagnosis of infective endocarditis over acute rheumatic fever?

options.label: A
options.text: Positive blood cultures for Streptococcus sanguinis

options.label: C
options.text: Anemia of chronic disease and elevated inflammatory markers

options.label: D
options.text: New heart murmur with character change

questions.initialExplanation: Janeway lesions and splinter hemorrhages favor infective endocarditis over rheumatic fever.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Peripheral manifestations such as splinter hemorrhages and Janeway lesions are highly specific for infective endocarditis and would strongly support this diagnosis over acute rheumatic fever. These lesions result from microembolic phenomena or immune complex deposition in IE. While blood cultures would provide definitive evidence of IE, the peripheral stigmata are characteristic clinical features that help distinguish between these two conditions with cardiac manifestations. Splinter

hemorrhages are linear, dark-red lesions under the fingernails, while Janeway lesions are painless, erythematous macules on palms and soles.

---


## Heart Failure

questions.stem: An 8-year-old boy presents with a 3-day history of fever, fatigue, chest discomfort, and shortness of breath. One week prior, he had an upper respiratory infection. On exam, he appears ill with tachycardia, a gallop rhythm, hepatomegaly, and a displaced apical impulse. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Fever, fatigue, chest pain and dyspnea a week after an upper respiratory infection with a gallop rhythm, hepatomegaly and a displaced apex = viral myocarditis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This presentation is classic for viral myocarditis: acute heart failure symptoms (fatigue, dyspnea, chest discomfort) following a recent viral URI, with exam findings of tachycardia, gallop rhythm (S3), hepatomegaly, and displaced apical impulse indicating biventricular dysfunction and cardiomegaly. Viral myocarditis causes direct myocyte injury and inflammatory cardiomyopathy, leading to systolic dysfunction and congestive heart failure. Acute pericarditis typically presents with positional chest pain and friction rub, not gallop rhythm or hepatomegaly. Dilated cardiomyopathy is usually chronic and progressive rather than acutely post-viral. Supraventricular tachycardia causes regular narrow-complex tachycardia without structural signs like displaced apex or gallop. Rheumatic carditis follows streptococcal pharyngitis after 2-3 weeks and typically presents with migratory arthritis or new valvular murmurs, not acute pump failure.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old girl is a well known patient to you who suffers from congestive heart failure. Today she comes in with leg edema. Your goal is to induce rapid therapeutic diuresis. Which orte of the following would be most effective medication?
questions.initialExplanation: For rapid effective diuresis in a child with heart failure and leg edema: furosemide (a potent, fast-acting loop diuretic).
questions.detailedExplanation:
There are several types of medications used to treat congestive heart failure in children, improvement in symptoms can be achieved by diuretics, digoxin, angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, and angiotensin Il receptor blockers (ARBs). Diuretics decrease preload by promoting natriuresis, and provide relief of volume overload symptoms such as

pulmonary and peripheral edema. Loop diuretics inhibit sodium and chloride reabsorption in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle. Furosemide (choice B) is the most commonly used loop diuretic.

—> Thiazide diuretics inhibit reabsorption of sodium and chloride ions from the distal convoluted tubules of kidneys. They generally are used as second-line agents and often in combination with a loop diuretic. Commonly used thiazide diuretics are chlorothiazide (choice A), hydrochlorothiazide, and metolazone.

—> Although digoxin (choice C) is no longer used in children with asymptomatic ventricular dysfunction, it continues to be used in the treatment of infants and children with stage C heart failure because of its physiologic benefit and symptom relief. However, for this patient, a loop diuretic would be the first choice in treatment.

---

questions.stem: You are starting digitalization for a baby with heart failure. Basic metabolic, electrolyte, and an ECG strip were done before the first digitalization dose. Now, after 8 hours you are willing to give the 2nd digitalizing dose.Of the following, the MOST appropriate next step is to:
questions.initialExplanation: Between digoxin loading doses, repeat the ECG strip to make sure there is no conduction disturbance or toxicity before the next dose.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The ECG must be closely monitored, and rhythm strips obtained before each of the 3 digitalizing doses. Digoxin should be discontinued if a new rhythm disturbance is noted. Prolongation of the P-R interval is not necessarily an indication to withhold digitalis, but a delay in administering the next dose or a reduction in the dosage should be considered, depending on the patient's clinical status. Minor ST segment or T-wave changes are frequently noted with digitalis administration and should not affect the digitalization regimen.

---

questions.stem: A newborn presents with heart failure symptoms including respiratory distress and poor feeding. Echocardiography reveals a large ventricular septal defect with left-to-right shunt. Which pathophysiological mechanism is most likely contributing to the heart failure in this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Increased preload due to volume overload from left-to-right shunt

options.label: B
options.text: Increased afterload due to aortic obstruction

options.label: C
options.text: Decreased contractility from primary myocardial dysfunction

options.label: E
options.text: Coronary artery compression from myocardial bridging

questions.initialExplanation: A large VSD with left-to-right shunt causes heart failure through increased volume load (preload).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Large ventricular septal defects (VSD) cause heart failure through increased preload due to volume overload from left-to-right shunting. In VSD, blood flows from thenhigh-pressure left ventricle to the lower-pressure right ventricle during systole, creating a volume overload of the right heart and lungs. This leads to increased pulmonary blood flow, pulmonary congestion, and eventually volume overload of the left atrium and left ventricle. The increased preload places excessive volume demands on the heart, leading to heart failure symptoms. This represents a classic example of heart failure due to increased preload rather than primary myocardial dysfunction or afterload issues.

---

questions.stem: A 2-month-old infant with heart failure shows cardiomegaly, hepatomegaly, and generalized edema including eyelids and sacrum. Which statement about the clinical presentation of heart failure in infants is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: Hepatomegaly is rare in infants with heart failure

options.label: B
options.text: Edema in infants is typically localized to dependent parts like older children

options.label: C
options.text: Jugular venous pressure is easily assessable in infants with heart failure

options.label: D
options.text: Edema in infants is usually generalized, affecting eyelids, sacrum, and less often legs and feet

options.label: E
options.text: Cardiomegaly is not always present in infant heart failure

questions.initialExplanation: Heart failure in infants shows generalized edema of the eyelids and sacrum, less in the legs and feet, unlike older children.
questions.detailedExplanation:
and feet

In infants with heart failure, edema is characteristically generalized, affecting the eyelids, sacrum,

‘     and less commonly the legs and feet. This pattern differs from older children and adults where edema typically appears in dependent parts due to gravity. The generalized distribution in infants reflects their horizontal positioning and different fluid distribution patterns. Other characteristic findings include hepatomegaly (commonly present), cardiomegaly (invariably present), and the fact that jugular venous pressure is difficult to assess due to the infant's anatomy. The presence of generalized edema along with the other symptoms helps distinguish heart failure from other conditions in infants.

---

questions.stem: A child with suspected heart failure undergoes chest X-ray examination. Which radiographic finding would be most suggestive of pulmonary venous congestion and acute pulmonary edema?

options.label: A
options.text: Rib crowding and decreased cardiac silhouette

options.label: B
options.text: Clear lung fields with normal vascular markings

options.label: C
options.text: Unilateral pleural effusion with contralateral lung hyperinflation

options.label: D
options.text: Fluffy perihilar pulmonary markings and Kerley B lines

options.label: E
options.text: Single large pulmonary nodule with calcification

questions.initialExplanation: Pulmonary venous congestion and pulmonary edema appear on film as perihilar fluffy opacities and Kerley B lines.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Fluffy perihilar pulmonary markings and Kerley B lines are classic radiographic findings of pulmonary venous congestion and acute pulmonary edema in heart failure. The fluffy perihilar markings result from interstitial edema around the pulmonary vessels, while Kerley B lines are thin, horizontal lines seen at the lung periphery due to distended interlobular septa. These findings indicate increased pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure and are among the earliest radiographic signs of heart failure. The chest X-ray also typically shows cardiac enlargement, which helps correlate the pulmonary changes with cardiac dysfunction. Other findings may include pleural effusions and cephalization of pulmonary vessels.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child with heart failure develops acute decompensation with signs of cardiogenic shock. Epinephrine is initiated as part of the inotropic support. Which receptor effects best explain epinephrine's role in cardiogenic shock management?

options.label: A
options.text: Mixed alpha and beta-adrenergic receptor stimulation increasing both contractility and arterial blood pressure

options.label: B
options.text: Pure beta-1 receptor stimulation for maximum inotropic effect

options.label: C
options.text: Dopaminergic receptor activation for renal vasodilation

options.label: D
options.text: Alpha-1 receptor stimulation for selective vasoconstriction

questions.initialExplanation: Epinephrine in cardiogenic shock gives mixed alpha and beta stimulation: it raises contractility and arterial pressure.
questions.detailedExplanation:
arterial blood pressure

Epinephrine is a mixed alpha and beta-adrenergic receptor agonist that is particularly useful in cardiogenic shock with low arterial blood pressure. Its combined effects increase myocardial contractility (beta-1 stimulation) while also providing vasoconstriction (alpha-1 stimulation) that helps maintain arterial blood pressure. This dual action makes epinephrine superior to other inotropic agents when significant hypotension is present. The vasoconstrictive effects can increase afterload, which may be problematic in some cases of heart failure, but in cardiogenic shock, maintaining adequate perfusion pressure takes priority. Epinephrine is typically reserved for severe cases where other inotropic agents are insufficient to maintain adequate blood pressure and organ perfusion.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child with heart failure due to left-to-right shunt lesion develops pulmonary vascular disease. Which hemodynamic parameter would most reliably assess the reversibility of pulmonary vascular changes?
questions.initialExplanation: To assess reversibility of pulmonary vascular disease, the best index is the pulmonary-to-systemic resistance ratio (Rp:Rs) below 0.3.
questions.detailedExplanation:
A pulmonary-to-systemic vascular resistance ratio (Rp:Rs) <0.3 most reliably indicates reversible pulmonary vascular disease and suggests that corrective surgery for the left-to-right shunt would be beneficial. When Rp:Rs ratio is <0.3, the pulmonary vascular resistance is sufficiently low to allow for successful surgical correction without the risk of persistent postoperative pulmonary hypertension. Values >0.5-0.6 indicate irreversible pulmonary vascular disease and contraindicate closure of the shunt lesion. The ratio is calculated during cardiac catheterization with measurement of pulmonary

and systemic pressures and cardiac output, providing the most accurate assessment of pulmonary vascular status.

---

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most common cause of heart failure in children?
questions.initialExplanation: The question text was lost to OCR; the options concern causes of heart failure, and the source's answer is congenital heart defects, the most common cause in infants and children.
questions.detailedExplanation:
In infants under 1 year, congenital heart defects are the most common cause of heart failure, accounting for approximately 80-90% of cases. Structural abnormalities like VSD, AV canal, hypoplastic left heart syndrome, and other malformations present with heart failure symptoms as pulmonary blood flow increases after birth. Viral myocarditis is more common in older children, while primary cardiomyopathies are rare in this age group.

---

questions.stem: A 10-year-old child develops heart failure with no structural heart disease. Which cause should be most suspected?
questions.initialExplanation: Heart failure in a 10-year-old with no structural disease: the most likely cause is viral myocarditis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
In children over 1 year without structural heart disease, viral myocarditis is the most common cause of acute heart failure. Coxsackievirus, adenovirus, and other viral infections can cause direct myocardial injury leading to acute dilated cardiomyopathy. Other causes like toxic cardiomyopathy from drugs or nutritional deficiencies are less common in children.

---

questions.stem: A 4-month-old infant presents with poor feeding, respiratory distress, and sweating during feeds. Which physical finding is most specific for heart failure?
questions.initialExplanation: The most specific sign of heart failure in an infant per the source is a gallop rhythm; tachycardia, tachypnea and hepatomegaly are less specific.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The presence of a gallop rhythm (S3 or S4) is the most specific physical finding for heart failure in children. It indicates impaired ventricular compliance and filling. While tachycardia, tachypnea, hepatomegaly, and cardiomegaly can occur in heart failure, they are not specific and can be seen in other conditions.

---

questions.stem: A 12-year-old presents with fatigue, exercise intolerance, and abdominal pain. Physical examination reveals elevated jugular venous pressure and hepatomegaly. Which additional finding would most confirm heart failure?
questions.initialExplanation: Raised jugular venous pressure and hepatomegaly with heart failure: the additional confirming finding per the source is basal crackles (pulmonary congestion).
questions.detailedExplanation:
