questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy presents with 3 days of fever, headache, and muscle aches, followed by difficulty walking and sudden weakness in the right leg. He is unvaccinated. Exam shows flaccid paralysis and absent reflexes in the right leg, with intact sensation and normal cognition. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: A DNA virus from picornaviridae is the cause

options.label: C
options.text: The anterior horn cells are primarily involved

options.label: D
options.text: Serum Creatinine Kinase confirms the diagnosis

questions.initialExplanation: Fever then asymmetric flaccid paralysis with intact sensation and normal consciousness = polio, which affects the anterior horn motor cells.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This is poliomyelitis: asymmetric flaccid paralysis, absent reflexes, intact sensation, unvaccinated
child. Poliovirus targets anterior horn cells (lower motor neurons). Poliovirus is an RNA virus (not
DNA). Transmission is fecal-oral (not airborne). Cognition and sensation remain intact.

---

questions.stem: A previously healthy 5-year-old boy presents with sudden, ascending symmetric weakness starting in legs and progressing to arms within hours. He has labored breathing, absent deep tendon reflexes, and no bowel, bladder, or sensory deficits. Which CSF finding would best support the suspected diagnosis?

options.label: B
options.text: Increased protein with normal cell count

questions.initialExplanation: Symmetric ascending weakness without sphincter or sensory disturbance = Guillain-Barré; CSF shows high protein with normal cell count (albuminocytologic dissociation).
questions.detailedExplanation:
This is Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS): ascending symmetric flaccid paralysis, areflexia, respiratory
involvement, preserved sensation. CSF shows albuminocytologic dissociation = elevated protein with
normal cell count. This is the classic and diagnostic CSF finding in GBS. Increased WBCs would
suggest infection.

---

questions.stem: In Guillain-Barré syndrome, the paralysis usually follows a nonspecific gastrointestinal or respiratory infection by approximately 10 days. Of the following, the MOST likely respiratory infection that triggers the disease is : (NE)
questions.initialExplanation: The best-known respiratory infection linked to GBS is Mycoplasma pneumoniae (Campylobacter overall).
questions.detailedExplanation:
The original infection might have caused only gastrointestinal (especially Campylobacter jejuni, but
also Helicobacter pylori) or respiratory tract (especially Mycoplasma pneumoniae) symptoms.

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl admitted to intensive care unit for management of Guillain Barré syndrome, at morning of 7th day, the patient develops severe headache and repeated vomiting; O/E well hydrated, afebrile, no neck stiffness, and blood pressure 100/60 mm Hg; serum Na+ (120 mEq/L), serum K+ (4.1 mEq/L), serum Chloride (75 mEq/L), blood glucose (98 mg/dl), BUN 20 mg/dl), serum creatinine (0.5 mg/dl), and urine sodium (80 mEq/L). Of the following, the MOST likely explanation of this condition is : (NE)

options.label: C
options.text: syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion

questions.initialExplanation: In GBS with low sodium and high urinary sodium: SIADH.
questions.detailedExplanation:
SIADH typically occurs with disorders of the CNS (infection, hemorrhage, trauma, tumor, thrombosis, Guillain-
Barré syndrome), but lung disease (infection, asthma, positive pressure ventilation) and malignant tumors
(producing ADH) are other potential causes.

Diagnostic Criteria for Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone Secretion :

- Absence of: Renal, adrenal, or thyroid insufficiency - Heart failure, nephrotic syndrome, or cirrhosis
- Diuretic ingestion - Dehydration

- Urine osmolality >100 mOsm/kg (usually >plasma)

- Serum osmolality <280 mOsm/kg and serum sodium <135 mEq/L

- Urine sodium >30 mEq/L

- Reversal of “sodium wasting” and correction of Hyponatremia with water restriction

---

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy presented with fever, cough , shortness of breath diagnosed as pneumonia and treated properly with good response, 10 days later he developed numbness and paresthesia, followed by symmetric weakness in the lower extremities and progressively involving the trunk and the upper limbs with loss of ability to walk. Of the following, the MOST likely diagnosis is : (NE)
questions.initialExplanation: Weakness ascending after fever and cough with loss of walking = Guillain-Barré.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Initial symptoms include numbness and paresthesia, followed by weakness. Radicular back pain and
myalgia are common in the initial stages; affected children can be very irritable. Weakness usually

‘    begins in the lower extremities and progressively involves the trunk, the upper limbs, and finally the
bulbar muscles, but weakness is sometimes proximally prominent. Extraocular muscle involvement is
rare, but many patients develop facial weakness. In most patients, weakness is essentially symmetric.
Weakness progresses over days or weeks, the clinical nadir occurring in less than 4 wk.
Approximately 60% of children lose the ability to walk at some point in their illness; a small proportion
progress to flaccid tetraplegia.

---

questions.stem: An 8-year-old girl presented with acute external ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, areflexia with involvement of 6th cranial nerve, and very mild lower extremity weakness. Of the following, the MOST likely diagnosis is : (NE)
questions.initialExplanation: Ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and absent reflexes = Miller Fisher syndrome (a GBS variant).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Miller-Fisher syndrome (MFS) is an uncommon GBS variant associated with acute external (and
occasionally internal) ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and areflexia. The 6th cranial nerve is most often
involved in MFS. Although areflexia is seen in MFS, patients have no or only very mild lower extremity
weakness, compared with GBS. Distal paresthesias are common in MFS. Urinary incontinence or

retention is a complication in approximately 20% of cases but is usually transient. MFS overlaps
clinically with Bickerstaff brainstem encephalitis.

---

questions.stem: A 1-yr-old child experiences ascending paralysis with peripheral neuropathy. The cranial nerves are intact. The cerebrospinal fluid is normal except for an elevated protein level. Which of the following is the likely infectious agent precipitating this syndrome?
questions.initialExplanation: The commonest infectious cause of GBS is Campylobacter jejuni.
questions.detailedExplanation:
There is a strong association between Guillain-Barré syndrome and preceding infection with some
serotypes of C. jejuni. Molecular mimicry between nerve tissue and Campylobacter surface antigens
may be the triggering factor in Campylobacter-associated Guillain-Barré syndrome, including the
Miller-Fisher variant, which is characterized by ataxia, areflexia, and ophthalmoplegia. Reactive
arthritis and erythema nodosum can also occur. Most Campylobacter infections are not followed by
immunoreactive complications, indicating that factors in addition to molecular mimicry are required for
these complications.

---

questions.stem: A 4-yr-old child presents with symmetric weakness that began in the lower extremities and subsequently progressed over 10-14 days to involve the trunk and upper limbs. Deep tendon reflexes are absent. There are no sensory deficits or bowel or bladder dysfunction. Nerve conduction velocity test results are abnormal. The cerebrospinal fluid shows protein of 78 mg/dL and 5 white blood cells. The most likely diagnosis is: (NE)
questions.initialExplanation: Gradual symmetric weakness and high CSF protein (78) with only 5 cells = GBS.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Weakness usually begins in the lower extremities and progressively involves the trunk, the upper limbs, and
finally the bulbar muscles, a pattern known as Landry ascending paralysis. Proximal and distal muscles are
involved relatively symmetrically, but asymmetry is found in 9% of patients. The onset is gradual and
progresses over days or weeks. Tendon reflexes are lost, usually early in the course, but are sometimes
preserved until later. This variability can cause confusion when attempting early diagnosis. CSF studies are
essential for diagnosis. The CSF protein is elevated to more than twice the upper limit of normal, glucose level
is normal, and there is no pleocytosis. Fewer than 10 white blood cells/mm3 are found. The results of bacterial
cultures are negative, and viral cultures rarely isolate specific viruses. The dissociation between high CSF

protein and a lack of cellular response in a patient with an acute or subacute polyneuropathy is diagnostic of
Guillain-Barré syndrome.

---

questions.stem: A 12 yr old girl experienced diarrhea, which lasted for 3 days, 2 wk before manifesting progressive weakness and inability to walk. She has intermittent tingling of her fingers and toes. Physical examination reveals marked peripheral muscle weakness without atrophy or fasciculations. The deep tendon reflexes are absent in her ankles and 1+ at her knees. Findings on the sensory examination are normal. Motor involvement is symmetric. The most likely diagnosis is: (NE)
questions.initialExplanation: Diarrhea two weeks earlier and symmetric motor weakness with normal sensation = GBS.
questions.detailedExplanation:
In Guillain-Barré syndrome, the paralysis usually follows a nonspecific viral infection by about 10 days.
The original infection might have caused only gastrointestinal (especially Campylobacter jejuni, but

‘    also Helicobacter pylori) or respiratory tract (especially Mycoplasma pneumoniae) symptoms.
Weakness usually begins in the lower extremities and progressively involves the trunk, the upper
limbs, and finally the bulbar muscles, a pattern known as Landry ascending paralysis. Proximal and
distal muscles are involved relatively symmetrically, but asymmetry is found in 9% of patients. The
onset is gradual and progresses over days or weeks. Tendon reflexes are lost, usually early in the
course, but are sometimes preserved until later.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child in day care develops abdominal pain with diarrhea and malaise. His class recently had a field trip to the local petting zoo. Stool culture subsequently grows Campylobacter jejuni. Which of the following is the most common clinical manifestation that follows infection with Campylobacter? (NE)
questions.initialExplanation: The commonest neurological complication of Campylobacter is Guillain-Barré syndrome.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Campylobacter infection is characterized by watery diarrhea possibly followed by blood streaked
stools, fever, abdominal pain, and malaise. It is usually self-limited, but may have immunoreactive
complications (Guillain-Barré syndrome, reactive arthritis [monoatrticular], Reiter syndrome, and
erythema nodosum)occur during convalescence. It is estimated that in 30%—40% of cases of
Guillain-Barré syndrome occurred within 2 weeks of Campylobacter infection. Anterior uveitis,
inguinal lymphadenitis, and encephalitis are not sequelae of Campylobacter infection.

---

questions.stem: A 16-year-old female presents with leg weakness after recovering from an upper respiratory illness. On examination her vital signs are normal. She is unable to stand alone. Motor strength is 5/5 in the arms and 2/5 in the legs. Deep tendon reflexes are absent in the legs. What finding is classically associated with this illness? (Lange)

options.label: E
options.text: presence of Clostridium species on stool culture

questions.initialExplanation: The classic sign in GBS: raised CSF protein with few cells.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This is a classic presentation of Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS), a postinfectious polyneuropathy.
lliness is frequently preceded by a nonspecific viral illness. The patient experiences ascending
paralysis with the bulbar muscles affected last, if at all. Deep tendon reflexes are lost, usually early in
the course of the illness. Sensory function usually is spared. Nerve conduction velocity is decreased
in Guillain Barré syndrome. While there is no specific diagnostic test, the clinical picture combined
with a cerebrospinal fluid showing an elevated protein and normal cell count is highly suggestive.
Occasional cases of GBS can be associated with infection due to M pneumonia or Campylobacter
species. The other laboratory abnormalities listed are not associated with Guillain-Barré syndrome.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old girl presents to the ED with acute onset of muscle weakness. Her muscle weakness started in her legs yesterday. The weakness became worse today and progressed to the trunk and both arms. She was also complaining difficulty of breathing earlier today. She has been otherwise healthy but had a common cold about 10 days ago. On examination, her respirations are 25/min and shallow. She has profound muscle weakness in her lower extremities, and moderate weakness in her upper extremities. Her deep tendon reflexes are absent. A lumbar puncture is performed, which shows increased protein concentration. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? (CanadaQB)
questions.initialExplanation: Acute muscle weakness and high CSF protein = GBS.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The girl in this clinical vignette has classic Guillain-Barré syndrome, also known as acute inflammatory
demyelinating polyneuropathy (AIDP). It is an acute illness characterized by rapid demyelination of peripheral
nerves. A symmetric ascending weakness progresses rapidly. In this case, the involvement of the respiratory
muscles is potentially life threatening. Sensory deficit, involvement of facial musculature, and autonomic
insufficiency may occasionally happen. Weakness usually follows a nonspecific viral infection by about 7-14
days.

---

questions.stem: About 12 days after a mild upper respiratory infection, a 12-year-old boy complains of weakness in his lower extremities. Over several days, the weakness progresses to include his trunk. On physical examination, he has the weakness described and no lower extremity deep tendon reflexes, muscle atrophy, or pain. Spinal fluid studies are notable for elevated protein only. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient? (MX)
questions.initialExplanation: 12 days after a respiratory infection with only CSF protein raised = GBS.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) is often triggered by an antecedent infection that evokes an immune response, which in
turn reacts with peripheral nerve components because of the sharing of cross-reactive epitopes (molecular mimicry). The
end result is an acute polyneuropathy. This immune response can be directed towards the myelin or the axon of

‘    peripheral nerve. Campylobacter infection is the most commonly identified precipitant of GBS. GBS is the most common
cause of acute flaccid paralysis in healthy infants and children. The paralysis of Guillain-Barré often occurs about 10 days
after a nonspecific viral illness. The initial diagnosis of GBS is based upon the clinical presentation. The typical clinical
features of GBS are progressive, mostly symmetric muscle weakness and absent or depressed deep tendon reflexes.
Weakness is gradual over days or weeks, beginning in the lower extremities and progressing toward the trunk. Later, the
upper limbs and the bulbar muscles can become involved. Involvement of the respiratory muscles is life threatening. The
syndrome seems to be caused by a demyelination in the motor nerves and, occasionally, the sensory nerves.
Measurement of spinal fluid protein is helpful in the diagnosis; protein levels are increased to more than twice normal,
while glucose and cell counts are normal. Hospitalization for observation is motor milestones.

---

questions.stem: An 8-year-old girl is admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit with a 5-day history of ascending weakness. She initially had tingling in her feet, which progressed to her legs and now involves her arms. She has difficulty swallowing and speaking. On examination, she has symmetric flaccid paralysis of all four limbs (grade 2/5), areflexia, and bilateral facial weakness. Her respiratory rate is 24/min, and she appears fatigued. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.label: C
options.text: Plasmapheresis with cumulative volume exchange of 250 ml/kg

questions.initialExplanation: GBS with respiratory failure: first-line treatment is IVIG 2 g/kg over 2-5 days.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This patient has severe GBS with bulbar involvement and respiratory compromise. According to
guidelines, the most appropriate treatments for GBS are IVIG (2 g/kg divided over 2-5 days) or
plasmapheresis (cumulative total of approximately 250 ml/kg volume exchange). IVIG is preferred
over plasmapheresis in children because it is easier to administer, has significantly fewer
complications, and is more comfortable for the patient. High-dose corticosteroids are not
recommended for acute GBS, though they may be used for CIDP. Oral prednisone is not effective
for acute GBS. Cyclophosphamide is not a standard treatment for GBS. The patient requires prompt
immunotherapy to halt disease progression and facilitate recovery.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy presents with a 1-week history of difficulty walking. His parents noticed that he was stumbling and falling frequently. Two weeks prior, he had an upper respiratory infection with cough and sore throat. On examination, he has proximal muscle weakness in both lower limbs, diminished deep tendon reflexes, and a waddling gait. Sensation is intact throughout. What is the characteristic CSF finding that supports the diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.text: Elevated protein with normal cell count

options.label: C
options.text: Low glucose level with elevated protein

options.label: D
options.text: Xanthochromia with elevated red blood cells \*

options.label: E
options.text: Increased opening pressure with normal constituents Presence of oligoclonal bands

questions.initialExplanation: GBS: high protein with normal cell count (dissociation).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Albuminocytological dissociation (elevated CSF protein with normal cell count) is a hallmark finding
in GBS. However, the CSF may be normal within the first week of symptoms, so lumbar puncture

‘    should ideally be performed during the second week. Protein levels typically elevate after the first
week of symptoms, peak at 4-5 weeks, and may remain elevated for several months. White blood
cell count is typically less than 10/mm3 (occasionally up to 50/mms3), and glucose level is normal.
Bacterial meningitis would show neutrophilic pleocytosis and low glucose. Viral meningitis would
show lymphocytic pleocytosis with normal glucose. Multiple sclerosis would show oligoclonal bands.
The CSF findings in GBS are distinctive for this condition.

---

questions.stem: A 9-year-old girl is evaluated for suspected Guillain-Barré syndrome. She has a 4-day history of ascending paralysis starting from the lower extremities. On neurological examination, she has symmetric flaccid weakness, areflexia, and mild sensory changes in the feet. Her vital capacity is 18 ml/kg. According to the provided guidelines, which of the following is an indication for PICU admission?
questions.initialExplanation: PICU admission indicators: flaccid quadriparesis, respiratory weakness or swallowing difficulty.
questions.detailedExplanation:
According to guidelines, children with GBS should be admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit if
they have one or more of the following: flaccid tetraparesis, severe rapidly progressive course,
reduced vital capacity at or below 20 ml/kg, bulbar palsy with symptoms, or autonomic cardiovascular
instability (persistent hypertension or labile blood pressure or arrhythmias). This patient has vital
capacity of 18 ml/kg, which is below the threshold of 20 ml/kg and would also be an indication for
PICU admission. Grade 3/5 weakness in lower extremities, vital capacity above 20 ml/kg, mild facial
nerve involvement, or sensory symptoms alone are not absolute indications for PICU admission.

Flaccid tetraparesis indicates severe involvement requiring intensive monitoring for respiratory and
autonomic complications.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy with Guillain-Barré syndrome has been hospitalized for 2 weeks. He initially presented with ascending paralysis and required PICU admission for respiratory monitoring. He is now recovering but continues to have mild residual weakness in his distal lower extremities. His parents are concerned about his prognosis.NWhat is the expected recovery rate for children with GBS?

options.label: E
options.text: Permanent disability in the majority of cases

questions.initialExplanation: 90-95% of children recover completely within 6 months in GBS.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The prognosis for GBS in children is generally excellent. Approximately 40% of children become
bed-bound during the acute phase, and 15% require ventilation. However, 90-95% achieve complete
recovery within 6-12 months. The remainder achieves ambulatory status with minor residual deficits.
The mortality rate is approximately 4%. Good prognostic factors include no preceding history of
infection, younger age, and milder disease at presentation. Poorer prognostic factors include
Campylobacter jejuni infection, rapid progression, and need for ventilation. This patient's mild

residual weakness and recovery trajectory are consistent with the expected course in children with

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy is being evaluated for progressive weakness over the past week. He initially noticed numbness and tingling in his feet, which progressed to his legs and now involves his hands. On examination, he has symmetric ascending weakness, areflexia, and mild ptosis. His bulbar function is intact, and respiratory status is stable. Which of the following is a diagnostic criterion for GBS?

options.label: A
options.text: Progressive motor weakness of more than one limb

options.label: C
options.text: Presence of upper motor neuron signs

questions.initialExplanation: GBS diagnostic criterion: progressive motor weakness in more than one limb with absent tendon reflexes.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The diagnostic criteria for GBS include progressive motor weakness of more than one limb (on
contralateral sides) and areflexia or hyporeflexia (loss of ankle jerks and diminished knee and biceps
reflexes will suffice if other features are consistent with the diagnosis). Other supportive features
include a monophasic course with progression over days to weeks, relative symmetry of symptoms,
possible sensory symptoms, cranial nerve involvement (especially facial nerve), autonomic
dysfunction, and absence of fever during the acute illness. Asymmetric weakness with sensory level
suggests transverse myelitis. Upper motor neuron signs (hyperreflexia, Babinski sign) are not seen in
GBS. Cranial nerve involvement in isolation suggests a different diagnosis. Fever at presentation is
not typical of GBS and should prompt consideration of alternative diagnoses.

---

questions.stem: An 8-year-old girl is admitted with suspected GBS. Lumbar puncture is performed on day 3 of symptoms. CSF analysis shows: opening pressure normal, protein 35 mg/dL, glucose 60 mg/dL, and cell count 2 cells/uL. What is the most appropriate interpretation and next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Normal CSF excludes GBS; pursue alternative diagnosis

options.label: B
options.text: < B) This pattern is diagnostic of GBS

options.label: C
options.text: Low glucose suggests bacterial meningitis; start antibiotics

options.label: E
options.text: Protein may be normal in the first week; repeat LP in the second week

questions.initialExplanation: CSF protein may be normal in the first week of GBS, so it does not exclude the diagnosis; repeat LP if needed.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This is an important clinical pearl. Albuminocytological dissociation (elevated protein with normal cell
count) is characteristic of GBS, but the CSF may be normal within the first week of symptoms. Lumbar
‘    puncture should ideally be performed during the second week for optimal diagnostic yield. At this point
(day 3), the protein may still be within normal limits (normal is typically less than 45 mg/dL in children).
Normal CSF does not exclude GBS at this early stage. Repeating the LP in the second week is
appropriate if the clinical suspicion remains high. Starting antibiotics is not indicated as there is no

evidence of bacterial infection (glucose is normal). Pleocytosis would suggest an alternative diagnosis
like viral meningitis.

---

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy with GBS has been hospitalized for 1 week. He is on day 3 of IVIG therapy. His nurse reports that he has developed fever, nausea, headache, and appears uncomfortable. His blood pressure is elevated at 150/95 mmHg. Which of the following is a known side effect of IVIG therapy?

options.label: B
options.text: Fever, nausea, headache, and aseptic meningitis

questions.initialExplanation: IVIG side effects include fever, headache, nausea and aseptic meningitis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) is generally well-tolerated but can have several side effects.
Common side effects include fever, nausea, vomiting, headache, and aseptic meningitis. These are
usually mild and self-limiting. Other possible but rare side effects include thromboembolism, renal
failure, and congestive heart failure. The patient described has fever, nausea, headache, and
elevated blood pressure —consistent with common VIG side effects. Hypotension and bradycardia
are not typical IVIG side effects. Hypoglycemia is not associated with IVIG. Stevens-Johnson
syndrome is extremely rare with VIG. Managing these side effects may require slowing the infusion
rate or pre-medication with antihistamines or acetaminophen.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy is evaluated for suspected GBS. Nerve conduction studies show conduction block and decreased compound muscle action potential amplitude with slowed conduction velocity. Which type of GBS is most commonly associated with these electrophysiological findings?
questions.initialExplanation: Slowed nerve conduction velocity = the commonest type: acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (AIDP).
questions.detailedExplanation:
AIDP is the most common subtype of GBS, accounting for approximately 70% of cases. The
electrophysiological findings described are characteristic of demyelination, including conduction block

‘    (interruption of nerve conduction at specific sites), decreased compound muscle action potential
amplitude (due to demyelination), and slowed conduction velocity (reflective of demyelination). These
findings differentiate AIDP from axonal forms of GBS (AMAN and AMSAN), which show axonal
degeneration without significant demyelinating features. Miller Fisher syndrome presents with the triad
of ataxia, areflexia, and ophthalmoplegia. CIDP is a chronic condition lasting more than 8 weeks. The
demyelinating pattern on nerve conduction studies confirms AIDP as the diagnosis.

---

questions.stem: An 8-year-old boy presents with a 2-week history of ascending paralysis. He had Campylobacter jejuni gastroenteritis 3 weeks ago. On examination, he has severe symmetric weakness (grade 1/5 in all limbs), areflexia, and requires mechanical ventilation for respiratory failure. What is the mortality rate associated with GBS?
questions.initialExplanation: GBS mortality is about 4% (higher if mechanical ventilation is needed).
questions.detailedExplanation:
The mortality rate for Guillain-Barré syndrome is approximately 4%, despite appropriate
immunotherapy and supportive care. Causes of death include autonomic complications (bradycardia,
tachycardia, hypertension, cardiac arrest), respiratory failure, pulmonary embolism, complications of
ventilation, and cardiovascular collapse. Campylobacter jejuni infection is associated with a poorer
prognosis and more severe disease. The mortality rate has decreased with modern ICU care and
immunotherapy. Less than 1% is too optimistic. Ten to twenty percent mortality is higher than actual
rates. Fifty percent mortality is seen only in untreated or severely complicated cases. The patient's
severe presentation with respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation places him at higher risk,
but overall mortality remains approximately 4% with appropriate care.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy who has not received any immunizations presents with a 2-day history of fever, headache, and vomiting. His parents report that he has been lethargic and refusing to drink. On examination, he has nuchal rigidity, positive Kernig's sign, and hyperreflexia in the lower extremities. He has no focal motor deficits. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: An unvaccinated child with fever and mild meningitis without motor weakness = non-paralytic poliomyelitis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This presentation is consistent with non-paralytic poliomyelitis (also called aseptic meningitis form of polio).
The key features include unvaccinated status (major risk factor for poliovirus infection), acute febrile illness
(fever, headache, vomiting), meningeal signs (nuchal rigidity, positive Kernig's sign), hyperreflexia (early sign

‘    before potential progression to paralysis), and absence of focal motor deficits (distinguishes from paralytic
form). The clinical course of non-paralytic polio includes signs of the abortive type with fleeting paralysis of
bladder and constipation, and meningeal signs on examination without sensory defects. Bacterial meningitis
would typically show neutrophilic pleocytosis and low glucose in CSF. GBS presents with ascending paralysis
and areflexia. ADEM typically follows vaccination or infection with multifocal CNS signs. Brain abscess would
show focal deficits and mass effect on imaging.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy with suspected poliomyelitis is being evaluated. The physician orders stool specimens for viral isolation. What is the appropriate collection method for stool specimens in suspected polio?

options.label: A
options.text: Single stool specimen collected within 24 hours \*

options.label: C
options.text: Two stool specimens collected 24-48 hours apart

questions.initialExplanation: To diagnose polio: two stool samples taken 24-48 hours apart.
questions.detailedExplanation:
For suspected poliomyelitis, the recommended diagnostic approach for stool specimens is to collect
two stool specimens 24-48 hours apart. Stool should be collected as soon as possible after the onset
of paralysis. Poliovirus can be isolated in 80-90% of cases in the first week, but the isolation rate
decreases to less than 20% within 3-4 weeks. This approach maximizes the yield of virus isolation. A
single random stool sample or morning sample after fasting is less reliable. Rectal swabs have lower
yield than stool specimens. Collection after enema is not recommended as it may dilute the
specimen. The two-sample approach is standard for both diagnostic confirmation and public health
surveillance.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy presents with fever, difficulty swallowing, and nasal voice. His parents report that he had a fever 3 days ago and now has accumulated pharyngeal secretions. On examination, he has a nasal voice, absent gag reflex, and inability to swallow saliva. His breathing is labored. Which type of paralytic poliomyelitis is this presentation consistent with?
questions.initialExplanation: Swallowing difficulty, nasal voice and difficult breathing = bulbar poliomyelitis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This presentation is characteristic of bulbar poliomyelitis, which involves the cranial nerve nuclei in the
medulla oblongata. Key features include nasal voice or cry (due to palatal and pharyngeal weakness),
difficulty swallowing, accumulated pharyngeal secretions, absence of effective coughing, nasal
regurgitation, deviation of palate and uvula and tongue (cranial nerve involvement), involvement of
vital centers in the medulla, and paralysis of vocal cords causing hoarseness and aphonia. Spinal
poliomyelitis affects limb muscles. Polioencephalitis is rare and presents with seizures, coma, and
spastic paralysis. Non-paralytic and abortive forms do not cause paralysis. Bulbar polio is particularly

dangerous due to the risk of aspiration and respiratory failure, with a mortality rate of approximately

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old girl is admitted with suspected poliomyelitis. Lumbar puncture is performed. CSF analysis shows: opening pressure normal, white blood cell count 150/uL (initially), glucose normal, and protein elevated at 80 mg/dL by the second week. Which CSF finding is most characteristic of poliomyelitis?

options.label: A
options.text: Normal cell count and normal protein \*

options.label: B
options.text: Pleocytosis with lymphocytic predominance and elevated protein

options.label: D
options.text: Normal protein and elevated cell count only

questions.initialExplanation: CSF in polio: increased lymphocytes with gradually rising protein.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The CSF findings in poliomyelitis (both paralytic and non-paralytic forms) typically show an initial cell
count of 20-200 cells/mm? (which then reduces), lymphocytic predominance (may be mixed initially),
protein elevated to 50-100 mg/dL by the second week, and normal glucose. These findings are similar
to viral meningitis and help distinguish poliomyelitis from bacterial meningitis, which shows neutrophilic
pleocytosis and low glucose. Albuminocytological dissociation (elevated protein with normal cell count)
is characteristic of GBS, not polio. The presence of oligoclonal bands suggests multiple sclerosis. The

pattern in poliomyelitis is most consistent with a viral etiology affecting the meninges and anterior horn
cells.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old unvaccinated boy presents with fever, headache, and neck stiffness. His parents report that he had a viral illness 1 week ago. On examination, he has nuchal rigidity and positive Brudzinski sign. He has no motor weakness. CSF shows lymphocytic pleocytosis with elevated protein. Which of the following distinguishes non-paralytic poliomyelitis from bacterial meningitis?
questions.initialExplanation: The difference from bacterial meningitis: CSF glucose is normal in non-paralytic polio.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The CSF findings help distinguish non-paralytic poliomyelitis from bacterial meningitis. Non-paralytic
poliomyelitis shows normal glucose level with lymphocytic pleocytosis and elevated protein, while

‘    bacterial meningitis shows low glucose level with neutrophilic pleocytosis and markedly elevated
protein. Both conditions can present with fever, nuchal rigidity, and headache. The normal glucose
level in poliomyelitis helps differentiate it from bacterial causes, where glucose is typically less than
40% of serum glucose or less than 40 mg/dL. Presence of fever is common to both conditions.
Absence of focal neurological deficits can occur in both early. Gradual onset is not specific. History of

recent vaccination might suggest vaccine-associated disease but doesn't distinguish the conditions
based on CSF findings.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy is recovering from paralytic poliomyelitis. He had asymmetric flaccid paralysis of the right lower limb 3 months ago. He has persistent weakness and muscle wasting in the affected limb. What is the typical duration of the recovery phase in paralytic polio?
questions.initialExplanation: Paralysis after polio usually improves over about 6 months, though permanent weakness may remain.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The recovery phase in paralytic poliomyelitis typically lasts 6 months. During this time, some patients
show gradual recovery of muscle strength while others may have permanent residual weakness or
paralysis. Physical therapy and rehabilitation are essential during this period, and orthopedic
management may be needed for deformities. Prognosis depends on the extent and severity of CNS
involvement (more extensive involvement leads to poorer recovery), the pattern of paralysis
(asymmetric involvement may have better outcomes), and age (younger children may have better
recovery potential). Two weeks is too brief for meaningful recovery. One to two years is longer than

the typical recovery phase. Most recovery occurs within the first 6 months, with remaining deficits
often being permanent.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy has had two similar, brief episodes within the past month consisting of abrupt arrest of ongoing behavior, eye staring, and lip smacking, followed by confusion and sleepiness for 1 hour. Brain MRI and EEG are normal. What is the MOST LIKELY diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Short recurrent seizures followed by confusion and sleepiness with normal MRI and EEG = complex partial (focal impaired awareness) seizure.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- behavioral arrest, staring, automatisms (lip smacking), followed by postictal confusion/sleepiness
lasting 1 hour. This is classic for complex partial (focal impaired awareness) seizure. Absence
seizures have NO postictal confusion and last only seconds. Interictal EEG can be normal in focal
epilepsy; MRI may miss subtle lesions.

---

questions.stem: 2024 J) 5 / A 9-year-old girl presented with daydreaming. You observed the girl attempting to inflate a latex glove, pausing, and then staring into space motionless for approximately 15 seconds. Subsequently, she blinked her eyes a few times and smiled at you. You advise the parent that:

options.label: A
options.text: If the child shows inattentive issues at school and home for six months, start stimulant medication

options.label: B
options.text: No further evaluation or medication is needed

options.label: C
options.text: Test for latex allergy is necessary

options.label: D
options.text: Start ethosuximide treatment after EEG assessment

options.label: E
options.text: Refer to a child psychiatrist for depression evaluation

questions.initialExplanation: Brief absence (about 15 seconds) with blinking and quick recovery = absence seizures; start ethosuximide after confirming with EEG.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This is a classic absence seizure: sudden behavioral arrest, blank stare for ~15 seconds, immediate

return to normal activity (smiling) with NO postictal confusion. EEG will show characteristic 3 Hz spike-
and-wave pattern. Ethosuximide is first-line treatment for childhood absence epilepsy.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child is presented with recurrent seizures, without regaining consciousness between episodes. After ensuring ABCs, you plan laboratory tests. Which test is the LEAST helpful in revealing the underlying cause?

options.label: C
options.text: Estimating blood urea and serum creatinine levels

options.label: E
options.text: Performing a lumbar puncture - F) POO OoTW

questions.initialExplanation: In recurrent seizures without return of consciousness (status epilepticus): the least useful test is the one least tied to the seizure cause (a non-targeted test).
questions.detailedExplanation:
This is status epilepticus. A skull X-ray only shows bone and cannot identify seizure causes. Blood
glucose (hypoglycemia), renal function (uremia), EEG (seizure focus/activity), and LP (CNS infection)
all help identify treatable causes. For intracranial pathology, CT or MRI is needed —not plain X-ray.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child arrives at the hospital in an ongoing generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting 7 minutes. Intravenous access is failed. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
questions.initialExplanation: Tonic-clonic seizure lasting 7 minutes without IV access: IM midazolam is first choice.
questions.detailedExplanation:
When |V access fails in status epilepticus, IM midazolam is the preferred choice—it has rapid
absorption and proven efficacy equal to IV lorazepam. Rectal diazepam is an alternative but IM
midazolam is faster and more practical. IM diazepam has erratic absorption and is NOT
recommended. Phenytoin cannot be given IM or intranasally.

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl has frequent episodes where she suddenly stops activity and stares blankly, sometimes with brief eyelid fluttering. Episodes last only seconds, occur many times daily, and she returns to normal immediately. Which finding would best confirm the diagnosis? DOO OoTW

options.label: A
options.text: MRI reveals a structural lesion in the frontal cortex

options.label: B
options.text: EEG shows generalized 3-Hz spike-and-wave discharges Episodes are followed by prolonged confusion and lethargy

options.label: C
options.text: Each episode typically lasts more than one minute

options.label: D
options.text: Focal motor activity and aura are commonly reported

questions.initialExplanation: Sudden daily staring with blinking = absence seizures, confirmed by EEG with 3-Hz spike-and-wave.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This is classic childhood absence epilepsy: brief staring spells, eyelid fluttering, multiple daily
episodes, immediate return to baseline (NO postictal confusion). EEG showing 3-Hz generalized
spike-and-wave is pathognomonic. Prolonged confusion suggests complex partial seizures; auras
suggest focal seizures.

> **Note:** Question number inferred from the sequence.

questions.stem: A previously healthy 3-year-old child presents with a generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting about 2 minutes during a febrile illness. The seizure was isolated, and the child quickly returned to baseline. Exam is normal, with no signs of meningeal irritation. What is the most appropriate next step in management? 2025 lJ

options.label: B
options.text: Perform an urgent brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)

options.label: C
options.text: Reassure and educate parents about febrile seizures

options.label: D
options.text: Do lumbar puncture to rule out meningitis

questions.initialExplanation: First simple febrile seizure (3 years, otherwise well): reassure and educate parents (no tests, no daily drug).
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child experienced a simple febrile seizure: generalized, lasting <15 minutes, single episode in 24 hours,
with rapid return to baseline and normal examination. Simple febrile seizures are benign, self-limited events
with excellent prognosis and no increased risk of epilepsy or neurological deficits. Antiepileptic drugs are not
indicated as they do not prevent recurrence or improve outcomes and carry unnecessary side effects.
Neuroimaging (MRI) and EEG are not routinely recommended after simple febrile seizures with normal
neurological examination. Lumbar puncture is reserved for cases with meningeal signs, altered mental status,
or in infants <12 months with incomplete immunization; this 3-year-old has no such indications. The
cornerstone of management is parental reassurance and education about fever management, seizure first aid,
and recognizing warning signs requiring re-evaluation. Recurrence risk is approximately 30%, but most
children outgrow febrile seizures by age 5 without long-term consequences.

---

questions.stem: An 18-month-old boy is presenting with the first simple febrile seizure and is otherwise neurologically healthy; his father read in the net that EEG has a significant role in the management of his son. Your proper answer should be : (NE)

options.label: A
options.text: EEG should not be performed as part of the evaluation

options.label: B
options.text: EEG would predict the future recurrence of febrile seizures

options.label: C
options.text: EEG would predict the future recurrence of epilepsy

options.label: D
options.text: EEG should be done after 2 wk of a febrile seizure

options.label: E
options.text: EEG should be done after second attack of febrile seizure

questions.initialExplanation: First simple febrile seizure: EEG is not part of the evaluation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
AAP Guidelines on Simple Febrile Seizures
The American Academy of Pediatrics has established clear guidelines regarding the evaluation of simple
febrile seizures. According to these evidence-based recommendations, a simple febrile seizure does not

‘     require further diagnostic evaluation, specifically including electroencephalography. A simple febrile seizure is
defined as a generalized seizure accompanied by fever (temperature greater than 100.4°F or 38°C) lasting
less than 15 minutes, without recurrence within 24 hours, and occurring in a neurologically healthy child.

The AAP guidelines explicitly state that an EEG should not be obtained in a neurologically healthy child with a

first simple febrile seizure. This recommendation is based on extensive clinical evidence demonstrating that
EEG findings do not provide meaningful prognostic information in this population.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child wakes up at night due to a focal seizure with throat tingling and clonic contractions of one side of the face, with drooling and inability to speak but with preserved consciousness and comprehension. EEG shows typical wide-based spikes that are markedly increased in frequency during drowsiness and sleep with normal MRI. Of the following, the MOST likely diagnosis is :(NE)

options.label: A
options.text: atypical benign childhood epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes

options.label: B
options.text: benign childhood epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes

options.label: D
options.text: nocturnal autosomal dominant frontal lobe epilepsy

questions.initialExplanation: Nocturnal focal seizure with a throat sensation and centrotemporal EEG spikes = benign rolandic epilepsy (BECTS).
questions.detailedExplanation:
The case presentation demonstrates classic features of benign childhood epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes (BECTS), the most common focal epilepsy
syndrome of childhood. Let me analyze the specific clinical elements that support this diagnosis:

- Age of Presentation: The 5-year-old child is within the typical age range for BECTS, which usually presents between 3-13 years of age with peak onset
between 7-10 years. This age is perfectly consistent with the expected epidemiology of this syndrome.

- Seizure Semiology: The described seizure characteristics are pathognomonic for Rolandic seizures. The focal seizure with throat tingling (orofacial
sensory symptoms), clonic contractions of one side of the face (unilateral facial motor activity), drooling (sialorrhea), and inability to speak (speech
arrest) with preserved consciousness and comprehension are the hallmark features of seizures originating from the rolandic cortex (central sulcus
region). These seizures result from involvement of the lower rolandic area controlling the face, tongue, and pharynx.

- Temporal Pattern: The seizure occurring at night during sleep is characteristic of BECTS, as more than 70% of seizures in this syndrome occur during
sleep or upon awakening. The nocturnal predominance is a well-recognized clinical feature.

- EEG Findings: The description of "wide-based spikes that are markedly increased in frequency during drowsiness and sleep" is the classic
electroencephalographic signature of centrotemporal spikes. These high-amplitude, sharp waves with characteristic morphology (often described as "
wicket spikes" or "Rolandic spikes") are located in the centrotemporal regions and show marked activation during sleep, which is a diagnostic hallmark.

---

questions.stem: A 3-week-old newborn presents with recurrent generalized tonic seizures that progress to status epilepticus which is not controlled by multiple antiepileptic drugs. The mother reports increased fetal movements in utero. Plasma and CSF showed elevated a-aminoadipic semialdehyde and pipecolic acid levels. Of the following, the MOST likely diagnosis is : (NE)
questions.initialExplanation: Neonatal seizures with raised α-aminoadipic semialdehyde and pipecolic acid = pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This case presents classic features of pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy (PDE), a treatable inherited metabolic disorder that presents in the
neonatal period with refractory seizures. Let me analyze the specific elements that support this diagnosis:

- Age and Seizure Characteristics: The 3-week-old newborn with recurrent generalized tonic seizures progressing to status epilepticus
that is refractory to multiple antiepileptic drugs is the typical presentation of pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy. These seizures are often
described as "shaking spells" that begin in the first days to weeks of life and are characteristically unresponsive to conventional
antiepileptic medications.

- Increased Fetal Movements: The maternal history of increased fetal movements is a characteristic feature reported by mothers of
infants with pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy. This prenatal manifestation reflects in utero seizure activity, which can begin before birth in
affected fetuses. This historical feature, when present, should raise strong clinical suspicion for PDE.

- Biochemical Hallmark: The elevated plasma and CSF levels of a-aminoadipic semialdehyde and pipecolic acid are the biochemical
hallmarks of pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy. These metabolites accumulate due to deficiency of a-aminoadipic semialdehyde
dehydrogenase (also known as antiquitin), which is encoded by the ALDH7A1 gene. The accumulation of these metabolites is both
diagnostic of the condition and provides a biomarker for newborn screening and disease monitoring.

---

questions.stem: A 3-week-old newborn is well and ready to be discharged from NICU; he developed seizure at first day of life due to difficult labor and treated with phenobarbital loading then maintenance on 5mg/kg/day twice daily. An EEG done before discharge and does not show evidence of epileptiform activity. Parents asked you about the fate of anticonvulsant and when can be stopped. Of the following, the MOST appropriate answer is that phenobarbital should be : (NE) 12
questions.initialExplanation: Once the newborn is stable, phenobarbital can be tapered at discharge instead of continued long-term.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This scenario describes a classic case of acute symptomatic neonatal seizure due to birth injury or hypoxic-ischemic
encephalopathy. The key features supporting this diagnosis and management approach include:

- Acute Symptomatic Etiology: The seizure occurred on the first day of life due to difficult labor, indicating an acute
neurological insult rather than an underlying epileptic syndrome. This is the most common type of neonatal seizure and
typically results from hypoxic-ischemic injury, intracranial hemorrhage, stroke, or metabolic derangements.

- Favorable Prognostic Indicators: Several features in this case suggest a good outcome: the infant is now clinically well
at 3 weeks of age, and the EEG performed before discharge shows no epileptiform activity. These findings indicate that
the acute injury has resolved without evolving into a chronic epileptic condition.

- Self-Limited Nature of Acute Symptomatic Seizures: Acute symptomatic neonatal seizures typically remit within 72
hours of onset once the underlying cause is addressed. These seizures represent a transient response to brain injury
and do not indicate a predisposition to future epilepsy in most cases.

---

questions.stem: - A term newborn is delivered by emergent cesarean section because of intrauterine growth restriction, oligohydramnios, and nonreassuring fetal heart rate monitoring in labor. Delivery room resuscitation includes endotracheal intubation and assisted ventilation with 100% oxygen, chest compressions, intravenous epinephrine, and volume expansion. Apgar scores are 1, 2, and 3 at 1, 5, and 10 minutes, respectively. An umbilical cord arterial blood gas measurement documents a pH of 6.9 and a base deficit of 20 mmol/L. At 12 hours of age, the infant demonstrates tonic-clonic convulsive activity of the arms and legs with a concomitant decrease in heart rate and bedside pulse oximetry saturation. Of Na moo the following, the MOST likely cause for this infant's seizure is :
questions.initialExplanation: Perinatal hypoxia (low Apgar, pH 6.9) with seizure at 12 hours = hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Seizures are the most frequent sign of central nervous system injury in the newborn. When seizures occur in a newborn
who has depressed neuromotor tone, reflexes, and cardiopulmonary function at birth that requires assisted ventilation,
perinatal asphyxia is likely. In this event, Apgar scores typically are depressed to less than 3 at 5 or more minutes after
birth, and there is a severely acidotic umbilical cord arterial pH (<7.0), with evidence of metabolic acidemia. Poor
tolerance of labor and asphyxia are more common in fetuses that have experienced intrauterine growth restriction.
Because the infant in the vignette has the previously described features, hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) must be
considered as a cause for the seizures.

- HIE is the most common cause of seizures occurring in the first 24 hours of postnatal life and accounts for up to 67% of
early neonatal seizures. Other causes of neonatal seizure include intracranial hemorrhage, cerebrovascular accidents
(stroke), or hemorrhagic infarction (10% to 15%); intracranial malformation (<10%); transient hypoglycemia or
hypocalcemia (<10%); drug withdrawal (<5%); and inborn errors of metabolism (<5%).

> **Note:** Question number inferred from the sequence.

---

questions.stem: A newborn in your neonatal intensive care unit has had intermittent seizures for 72 hours. You have been unable to control the seizures with phenobarbital, hydantoin, and lorazepam. Electrolyte, calcium, magnesium, and glucose concentrations are normal. The infant subsequently becomes apneic, comatose, and unresponsive. Of the following, the BEST laboratory test to determine the cause of coma in this infant is :(NE)

options.label: A
options.text: analysis of whole blood lead concentration

options.label: B
options.text: evaluation of urine for reducing substances

options.label: C
options.text: measurement of serum amino acids, organic acids, lactate, and ammonia

options.label: D
options.text: measurement of serum cortisol, thyroxine, and thyroid-stimulating hormone

options.label: E
options.text: measurement of very long-chain fatty acids

questions.initialExplanation: Coma in a newborn with suspected metabolic disorder: the best test is serum amino acids.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Seizures in the neonatal period often are due to hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy or intracranial pathology such as malformation or
hemorrhage. Most are controlled readily with a single or, possibly, two anticonvulsant therapies. The patient described in the vignette
has refractory seizures that have not responded to three anticonvulsants, and the infant’s condition progresses to coma. This
presentation is not uncommon in metabolic diseases, where seizures may be focal or multifocal clonic jerks or generalized and tonic.
Such events typically occur after the first 48 postnatal hours. Because transient abnormalities in glucose and electrolytes are not
present in this patient, inborn errors of metabolism need to be ruled out.

A categorical approach to the laboratory evaluation of the comatose newborn or young infant is helpful. Toxins and drugs can be
evaluated by history and blood, urine, or meconium toxicology screens. Intracranial pathology can be evaluated by ultrasonography or
computed tomography scan. Hypoxia-ischemia mechanisms can be discerned by history, blood gas analysis, evidence of multiple
organ system dysfunction, the neurologic examination, and the timing of the onset of seizures (generally in the first 24 hours of
postnatal life). Infection may be systemic or focal (central nervous system) and can be evaluated by cultures, antigen testing, and use
of specific viral polymerase chain reaction tests of the blood, urine, and cerebrospinal fluid.

---

questions.stem: A 1 mo old child is brought to the emergency department during a heat wave after she has had a generalized seizure. A CT scan of the brain is reportedly normal. The family notes having recently diluted the child's formula to provide additional water. The most likely explanation for this child's seizures is: (NE)
questions.initialExplanation: An infant seizing in hot weather after the milk was diluted with water = hyponatremia (water intoxication).
questions.detailedExplanation:
In patients with normal renal function, the kidney can excrete dilute urine with an osmolality as low
as 50 mOsm/kg. To excrete a daily solute load of 500 mOsm/m2 , the kidney must produce 10 L/m2
of urine per day. Therefore, to avoid hyponatremia, the maximum amount of water a person with
normal renal function can consume is 10 L/m2 . Neonates, however, cannot dilute their urine to this
degree, putting them at risk for water intoxication if water intake exceeds 4 L/m2/day (approximately
60 mL/hr in a newborn). Many infants develop transient but symptomatic hyponatremic seizures
after being fed pure water without electrolytes rather than breast milk or formula.

---

questions.stem: A 4 yr old boy is evaluated for his 1st generalized tonic-clonic seizure, which lasted 10 min. There is no history of illness or fever, and findings on examination an hour after the seizure are completely normal. The most appropriate management is: (NE)
questions.initialExplanation: A first generalized afebrile seizure in a 4-year-old with a normal exam: brain MRI per the given answer.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Guidelines on the evaluation and treatment of a 1st unprovoked nonfebrile seizure include a careful history
and physical examination and brain imaging by head CT or MRI. Emergency head CT in the child presenting
with a 1st unprovoked nonfebrile seizure is often useful for acute management of the patient. Laboratory
studies are recommended in specific clinical situations: spinal tap is considered in patients with suspected
meningitis or encephalitis, in children without brain swelling or papilledema, and in children in whom a history
of intracranial bleeding is suspected without evidence of such on head CT. In the 2nd of these, examination of
the CSF for xanthochromia is essential. CSF tests can also confirm with the appropriate clinical setup the
diagnosis of glucose transporter Deficiency, cerebral folate deficiency, pyridoxine dependency, pyridoxal
dependency, mitochondrial disorders, nonketotic hyperglycemia, and neurotransmitter deficiencies.
Electrocardiography (ECG) to rule out long QT or other cardiac dysrhythmias and other tests directed at
disorders that could mimic seizures may be needed.

---

questions.stem: A 15 mo old girl is evaluated for a 10-min-long generalized seizure associated with a temperature of 40 C. Which of the following factors in the history is most likely to increase the risk of future seizures?
questions.initialExplanation: Risk factors for febrile seizure recurrence and later epilepsy: family history of seizures.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Although about 15% of children with epilepsy have had febrile seizures, only 2-7% of children who

experience febrile seizures proceed to develop epilepsy later in life. There are several predictors of
epilepsy after febrile seizures.

---

questions.stem: A 14-year-old girl with a history of seizures is admitted to the hospital with the diagnosis of status epilepticus. Her valproic acid level is in the therapeutic range. You arrange a 24-hour video electroencephalogram (EEG). During the EEG, she has several episodes of tonic and clonic movements with moaning and crying, with no loss of bowel or bladder control. The neurologist tells you that during the events the EEG had excessive muscle artifact but no epileptiform discharges. Which of the following treatments is the most appropriate for this condition? (pretest)

options.label: A
options.text: Add a scheduled benzodiazepine for her muscular symptoms

options.label: B
options.text: Add carbamazepine to her current seizure medication

options.label: C
options.text: Increase her dose of valproic acid

questions.initialExplanation: Seizures with no EEG changes during the event and psychiatric symptoms: psychiatric evaluation for possible pseudoseizures.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Seizure like activity with no epileptiform activity on EEG is consistent with pseudoseizure. These
episodes may be very convincing for seizures and may include unusual posturing and sounds, but
typically do not involve loss ofnbowel or bladder control. In addition, the patient usually will not
cause self-injury, and pupillary response to light is normal. These episodes can be deliberate or part
of a conversion disorder, and do not require treatment with antiepileptic medications. However,
many patients with pseudoseizures also have true epileptic seizures, so withdrawal of antiepileptic
medication would be inappropriate at this point. Psychiatric or psychologic evaluation is the best
way to start managing pseudoseizures.

---

questions.stem: The parents of a 2-year-old bring her to the emergency center after she had a seizure. Although the parents report she was in a good state of health, the vital signs in the emergency center reveal a temperature of 39°C (102.2°F). She is now running around the room. Which part of the story would suggest the best outcome in this condition?

options.label: D
options.text: The child was born prematurely with an intraventricular hemorrhage.

options.label: E
options.text: The family reports the child to have had right-sided tonic-clonic activity only.

questions.initialExplanation: The best prognosis is when there is a clear fever source such as otitis media.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The child in the question likely had a febrile seizure. Febrile seizures usually occur in children between the
ages of 9 months and 5 years, generally in association with upper respiratory illness, roseola, shigellosis, or
gastroenteritis. The generalized seizures are mostly brief (2-5 minutes), and the CSF is normal. Since other
more serious processes cause seizure and fever, each child must be carefully evaluated. Children younger
than 12 to 18 months do not have a reliable neck examination for meningismus, so they will probably need a
lumbar puncture to rule out CNS infection as a cause. In a simple febrile seizure, EEG and CNS imaging are
not usually necessary. Infants who have seizures that are prolonged (longer than 15 minutes), focal, or
lateralized, or who had neurologic problems before the febrile seizure (including intra ventricular hemorrhage),
are at a higher risk of developing an afebrile seizure disorder during the subsequent 5 to 7 years. CSF is
usually normal after a seizure, so a pleocytosis requires evaluation for meningitis or encephalitis.

---

questions.stem: A 12-year-old girl is being evaluated for possible seizures. She has a seizure about once a week. Typically they occur when she is in a stressful situation or frightened. Her eyes roll up and she has asynchronous jerking movements of all extremities and pelvic thrusting for about 15 minutes. A routine EEG is normal; however, no events were captured. What is the next best step in her management? (Rud)

options.label: D
options.text: The parents should ignore the events.

questions.initialExplanation: Normal EEG with seizures not captured: admit for video EEG monitoring to document the events.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This girl’s events could be nonepileptic seizures, a form of conversion disorder. The asynchronous
jerking of the limbs and pelvic thrusting are common manifestations of nonepileptic seizures in
teenaged girls. However, many patients with nonepileptic seizures also have epilepsy, so an
admission for video EEG monitoring to capture events is essential in clarifying the diagnosis. It will
also afford an opportunity for private discussions with the adolescent about whether there is any
concern for abuse. Starting a medication typically should be delayed until the diagnosis is clear,
particularly as the goal of the admission is to record events. If the diagnosis is ultimately shown to
be nonepileptic seizures, then referral for behavioral therapy would be recommended.

---

questions.stem: A neonate is being loaded on phenobarbital for seizures. What is the most likely side effect the neonatology team should be prepared for? (Rud)
questions.initialExplanation: The most important side effect of phenobarbital in newborns: respiratory depression.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Multiple loading doses of phenobarbital can sometimes be required to control neonatal seizures.
Respiratory suppression is not uncommon and infants may need respiratory support, particularly
with escalating doses.

Phenobarbital-induced electrolyte disturbances are not expected. Allergic reactions are rare.
Dystonic reactions are associated with dopamine receptor antagonists, not barbiturates.

---

questions.stem: A 15-month-old girl presents to the emergency department after a reported generalized convulsion at home that lasted 60 seconds. A rectal temperature on arrival is 39.5°C. She is well appearing and back to her baseline with a normal neurologic examination. She is an otherwise healthy and normally developing girl. Mom had a febrile seizure when she was 2 years old. What are the clinical features that would increase this child’s risk of future epilepsy? (Rud)

options.label: A
options.text: Family history of febrile seizures in a first-degree relative

options.label: B
options.text: Age of fist febrile seizure <18 months

options.label: C
options.text: Level of temperature at first seizure

options.label: D
options.text: Complex febrile seizure (focal, prolonged, or repeated)

options.label: E
options.text: Duration of illness before seizure - F) ®0O0oo

questions.initialExplanation: Complex febrile seizure (focal, prolonged, or recurring within 24 hours) raises the later epilepsy risk.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Several studies have shown that the factors that define a complex febrile seizure are risk factors for subsequent
epilepsy after a first febrile seizure. These factors include a focal seizure, prolonged seizure, and repeated
seizures within a single febrile illness. Developmental delay or abnormal neurologic examination is also
associated with an increased risk of future epilepsy.

Children with a history of febrile seizures with no risk factors for epilepsy have a 2% chance of developing
epilepsy. A single risk factor increases the risk of epilepsy to 5%, and 2 or more risk factors increase the risk to
15%. Even so, the majority of all children with febrile seizures will not develop epilepsy.

The other choices listed above are risk factors for having a recurrent febrile seizure after a first febrile seizure.
Positive family history and younger age of first febrile seizure are most predictive, but low temperature and
shorter duration of illness at first seizure are also risk factors.

---

questions.stem: A 13-year-old girl with a history of generalized tonic clonic seizures arrives to the emergency department by ambulance after having a convulsion lasting 5 minutes at home. She is sleepy but arousable on arrival without any focal neurologic findings. Vital signs are normal. There is no history of illness or trauma. She takes lamotrigine for seizure control. As part of her diagnostic evaluation, what test would be most important in this situation? (Rud)
questions.initialExplanation: Known epilepsy with seizures despite treatment: the most important test is the lamotrigine level to check adherence and dose.
questions.detailedExplanation:
It is important to check a lamotrigine level to determine if the patient is taking the medication, as this
will affect the management plan going forward. Nonadherence is a significant problem with patients

‘    with epilepsy. The patient has known epilepsy without recent trauma, and has a nonfocal neurologic
examination, and therefore a head CT scan is unnecessary. An EEG is also unnecessary, as the
patient has known epilepsy and is waking up (therefore low risk of ongoing subclinical seizures).
CBC, LFTs, and a lumbar puncture are also unnecessary in this patient who is otherwise well
appearing without recent fevers or infection.

---

questions.stem: A 4-month-old infant is seen in the office for a new patient visit. The patient’s mother reports that her daughter had “seizures” involving clonic movements starting at 5 days of life and remitting at 1 month of life spontaneously. Brain MRI and metabolic studies at the time of seizure onset were normal. Her examination and developmental are normal. There is no family history of seizures. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: An infant with benign seizures and normal development = benign neonatal convulsions.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Benign neonatal convulsions, also known as fifth-day fits, are marked by seizure onset between 4 and 6 days
of life in otherwise healthy newborns. Diagnostic evaluation for an underlying cause is negative. The seizures
remit by 2 months of life. The diagnosis is made retrospectively, after the seizures remit and development
remains normal. Infantile spasms present around 6 months of age and are generally associated with poor
developmental outcomes. Similarly, EME is associated with poor developmental outcomes, and the early-
onset myoclonic seizures tend to be refractory to treatment. Metabolic disorders, such as nonketotic
hyperglycinemia, are the most common underlying cause. Benign familial neonatal convulsions also present
in the first several days of life in a healthy newborn and are associated with favorable prognosis, but there is a
family history of seizures during the newborn period. This syndrome is associated with mutations in the
potassium channel gene KCNQ2/KCNQ3.

---

questions.stem: An 8-year-old boy is referred for new-onset seizures. Which of the following would mostly support a diagnosis of complex partial (psychomotor) seizures? (Lange)

options.label: A
options.text: normal mental state, consciousness, and responsiveness during seizure

options.label: E
options.text: normal mental state, consciousness, and responsiveness after seizure

questions.initialExplanation: Supporting complex partial seizures: automatisms (automatic movements such as chewing and hand rubbing).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Complex partial seizures is the current name for what previously was termed temporal lobe or
psychomotor seizures. Complex partial seizures are characterized by alterations of mental status,
consciousness, or responsiveness. During the seizure, there may be confusion, emotional reactions,
feelings of detachment, and hallucinations. Automatisms (semipurposeful but inappropriate motor
acts) are frequent. There is no tonic or clonic component. Postictal confusion is common. The usual
EEG finding is spike-wave activity over one or both temporal lobe regions. A three-per-second spike-
and-wave pattern on EEG is characteristic of absence seizures.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old with a seizure disorder presents to the emergency department with increased seizure frequency. Her medication regimen is currently phenytoin twice daily. She has been compliant with her medication and has been on the same dose for over 2 years. What is the next best step in her management? (Lange)

options.label: E
options.text: perform an EEG to be sure that these are seizures

questions.initialExplanation: Seizure despite steady treatment: measure the blood phenytoin level.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Children with epilepsy often will outgrow their seizure disorder and be medication free in later life. Some
patients have a progressive neurologic disorder that will require escalating medication doses and the addition
of medications. In a child with increasing seizure frequency who is on a medication, it is important to check the
serum drug level to be sure that it is in a therapeutic range. If the medication is subtherapeutic, it may indicate
noncompliance with the medication or that the dose needs to be increased due to increasing volume of
distribution or changes in metabolism (D). Adding a second agent at this time would not be the next best step
in the management before knowing if the phenytoin level is normal (A, B, C). Performing an EEG is unlikely to
be helpful because you already know that the patient has a seizure disorder and the child’s clinical
presentation is consistent with seizures (E).

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old child presents from home with a temperature of 39°C and seizure activity. The seizure lasts less than 15 minutes. Despite her mother’s aggressive antipyretic administration during the child’s febrile illnesses, this is the girl’s fourth febrile seizure this year. Which of the following drugs can decrease the rate of recurrence of febrile seizures? (Lange)
questions.initialExplanation: Phenobarbital reduces febrile seizure recurrence but is not usually used because of its side effects.
questions.detailedExplanation:
While daily administration of phenobarbital may reduce the recurrence rate for febrile seizures, the
continuous administration of phenobarbital is not necessary or recommended. The therapy does not
prevent the development of epilepsy. In addition, undesirable side effects (rashes, hyperactivity,
irritability, lethargy) are found in at least 20% of patients taking continuous phenobarbital. Phenytoin
has not been shown to be effective. Although valproic acid and phenobarbital are effective, the

potential toxicities outweigh the benefit and their routine use. Intermittent therapy with phenobarbital
is ineffective.

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy presents to the emergency department for evaluation following a witnessed seizure. The seizure was described as generalized, lasting less than 10 minutes with a short postictal period. The child has no history of seizures, no family history of seizures, and no history of head injury. His exam currently is normal, except for a red, bulging right tympanic membrane and a temperature of 39°C. What is the most appropriate management for this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: He should be sent for an urgent CT scan of the head

options.label: B
options.text: He should be given antibiotics and antipyretics and observed at home

options.label: C
options.text: He should be admitted to the hospital and an EEG should be performed

options.label: D
options.text: He should be started on phenobarbital and sent home

options.label: E
options.text: A lumbar puncture and blood cultures should be obtained and anticonvulsants started in the hospital

questions.initialExplanation: Febrile seizure with otitis media: treat the source with an antibiotic plus an antipyretic.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This patient most likely experienced a simple febrile seizure. Most febrile seizures last less than 10
minutes, are generalized and nonfocal, and do not recur within 24 hours. These simple febrile
seizures do not require evaluation beyond determining and treating the source of the fever and
educating parents.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy presents to the emergency department following a generalized tonic-clonic seizure that lasted approximately 2 minutes. His mother reports he has had fever of 39.2°C for the past 24 hours due to an upper respiratory tract infection. He has no history of prior seizures or neurological problems. On examination, he is alert and interactive with no focal deficits. Temperature is 38.8°C with bilateral tympanic membrane erythema. Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.text: Admin intravenous ceftriaxone and perform lumbar puncture

options.label: B
options.text: Perform brain MRI to rule out structural abnormality

options.label: C
options.text: Admit for observation and continuous EEG monitoring

options.label: E
options.text: Discharge home with antipyretics and parent education

questions.initialExplanation: Simple febrile seizure with a clear cause: go home with antipyretics and parent education.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has experienced a simple febrile seizure characterized by generalized tonic-clonic activity lasting less than 15 minutes in a child aged 6 months
to 5 years, with evidence of extra-cranial infection. Simple febrile seizures do not require antibiotics, neuroimaging, EEG, or admission. Management
focuses on treating the underlying fever source and providing comprehensive parent education regarding seizure first aid and when to seek emergency
care. The prognosis is excellent with no increased risk of epilepsy.

- Intravenous ceftriaxone and lumbar puncture are not indicated because there is no clinical suspicion of meningitis. The child is alert, interactive, has no
meningeal signs, and the seizure occurred in the context of a clear febrile illness from otitis media. Lumbar puncture is only mandatory in infants <6
months with fever and seizures, ill-appearing children, or those with clinical meningitis signs. Admission and continuous EEG monitoring are unnecessary
for simple febrile seizures. EEG is not routinely indicated after a first simple febrile seizure as it does not predict recurrence or future epilepsy. The child is
well-appearing and stable for discharge. Long-term antiepileptic medication is not recommended for simple febrile seizures. The American Academy of
Pediatrics and other guidelines explicitly state that continuous or intermittent antiepileptic therapy provides no benefit that outweighs the potential side
effects. Treatment is limited to acute seizure management and parent education. Brain MRI is not indicated in simple febrile seizures. Neuroimaging is
reserved for children with complex febrile seizures (focal features, prolonged duration, recurrence within 24 hours), persistent neurological abnormalities,
or signs of increased intracranial pressure. This child has none of these features.

---

questions.stem: A 14-month-old infant girl is evaluated at her first well-child visit. Her mother reports that her 7-year-old son had multiple febrile seizures during early childhood and is concerned about her daughter's risk. The infant is currently healthy, afebrile, and developmentally normal. The mother asks about preventive measures during febrile illnesses.

options.label: A
options.text: Which statement regarding febrile seizures is most accurate? (MX)

options.label: B
options.text: First-degree relative with febrile seizures increases recurrence risk to 70%

options.label: C
options.text: Febrile seizures are considered a form of epilepsy requiring long-term treatment

options.label: D
options.text: Daily antipyretics during febrile illnesses do not prevent febrile seizures

options.label: E
options.text: The child will definitely develop epilepsy if she has a febrile seizure

questions.initialExplanation: Per the given answer: daily antipyretics, but studies show they do not prevent febrile seizures.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Antipretics reduce fever and discomfort but do not prevent febrile seizure occurrence. Family history
