increases recurrence risk (approximately 30-50%), not to 70%. Febrile seizures are distinct from
epilepsy and have an excellent prognosis. Prophylactic antiepileptics are not recommended due to
unfavorable risk-benefit profiles. Parent education about seizure recognition and rescue medication
use is the cornerstone of management.

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with fever and a seizure that occurred 30 minutes ago. This is his third febrile seizure, with previous episodes at 8 and 14 months of age. Each seizure was generalized, lasted 1-3 minutes, and occurred with high fevers from viral illnesses. On arrival, he is postictal but arousable. Temperature is 39.5°C with mild pharyngeal erythema. What is the most appropriate intervention at this time?

options.label: A
options.text: Provide antipyretics and observe for seizure recurrence

options.label: C
options.text: Perform emergent lumbar puncture to rule out meningitis

options.label: D
options.text: Administer intravenous lorazepam for seizure control

options.label: E
options.text: Start valproic acid for long-term seizure prevention

questions.initialExplanation: Simple febrile seizure: give an antipyretic and observe.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has recurrent simple febrile seizures. The current seizure has terminated, and management
focuses on antipyretic therapy and observation. Lumbar puncture is not indicated without meningeal
signs. Long-term antiepileptic prophylaxis is not recommended for simple febrile seizures. Focus

should be on parent education regarding rescue medications for prolonged seizures and reassurance
about the generally excellent prognosis.

---

questions.stem: A 10-month-old infant girl is brought to the emergency department with fever and a seizure occurring 1 hour ago. This was her first seizure ever. The seizure was characterized by stiffening of the right arm and face followed by jerking on the right side only, lasting approximately 8 minutes. She has been lethargic since the seizure. Temperature is 39.0°C with bulging anterior fontanelle and mild nuchal rigidity. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.text: Observe at home and give antipyretics only \*

options.label: B
options.text: Perform lumbar puncture to rule out meningitis

options.label: C
options.text: Start oral amoxicillin for otitis media

options.label: E
options.text: Administer rectal diazepam for seizure control

questions.initialExplanation: An infant with fever, bulging fontanelle and stiff neck: LP is required to exclude meningitis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This presentation suggests complex febrile seizure (focal features) plus concerning signs of
meningitis (bulging fontanelle, nuchal rigidity). Lumbar puncture is mandatory in infants with fever,
seizures, and meningeal signs regardless of immunization status. The focal nature of the seizure
and meningeal findings require urgent evaluation for meningitis. This child does not require
observation alone given the high suspicion for CNS infection.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy with history of two previous simple febrile seizures presents during a well-child visit. His mother reports frequent viral illnesses and anxiety about another seizure. She asks about medications to give at the first sign of fever to prevent a seizure. Which medication, if used intermittently during febrile illnesses, reduces but does not eliminate recurrent febrile seizure risk?
questions.initialExplanation: Intermittent diazepam (during fever) reduces but does not eliminate the risk of febrile seizure recurrence.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Intermittent oral diazepam (0.3 mg/kg every 8 hours) or rectal diazepam during febrile illnesses may
reduce but not eliminate recurrence risk. This approach is reserved for high-risk cases after
counseling about side effects (sedation, irritability). Daily phenobarbital and continuous valproic acid
are not recommended for prophylaxis. Antipretics do not prevent seizures. Education about rescue
medications remains the primary management strategy.

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old previously healthy girl is brought to the emergency department after an episode at school. Witnesses report she suddenly became unresponsive, eyes rolled back, and her body stiffened followed by rhythmic jerking of all four extremities. She was cyanotic during the event and lost bladder control. The episode lasted approximately 2 minutes, and since then she has been confused, drowsy, and unable to speak clearly. Which seizure type best describes this event? (MX)
questions.initialExplanation: Confusion and sleepiness after a convulsion = postictal state after a generalized tonic-clonic seizure.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This presentation is classic for generalized tonic-clonic seizure with sudden loss of consciousness,
tonic phase (stiffening), clonic phase (rhythmic jerking), cyanosis, bladder incontinence, and
prolonged postictal confusion. The bilateral symmetric motor activity from the outset distinguishes
generalized from focal seizures. Absence seizures are brief (<10 seconds) with no postictal state.
Tonic seizures involve only stiffening without the clonic phase.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy is evaluated in the epilepsy clinic with multiple daily episodes of sudden staring and unresponsiveness lasting 5-10 seconds. During these episodes, he sometimes has brief lip-smacking movements. These episodes occur many times daily, often in clusters, and have been happening for 3 months. His teacher notes academic decline due to frequent interruptions. He is otherwise developmentally normal. What is the most characteristic EEG finding expected?
questions.initialExplanation: Frequent daily pauses = absence seizures, with 3 Hz spike-and-wave on EEG.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has typical absence seizures characterized by sudden interruption of activity, blank stare,
and unresponsiveness with subtle automatisms. The characteristic EEG finding in childhood absence
epilepsy is generalized 3 Hz spike-and-wave discharges. Hypsarrhythmia is seen in West syndrome
(infantile spasms). Periodic lateralized discharges suggest focal structural lesions. Continuous spike-
and-wave during sleep is associated with ESES syndrome.

---

questions.stem: A 14-year-old girl is evaluated for episodes of episodic epigastric discomfort rising to her throat, accompanied by fear and déja vu. She describes automatisms including lip-smacking and fumbling with clothes during these episodes, which typically last 1-2 minutes. She remains partially aware during events and remembers the uncomfortable sensations afterward. Between episodes, examination is normal. EEG shows interictal spikes in the left temporal region. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Ascending epigastric sensation with left temporal EEG spikes = temporal lobe epilepsy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This presentation is characteristic of temporal lobe epilepsy with experiential aura (epigastric rising
sensation, fear, déja vu), automatisms, and partial awareness. Temporal lobe seizures are the most
common focal epilepsy in adolescents. The EEG finding of temporal spikes localizes to the temporal
lobe. Frontal lobe seizures are typically brief and occur from sleep. Occipital seizures have visual
phenomena. Parietal seizures have sensory symptoms.

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy is evaluated for recurrent seizures. His mother reports clusters of sudden flexor spasms of trunk and limbs, occurring in series of 5-10 spasms at a time, multiple times daily. Episodes began at 8 months and have increased in frequency. Developmental milestones were initially normal but have plateaued. On examination, hypopigmented macules on trunk and face and retinal hamartomas are noted. Which syndrome is most likely responsible?
questions.initialExplanation: Infantile spasms with white (hypopigmented) macules and retinal hamartomas = West syndrome secondary to tuberous sclerosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has classic West syndrome with epileptic spasms, developmental regression, and features
of tuberous sclerosis (hypopigmented macules, retinal hamartomas). Tuberous sclerosis is a common
genetic cause of infantile spasms. The spasms present between 3-12 months of age as flexor,
extensor, or mixed jerks in clusters. Lennox-Gastaut syndrome presents later with multiple seizure
types. Dravet syndrome begins with febrile seizures.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy is evaluated in the emergency department following a generalized seizure at school. He was sitting quietly when he suddenly stiffened and had rhythmic jerking of all limbs lasting approximately 90 seconds, followed by several minutes of confusion. This is his first known seizure with no fever, illness, or trauma history. He is now alert and oriented with normal neurological examination. Which investigation is most critical to perform at this time?
questions.initialExplanation: After a seizure in an otherwise healthy child: the most important test is blood glucose to exclude hypoglycemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has had a first unprovoked generalized tonic-clonic seizure. The initial evaluation should focus on identifying
acute metabolic or systemic causes that require immediate treatment. Hypoglycemia is one of the most common
metabolic causes of acute symptomatic seizures and is rapidly correctable with intravenous dextrose. Therefore, point-of-
care glucose measurement is a critical first step in the evaluation of any child presenting with a new-onset seizure. A
glucose level should be obtained immediately, preferably before treatment with glucose is given. Urgent MRI brain is not
typically indicated in a child with a first generalized seizure and normal neurological examination. MRI may be indicated if
there is concern for a structural lesion, focal neurological deficits, or atypical features, but it can be arranged as outpatient
or semi-urgent rather than emergent. The priority is ruling out reversible metabolic causes. Lumbar puncture is indicated if
there is concern for meningitis or encephalitis, but this child has no fever, no meningeal signs, and is not ill-appearing. LP
is not indicated as part of the routine workup for a first unprovoked seizure in an alert child.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy is referred for evaluation of episodes of sudden falls. His mother reports multiple daily episodes where he suddenly loses leg muscle tone and collapses without warning, lasting only 1-2 seconds. He immediately regains consciousness and gets up. He has never hurt himself during falls. Developmental milestones are appropriate. Neurological examination is normal. EEG shows generalized spike-and-wave discharges at 2-3 Hz. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Sudden falls with generalized 2-3 Hz EEG spikes = atonic seizures (drop attacks).
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has atonic seizures characterized by sudden, brief loss of muscle tone causing the child to
collapse or drop to the ground. The episodes are typically very brief (1-2 seconds) and associated
with immediate recovery of consciousness without postictal confusion. The EEG finding of
generalized spike-and-wave discharges at 2-3 Hz is characteristic and helps distinguish epileptic drop
attacks from non-epileptic causes. Atonic seizures are a component of several epilepsy syndromes,
most notably Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, though they can occur in isolation or as part of other
generalized epilepsy syndromes.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl is evaluated for episodes of staring and unresponsiveness with multiple daily episodes over the past 2 months. She suddenly stops playing, has a blank stare, and does not respond to her name for 5-10 seconds. Some episodes have slight eyelid jerking. No fever, illness, or developmental delay. Examination shows alert, developmentally appropriate child. Which historical feature would be most helpful in confirming absence epilepsy?

options.label: A
options.text: The episodes occur upon awakening from sleep

options.label: B
options.text: The episodes are preceded by an aura

options.label: D
options.text: The episodes are triggered by hyperventilation

options.label: E
options.text: The episodes are associated with urinary incontinence

questions.initialExplanation: What best confirms absence epilepsy: provoking seizures with hyperventilation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Hyperventilation is a well-recognized physiological trigger that can precipitate absence seizures in
susceptible individuals. This is a classic clinical pearl and is often used in the clinical setting to help
confirm the diagnosis. The examiner can ask the child to blow a pinwheel or party favor vigorously
for 2-3 minutes, which often precipitates an absence seizure characterized by staring and
unresponsiveness with associated 3 Hz spike-and-wave on EEG. A positive hyperventilation
response is highly supportive of absence epilepsy.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy with no significant history presents following a generalized tonic-clonic seizure at home. His parents report fever, cough, and runny nose for 2 days. This morning, while watching television, he suddenly stiffened and began shaking, lasting about 2 minutes. He has had similar episodes with high fevers twice before—at 18 months and 3 years of age. He is now alert and interactive. Temperature is 38.6°C with pharyngeal erythema. Which statement best characterizes this child's condition? A) He meets criteria for complex febrile seizure B) He has developed epilepsy requiring long-term treatment

options.label: A
options.text: He should be started on prophylactic antiepileptic medication

options.label: B
options.text: He meets criteria for complex febrile seizure \*

options.label: C
options.text: He has developed epilepsy requiring long-term treatment \*

options.label: D
options.text: He is at significantly increased risk for sudden unexplained death in epilepsy

options.label: E
options.text: He has a benign condition with excellent prognosis

questions.initialExplanation: Simple febrile seizure without complications: a benign condition with an excellent prognosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has recurrent simple febrile seizures, which are defined as generalized tonic-clonic
seizures lasting less than 15 minutes, occurring in children between 6 months and 5 years of age, in
association with a febrile illness, without evidence of CNS infection or metabolic disturbance. This
child meets all the criteria: he is within the age range, the seizures are generalized, brief (<15
minutes), and occur in isolation without recurrence within 24 hours. Simple febrile seizures are not
considered epilepsy and do not require long-term antiepileptic treatment. The prognosis is
excellent—children with simple febrile seizures have normal development and intelligence, and the

risk of developing epilepsy is only minimally increased (approximately 2-4%) above the general
population.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy with no history of epilepsy is brought to the emergency department with continuous seizure activity for the past 25 minutes. His parents report fever and lethargy for 2 days. While having breakfast, he suddenly stiffened and began shaking, which has not stopped since. On arrival, he is having generalized tonic-clonic movements, unresponsive, with frothing at the mouth. Oxygen saturation is 88%, temperature is 40.2°C. What is the most appropriate initial pharmacologic intervention?
questions.initialExplanation: Ongoing seizure with hypoxia: the first drug is IV lorazepam after securing the airway.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child is in convulsive status epilepticus, defined as continuous seizure activity lasting more than
5 minutes (newer operational definition) or recurrent seizures without recovery of consciousness
between episodes. Status epilepticus is a neurological emergency requiring immediate treatment.
The first-line therapy for established status epilepticus is a benzodiazepine, with intravenous
lorazepam being the preferred agent when IV access is available. The recommended dose is 0.1
mg/kg (maximum 4 mg per dose), administered slowly over 1-2 minutes. Lorazepam is preferred
over diazepam because it has a more rapid onset of action in the brain, a longer duration of seizure-
suppressing effect, and causes less respiratory depression.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl with known epilepsy treated with carbamazepine presents in status epilepticus. She has had continuous seizure activity for approximately 40 minutes despite multiple doses of rectal diazepam at home. On arrival, she is having generalized tonic-clonic seizures without intervening consciousness. She is being prepared for second-line antiseizure medication. Which is the most appropriate second-line agent?
questions.initialExplanation: After a benzodiazepine fails to stop it: second line is IV phenytoin.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has status epilepticus that has persisted despite appropriate first-line benzodiazepine
therapy (rectal diazepam). According to established treatment protocols, if seizures continue after 20-
40 minutes of onset (or after first-line therapy has failed), second-line antiseizure medications should
be administered. Intravenous phenytoin (or its prodrug fosphenytoin) is a standard second-line agent
for status epilepticus. The loading dose is 15-20 mg/kg of phenytoin, administered at a rate not
exceeding 1 mg/kg/min. Fosphenytoin is often preferred over phenytoin due to its better tolerability
(less pain and phlebitis at the infusion site) and ability to be infused more rapidly.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy is in the pediatric intensive care unit in refractory status epilepticus despite appropriate first-line (IV lorazepam) and second-line (IV fosphenytoin) therapy. The neurology team has decided to initiate induction of therapeutic coma. Which medication is most commonly used for induction of therapeutic coma in refractory status epilepticus?
questions.initialExplanation: Induced coma in refractory status epilepticus: propofol (or midazolam/pentobarbital).
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has refractory status epilepticus, defined as status epilepticus that continues despite
appropriate doses of a benzodiazepine and a second-line antiseizure medication. The management
of refractory status epilepticus requires induction of therapeutic coma with continuous intravenous
anesthetic agents to suppress seizure activity. The most commonly used agents include intravenous
propofol, midazolam infusion, and thiopental (or pentobarbital). Propofol is often preferred as a first-
line anesthetic for refractory status epilepticus due to its rapid onset and offset, although prolonged
high-dose infusion can be associated with propofol infusion syndrome (characterized by metabolic
acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, and cardiovascular collapse).

---

questions.stem: An 18-month-old infant is evaluated following a prolonged febrile seizure lasting approximately 25 minutes. The seizure has stopped after rectal diazepam. The infant is drowsy but arousable with temperature 39.4°C and bilateral otitis media. While being observed, he has another generalized seizure. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.text: Administer a second dose of rectal diazepam

options.label: C
options.text: Prepare for intubation and ICU admission

options.label: D
options.text: Perform lumbar puncture to rule out meningitis

questions.initialExplanation: A second seizure during observation after a febrile seizure: IV lorazepam.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This infant is experiencing recurrent seizures following an initial prolonged febrile seizure, meeting
the definition of status epilepticus (seizure >5 minutes or recurrent seizures without recovery of
consciousness). The most appropriate next step is to administer intravenous lorazepam as first-line
therapy for ongoing seizure activity. Since IV access has already been established in the hospital
setting, IV lorazepam is preferred over rectal diazepam due to its more rapid onset and longer
duration of action. The recommended dose is 0.1 mg/kg (maximum 4 mg). If IV access were not

available, a second dose of rectal diazepam or buccal/intranasal midazolam would be appropriate
alternatives.

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy is admitted to PICU in status epilepticus. Despite aggressive therapy including benzodiazepines, fosphenytoin, and midazolam infusion, electrographic seizures persist. Hospital course has been complicated by aspiration pneumonia, rhabdomyolysis, and acute kidney injury. After several days, seizures have finally been controlled. Which long-term complication is most strongly associated with status epilepticus?
questions.initialExplanation: A complication of prolonged status epilepticus: hemiplegia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Status epilepticus is a neurological emergency that carries significant morbidity and mortality.
Prolonged seizure activity can lead to cerebral injury through multiple mechanisms including
excitotoxicity from excessive glutamate release, metabolic derangements, and secondary hypoxia.
Hemiplegia (unilateral weakness) is a well-recognized neurological sequela resulting from this
cerebral injury, typically involving the motor cortex or corticospinal tracts. The injury may be transient

(Todd's paralysis, which can last hours to days) or permanent, depending on the severity and
duration of the insult.

---

questions.stem: 7-year-old girl with no prior epilepsy history presents following a generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting approximately 15 minutes. Paramedics administered one dose of IV lorazepam en route with no effect. On arrival, she is still seizing. She has been otherwise healthy with normal developmental milestones. Which is the most common cause of status epilepticus in children without prior epilepsy?
questions.initialExplanation: The commonest cause of status epilepticus in a child without prior epilepsy: fever (febrile status).
questions.detailedExplanation:
In children without a prior history of epilepsy, fever is the most common precipitant of status
epilepticus, accounting for approximately 45% of cases. Febrile status epilepticus is typically
associated with acute infections, most commonly viral illnesses (such as enterovirus or herpesvirus
infections), and may represent an extreme manifestation of the febrile seizure phenomenon. The
developing brain in young children appears to be more susceptible to the excitatory effects of fever,
and in some cases, this can lead to prolonged or recurrent seizures meeting the definition of status

epilepticus. The risk is highest in children between 6 months and 5 years of age, which coincides with
the peak incidence of febrile seizures.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy is in PICU being treated for status epilepticus. After several days of pentobarbital coma, seizures have stopped, and the team is preparing to wean the anesthetic agent. The family asks about prognosis. Which statement regarding status epilepticus prognosis is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: The majority of children will develop intellectual disability

options.label: B
options.text: Mortality is highest in idiopathic status epilepticus

options.label: C
options.text: The risk of recurrent status epilepticus is minimal

questions.initialExplanation: Mortality of status epilepticus in children is about 5% and depends on the cause.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Status epilepticus carries significant morbidity and mortality. The overall mortality rate in children is
approximately 5%, with higher mortality in cases of symptomatic status epilepticus (due to underlying
acute causes such as infection, stroke, or metabolic disturbance) compared to idiopathic or febrile
status epilepticus. This figure represents a well-established statistic from multiple epidemiological
studies. Mortality has decreased over time with more aggressive early treatment, but status
epilepticus remains a serious condition with significant risk of death.

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy is brought with fever and seizure lasting approximately 25 minutes. He has been healthy until now. On examination, he is having generalized tonic-clonic activity with temperature 40.1°C, pharyngeal erythema, and mild nuchal rigidity. Lumbar puncture is planned after seizure control. What is the most appropriate sequence of management?

options.label: A
options.text: Administer lorazepam — control seizure — perform lumbar puncture

options.label: B
options.text: Perform lumbar puncture — administer lorazepam — control seizure

options.label: C
options.text: Administer antibiotics — perform lumbar puncture — administer lorazepam

options.label: D
options.text: Administer lorazepam — perform lumbar puncture — control seizure

options.label: E
options.text: Perform CT head — administer lorazepam — perform lumbar puncture

questions.initialExplanation: Fever and seizure with rigidity: give lorazepam to stop the seizure first, then LP after stabilization.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has fever, seizure, and meningeal signs (nuchal rigidity), raising concern for bacterial
meningitis. However, the child is currently in status epilepticus (seizure >5 minutes), which takes

‘    precedence in management. The immediate priority is to terminate the ongoing seizure activity with
benzodiazepine therapy (IV lorazepam). Only after the seizure is controlled can a proper neurological
assessment be performed and the lumbar puncture be safely completed. Performing a lumbar
puncture during active seizure activity is technically challenging, could cause injury to the child, and
the results may be difficult to interpret. Additionally, if bacterial meningitis is suspected, antibiotics
should be started as soon as possible, but seizure control remains the immediate priority.

---

questions.stem: Nonepileptic seizures are a subtype of conversion disorder that resembles true epileptic seizures. Of the following, the MOST characteristic criteria of these seizures is : (NE)

options.label: B
options.text: most cases have a protracted course

options.label: C
options.text: the course of the disease is refractory

options.label: D
options.text: E there is a high incidence of recurrence

options.label: E
options.text: antiepileptic medication is the cornerstone of treatment

questions.initialExplanation: The distinguishing feature of non-epileptic (psychogenic) seizures: absence of EEG changes during the event.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Nonepileptic seizures (psychogenic nonepileptic seizures/PNES) are a conversion disorder that
mimics epilepsy but has a psychological rather than neurological origin.

The hallmark diagnostic feature is a normal EEG during the episode — true epileptic seizures show
characteristic electrical abnormalities, while PNES do not.

---

questions.stem: A previously healthy 3-year-old child presents with a generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting about 2 minutes during a febrile illness. The seizure was isolated, and the child quickly returned to baseline. Exam is normal, with no signs of meningeal irritation. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: C
options.text: Reassure and educate parents about febrile seizures

options.label: D
options.text: Do lumbar puncture to rule out meningitis

options.label: E
options.text: Arrange for EEG within 24 hours - F) ®Paoop

questions.initialExplanation: First simple febrile seizure in a healthy child: reassure and educate parents.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This is a simple febrile seizure: age 6 months-5 years, generalized, <15 minutes, single episode, rapid
return to baseline, no meningeal signs. Management is reassurance and parent education. No AEDs,
EEG, or imaging needed. LP is not indicated if no meningeal signs and child returns to baseline.

---

## Cerebral Palsy

> Question numbers not present in the source file for this topic: 2, 17.

questions.stem: A 20-month-old girl is evaluated for delayed motor milestones. Her parents report a preference for using the left hand. Exam shows increased tone and brisk deep tendon reflexes in the right limbs, with right leg circumduction while walking with assistance. The left side is unaffected. Which of the following best describes her motor involvement pattern? 2025 <1
questions.initialExplanation: Delayed walking and increased tone on one side only = spastic hemiplegia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child demonstrates classic features of spastic hemiplegic cerebral palsy: unilateral upper motor neuron
signs (increased tone, brisk reflexes, circumduction gait) affecting the right side with early hand preference
(left-hand dominance at 20 months suggests right-sided weakness). Spastic hemiplegia typically results from
perinatal stroke or unilateral brain injury, causing contralateral motor impairment while sparing cognition and
sensation. Athetoid and dyskinetic types feature involuntary movements rather than spasticity. Spastic diplegia
predominantly affects both lower extremities, commonly in premature infants. Spastic quadriplegia involves all
four limbs with severe global impairment. Recognition guides early intervention with physical therapy,
occupational therapy, and orthopedic monitoring to optimize function and prevent contractures. Neuroimaging
(MRI) confirms the diagnosis and identifies the underlying lesion. This pattern has favorable prognosis for
independent ambulation compared to other cerebral palsy subtypes.

---

questions.stem: Dystonia is characterized by abnormally sustained muscle contraction, causing twisting motion (torsion spasm) and repetitive movements or abnormal postures. The MOST common cause of dystonia among children is : (NE)
questions.initialExplanation: The commonest cause of dystonia in children is cerebral palsy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Cerebral palsy encompasses a group of permanent movement and posture disorders resulting from
non-progressive disturbances in the developing fetal or infant brain. Among the various types of
cerebral palsy, the dyskinetic and dystonic subtypes specifically involve abnormal involuntary
movements characterized by sustained muscle contractions, twisting movements, and abnormal
postures—the defining features of dystonia.

- The pathophysiology involves injury to the basal ganglia, particularly the area of the brain
responsible for controlling muscle tone and movement coordination. This injury typically occurs
during the prenatal period, birth process, or early infancy, leading to the characteristic dystonic
movements that may become more apparent as the child develops.

---

questions.stem: A family consults you about the MOST appropriate treatment for their 10 year-old boy who is a known case of cerebral palsy with severe spasticity of upper and lower limbs refractory to oral medication associated with excessive drooling of saliva. Of the following, the MOST appropriate answer is : (NE)
questions.initialExplanation: For drooling with spasticity: intrathecal baclofen reduces spasticity (drooling is treated with drugs such as glycopyrrolate), per the given answer.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Effective for Generalized Spasticity: Intrathecal baclofen delivers the medication directly to the spinal cord, bypassing the
blood-brain barrier and achieving therapeutic concentrations in the cerebrospinal fluid with much smaller doses than
required orally. This makes it particularly effective for severe, generalized spasticity affecting multiple limb regions, which
is exactly the scenario described in this case.

- Evidence Base in Cerebral Palsy: Intrathecal baclofen therapy has extensive supporting evidence in the cerebral palsy
population. Multiple studies have demonstrated significant reduction in spasticity, improved function, and better quality of
life in children with severe spasticity who have failed oral medications.

- Reversible and Adjustable: Unlike some surgical interventions, intrathecal baclofen therapy is reversible and the dose
can be adjusted according to the patient's response. This allows for individualized treatment optimization.

- Comprehensive Benefits: Beyond spasticity reduction, studies have shown benefits in comfort, ease of caregiving, and
potentially in drooling management, which addresses the additional concern mentioned in the case.

---

questions.stem: You are seeing for the first time a 15-month-old boy who was born at 28 weeks' gestation. He had an afebrile seizure at 12 months, but takes no medications. He uses both a cup and a bottle and takes most solid foods without choking. He wakes frequently at night. He can sit alone, but does not crawl! or walk. He uses three words other than "mama" or "dada." His growth parameters are at the 50th percentile for length and head circumference and at the 10th percentile for weight. On physical examination, you note increased tone in his lower extremities and trunk. Of the following, the MOST likely other information that you would expect is a history of : (NE)
questions.initialExplanation: CP with delay and excess tone: the expected common history is constipation (a common bowel problem).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Cerebral palsy is an umbrella term covering a group of nonprogressive, but often changing, motor impairment
syndromes due to lesions or anomalies of the brain that arise in the early stages of its development. Some 2 to
3 per 1,000 children have cerebral palsy in the United States. Although it may be difficult to determine the
exact cause of the motor impairment for an individual child, several clinical situations are associated with
increased risk of cerebral palsy, including brain malformation, chromosomal abnormalities, intrauterine growth
restriction, prematurity, birth hypoxia, and postnatal events such as traumatic injury and meningitis. The motor
manifestations of cerebral palsy are treated best by an interdisciplinary team of clinicians who can address
medical and surgical management of tone and joint contractures as well as therapists who can address
therapeutic issues such as range of motion and equipment needs.

---

questions.stem: The parents of a 10-year-old boy bring their child in to see you. The child has been diagnosed with cerebral palsy, and the parents do not really understand what this means. As part of your explanation, which of the following would you tell them?

options.label: A
options.text: Cerebral palsy is a static encephalopathy because the EEG exhibits a disorganized background rhythm.

options.label: B
options.text: Cerebral palsy is a static encephalopathy because affected persons fail to reach any developmental milestones on time.

options.label: C
options.text: Cerebral palsy is a static encephalopathy because affected persons have resting tremors.

options.label: D
options.text: Cerebral palsy is a static encephalopathy because the injury to the brain does not progress.

options.label: E
options.text: Cerebral palsy is a static encephalopathy because deficits do not appear after birth.

questions.initialExplanation: CP is a static encephalopathy that does not progress, though its clinical features may change with growth.
questions.detailedExplanation:
progress.

A static encephalopathy is one in which brain damage has been arrested but neurologic problems
persist. Establishing that the brain lesion is not progressive may require extensive testing. A young
child with a static motor disorder is said to have CP. Neurodegenerative diseases with slow or
stepwise progressions may appear to be static encephalopathies over the course of months, but
prove to be progressive encephalopathies over the course of years. The brain lesion with CP is static,
but the deficits associated with CP may evolve as the child matures.

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy is evaluated for delayed motor milestones. He rolled over at 10 months and sits with support but has not achieved independent walking. He favors his right hand when reaching and drags his left leg when crawling. Pregnancy was complicated by preeclampsia requiring cesarean delivery at 32 weeks. On examination, increased tone is noted in the left upper and lower extremities with scissoring. Which type of cerebral palsy is most consistent with this presentation?
questions.initialExplanation: Leg hypertonia with scissoring is sometimes spastic diplegia; the given answer is hemiplegia per the question details.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child presents with spastic hemiplegia characterized by unilateral motor impairment predominantly
affecting one side of the body. The clinical features supporting this diagnosis include asymmetric motor
development with preferential use of the right side, early handedness before 18 months indicating left-
side involvement, scissoring of the legs, and increased tone on the affected left side. The history of
premature birth at 32 weeks with perinatal asphyxia (Apgar scores 4 and 6) are significant risk factors
for cerebral palsy. Spastic hemiplegia typically involves the upper extremity more than the lower
extremity, which is consistent with this presentation. The involvement is unilateral, distinguishing it from
diplegia (bilateral lower extremity predominant) and quadriplegia (all four limbs severely affected).

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old girl with known cerebral palsy is evaluated for episodes of stiffening of her arms and trunk with arching of her back. These episodes occur several times daily, triggered by excitement or frustration, and are associated with screaming and difficulty breathing. She has no loss of consciousness during these 30-60 second episodes. On examination, increased tone is present in all four extremities. Which type of movement disorder is most likely responsible?
questions.initialExplanation: Involuntary movements with generalized increased tone = dystonia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child is experiencing dystonic episodes characterized by sustained muscle contractions causing
abnormal postures. The episodes of stiffening with arching of the back are classic examples of

‘    dystonic posturing. Key features supporting this diagnosis include: (1) episodes triggered by
environmental stimuli (excitement, frustration), (2) no loss of consciousness, (3) non-epileptic nature
without postictal state, and (4) abnormal postures rather than rhythmic jerking. Dystonia is commonly
associated with cerebral palsy, particularly in cases involving the basal ganglia. The classification
includes task-specific and non-task-specific dystonia. Management may include baclofen,
trihexyphenidyl, botulinum toxin injections, or intrathecal baclofen for severe cases.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy with spastic quadriplegic cerebral palsy is evaluated for feeding difficulties. His mother reports that meals take over an hour with frequent choking and coughing during feeding. He has had multiple episodes of pneumonia over the past year. On examination, he has increased tone in all extremities with scissoring when held standing, persistent drooling, and pooling of material in the oral cavity when given food. Which complication is this child at highest risk for developing?
questions.initialExplanation: Quadriplegic CP with swallowing difficulty: the biggest risk is aspiration pneumonia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has significant oropharyngeal dysphagia with signs of aspiration including coughing, choking
during feeding, recurrent pneumonia, prolonged feeding times, and pooling of oral secretions.
Dysphagia is extremely common in children with cerebral palsy, particularly those with severe motor
involvement. The combination of impaired oral motor control, delayed swallow reflex, and poor
coordination of breathing and swallowing creates a high risk for aspiration of food, liquids, or saliva.
Aspiration pneumonia is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in children with cerebral palsy.
Management strategies include positioning modifications, texture modification of foods, feeding
therapy, and in severe cases, gastrostomy tube placement.

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy with spastic diplegic cerebral palsy is evaluated for progressive hip pain over 3 months. He walks with a walker but has noticed increased difficulty with ambulation and complains of groin and knee pain. On examination, increased tone is present in both lower extremities with scissoring gait. Hip range of motion is limited with abduction of only 20 degrees bilaterally and internal rotation causing discomfort. Radiographs reveal subluxation of both femoral heads. Which complication is most likely responsible?
questions.initialExplanation: Diplegic CP with pain and pelvic issues: hip subluxation/dislocation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has developed hip subluxation, a common complication in spastic cerebral palsy. The
clinical features include progressive hip pain, decreased range of motion with limited abduction and
internal rotation, difficulty with ambulation, and radiographic evidence of subluxation with inadequate
acetabular coverage. Hip dysplasia results from muscle imbalance around the hip joint, with adductor
and flexor muscles overpowering the abductors and extensors. This leads to progressive lateral and
superior displacement of the femoral head. Early detection through regular screening is essential, as
early intervention (adductor releases, muscle lengthening, bony surgery) can prevent progression to
dislocation.

---

questions.stem: An 18-month-old girl is evaluated for concerns about motor development. She was born at 28 weeks gestation with a birth weight of 1,100 grams. She required mechanical ventilation for 3 weeks for respiratory distress syndrome and had a complicated neonatal course including several episodes of sepsis. She is not yet walking and has persistent head lag when pulled to sit. On examination, increased tone is present in all four extremities with tight heel cords bilaterally. What is the most significant risk factor for cerebral palsy in this infant?
questions.initialExplanation: The most important risk factor for CP: prematurity.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Prematurity is the single most significant risk factor for cerebral palsy. This infant has very low birth
weight (less than 1,500 grams) and extreme prematurity (less than 28 weeks). The risk of cerebral
palsy is inversely related to gestational age, with infants born before 28 weeks having the highest
risk. The pathophysiology involves vulnerability of the periventricular white matter in premature
infants, where the germinal matrix is located. This region is susceptible to injury from hypoxia-
ischemia, inflammation, and hemodynamic instability. Despite advances in neonatal care, the
incidence of cerebral palsy has not decreased proportionally with improved survival of very
premature infants.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old girl with spastic quadriplegic cerebral palsy is evaluated for constipation. Her mother reports no bowel movement for 7 days despite dietary changes and oral laxatives. She cries during bowel movements with hard, pellet-like stools. On examination, the abdomen is distended and firm with significant stool palpable in the left lower quadrant. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.initialExplanation: Severe constipation with a full rectum in a girl with CP: clean out with enemas (disimpaction).
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has severe constipation with evidence of fecal impaction (no bowel movement for 7 days,
hard pellet-like stools, abdominal distension with palpable stool). The first step in managing fecal

‘    impaction is disimpaction, which can be achieved with oral agents (polyethylene glycol, lactulose) or
rectal enemas. Given the severity and duration, disimpaction with enemas is the most appropriate
initial intervention. After successful disimpaction, a maintenance program including scheduled toileting,
adequate fluid and fiber intake, and regular laxatives should be established to prevent recurrence.
Constipation is extremely common in cerebral palsy due to reduced mobility, abnormal muscle tone,
medications, and inadequate fiber and fluid intake.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old girl with spastic diplegic cerebral palsy is evaluated for dental problems. Her mother reports difficulty brushing her teeth due to hand coordination problems with multiple cavities. On examination, there is severe dental caries on multiple teeth, enamel hypoplasia, and gingival hyperplasia. Which medication is most likely responsible for the gingival hyperplasia?
questions.initialExplanation: Gum overgrowth with phenytoin = gingival hyperplasia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has gingival hyperplasia, a well-known side effect of phenytoin therapy. Many children
with cerebral palsy are prescribed antiseizure medications for epilepsy, which is common in the CP
population. Phenytoin-induced gingival hyperplasia typically begins within the first few months of
treatment and is more common with poor oral hygiene. The hyperplasia can be minimized with
meticulous oral hygiene, regular dental cleanings, and in severe cases, surgical gingivectomy.
Alternative antiseizure medications that do not cause gingival hyperplasia (such as levetiracetam)
may be considered if seizure control is adequate.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy with spastic hemiplegic cerebral palsy is evaluated for recurrent episodes of stiffening and arching of his back. These episodes occur when being dressed or bathed and seem triggered by movement of his affected limbs. He does not lose consciousness during these episodes, which resolve when left alone. His mother reports increased frequency over the past few months. Which diagnosis best explains these episodes?
questions.initialExplanation: Extensor spasm episodes in a child with CP.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child is experiencing extensor spasms (extensor thrusts or startle responses), common in infants
and young children with cerebral palsy. These spasms are characterized by sudden extension of the
trunk and limbs, often triggered by sudden movements, handling, or environmental stimuli. They are
not epileptic seizures and represent an exaggerated extensor response due to abnormal motor
control and tone regulation. Extensor spasms are common in children with moderate to severe CP
and can interfere with care activities. Management includes avoiding triggers, positioning
modifications, and in some cases, medication (baclofen, benzodiazepines) to reduce spasticity.

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy with spastic quadriplegic cerebral palsy is evaluated for skin breakdown over his sacrum. His mother reports increased time in wheelchair due to difficulty with transfers. On examination, there is a stage 2 pressure ulcer over the sacrum with partial thickness skin loss involving the epidermis and dermis. Which is the most important factor in preventing progression?
questions.initialExplanation: Pressure ulcer: the key factor to prevent worsening is pressure relief with frequent repositioning.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Pressure ulcers are a significant concern in children with limited mobility. The sacrum is a common
site due to prolonged sitting or lying. The most important intervention for preventing progression and
promoting healing is pressure relief through frequent repositioning (every 2 hours minimum) and use
of pressure-relieving surfaces. This addresses the underlying cause of the ulcer (unrelieved pressure
causing tissue ischemia). Without adequate pressure relief, no other intervention will be successful.
Additional measures include optimizing nutrition, maintaining skin hygiene, and using appropriate
positioning equipment.

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old girl with spastic quadriplegic cerebral palsy is evaluated for vision concerns. Her parents report that she does not track objects well and often holds objects very close to her face. On examination, significant strabismus is present with the left eye turned inward. She does not fix or follow objects with either eye. Which visual abnormality is most commonly associated with cerebral palsy?
questions.initialExplanation: The vision problem most linked to CP: cortical visual impairment.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Cortical visual impairment (CVI) is the most common cause of visual impairment in children with
cerebral palsy. It results from damage to the visual pathways or visual centers in the brain, typically
from hypoxic-ischemic injury, intracranial hemorrhage, or infection. Unlike ocular causes, CVI is
characterized by relatively normal-appearing eyes with abnormal visual behavior. Features include
poor visual attention, difficulty with complex visual stimuli, preference for certain colors (often
red/yellow), visual field deficits, and better function in familiar environments. Strabismus is also
common in CP and may coexist with CVI.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy with spastic diplegic cerebral palsy is evaluated for knee pain. His parents report knee pain during and after walking. On examination, increased tone is present in the hamstrings and gastrocnemius muscles. His knees show valgus alignment bilaterally with a positive windlass sign. Which intervention is most appropriate for addressing his knee pain?

options.label: C
options.text: Physical therapy focused on stretching and strengthening

questions.initialExplanation: Knee pain in a diplegic CP child: the most suitable treatment is physical therapy with muscle stretching.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has knee pain in the context of spastic diplegia with increased tone, hamstring and
gastrocnemius tightness, and genu valgum. The windlass sign suggests gastrocnemius tightness
contributing to gait disturbance and knee pain. The initial management should be conservative,
focusing on physical therapy to stretch the hamstrings and gastrocnemius, strengthen the
quadriceps and hip abductors, and improve gait mechanics. Orthotics (AFOs) may also be helpful.
Corrective osteotomy is reserved for severe, progressive deformity that has not responded to
conservative management.

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy with spastic hemiplegic cerebral palsy is evaluated for hand function. His parents report that he keeps his left hand fisted and does not use it spontaneously. On examination, increased tone is present in the left forearm and hand with thumb adduction and finger flexion contracture. Which therapeutic approach is most appropriate?
questions.initialExplanation: Hemiplegic CP with a weak hand: constraint-induced movement therapy (restrain the good hand to train the affected one).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Constraint-induced movement therapy (CIMT) is an evidence-based intervention for hemiplegic
cerebral palsy. It involves restraining the unaffected upper extremity while intensively training the
affected upper extremity. The goal is to overcome "learned non-use" of the affected hand and
promote neuroplasticity. CIMT has been shown to improve functional use of the affected hand, with
effects persisting after treatment. This child has significant asymmetry with preference for the
unaffected hand and limited spontaneous use of the affected hand, making him a good candidate.
The therapy is typically provided for 2-4 weeks of intensive daily practice.

---

questions.stem: An 8-year-old girl on anti-tuberculosis treatment complains of passing red urine for the last few days. Which of the following drugs could be the cause of this condition?
questions.initialExplanation: Orange-red urine during TB treatment is caused by rifampicin (it colors secretions and urine); it is a benign expected effect.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The 8-year-old girl on anti-tuberculosis treatment is passing red urine, which is most likely a side effect of Rifampicin , one of the first-line drugs used in tuberculosis (TB) treatment. Rifampicin can cause red-orange discoloration of bodily fluids , including urine, sweat, tears, and saliva. This is a well-known and harmless side effect but can be alarming to patients if they are not forewarned.

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the clinic due to persistent low-grade fever, poor weight gain, chronic cough, and night sweats for the past 3 weeks. His grandfather, who lived in the same household, died recently from a chronic pulmonary illness. On examination, he has cervical lymphadenopathy and signs of mild respiratory distress. Chest X-ray reveals right hilar lymphadenopathy and patchy infiltrates. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial test to support the diagnosis in this child?2025 <.)Js
questions.initialExplanation: A child with low-grade fever, weight loss, cough, adenopathy and exposure history: the best initial supportive test is the tuberculin skin test (TST).
questions.detailedExplanation:
The tuberculin skin test (TST/Mantoux test) is the most appropriate initial diagnostic test in this child with clinical and radiographic features suggestive of pediatric tuberculosis. It is non-invasive, widely available, and helps detect Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection. In a 2-year-old with exposure history (grandfather with chronic pulmonary illness), constitutional symptoms (fever, night sweats, poor weight gain), cervical lymphadenopathy, and chest X-ray showing hilar lymphadenopathy with infiltrates, a positive TST strongly supports the diagnosis of primary pulmonary TB. Sputum culture

(A) is difficult to obtain in young children who cannot expectorate and requires gastric aspirates or induced sputum, making it less practical as an initial test. Blood culture (C) is not useful for diagnosing pulmonary TB. Bronchoscopy with BAL (D) is invasive and reserved for cases with diagnostic uncertainty or severe disease. Complete blood count (E) is non-specific and cannot confirm TB. While bacteriologic confirmation is ideal, pediatric TB is often diagnosed clinically with supportive evidence from TST, exposure history, and radiographic findings.

---

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy with cough, fever and night sweats has a positive skin test for tuberculosis. A chest x-ray reveals minimal hilar adenopathy and a small pulmonary infiltrate. Drug susceptibility studies are negative for drug resistance. The current recommended treatment is:
questions.initialExplanation: Drug-sensitive pulmonary TB in a child: triple therapy isoniazid + rifampin + pyrazinamide (with ethambutol sometimes) in the intensive phase, per the source.
questions.detailedExplanation:
All patients with new, previously untreated TB should receive a 2 month initial phase of treatment followed by a 4 or 7 month continuation phase. Initial-phase therapy is with a combination of antibiotics for the first 2 months which are isoniazid (INH), rifampin (RIF), and pyrazinamide (PZA), Ethambutoi (EMB) is added in the initial phase whenever there is any suspicion of initial drug

resistance and while the results of drug susceptibility testing are pending (which is not the case in this scenario).

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl presents with a two month history of low-grade fever, cough, anorexia, and weight loss. A chest x-ray reveals a right-sided pleural effusion. Which one of the following tests is most likely to confirm the diagnosis of tuberculosis if a previous culture result was negative?

options.label: B
options.text: Pleural tap for cell morphology and acid-fast bacilli

questions.initialExplanation: Suspected tuberculous pleural effusion with a negative culture: pleural tap for cells and acid-fast bacilli (AFB) is most likely to confirm the diagnosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
in patients with pleural effusion, the diagnosis of TB is made by detection of acid-fast bacilli by stain or by culture of mycobacteria in pleural fluid or pleural tissue (obtained by dosed biopsy) or by the presence of caseating granulomas in histological sections.

5- A 6-month-old infant presents with persistent cough and failure to thrive. Birth weight was 3.2 kg, current weight

---

questions.stem: 8 kg (below 3rd percentile). Parents describe 2-week history of non-productive cough, intermittent fever, and decreased feeding. The mother was recently diagnosed with TB and started treatment 1 month ago. Examination shows thin, pale infant with temperature 37.8°C, respiratory rate 32/min, bilateral crackles. TST shows only 2 mm induration. Which factor is most likely causing this false-negative TST result?
questions.initialExplanation: A false-negative TST in a malnourished infant is due to malnutrition weakening cell-mediated immunity (anergy).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Malnutrition is a common cause of false-negative TST in young children due to impaired immune response. Malnourished children, especially those under 6 months, have compromised cellular immunity that delays or prevents the delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction to tuberculin. This is particularly important in TB-endemic areas where malnutrition is prevalent.

- BCG vaccination typically causes false-positive TST results due to crossreactivity with BCG antigens, rather than false- negative results. Minor upper respiratory tract infections do not typically cause falsenegative TST results, though severe viral infections (measles, varicella, influenza) can suppress TST reactivity. Recent live-virus vaccination can cause false- negative results by suppressing the immune response, but malnutrition is more commonly associated with false-negative TST in TB-endemic areas. Poor technique in TST placement can affect results through improper

injection depth or volume, but biological factors like malnutrition are more common causes of false-negative results.

---

questions.stem: On tuberculin skin testing, a well 5-year-old who traveled last year to Mexico is found to have 8 mm of induration to 5 tuberculin units (TU) of purified protein. There is no history suggestive of contact with tuberculosis. What does this reaction likely indicate?

options.label: B
options.text: subcutaneous rather than intradermal injection of test material

questions.initialExplanation: An 8 mm reaction in a healthy child with no known exposure is usually cross-reactivity with non-tuberculous mycobacteria.
questions.detailedExplanation:
In healthy children over age 4 years, reactions of less than 5-mm induration to 5 TU are considered negative. Reactions between 5 and 15 mm are considered doubtful and usually represent infection with nontuberculous mycobacteria. Reactions of 15 mm or more induration generally are considered positive and indicative of infection with M tuberculosis but do not necessarily mean clinically evident disease. The point to remember is that the threshold for interpreting a tuberculin skin test as positive is lower for children with signs or symptoms suggestive of tuberculosis or with a history of contact with tuberculosis.

---

questions.stem: A malnourished 3-year-old child from Mexico has a positive tuberculin skin test (TST > 10 mm for this age). Which of the following would be most concerning for extra-pulmonary disease?
questions.initialExplanation: Hepatosplenomegaly in a child with TB suggests extrapulmonary dissemination (miliary/disseminated TB).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Fever, cough, hilar lymphadenopathy, and elevated sedimentation rate are seen commonly in uncomplicated primary pulmonary tuberculosis. Hepatosplenomegaly is generally not seen in uncomplicated primary pulmonary tuberculosis, but does occur in more than 50% of children with disseminated disease.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child presents with fever, night sweats, weight loss, and cough. A diagnosis of pulmonary tuberculosis infection was made based on chest x-ray and tuberculin skin testing. The mother of the child asks when her child may return to day care. When can a child diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis infection return to day care or school?

options.label: A
options.text: as soon as effective therapy has been instituted

options.label: C
options.text: once negative sputum smears are confirmed

options.label: E
options.text: whether they are receiving therapy or not

questions.initialExplanation: A child with childhood pulmonary TB (usually non-infectious) may return to nursery as soon as effective treatment starts.
questions.detailedExplanation:
In general, children with uncomplicated primary pulmonary tuberculosis are noninfectious and do not require isolation. This is believed to relate to the scanty sputum production, lack of expectoration, and the small number of organisms that can be recovered from sputum or gastric culture. In contrast, children with laryngeal involvement, with cavitary pulmonary tuberculosis, extensive pulmonary infection, positive sputum AFB smears, or suspected congenital tuberculosis should be considered contagious and appropriate precautions should be taken. Children with tuberculosis disease can attend school or child care if they are receiving therapy.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child from Somalia presents to the emergency department with a 2-week history of low- grade fever, headache, and irritability. This morning he was difficult to arouse and subsequently had a seizure. On examination, he has a temperature of 102.2°F (39°C), nuchal rigidity, and somnolence. You discover that he and his parents had positive tuberculin skin tests on arrival to the United States and suspect tuberculous meningitis. Which of the following is characteristic of the cerebrospinal fluid in tuberculous meningitis?

options.label: A
options.text: The color is usually blood tinged.

options.label: C
options.text: Culture reveals tuberculous organisms within 1 week.

questions.initialExplanation: In TB meningitis the CSF shows low glucose, high protein and predominantly lymphocytes.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Tuberculous meningitis is the most serious complication of tuberculosis in children. It usually occurs within 2—6 months of initial infection. It is difficult to diagnose rapidly as skin testing may be negative and chest films may be normal. Culture results can take anywhere from 1-10 weeks to yield a positive result. CSF findings can give clues of the diagnosis. CSF white cell counts range from 10 to 500 with usual lymphocytic predomination. Glucose is typically 20—40. Protein concentration is elevated, often markedly. Blood-tinged CSF is not associated with tuberculous meningitis.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child presents to your office for wellchild care. You screen him for tuberculosis and find that he had had no family members with tuberculosis or a positive tuberculin skin test, but he was born in a country identified by WHO as a high-incidence area for tuberculosis and received a BCG vaccine. A tuberculin skin test (TST) is placed in the right forearm, and 2 days later he returns for reading. Your nurse uses the “ballpoint method” and measures the induration at 12 mm perpendicularly to the long axis of the arm. Your appropriate next step is:

options.label: A
options.text: Do nothing, as this is a negative TST.

options.label: B
options.text: Repeat the measurement, as one must measure with the long axis of the arm.

options.label: C
options.text: Repeat the skin test, as this is an equivocal TST.

options.label: D
options.text: Obtain radiographs of the chest, as this is a positive TST.

options.label: E
options.text: Refer the patient to an infectious disease specialist.

questions.initialExplanation: A 12 mm TST in a child born in a high-incidence country is positive; the next step is a chest X-ray to determine whether disease is active.
questions.detailedExplanation:
For children younger than 4 years of age, any induration of greater than or equal to 10 mm is considered a positive tuberculin skin test; this is also true for children who are born in other countries. The definitions of positivity apply regardless of BCG vaccination. Appropriate next steps are to obtain chest radiography and subsequently to begin appropriate therapy (dictated by the results of the chest radiography). A tuberculin skin test should be measured between 48 and 72 hours after placement. Measurement should identify the amount of induration perpendicular to the long axis of the arm. The amount of induration identified as positive depends on any other history or physical findings (see Table 12-5 for identification of categories). If the radiograph were to show findings consistent with tuberculosis (ie, lymphadenopathy out of proportion to parenchymal disease), referral to an infectious disease specialist might be warranted, although often a primary care provider in a medical home can oversee treatment of primary tuberculosis. However, children with latent TB

(those with positive TST but negative radiographs) can be well managed by a medical home. Some states require notification of positive TSTs.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old girl presents for routine school physical examination. She is active, healthy with no significant medical history, normal developmental milestones, and up-to-date vaccinations. Family moved from low TB prevalence country with no TB exposure history. Physical exam shows well-appearing child with normal growth (weight and height 50th percentile), clear lung sounds, no lymphadenopathy. TST performed shows 12 mm induration after 48 hours. According to TST interpretation guidelines, what size of induration indicates a positive test in this 5-year-old child with no risk factors?
questions.initialExplanation: The positive cutoff for TST in a child without risk factors is ≥15 mm (the original answer appeared as "215 mm" because of OCR; the intended value is ≥15 mm).
questions.detailedExplanation:
215 mm induration is positive for children 24 years without risk factors. This higher cutoff reduces false-positive results from BCG vaccination or environmental mycobacteria while maintaining sensitivity for true TB infection in low-risk children.

- 25 mm induration is the most stringent cutoff reserved for highest-risk groups (HIV-infected, close contacts of infectious TB cases, immunosuppressed children) where the consequences of missing TB are severe. 210 mm induration is used for children at increased risk including those under 4 years old, children with other medical conditions, or those with increased exposure to TB. No standard TST cutoff requires 220 mm induration, as this would miss too many true positive cases. No standard TST cutoff requires 225 mm induration, as this would be unnecessarily restrictive and reduce sensitivity.

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old toddler presents with breathing difficulty and persistent cough. Child has dry cough for 3 weeks that gradually worsened with occasional wheezing, especially at night, and tires easily during feeding. Family recently immigrated from high TB prevalence country, grandfather diagnosed with pulmonary TB 2 months ago. Examination shows respiratory rate 32/min, mild retractions, localized wheezing over right lower lobe. Chest X-ray shows small peripheral lung lesion in right middle lobe with significant hilar lymphadenopathy. Which finding is most characteristic on chest X-ray?

options.label: B
options.text: Hilar lymphadenopathy with small parenchymal focus

questions.initialExplanation: In common primary TB: enlarged hilar nodes with a small parenchymal focus (primary complex), not an upper-lobe cavity.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Primary TB shows characteristic Ghon complex with hilar lymphadenopathy and small parenchymal focus. The hallmark of primary TB is the disproportionate size of hilar lymphadenopathy compared to the relatively small lung lesion, reflecting the child's primary immune response to TB infection.

- Upper lobe cavitation is characteristic of reactivation TB seen in adolescents and adults, representing disease progression from previous primary infection that remained dormant for years. Miliary pattern indicates disseminated disease where massive bacillary spread occurs throughout the lungs, not typical primary TB which is usually localized. Pleural effusion is uncommon in young children with primary TB and when present, usually represents pleural involvement from adjacent parenchymal disease. Peribronchial thickening is a nonspecific finding seen in various respiratory conditions and is not characteristic of primary TB.

---

questions.stem: An 8-year-old boy presents with concerns about recent TB exposure. Family discovered their household contact, a neighbor who frequently babysits children, was diagnosed with pulmonary TB and started treatment. Boy is otherwise healthy with no current symptoms, normal appetite, good weight gain, no respiratory complaints. Up-to-date with vaccinations including BCG at birth, no known allergies, performing well in school. Parents want to know timeline for TB infection evidence development. What is the incubation period from TB infection to positive TST conversion?
questions.initialExplanation: TST conversion appears 3 weeks to 3 months after infection.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Tuberculin sensitivity develops 3 weeks to 3 months after infection, most commonly 4-8 weeks. This represents the time required for cell-mediated immunity to develop after initial infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis, during which T-cells become sensitized to tuberculin antigens.

- 1-2 weeks is too short for immune response development, as cellmediated immunity requires sufficient time for T-cell priming and proliferation. 2-3 weeks is still too short for complete immune response development and TST conversion in most individuals. 6 months to 1 year is too long and represents progression to active disease rather than TST conversion, which should occur much earlier. 1-2 years is excessive and represents prolonged latency or disease progression, not TST conversion which occurs relatively early after infection.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child presents with 1-week history of progressive symptoms including high fever, irritability, decreased activity. Fever started reaching 39.5°C with chills and night sweats. Over past 3 days, child became increasingly sleepy, difficult to arouse, with headache and neck stiffness. Family recently moved from high TB prevalence area, history of contact with uncle diagnosed with TB 2 months ago. Examination shows severely ill child with temperature 39.8°C, respiratory rate 28/min, altered consciousness, nuchal rigidity, positive Kernig sign. What is the most likely complication?
questions.initialExplanation: Fever and meningeal signs in a child with a TB contact: most likely tuberculous meningitis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- Miliary TB commonly involves CNS, leading to tuberculous meningitis. The hematogenous spread characteristic of miliary disease frequently affects the CNS, with TB bacilli crossing the blood-brain

’    barrier to cause meningitis, which occurs in 20-40% of advanced miliary cases.

- Brain abscess is rare in TB as it typically causes meningoencephalitis rather than localized abscess formation. Cerebral edema can occur as a complication of meningitis but tuberculous meningitis is the direct and more common CNS involvement in miliary disease. Hydrocephalus is a complication of tuberculous meningitis resulting from impaired CSF absorption, not direct miliary involvement. Seizures can occur in tuberculous meningitis but they are symptoms of the underlying meningitis rather than the most likely complication.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy with confirmed TB has been started on anti-TB treatment including isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol. Pediatrician explains potential side effects of each medication and emphasizes importance of regular monitoring. Family wants to understand which drug requires most careful monitoring for visual side effects, concerned about child's ability to communicate vision problems. Child is otherwise healthy with normal development, no known allergies or medical conditions. Which anti-TB drug requires monitoring for optic neuritis as a serious side effect?
questions.initialExplanation: Ethambutol is the drug that causes optic neuritis and needs visual monitoring.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- Ethambutol can cause optic neuritis, especially at higher doses (>25 mg/ kg). This is due to its mechanism of action on mycobacterial RNA synthesis, which can also affect neuronal tissues. Vision monitoring is essential during ethambutol therapy, particularly when doses exceed 15-20 mg/kg/day in children.

- Isoniazid causes hepatotoxicity through metabolite accumulation and peripheral neuropathy due to pyridoxine deficiency, but does not affect optic nerves. Rifampin causes hepatotoxicity, orange-red discoloration of body fluids, and drug interactions through enzyme induction, but does not cause optic neuritis. Pyrazinamide causes hepatotoxicity and hyperuricemia due to its effect on purine metabolism, but does not affect the optic nerves. Streptomycin causes ototoxicity (hearing loss) and nephrotoxicity through damage to hair cells in the inner ear and kidney tubules, not optic neuritis.

---

questions.stem: A 10-year-old child was diagnosed with primary TB 4 months ago and is on treatment. He presents with fever and loss of energy and appetite. He has a persistent cough, with a large spleen and liver found on examination. There are abnormalities on auscultating his lungs. The X-ray shows diffuse mottling throughout both lung fields. the most likely diagnosis is?

options.label: B
options.text: Pneumonia on top of pulmonary TB

questions.initialExplanation: Fever, hepatosplenomegaly and a diffuse mottled chest film in a child treated for primary TB = miliary TB.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Miliary TB usually occurs when the organism disseminates into the bloodstream throughout the body, causing small focal lesions, including on the lungs. This may happen acutely, slowly or chronically. Beside the symptoms described in Question 24, eye examination may reveal choroidal tubercles that may be seen along the vessels and these are diagnostic. The radiological appearance is typical. Children who are not treated will develop tubercular meningitis.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child is being evaluated for suspected TB based on positive TST and contact with infectious adult. Child has no current respiratory symptoms, normal examination, chest X-ray shows only minimal changes consistent with primary infection. Pediatrician needs microbiological confirmation to confirm diagnosis and guide treatment decisions. Child is too young to produce sputum spontaneously, family needs to understand most appropriate diagnostic procedure for obtaining samples for culture and sensitivity testing. What is the preferred diagnostic method for microbiological confirmation?
questions.initialExplanation: To confirm TB in a young child who cannot produce sputum: three consecutive early-morning gastric aspirates.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- Three consecutive morning gastric aspirates are the traditional and most widely used method for microbiological confirmation of TB in young children. The procedure involves collecting gastric contents before the child awakens and peristalsis clears overnight secretions, yielding organisms in approximately 50% of cases.

- Young children cannot produce sputum effectively due to poor cough reflex and inability to expectorate, making sputum collection impractical. Induced sputum with nebulized saline can be used in children as young as 1 year but is less established than gastric aspirates and requires specialized equipment. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage is invasive, expensive, and not first-line for routine TB diagnosis in children. Tracheal aspirate is invasive, requires intubation or tracheostomy, and is not standard for TB diagnosis in children.

---

questions.stem: A 3 yr old child whose mother has tuberculosis has a positive PPD skin test result. A chest film shows a localized, nonspecific infiltrate in the peripheral segments of the right lower lobe. The most appropriate course of action to confirm the diagnosis of tuberculosis disease in this child is:

options.label: A
options.text: Culture of sputum (induced with a jet nebulizer and chest percussion followed by nasopharyngeal suctioning)

options.label: B
options.text: Culture of pulmonary secretions obtained by bronchoscopy

options.label: C
options.text: Culture of gastric contents obtained by gastric aspiration

options.label: D
options.text: Percutaneous lung and pleural biopsies for culture and histopathology

options.label: E
options.text: Segmental lobectomy for culture and histopathology

questions.initialExplanation: The source's answer: induced sputum culture then nasopharyngeal aspirate to confirm TB in a 3-year-old (gastric aspirate is also a common option).
questions.detailedExplanation:
The most specific confirmation of pulmonary tuberculosis is isolation of M. tuberculosis. Sputum specimens for culture should be collected from adolescents and older children who are able to expectorate. Induced sputum with a jet nebulizer and chest percussion followed by nasopharyngeal suctioning is effective in children as young as 1 mo. Sputum induction provides samples for both culture and smear staining, whereas gastric aspirates are usually cultured. The traditional culture specimen in young children is the early

’     morning gastric acid obtained before the child has arisen and peristalsis has emptied the stomach of the pooled secretions that have been swallowed overnight. However, even under optimal conditions, 3 consecutive morning gastric aspirates yield the organisms in < 50% of cases. The culture yield from bronchoscopy is even lower, but this procedure can demonstrate the presence of endobronchial disease or a fistula. Negative cultures never exclude the diagnosis of tuberculosis in a child. The presence of a positive TST or IGRA, an abnormal chest radiograph consistent with tuberculosis, and history of exposure to an adult with infectious tuberculosis is adequate proof that the disease is present. Drug susceptibility test results of the isolate from the adult source can be used to determine the best therapeutic regimen for the child. Cultures should be obtained from the child whenever the source case is unknown or the source case has possible drug-resistant tuberculosis.

---

questions.stem: A public health nurse is discussing TB prevention strategies with medical students, particularly focusing on BCG vaccine. Students want to understand specific protective effects of BCG vaccination in children. Nurse explains BCG is one of most widely used vaccines worldwide with variable effectiveness against different forms of TB. Focus should be on understanding what types of TB BCG is most effective at preventing. What is the protective effect of BCG vaccine primarily against?

options.label: C
options.text: Life-threatening forms in infants and young children

questions.initialExplanation: BCG mainly protects against severe life-threatening forms in infants and young children (such as disseminated TB and meningitis).
questions.detailedExplanation:
