- BCG primarily prevents severe, life-threatening forms of TB (meningitis, miliary) in infants and young children with an efficacy of 70-80%. This protective effect is most pronounced in the first 5-10 years of life and represents the primary public health benefit of BCG vaccination.

- BCG does not protect against all forms of TB, particularly pulmonary TB in adults, where protection is variable and often limited. BCG has limited and inconsistent effect on pulmonary TB in adults, with protection ranging from 0-80% depending on population and strain. BCG does not prevent latent TB infection but may reduce the

progression from infection to active disease. There is no specific protection against drug-resistant strains, as resistance develops regardless of vaccination status.

---

questions.stem: Which one of the following options is the most appropriate test to differentiate pulmonary tuberculosis (TB) from sarcoidosis?
questions.initialExplanation: To differentiate pulmonary TB from sarcoidosis: Mantoux is positive in TB and usually negative in sarcoidosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Sarcoidosis and pulmonary TB have many similarities in presentation. They both can be associated with vague systemic symptoms of fever, night sweats, and weight loss. They both cause cough and might appear similar on CXR and other imaging modalities. There might be also an overlap syndrome in which both conditions coexist.

Both TB and sarcoidosis are granulomatous diseases; however, tuberculosis has a caseating granuloma as opposed to sarcoidosis, which presents with non-caseating epithelioid cell granuloma.

Misdiagnosis of sarcoidosis as TB results in futile anti-TB treatment while the sarcoidosis remains unattended. Conversely, a patient with misdiagnosed TB as sarcoidosis may be treated with corticosteroids that worsen the TB due to induction of immunodeficiency. Therefore, it is imperative to distinguish between these two. A tuberculin skin test (TST), also known as Mantoux test, is the most appropriate initial tool to apply for differentiation between these two. A negative TST suggests sarcoidosis versus TB. A positive test, however, should prompt extensive investigations for TB. A patient with a positive TST may be infected with TB, or the result might just be false positive e.g. due to previous BCG vaccination.

---

questions.stem: As part of a health check, an immigrant Sudanese woman is found to have a positive tuberculin skin test(TST). A chest X-ray is obtained with inconclusive results. Sputum microscopy and culture are positive for tuberculosis (TB). She is planned to be started on four-drug therapy. She has a 4-year-old son and you make arrangements for him to have an interferon gamma release assay (IGRA) which turns out positive. The child is healthy and has no symptoms. Which one of the following would be the next best step in management?

options.label: C
options.text: Repeat the IGRA for the child.

questions.initialExplanation: An asymptomatic child with a positive IGRA and a contact with active TB: next step is a chest X-ray to exclude active disease before deciding treatment.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child is has been exposed to active TB infection and has a positive IGRA, but is asymptomatic. By definition, this child has latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI). LTBI means the patient has been infected with Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB), but does not have active tuberculosis. Unlike patients with active TB, those with LTBI cannot transmit the MTB to others. Generally, for patients with LTBI, there is a 10% lifetime risk of developing active TB ( 5% in the first 2 years after infection and 0.1% per year thereafter).

To diagnose the latent TB, 2 tests can be used:

Tuberculin skin test (TST), also known as Mantoux test

---

questions.stem: An indigenous woman has brought her three-year-old son to your GP clinic on the advice of an Aboriginal liaison in her community. She was diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis 13 months ago and was treated with standard quadruple therapy. She wants to know if her son may have contacted TB from her. On physical examination, the child has no symptoms. You order a Quantiferon-TB Gold test for the child, the result of which comes back positive. Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step in management of this child?

options.label: E
options.text: Obtain sputum sample for acid fast bacilli microscopy and culture.

questions.initialExplanation: An asymptomatic child with a positive QuantiFERON: first a chest X-ray to decide between latent TB infection (LTBI) and active disease.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has been in close contact with a person with active TB (his mother), and there are chances that he also has contracted the infection. In fact, the positive Quantiferon-TB Gold test indicates that he has TB infection. The next question to

answer is whether he has latent TB infection (LTBI) or active TB infection.

With a positive Quantiferon-TB Gold (IGRA) or tuberculin skin test (TST) [also termed as Mantoux test] in an asymptomatic patient, the next step is always obtaining a chest X-ray. If the chest X-ray is clear, the patient does not have active TB and

should be treated for LTBI by monotherapy with isoniazid for 6-9 months.

If the chest X-ray shows abnormalities in favor of TB infection, the next is obtaining three sputum samples for acid fast bacilli (AFB) stain and culture. If all the three samples are negative, active TB infection is excluded and the patient should be

treated for LTBI. With even one positive sample, active TB infection is the diagnosis, and the patient should be treated with standard quadruple therapy.

This child is asymptomatic and has a positive Quantiferon-TB Gold test. For him, obtaining an X-ray would be the most appropriate next

step in management.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child is diagnosed with TB meningitis and started on anti-TB treatment with isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and aminoglycoside. Child presented with 2-week history of progressive symptoms including fever, headache, irritability, and vomiting. Examination shows signs of meningeal irritation with nuchal rigidity and positive Kernig sign, but child remains alert and oriented. Pediatrician needs to decide on adjunctive therapy to improve outcomes and reduce risk of inflammatory response complications. When should corticosteroids be added?

options.label: A
options.text: Only if there's evidence of cerebral edema

options.label: B
options.text: Routinely from the beginning of treatment

options.label: C
options.text: Only if the child develops seizures

options.label: D
options.text: After 1 week of anti-TB therapy if no improvement

options.label: E
options.text: Only in severe cases with altered consciousness

questions.initialExplanation: TB meningitis: corticosteroids are added routinely from the start to reduce inflammation and complications.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- Corticosteroids are routinely recommended in TB meningitis to reduce inflammation and complications from the beginning of treatment. They help decrease cerebral edema, intracranial pressure, and inflammatory response to TB antigens, improving survival and neurological outcomes.

- Corticosteroids should not be conditional on evidence of cerebral edema - they are recommended routinely for all TB meningitis cases regardless of edema presence. corticosteroids are not used only when seizures develop - they are used prophylactically to prevent complications including seizures, not reactively. Corticosteroids should be started immediately with anti-TB therapy, not delayed for a week or until no

improvement is seen. Corticosteroids are not reserved only for severe cases - they are indicated in all stages of TB meningitis to reduce inflammatory complications.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old girl presents with 3-week history of cervical lymphadenopathy gradually increasing in size. Parents noticed small neck lump 3 weeks ago that has grown to approximately 2 cm diameter. Child has been experiencing low-grade evening fever, decreased appetite, and night sweats. Lymph node is firm, non-tender, doesn't move freely with swallowing. No history of recent upper respiratory infection, skin infections, or cat exposure. Family recently immigrated from high TB prevalence country. Examination shows single, firm, non-tender cervical lymph node measuring about 2 cm. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: A hard painless cervical node growing gradually with evening fever and night sweats in a family from an endemic area = scrofula (TB lymphadenitis).
questions.detailedExplanation:
- TB lymphadenitis (scrofula) is the most common extrapulmonary TB in children with these characteristics. The presentation with discrete, non-tender, firm cervical lymphadenopathy along with systemic symptoms like fever and night sweats is classic for TB lymphadenitis, which represents lymphatic spread from pulmonary focus.

- Bacterial lymphadenitis is usually tender, warm, and has an acute onset with rapid progression, contrasting with the chronic, non-tender nature of TB lymphadenitis. Lymphoma can cause similar symptoms and lymph node characteristics but is less common than TB in endemic areas and often presents with more systemic "B symptoms." Cat scratch disease typically has a history of cat exposure, regional lymphadenopathy, and often a primary skin lesion, with different epidemiology. Mononucleosis typically causes generalized lymphadenopathy affecting multiple lymph node groups, not isolated cervical involvement.

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy presents with breathing difficulty and persistent cough. Child has dry cough for 2 weeks that progressively worsened with episodes of wheezing sounding like whistle when breathing. Wheeze is particularly noticeable at night, seems to improve somewhat during day. No history of fever, but child has been less playful and tires easily during activities. Family recently moved from high TB prevalence country, history of contact with neighbor recently diagnosed with tuberculosis. Examination shows localized wheezing over right lower lobe, decreased breath sounds, mild respiratory distress. In primary pulmonary tuberculosis, what causes bronchial obstruction leading to wheeze?

options.label: C
options.text: External compression by enlarged lymph nodes

questions.initialExplanation: Wheeze in primary TB is due to external compression of the bronchi by enlarged lymph nodes.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- Enlarged hilar lymph nodes can compress bronchi, causing obstruction and wheeze. In primary TB, the characteristic Ghon complex involves hilar lymphadenopathy that can compress adjacent bronchi, leading to localized wheezing that may be mistaken for asthma.

’      - Secretion accumulation in airways is not the primary mechanism of obstruction in primary TB, though it can contribute to symptoms. TB doesn't typically cause allergic bronchospasm - the wheeze is mechanical from lymph node compression rather than allergic in nature. Tracheomalacia (weakness of tracheal walls) is not a

characteristic feature of TB. Foreign body aspiration is unrelated to TB and would present with different historical features.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old girl is brought to pediatric clinic after household contact diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis. Child has no current symptoms, normal examination, normal chest X-ray, but TST is positive at 12 mm induration. This indicates latent TB infection rather than active disease. Pediatrician needs to decide on treatment to prevent progression from latent infection to active disease. Child is otherwise healthy with no underlying medical conditions, good nutritional status, no contraindications to medication. Family committed to ensuring treatment completion. What is the most appropriate treatment for latent TB infection in a child?
questions.initialExplanation: Treatment of latent TB infection (LTBI) in a child: isoniazid for 9 months per the source.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- Isoniazid for 9 months is the standard treatment for latent TB infection in children, providing optimal protection against progression to active disease. This regimen achieves the best balance of efficacy and adherence in the pediatric population.

- Rifampin monotherapy for 4 months is an alternative regimen but not first-line for latent infection in children. Six months of isoniazid provides suboptimal protection compared to the 9-month regimen, with higher rates of treatment failure. Combination therapy with INH and RIF for 3 months is used for active disease, not latent infection, and is shorter than standard latent infection treatment. Treatment is definitely indicated for latent TB infection in children to prevent progression to active disease, which can be more severe in young children.

---

questions.stem: A newborn infant presents at 2 weeks of age with respiratory distress, fever, poor feeding. Mother developed persistent cough and weight loss during last trimester but wasn't diagnosed with tuberculosis until after delivery. Infant was born at term with initial Apgar scores 8 and 9, but developed breathing difficulties within first week of life. Family history reveals mother was treated for pneumonia during pregnancy but later tests confirmed pulmonary tuberculosis. Infant has been formula-fed since birth, showing signs of lethargy, poor suck, respiratory distress with intercostal retractions. In congenital tuberculosis, what is the most important maternal risk factor?
questions.initialExplanation: The most important maternal risk factor for congenital TB is active pulmonary TB during pregnancy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- Maternal active pulmonary TB during pregnancy or at delivery is the key risk factor for congenital TB. The infant can be infected in utero through hematogenous spread or during delivery through aspiration of infected amniotic fluid or maternal genital secretions. Previous history of TB without active disease during pregnancy is less significant as it doesn't provide a source of infection for the fetus. BCG vaccination is protective against TB and reduces the risk of severe disease, making it a preventive factor rather than a risk factor. HIV infection increases TB risk but active maternal TB during delivery is the more direct and immediate risk factor for congenital TB. Poor nutrition during pregnancy is a risk factor for various pregnancy complications but is not specifically the primary risk factor for congenital TB.

---

questions.stem: An 8-year-old child presents with 2-week history of chest pain, shortness of breath, lowgrade fever. Pain is sharp, worse with deep breathing. Examination shows decreased breath sounds at right base with dullness to percussion. Chest X-ray shows moderatesized pleural effusion on right side with underlying pulmonary infiltrates. Thoracentesis is performed and pleural fluid analyzed. Fluid appears straw-colored, laboratory studies show elevated protein, low glucose, cell count with lymphocytic predominance. Which diagnostic finding is most characteristic of tuberculous pleural effusion?
questions.initialExplanation: Typical tuberculous pleural effusion: yellow fluid with high protein, low glucose and lymphocytic predominance.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- Tuberculous pleural effusion characteristically shows lymphocytic predominance as the disease progresses. Initially, there may be neutrophil predominance, but by the time the effusion is clinically apparent, lymphocytes usually dominate the differential.

- Bloody pleural fluid is more typical of malignancy, trauma, or pulmonary embolism, not tuberculous pleural effusion which is typically yellow or straw-colored. Protein is elevated (2-4 g/dL) but not usually >6 g/dL in TB pleural effusion, which helps differentiate from empyema. Glucose is typically low-normal (20-40 mg/dL) rather than high, due to increased glucose consumption by activated inflammatory cells. While neutrophils may predominate early, lymphocytes characteristically predominate in established tuberculous pleural effusions.

---


## Diphtheria | Tetanus | Pertussis

questions.stem: The following bacterial infection can be prevented by a vaccine. Which one of the following can be prevented by toxoid vaccine?
questions.initialExplanation: Toxoid vaccines protect against diphtheria (Corynebacterium diphtheriae) because the disease is caused by its toxin; the same applies to tetanus.
questions.detailedExplanation:
A toxoid vaccine is a type of vaccine that is made from inactivated toxins (toxoids) produced by certain bacteria. The toxoid vaccine works by stimulating the immune system to produce antibodies against the toxin, rather than the bacterium itself.

Corynebacterium diphtheriae , the causative agent of diphtheria, produces a potent exotoxin that is

responsible for the severe symptoms of the disease. The diphtheria toxoid vaccine (usually given as part of the DTP vaccine , which also protects against tetanus and pertussis) contains an inactivated form of the diphtheria toxin, which induces immunity against the harmful effects of the toxin.

---

questions.stem: A healthy 14-year-old boy sustained an injury to his right hand. Ten days post-injury, he presented with generalized spasms followed by sore throat that later progressed to trismus, rigidity of the jaw muscles, and sustained generalized muscle spasms. Given the patient's lack of immunization, tetanus infection was suspected. Which of the following statements regarding the management of this case is least accepted?

options.label: B
options.text: Tetanus antitoxin (TAT) should be given if TIG is unavailable

options.label: C
options.text: Surgical debridement and wound care are necessary

options.label: D
options.text: Supportive care, including keeping the patient in a quiet and darkened room

options.label: E
options.text: Administration of high doses of Tetracycline drugs

questions.initialExplanation: Tetanus treatment includes TIG (or TAT), wound cleaning and supportive care in a quiet room; high-dose tetracycline is not acceptable (the accepted antibiotics are metronidazole or penicillin).
questions.detailedExplanation:
This 14-year-old boy presents with classic symptoms of tetanus , including trismus (lockjaw), generalized muscle spasms, and rigidity. Tetanus is caused by the toxin produced by Clostridium tetani , a spore-forming anaerobic bacterium that typically enters the body through contaminated wounds. Since the patient has no history of immunization, tetanus infection is a reasonable suspicion.

The management of tetanus focuses on neutralizing the toxin, controlling symptoms, preventing further toxin production, and supportive care.

Least accepted practice : While antibiotics like metronidazole or penicillin are commonly used to kill Clostridium tetani and prevent further toxin production, tetracycline drugs are not the first-line choice for treating tetanus.

Metronidazole is preferred because it effectively targets Clostridium tetani and does not interfere with GABAergic neurotransmission (unlike penicillin, which may exacerbate neuromuscular blockade).

High doses of tetracyclines are not recommended because they are less effective against Clostridium tetani and are associated with side effects such as photosensitivity and gastrointestinal upset.

---

questions.stem: 2024 )')s 1 A 66-year-old child is brought in with a persistent cough. The pediatrician suspects pertussis. The gold standard tool for confirming the diagnosis is:
questions.initialExplanation: The gold standard to confirm pertussis is culture of a nasopharyngeal swab.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Pertussis , also known as whooping cough, is caused by the bacterium Bordetella pertussis . It is characterized by a persistent, paroxysmal cough that can last for weeks. Confirming the diagnosis of

pertussis requires specific laboratory tests, and the gold standard for diagnosis is nasopharyngeal culture .

---

questions.stem: A 4-month-old boy develops fever of 38.4 C and is fussy for 2 hours after immunization with the DTaP vaccine. Which of the following steps should be taken in the next visit at the age of 6 months?

options.label: A
options.text: Administer half the usual dose of the DTaP vaccine

options.label: B
options.text: Administer the DTaP vaccine with instructions for fever control

options.label: C
options.text: Defer all immunization until the infant is 12 months old

options.label: D
options.text: Defer immunization, and instead administer DT vaccine

options.label: E
options.text: No further immunization with the DTaP vaccine

questions.initialExplanation: A temperature of 38.4 after DTaP is not a contraindication to the next dose; give it with advice on fever control.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The 4-month-old boy developed a low-grade fever (38.4°C) and fussiness shortly after receiving the DTaP vaccine . These are common, mild side effects of the DTaP vaccine and do not indicate any contraindication to future doses. The appropriate action at the next visit (at 6 months) is to continue

the immunization schedule as planned , while providing guidance to the parents on managing fever and discomfort.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old unvaccinated boy recently presented with a diagnosis of Diphtheria. The bull-neck appearance of Diphtheria presentation is most likely due to:
questions.initialExplanation: The bull neck in diphtheria results from soft-tissue edema and cervical lymphadenopathy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The bull-neck appearance in diphtheria is a classic clinical feature caused by marked soft tissue edema of the neck, often accompanied by enlarged and inflamed cervical lymph nodes. This swelling is due to the intense inflammatory response triggered by the diphtheria toxin , which is produced by Corynebacterium diphtheriae . The toxin causes local tissue damage and inflammation, leading to the characteristic thick, grayish pseudomembrane formation in the throat and surrounding tissues.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old unvaccinated child presents with low-grade fever, sore throat, and difficulty swallowing. Exam shows a thick gray-white pseudomembrane over the tonsils and soft palate that bleeds on contact. Stridor is present, and the airway has been stabilized in the emergency department. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: D
options.text: Await throat culture before starting treatment

options.label: E
options.text: Order chest X-ray to rule out lower respiratory infection

questions.initialExplanation: A bleeding gray-white membrane on the tonsils with stridor in an unvaccinated child = diphtheria; next step is antitoxin plus antibiotic without waiting for culture.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Diphtheria is a medical emergency where the exotoxin causes local tissue necrosis and systemic complications (myocarditis, neuropathy). Diphtheria antitoxin neutralizes circulating unbound toxin and must be administered immediately upon clinical suspicion without awaiting culture confirmation, as delayed treatment increases mortality. Antibiotics (erythromycin or penicillin) eliminate Corynebacterium diphtheriae, halt further toxin production, and reduce transmission. Corticosteroids (A) lack proven benefit in diphtheria management. Antibiotics alone (B) fail to neutralize circulating toxin already causing damage. Awaiting throat culture (D) dangerously delays life-saving antitoxin therapy. Chest X-ray (E) may assess complications but is not the priority intervention. Prompt antitoxin administration, ideally after skin testing for hypersensitivity, combined with antibiotics and continued airway monitoring, aligns with WHO and CDC guidelines.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy is admitted with signs of generalized tetanus: trismus, rigidity, and opisthotonos. He sustained a deep foot wound a week ago while playing barefoot. His vaccinations are up to date. He is conscious and stable but has painful muscle spasms. What is the best immediate step in management?

options.label: C
options.text: Administer tetanus immunoglobulin and start antibiotics

options.label: D
options.text: Start calcium infusion to relieve spasms

options.label: E
options.text: Observe and monitor without intervention unless symptoms worsen

questions.initialExplanation: Generalized tetanus is treated with TIG plus antibiotic and wound cleaning, even with complete vaccination per the source.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has generalized tetanus requiring immediate intervention to neutralize circulating toxin and eliminate the bacterial source. Human tetanus immunoglobulin (TIG) binds and neutralizes unbound tetanospasmin, preventing further neurological damage, while metronidazole (preferred) or penicillin eliminates Clostridium tetani to halt ongoing toxin production. Although vaccinations are up to date, tetanus can still occur with heavy inoculum or waning immunity; a tetanus toxoid booster should also be administered at a separate site to stimulate active immunity, as natural infection does not confer protection. Surgical wound debridement removes necrotic tissue and anaerobic conditions favoring bacterial growth. Muscle spasms require benzodiazepines and supportive care in a quiet environment. Calcium infusion has no role in tetanus management. Delaying TIG or antibiotics risks progression to respiratory failure, autonomic instability, or death.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy is diagnosed with pertussis after 10 days of persistent coughing and post-tussive vomiting. He lives with a 3-week-old sibling who is currently asymptomatic. What is the most appropriate intervention for the infant sibling?
questions.initialExplanation: Prophylaxis for a 3-week-old exposed to pertussis: azithromycin for 5 days (safe in young infants).
questions.detailedExplanation:
For a 3-week-old infant exposed to pertussis, azithromycin for 5 days is the preferred post-exposure prophylaxis per CDC guidelines. Macrolide antibiotics effectively eradicate Bordetella pertussis from the nasopharynx, preventing disease onset and reducing transmission. Azithromycin is favored over erythromycin in infants <1 month due to significantly lower risk of infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, a serious complication associated with erythromycin use in this age group. Clarithromycin lacks sufficient safety data for neonates. Penicillin and trimethoprim have no activity against B. pertussis. Prophylaxis should be initiated within 21 days of exposure, regardless of vaccination status, as the infant is too young to have completed the primary DTaP series. Close monitoring for cough or respiratory symptoms remains essential, and the infant should receive age-appropriate pertussis vaccination starting at 6 weeks.

---

questions.stem: There has been a recent increase in cases of pertussis in your community. When counseling a family who declines immunization, you should inform them of the common manifestations of pertussis. Which of the following is a typical presentation of pertussis infection?

options.label: A
options.text: 4 or 5 days of high fever followed by croupy cough

options.label: B
options.text: sudden onset of fever and cough

options.label: C
options.text: gradual onset of cough, followed by abrupt onset of fever and whooping

options.label: D
options.text: mild upper respiratory symptoms followed by paroxysmal cough

questions.initialExplanation: Pertussis begins with mild upper respiratory symptoms and then becomes paroxysmal cough.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Pertussis classically begins with a catarrhal stage indistinguishable from a common cold and lasts up to a week. This is followed by gradual worsening of the cough, finally reaching the paroxysmal stage, characterized by thick, tenacious secretions and fits of forceful coughing that often end in a whoop as the child is finally able to take a full breath. Fever is usually mild or absent.

---

questions.stem: The mother of the family in the previous question develops paroxysmal cough a few weeks later. Her infant is subsequently admitted to the hospital with apneic episodes. Which of the following white blood cell counts is most suggestive of pertussis?
questions.initialExplanation: Pertussis gives leukocytosis with lymphocyte predominance (about 20,000 with 65% lymphocytes).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Pertussis usually is associated with a marked absolute lymphocytosis. Peripheral white blood cell counts in the range of 20,000-30,000/mm3 with a majority of lymphocytes are characteristic of this infection. This is a useful and important diagnostic feature.

---

questions.stem: A 2-month-old female presents with a 4-day history of coughing spells that last at least 30 seconds. After the coughing spells she vomits. She is otherwise well. Laboratory evaluation reveals a peripheral white blood cell count of 42,000/mm3 with 86% lymphocytes. Which of the following prophylaxis should the family and day-care contacts of this child receive?
questions.initialExplanation: An infant with paroxysmal cough and WBC 42,000 with lymphocyte predominance = pertussis; prophylaxis for contacts with erythromycin (a macrolide).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Erythromycin has historically been the drug of choice to prevent spread of pertussis though currently, azithromycin is generally preferred as therapy. On rare instances Bordetella pertussis has been found to be macrolide resistant; in such a case, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is an alternative but its efficacy is less well documented. Treatment of the index case generally will eradicate the organism from the tracheobronchial tree and reduce spread. Although erythromycin alters the clinical course of pertussis when given early in the paroxysmal stage, it does not seem to alter the clinical course if started later in the illness. A 14-day course of erythromycin is recommended for prevention and treatment of pertussis; a 5 day course is recommended for azithromycin.

---

questions.stem: A 6-month-old female develops a persistent cough with progressively worsening paroxysms and cyanosis. There is occasional posttussive emesis. The child is afebrile. Between coughing spells, the physical examination is normal. At this time, what would be most important question to ask the family regarding patient history?

options.label: E
options.text: family history of reactive airways disease

questions.initialExplanation: An infant with paroxysmal cough, cyanosis and post-tussive vomiting: the most important question is about immunizations.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This history is highly suggestive of pertussis. The clinical course is divided into three stages: (1) the catarrhal stage, 2-10 days in duration, characterized by rhinorrhea, lacrimation, and sometimes low-grade fever; (2) the paroxysmal stage, lasting 1-6 weeks, during which there are intermittent episodes of coughing that may terminate with a forced inspiration against a partially closed glottis resulting in a “whoop” or may terminate with vomiting; (3) the convalescent stage, lasting up to 6 months, during which the coughing episodes gradually resolve. Infants with pertussis often do not whoop because of their inability to generate sufficient inspiratory forces. Between episodes of cough, the examination is often normal. Of the choices given, the immunization status is of most importance.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy presents with sore throat and fever for 2 days. His parents notice a graywhite membrane covering his left tonsil that extends to the uvula. The child appears ill with difficulty swallowing and has enlarged cervical lymph nodes. The family recently immigrated from a country where vaccination coverage is low. Physical examination reveals soft tissue swelling in the neck giving a "bull-neck" appearance. The membrane is adherent and bleeds when attempts are made to remove it. What is the most appropriate initial treatment for this child?
questions.initialExplanation: A gray-white adherent bleeding membrane with bull neck in a child from a low-coverage country = diphtheria; treat with antitoxin plus antibiotic.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- Diphtheria antitoxin is the mainstay of therapy and should be administered immediately based on clinical diagnosis, regardless of laboratory confirmation. This neutralizes circulating toxin and prevents systemic complications. Antibiotics (erythromycin or penicillin) are given to halt toxin production and prevent transmission.

- Oral erythromycin alone is insufficient - antitoxin is essential for neutralizing toxin and must not be delayed waiting for antibiotic effects. IV penicillin alone is inadequate - while effective against the organism, it doesn't neutralize the toxin that's already causing damage. Supportive care alone is dangerous - antitoxin is life-saving and must be given immediately to prevent cardiomyopathy and neuropathy. Corticosteroids are not recommended in diphtheria treatment and may worsen outcomes by affecting immune response.

---

questions.stem: A 2-month-old male presents with a cough that has persisted for over 2 weeks. Mother has noted he coughs in spells and at the end of these spells, he vomits. She feels he has lost weight. On examination, you note a thin male infant who otherwise appears normal. Complete blood count reveals 30,000 white blood cells with 95% lymphocytes. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: An infant with coughing fits followed by vomiting and WBC 30,000 with 95% lymphocytes = pertussis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Pertussis is most deadly for young infants. Complications include pneumonia, seizures, encephalopathy, and apnea. The case fatality rate in the United States is 1% for those infants less than 2 months of age. In adolescents, the illness more likely presents as a persistent cough. For those in between these age groups, the more classic picture is seen: paroxysms of 10-30 uninterrupted staccato coughs followed by a long loud gasping inspiration known as a “whoop,” accompanied by an absolute lymphocytosis. Following implementation of pertussis immunization in the 1950s, the number of annual US cases fell dramatically. Pertussis incidence has increased since 1980 in the US and increase in incidence has been most notable for adolescents and adults. In 2005, pertussis containing vaccine (Tdap) for adolscents and adults has been available with hopes that implementation will reduce the large group of susceptibles and decrease the risk of disease in infants too young to immunize.

---

questions.stem: You have diagnosed a 1-year-old infant with pertussis after he presents with difficulty breathing and “fits” of coughing for the past 2 days. Which of the following is the most common complication of pertussis?
questions.initialExplanation: The most common complication of pertussis is pneumonia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
There are numerous complications associated with pertussis. The most common complications are pneumonia (22%) and otitis media. Seizures (2%) and encephalopathy (<1%) are uncommon. For infants less than 2 months of age, the fatality rate is 1%. Rib fractures secondary to violent fits of coughing have been reported in adults and adolescents with pertussis. In general, pertussis is an afebrile condition. As a result, if a fever is noted, it is important to check for a secondary bacterial infection, such as otitis or pneumonia.

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy is recovering from respiratory diphtheria treated 2 weeks ago. He now develops irregular heart rhythm and complains of chest pain. His heart rate is 120/min with irregular beats, and he appears short of breath with minimal exertion. Examination reveals gallop rhythm and peripheral edema. The treatment with antitoxin was delayed by 3 days due to unavailability. His ECG shows ST-T wave changes and frequent premature beats. What is the most likely cause of these cardiac symptoms?
questions.initialExplanation: Weeks after diphtheria: arrhythmia and heart failure from the diphtheria toxin = diphtheritic myocarditis (toxic cardiomyopathy).
questions.detailedExplanation:
- Toxic cardiomyopathy occurs in up to 25% of patients with respiratory diphtheria and is responsible for 50% of deaths. It results from diphtheria toxin affecting myocardial cells, causing arrhythmias, heart failure, and can occur 1-3 weeks after initial infection, especially when antitoxin is delayed.

- Viral myocarditis is less likely given the recent diphtheria history and timeline - diphtheritic cardiomyopathy is the more probable diagnosis. Antitoxin reactions are immediate and allergic in nature, not delayed cardiac complications. Penicillin toxicity doesn't cause delayed cardiomyopathy and is unlikely with standard dosing. Stress-induced cardiomyopathy doesn't typically present with this timeline and rhythm pattern after infection.

---

questions.stem: A 14-day-old infant presents with difficulty breathing and grunting. The diagnosis of pertussis is confirmed via polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing on nasopharyngeal swab specimen. What is the appropriate plan for prophylaxis?

options.label: A
options.text: Prophylaxis is given to unimmunized individuals only for 14 days after the last contact.

options.label: B
options.text: Household and day care contacts of confirmed pertussis patients should receive antibiotic prophylaxis for 14 days after the last contact.

options.label: C
options.text: Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole is the drug of choice for prophylaxis for 21 days after the last contact.

options.label: D
options.text: Prophylaxis for 21 days is needed only for the personnel who intubate the patient.

options.label: E
options.text: There is no prophylaxis needed, as pertussis is a self-limiting disease.

questions.initialExplanation: Prophylaxis for household and daycare contacts of a confirmed pertussis case: antibiotic for 14 days after last contact.
questions.detailedExplanation:
antibiotic prophylaxis for 14 days after the last contact.

Although bacterial culture is considered the “gold standard” for diagnosis, PCR testing on nasopharyngeal swab specimens for pertussis is becoming the most widely used diagnostic procedure.

Household and day care contacts of confirmed pertussis patients should receive antibiotic prophylaxis for 14 days after the last contact. Prophylaxis is indicated regardless of prior immunization status. Macrolides are the drugs of choice at the same dosages used for therapy.

---

questions.stem: An 8-year-old boy with diphtheria is being discharged after completing 14 days of antibiotic therapy. His throat culture is now negative, and he has recovered from the acute infection. The family asks about prevention measures for other family members. The parents are concerned about their 3-year-old daughter who is fully vaccinated and their 6-month-old son who has received only 2 doses of diphtheria vaccine. What is the most appropriate preventive measure for the family contacts?

options.label: B
options.text: Antibiotic prophylaxis for symptomatic contacts only

options.label: C
options.text: Antibiotic prophylaxis and vaccine booster for all household contacts

questions.initialExplanation: Contacts of a diphtheria case: all household contacts get antibiotic prophylaxis plus a booster vaccine dose.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- All household contacts should receive antibiotic prophylaxis (erythromycin for 10 days or benzathine penicillin G injection) regardless of immunization status. Additionally, diphtheria toxoid booster should be given to those who haven't received a booster within 5 years, and children need completion of their vaccine series.

- No measures are insufficient - asymptomatic carriers can transmit infection, and boosting immunity is important. Antibiotic prophylaxis should be given to all contacts regardless of symptoms to eliminate carriage and prevent spread. Isolation is not necessary once the patient has completed treatment and has negative cultures. Monthly cultures are not standard practice and don't address the need for prophylaxis and vaccination.

---

questions.stem: You are advising the mother of a 2 mo old infant about recommended immunizations. She has read about pertussis vaccine and questions you on the acellular pertussis vaccine you are recommending. You should advise her that compared with whole-cell pertussis vaccine, the acellular vaccine:

options.label: A
options.text: Is more effective in preventing pertussis

options.label: C
options.text: Is less likely to cause seizures

options.label: D
options.text: Is less likely to cause encephalopathy

options.label: E
options.text: Is less likely to cause anaphylaxis

questions.initialExplanation: Acellular pertussis vaccine is less likely to cause seizures than whole-cell vaccine.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Mild local and systemic adverse events as well as more serious events (including high fever, persistent crying of = 3 hr in duration, hypotonic hyporesponsive episodes, and seizures) occur significantly less frequently among infants who receive DTaP than in those who receive DTP vaccine.

---

questions.stem: A 6-month-old boy is brought to your office by his mother with persistence bouts of cough for the past 2 weeks. Every bout of cough is associated with cyanosis of the face and usually followed by vomiting. Which one of the following is the next step in management?

options.label: A
options.text: Nasopharyngeal aspirate and review in 24 hours.

options.label: B
options.text: Immunization at this visit with dTP and review in 24 hours.

options.label: C
options.text: Start him on clarythromycin and review in 24 hours.

questions.initialExplanation: A 6-month-old with coughing fits, cyanosis and vomiting: likely pertussis; needs admission because of the risk of apnea.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The clinical picture suggests respiratory infection with Bordetella pertussis. Pertussis (whooping cough) is a bacterial respiratory infection caused by the organism, Bordetella pertussis (a Gram negative bacillus). It is highly infectious and is spread by respiratory droplets to 70—100% of susceptible household contacts and 50-80% of susceptible school contacts. Pertussis infection occurs worldwide, it affects all age groups, and is most serious in young, unprotected infants. It commonly occurs in teenagers and young adults who have not been immunized or with waning immunity. Patients are infectious just before, and for 21 days after, the onset of cough if left untreated. If treated early with antibiotics, the period of infectivity usually lasts 5 days or less after the commencement of therapy. Maternal antibody does not give adequate protection against pertussis; therefore, babies can be infected before being immunized. The indications for hospitalization/pediatric consultation include the following:

- Infants less than 6 months of age

- Any child who has had apnea, cyanosis, pneumonia, or encephalopathy as a complication of pertussis. With cyanosis following the attacks of cough, this child needs to be admitted to the hospital as the most important next step in management.

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old child is being evaluated for suspected pertussis. The child has had cough for 2 weeks with paroxysmal episodes, whooping, and post-tussive vomiting. The parents report that the child's 5- year-old sibling had similar symptoms 3 weeks ago that resolved. The family recently moved from another country where pertussis vaccination rates are low. What diagnostic test is the gold standard for confirming pertussis?
questions.initialExplanation: The gold standard to confirm pertussis is culture of a nasopharyngeal swab on special medium; PCR is faster but not the standard.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- Isolation of Bordetella pertussis in culture remains the gold standard for diagnosis of pertussis. This requires appropriate culture media (Regan-Lowe or BordetGengou) and takes several days but provides definitive confirmation.

- Chest X-ray findings are not diagnostic and may be normal or show nonspecific changes. Leukocyte count shows lymphocytosis but is not diagnostic on its own. PCR is rapid and sensitive but culture remains the gold standard for definitive diagnosis. Serology can be useful but is not the gold standard and may be affected by vaccination status.

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old male child brought to your clinic with a two-week history of paroxysms of a cough and vomiting at the end of coughing episodes during school holidays. The cough is dry and is worse at night. His mother is worried whether he should go to school which is going to start within two days after holidays.What will you do next?

options.label: D
options.text: Exclude from the school and start antibiotics

questions.initialExplanation: A child with paroxysmal cough and post-tussive vomiting: exclude from school and start antibiotic to reduce transmission.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has developed symptoms of a whooping cough or pertussis. It is caused by Bordetella pertussis. The incubation period is 7-14 days. The illness is characterized by three stages-catarrhal, paroxysmal and convalescent. This child should be given antibiotics to reduce the period of communicability within three weeks of symptoms onset. There is no evidence that the antibiotics make any improvement in symptoms. Exclude from school until five days after starting appropriate antibiotic treatment, or for 21 days from onset of coughing. Cough mixtures are ineffective.

---

questions.stem: A 14-year-old high school student arrives to your clinic for well-child care. In reviewing his records you determine that his most recent immunization for tetanus was at 4 years of age. Which of the following should you recommend?

options.label: C
options.text: Diphtheria toxoid, whole cell pertussis, and tetanus toxoid (DPT) booster

options.label: D
options.text: Tetanus toxoid and tetanus immune globulin

options.label: E
options.text: Tetanus toxoid, reduced diphtheria toxoid, and acellular pertussis vaccine adsorbed (Tdap)

questions.initialExplanation: An adolescent whose last tetanus dose was at age 4: give Tdap (tetanus and diphtheria toxoids with acellular pertussis) as the adolescent booster.
questions.detailedExplanation:
(Tdap)

Until 2006, the correct answer would have been a booster immunization with adult Td (which generally is given every 10 years to maintain immunity against both diphtheria and tetanus). However, recognition of an increased incidence of pertussis in adolescents and young adults (and that this group serves as a reservoir for disease in infants) has led to a vaccine that incorporates immunity also against pertussis. Current recommendations are for the new Tdap to replace the Td to help eliminate pertussis.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old unimmunized child fell while playing in an old barn and sustained a laceration to his leg. After local wound care, what would be the most appropriate management regarding tetanus prophylaxis?

options.label: C
options.text: give Td and tetanus immune globulin

options.label: D
options.text: give DTaP and tetanus immune globulin

questions.initialExplanation: An unvaccinated child with a contaminated wound: give DTaP (vaccine) with tetanus immune globulin.
questions.detailedExplanation:
If a child is unimmunized, or immunization is incomplete for tetanus, a dose of the appropriate vaccine for age should be given, along with tetanus immune globulin (TG) if the wound is considered dirty. As this child is 5 years old, DTaP would be the best choice according to the childhood immunization schedule

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl presents with skin lesions on her legs that have been present for 1 week. The lesions are described as punched-out ulcers with gray membrane covering the base. the child appears otherwise well with no respiratory symptoms. She has been playing in the dirt near a construction site where workers have been excavating soil. Her vaccination status is unknown, and she has no history of previous skin infections. What is the most appropriate diagnostic approach for these skin lesions?
questions.initialExplanation: Ulcerated skin lesions with a gray membrane in a child after soil exposure: suspect cutaneous diphtheria; diagnose by culture on a selective medium.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- Skin lesions suspicious for cutaneous diphtheria should be cultured on selective medium (Loeffler's medium or tellurite medium) that inhibits competing organisms. The laboratory must be specifically notified to use selective medium for Corynebacterium diphtheriae detection.

- Clinical appearance is suggestive but requires laboratory confirmation for definitive diagnosis and to guide treatment and public health measures. Viral culture is not appropriate for bacterial diphtheria infection. Fungal culture would be indicated for fungal infections, not bacterial diphtheria. Skin biopsy is not necessary for diagnosis and culture is the preferred diagnostic method.

---

questions.stem: As a visiting physician in a developing country, you are asked to see a 2 yr old child who presents with a history of fever, dysphagia, and lethargy. Physical examination shows a graybrown leather-like adherent membrane over the posterior oropharynx and hypopharynx. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.initialExplanation: A gray-brown adherent pharyngeal membrane with fever and difficulty swallowing = diphtheria.
questions.detailedExplanation:
In a classic description of 1,400 cases of diphtheria in California (1954), the primary focus of infection was the tonsils or pharynx (94%), with the nose and larynx the next 2 most common sites. After an average incubation period of 2-4 days, local signs and symptoms of inflammation develop. In tonsillar and pharyngeal diphtheria, sore throat is the universal early symptom: Only half of patients have fever, and fewer have dysphagia, hoarseness, malaise, or headache. Mild pharyngeal injection is followed by unilateral or bilateral tonsillar membrane formation, which can extend to involve the uvula (which may cause toxin-mediated paralysis), soft palate, posterior oropharynx, hypopharynx, or glottic areas. Underlying soft tissue edema and enlarged lymph nodes can cause a bull-neck appearance. The degree of local extension correlates directly with profound prostration, bull-neck appearance, and fatality due to airway compromise or toxin-mediated complications. The characteristic adherent membrane, extension beyond the faucial area, dysphagia, and relative lack of fever help differentiate diphtheria from exudative pharyngitis caused by Streptococcus pyogenes or Epstein-Barr virus. Vincent angina, infective phlebitis with thrombosis of the jugular veins (Lemierre disease), and mucositis in patients undergoing cancer chemotherapy are usually differentiated by the clinical setting.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old is brought in to the emergency department. His parents report that he stepped on a rusty nail in their kitchen about two hours ago, His immunization card reveals that he had his DTaP vaccinations at 2 , 4, 6 months and 18 months of age and a booster DT vaccination one year ago. What would you recommend for management of this patient?

options.label: C
options.text: Vaccination with tetanus and diphtheria toxoids

questions.initialExplanation: A child who completed the DTaP series with a booster a year ago and a rusty nail wound: no additional dose is needed.
questions.detailedExplanation:
There are four combination vaccines used to prevent diphtheria, tetanus and pertussis: DTaP, Tdapr DT,and Td, Two of these (DTaP and DT) are given to children younger than 7 years of age, and two (Tdap and Td) are given to older children and adults.

Children should get 5 doses of DTaP, one dose at each of the following ages: 2, 4, 6, and 15-18 months and 4- 6 years. DT does not contain pertussis, and is used as a substitute for DTaP for children who cannot tolerate pertussis vaccine.

Td is a tetanus-diphtheria vaccine given to adolescents and adults as a booster shot every 10 years, or after an exposure to tetanus under some circumstances. Tdap is similar to Td but also containing protection against pertussis. A single dose of Tdap is recommended for adolescents 11 or 12 years of age, or in place of one Td booster in older adolescents and adults age 19 through 64.

---

questions.stem: A 1-year-old child presents for a well-child check-up, but the parents are concerned about giving the child his immunizations. Which of the following is a true contraindication to the administration of the fourth DTaP (diphtheria, tetanus toxoid, and acellular pertussis) vaccine?

options.label: A
options.text: Child is currently on amoxicillin for an otitis media

options.label: B
options.text: Positive family history of adverse reactions to DTaP vaccine

options.label: C
options.text: A past history of infantile spasms

options.label: E
options.text: Prolonged seizures 6 days after the last DTaP vaccine

questions.initialExplanation: The true contraindication to the 4th DTaP dose is encephalopathy or prolonged seizures after the previous dose; antibiotics and mild fever are not contraindications.
questions.detailedExplanation:
There are few true contraindications to vaccines, but many misconceptions about contraindications. The one contraindication for all vaccines is a prior history of a severe allergic reaction to a component

’     of the vaccine. For the DTaP, another contraindication is the occurrence of encephalopathy (such as coma, altered level of consciousness, or prolonged seizures) within 7 days of administration of the previous dose. Minor illnesses; current antibiotic therapy; history of local reaction (such as erythema or swelling) after previous immunizations; family history of seizures, SIDS, or adverse events due to DTaP; and stable, nonprogressive neurologic conditions (eg, cerebral palsy, controlled seizure disorder, or developmental delay) are not contraindications.

---

questions.stem: A 2-week-old infant presents with apnea. The infant was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy. The mother of this baby had rhinorrhea and cough that started 3 weeks ago and now she has a severe persistent cough with post-tussive emesis. Which treatment should be initiated?
questions.initialExplanation: A 2-week-old with apnea and a mother with paroxysmal cough = pertussis; treat with azithromycin.
questions.detailedExplanation:
There are many causes of apnea in infants. The extent of the diagnostic workup depends on many factors such as history and physical examination findings. In this case, the symptoms of the mother should raise significant concern for presence of pertussis, a well-recognized cause for apnea in young infants. Pertussis, caused by B pertussis, is endemic and the annual incidence has risen in the past year. Coughing adolescents and adults currently are the major reservoir for B pertussis. Erythromycin for 14 days in the past has been the standard treatment but current recommendations suggest azithromycin is effective and a shorter duration of therapy is needed. It should be instituted when pertussis is suspected or confirmed to limit the spread of infection; the clinical benefit to the patient who has been coughing for longer than 2

weeks is neglible. New vaccines recently have been licensed for booster immunizations of adolescents and adults (Tdap) and will hopefully serve to reduce the risk of exposure of young infants to the pool of susceptible older patients.

---

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy is diagnosed with diphtheria and started on treatment. On the second day of hospitalization, he develops hives, wheezing, and low blood pressure shortly after receiving diphtheria antitoxin. His vitals show blood pressure 85/50 mmHg, heart rate 130/min, and respiratory rate 24/min. He appears anxious and has diffuse urticaria covering his trunk and extremities. What is the most likely diagnosis and immediate treatment?
questions.initialExplanation: Anaphylaxis after diphtheria antitoxin (urticaria, wheeze, hypotension): immediate epinephrine.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- Anaphylactic reaction to diphtheria antitoxin requires immediate epinephrine administration. This is a medical emergency with rapid onset (minutes to hours) following exposure, presenting with hypotension, bronchospasm, and urticaria.

- Serum sickness occurs 1-2 weeks after exposure with different timing and presentation - this is immediate anaphylaxis requiring epinephrine. This is not an antibiotic reaction - timing and symptoms suggest antitoxin-related anaphylaxis. Sepsis wouldn't develop this rapidly and the temporal relationship to antitoxin administration suggests allergic reaction. This is not an anxiety reaction but a true allergic emergency requiring immediate epinephrine.

---

questions.stem: Pharyngeal diphtheria may be misdiagnosed with exudative pharyngitis caused by streptococcus pyogenes or Epstein-Barr virus. Which of the following features is characteristic of pharyngeal diphtheria rather than exudative pharyngitis?

options.label: B
options.text: Extension of the membrane beyond the faucial area

questions.initialExplanation: Pharyngeal diphtheria is characterized by a membrane extending beyond the tonsillar area (faucial), whereas exudative pharyngitis does not extend.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The characteristic adherent membrane, extension beyond the faucial area, dysphagia, and relative lack of fever help differentiate diphtheria from exudative pharyngitis.

---

questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy presents with jaw stiffness and difficulty opening his mouth for 2 days. He was injured while playing in a dirty sandbox 1 week ago, sustaining a deep puncture wound on his leg that was not properly cleaned. His vaccination records show he received his last tetanus booster at age 5. Examination reveals trismus (lockjaw), neck muscle stiffness, and difficulty swallowing. He appears anxious and alert, complaining of muscle spasms triggered by minor stimuli. What is the most appropriate initial treatment for this patient?
questions.initialExplanation: A patient with tetanus (trismus) and a deep wound: give tetanus immunoglobulin with antibiotic first, along with cleaning.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- Tetanus immunoglobulin (TIG) should be given immediately to neutralize circulating tetanus toxin before it binds at distant muscle groups. This must be combined with antibiotics (penicillin) to eradicate Clostridium tetani from the wound site.

- Antibiotics alone are insufficient - TIG is essential to neutralize toxin already in circulation. Wound debridement is important but doesn't address the toxin already in circulation - TIG is the priority. Muscle relaxants treat symptoms but don't address the underlying toxin - TIG is the definitive treatment. Sedation is supportive but doesn't neutralize toxin - TIG and antibiotics are the cornerstone of treatment.

---

questions.stem: A 16-year-old boy presents with tetanus following a foot injury from a rusty nail. He is being treated in the intensive care unit with mechanical ventilation due to respiratory muscle involvement. His family asks about prevention of tetanus in the future. He received his childhood vaccinations but his last tetanus booster was 8 years ago. The wound has been properly cleaned and debrided. What is the most appropriate tetanus prevention strategy for this patient?

options.label: B
options.text: Single booster dose of tetanus toxoid

questions.initialExplanation: After recovery from tetanus a booster of tetanus toxoid is needed because natural infection does not confer immunity.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A single booster dose of tetanus toxoid is appropriate for previously immunized individuals who have had their last booster more than 5 years ago. This enhances immunity and provides long-term protection against future tetanus exposure.

- No additional vaccination is insufficient - boosters are recommended every 10 years or after high-risk injuries. Complete primary series is not needed in previously immunized individuals. Immunoglobulin is

for immediate protection but doesn't provide longterm immunity. Watchful waiting is inappropriate when boosters are clearly indicated.

---

questions.stem: A 6-month-old male infant is brought to your clinic by his mother for receiving his third dose of DTPa vaccine. He has received his previous doses at 6 weeks and 4 months of age. The child sneezes, has a runny nose and a fever of 38.2°. Exam findings are consistent with upper respiratory tract infection (URTI). According to the mother, last time he received his DTPa vaccine, he developed a huge swelling at the injection site. Which one of the following is the most appropriate management regarding vaccination with DTPa in this situation?

options.label: C
options.text: Do not give the pertussis component.

questions.initialExplanation: An infant after a previous DTPa dose with a large local swelling and a mild cold with low fever: give the dose now; mild fever and local swelling are not contraindications.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The acronym DTPa, using capital letters, signifies child formulations of diphtheria, tetanus and acellular pertussis- containing vaccines. The acronym dTpa is used for formulations that contain substantially lesser amounts of diphtheria toxoid and pertussis antigens than child (DTPa-containing) formulations; dTpa vaccines are usually used in adolescents ’     and adults. Pertussis-containing vaccine is recommended in a 3-dose primary schedule for infants at 2, 4 and 6 months of age. Due to the high morbidity and occasional mortality associated with pertussis in the first few months of life, the first dose can be given as early as 6 weeks of age. Giving a first dose at 6 weeks of age rather than 2 months of age is estimated to prevent an additional 8% of infant pertussis cases. The next scheduled doses should still be given at 4 months and 6 months of age. Extensive limb swelling, defined as swelling and/or redness involving at least half the circumference of the limb and the joints both above and below the injection site is a recognized adverse event that occurs rarely following booster doses of DTPa. Such reaction begins within 48 hours of vaccination, last for 1 to 7 days and

resolve completely without sequelae. History of such event is not a contraindication to the vaccine use. No change in the formulation is required or recommended either.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child is brought to the pediatric clinic after stepping on a rusty nail. The wound is deep and contaminated with dirt. The parents are unsure about the child's vaccination status. The wound requires cleaning and the family wants to know about tetanus prevention. The child appears otherwise well with no signs of infection. What is the most appropriate tetanus prevention approach?

options.label: D
options.text: Tetanus toxoid, immunoglobulin, and wound cleaning

questions.initialExplanation: A deep contaminated wound with unknown immunization status: tetanus toxoid with tetanus immunoglobulin and wound cleaning.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- For dirty wounds with uncertain vaccination status, both tetanus toxoid (for active immunity) and tetanus immunoglobulin (for immediate passive protection) are indicated, along with proper wound cleaning and debridement. This provides both immediate and long-term protection.

- Wound cleaning alone is insufficient for tetanus prevention in high-risk situations. Toxoid alone provides protection but immunoglobulin is needed for immediate protection in dirty wounds with uncertain immunity. Immunoglobulin provides immediate protection but doesn't provide long-term immunity. Antibiotics help prevent infection but don't provide specific tetanus protection.

---

questions.stem: A 14-year-old boy is being treated for tetanus in the hospital. His spasms are controlled with medication, but he has developed pneumonia and requires respiratory support. The medical team is discussing prognosis and wants to counsel the family about recovery expectations. The patient's trismus has begun to improve after 2 weeks of treatment. What is the typical duration of tetanus illness?
questions.initialExplanation: Typical duration of tetanus per the source is 2-4 months (spasms may last weeks then improve slowly).
questions.detailedExplanation:
- The typical course of tetanus involves severe spasms in the first week, stabilization in the second week, and gradual recovery over 2-4 months. Complete recovery is the norm with proper supportive care, though some patients may have residual weakness. One week is too short - tetanus requires weeks to months for recovery. 2-4 weeks is too short for complete recovery - this represents the acute

phase only. 6-12 months is longer than typical and suggests complications. Permanent disability is not typical - most patients recover completely with proper care.

---

questions.stem: A 3-month-old infant presents with episodes of coughing followed by cyanosis and apnea. The parents describe the cough as occurring in bursts, sometimes lasting for several minutes. The baby was born at term and received one dose of DTaP vaccine at 2 months of age. Over the past week, the cough has worsened, especially at night. Examination shows a well-nourished infant with occasional paroxysmal coughing episodes during the examination. What is the most characteristic feature that differentiates pertussis from other respiratory infections in infants?

options.label: B
options.text: Paroxysmal cough with whoop and post-tussive emesis

questions.initialExplanation: The characteristic feature of pertussis in infants: paroxysmal cough with a whoop and post-tussive vomiting.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- The hallmark of pertussis is paroxysmal coughing with a characteristic whoop and post-tussive emesis. In infants, this may present with cyanosis and apnea rather than the classic whoop. This pattern is distinctive and differentiates pertussis from other respiratory infections.

- High fever is not characteristic of pertussis - fever is usually low-grade or absent. Rash is not associated with pertussis and suggests other infections. Wheezing is more typical of asthma or

bronchiolitis, not pertussis. While rhinorrhea occurs in the catarrhal stage, it's not the distinguishing feature.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old child is in the paroxysmal stage of pertussis. The parents report that the child has coughing fits every 15-20 minutes during the day and night. During these episodes, the child appears to cough continuously for 30-45 seconds, then makes a loud whooping sound during inspiration. The child vomits after many episodes and appears exhausted between coughing spells. What is the most appropriate antimicrobial treatment for this child?
questions.initialExplanation: A child in the paroxysmal stage of pertussis: give azithromycin for 5 days.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- Azithromycin (10 mg/kg/day in a single dose for 5 days) is the preferred treatment for pertussis. It shortens the infectious period and may reduce transmission,though it has limited effect on symptoms once in the paroxysmal stage.

- Amoxicillin is not effective against Bordetella pertussis and is not recommended. Cephalexin is not effective against pertussis and is not a recommended alternative. Antibiotics are recommended to reduce transmission, even in later stages. IV vancomycin is not indicated for pertussis and is used for serious Grampositive infections.

---


## Infectious Mononucleosis | PUO

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy presented with fever for the last 3 days, associated with headache and sore throat. He had frequent episodes of vomiting and abdominal pain. He appears ill, febrile, skin rash, with tender bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy, the tongue covered with heavy white coat with obvious red papillae protruded. The tonsils were red and edematous. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.initialExplanation: The source's answer is infectious mononucleosis (fever, sore throat, cervical adenopathy), but the description of a strawberry tongue with prominent papillae resembles scarlet fever; check the original.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The clinical presentation of fever, headache, sore throat, vomiting, abdominal pain, tender bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy, and a characteristic "white-coated tongue" with red papillae protruding (referred to as " strawberry tongue") , along with red and edematous tonsils. These findings are highly suggestive of infectious mononucleosis , which is caused by the Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) .

Scarlet fever is caused by group A Streptococcus (GAS) and is associated with a sore throat, fever, and a characteristic sandpaper-like rash that starts on the trunk and spreads outward. While scarlet fever can cause a "strawberry tongue," it does not typically present with tender cervical lymphadenopathy or systemic symptoms like vomiting and abdominal pain. This option is less likely .

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy recently diagnosed with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection returns for follow-up. His fever and fatigue have improved, but laboratory tests show neutropenia. He is clinically stable, with mild cervical lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly, and no new medications. What is the most likely cause of his neutropenia?
questions.initialExplanation: Neutropenia after EBV is due to transient bone marrow suppression caused by the virus itself.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Neutropenia is a well-recognized hematologic manifestation of Epstein-Barr virus infection, occurring in up to 50% of cases due to transient bone marrow suppression and peripheral immune-mediated destruction. EBV infects B-lymphocytes and disrupts normal hematopoiesis, leading to cytopenias that typically resolve spontaneously as the infection clears. The child's clinical improvement with persistent mild lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly supports resolving infectious mononucleosis rather than a new process. Bacterial superinfection would typically cause neutrophilia and clinical deterioration. Transformation to leukemia is exceedingly rare acutely and would present with additional abnormalities like blasts, severe pancytopenia, or progressive symptoms. Vitamin B12 deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia with macrocytosis, not isolated neutropenia, and develops chronically.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old child presents with a 3-week history of daily fever reaching up to 39.5°C, associated with malaise and decreased appetite. The child has no cough, rash, or recent travel history. On examination, he appears tired, mildly pale, with no lymphadenopathy, organomegaly, or joint swelling. Initial workup, including complete blood count, urinalysis, chest X-ray, and blood cultures, is unremarkable. Inflammatory markers are elevated (ESR 75 mm/h, CRP 45 mg/L). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the evaluation of this child's condition?

options.label: C
options.text: Repeat CBC and wait one week

options.label: D
options.text: Repeat chest X-ray in one week

questions.initialExplanation: A prolonged fever of unknown origin with high inflammatory markers and normal initial tests: per the source the next step is bone marrow aspiration/biopsy (to exclude leukemia).
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has fever of unknown origin (FUO) with prolonged high-grade fever, elevated inflammatory markers, pallor, and constitutional symptoms despite unrevealing initial workup. Bone marrow aspiration is the most appropriate next step to exclude occult malignancy such as leukemia, which can present with fever before peripheral blood abnormalities appear. It also diagnoses hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH), a life- threatening condition causing persistent fever and inflammation. Disseminated infections like tuberculosis, histoplasmosis, or brucellosis may be identified through marrow culture and histopathology when other studies are negative. Abdominal ultrasound is less likely to yield diagnosis without focal abdominal findings or organomegaly. Repeating tests or delaying evaluation risks missing treatable conditions in a child with significant inflammatory markers. Antinuclear antibody testing has low specificity and is premature before excluding infection and malignancy.

---

questions.stem: You examine an 18-year-old male college student with a 5-day history of fever, sore throat, and fatigue. Physical examination reveals an exudative tonsillitis and bilateral enlarged and slightly tender posterior cervical lymph nodes. The spleen is palpable 3 cm below the rib cage. Which agent is most likely responsible for this patient’s illness?
questions.initialExplanation: Fever, exudative tonsillitis, posterior cervical adenopathy and splenomegaly in a young person = Epstein-Barr virus (mononucleosis).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Although this question also is quite straightforward, it potentially is more difficult than the preceding questions because several of the agents listed can explain many of the features of this adolescent's illness. If you read the instructions carefully, you noted that you were asked to select the one best answer, which does not imply that all other choices are totally without merit. Consider which of the above choices best fits the clinical scenario, and therefore, which is most likely responsible for this patient's illness. The correct answer is (D).

‘      The agent most likely responsible for this child’s illness is the Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). The clinical picture is strongly suggestive of mononucleosis. Although this patient could be infected with group A streptococcus or adenovirus, several features are much more characteristic of EBV infection than either of these. They include the fact that the child is a college student, the presence of splenomegaly, and the fact that the adenopathy is posterior rather than anterior and is only slightly tender. While these findings also could be explained by toxoplasmosis, this diagnosis is rarely confirmed as a cause of acute exudative tonsillitis and cervical adenitis in the United States. Although it is appropriate to think of diphtheria in patients with acute exudative tonsillitis, there is nothing specific in this case to suggest that diagnosis. Infectious mononucleosis is clearly the most likely diagnosis.

---

questions.stem: A 16-year-old boy presents with fever, fatique, and sore throat. Examination reveals exudative pharyngitis, generalized lymphadenopathy, and mild splenomegaly. Laboratory studies show elevated WBC count with presence of atypical lymphocytes. What is the best action?

options.label: A
options.text: no participation in contact sports for next 2-4 weeks

options.label: C
options.text: 2-week treatment with oral acyclovir and prednisone

questions.initialExplanation: A teenager with mononucleosis and splenomegaly: avoid contact sports for 2-4 weeks to prevent splenic rupture.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Signs and symptoms in this patient are consistent with infectious mononucleosis most likely caused by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). A presumptive diagnosis can be made with typical clincal presentation and presence of atypical lymphocytosis. Serologic testing can confirm the diagnosis. Very few healthy adolescents with infectious mononucleosis experience severe complications. The most feared complication is splenic rupture which has a reported occurrence rate of 0.2% in adults and is usually associated with blunt trauma to the abdomen. Participation in contact sports should therefore be avoided for several weeks or until splenomegaly has resolved. Corticosteroids are indicated only if there is severe airway obstruction because of tonsillar enlargement. Acyclovir does not alter the course of the disease.

questions.stem: A young man presents with symptoms of ongoing fever and sore throat for the past week along with mild headache and malaise. On examination of the oropharynx, he has reddened and enlarged tonsils without exudate with fine petechiae over the uvula and soft palate. There is bilateral cervical adenopathy present. Abdominal examination reveals an enlarged spleen. A rapid group A Streptococcus test from yesterday is negative. Hematologic tests from the day before show a slightly elevated white blood cell count and a mild thrombocytopenia of 120,000 platelets/uL. A blood smear is obtained. The best treatment for the patient’s condition is:
questions.initialExplanation: A young person with fever, sore throat, palatal petechiae and splenomegaly and a negative strep test: likely mononucleosis; treatment is symptomatic only.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This patient’s symptoms and findings are all compatible with mononucleosis, generally treated with antipyretics. Acyclovir, while used for other herpes viruses, has not been generally effective in treating EBV. Corticosteroids are reserved for severe EBV disease (airway obstruction, neurologic complications, fulminant hepatitis, myocarditis, pericarditis, thrombocytopenic purpura, or hemolytic anemia). The patient’s blood smear shows reactive lymphocytes, not cancerous cells, although a heterophil antibody test can help differentiate mononucleosis from oncologic problems. The patient is unlikely to have streptococcal pharyngitis and amoxicillin may additionally exacerbate the patient’s condition by causing a morbilliform rash.

---

questions.stem: A 15-year-old boy is diagnosed with infectious mononucleosis and started on amoxicillin for presumed bacterial pharyngitis. On the third day of antibiotic therapy, he develops a diffuse maculopapular rash covering his trunk and extremities. His temperature is normal and he feels better overall. The rash is intensely pruritic and the family is concerned about a drug allergy. What is the most likely explanation for this rash?
questions.initialExplanation: A rash after amoxicillin in a patient with mononucleosis is not true allergy but the well-known ampicillin-induced rash of this disease.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- CMaculopapular rash occurs in approximately 80% of patients with EBV mononucleosis who receive aminopenicillins (ampicillin, amoxicillin). This is not a true drug allergy but a characteristic reaction specific to EBV infection. The rash typically appears 5-9 days after starting the antibiotic.

- This is not a true penicillin allergy - the rash would have appeared sooner with true allergy and might include urticaria or anaphylaxis. EBV-associated rash occurs in only 10% of patients and wouldn't be specifically related to antibiotic timing. Viral exanthem would not be temporally related to antibiotic administration. Contact dermatitis would be localized to contact areas, not diffuse.

---

questions.stem: A previously well 12-year-old presents with fever, sore throat, and general malaise. On physical examination, you notice generalized lymphadenopathy, exudative pharyngitis, and splenomegaly. Laboratory evaluation reveals elevated serum transaminase levels. What is the organism most likely responsible for these findings?
questions.initialExplanation: Fever, exudative sore throat, adenopathy, splenomegaly and raised transaminases = Epstein-Barr virus.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The clinical and laboratory findings described are most suggestive of infectious mononucleosis from
