Epstein-Barr virus. Hepatic involvement evidenced by elevated serum transaminase levels is common. Syphilis, HBV, rubella, and toxoplasmosis do not present with this constellation of symptoms.

---

questions.stem: A 15-year-old has exudative tonsillitis, cervical adenitis, and splenomegaly. His monospot test is positive. Which of the following is the most common complication encountered?

options.label: A
options.text: chronic fatigue lasting greater than 6 months

questions.initialExplanation: The most common complication of mononucleosis per the source is airway obstruction due to tonsillar enlargement.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Infectious mononucleosis syndrome generally presents with exudative pharyngitis that may be associated with petechiae or erythematous macules on the palate. A rash occurs occasionally and splenomegaly may be noted. Airway obstruction secondary to markedly enlarged tonsils is an infrequent but important complication.

---

questions.stem: A 14-year-old girl with infectious mononucleosis develops increasing difficulty breathing and stridor. Her tonsils are enlarged with exudate, and she appears anxious with labored breathing. The cervical lymph nodes are significantly enlarged, and she is having difficulty swallowing her own secretions. Oxygen saturation is 92% on room air. The parents report that her breathing worsened over the past 6 hours. What is the most appropriate immediate intervention?
questions.initialExplanation: Upper airway obstruction from tonsillar hypertrophy in mononucleosis: the source's answer is corticosteroids to reduce edema (with monitoring and airway protection if worsening).
questions.detailedExplanation:
- Corticosteroids are recommended for management of impending airway obstruction in infectious mononucleosis. They reduce tonsillar and lymphoid tissue swelling, which can be life-threatening. This is the most appropriate intervention before considering more invasive procedures.

- Nebulized epinephrine is used for croup, not for airway obstruction from mononucleosis. Oxygen alone is insufficient for significant airway obstruction. Emergency intubation may be necessary if steroids fail, but steroids should be tried first. IV antibiotics are not indicated as this is viral, not bacterial infection.

---

questions.stem: A 12-year-old child presents with fever, sore throat, and fatigue for 1 week. Examination reveals generalized lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, and pharyngitis with exudate. Blood tests show marked lymphocytosis with atypical lymphocytes. The Monospot test is negative. The child has no travel history or unusual exposures. What is the most appropriate next diagnostic step?

options.label: C
options.text: Start amoxicillin for presumed bacterial infection

questions.initialExplanation: A full mononucleosis picture with a negative Monospot (common in young children): the next step is EBV-specific serology (VCA and EBNA).
questions.detailedExplanation:
- EBV-specific serology for viral capsid antigen (VCA) and EBV nuclear antigen (EBNA) should be performed when heterophile antibody test is negative but clinical suspicion remains high. Specific antibodies provide definitive diagnosis and can distinguish acute from past infection.

- While repeat testing might be considered, proceeding to specific serology is more appropriate for timely diagnosis. Amoxicillin should be avoided as it can cause rash in EBV infection and isn't indicated for viral pharyngitis. Bone marrow biopsy is invasive and not indicated for typical mononucleosis presentation. CT scan is not needed for diagnosis and involves unnecessary radiation exposure.

---

questions.stem: A pregnant woman has come to you because two days after babysitting her friend’s son, he was diagnosed with infectious mononucleosis. She is worried about herself and her baby’s well-being. Currently she is asymptomatic. Which one of the following will be the most appropriate action for now?

options.label: A
options.text: Order an ultrasound for assessment of fetal hydrops.

options.label: D
options.text: Tell her to come back if any symptoms develop.

questions.initialExplanation: A pregnant woman exposed to a mononucleosis patient, asymptomatic: the source's answer is to return if symptoms develop; no tests or interventions now.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is a human herpes virus with variable incubation period that may cause infectious mononucleosis. This virus can remain latent in the body and become reactivated at a later time.

EBV is more common among women aged 15 and 19 years, but in developing countries it is more common among children. The route of transmission is sharing oral secretions (saliva). EBV has an incubation period of 2-7 weeks after exposure.

Clinical features of EBV include: Fever, Sore throat, Lymphadenopathy, Characteristic increase in the percentages of monocytes and lymphocytes (mononucleosis and lymphocytosis), Hepatosplenomegaly, Rise in hepatic transaminases

---

questions.stem: A 20-year-old university student, presented with sore throat, fever and malaise for 3 days. Examination findings are positive for generalized lymphadenopathy, enlarged tonsils, erythematous pharynx. Investigation done shows lymphocytosis with atypical lymphocytes on peripheral blood smear and elevated liver enzymes. What is your provisional diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Sore throat, fever, generalized adenopathy with atypical lymphocytes and raised liver enzymes = infectious mononucleosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The correct answer is infectious mononucleosis (glandular fever), occurs mostly in persons aged from 15-24. After the prodromal period of chills, sweats and malaise, the disease presents with the classical triad of severe sore throat, fever (38-40 degree Celcius) and lymphadenopathy (mostly anterior and posterior cervical nodes, also in axillary and inguinal nodes). Other findings: enlarged tonsils, erythematous pharynx with thick exudate, palatal petechiae. 50% has splenomegaly, 10-15% has

hepatomegaly and 5% is icteric. FBE and peripheral blood film show lymphocytosis with >10% atypical/reactive lymphocytes (Downey cells). Consider a heterophile/Monospot test. Elevated aminotransferases + pharyngitis strongly suggest the diagnostic possibility of IM. Patients with fever, pharyngitis, and lymphadenopathy may have infection due to group A streptococcus, Arcanobacterium haemolyticum, cytomegalovirus (CMV), acute HIV, or, rarely, Toxoplasma gondii.

---

questions.stem: A 12 yr old boy has been seen as an outpatient several times over the past 3 wk for fever (temperature 38-40°C). His CBC count and differential count have been normal on 2 occasions, his urinalysis is normal, and results of 2 Monospot tests done a week apart are negative. His ESR is 42 mm/hr. His physical examination has been normal at each visit. Which of the following is most likely to give a clue as to the cause of his fever?

options.label: B
options.text: Radiographs of the chest, sinuses, and mastoids

questions.initialExplanation: Fever for 3 weeks with normal tests: what most helps find the cause is a complete medical history.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The evaluation of fever of unknown origin requires a thorough history and physical examination

supplemented by a few screening laboratory tests and additional laboratory and radiographic tests as indicated by the history or abnormalities on examination or initial screening.

---

questions.stem: A 16-year-old boy with infectious mononucleosis develops petechiae and easy bruising. His platelet count is 40,000/mms3, and he has no other bleeding manifestations. The splenomegaly has improved, and he otherwise feels well. The family is concerned about the low platelet count and asks about treatment options. What is the most appropriate management approach for this thrombocytopenia?
questions.initialExplanation: Thrombocytopenia associated with mononucleosis without major bleeding: observation only.
questions.detailedExplanation:
EBV-associated thrombocytopenia in infectious mononucleosis is typically mild and self-limited, resolving spontaneously as the viral illness improves. In this adolescent with a platelet count of 40,000/mms3, petechiae, and easy bruising but no active mucosal or internal bleeding, observation with serial monitoring is the appropriate initial management. Platelet transfusion is reserved for life-threatening hemorrhage or extremely low counts with active bleeding. Corticosteroids or IV immunoglobulin may be considered for severe thrombocytopenia with significant bleeding, but are not indicated for asymptomatic mild-moderate cases. Splenectomy has no role in acute EBV-related thrombocytopenia. Counsel the family about bleeding precautions, including avoiding NSAIDs, contact sports, and activities with trauma risk. Most cases normalize within 2—4 weeks without specific intervention.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy presents with fever for 4 weeks. Specifically, he has been documented with an oral temperature =38.0°C (100.4°F) at least 5 times per week for the last 4 weeks. History is unremarkable. Physical examination is also noncontributory. After 1 week of outpatient investigation, no etiology for the fevers has been noted. He has no risk factors or evidence of immunodeficiency. Which of the following is the most likely etiology?
questions.initialExplanation: FUO in a 4-year-old after a week of work-up: the most likely outcome is that no etiology is identified, as most cases end without a diagnosis and resolve spontaneously.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The patient fulfills the criteria for fever of unknown origin (FUO). The definition of FUO requires an immunologically normal host with oral or rectal temperature 238.0°C (100.4°F) at least twice a week for more than 3 weeks, a noncontributory history and physical examination, and 1 week of outpatient investigation. More than two thirds of children with FUO resolve their fevers without determination of cause; thus, extensive workup in an otherwise well-appearing child may not need to be conducted until >3 to 6 weeks of fever have been sustained. Infectious etiologies account for approximately 40%

of identified etiologies, and among those the most common sources are B. henselae infection, EBV infection, and UTIs.

---

questions.stem: A 15-year-old girl with infectious mononucleosis develops severe headache, neck stiffness, and photophobia. She becomes increasingly confused and has difficulty focusing on objects. The symptoms developed over 24 hours. Physical examination shows nuchal rigidity and positive Kernig sign. Her mental status is altered. What is the most likely neurological complication?
questions.initialExplanation: Fever, headache, neck stiffness and confusion with mononucleosis: the likely neurological complication is EBV encephalitis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- EBV has been implicated in virtually every form of infection-related neurological disorder, including encephalitis, meningitis, and cranial nerve palsies. The timeline and presentation are consistent with EBV neurological involvement, which can be severe but typically has good recovery with supportive care.

- While bacterial meningitis is possible, the recent EBV diagnosis makes EBV encephalitis more likely. Cerebral edema can occur but wouldn't typically present with these specific neurological signs. Stroke is less common and wouldn't present with this acute timeline. Brain abscess is rare and wouldn't typically present with meningeal signs.

---

questions.stem: A 18-year-old college student is diagnosed with infectious mononucleosis and wants to know about long-term complications. He is concerned about his risk of developing cancer since his uncle had lymphoma. The student is otherwise healthy and recovering well from the acute infection. Which malignancy is most strongly associated with EBV infection?
questions.initialExplanation: The tumor most associated with EBV per the source: Hodgkin lymphoma (also Burkitt lymphoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma).
questions.detailedExplanation:
- Hodgkin lymphoma has the strongest association with EBV infection among common malignancies. EBV DNA is found in Reed-Sternberg cells in a significant percentage of Hodgkin lymphoma cases, particularly in children and young adults.

- Lung cancer is not strongly associated with EBV infection. Breast cancer has no established association with EBV. Colorectal cancer is not associated with EBV. Skin cancer is not related to EBV infection.

---

questions.stem: A 14-year-old boy with infectious mononucleosis complains of persistent fatigue 6 weeks after symptom onset. He returned to school but feels exhausted after minimal activity and needs to sleep more than usual. The acute symptoms resolved, and his spleen size is normal. His parents are concerned about chronic fatigue syndrome. What is the expected course of fatigue in infectious mononucleosis?

options.label: A
options.text: Fatigue should resolve completely by 4 weeks

options.label: B
options.text: No fatigue should occur in young patients

options.label: E
options.text: Prolonged fatigue lasting weeks to months is common

questions.initialExplanation: Prolonged fatigue for weeks to months is common after mononucleosis and does not mean chronic fatigue syndrome or treatment failure.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- Prolonged fatigue that may wax and wane for weeks to months is a common complaint after infectious mononucleosis. This fatigue syndrome can persist beyond the acute illness and is a recognized feature of EBV infection recovery.

- Complete resolution by 4 weeks is not typical - prolonged fatigue is common. While fatigue can be prolonged, progression to chronic fatigue syndrome is not inevitable. Persistent fatigue does not indicate treatment failure - it represents normal recovery pattern. Fatigue occurs at all ages and is not age-dependent.

---

questions.stem: A 12-year-old child presents with fever of 38.5°C for 4 weeks. The fever occurs daily, usually in the evening, and is associated with night sweats and weight loss of 3 kg. The child appears ill but has no localizing symptoms. Multiple visits to healthcare providers have not identified the cause despite basic investigations including complete blood count, chest X-ray, and urine analysis. According to the standard definition, what additional criteria must be met for this to qualify as classic FUO?

options.label: B
options.text: More than 2 outpatient visits or 1 week of hospital evaluation

options.label: C
options.text: Failure to respond to empirical antibiotics

questions.initialExplanation: The classic FUO definition: fever ≥3 weeks with more than two outpatient visits or a week of in-hospital work-up without a diagnosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- Classic FUOQ is defined as fever documented by a healthcare provider for which the cause cannot be identified after 3 weeks of evaluation as an outpatient OR after 1 week of evaluation in the hospital. The child needs either additional outpatient visits or hospital admission to meet the full definition.

- The standard definition is 3 weeks, not 6 weeks. Response to empirical antibiotics is not part of the

FUO definition. Hospitalization is one option but not required - outpatient evaluation for 3 weeks also qualifies. Specialist consultation is not part of the formal definition.

---

questions.stem: A 8-year-old child with prolonged fever underwent extensive outpatient investigations with no diagnosis. The child is now admitted to the hospital for further evaluation. The pediatric team is planning a systematic approach to identify the cause of FUO. Which of the following should be the emphasis in the initial hospital evaluation?

options.label: A
options.text: Ordering a comprehensive battery of tests immediately

options.label: E
options.text: Careful observation, detailed history, and focused physical examination

questions.initialExplanation: Initial in-hospital evaluation of FUO focuses on close observation, detailed history and a targeted clinical examination.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- The cornerstone of FUO evaluation is careful observation, talking to the patient, and thinking about the case. A detailed history and thorough physical examination are more valuable than extensive testing in many cases. "There is no substitute for observing the patient, talking to him and thinking about him."

- Avoid indiscriminately ordering a large battery of tests - this wastes resources and may lead to false positives. Empirical antibiotic treatment should generally be avoided until diagnosis is established, except in specific circumstances. Multiple specialist referrals without initial systematic evaluation can lead to fragmentation of care. Invasive procedures should be reserved for when indicated by clinical findings, not done routinely.

---

questions.stem: A 10-year-old child with FUO has the following additional history: fever, joint pain in knees and ankles, and a history of recent travel to a farm where the family consumed unpasteurized milk. The physical examination reveals a new heart murmur that wasn't present previously. The child appears pale and has tender lymph nodes. Which investigation should be prioritized based on this history?

options.label: D
options.text: CT scan of chest and abdomen

questions.initialExplanation: Joint pain and fever with unpasteurized milk exposure and a new murmur: suspect brucellosis with endocarditis; the priority is an echocardiogram.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- The history of unpasteurized milk consumption, fever, heart murmur, and systemic symptoms is highly suggestive of bacterial endocarditis, most likely from Brucella or other zoonotic infections.

‘     Echocardiography should be prioritized to evaluate for vegetations and assess cardiac involvement.

- Joint aspiration might be considered but cardiac involvement is more immediately concerning. Bone marrow biopsy is invasive and not first-line for this presentation. CT scan might be useful but cardiac evaluation should be immediate priority. Autoimmune panel is less urgent than evaluating for bacterial endocarditis.

---

questions.stem: A 15-year-old teenager with FUO has been hospitalized for 1 week with no diagnosis. The child has developed respiratory distress and appears toxic. Recent chest X-ray shows a new infiltrate, and blood cultures are pending. The medical team is considering empirical therapy. What is the most appropriate indication for empirical treatment in FUO?

options.label: B
options.text: Patients who have been hospitalized for 1 week

options.label: C
options.text: Clinically deteriorating patients with suspicion of bacteremia or sepsis

options.label: E
options.text: Children who have failed outpatient therapy

questions.initialExplanation: Empiric treatment in FUO is justified in clinically deteriorating patients with suspected bacteremia or sepsis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- Empirical therapy is indicated in clinically deteriorating patients with suspicion of bacteremia or sepsis. This is one of the specific situations where treatment before diagnosis is warranted, particularly when the patient appears toxic or is clinically deteriorating.

- Not all hospitalized FUO patients need empirical therapy - this should be selective. Duration of hospitalization alone is not an indication. Elevated inflammatory markers alone don't mandate

empirical treatment. Failed outpatient therapy alone doesn't justify empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old child with FUO has persistent fever and elevated inflammatory markers. The child has been receiving multiple antibiotics empirically in different hospitals. Current blood tests show elevated liver enzymes, and the child appears jaundiced. No source of infection has been identified despite extensive testing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: FUO with jaundice and raised liver enzymes after multiple antibiotics with no infectious source: most likely drug-induced hepatitis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- Drug-induced hepatitis is highly likely given the history of multiple antibiotics and no infectious source identified. This represents a common iatrogenic cause of FUO, where the treatment itself becomes the problem.

- While viral hepatitis is possible, the temporal relationship to multiple antibiotics suggests drug- induced. Autoimmune hepatitis doesn't typically present this acutely. Wilson disease is chronic and wouldn't present with this acute timeline. No evidence of ongoing sepsis despite extensive investigations.

---

questions.stem: A 9-year-old child with FUO has been thoroughly investigated with normal basic tests. The child's fever pattern is unusual, occurring only when parents are present and not when alone with nurses. The child appears comfortable when alone but becomes febrile when parents visit. Temperature recordings by nursing staff consistently show normal values. What is the most likely explanation for this presentation?
questions.initialExplanation: A fever present only when parents are around and not recorded by nurses: factitious fever.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- Factitious fever (factitious disorder imposed on another, in this case likely by parents) is suggested by the pattern of fever only when parents are present, normal temperatures when alone with nurses, and the unusual fever pattern. This is one of the recognized causes of FUO that defies diagnosis.

- Drug fever would be more consistent and wouldn't show this pattern of occurring only with parents. Familial Mediterranean fever has characteristic patterns and genetic association. Kawasaki disease would have typical clinical features and laboratory findings. Tuberculosis would show more consistent fever pattern and likely have other signs.

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old child with FUO has undergone Level 1 investigations (CBC, ESR, CRP, metabolic panel, cultures, chest X-ray) with normal results. The child has persistent fever but appears otherwise well. The medical team is planning the next level of investigation. What should be included in Level 2 investigations for FUO?

options.label: B
options.text: Echocardiography, CT scan, bone scan, serology, autoimmune tests

questions.initialExplanation: Second-tier FUO tests: echocardiography, CT, bone scan, serology and autoimmune tests.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- Level 2 investigations for FUO include echocardiography (for endocarditis), CT scans (for occult abscesses), bone scan (for osteomyelitis), serology (for viral infections), and autoimmune tests (for connective tissue diseases). These are more specialized tests used when Level 1 investigations are unrevealing.

- Tissue biopsy and endoscopy represent Level 3 investigations, not Level 2. Bone marrow biopsy is not typically Level 2 and is more invasive. Repeating Level 1 tests is not indicated when results are normal. MRI of brain alone is insufficient for systematic FUO evaluation.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child with FUO has been admitted for evaluation. The child has no localizing signs but appears ill with persistent high fevers. The medical team is deciding on empirical treatment while awaiting culture results. Which of the following is an appropriate indication for empirical therapy in FUO?

options.label: C
options.text: All children with FUO for 3 weeks

options.label: D
options.text: Critically ill child with possible disseminated tuberculosis

options.label: E
options.text: Patients who have had negative cultures

questions.initialExplanation: Among indications for empiric therapy in FUO: a critically ill child with possible disseminated TB.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- Antituberculosis drugs in critically ill children with possible disseminated tuberculosis is an appropriate indication for empirical therapy in FUO. This represents a situation where delay in treatment could be life-threatening and the benefits outweigh the risks.

- Nonsteroidal agents for presumed JIA is appropriate, but the question asks for antituberculosis drugs specifically. Duration alone is not an indication for empirical therapy. Elevated inflammatory markers alone don't justify empirical treatment. Negative cultures alone don't indicate need for empirical therapy.

---


## Varicella - Zoster

questions.stem: A 66-year-old girl is brought in with a sudden fever and rash spreading from her trunk to her face and extremities. The pediatrician suspects chickenpox. What are the characteristic clinical features of primary varicella infection:

options.label: A
options.text: Maculopapular nature of skin rash over the trunk

options.label: B
options.text: Different stages of maturation of the skin lesions at the same time

options.label: C
options.text: Spiking fever during the course of disease

questions.initialExplanation: The hallmark of varicella: skin lesions at different stages of maturation at the same time (macules, papules, vesicles and crusts together).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Primary varicella infection, commonly known as chickenpox , is caused by the varicella-zoster virus (VZV) . lt is a highly contagious disease that typically affects children and presents with characteristic clinical features. The hallmark feature of chickenpox is the presence of skin lesions in different stages of maturation simultaneously .

---

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy, post renal transplant on immunosuppressants, is exposed to a classmate with chickenpox. He has no prior varicella infection or vaccination. What is the most appropriate post- exposure prophylaxis?
questions.initialExplanation: An immunosuppressed patient (kidney transplant) exposed to varicella without immunity: post-exposure prophylaxis with varicella-zoster immune globulin (VZIG).
questions.detailedExplanation:
This immunocompromised child (post-renal transplant) is at high risk for severe, potentially fatal varicella and requires immediate post-exposure prophylaxis. Varicella-zoster immune globulin (VZIG) provides passive immunity through neutralizing antibodies and is recommended for high-risk susceptible individuals, including immunocompromised patients. It should be administered within 10 days of exposure (ideally within 96 hours) to prevent or modify disease severity. The varicella vaccine is contraindicated as it is live attenuated and could cause disseminated infection in immunocompromised hosts. Acyclovir prophylaxis is less effective than passive immunization for severely immunocompromised patients. No prophylaxis is dangerous, as mortality reaches

15-20% in this population. VZIG provides immediate protection while avoiding the risks of live vaccines or inadequate antiviral prophylaxis in this vulnerable patient.

---

questions.stem: For the past three days, an 11-year-old white male has had several small, circular lesions on the left side of his lower forehead and nose, extending to the tip of his nose. On examination you note grouped vesicles, several of which are scabbed. The patient also complains of burning pain in the area of the lesions. He had a sore throat with a fever 5 days ago, but is now improved. His stepfather reports he is up-to-date on immunizations, but a specific immunization record is not available. His history and examination are otherwise unremarkable. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.initialExplanation: Clustered vesicles on the forehead and nose with burning pain in a one-sided dermatomal distribution = herpes zoster (shingles).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Clustered circular lesions with accompanying dysesthesia in a dermatone are characteristic of herpes zoster, which may occur after a stressful event or infection in both children and adults. For herpes zoster to occur, there must be a previous primary varicella infection or immunization. Herpes zoster is less likely to be associated with significant post-herpetic neuraigia in children than in adults.

---

questions.stem: A 16-year-old immunocompetent student develops varicella. Her mother asks about the contagious period and when she can return to school safely. What is the period of highest transmission risk for varicella?

options.label: A
options.text: From 2 days before rash onset until all lesions are crusted

options.label: C
options.text: From 3 days before rash until vesicles appear

options.label: D
options.text: From the first day of fever until the rash disappears

options.label: E
options.text: From rash onset until 1 week after crusting

questions.initialExplanation: Varicella is contagious from about 2 days before the rash until all lesions have crusted; the answer is from 2 days before rash onset until all lesions crust.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Varicella is most contagious from 2 days before the onset of rash until all vesicles have crusted. This represents the period of highest virus shedding and transmission risk. The virus is transmitted through airborne particles and direct contact with infected lesions.

- The contagious period extends beyond day 5 of rash until crusting is complete. The contagious period starts 2 days before rash onset, not 3 days. Transmission risk decreases significantly after vesicles crust. The contagious period ends when crusting is complete, not 1 week later.

---

questions.stem: A mother calls you frantic because she has just been diagnosed with varicella (chicken pox). She delivered a term infant 7 days ago that appears to be eating, stooling, and urinating without difficulty. The child has been afebrile and seems to be doing well. Which of the following is the most appropriate step in management?

options.label: A
options.text: Isolate the infant from the mother.

options.label: B
options.text: Hospitalize the infant in the isolation ward.

options.label: D
options.text: Administer varicella-zoster immunoglobulin to the infant.

options.label: E
options.text: Advise the mother to continue regular well-baby care for the infant.

questions.initialExplanation: A mother who developed varicella 7 days after delivery (not around delivery) and a healthy baby with maternal antibodies: continue normal care without isolation or drugs.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Per CDC recommendations, varicella-zoster immunoglobulin (VZIG) should be administered to the infant immediately after delivery if the mother had the onset of varicella within 5 days prior to delivery, and immediately upon diagnosis if her chicken pox started within 2 days after delivery. If untreated, about half of these infants will develop serious varicella as early as 1 day of age. If a normal full-term newborn is exposed to chicken pox 2 or more days postnatally, VZIG and isolation are not necessary because these babies appear to be at no greater risk for complications than older children. Acyclovir may be used in infants at risk for severe varicella, such as those infants exposed perinatally.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old unimmunized child has fever of 104°F (40°C) and cropped vesicles on the trunk with scattered scabbed lesions. Which of the following infections is the likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: An unvaccinated child with high fever and successive vesicles on the trunk with crusted lesions = varicella.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Of the so-called common childhood diseases listed in this question, primary varicella infection (or chickenpox) is most likely to present with a generalized, pruritic vesicular rash and mild fever. The typical exanthem appears first on the scalp, face, or trunk. New crops of lesions develop over a 1-7

day period. Progression from vesicle to pustule to crusted scab occurs quickly such that lesions of all stages are present after the first 48 hours.

---

questions.stem: A 3-month-old infant is brought to the emergency department with severe varicella. Him mother developed varicella 3 days before delivery and the baby was born with widespread vesicular rash, respiratory distress, and hepatomegaly. What is the mortality rate for this presentation of neonatal varicella?
questions.initialExplanation: Neonatal varicella when the mother is infected 3 days before delivery carries a high mortality, up to 30% per the source.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Neonatal varicella acquired perinatally when the mother develops primary varicella infection around delivery has a mortality rate of approximately 30%. The severe form includes widespread rash, pneumonia, hepatitis, and can be fatal without appropriate management.

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old unimmunized child presents with fever and vesicular rash. You notice about 300 lesions, some of which were crusted. You suspect varicella infection. Which of the following is a TRUE statement about varicella?

options.label: A
options.text: It has an incubation period of 5-7 days.

options.label: B
options.text: The rash is confluent, centrifugal, and pustular.

options.label: C
options.text: It is associated with Koplik spots.

options.label: D
options.text: There is a high risk of shingles.

options.label: E
options.text: It can cause visceral dissemination in the immunocompromised host.

questions.initialExplanation: Varicella can cause serious visceral dissemination in immunocompromised patients.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The rash of varicella follows an incubation period of 10-21 days. There is the onset of a very pruritic rash, with crops of lesions that begin as papules and progress to vesicles and finally crusted scabs. Typically, all three stages of skin lesions are identified on clinical examination. Fever usually is mild to moderate. While a generally self-limited and benign course is noted, severe disease may occur occasionally in the otherwise healthy host, especially adolescents and adults. A progressive and severe disease with visceral dissemination is seen in 30%—-50% of children with lymphoproliferative malignancies, solid tumors, or posttransplantation with the development of hepatitis, encephalitis, and

pneumonia. Fatal disease has also been reported in those treated with highdose corticosteroids and in those with other defects of T-cell function.

---

questions.stem: The mother of an 8-year-old boy with a history of biliary atresia, s/p liver transplant at 7 months of age, calls your clinic. Her son was at a sleepover party 2 nights ago with a friend who was diagnosed with chicken pox the next day. His current immunosuppression includes tacrolimus and prednisone. The mom reports her son is well, without any signs of illness. What is the appropriate management of this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Monitor for chicken pox lesions and give varicella immune globulin if he develops any

options.label: B
options.text: Measure serum IgM and IgG levels to varicella and prescribe immune globulin if IgM positive

options.label: C
options.text: Prescribe antibiotics to prevent superinfection of any developing varicella lesions

options.label: D
options.text: Administer varicella immune globulin and continue to monitor for signs of illness

options.label: E
options.text: Monitor for signs of chicken pox and treat symptoms of illness

questions.initialExplanation: A patient after liver transplant on immunosuppressants exposed to varicella: give varicella immune globulin (VZIG) and monitor for disease.
questions.detailedExplanation:
It is notable that the boy in this vignette received his transplant prior to his first birthday, thus it is unlikely that he ever received live-virus vaccines such as MMR and varicella. Consequently, it is imperative to administer the immune globulin as quickly as possible. Given the severity of infection that can occur in these patients, it is not appropriate to delay treatment by monitoring for symptoms or checking labs (Answers a, b, and d). An immunocompromised patient is at higher risk of bacterial superinfection of varicella lesions; however, until evidence of this occurs, it is not appropriate to prescribe antibiotics (Answer c).

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old immunocompetent child with varicella develops fever and increasing lethargy on day 4 of illness. His parents note worsening rash and breathing difficulty. Examination reveals extensive rash and signs of respiratory distress. What is the most likely complication and appropriate treatment?

options.label: A
options.text: Secondary bacterial pneumonia requiring IV antibiotics

questions.initialExplanation: Varicella with dyspnea and fever in an immunocompetent child: the likely complication is varicella pneumonitis; treat with IV acyclovir.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Varicella pneumonitis is a serious complication of varicella infection that can present with respiratory distress, fever, and constitutional symptoms. It requires intravenous acyclovir therapy as this is an invasive viral complication that benefits from systemic antiviral treatment.

- While bacterial pneumonia can occur, the timing and presentation suggest varicella pneumonitis. Cellulitis would present with localized erythema and warmth, not respiratory symptoms. Myocarditis is rare and would present with cardiac symptoms primarily. Menigoencephalitis would present with neurological symptoms rather than primaryrespiratory distress.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child with varicella develops painful, swollen, and red skin lesions on his arms that are warm to touch. The lesions have progressed beyond the typical vesicular stage and show signs of bacterial superinfection. What is the most likely causative organism and appropriate antibiotic choice?
questions.initialExplanation: Secondary bacterial infection of varicella lesions: the most common organisms are Staphylococcus aureus (and group A Strep); the chosen treatment here is oral dicloxacillin.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The most common complication of varicella is secondary bacterial infection, usually with Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes. S. aureus infections typically present with the described symptoms and are best treated with anti-staphylococcal penicillins like dicloxacillin.

- While Group A Streptococcus can cause skin infections, S. aureus is more common in varicella complications. Pseudomonas infections are uncommon in this setting and ciprofloxacin is not firstline.

This presentation suggests bacterial superinfection, not viral reactivation. Candida infection would present differently and is not the most common complication.

---

questions.stem: A 40-year-old pregnant woman at 18 weeks gestation develops varicella. She is concerned about potential fetal effects and asks about the risk of congenital varicella syndrome. What is the critical period for congenital varicella syndrome development?
questions.initialExplanation: The risk period for congenital varicella syndrome is the first 20 weeks of pregnancy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Congenital varicella syndrome results when a mother is infected with varicella during the first 20 weeks of pregnancy. This represents the period when the developing fetus is most susceptible to the teratogenic effects of VZV infection, leading to characteristic congenital abnormalities.

---

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman presents to your clinic at 26 weeks gestation. She is worried because 24 hours ago, she came in contact with a child who had chickenpox. Her pre-pregnancy IgG against chickenpox was negative, and she missed her prenatal chickenpox vaccine. On examination, she is asymptomatic. Which one of the following would be the next best step in management?

options.label: A
options.text: Check varicella zoster virus IgM level.

options.label: E
options.text: No action is needed because she is asymptomatic.

questions.initialExplanation: A 26-week non-immune pregnant woman exposed to varicella 24 hours ago: give varicella zoster immunoglobulin (VZIG) as prophylaxis for the mother.
questions.detailedExplanation:
In the absence of a postive IgG antibody in prenatal assessment, the patient should be informed of her susceptibility to varicella infection, and warned about risks of exposure to other individuals, who may have acute varicella.

If a susceptible pregnant woman is exposed to someone with chickenpox, serologic assessment for varicella zoster virus (VZV IgG) should be performed and varicella zoster immunoglobulin (VZIG) given as prophylactic treatment if the patient is within the 96 hours of exposure.

If >96 hours, the following patients should still be treated prophylactically with aciclovir (preferred) or valacilovir after exposure:

If in the second half of pregnancy

There is a history of an underlying lung disease

The woman is immunocompromised

The woman is smoker

The patient has no history of chickenpox or vaccination against VZV, and a prenatal IgG has been negative. For this patient serology is not required. Since she has presented within 96 hours of exposure, the next step in management would be treating her with prophylactic IVIG (VZIG).

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old child has completed varicella illness and all skin lesions have crusted over. The parents ask when their child can resume normal activities including contact sports. What is the appropriate recommendation regarding return to activities?

options.label: A
options.text: Can return immediately as lesions are crusted

options.label: B
options.text: Wait 1 week after crusting for full clearance

options.label: C
options.text: Wait 2 weeks after crusting for complete viral clearance

options.label: D
options.text: Avoid contact sports for 3-4 weeks due to splenomegaly risk

options.label: E
options.text: Resume all activities except swimming for 1 month

questions.initialExplanation: After all varicella lesions have crusted the child may return to activities immediately since the virus is no longer contagious.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Susceptible healthy children may be considered noncontagious after all lesions have crusted. Once crusting is complete, the risk of transmission is minimal and normal activities can be resumed. This represents the end of the infectious period for practical purposes.

- No additional waiting period is necessary once crusting is complete. The 2-week waiting period is not evidence-based for varicella. Splenomegaly is not a typical complication of varicella; this description fits infectious mononucleosis. Swimming restrictions are not specifically indicated once crusting is complete.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl develops a mild fever and itchy rash that started as small red spots on her scalp and face. Her mother notices the rash is spreading downward to her trunk and arms. The lesions have different appearances - some look like small water blisters while others have formed yellow-brown crusts. What is the characteristic sequence of lesion development in varicella?
questions.initialExplanation: Sequence of varicella lesions: macules, then papules, then vesicles, then crusts.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The typical exanthem of varicella begins as erythematous, pruritic macules that develop into papules and fluid-filled vesicles, followed by crusting. This sequence represents the characteristic progression of varicella lesions. The presence of all stages simultaneously is one of the most characteristic features.

- Pustules are not typically part of the varicella lesion sequence. Ulceration is not a normal stage in varicella lesion progression. Pustules appearing before vesicles is not characteristic of varicella. Vesicles appearing first is not the typical sequence.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old immunocompetent child with varicella develops joint swelling and pain in his knees and ankles. His parents notice he is reluctant to walk and appears uncomfortable. Examination reveals warm, swollen joints with limited range of motion. What is the most appropriate management approach for this complication?

options.label: A
options.text: IV antibiotic therapy for septic arthritis

questions.initialExplanation: Reactive arthritis accompanying varicella is treated supportively with anti-inflammatory drugs and is not a septic arthritis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Varicella can cause arthritis as a complication, which is typically viral and self-limiting. Management is supportive with anti-inflammatory medications, rest, and monitoring. The joint involvement is usually transient and resolves with the viral infection.

- IV antibiotics are not indicated for viral arthritis, Joint aspiration is not necessary for viral arthritis, Intra-articular steroids are not indicated for viral arthritis, Surgical drainage is unnecessary for viral joint inflammation.

---

questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy with leukemia on chemotherapy develops extensive varicella with more than 100 lesions involving multiple body regions, high fever, and respiratory symptoms. His mother asks about the specific treatment needed for his condition. What is the most appropriate antiviral therapy for this immunocompromised child with varicella?

options.label: A
options.text: Oral acyclovir 800 mg five times daily

options.label: C
options.text: Topical acyclovir cream applied to all lesions

options.label: D
options.text: Valacyclovir oral therapy, 1g three times daily

questions.initialExplanation: Severe disseminated varicella in a child with leukemia on chemotherapy: IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Immunocompromised patients with varicella should receive intravenous acyclovir at 10mg/kg every 8 hours. This is because they are at high risk for severe disease, disseminated infection, and complications. IV acyclovir provides adequate tissue penetration and viral suppression in immunocompromised hosts.

- Oral acyclovir is insufficient for severe immunocompromised disease, Topical therapy is inadequate for systemic viral infection, Valacyclovir may not provide sufficient dosing for severe disease, Immunocompromised patients require specific antiviral therapy.

---

questions.stem: A 9-month-old infant is brought to the pediatrician with a fever and rash. Her parents mention that the baby was exposed to an older sibling with chickenpox 14 days ago. The examination reveals a generalized vesicular rash with lesions in various stages of development. What is the incubation period for varicella in this case?
questions.initialExplanation: The incubation period of varicella is 10-21 days (up to 28 days after VZIG).
questions.detailedExplanation:
The incubation period for varicella is typically 10-21 days after exposure. In this case, the 14-day interval between exposure and symptom onset falls within the expected incubation period. This period can vary slightly depending on age and immune status of the exposed individual.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old child with varicella develops severe headache, neck stiffness, and altered mental status on day 6 of illness. His parents report he seems confused and is complaining of sensitivity to light. Examination reveals signs of meningeal irritation and decreased consciousness. What is the most likely complication and appropriate investigation?

options.label: B
options.text: Bacterial meningitis - Start empirical antibiotics only

options.label: C
options.text: Varicella meningoencephalitis - Perform lumbar puncture after stabilization

options.label: D
options.text: Reye syndrome - Check ammonia and liver enzymes

questions.initialExplanation: Headache, neck stiffness and confusion on day 6 of varicella: varicella meningoencephalitis; evaluate with a lumbar puncture after stabilization.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Varicella meningoencephalitis is a known complication of varicella infection that can present with headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, and altered mental status. Lumbar puncture should be performed after stabilization to confirm the diagnosis and rule out bacterial meningitis, which would require immediate antibiotic therapy.

- While bacterial meningitis must be considered, the temporal relationship to varicella suggests viral meningoencephalitis, CT scan before lumbar puncture is indicated when focal neurological signs are present, Mannitol is used for cerebral edema but the primary concern is encephalitis, Febrile seizures typically occur with high fever and are usually brief.

---


## Measles | Rubella | Mumps

questions.stem: An 8-year-old girl is brought in with fever, headache, and swollen salivary glands. Which of the following complications is more in favor of mumps than other viral infections?
questions.initialExplanation: What favors mumps over other viruses is aseptic meningitis, not rash or otitis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The clinical presentation of an 8-year-old girl with fever, headache, and swollen salivary glands is highly suggestive of mumps , which is caused by the mumps virus (a paramyxovirus). Mumps is well- known for its association with certain complications, particularly aseptic meningitis , which is more characteristic of mumps than other viral infections.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old unvaccinated child presents with 5 days of fever, cough, and coryza. A rash appeared yesterday, starting on the face and neck and spreading to the trunk and limbs. On exam, the child is febrile and irritable, with conjunctivitis, a generalized maculopapular rash, and white spots with red halos on the buccal mucosa near the molars. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Fever, cough, coryza, conjunctivitis and white buccal spots (Koplik) then a rash starting on the face = measles.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This presentation is classic for measles: unvaccinated child, prodromal fever with the "3 C's" (cough, coryza, conjunctivitis), followed by a maculopapular rash spreading cephalocaudally from face to limbs. The pathognomonic finding is Koplik spots—white lesions with red halos on the buccal mucosa near the molars—which appear 1-2 days before the rash and confirm the diagnosis. Erythema infectiosum causes a " slapped cheek" rash without Koplik spots or prominent respiratory symptoms. Roseola presents with rash appearing after fever defervescence, typically in younger infants. Rubella causes a milder rash with postauricular lymphadenopathy but lacks Koplik spots and severe prodrome. Varicella produces vesicular lesions in different stages, primarily on the trunk.

---

questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy presents with fever, headache, and painful swelling of the parotid glands. He is diagnosed clinically with mumps. Which of the following is the MOST likely complication of his condition?
questions.initialExplanation: The most common complication of mumps in children is aseptic meningitis; orchitis is more common after puberty.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Aseptic meningitis is the most common complication of mumps across all age groups, occurring in 10-15% of cases. While orchitis is frequent in post-pubertal males (15-30%), a 12-year-old may be pre-pubertal or early pubertal, making meningitis the more universally likely complication regardless of pubertal status. Mumps virus has neurotropic properties, causing lymphocytic pleocytosis with headache, neck stiffness, and fever that typically resolve without sequelae. Pancreatitis (~4%), sensorineural hearing loss (1-4%), and Guillain-Barré syndrome are recognized but less frequent complications. Recognizing aseptic meningitis as the predominant complication guides appropriate evaluation for meningeal signs and cerebrospinal fluid analysis when indicated. Supportive management with analgesics and hydration is usually sufficient.

---

questions.stem: The mother of a 6-month-old child seeing you for a well visit, requests immunization against measles as she has heard it is present in the community. At what age should the first dose of live attenuated measles vaccine (as MMR) be routinely administered in the absence of a community measles outbreak?

options.label: E
options.text: At the time of school entry

questions.initialExplanation: The first MMR dose is routinely given at 12-15 months (outside an outbreak).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Ordinarily, the first dose of live attenuated measles vaccine (combined with mumps and rubella as the MMR vaccine) should be administered between 12 and 15 months of age to maximize the likelihood that transplacentally acquired antibodies have disappeared completely from the child’s blood. Otherwise, these antibodies may blunt the infant's immunologic response to the vaccine. On the other hand, administration of the vaccine should not be delayed much beyond 15 months because of the seriousness of measles infection. It is recommended that a second dose of the vaccine be given when the child enters elementary school. In areas where, or at times when, measles is epidemic, it is recommended that an initial dose of monovalent measles vaccine be given as early as 6 months of age, followed by the two MMRs as noted.

---

questions.stem: A 17-month-old nonimmunized child has had fever for 4 days and now has a maculopapular rash. She is seen in clinic and diagnosed as having measles. There is a 4-month-old sibling at home. What is the appropriate management for the sibling?

options.label: A
options.text: immediate immunization with live attenuated measles vaccine

options.label: B
options.text: immediate immunization with killed measles vaccine

options.label: C
options.text: a single dose of immune globulin (IG)

options.label: D
options.text: IG plus live attenuated measles vaccine

questions.initialExplanation: A 4-month-old (too young for vaccine) exposed to measles: give immune globulin (IG) as post-exposure prophylaxis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Active immunization with live measles vaccine at the time of contact is too late to assure protection. Additionally, children should not receive the vaccine before the age of 6 months to assure an adequate immunologic response. The recommended management of susceptible siblings of a contact case is the use of a preventive dose of gamma globulin (0.25 mg/kg) and later immunization with the live-virus vaccine. In the past, when most women had natural measles infection, maternal IgG levels of measles antibody were very high, and transplacental IgG afforded the young infant relatively strong protection. Cases of measles infection in this agegroup were often milder than in older children. Such is not the case now. Many mothers have low levels of measles antibody (from immunization rather than natural infection), and their infants are susceptible to severe measles infection.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old presents with a 2-day history of fever, conjunctivitis, hacking cough, and congestion. According to the mother, there is no “bark” and there is no “whoop” with his cough. Examination of his mouth is notable for pinpoint white dots on a red base. The patient moved 3 years ago from Australia at 1 year of age. His parents have refused immunizations. Which vitamin supplement would you include in your treatment plan?
questions.initialExplanation: Measles: give vitamin A as part of treatment since it reduces complications and mortality.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The child in this vignette has measles. The lesions in the mouth are Koplik spots, which are pathognomonic for measles. Although measles usually presents with a rash, the rash usually appears after the fever, cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis. Vitamin A deficiency is associated with decreased resistance of infection. In addition, although vitamin A deficiency is rare in the United States, there is an association between measles infection and vitamin A deficiency. As a result, the American Academy of Pediatrics recommends consideration of treatment with vitamin A for all children hospitalized for measles.

---

questions.stem: Twelve children in a local Amish community have contracted a similar infection. They all present with a rising fever, conjunctivitis, cough and cold symptoms, and a maculopapular rash that appears on days 3 to 4 of fevers and that spreads from the hairline downward within a 24-hour span. All 12 children attend school together and 11 of the 12 are unvaccinated. One of the boys in the group is noted to have a few white lesions on his oral mucosa surrounded with red areolae. Which of the following is the most common complication of this disease process?
questions.initialExplanation: The most common complication of measles is acute otitis media; SSPE is rare and appears years later.
questions.detailedExplanation:
All of the answers listed can be complications of measles infection, which is the viral cause of the outbreak in the clinical scenario above. Unlike measles, rubella is generally without a cough and has a milder course. The oral lesions described in the case (Koplik spots) are pathognomonic for measles. Of the complications listed, otitis media (and more generally pyogenic bacterial infections) is relatively common following measles infection. Some sources argue for universal antibiotic prophylaxis following measles infection, although this has only been shown to decrease the incidence of pneumonia but not mortality. It must also be weighed against increasing microbial resistance. Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis is quite rare with a case rate of 1:10,000 cases. Corneal ulcers following measles are uncommon in children who are not malnourished (particularly as regards vitamin A). Myocarditis is rare, although transient electrocardiographic abnormalities are common. Spontaneous bleeding is rare, although mild thrombocytopenia is not uncommon.

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old unvaccinated child is exposed to measles at school. His parents are concerned about prevention and ask about post-exposure prophylaxis. What is the most appropriate post-exposure intervention for this child?

options.label: C
options.text: Immune globulin within 6 days of exposure

questions.initialExplanation: Post-exposure prophylaxis for an unvaccinated 7-year-old: MMR vaccine immediately (within 72 hours) per the source, and IG for those who cannot be vaccinated.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Post-exposure prophylaxis with MMR vaccine within 72 hours of exposure is effective for preventing or modifying measles in susceptible individuals. This is the preferred intervention for healthy children over 12 months of age.

- Vitamin A is for treatment, not prophylaxis, Immune globulin is reserved for infants <12 months or immunocompromised patients, No specific antiviral therapy exists for measles, Isolation is for confirmed cases, not exposed individuals.

---

questions.stem: A 14-year-old boy develops repetitive attacks of myoclonic jerks not associated with loss of consciousness. He has been experienced poor academic experience, irritability, reduced attention span, and temper outbursts few months ago. He has a history of measles infection at the age of 4 year. EEG shows suppression-burst episodes. Of the following, his cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) MOST likely reveals :
questions.initialExplanation: A teenager with myoclonic jerks, school and behavior decline, a history of childhood measles and EEG with suppression-burst = SSPE; the CSF shows elevated measles antibody.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis in SSPE reveals normal cells but elevated IgG and IgM antibody titers in dilutions >1:8.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl has been exposed to an index case with measles in the nursery home 4 days ago. She doesn’t receive any vaccine yet. Of the following, the MOST appropriate management to prevent or modify infection is :
questions.initialExplanation: An unvaccinated girl exposed to measles 4 days ago (beyond 72 hours): give immunoglobulin to modify or prevent disease.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The vaccine is effective in prevention or modification of measles if given within 72 hr of exposure. Immunoglobulin may be given up to 6 days after exposure to prevent or modify infection.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy presents with a 3-day history of a cough, coryzal symptoms and conjunctivitis. He then develops a high fever and a blotchy red maculo-papular rash which starts behind his ears and spreads to his face and then to the rest of his body. the most likely diagnosis is :
questions.initialExplanation: Cough, coryza and conjunctivitis then high fever and a rash starting behind the ears, then face and body = measles.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Measles is an infection of the respiratory system caused by paramyxovirus, which is an RNA virus. Symptoms include fever, cough, runny nose, red eyes and a generalised maculo-papular erythematous rash which starts behind the ears and spreads sequentially to the face, arms, chest, abdomen, back and legs. Koplik’s spots in the mouth are pathognomonic, but are usually only seen in the prodromal phase and have usually disappeared by the time the rash appears. The diagnosis can be confirmed by serology. Complications include interstitial pneumonitis, encephalomyelitis and subacute sclerosing panencephalitis.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child with measles develops a red maculopapular rash that started on the forehead and behind the ears. The rash has spread downward to the trunk and extremities. The child's fever is very high and she appears very ill. What is the pattern and progression of measles rash development?

options.label: A
options.text: Begins on extremities, spreads to trunk, fades randomly

options.label: B
options.text: Begins on trunk, spreads upward, fades from top down

options.label: C
options.text: Begins on face, spreads to trunk, fades within 3 days

options.label: D
options.text: Begins on forehead, spreads downward, fades from bottom up

options.label: E
options.text: Begins on trunk and face simultaneously, spreads uniformly

questions.initialExplanation: The measles rash starts at the forehead and behind the ears and spreads downward. The source's answer D says it fades from bottom to top, whereas references usually say it fades in the order it appeared; check the original.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Measles rash typically begins on the forehead, behind the ears, and upper neck as red maculopapular eruption, then spreads downward to torso and extremities. After reaching its peak, the rash fades in the same progression as it evolved, from the top downward.

- The rash doesn't start on the trunk or spread upward, Rash lasts longer than 3 days and follows specific pattern, The progression is not random - it follows specific downward spread, The rash doesn't start simultaneously on multiple areas.

---

questions.stem: A mother brings her 7-year-old son who has measles and wants to know if the child needs to be excluded from school. The diagnosis was made when the typical rash developed 6 days ago and he has not attended his class since then. The teacher has informed her that all children in the class has been immunized against measles. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate advice?

options.label: B
options.text: He should be excluded from school for a total period of 14 days after the rash.

options.label: C
options.text: He should be excluded for another 4 days.

options.label: D
options.text: He shoudl receive MMR vaccine before he can go back to school.

options.label: E
options.text: He can go to school when the rash completely resolves.

questions.initialExplanation: A measles patient is isolated from 4 days before the rash to 4 days after; 6 days after the rash the contagious period is over, so no extra isolation is needed.
questions.detailedExplanation:
All children with measles should be excluded from school for at least 4 days after the onset of the rash.

Immunized and immune contacts are not excluded. Non-immunized contacts of a case are to be excluded from child care until 14 days after the first day of appearance of rash in the last case, unless immunized within 72 hours of first contact during the infectious period with the first case. All immunocompromised children should be excluded until

14 days after the first day of appearance of rash in the last case.

Since more than 4 days has passed since the onset of the rash no more exclusion is required and he can go back to school.

Vaccination is not indicated anymore because this child will have life-long immunity to measles. However, MMR vaccine should still be given for protection against rubella and mumps at due time.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child has been diagnosed with acute lymphoblastic leukaemia two years ago and has been in remission since the treatment completed. Which of the following vaccines can not been given to this child?
questions.initialExplanation: Live vaccines such as MMR must not be given to an immunocompromised child; the source's answer is that MMR is the vaccine not given to this child.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has a history of leukaemia and thus is considered immunosuppressed. All live vaccines are contraindicated in patients with a history of immunosuppression. These live vaccines include Measles, mumps, rubella (MMR combined vaccine), Rotavirus, Chickenpox (Varicella Zoster) and Yellow fever vaccine. All other vaccines in the list such as DPT, tetanus toxoid, influenza and inactivated polio are inactivated vaccines and are safe is used in this clinical situation.

---

questions.stem: An 8-month-old infant with measles is hospitalized. The medical team is planning isolation precautions for infection control. What is the appropriate duration of isolation for measles patients?

options.label: A
options.text: From rash onset until fever resolves

options.label: B
options.text: From 3 days before to 4 days after rash onset

questions.initialExplanation: Measles isolation period: from 3-4 days before the rash until 4 days after it appears.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Measles patients are infectious from 3 days before rash onset until 4-6 days after the rash appears. This represents the period of highest transmission risk, and isolation precautions should be maintained during this timeframe.

- Isolation is not based on fever resolution, Unlike varicella, crusting is not the end point for measles

isolation, The 7-day duration doesn't match the infectious period, IgM testing is not used to determine isolation duration.

---

questions.stem: A 10-month-old infant is exposed to measles. The parents ask about prevention since the child hasn't received the measles vaccine yet. What is the most appropriate prophylaxis for this infant?
questions.initialExplanation: A 10-month-old unvaccinated infant exposed to measles: give immune globulin within 5-6 days of exposure.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Infants younger than 12 months who are exposed to measles should receive immune globulin (0.25 ml/kg IM) within 5 days of exposure. This provides passive immunity and can prevent or modify the infection in this high-risk age group.

- MMR vaccine is not typically given before 12 months of age, Vitamin A is for treatment, not prophylaxis, Acyclovir is not effective for measles prevention, Isolation is for confirmed cases, not prophylaxis.

---

questions.stem: The child shown below presents with a 3-day history of malaise, fever to 41.1°C (106°F), cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis. He then develops erythematous, maculopapular rash pictured. He is noted to have white pinpoint lesions on a bright red buccal mucosa in the area opposite his lower molars. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Fever 41°C, cough, coryza, conjunctivitis and a maculopapular rash with white buccal spots near the molars (Koplik) = measles.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The picture and clinical history presented are most common for the diagnosis of measles (rubeola). This is an uncommon disease in areas where immunization rates are high, but sporadic outbreaks do occur. The rash typically lasts 6 days. Complications are common, including pneumonia, laryngitis, myocarditis, and encephalitis.

Parvovirus B19 causes erythema infectiosum (fifth disease), which presents with low-grade fever, headache, and mild upper respiratory infection (URI) symptoms; the rash is “slapped cheek” in appearance. Rubella in this age of child would present with mild URI symptoms, retroauricular, posterior cervical and postoccipital lymphadenopathy, and then a diffuse erythematous macular-papular rash that clears in about 72 hours. Herpes, depending on where it presents, usually is found to have thin-walled vesicles on an erythematous bases. Varicella presents with fever, malaise, headache, moderate fever 37.8°C to 38.9°C (100°F to 102°F), and then crops of intensely pruritic red macules that evolve into fluid-filled vesicles.

---

questions.stem: A mother comes with her son who has measles rash for 6 days and he has been at home since the onset of rash.She is asking when he can return to school. What is the most appropriate response?

options.label: D
options.text: Arrange measles serology before any school exclusion

questions.initialExplanation: After 6 days from the onset of the measles rash the child is no longer contagious and may return to school now.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has developed measles rash and he already spent 6 days at home since the onset of rash. Usually school exclusion is recommended for 4 days from the onset of rash in a measles case.

If there is any doubt, urgent measles serology can be arranged. Immune and immunised contacts are not excluded. Non-immunised contacts are excluded from childcare until 14 days after the rash onset. All immune suppressed children should be excluded until 14 days after rash onset in the last case in the facility.

Calling infectious disease is not usually required as diagnosis is usually very obvious with typical measles rash.

---

questions.stem: A 21-year-old woman has just delivered a term infant. She has had only one visit to her obstetrician, and that was at about 6 weeks of pregnancy. She provides her laboratory results from that visit. The delivered infant is microce-phalic, and has cataracts, a heart murmur, and hepatosplenomegaly. Your further evaluation of the child demonstrates thrombocytopenia, mild hemolytic anemia, and, on the echocardiogram, patent ductus arteriosus and peripheral pulmonary artery stenosis. Which of the following maternal laboratory tests done at 6 weeks of gestation is likely to explain the findings in this child?

options.label: B
options.text: Positive rapid plasma reagin (RPR) with negative Microhemagglutination Treponema pallidum test (MHATP)

questions.initialExplanation: Microcephaly, cataract, murmur (PDA and pulmonary stenosis) and hepatosplenomegaly: congenital rubella; the explanation is the mother's negative rubella titer (not immune).
questions.detailedExplanation:
When German measles (rubella) occurs during the first 2 months of pregnancy, it has a severe effect on the fetus, including cardiac defects, cataracts, and glaucoma. The most common cardiac defects are patent ductus arteriosus, which can be accompanied by peripheral pulmonary artery stenosis, and atrial and ventricular septal defects. Myriad other complications vary in incidence with the timing of the infection during pregnancy, including thrombocytopenia, hepatosplenomegaly, hepatitis, hemolytic anemia, microcephaly, and a higher risk of developing insulindependent diabetes mellitus. The mother’s negative rubella titer early in the pregnancy indicates she is susceptible to the infection and its sequelae; her titer undoubtedly now is positive.

A positive hepatitis B surface antibody indicates successful vaccination or old, resolved infection. The positive RPR (a screening test for syphilis) with negative MHATP (the confirmatory test for syphilis) points away from this TORCH infection, but can be associated with a variety of conditions, such as systemic lupus erythematosus or other collagen vascular diseases. The triple screen, usually done at 16 to 18 weeks’ gestation, identifies infants at risk for conditions such as Down syndrome or neural tube defects. The positive varicella titer indicates either previous natural infection or successful vaccination.

---

questions.stem: You were called to the neonatal nursery to see an infant with the following features: growth retardation, rash, and absent red reflexes. On your examination, the baby is very small, with bluish purpuric skin lesions, and obvious cataracts. The baby also has a heart murmur. You suspect congenital infection. What is the most likely etiology?
questions.initialExplanation: Growth delay, blueberry-like purpuric rash, cataract and murmur = rubella (congenital rubella).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Infants congenitally infected with rubella excrete the virus in urine and pharyngeal secretions and can be infectious for many weeks or months. Such infants pose a definite hazard to nonimmune family members, caretakers, as well as medical and nursing personnel. Pregnant females who are not certain of their rubella immunity status should not handle these infants or their secretions. Infants with perinatally acquired HIV are generally asymptomatic at birth. An infant with congenital CMV and toxoplasmosis may have a similar presentation to congenital rubella, although cataracts and congenital heart disease are not typical manifestations. In addition, patients with toxoplasmosis may have scattered cerebral calcifications, while patients with CMV may have periventricular calcifications.

---

questions.stem: You are counseling a primigravid woman who has been found to be rubella nonimmune on prenatal laboratory evaluation. She asks you if her fetus is at risk for malformations. When is maternal infection with rubella virus most commonly associated with congenital defects?

options.label: A
options.text: in the first 4 weeks of gestation

options.label: C
options.text: in the third or fourth month

options.label: E
options.text: anytime during pregnancy or B? Infection in the first 4 weeks can cause severe defects, but many such pregnancies are lost spontaneously

questions.initialExplanation: The highest risk of congenital rubella defects is in the first month of pregnancy, and many such pregnancies miscarry.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Congenital malformations, stillborns, and abortions all have been reported with rubella infection during pregnancy. The congenital rubella syndrome consists of ophthalmologic, cardiac, auditory, and neurologic abnormalities with rates as high as 85% if infection occurs in the first 4 weeks of gestation, decreasing to 20%—30% during the second month, and 5% during the third or fourth month. These infants may continue to excrete rubella virus for 1 year or more after birth and pose a risk of infection for susceptible hosts.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old immunocompetent child with measles develops fever, ear pain, and decreased hearing. Examination reveals a bulging tympanic membrane with purulent discharge. What is the most likely complication and appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.text: Viral otitis media requiring supportive care

options.label: D
options.text: Sensorineural hearing loss requiring audiology referral

questions.initialExplanation: Purulent otitis media after measles: a bacterial complication needing antibiotics (bacterial otitis media).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Otitis media is a common complication of measles and is typically bacterial, often caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae or Haemophilus influenzae. Bacterial otitis media following measles requires appropriate antibiotic therapy to prevent hearing loss and other complications.

---

questions.stem: A pregnant woman in the 1st trimester is exposed to an index case of rubella. Lab tests confirms recent infection. She refused to terminate pregnancy. Of the following, the MOST appropriate management is:
questions.initialExplanation: A first-trimester pregnant woman with rubella who refused abortion: the source's answer is immunoglobulin (although its effectiveness is limited).
questions.detailedExplanation:
The routine use of immunoglobulin for susceptible pregnant women exposed to rubella is not recommended and is considered only if termination of pregnancy is not an option because of maternal preferences, understanding that prophylaxis may reduce the risk for clinically apparent infection but does not guarantee prevention of fetal infection.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child with measles develops severe diarrhea, abdominal pain, and signs of dehydration. The child appears malnourished and is losing weight rapidly. What nutritional intervention is most critical for this presentation?
questions.initialExplanation: Measles with severe diarrhea and malnutrition: the most important nutritional treatment is vitamin A (reduces diarrhea duration and complications).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Vitamin A deficiency increases the severity of measles and associated complications, including gastrointestinal manifestations. Vitamin A therapy is crucial for children with measles, particularly in malnourished populations, as it reduces mortality and severity of diarrhea and other complications.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old child presents with a mild illness consisting of low-grade fever, sore throat, and red eyes. Examination reveals tender lymph nodes behind the ears and on the back of the neck. A faint rash with small red spots is beginning to appear on the face. What is the most characteristic clinical feature described?
questions.initialExplanation: The distinguishing feature of rubella: retroauricular and posterior cervical lymphadenopathy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The most characteristic sign of rubella is retroauricular, post-cervical, and post-occipital lymphadenopathy. The lymph nodes are tender and appear 24 hours before the rash starts, then may remain for one week. This lymphadenopathy is more distinctive than the mild prodromal symptoms or rash.

- Koplik spots are specific to measles, The rash in rubella is not typically confluent, Forchheimer spots

may occur but are not the most characteristic feature, Parotid swelling is associated with mumps, not rubella

---

questions.stem: A 34-year-old Aboriginal woman is found to be IgM positive, but IgG negative after exposure to a child with rubella during the first trimester of pregnancy. Rubella infection is confirmed with repeated serology testing showing not only a positive IgM, but also rising titers of IgG. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: C
options.text: Check rubella serology again and get the test reported from another laboratory.

questions.initialExplanation: Confirmed rubella in the first trimester (positive IgM and rising IgG): the correct option per the source is termination of pregnancy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The positive IgM for rubella indicates active rubella infection. In such cases, repeating the test is indicated. If IgM is still poitive, diagnosis of rubella infection is confirmed. No further testing from another laboratory (option

C) is required.

If rubella infection occurs in the first trimester of pregnancy, the risk of fetal infection and damage is high (85% in the first 2 months of pregnancy, and 50 -80% in the third month); therefore, termination of pregnancy is usually recommended.

NHIG (option B) has been used in trials for prophylaxis and prevention of congenital rubella syndrome after contact to a case with rubella infection.
