The results have been discouranging; therefor, it is not advised for prophylaxis. This woman, on the other hand, has establsihed infection and NHIG wil not be of benefit as primary prevention.

---

questions.stem: A pregnant elementary school teacher, aged 24 years, presents to your GP office after she found that one of the students in her class has been recently diagnosed with rubella by his GP; the diagnosis however was not confirmed by serologic studies. Her last vaccination against rubella was when she was 12 years. Which one of the following would be the next best step in management?

options.label: A
options.text: No action is required; reassure her.

options.label: C
options.text: Confirm the diagnosis of rubella in the sick child with rubella serology testing.

options.label: D
options.text: Give her a booster dose of MMR vaccine.

options.label: E
options.text: Advise her to terminate the pregnancy.

questions.initialExplanation: A pregnant teacher exposed to a suspected rubella case, aged 24, last vaccinated at 12: the step is rubella serology to determine immunity.
questions.detailedExplanation:
All pregnant women with contact with a person, who has confirmed diagnosis of rubella infection or is suspicious of having the disease, should be offered serologic testing (both IgM and IgG) for rubella as the most appropriate next step in management. However, if the patient had been screened for rubella IgG in the first trimester and had a positive IgG with titers >10 IU/ml, no further serologic testing would have been indicated.

(Option A) Taking no action is incorrect as serologic testing is indicated in all pregnant patients after contact to a rubella or rubella-like infection, unless the woman has been documented to be immune in the current pregnancy using IgG titers as mentioned earlier.

(Option C) There is no need for serologic testing in the index case (the child in this scenario).

(Option D) Rubella-containing vaccines (MMR, MMRYV) are live attenuated vaccines and contraindicated throughout pregnancy.

Advising the patient to terminate the pregnancy is recommended if there is a with definite diagnosis of rubella infection (confirmed by serology) in the first trimester, as it is associate with fetal anomalies in almost 85% of cases.

---

questions.stem: An 18-year-old girl was vaccinated against rubella as a part of antenatal work up and was advised to avoid pregnancy for at least 3 months. She was found to be pregnant 4 weeks after the rubella vaccination and is concerned about the outcome. Which one of the following would be the correct management?
questions.initialExplanation: Pregnancy 4 weeks after rubella vaccine: reassure; no malformation risk has been shown from the vaccine.
questions.detailedExplanation:
It is recommended that women who receive rubella vaccine avoid pregnancy for 3 months post- vaccination, despite the fact that no study has proven the increased risk of congenital rubella syndrome if the patient becomes pregnant during this period.

If a patient becomes pregnant within 3 months of receiving the vaccine, reassurance is all needed and pregnancy should be continued.

Termination of pregnancy is considered if there is serological evidence of rubella infection during first trimester of pregnancy.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child develops fever, runny nose, red eyes, and cough for 2 days. His mother notices small grayish-white spots with red borders on the inside of his cheeks near his back teeth. The child appears more uncomfortable in bright light. What is the most pathognomonic sign described in this presentation?
questions.initialExplanation: The distinguishing sign of measles is Koplik spots on the buccal mucosa.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Koplik spots are grayish-white dots with reddish areolae that appear on the inner aspects of the cheeks at the

level of premolars. They are pathognomonic for measles and typically appear 1-4 days Before the onset of rash. The red borders and location near molars are characteristic features.

- Photophobia and conjunctivitis are common symptoms but not pathognomonic, Forchheimer spots are associated with rubella, not measles, Retroauricular lymphadenopathy is characteristic of rubella, Facial rash occurs later in the disease progression

---

questions.stem: A newborn has bilateral cataracts and microphthalmia, intrauterine growth retardation, hemorrhagic skin lesions scattered throughout the body, harsh systolic murmur heard at the left sternal border and radiating to the lung fields. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Cataract, microphthalmia, IUGR, purpuric skin lesions and a murmur = congenital rubella.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Congenital rubella infection affects all organ systems. Infants will be small, with intrauterine growth retardation. They may also manifest cataracts, microphthalmia, myocarditis, and a red or purple macular rash (“blueberry muffin” rash). Structural heart defects (such as a patent ductus arteriosis, pulmonary artery stenosis, and septal defects) are typical of congenital rubella, but not in the other TORCH infections. Laboratory anomalies may include a hemolytic anemia with thrombocytopenia, elevated liver functions, and pleocytosis in the spinal fluid. Affected children do not have a good

prognosis. Congenital rubella is not commonly seen in developed countries with high immunization rates.

---

questions.stem: A 25-year-old pregnant woman in her first trimester develops a mild illness with lowgrade fever and a faint rash. She is concerned about potential effects on her unborn baby. What is the most critical period for congenital rubella syndrome development?
questions.initialExplanation: The most dangerous period for congenital rubella malformations is the first 8 weeks of pregnancy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Congenital rubella syndrome occurs when maternal infection occurs during the first 8 weeks of pregnancy, with the highest risk of severe defects during organogenesis. The first 8 weeks represent the most critical period for teratogenic effects. The risk is not uniform throughout pregnancy, The highest risk is in early pregnancy, not second trimester, Third trimester infection carries much lower risk of congenital defects, Labor and delivery exposure leads to neonatal infection, not congenital syndrome.

---

questions.stem: You are working in a clinic in rural Mexico and examine an 8-year-old boy who has a rectal temperature of 100°F (38°C), bilateral tender parotid swelling, and pain when you flex his neck. He has been complaining of a headache. His immunization history is unknown. What is the most likely cause of this child’s infection?
questions.initialExplanation: Painful bilateral parotid swelling with neck stiffness and headache = mumps with meningitis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Mumps causes subclinical infection in one-third of cases. The most common manifestation is unilateral parotid swelling that becomes bilateral with a prodrome of headache, fever, abdominal pain, and anorexia. EBV infection typically manifests as exudative pharyngitis and cervical chain adenopathy. Brucellosis is a systemic illness that typically causes fever, joint pain, malaise, and anorexia. Leukemia may vary in presentation, but often presents with fever, hematologic abnormality, petechial rash, and nonspecific complaints. The initial sign of cysticercosis in children is oftentimes a seizure in an otherwise healthy child.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child with rubella develops a rash that begins on the face and spreads quickly to the trunk and extremities. By the second day of the rash, the facial eruption has already begun to fade. What is the typical duration and characteristics of rubella rash?

options.label: A
options.text: Maculopapular rash lasting 7-10 days with upward spread

options.label: B
options.text: Vesicular rash lasting 4-5 days with crusting

options.label: C
options.text: Maculopapular rash lasting 3 days with downward spread

options.label: D
options.text: Purpuric rash lasting 10 days with no pattern

options.label: E
options.text: Erythematous rash lasting 1-2 days with rapid resolution

questions.initialExplanation: The rubella rash is maculopapular, spreads downward and lasts about 3 days (shorter than measles).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Rubella is often called "three-day measles" because the rash typically lasts about three days. It begins on the face and spreads quickly, often fading from the face by the time it appears on the trunk. The rash is maculopapular and typically resolves by the third day.

---

questions.stem: A 2-month-old infant is born with low birth weight, cataracts, and a heart murmur. The mother had a mild illness with fever and rash during early pregnancy. What is the most likely cardiac abnormality in congenital rubella syndrome?
questions.initialExplanation: The most common cardiac defect in congenital rubella syndrome is PDA (often with pulmonary artery stenosis).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) is the most frequently reported cardiac defect in congenital rubella

syndrome. Other cardiac abnormalities include peripheral pulmonary artery stenosis, but PDA is the classic cardiac manifestation of maternal rubella infection.

---

questions.stem: A pregnant woman at 20 weeks gestation is exposed to rubella. She asks about isolation precautions to prevent transmission to others. What is the period of highest communicability for rubella?

options.label: A
options.text: From 5 days before to 6 days after rash onset

options.label: B
options.text: From 2 days before to 4 days after rash onset

options.label: C
options.text: From symptom onset until rash resolves

questions.initialExplanation: The peak contagious period of rubella is from 5 days before the rash to 6 days after it.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The period of highest communicability for rubella is from 5 days before the rash appears until 6 days

following the appearance of the rash. During this period, virus shedding in nasopharyngeal secretions is at its peak.

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy develops fever, headache, and pain when eating acidic foods. Examination reveals swelling of the parotid gland on one side, with the ear lobe pushed upward and outward. What is the characteristic pattern of parotid gland involvement in mumps?

options.label: B
options.text: Unilateral initially, becoming bilateral in 70% of cases

questions.initialExplanation: Mumps begins with unilateral parotid swelling that becomes bilateral in most cases (about 70%).
questions.detailedExplanation:
In mumps, parotid swelling typically starts unilaterally and becomes bilateral in approximately 70% of cases. The swelling usually affects one parotid gland first, and the other gland may swell a day or two later. The upward and outward displacement of the ear lobe is characteristic.

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old child with mumps develops sudden onset of severe unilateral hearing loss. Audiometry confirms profound sensorineural hearing loss. What is the significance of this complication?

options.label: A
options.text: It is temporary and resolves spontaneously

options.label: C
options.text: It is typically permanent and requires hearing rehabilitation

options.label: D
options.text: It responds well to antiviral therapy

options.label: E
options.text: It can be prevented with early antibiotic treatment

questions.initialExplanation: Sensorineural hearing loss after mumps is usually permanent and needs audiological rehabilitation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Sensorineural hearing loss is a serious complication of mumps that is typically permanent. It can occur suddenly and may be unilateral or bilateral. Once established, the hearing loss usually does not recover, requiring long-term hearing rehabilitation and support.

- Mumps-related hearing loss is typically permanent, not temporary, Surgical intervention is not effective for sensorineural hearing loss.

D) No specific antiviral therapy exists for mumps

E) Antibiotics don't prevent viral complications of mumps

---


## Scarlet Fever | Roseola | Erythema Infectiosum

questions.stem: A 3-month-old boy has a maculopapular rash that appeared on the face then spread all over the body. It has been preceded by very high fever for 3 days. Today he looks well active, afebrile with this rash. The most likely causative agent is:-
questions.initialExplanation: High fever for 3 days then sudden resolution with a maculopapular rash in an infant = roseola infantum (exanthem subitum), caused by HHV-6.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The clinical presentation described—a high fever for 3 days followed by the appearance of a maculopapular rash once the fever subsides —is classic for roseola infantum , which is caused by Human Herpes Virus Type 6 (HHV-6) .

---

questions.stem: A previously healthy 7-year-old child presents with a 2-day history of high-grade fever, sore throat, and a generalized rash. On examination, the child is febrile and has a coarse, erythematous rash resembling sandpaper, which began on the neck and upper chest and has now spread to the trunk. Oral examination reveals a "strawberry tongue" and pharyngeal redness, with no conjunctivitis, runny nose, or oral ulcers. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Fever, sore throat and a sandpaper-like rash starting on the neck and chest with a strawberry tongue = scarlet fever (group A Streptococcus).
questions.detailedExplanation:
This presentation is classic for scarlet fever: high-grade fever, sore throat, coarse sandpaper-like erythematous rash starting on the neck/chest and spreading centrally, and strawberry tongue with pharyngeal erythema. Scarlet fever results from Group A Streptococcus pharyngitis producing erythrogenic toxin, which causes the characteristic rash and mucosal changes. The absence of conjunctivitis, coryza, or Koplik spots effectively excludes measles, while the rash timing and morphology rule out roseola (rash after fever defervescence) and erythema infectiosum (slapped-cheek appearance). Rubella typically presents with milder symptoms and prominent postauricular lymphadenopathy without sore throat or strawberry tongue.

---

questions.stem: A 9-month-old previously healthy boy presents with sudden high-grade fever lasting 3 days, during which he was irritable. After the fever abruptly resolved, he developed a faint maculopapular rash on the trunk and returned to normal activity. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: High fever for 3 days that suddenly resolves with a mild truncal rash in a 9-month-old = roseola infantum.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This presentation is classic for roseola infantum (exanthem subitum): sudden high-grade fever for 3 days in an infant, followed by abrupt defervescence and appearance of a faint maculopapular rash on the trunk as the child returns to normal activity. Human herpesvirus type 6 (HHV-6) is the primary causative agent, typically affecting children aged 6-24 months. The hallmark "rash after fever" sequence distinguishes roseola from measles, rubella, or scarlet fever, where rash appears during ongoing fever. Erythema infectiosum presents with "slapped cheek" facial rash and lacy extremity involvement, not truncal rash post-defervescence. Infectious mononucleosis is uncommon in infants and presents with pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly.

---

questions.stem: A 12-year-old previously healthy girl presents with a 5-day history of facial rash followed by joint pain. The rash began with "slapped cheek" facial redness and later spread to the trunk and limbs in a lacy, reticular pattern, sparing palms and soles. She is afebrile and appears well. The physician advises no need for isolation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Red cheeks ("slapped cheek") then a lacy reticular rash on the trunk and limbs with joint pain and no fever = erythema infectiosum (fifth disease, parvovirus B19).
questions.detailedExplanation:
This presentation is classic for erythema infectiosum (Fifth disease) caused by parvovirus B19: "slapped cheek" facial erythema followed by a lacy, reticular rash on the trunk and limbs, with arthralgias common in adolescent females. The child appears well and afebrile because the rash represents an immune-mediated phenomenon occurring after viral clearance, meaning she is no longer contagious—hence no isolation is required. Scarlet fever produces a sandpaper-like rash with strawberry tongue and requires antibiotics. Roseola infantum affects younger infants with rash appearing after fever defervescence, not with facial slapped-cheek appearance. Infectious mononucleosis causes pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, and fatigue without this characteristic rash pattern. Aplastic anemia is a complication of parvovirus B19 in patients with hemolytic disorders, not healthy children with typical rash.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl has a mild febrile illness with mild URI symptoms. She has an erythematous rash on both cheeks. Her pregnant mother had arthralgias of the hands wrists, knees, and ankles a week ago. What should be the next action?

options.label: A
options.text: Closely monitor the child’s sibling who has spherocytosis.

options.label: B
options.text: Exclude the child from daycare until rash has resolved.

options.label: C
options.text: Exclude the pregnant daycare providers until no further cases are diagnosed for 2 weeks.

options.label: E
options.text: Give the sibling with spherocytosis IVIG.

questions.initialExplanation: A girl with slapped cheeks, a pregnant mother with joint pain and a brother with hereditary spherocytosis: the brother is at risk of aplastic crisis from parvovirus B19, so monitor him closely.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The child and mother exhibit classical symptoms of human parvovirus B19 infection also called fifth disease or erythema infectiosum. Prodromal symptoms are usually mild and diagnosis is often made when the characteristic rash appears. Initally the rash starts on the face and children have what is often described as a “slapped-cheek” appearance. The rash spreads readily to the rest of the body with a diffuse macular erythema. Central clearing of the macules then occurs rapidly and gives the rash a lacy, reticulated appearance. Joint symptoms are very common in adults and may be the only clinical manifestation of parvovirus B19 infection. The primary target of parvovirus B19 is the erythroid cell line. Children with erythema infectiosum are most infectious prior to the onset of the rash, therefore, exclusion from school or day care after the rash develops is not indicated. Pregnant caregives in day care or schools need not be excluded. Parvovirus B19 has also been associated with hydrops fetalis in pregnant women. it also can cause a more serious transient aplastic crisis in patients with chronic hemolytic diseases. Postexposure prophylaxis with VIG for pregnant women or patients with chronic hematologic disorders is not indicated.

questions.stem: A pregnant mother is picking up her child from day care when she is informed that there was a recent outbreak of parvovirus. She brings her child into the clinic the following day where her daughter is diagnosed with erythema infectiosum based on low-grade fever and a reticular, macular rash that appeared overnight. The mother is pregnant at 15 weeks and as such asks that her child be formally tested. The daughter is found to be IgM positive and IgG positive. Given concern for fetal effects the mother undergoes testing with the following results: IgM negative and IgG positive. Based on these findings the best recommendation would be to:

options.label: A
options.text: Repeat the mother’s antibody testing in 2 to 3 weeks.

options.label: C
options.text: Tell the mother that no further testing is necessary.

options.label: D
options.text: Conduct parvovirus PCR testing from the mother’s serum.

options.label: E
options.text: Conduct parvovirus IgM testing from fetal cordocentesis at 22 weeks.

questions.initialExplanation: A 15-week pregnant mother with negative IgM and positive IgG = past immunity (old infection); no further tests needed.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The child in this case has had a recent infection with parvovirus B19, which, if acquired during pregnancy, can occasionally cause complications such as fetal wastage, fetal hydrops, and stillbirths,

’    although in the majority of cases the fetus suffers no adverse effects. In the above case, despite the child having had a recent infection with human parvovirus, the mother’s titers demonstrate that she is already immune, and thus requires no further testing or evaluation. If she were negative for both IgM and IgG, then retesting in 2 to 3 weeks is advised. If the mother’s IgM were positive, regardless of her IgG, it is generally recommended that the fetal ultrasound be followed weekly to evaluate for possible complications. PCR testing of the mother’s serum, while feasible, is generally more expensive and not as helpful as antibody titers. Cordocentesis for IgM is occasionally done for possible congenital rubella infections but is not used for parvovirus.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old girl develops low grade fever, headache, and flu-like illness. She then develops bilateral cheeks erythema followed by diffuse macular rash over the trunk and extensors of extremities, with central clearing in some areas giving a reticulate appearance. Soles and palms are spared. Of the following, the MOST likely diagnosis is :
questions.initialExplanation: Red cheeks then a reticular rash on the trunk and limbs sparing palms and soles = erythema infectiosum.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The most common manifestation of Parvo virus B19 is erythema infectiosum (fifth disease). The initial stage is an erythematous facial flushing (slapped-cheek appearance). The rash spreads rapidly or concurrently to the trunk and proximal extremities as a diffuse macular erythema in the second stage. Central clearing of macular lesions occurs promptly, giving the rash a lacy, reticulated appearance.

---

questions.stem: A 10-year-old child with sickle cell anemia develops sudden pallor, fatigue, and shortness of breath. His parents mention that several children at school have had a "slapped cheek" appearance recently. Laboratory tests show severe reticulocytopenia. What is the most likely mechanism of this complication?

options.label: A
options.text: Direct viral invasion of bone marrow

options.label: B
options.text: Parvovirus B19 infection of erythrocyte precursor cells

options.label: C
options.text: Autoimmune destruction of red blood cells

options.label: E
options.text: Nutritional deficiency due to poor appetite

questions.initialExplanation: Aplastic crisis in a sickle cell patient: parvovirus B19 infects red cell precursors and halts their production (reticulocytopenia).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Parvovirus B19 infects erythroid precursor cells in the bone marrow, causing severe reticulocytopenia that lasts 7-10 days. In children with underlying hemolytic anemias (like sickle cell disease), this

temporary cessation of red blood cell production can precipitate an aplastic crisis, requiring urgent medical intervention.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old child develops a maculopapular rash on the trunk and extremities that forms a characteristic lacy, reticular pattern. The child mentions the rash comes and goes in waves over the past week. What is this characteristic rash pattern called?
questions.initialExplanation: The lacy reticular pattern is the characteristic rash of erythema infectiosum.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The second stage of erythema infectiosum (fifth disease) is characterized by a maculopapular rash on the trunk and extremities that forms a lacy, reticular pattern. This pattern is quite distinctive and occurs

1-4 days after the initial facial rash.

---

questions.stem: A 23-year-old female presents to your office for advice. She works at a childcare centre. She is 12 weeks pregnant and she was exposed to a child with slapped cheek fever 2 weeks ago. What will you do next?

options.label: A
options.text: Reassure her it does not cause any issues in pregnancy

questions.initialExplanation: A 12-week pregnant woman exposed to a child with fifth disease: check parvovirus B19 serology to determine immunity or infection.
questions.detailedExplanation:
“Slapped cheek” is a viral infection caused by a virus called parvovirus B19. It is also called fifth disease’ or erythema infectiosum.

About 50% of pregnant women are immune to parvovirus B19. So, these women and their babies are usually protected from getting the virus and fifth disease.Pregnant women who are not immune do not have serious complications after they are exposed to others with the fifth disease.

The baby may develop anemia and miscarriage can also happen. So the serology for the Parvovirus B19 should be requested.

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy presents to the office with an intermittent fever of 40°C (f 04°F) for the past three days. The physical examination reveals no source of infection. However, you notice faint pink maculopapular rash on his trunk. The patient does not appear toxic, and the parents feel that he appears well between fevers. They also add that the rash was not seen earlier. The differential diagnosis includes:
questions.initialExplanation: Fever 40°C for three days without a focus then a faint pink rash in a 2-year-old = roseola.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Roseola (choice D) is characterized by 3 days of high fever, which disappears suddenly as the typical rash appears. Roseola is typically characterized by a history of 3 days of high fever (often up to 40°C) followed by rapid defervescence and a characteristic rash (fades within a few hours to 2 d)

which is:

- Maculopapular or erythematous

- Typically beginning on the trunk and may spread to involve the neck and extremities

- Nonpruritic

- Blanches on pressure

---

questions.stem: A 10-month-old child has a temperature of 104°F (40°C) for 4 days without other signs. On the fourth day a rose pink, maculopapular rash appears and the temperature returns to normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: An infant with high fever for 4 days then a pink rash with fever resolution = roseola; the cause is human herpesvirus 6.
questions.detailedExplanation:
High fever without other signs and clearing of the fever on appearance of a rash are characteristic of roseola and is the defining clinical expression of primary infection with human herpes virus 6. In measles infection, fever continues for several days after the appearance of the rash. The same is true for the several types of typhus. In infection to echovirus, the rash and fever usually appear together. The rash of scarlet fever often appears at the time of temperature elevation.

---

questions.stem: An 8-month-old boy develops high grade fever associated with fussiness and irritability. Three days later, there is abrupt defervescence with the appearance of rose-colored, nonpruritic, 2-3 mm morbilliform rash over the trunk. He is a breast fed infant, and his vaccination history is complete up to his age. Of the following, the MOST likely diagnosis is :
questions.initialExplanation: An infant with fever followed by a pink rash after sudden defervescence = exanthem subitum (roseola).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Roseola infantum (exanthem subitum, or sixth disease) is an acute, selflimited disease of infancy and early childhood. It is characterized by the abrupt onset of high fever, which may be accompanied by fussiness. The fever usually resolves acutely after 72 hr (crisis) but may gradually fade over a day

(lysis) coincident with the appearance of a faint pink or rose-colored, nonpruritic, 2-3 mm morbilliform rash on the trunk.

---

questions.stem: A 25-year-old pregnant woman in her second trimester is exposed to a child with fifth disease at her workplace. She is concerned about potential effects on her pregnancy. What is the highest risk period for miscarriage due to parvovirus B19 infection during pregnancy?
questions.initialExplanation: The highest risk of miscarriage from parvovirus B19 is in the first half of pregnancy, especially the second trimester per the source.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Parvovirus B19 infection during pregnancy has been implicated in causing miscarriage, with the highest risk occurring during the second trimester. This is when the virus can cross the placenta and cause fetal hydrops or death. The second trimester represents a critical period in fetal development when the fetal immune system is becoming more active, but the protective mechanisms are not yet fully mature. During this period, parvovirus B19 can cross the placental barrier and infect fetal erythroid precursors, similar to the mechanism seen in adults. The fetal consequences depend on the timing and severity of infection. Early in the second trimester, the fetus is still highly dependent on active erythropoiesis for tissue oxygenation because fetal red blood cells have a shorter lifespan than adult cells. Parvovirus B19 infection causes severe fetal anemia by suppressing erythropoiesis, leading to congestive heart failure and generalized edema (hydrops fetalis). The increased cardiac workload from severe anemia, combined with viral myocarditis, can lead to high-output cardiac failure and subsequent death. The risk of miscarriage is highest between 14-20 weeks gestation, with fetal mortality rates approaching 10% when maternal infection occurs during this critical window. This timing is different from congenital infections like rubella, where the first trimester poses the highest risk for structural malformations.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child with erythema infectiosum develops joint pain and swelling in both knees and ankles. The child is reluctant to walk and appears uncomfortable with movement. What is the most appropriate management for this complication?
questions.initialExplanation: Arthritis accompanying fifth disease is treated with NSAIDs.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Arthritis or arthralgia can occur in children with erythema infectiosum, particularly affecting large joints.

Management is supportive with NSAIDs for pain and inflammation, along with rest. This is typically self- limiting and resolves as the viral infection resolves.

---

questions.stem: A 9-year-old child with known erythema infectiosum develops sudden onset of severe headache, vomiting, and ataxia. The child appears lethargic and has difficulty with coordination. What is the most serious neurological complication that can occur with parvovirus B19 infection?
questions.initialExplanation: The most serious neurological complication of parvovirus B19 per the source is encephalitis from direct viral invasion.
questions.detailedExplanation:
While rare, encephalitis can occur as a neurological complication of parvovirus B19 infection. This

represents direct viral invasion of the central nervous system and requires urgent evaluation and supportive management.

---

questions.stem: A mother brings her 18-months old male child with a 3-day history of high grade fever that resolves abruptly followed by the development of rash starting on the neck and trunk and spreading to the face and extremities. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: High fever for 3 days that resolves suddenly, then a rash on the neck and trunk spreading to the face and limbs = roseola infantum.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has a clinical diagnosis of roseola. Classical roseola begins with a fever that may exceed 40°C (104°F) and lasts for three to five days. The fever often is accompanied by irritability, although most children with roseola are otherwise well-appearing, active, and alert. As the child’s fever abates, a blanching macular or maculopapular rash develops, starting on the neck and trunk and spreading to the face and extremities. Human herpes virus 6 (HHV-6) is the most frequent cause of roseola. Erythema infectiosum, in which the rash is prominent on the cheeks and which usually, affects school-age children.lt is caused by Human Parvo B19 virus. Rubeola (measles) is distinguished by a prodrome of coryza, cough, and Koplik spots. The rash classically begins on the face and spreads down the body. In rubella, the rash and fever occur simultaneously. The rash classically starts on the face and spreads down the body.

---

questions.stem: An 18-month old female infant is brought to your clinic due to an onset of red maculopapular rash on her trunk. Symptoms reported by mother include high-grade fever and mild coryza for last 3 days however she has still been quite active.Her temperature has returned to normal today. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: An active infant with high fever for 3 days and a rash after the temperature falls = roseola infantum.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Roseola infantum is a viral infection usually affecting children between the ages of 6-18 months. The patient typically develops high fever up to 40 degrees Celsius but is otherwise not particularly unwell. There may be mild cervical lymphadenopathy and pharyngitis.

After three days, the temperature usually returns suddenly to normal and the patient develops a red macular or maculopapular non-desquamating rash which is truncal, usually sparing the face and limbs. The rash abates within two days.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old child presents with sudden onset fever up to 40.5°C, sore throat, and headache. Examination reveals a fine maculopapular rash with sandpaper texture on an erythematous background that began on the trunk and is spreading to involve the entire body. What is the most characteristic feature of the rash described?
questions.initialExplanation: The characteristic feature of the scarlet fever rash is a fine sandpaper texture on a red background.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The characteristic rash of scarlet fever is described as having a "sandpaper texture" on an erythematous background. The texture is more important than the appearance in diagnosis. The rash typically begins on the trunk and spreads to involve most of the body within hours to days. This sandpaper texture results from the inflammatory response to the pyrogenic exotoxins (particularly streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxins A and B) produced by the Group A Streptococcus bacteria. These superantigens trigger a massive immune response that causes widespread capillary dilation and inflammatory changes in the skin. The fine, raised nature of the erythematous rash creates the characteristic sandpaper feel when touched gently with the fingertips. This texture sensation is often more reliable for clinical diagnosis than the visual appearance, which can vary significantly in intensity from child to child. The sandpaper rash typically spreads very rapidly, often within hours, reflecting the systemic nature of the toxin-mediated response. Understanding that this is primarily a textural rather than visual diagnostic feature helps clinicians distinguish scarlet fever from other childhood exanthems, particularly when the visual appearance might be confused with viral rashes or drug reactions. The texture is best assessed by light

touch rather than firm pressure, as firm pressure will cause the erythema to blanch, obscuring the fine papular texture that is pathognomonic for scarlet fever.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child with scarlet fever develops deep, red, non-blanching lesions in the antecubital and popliteal areas. The child also has circumoral pallor - pale skin around the mouth while the rest of the face is flushed. What is the name given to the deep red lesions in skin folds?
questions.initialExplanation: Deep red lines in skin folds (elbow and knee) in scarlet fever are called Pastia lines.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Pastia's lines are deep, red, non-blanching linear lesions that occur in the antecubital and popliteal

areas in scarlet fever. They are a characteristic sign of the disease and help distinguish it from other exanthems.

A) Koplik spots are seen in measles, not scarlet fever

B) Forchheimer spots occur in rubella

D) Janeway lesions are associated with infective endocarditis

E) Osler nodes are also associated with infective endocarditis

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old child with scarlet fever has a white coating on the dorsum of the tongue early in the illness, but by day 3 the coating has desquamated to reveal a swollen, red, and mottled tongue that resembles a strawberry. What is the significance of this tongue change?

options.label: B
options.text: It represents the progression from white coat to strawberry tongue

options.label: C
options.text: It shows the development of glossitis from vitamin deficiency

options.label: D
options.text: It suggests allergic reaction to antibiotics

questions.initialExplanation: The white then strawberry tongue represents progression from a white coating to a red, swollen tongue.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The progression from a white coating on the tongue early in scarlet fever to a swollen, red, mottled " strawberry tongue" is characteristic of the disease. This represents the normal progression of the enanthem in scarlet fever.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child with suspected scarlet fever needs laboratory confirmation. The rapid streptococcal antigen test comes back negative, but the clinical presentation is highly suggestive. What is the most appropriate next step for diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: A negative rapid strep test with strong clinical suspicion: do a throat culture to confirm the diagnosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
When the rapid streptococcal antigen test is negative but clinical suspicion remains high, a throat culture should be performed. Throat culture has the best sensitivity (>90%) and is considered the gold standard for diagnosing group A streptococcal pharyngitis.

A) Empiric therapy without confirmation may be appropriate in some cases, but culture provides definitive diagnosis

B) Repeating the rapid test is not as reliable as culture

D) CBC may show leukocytosis but is not diagnostic

E) Heterophile antibodies are for EBV infection, not streptococcal infection

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old child with scarlet fever develops ear pain, fever, and decreased hearing. Examination reveals a bulging, erythematous tympanic membrane with purulent discharge. What is the most likely complication and appropriate management?

options.label: B
options.text: Sensorineural hearing loss requiring audiology referral

options.label: D
options.text: Viral upper respiratory infection requiring supportive care

questions.initialExplanation: Otitis media with fever, pain and purulent discharge after scarlet fever: the complication is otitis media needing antibiotics.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Acute otitis media is a common complication of scarlet fever. The child needs appropriate antibiotic

therapy targeting both the streptococcal infection and potential bacterial pathogens commonly causing otitis media.

B) Sensorineural hearing loss is not typical of acute otitis media

C) Mastoiditis would present with more severe symptoms and signs

D) The clinical picture suggests bacterial infection, not viral

E) This is not simply eustachian tube dysfunction

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old child with scarlet fever develops desquamation of the skin, particularly on the fingertips and toes, about 2 weeks after the onset of illness. What is the significance of this desquamation?

options.label: B
options.text: It represents a drug allergy to penicillin

options.label: C
options.text: It is a normal part of the recovery phase of scarlet fever

questions.initialExplanation: Skin peeling of the fingers two weeks after scarlet fever is a normal part of recovery.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Desquamation, particularly of the fingertips and toes, occurs 1-3 weeks after the onset of scarlet fever

and is a normal part of the recovery phase. This represents the natural healing process of the skin after the acute inflammatory phase.

---

questions.stem: A 10-month-old infant develops high fever (39°C) for 3-5 days. The parents report that despite the high fever, the baby behaves normally and is playful. The fever then abruptly resolves, and 12-24 hours later, a rose-colored rash appears on the trunk. What is the most distinctive feature of this presentation?

options.label: A
options.text: High fever with irritability and decreased activity

options.label: C
options.text: Rash that spreads to face and extremities rapidly

options.label: D
options.text: Persistent fever lasting more than 7 days

options.label: E
options.text: Fever that resolves before the rash appears

questions.initialExplanation: The key point in roseola: the fever resolves before the rash appears (the two do not occur together).
questions.detailedExplanation:
The most distinctive feature of roseola infantum is that the fever resolves first, and then a rash appears 12-24 hours later. This is the key feature that distinguishes roseola from other childhood exanthems where fever and rash typically occur together. This characteristic temporal relationship is crucial for clinical diagnosis and parental counseling. During the 3-5 day febrile phase, children with roseola often maintain their normal activity level and demeanor despite having high fever (often 39- 40°C), which is reassuring but can be confusing for parents who expect their child to appear ill during high fevers. The abrupt defervescence of fever followed by the appearance of a rose-pink maculopapular rash represents the body's successful control of the viral infection.

---

questions.stem: A 6-month-old infant with roseola infantum has not yet developed the characteristic rash but has had high fever for 4 days. The parents are concerned and ask about the expected course. What is the typical duration of fever in roseola infantum?
questions.initialExplanation: The typical duration of fever in roseola infantum is 3-5 days.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Fever in roseola infantum typically persists for 3-5 days, then typically resolves abruptly. This is followed by the appearance of the characteristic rash 12-24 hours after fever resolution.

A) 1-2 days is shorter than typical for roseola

C) 5-7 days may occur but 3-5 days is more characteristic

D) Fever lasting 7-10 days exceeds the typical range

E) Fever lasting more than 2 weeks suggests an alternative diagnosis

---

questions.stem: A 20-month-old boy presents with delayed walking and bowed legs. He was exclusively breastfed until 12 months, has limited sun exposure, and his diet lacks fortified foods. Examination reveals frontal bossing, widened wrists, and rachitic rosary. Laboratory studies show low calcium, low phosphate, and elevated alkaline phosphatase. X-rays demonstrate metaphyseal cupping and fraying. Which of the following is LEAST likely to be a complication of this condition?
questions.initialExplanation: Complications of rickets: hypocalcemia, delayed fontanelle closure, fractures and hypocalcemic seizures. Intracranial calcifications are a complication of hypoparathyroidism, not rickets.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This clinical presentation is classic for nutritional rickets, resulting from vitamin D deficiency. The risk
factors identified in the case —exclusive breastfeeding without vitamin D supplementation, limited sun
exposure, and lack of fortified foods—are all consistent with vitamin D deficiency rickets. The physical
examination findings (frontal bossing, widened wrists, rachitic rosary) and radiographic features
(metaphyseal cupping and fraying) are pathognomonic for rickets.

- Vitamin D deficiency leads to decreased intestinal calcium absorption, resulting in hypocalcemia.
This stimulates parathyroid hormone (PTH) secretion, which causes phosphaturia (phosphate wasting
in the urine) and bone demineralization as the body attempts to maintain serum calcium levels. The
elevated alkaline phosphatase reflects increased osteoblastic activity as the body attempts to repair
the demineralized bone.
