questions.stem: You are examining a 10-month-old male infant during a routine visit; you find that he has wide wrists. He is still breast fed. X-ray of the wrist joint shows signs of rickets. Of the following, the BEST reflection of vitamin D deficiency is : (NE)
questions.initialExplanation: The best marker of vitamin D status is the serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D level.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Serum concentration of 25-hydroxyvitamin D is considered the best indicator of vitamin D status for several
critical reasons:

1. Gold Standard for Assessment:

- 25-hydroxyvitamin D is the major circulating form of vitamin D in the blood

- It has a long half-life of approximately 2-3 weeks, providing a stable reflection of vitamin D stores
- It represents the total vitamin D available for conversion to the active form

- Levels below 20 ng/mL typically indicate vitamin D deficiency

2. Reliability in Clinical Practice:

- Unlike 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, 25(OH)D levels are not regulated by PTH or calcium levels

- It directly reflects dietary intake and cutaneous synthesis of vitamin D

- Most clinical guidelines recommend measuring 25(0OH)D to diagnose vitamin D deficiency

---

questions.stem: Rickets is defined as decreased bone mineralization in growing children. Hypocalcemia may accompany rickets. Of the following, the condition that causes hypocalcemia rather than rickets is : (NE)
questions.initialExplanation: Hypocalcemia without rickets occurs in primary hypoparathyroidism because low PTH does not produce high bone turnover.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Primary hypoparathyroidism is characterized by inadequate parathyroid hormone (PTH) secretion, leading to distinct
metabolic abnormalities that explain why it causes hypocalcemia but not rickets:

Pathophysiology:

- PTH deficiency — | renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity — | 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D synthesis

- PTH deficiency — | bone resorption — | calcium release from bone

- PTH deficiency — | renal calcium reabsorption — increased urinary calcium losses

Net result: Hypocalcemia with normal or elevated phosphate

Why No Rickets Develops:

- Rickets requires a state of secondary hyperparathyroidism with high bone turnover

- In hypoparathyroidism, PTH is low, not elevated

- Low PTH suppresses bone remodeling and osteoclastic activity

Without active bone turnover and the mineral-metabolism disturbances seen in vitamin D deficiency, defective bone mineralization (rickets) does not
occur, The bone disease in hypoparathyroidism is typically osteosclerosis or normal bone density, not the demineralization seen in rickets

---

questions.stem: A 16-month-old black male is seen in clinic for a well child visit. On history, his mother states that he has not started to walk and was exclusively breast fed until 14 months. On physical exam, his anterior fontanelle is open, wrists appear thickened, and he is below the 3 rd percentile for both length and weight. Which of the following laboratory results are most consistent with his diagnosis? (Rud)

options.label: A
options.text: Decreased calcium, increased phosphate, normal alkaline phosphatase, normal parathyroid hormone (PTH)

options.label: B
options.text: Decreased calcium, decreased phosphate, increased alkaline phosphatase, increased PTH

options.label: C
options.text: Increased calcium, decreased phosphate, decreased alkaline phosphatase, increased PTH

options.label: D
options.text: Decreased calcium, decreased phosphate, decreased alkaline phosphatase, decreased PTH

options.label: E
options.text: Increased calcium, increased phosphate, increased alkaline phosphatase, increased PTH

questions.initialExplanation: Nutritional rickets: low Ca and phosphate with high alkaline phosphatase and high PTH.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has rickets, which is most likely due to decreased vitamin D intake. Breast milk is deficient in vitamin
D and recommendations state that breastfeeding mothers should take 1000 IU of vitamin D daily while their
infant should receive 400 IU of vitamin D per day. Individuals with darkly pigmented skin are at an increased
risk for vitamin D deficiency. As the child in this case is black and was exclusively breast fed, he is at high risk
for vitamin D deficiency. In children with rickets, delayed closure of fontanelles can be seen along with short
stature, poor weight gain, and delayed walking. Common findings on radiographs include cupping and fraying
of the metaphyses of the long bones and demineralization. In mild vitamin D deficient rickets, laboratory
abnormalities are more subtle and calcium, phosphate, and parathyroid levels may be normal with an
increased alkaline phosphatase. In more severe cases, calcium and phosphate are low with a notable
increase in alkaline phosphatase and PTH.

---

questions.stem: An 8-month-old Caucasian male is brought into your pediatric clinic for a routine check up. Upon examination you note severely bowed legs and flaring of both wrists. Feeding history reveals he is formula fed and receives a daily multivitamin supplement. Laboratory results demonstrate the following: high 25 (OH)2 D,low 1,25(0H)2D, low calcium, and normal phosphorous. What diagnosis is most consistent with these findings? (Lange)
questions.initialExplanation: High 25(OH)D with low 1,25 and low calcium = vitamin D-dependent rickets type 1 (1-alpha hydroxylase deficiency).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Vitamin D refractory rickets type | is a rare cause of rickets. It results from impaired1-hydroxylation of 25(OH)2D
to 1,25(0OH)2D (the active form of vitamin D) and causes low calcium levels in the face of normal vitamin D
intake and absorption. Phosphate levels may be normal or slightly decreased in this disorder. Levels of 25(OH)
‘     2 D are usually normal or elevated while 1,25(0OH)2 D levels are low.
Hypophosphatemic rickets is characterized by low serum phosphate caused by abnormal renal phosphate loss.
It is an X-linked autosomal dominant disorder. Vitamin D deficiency rickets results from poor absorption and/or
poor intake of vitamin D. Both forms of vitamin D would be low in such children. Dark-skinned, breastfed
individuals born in the winter are at particular risk for vitamin D deficiency rickets.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child has mental retardation, shortness of stature, brachy dactyly (especially of the fourth and fifth digits), and obesity with round facies and short neck. The child is followed by an ophthalmologist for sub capsular cataracts, and has previously been noted to have cutaneous and subcutaneous calcifications, as well as perivascular calcifications of the basal ganglia. This patient is most likely to have which of the following features? (pretest)

options.label: E
options.text: Decreased bone density, particularly in the skull

questions.initialExplanation: Short stature, mental delay, short finger bones and basal ganglia calcification = pseudohypoparathyroidism (Albright), with high PTH.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The patient with the features listed likely has pseudohypoparathyroidism (Albright hereditary osteodys
trophy). Such patients have chemical findings of hypoparathyroidism (low calcium, high phosphorus),
but parathyroid hormone levels are high, indicating resistance to the action of this hormone.
Parathyroid hormone infusion does not produce a phosphaturic response. Phenotypically, these
patients demonstrate shortness of stature with delayed bone age, mental retardation, increased bone
density throughout the body (especially evident in the skull), brachydactyly (especially of the fourth
and fifth digits), obesity with round facies and short neck, subcapsular cataracts, cutaneous and sub
cutaneous calcifications, and perivascular calcifications of the basal ganglia.

---

questions.stem: A 39-week gestation infant was born after an uneventful pregnancy. Following delivery, the infant has respiratory distress and is found to have truncus arteriosis. Further examination reveals a low calcium (6.0 mg/dL) and low PTH. What is this child’s most likely diagnosis? (Rud)
questions.initialExplanation: Low calcium and low PTH in a newborn = DiGeorge syndrome (absent parathyroids).
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has DiGeorge syndrome as evidenced by the conotruncal defect of the heart and hypocalcemia due
to hypoparathyroidism. The classic presentation for this syndrome includes conotruncal heart defect (such as
tetralogy of Fallot, truncus ateriosus, aberrant right subclavian artery, and interrupted or right aortic arch),

‘    hypoplastic thymus, and hypocalcemia secondary to hypoparathyroidism. The hypoparathyroidism is not due to
an autoimmune process, but secondary to defects in the development of the 3 rd and 4 th pharyngeal
pouches, which causes parathyroid gland dysgenesis. Incidence ranges from 1:4000 to 1:10,000 births with
approximately 70% having isolated hypoparathyroidism. Partial or complete absence of the thymus can result in
an increased frequency of viral and fungal infections due to impaired cell-mediated immunity and defects in T

lymphocyte function. The most common genetic cause of sporadic DiGeorge syndrome is a microdeletion in
chromosome 22g11.2.

---

questions.stem: A 10-month-old breast-fed infant presents with swelling of wrists and ankles for the past 2 months. He was born at term and has been exclusively breast-fed without vitamin D supplementation. His mother keeps him indoors most of the time due to cultural practices. On examination, he has frontal bossing, widening of the wrists, and rachitic rosary. His serum calcium is 8.2 mg/dL, phosphorus 3.0 mg/dL, and alkaline phosphatase 450 U/L. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: A breastfed infant with swollen wrists, mildly low phosphorus and high ALP = nutritional vitamin D deficiency rickets.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This infant presents with classic clinical and laboratory features of nutritional vitamin D deficiency rickets.
The key risk factors include exclusive breast-feeding without vitamin D supplementation (breast milk is low
in vitamin D), limited sun exposure due to indoor lifestyle, and cultural practices preventing adequate
sunlight exposure. The clinical features —frontal bossing, wrist widening, and rachitic rosary—are
pathognomonic for rickets. The laboratory findings show hypophosphatemia (3.0 mg/dL) and elevated
alkaline phosphatase (450 U/L), with low-normal calcium, all consistent with active rickets.

- Nutritional vitamin D deficiency is the most common cause of rickets worldwide, particularly in breast-fed
infants who do not receive supplementation. The pathophysiology involves decreased intestinal absorption
of calcium and phosphorus, leading to secondary hyperparathyroidism and accelerated bone
demineralization at the growth plates.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the clinic with bowing of the legs and difficulty walking. His parents notice that his legs have been progressively bowing outward over the past year. He was born at term via normal delivery and has been on a regular diet. On examination, he has anterior bowing of both tibiae, widening of the wrists, and mild frontal bossing. His serum calcium is 9.5 mg/dL, phosphorus 3.2 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 320 U/L, and parathyroid hormone 65 pg/mL (normal 10-65 pg/mL). Which of the following radiological findings is most characteristic of this condition?

options.label: C
options.text: Increased bone density with rugger-jersey spine

questions.initialExplanation: The classic radiological sign of rickets: metaphyseal fraying and cupping.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child presents with clinical features of rickets, including bowing deformities, wrist widening, and frontal
bossing. The radiological hallmark of rickets is metaphyseal changes at the growth plates. These include:

- Fraying: Loss of the sharp, well-defined border of the metaphysis

- Cupping: Development of a concave depression at the end of the metaphysis

- Widening: Increased distance between the metaphysis and epiphysis

- Splaying: Flaring of the metaphyseal ends

These changes are most readily visualized on radiographs of the wrist (distal radius and ulna) but can be seen
at any growth plate. The fraying and cupping result from failure of mineralization at the growth plate cartilage,
leading to accumulation of unmineralized osteoid.

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old girl presents with inability to walk due to leg pain and deformity. She was born prematurely at 28 weeks gestation and has been in and out of the hospital for respiratory problems. She has been on total parenteral nutrition for prolonged periods. On examination, she has rachitic rosary, wrist and ankle widening, and mild bowing of the femurs. Her serum phosphorus is 2.5 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 380 U/L, and 25-hydroxyvitamin D is 25 ng/mL (sufficient >20 ng/mL). What is the most likely cause of rickets in this patient?
questions.initialExplanation: Adequate 25(OH)D with rickets: the cause is phosphorus deficiency.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This preterm infant with prolonged parenteral nutrition presents with rickets. The key finding is a normal 25-
hydroxyvitamin D level (25 ng/mL), which rules out vitamin D deficiency as the primary cause. The rickets in
this case is most likely due to phosphorus deficiency, which is common in preterm infants receiving parenteral
nutrition and can result from inadequate phosphate supplementation.

Phosphorus deficiency rickets (sometimes called "rickets of prematurity") occurs due to:

- Inadequate phosphorus intake in parenteral nutrition

- High growth rate of preterm infants requiring increased phosphate for bone mineralization

- Increased urinary phosphate losses in some premature infants

The treatment involves adequate phosphorus supplementation along with calcium and vitamin D. The rickets
of prematurity is distinct from nutritional vitamin D deficiency rickets and requires specific attention to
phosphate replacement.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy with known Fanconi syndrome is found to have bone deformities on routine examination. He has been on supportive treatment for his renal tubular disorder. On examination, he has widening of the wrists, mild frontal bossing, and genu valgum. His serum phosphorus is 2.2 mg/dL, bicarbonate 18 mEq/L, glucose 95 mg/dL, and amino acids are elevated in urine. Which mechanism best explains the development of rickets in this patient?
questions.initialExplanation: Fanconi syndrome loses phosphate through the kidneys and causes rickets.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This patient with Fanconi syndrome presents with rickets as a complication of his underlying renal tubular disorder.
Fanconi syndrome is characterized by generalized dysfunction of the proximal renal tubule, leading to impaired
reabsorption of phosphate, glucose, amino acids, bicarbonate, and other substances.

- The mechanism of rickets in Fanconi syndrome is primarily phosphate wasting due to defective proximal tubular
reabsorption. The resulting hypophosphatemia leads to impaired bone mineralization and rickets. The urinary findings
(elevated amino acids, normal glucose in this case) confirm the proximal tubular dysfunction.

Additional factors contributing to rickets in Fanconi syndrome include:

- Bicarbonate wasting leading to metabolic acidosis (which promotes bone demineralization)

- Possible associated vitamin D metabolism abnormalities

- Chronic kidney disease progression

Treatment requires addressing the underlying tubular disorder, phosphate supplementation, vitamin D analogs, and
correction of acidosis.

---

questions.stem: A 6-month-old infant presents with seizures. He was born at term to a mother with limited sun exposure during pregnancy. The infant is exclusively breast-fed without supplementation. On examination, he has frontal bossing, craniotabes, and positive Chvostek sign. His serum calcium is 6.8 mg/dL, phosphorus 5.5 mg/dL, and parathyroid hormone is 120 pg/mL (elevated). What is the most likely mechanism of hypocalcemia in this patient?

options.label: B
options.text: Vitamin D deficiency leading to decreased intestinal calcium absorption

questions.initialExplanation: An infant with seizure and high PTH: vitamin D deficiency reduces intestinal calcium absorption, so calcium falls.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This infant with vitamin D deficiency rickets presents with hypocalcemic seizures. The mechanism involves:

1. Vitamin D deficiency — decreased intestinal calcium absorption

2. Low serum calcium — stimulates parathyroid hormone secretion (secondary hyperparathyroidism)

3. PTH attempts to correct hypocalcemia by: Increasing bone resorption, Increasing renal calcium reabsorption,
Stimulating 1-alpha-hydroxylase to produce active vitamin D

4. However, with severe vitamin D deficiency, the compensatory mechanisms fail, leading to persistent hypocalcemia and
symptoms.

The elevated PTH (120 pg/mL) confirms secondary hyperparathyroidism, which is the appropriate physiological response
to hypocalcemia. The hypocalcemia in vitamin D deficiency is primarily due to impaired intestinal calcium absorption rather
than PTH deficiency or resistance.

- The clinical presentation with seizures is a medical emergency requiring prompt calcium replacement and vitamin D
therapy.

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the clinic with bilateral leg bowing noted over the past 6 months. His diet consists mainly of rice and vegetables with minimal dairy intake. He lives in a northern latitude and spends most of his time indoors. Examination reveals frontal bossing, rachitic rosary, and enlargement of both wrists and ankles. Radiographs of the wrists show metaphyseal cupping and fraying. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.label: A
options.text: Oral vitamin D 2,000-5,000 IU daily for 4-6 weeks

options.label: B
options.text: Intramuscular vitamin D 300,000-600,000 IU in divided doses

questions.initialExplanation: Treatment of vitamin D deficiency rickets: oral vitamin D 2000-5000 IU daily for several weeks.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has nutritional vitamin D deficiency rickets based on the dietary history (minimal dairy
intake), limited sun exposure (indoor lifestyle in northern latitude), and clinical and radiographic
findings. The treatment of nutritional vitamin D deficiency includes two strategies: high-dose vitamin D
(300,000-600,000 IU orally or intramuscularly as 2-4 divided doses over 1 day) or daily high-dose
vitamin D (2,000-5,000 IU/day over 4-6 weeks). Either strategy should be followed by daily vitamin D
intake of 400 IU/day.

- Daily high-dose vitamin D is generally preferred for most patients, while the observed high-dose
regimen is ideal when adherence is questionable. Calcium and phosphorus supplementation should
also be provided. Surgical correction is reserved for permanent deformities that do not improve with
medical treatment. Growth hormone is not indicated.

---

questions.stem: An 18-month-old girl presents with failure to thrive and recurrent respiratory infections. She was born at 28 weeks gestation and has been receiving parenteral nutrition since birth. Examination reveals a protruding abdomen, Harrison groove, and widening of the wrists. Serum phosphorus is low, alkaline phosphatase is elevated, and parathyroid hormone is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Rickets of prematurity occurs due to phosphate and calcium deficiency with normal PTH.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This preterm infant (28 weeks gestation) on long-term parenteral nutrition presents with rickets.
Rickets of prematurity is a well-recognized complication in very premature infants due to inadequate
mineral stores (calcium and phosphorus) at birth, increased mineral requirements for growth, and
limited enteral intake. The clinical features (failure to thrive, respiratory infections, protruding
abdomen, Harrison groove, wrist widening) and laboratory findings (low phosphorus, elevated alkaline
phosphatase, normal PTH) are consistent with this diagnosis.

- Unlike nutritional vitamin D deficiency rickets, rickets of prematurity is characterized by normal PTH
levels and primarily involves phosphate deficiency rather than vitamin D deficiency.

---

questions.stem: A 6-month-old infant is admitted with carpopedal spasm and laryngeal stridor. His mother reports that he has been exclusively breast-fed without vitamin D supplementation. Laboratory studies show serum calcium 6.2 mg/dL (normal 8.5-10.5), phosphorus 3.0 mg/dL (normal 4.0-7.0), and elevated parathyroid hormone. ECG shows prolonged QT interval. What is the most appropriate acute management?
questions.initialExplanation: Laryngospasm and carpopedal spasm with long QT: acute hypocalcemia, treated with IV calcium gluconate.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This infant presents with symptomatic hypocalcemia manifesting as carpopedal spasm, laryngeal
stridor, and prolonged QT interval. The underlying cause is nutritional vitamin D deficiency rickets
(exclusively breast-fed without supplementation). Acute management of symptomatic hypocalcemia

requires intravenous calcium to raise serum calcium levels rapidly and prevent complications such as
seizures and respiratory distress.

- After acute stabilization with IV calcium, the patient should be transitioned to oral calcium
supplements, which can typically be tapered over 2-6 weeks once adequate dietary calcium and

vitamin D therapy are established. Intravenous calcium gluconate is the standard of care for acute
symptomatic hypocalcemia.

---

questions.stem: A 14-month-old girl presents with swollen wrists and ankles. She was exclusively breast-fed for 12 months without vitamin D supplementation. Examination reveals frontal bossing, rachitic rosary, and widening of the distal radius and ulna on palpation. Serum calcium is low-normal, phosphorus is low, and 25-hydroxyvitamin D is markedly decreased. Which of the following is the most effective preventive measure?

options.label: A
options.text: Giving cow's milk instead of formula \*

options.label: B
options.text: Daily vitamin D 400 IU for breast-fed infants

questions.initialExplanation: Prevention of rickets in infants: vitamin D 400 IU daily for breastfed infants.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This infant has nutritional vitamin D deficiency rickets due to lack of vitamin D supplementation during
exclusive breast-feeding. Most cases of nutritional rickets can be prevented by universal administration
of a daily multivitamin containing 400 IU of vitamin D to children who are breast-fed. Breast milk has
low vitamin D content, so breast-fed infants rely on cutaneous synthesis or vitamin supplements.

- While maternal vitamin D supplementation during pregnancy can help prevent congenital rickets, the
key preventive measure for this infant is vitamin D supplementation. Sun exposure is important but
may be insufficient, especially in winter months or with increased skin pigmentation. Early introduction
of solid foods alone is not adequate prevention.

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy with chronic kidney disease stage 4 presents with bone pain and skeletal deformities. He has been on dialysis for 2 years. Laboratory studies show elevated parathyroid hormone, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, and low 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D levels. Radiographs show osteitis fibrosa cystica. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: CKD with osteitis fibrosa cystica = hyperparathyroid bone disease (renal osteodystrophy).
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child with end-stage renal disease presents with renal osteodystrophy, which encompasses
several bone diseases that occur in patients with chronic kidney disease. The laboratory findings

‘    (elevated PTH, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, low 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D) and radiographic
findings (osteitis fibrosa cystica) are characteristic of hyperparathyroid bone disease, a component of
renal osteodystrophy.
- In chronic kidney disease, decreased renal mass leads to decreased 1-alpha hydroxylase activity,
resulting in decreased 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D production. This causes hypocalcemia, which
stimulates secondary hyperparathyroidism. Hyperphosphatemia also develops due to decreased
phosphate excretion. Together, these lead to high-turnover bone disease characterized by increased
osteoclastic activity and bone resorption.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old girl presents with failure to thrive and proximal muscle weakness. She has a history of recurrent urinary tract infections. Examination reveals short stature, rachitic rosary, and wrist widening. Urinalysis shows glycosuria and aminoaciduria. Serum bicarbonate is low. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Failure to thrive, muscle weakness and sugar and amino acids in urine with acidosis = Fanconi syndrome.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child presents with features of rickets (failure to thrive, proximal muscle weakness, rachitic rosary,
wrist widening) along with glycosuria, aminoaciduria, and metabolic acidosis (low serum bicarbonate).
This constellation of findings is characteristic of Fanconi syndrome, which is a disorder of the proximal
renal tubule resulting in impaired reabsorption of glucose, amino acids, phosphate, bicarbonate, and
other substances.

- Fanconi syndrome can be caused by various conditions including genetic disorders (cystinosis,
Wilson disease), toxins, and metabolic diseases. The proximal tubular dysfunction leads to phosphate
wasting (causing rickets), bicarbonate wasting (causing metabolic acidosis), glucose and amino acid
wasting. This distinguishes it from other causes of rickets.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy presents with short stature and rickets not responding to standard vitamin D therapy. He has sparse hair and alopecia. Laboratory studies show very low 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D levels despite adequate 25-hydroxyvitamin D supplementation. His father has similar features. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Rickets unresponsive to vitamin D with a family history and high 1,25 = vitamin D-dependent rickets type 2.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Vitamin D-dependent rickets type 2 (also known as hereditary vitamin D-resistant rickets) is
characterized by end-organ resistance to 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D due to mutations in the vitamin D
receptor. Key features include early-onset severe rickets, hypocalcemia with secondary
hyperparathyroidism, very high levels of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (due to lack of feedback inhibition),
alopecia (a characteristic finding), and poor response to vitamin D therapy.

- The family history (father affected) suggests autosomal recessive inheritance. In contrast, vitamin D-
dependent rickets type 1 is due to 1-alpha hydroxylase deficiency, resulting in low 1,25-
dihydroxyvitamin D levels, and responds to physiological doses of calcitriol.

---

questions.stem: A 9-month-old exclusively breast-fed infant presents with bowed legs and swollen wrists. He was born at term and has never received vitamin D supplementation. His mother reports limited sun exposure due to cultural practices. On examination, he has frontal bossing, enlarged wrists and ankles, and bilateral tibial bowing. Radiograph of the wrist shows widening of the growth plate with cupping and fraying of the metaphysis. Which laboratory finding is most characteristic of this condition?

options.label: A
options.text: Low serum calcium, low serum phosphate, elevated alkaline phosphatase

options.label: B
options.text: Low serum calcium, high serum phosphate, normal alkaline phosphatase

options.label: C
options.text: Normal serum calcium, normal serum phosphate, elevated alkaline phosphatase

options.label: D
options.text: Low serum calcium, low serum phosphate, normal alkaline phosphatase

options.label: E
options.text: High serum calcium, low serum phosphate, elevated alkaline phosphatase

questions.initialExplanation: Nutritional rickets: low calcium, low phosphate and high ALP.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This infant presents with classic nutritional rickets due to vitamin D deficiency. The clinical features (bowed legs, swollen
wrists, frontal bossing) and radiographic findings (growth plate widening, cupping, fraying) are pathognomonic for rickets.
The characteristic laboratory findings in nutritional rickets include:

- Hypocalcemia: Due to impaired intestinal calcium absorption secondary to vitamin D deficiency

- Hypophosphatemia: Due to PTH-induced renal phosphate wasting combined with decreased intestinal absorption

- Elevated alkaline phosphatase: Reflects increased osteoblastic activity as the body attempts to mineralize the
unmineralized osteoid

The combination of low calcium and phosphate with elevated ALP distinguishes rickets from other conditions. In
hypoparathyroidism, phosphate would be elevated. In renal failure, both calcium and phosphate may be abnormal with
different patterns.

---

questions.stem: A 6-month-old exclusively breast-fed infant is found to have craniotabes and widened wrists. His mother has dark skin and wears covering clothing. Serum investigations show calcium 7.5 mg/dL, phosphate 4.5 mg/dL, and alkaline phosphatase 380 U/L. Radiograph of the wrist shows fraying and cupping of the distal radius and ulna. Which factor is the most significant risk factor for developing this condition?

options.label: B
options.text: Exclusive breast-feeding without vitamin D supplementation

questions.initialExplanation: The main risk for rickets in an exclusively breastfed infant: not giving vitamin D.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This infant has nutritional vitamin D deficiency rickets. The most significant risk factor is exclusive breast-feeding
without vitamin D supplementation. Breast milk contains very low levels of vitamin D (approximately 20-40 IU/L),
which is insufficient to meet infant requirements, especially in those with limited sun exposure.

Additional risk factors in this case include:

- Dark skin pigmentation (decreased cutaneous vitamin D synthesis)

- Maternal covering clothing (limited sun exposure)

- Young age (peak incidence at 6-18 months when growth is rapid)

While premature birth can lead to rickets of prematurity, this infant was born at term. Cow's milk allergy would
cause issues with calcium intake but is not the primary risk factor here. Maternal hyperparathyroidism would
cause different manifestations.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old girl with rickets has hypocalcemia, hypophosphatemia, elevated alkaline phosphatase, and elevated parathyroid hormone. Her serum 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is low. Treatment with high-dose vitamin D is initiated. Which parameter should be monitored most closely during initial treatment?
questions.initialExplanation: When treating rickets with high-dose vitamin D, monitor calcium early because of the risk of it falling.
questions.detailedExplanation:
During treatment of vitamin D deficiency rickets, the most important parameter to monitor is serum calcium.
The risk of hypercalcemia is significant because:

- Vitamin D therapy promotes intestinal calcium absorption

- Previously demineralized bone is actively taking up calcium

- PTH levels are elevated, promoting bone resorption

- Hypercalcemia can cause serious complications including nephrocalcinosis, soft tissue calcification, and
neurological symptoms. Initial treatment should include monitoring of serum calcium every 1-2 weeks during
the intensive phase, then monthly.

While phosphate, ALP, and urinary calcium are important, serum calcium is the most critical to monitor due to
the risk of life-threatening hypercalcemia. Symptoms of hypercalcemia include anorexia, nausea, vomiting,
polyuria, and lethargy.

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy presents with bowed legs. On examination, he has notching of the ear lobes and subcutaneous calcifications. Radiograph shows increased bone density at the metaphyses. Laboratory investigations reveal serum calcium 5.5 mg/dL, phosphate 7.5 mg/dL, and normal alkaline phosphatase. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Very low calcium, high phosphate and normal ALP = hypoparathyroidism.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has hypoparathyroidism, not rickets. The key features include:

- Severe hypocalcemia (5.5 mg/dL)

- Hyperphosphatemia (7.5 mg/dL) - opposite of rickets

- Notching of ear lobes and subcutaneous calcifications - characteristic physical findings in chronic
hypoparathyroidism

- Increased bone density on radiograph - opposite of the rarefaction seen in rickets

- Normal alkaline phosphatase - osteoblastic activity is not increased as in rickets

In rickets, the pattern is hypocalcemia, hypophosphatemia, and elevated alkaline phosphatase. The physical
findings (ear lobe notching, subcutaneous calcifications) and radiographic features (increased density) are
classic for chronic hypoparathyroidism due to long-standing hypocalcemia.

---

questions.stem: A 6-month-old infant presents with craniotabes and delayed fontanelle closure. His mother reports that he has had recurrent respiratory infections. On examination, he has a Harrison groove and rachitic rosary. His serum calcium is 7.8 mg/dL, phosphate is 3.8 mg/dL, and alkaline phosphatase is 350 U/L. Which complication is this child at highest risk for?
questions.initialExplanation: A severely rachitic infant is exposed to seizures because of low calcium.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This infant has severe nutritional vitamin D deficiency rickets with significant hypocalcemia (7.8 mg/dL). The most
immediate and serious complication is hypocalcemic seizures, which can occur when serum calcium falls below 7 mg/dL.
Additional complications include:

- Pathological fractures: Due to weakened bone (true, but seizures are more acute)

- Respiratory infections: Due to chest wall deformities and muscle weakness (increased risk, but not the highest immediate
risk)

- Respiratory distress: From chest wall deformities and hypotonia

- Long-term deformities: Bowing, short stature

The hypocalcemia in rickets results from impaired intestinal calcium absorption due to vitamin D deficiency. The
compensatory secondary hyperparathyroidism helps maintain calcium levels but contributes to hypophosphatemia.
Monitoring serum calcium and treating promptly are essential to prevent seizures.

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy presents with hypocalcemia and seizures. Laboratory investigations show serum calcium 5.8 mg/dL, phosphate 9.0 mg/dL, and PTH 8 pg/mL (low). His face is noted to have small chin, low-set ears, and hypertelorism. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Low calcium and seizure with a typical face (small chin, low-set ears) = DiGeorge syndrome.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2 deletion syndrome), characterized by:

- Hypoparathyroidism: Due to aplasia or hypoplasia of parathyroid glands

- Characteristic facies: Small chin (micrognathia), low-set ears, hypertelorism, nasal anomalies

- Cardiac anomalies: Conotruncal defects (tetralogy of Fallot, truncus arteriosus)

- Thymic hypoplasia: Immunodeficiency (variable severity)

- CATCH 22: Cardiac defects, Abnormal facies, Thymic hypoplasia, Cleft palate, Hypocalcemia

The combination of hypoparathyroidism with characteristic facial features strongly suggests DiGeorge

syndrome. The hypocalcemia is due to absent or hypoplastic parathyroid glands (fourth pharyngeal pouch
anomaly).

---

questions.stem: A 1-week-old infant presents with seizures. He was born at term to a mother with hyperparathyroidism who was treated with parathyroidectomy during pregnancy. Laboratory investigations show serum calcium 5.5 mg/dL, phosphate 9.0 mg/dL, and parathyroid hormone undetectable. What is the mechanism of hypocalcemia in this infant?

options.label: A
options.text: Maternal hypercalcemia suppressing fetal parathyroid function

questions.initialExplanation: An infant seizing with undetected PTH and high phosphate: a mother with hypercalcemia suppresses the fetal PTH.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This infant has hypocalcemia secondary to suppression of neonatal PTH secretion due to maternal hyperparathyroidism.
Maternal hypercalcemia crosses the placenta and suppresses fetal parathyroid gland development and function.

Key points:

- Maternal hyperparathyroidism causes elevated maternal calcium, which crosses the placenta

- Fetal parathyroid glands are suppressed by the high calcium environment

- After birth, the infant's calcium drops, but the parathyroid glands cannot respond adequately

- Result: Hypocalcemia with low PTH in the newborn period

This is a form of functional hypoparathyroidism that typically resolves as the parathyroid glands recover. Treatment is
supportive with calcium and vitamin D during the acute period.

In contrast, maternal hypoparathyroidism can cause fetal hyperparathyroidism and neonatal hypocalcemia due to different
mechanisms.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy with hypoparathyroidism is being treated with calcitriol and calcium supplements. His serum calcium has been maintained at 8.5-9.0 mg/dL. His mother reports that he has been having headaches and vomiting for the past week. What is the most likely cause of these symptoms?
questions.initialExplanation: In hypoparathyroidism with headache and vomiting: intracranial (basal ganglia) calcification is possible.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has chronic hypoparathyroidism with neurological symptoms (headache, vomiting) that could indicate
increased intracranial pressure. In long-standing hypoparathyroidism, intracranial calcifications can develop,
particularly in the basal ganglia, and may cause neurological symptoms.

Key points about intracranial calcification in hypoparathyroidism:

- Occurs in long-standing untreated or poorly controlled hypoparathyroidism

- Most commonly affects the basal ganglia, but can also involve the cerebellum, thalamus, and other areas

- Can cause neurological symptoms including headache, vomiting, visual changes, and cognitive impairment
- May be reversible with adequate calcium and vitamin D therapy

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy presents with seizures. Laboratory investigations show serum calcium 6.0 mg/dL, phosphate 8.5 mg/dL, and parathyroid hormone 350 pg/mL (elevated). His serum magnesium is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Low calcium, high phosphate and high PTH in a child with seizures suggests PTH resistance (pseudohypoparathyroidism).
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has pseudohypoparathyroidism (PHP), characterized by:

- Hypocalcemia (6.0 mg/dL), Hyperphosphatemia (8.5 mg/dL)

- Elevated PTH (350 pg/mL) - the key distinguishing feature

In PHP, the parathyroid glands are normal or hyperplastic and produce adequate PTH, but there is end-organ resistance to
PTH action. This causes the biochemical picture of hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia despite elevated PTH levels.

- In contrast, hypoparathyroidism would show low or undetectable PTH levels. The distinction is crucial because treatment
differs:

- Hypoparathyroidism: Calcium and vitamin D supplementation
- PHP: Same treatment, but genetic counseling is important

- PHP is classified into different types based on the pattern of hormone resistance and associated physical features.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy with hypoparathyroidism has a serum calcium of 6.5 mg/dL and presents with carpopedal spasm and laryngeal stridor. What is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.initialExplanation: Calcium falling to 6.5 with laryngospasm: emergency treatment is IV calcium gluconate.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has acute hypocalcemic tetany with laryngeal spasm, a medical emergency. The stridor indicates
laryngospasm, which can progress to complete airway obstruction and respiratory arrest.

The immediate treatment is intravenous calcium gluconate:

- 5-10 mL of 10% calcium gluconate at 0.5-1 mL/minute

- Monitor heart rate continuously during administration

- Repeat as needed until symptoms resolve

While intubation may be necessary if there is severe airway compromise, calcium administration should be
initiated immediately as it will reverse the laryngospasm. IV calcium works within minutes to raise serum
calcium and relieve muscle spasm.

Corticosteroids are not indicated for hypocalcemic tetany. Oral calcium and inhaled bronchodilators are too
slow and ineffective for this emergency.

Rickets & Parathyroid |

---

questions.stem: You are providing initial diabetes education to the parents of a 12-year-old recently diagnosed with type 1 diabetes. Which of the following should NOT be included in the initial treatment guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: Recognizing high blood glucose and testing ketones on sick days \*

options.label: B
options.text: Explaining the long-term risks of nephropathy and retinopathy

options.label: C
options.text: Preparing and injecting the correct dose of insulin subcutaneously at the proper time

options.label: D
options.text: Recognizing and treating symptoms of low blood glucose

options.label: E
options.text: Providing basic guidance on nutritional management and meal planning

questions.initialExplanation: Initial education focuses on insulin, hypoglycemia and nutrition; explaining long-term diabetes complications (retina, kidney) is not part of the initial guidance.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Initial diabetes education for a newly diagnosed child with type 1 diabetes should focus on essential,
immediately relevant information that the family needs to manage the condition safely and effectively. The goal
is to provide practical skills and knowledge that will allow the family to prevent acute complications while
avoiding overwhelming them with information about long-term complications that may not manifest for decades.
- The newly diagnosed patient and family are typically in a state of emotional distress and information overload.
Research in diabetes education emphasizes the importance of staged learning, where basic survival skills are
taught first, followed by more complex self-management concepts. Presenting too much information too quickly
can lead to poor retention and increased anxiety.

---

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy with type 1 diabetes presents with vomiting, dehydration, rapid breathing, and altered mental status. Laboratory studies show random glucose of 350 mg/dL, arterial pH of 7.2, and 3+ urinary ketones. Which option best reflects proper management?

options.label: A
options.text: Insulin bolus should be given before starting fluids \*

options.label: B
options.text: Fluid resuscitation should begin with 30 mL/kg over 4 hours

options.label: C
options.text: Intravenous bicarbonate should be administered to correct acidosis

options.label: D
options.text: Insulin infusion should continue at 0.05 units/kg/hour when glucose drops below 150 mg/dL

options.label: E
options.text: Potassium should be withheld if the serum potassium is within normal limits

questions.initialExplanation: In DKA the insulin infusion continues (0.05-0.1 unit/kg/hr) after fluids start; do not give routine insulin boluses or bicarbonate.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This patient presents with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), a life-threatening emergency requiring immediate
hospital treatment. The clinical features—vomiting, dehydration, rapid breathing (Kussmaul respirations), and
altered mental status—are classic for DKA. The laboratory findings confirm the diagnosis: hyperglycemia
(glucose 350 mg/dL), metabolic acidosis (pH 7.2, consistent with moderate DKA), and ketonuria.

- DKA results from absolute insulin deficiency combined with increased counterregulatory hormones (glucagon,
catecholamines, cortisol, growth hormone). This hormonal imbalance leads to increased hepatic glucose
production, decreased peripheral glucose utilization, and accelerated lipolysis with ketogenesis. The resulting
hyperglycemia causes osmotic diuresis, dehydration, and electrolyte losses. Metabolic acidosis develops from
the accumulation of ketone bodies (acetoacetate and 3-hydroxybutyrate).

---

questions.stem: A 13-year-old girl with a 6-year history of type 1 diabetes mellitus is admitted for the third time in two months due to diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). Her glucose monitoring records reveal episodes of severe hypoglycemia alternating with marked hyperglycemia, despite reported adherence to her insulin regimen. She has a background of anxiety and limited family support. Her HbA1c remains persistently elevated (>10%) and continuous glucose monitoring shows significant glycemic variability without a consistent pattern. What is the most likely diagnosis in this case?
questions.initialExplanation: Marked glucose swings without a fixed pattern despite insulin = brittle diabetes.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This patient demonstrates the classic presentation of "brittle diabetes," a term used to describe type 1
diabetes characterized by recurrent, unpredictable fluctuations in blood glucose levels that are difficult
to control despite apparent adherence to the treatment regimen. The repeated hospitalizations for
DKA, significant glycemic variability, and psychosocial stressors all point to this diagnosis.

- Brittle diabetes is characterized by recurrent, unexplained hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia leading
to frequent hospitalizations. The term was first coined in the 1930s and remains relevant today
despite advances in insulin therapy and glucose monitoring. While the term is somewhat dated and
controversial (as it may stigmatize patients), it describes a real clinical phenomenon in which
psychological, social, and behavioral factors significantly impact glycemic control.

---

questions.stem: A 12-year-old diabetic female presented with dehydration and decreased level of consciousness. You suspect the diagnosis of DKA, and during management, she deteriorated. Which of the following is MOST indicative of cerebral edema?
questions.initialExplanation: The key sign of cerebral edema in DKA: bradycardia (Cushing) with headache, altered consciousness and hypertension.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This patient presents with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) and has deteriorated during management, raising
concern for the development of cerebral edema, which is the most feared and life-threatening complication of
DKA treatment in children. Cerebral edema typically occurs within the first 12-24 hours of treatment and has a
mortality rate of approximately 20-25%, with many survivors suffering from permanent neurological sequelae.

- The exact mechanism of cerebral edema in DKA is not fully understood, but it is believed to result from
multiple factors including rapid changes in osmolality, generation of inflammatory mediators, and impaired
cerebral autoregulation. When DKA is treated, the rapid decrease in serum osmolality creates an osmotic
gradient that draws water into brain cells, causing cerebral swelling. Children are at particularly high risk due to
their relatively larger brain-to-skull ratio and different compensatory mechanisms compared to adults.

---

questions.stem: A 13-year-old diabetic child with poor control with HbA1c of 12% is seen in the endocrine clinic. The LEAST chronic complication of type 1 diabetes mellitus that needs to be examined is:

options.label: D
options.text: Lipohypertrophy at the site of injections

options.label: E
options.text: Positive prayers signs due to limited joint mobility

questions.initialExplanation: When reviewing poorly controlled diabetes we look for chronic complications (retina, kidney, nerves); "signs of dehydration" is not a chronic complication.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The question asks for the least relevant chronic complication to assess in a 13-year-old with long-
standing, poorly controlled type 1 diabetes (HbA1c 12%). Chronic complications of type 1 diabetes

include microvascular (retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy), macrovascular, and diabetes-specific
musculoskeletal or skin changes.

- Assessment of vision (B) screens for diabetic retinopathy, a well-known microvascular complication
that can begin in adolescence after several years of poor control.
Lipohypertrophy at injection sites (D) is a common local tissue reaction due to repeated insulin

injections and reflects suboptimal injection practices; it can affect insulin absorption and glycemic
control.

---

questions.stem: A 9-year-old girl develops polyuria, vomiting, abdominal pain, and deep acidotic breathing during an intercurrent illness. She has been diagnosed with type 1 diabetes mellitus 5 years ago. Lab investigations reveal: blood glucose, 600 mg/dL; blood pH, 7.28; serum bicarbonate concentration, 14 mEq/L; and ketones in urine are positive. Of the following, the MOST serious complication that may occur in this girl is : (NE)
questions.initialExplanation: The most dangerous complication of DKA in children: cerebral edema.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This patient presents with classic features of severe DKA:

- Hyperglycemia (glucose 600 mg/dL), Metabolic acidosis (pH 7.28, HCOs~ 14 mEq/L), Ketones in
urine

- Symptoms including polyuria, vomiting, abdominal pain, and deep (Kussmaul) breathing

Among the listed options, cerebral edema is the most feared and life-threatening complication of DKA
in children. It typically occurs 6—12 hours after initiation of treatment, although it can present at
diagnosis. It is the leading cause of mortality and severe neurological morbidity in pediatric DKA.

---

questions.stem: You are going to treat a 7-year-old boy with type 1 diabetes mellitus who develops DKA due to a recent infection. Examination reveals severe dehydration and deep acidotic breathing. Lab investigations shows: blood glucose, 450 mg/dL; blood pH, 7.2; and serum bicarbonate concentration, 14 mEq/L. Which of the following should be avoided during the treatment of this girl? (NE)
questions.initialExplanation: In DKA treatment bicarbonate is avoided in most cases because it may raise cerebral edema risk and lower potassium.
questions.detailedExplanation:
In the management of pediatric diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), intravenous sodium bicarbonate is generally contraindicated
and should be avoided in almost all cases.

- This patient—a 7-year-old boy with DKA (glucose 450 mg/dL, pH 7.2, HCOs™ 14 mEq/L) —requires standard DKA therapy:
fluid resuscitation, insulin infusion, and careful electrolyte replacement. However, bicarbonate administration offers no

proven benefit and carries significant risks, including:

- Paradoxical central nervous system acidosis

- Hypokalemia (due to intracellular shift of potassium)

- Impaired oxygen delivery (leftward shift of the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve)

- Potential worsening of cerebral edema

Current guidelines strongly advise against routine bicarbonate use in children with DKA. According to the BSPED (British Society for
Paediatric Endocrinology and Diabetes) guideline:

“Do not give intravenous sodium bicarbonate to children and young people with DKA. Only consider bicarbonate if there is life-
threatening hyperkalemia or cardiac arrest”.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old girl has been developed type 1 diabetes mellitus 6 months ago. She is on intensive control using multiple daily injections of insulin. A recent blood testing of HgbA1c is 6.5%. Of the following, the MOST frequent complication that may be encountered at this age is : (NE)
questions.initialExplanation: Young children on insulin are prone to recurrent hypoglycemia because they cannot express the symptoms.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This 5-year-old girl with type 1 diabetes mellitus on intensive insulin therapy with multiple daily injections and a relatively tight glycemic
control (HbA1c 6.5%) is at significant risk for recurrent hypoglycemia, which is the most frequent complication encountered in young

children with type 1 diabetes.

Why recurrent hypoglycemia is the most frequent complication:

1. Physiological vulnerability of young children: Young children have higher insulin sensitivity and lower glycogen stores compared to older patients,
making them more susceptible to hypoglycemia

2. Unpredictable eating patterns: Preschool-aged children have erratic food intake, making it difficult to match insulin dosing with carbohydrate
consumption

3. Immature counter-regulatory responses: Young children may have blunted glucagon and epinephrine responses to hypoglycemia, impairing their
ability to recognize and correct low blood glucose

4. Limited ability to communicate: Young children cannot always articulate hypoglycemia symptoms, leading to delayed recognition and treatment
5. Intensive insulin therapy: Multiple daily injection regimens, while providing better glycemic control, significantly increase hypoglycemia risk compared to
conventional therapy

6. Developmental factors: Rapidly growing children have changing insulin requirements, and physical activity patterns are unpredictable

---

questions.stem: Type 2 DM can be managed with lifestyle modifications, including nutrition therapy, increased exercise, and oral hypoglycemic agent (metformin); however, insulin therapy is necessary in special circumstances. Of the following, insulin treatment is required when there is : (NE)
questions.initialExplanation: Insulin is required in T2DM when there is ketonuria/ketosis (or a very high HbA1c).
questions.detailedExplanation:
In type 2 diabetes mellitus, insulin therapy is typically reserved for special circumstances when oral hypoglycemic agents
and lifestyle modifications are insufficient. The presence of ketonuria is a clear indication that insulin treatment is required.

Why ketonuria necessitates insulin therapy:

1. indicates severe insulin deficiency: Ketonuria demonstrates that the body has insufficient insulin to properly metabolize
glucose, forcing it to break down fats for energy through ketogenesis.

2. Risk of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA): Although DKA is more commonly associated with type 1 diabetes, it can occur in
type 2 diabetes during severe physiological stress (infection, trauma, surgery). The presence of ketones signals
impending or established ketoacidosis.

3. Absolute insulin deficiency state: The development of ketonuria indicates that the insulin deficiency has progressed

beyond what oral agents can address, requiring exogenous insulin to: Suppress lipolysis, Stop ketogenesis, Promote
glucose utilization ,Reverse the catabolic state

---

questions.stem: A 12-years-old girl presents to the ER with history of repeated vomiting and abdominal pain, in the preceded 4 days she suffered from frequent urination and excessive thirst. What is the next step in her management? (NE)
questions.initialExplanation: With vomiting, abdominal pain and thirst: the first step is measuring blood glucose to confirm hyperglycemia/DKA.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This 12-year-old girl presents with classic symptoms of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA): repeated vomiting, abdominal pain,

polyuria (frequent urination), and polydipsia (excessive thirst). These are the hallmark symptoms of new-onset type 1
diabetes mellitus.

Why blood glucose is the next step:

1. Immediate diagnosis confirmation: Checking blood glucose is the fastest and most critical initial test. A fingerstick
glucose can be performed at the bedside within seconds and will immediately reveal if significant hyperglycemia is present
2. Guides all subsequent management: If hyperglycemia is confirmed (typically >200 mg/dL), this sets in motion the DKA
protocol including fluid resuscitation, insulin therapy, and electrolyte monitoring

3. Resource-efficient: Blood glucose testing is rapid, inexpensive, and can be done before any other interventions or
investigations

---

questions.stem: An 8-year-old boy presents with abdominal pain and rapid breathing, his blood sugar is 483 mg/dI. What is the MOST appropriate next step in his management? (NE)
questions.initialExplanation: Abdominal pain, rapid breathing and glucose 483 mean DKA: give NS quickly (10 mL/kg/hr) before insulin.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child’s presentation is highly suggestive of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA):

- Hyperglycemia (glucose > 250 mg/dL), - Abdominal pain (common in pediatric DKA)

- Rapid/deep breathing (Kussmaul respirations due to metabolic acidosis)

In pediatric DKA, the initial priority is fluid resuscitation, not immediate insulin administration —especially if there are signs
of dehydration or hemodynamic instability.

Why fluid first?

- Insulin drives potassium and glucose into cells, which can worsen hypovolemia and precipitate shock or cerebral edema
if given before adequate volume expansion.

- Guidelines (e.g., ISPAD, BSPED, ADA) recommend:

Initial fluid bolus: 10 mL/kg of 0.9% normal saline over 30—60 minutes in children with signs of dehydration or poor
perfusion.

- Insulin infusion should be delayed until after initial fluid resuscitation (typically started 1-2 hours after fluids begin).

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-girl presents with history of polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia and decrease body weight, her investigation reveal blood glucose 321 mg/dl, Hb A1c 8 and ketones in urine —ve. What is the NEXT step in her management?
questions.initialExplanation: Diabetes symptoms and high glucose without ketones: start subcutaneous insulin (T1DM without DKA).
questions.detailedExplanation:
This 6-year-old child presents with classic symptoms of diabetes mellitus (polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, and weight
loss) with laboratory confirmation (blood glucose 321 mg/dl and HbA1c 8%). The critical clinical consideration here is the
patient's age and presentation.

Why insulin is the correct choice:

1. Age Factor: At 6 years old, this child falls in the age group where type 1 diabetes is overwhelmingly more common than type 2
diabetes. Type 2 diabetes is rare in young children and typically presents in adolescents with obesity and strong family history.

2. Clinical Presentation: The classic "3 Ps" with weight loss in a young child strongly suggests type 1 diabetes, even without
ketoacidosis.

3. Management Guidelines: For new-onset type 1 diabetes in children without DKA, subcutaneous insulin should be initiated
immediately. The absence of ketones indicates this is not DKA, but the child still requires insulin therapy.

4. Type 2 diabetes is unlikely: While the absence of ketones might suggest type 2 diabetes in an obese adolescent, in a 6-year-old with
these symptoms, type 1 diabetes is the presumptive diagnosis until proven otherwise.

---

questions.stem: You are evaluating a 14-year-old boy who has a body mass index of 40 kg/m2. His mother and 25- year-old sister have type 2 diabetes. A fasting blood glucose concentration for the boy is 110 mg/dL (6.1 mmol/L). Of the following, the MOST appropriate next step to screen for diabetes is to : (NE)

options.label: B
options.text: measure serum insulin and C-peptide concentrations

options.label: C
options.text: perform a 2-hour oral glucose tolerance test

options.label: D
options.text: E measure blood glucose 1 hour after a high-carbohydrate breakfast

options.label: E
options.text: repeat a fasting blood glucose measurement

questions.initialExplanation: An obese teen with a slightly high fasting result: do a 2-hour OGTT to diagnose diabetes/glucose intolerance.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The boy described in the vignette is at high risk for type 2 diabetes because of his elevated body mass index and strong
family history. His elevated fasting blood glucose value is worrisome but not diagnostic of diabetes. Criteria for the
diagnosis of diabetes are two random blood glucose values greater than 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) or one random value of
200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) with symptoms, a fasting plasma glucose greater than 126 mg/dL (6.7 mmol/L), or a 2-hour post
glucose tolerance test glucose value of greater than 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L). Therefore, a 2 hour oral glucose tolerance
test should be performed for the boy in the vignette to determine whether he meets the criteria for diabetes.

Although glycosylated hemoglobin values are elevated in diabetes that is not perfectly controlled, measurement of this
compound is not a good screening test for diabetes. Elevated insulin and C-peptide concentrations are found in any
individual who has insulin resistance. Levels may help differentiate type 1 (low insulin and C-peptide) from type 2 (high
insulin and C peptide) diabetes, but are not diagnostic of diabetes itself.

---

questions.stem: A 10-year-old child arrives with the complaint of new-onset bed-wetting. He has had no fever, his urine culture is negative, and he has had no new stresses in his life. He is well above the 95th percentile for weight as is much of his family. Which of the following is most helpful in making a diagnosis? (pretest)

options.label: C
options.text: Two-hour glucose during glucose tolerance test of 165 mg/dL

options.label: E
options.text: Symptoms alone are enough to make the diagnosis

questions.initialExplanation: New bedwetting with weight gain in the family: requires a fasting plasma glucose for diagnosis (>=126).
questions.detailedExplanation:
The criteria for diagnosis of diabetesmellitus, as established by the Expert Committee on the Diagnosis and
Classification of Diabetes Mellitus (sponsored by the American Diabetes Association) include a fasting glucose
level = 126 mg/dL, a 2-hour plasma glucose during an oral glucose tolerance test = 200 mg/dL, or symptoms of

‘    diabetes mellitus plus a random plasma glucose = 200 mg/dL. Acanthosis nigricans in children usually suggests
insulin resistance, but is not, in and of itself, diagnostic, nor are symptoms alone diagnostic. Previous standards
suggested a fasting glucose between 110 and 125 mg/dL or a 2-hour glucose during an oral glucose tolerance
test between 140 and 200 mg/dL indicated impaired glucose tolerance. Impaired (not yet diabetic) glucose
levels include fasting values between 100 and 125 mg/dL and impaired 2-hour values between 140 and 200
mg/dL. The bed-wetting in the question can be explained by increased liquid consumption due to the
hyperosmolar state caused by hyperglycemia.

---

questions.stem: An adolescent with type 1 diabetes returns for a follow-up visit after his annual checkup last week. You note that his serum glucose is elevated, and his glycosylated hemoglobin (hemoglobin A1C) is 16.7%. This finding suggests poor control of his diabetes over at least which of the following time periods? (pretest) 8 hours
questions.initialExplanation: HbA1c reflects control over about 2 to 3 months.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Glucose is nonenzymatically attached to hemoglobin to form glycosylated hemoglobin. The major
component of this reaction proceeds very slowly and is irreversible until the hemoglobin is destroyed.
The concentration of glycosylated hemoglobin thus reflects glucose concentration over the half-life of
the red cell, or about 2 to 3 months. The adolescent in the question may have had poor control of his
diabetes for longer than 2 to 3 months, but glycosylated hemoglobin is unable to determine this.

---

questions.stem: A previously healthy 10-year-old boy presents with a 2-day history of abdominal pain and vomiting. His mother thought that he had the flu since his older brother was recently diagnosed with a viral iliness. On exam, he is afebrile but appears ill as he is tachypneic and tachycardic. Laboratory testing reveals a plasma glucose of 745 mg/dL. His bicarbonate level is 6 mEq/L and his venous pH is 7.10. A urinalysis is positive for glucose and large ketones. The most appropriate first step in this patient’s management is which of the following? (Rud)

options.label: A
options.text: Start an insulin drip at 0.1 units per kg per hour

options.label: D
options.text: Bolus with normal saline at 20 mL/kg

questions.initialExplanation: DKA: the first step is a 0.9% NS bolus of 20 mL/kg.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The patient has new-onset diabetes and is presenting with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). The goals of
treatment of DKA are to restore perfusion, arrest ketone production, replace electrolyte losses, and

‘    avoid complications. The first line of treatment is to restore perfusion by giving NaCl (0.9%) at 20
mL/kg in the first 1 to 2 hours. After the initial fluid bolus, IV fluids should be given based on a
rehydration plan accounting for the degree of dehydration and maintenance fluid requirement. Insulin
should be started as an insulin drip at 0.1 units/kg/hr as a continuous infusion only after the initial fluid
expansion is completed. A bolus of insulin is unnecessary and should be avoided as this could
precipitously drop the serum blood sugar as well as increase the risk of cerebral edema. Bicarbonate
is not indicated in this clinical scenario and would increase the potential risk for complications.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old girl is admitted to the hospital with DKA. Her weight is 20 kg. She received 2 L of IV fluids initially when she arrived in the Emergency Department 6 hours ago. She had been feeling better and was conversational, but now she is more somnolent and difficult to arouse. Her blood sugar is 214 mg/dL, and she is on an insulin drip and IV fluids at 2 times maintenance. Which of the following is the most appropriate step in the management of this patient? (Rud)
questions.initialExplanation: DKA with neurological deterioration: cerebral edema is treated with mannitol.
questions.detailedExplanation:
A serious and potentially life-threatening complication of DKA is cerebral edema. As this patient is less than 5-
years old and received a large volume of fluids upon presentation (100 mL/kg), she is at high risk for cerebral
edema. Cerebral edema typically occurs 4-12 hours after starting treatment, but it can occur later or even
before treatment has started. Many if not all patients with DKA have some degree of cerebral edema, but most
are asymptomatic. Case reports have shown some benefit with mannitol. Close monitoring and rapid
recognition of cerebral edema may result in positive outcomes.

Treatment and clinical decision making should not be delayed for the results of a head CT. Bicarbonate is not
indicated and would increase the likelihood of cerebral edema. Intubation is not necessary unless respiratory
compromise is present. Hyperventilation has been associated with poor outcomes in patients with cerebral
edema. Besides mannitol, other early intervention measures include reduction in the IV fluid rate and elevation
of the head of the bed.

---

questions.stem: A 15-year-old obese African American girl has struggled with weight gain for many years. She presents with concerns of fatigue and lack of energy. Other review of systems is positive for increased thirst and urination over the past few weeks. Her weight is 120 kg and she has lost 5 kg in the last 2 months. On exam, she has darkening of the skin on the back and sides of her neck. She also has a vaginal yeast infection. A urinalysis reveals >1000 glucose and no ketones. Additional tests show that her plasma glucose is 256 mg/dL, bicarbonate is 26 mEqg/mL, and her hemoglobin A1c is 9.5%. Which of the following would be the most appropriate treatment? (Rud)

options.label: A
options.text: Refer her to a diabetes specialist to start insulin injections

options.label: B
options.text: Refer her to a dietitian to start a calorie-restricted diet

options.label: C
options.text: Refer her to a diabetes specialist to start metformin

options.label: D
options.text: Refer her to a diabetes specialist to start a sulfonylurea

options.label: E
options.text: Admit her to the hospital for IV fluids and an insulin drip

questions.initialExplanation: An obese teen girl with HbA1c 9.5%: refer to a diabetes specialist to start insulin.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The patient has new-onset diabetes based on her symptoms and elevated random plasma glucose. The diagnostic criteria
for diabetes includes symptoms of diabetes and a casual plasma glucose 2200 mg/dL; fasting plasma glucose 2126
mg/dL; 2-hour plasma glucose 2200 mg/dL during an oral glucose tolerance test; or a hemoglobin Alc 26.5%. If the patient

‘     is asymptomatic, then the test needs to be repeated on a second day to confirm the diagnosis. It is sometimes difficult to
determine if a patient has type 1 or type 2 diabetes, as obesity is increasing in all populations in the United States. As she
has a history of obesity, is from a high-risk ethnic population, and has signs of insulin resistance (acanthosis nigricans),
she most likely has type 2 diabetes. Regardless of whether she has type 1 or type 2 diabetes, she should be started on
insulin injections due to her markedly elevated hemoglobin A1c value of 9.5%. Due to glucose toxicity and {3 cell
dysfunction, neither metformin nor a sulfonylurea alone would be effective at this time. The patient does not have ketones
in her urine and her bicarbonate level is normal; therefore, she does not have DKA and does not need to be started on IV
fluids or an insulin drip. Referral to a dietitian would be helpful, but this is not the best initial management to improve her
blood sugar control.

---

questions.stem: An obese 11-year-old boy with diabetes mellitus is admitted to the hospital because of severe ketoacidosis and cardiovascular collapse. Which of the following electrolyte deficits would most likely cause death in this patient? (CanadaQB)
questions.initialExplanation: A diabetic patient with cardiac collapse: the most dangerous cause is low potassium resulting from DKA treatment.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Diabetics in DKA are at serious risk for profound hypokalemia, a potentially fatal condition. The
hypokalemia results from both profound dehydration and from an intracellular return of potassium to
cells after the requirement to buffer the acidosis has passed. During acidosis there is an exchange of
potassium for hydrogen with hydrogen moving intra-cellularly to be buffered.

---

questions.stem: A 12-year-old girl presents to the emergency department with a 3-day history of nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. She has been drinking more fluids than usual and urinating frequently. Her parents report she has been more tired and has lost weight over the past 2 weeks. On examination: temperature 37.2°C, heart rate 110/min, respiratory rate 28/min, blood pressure 100/65 mmHg. She appears dehydrated with dry mucous membranes. Her breath has a fruity odor. Random blood glucose is 420 mg/dL, and urinalysis shows 4+ glucose and positive ketones. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Glucose 420 with sugar and ketones in urine = diabetic ketoacidosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This clinical presentation is classic for diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). The key features include polyuria and
polydipsia (increased thirst and urination), weight loss, nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. The fruity breath
odor is characteristic of acetone, which is produced from ketone bodies. Random blood glucose of 420 mg/dL
with glucosuria and ketonuria confirms the diagnosis. DKA is defined by the triad of hyperglycemia (serum
glucose >200 mg/dL), metabolic acidosis (pH <7.25 or serum bicarbonate <15 mEq/L), and ketonemia or
ketonuria.

- Hypoglycemia would present with low blood glucose, not high. Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state is more
common in Type 2 diabetes and presents with severe hyperglycemia (>600 mg/dL) but without significant
ketosis. Lactic acidosis would have elevated lactate levels. Salicylate poisoning would have a history of
ingestion and different clinical findings.

---

questions.stem: A 12-year-old girl with Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus for 3 years presents with nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain for 1 day. She reports increased shortness of breath and fruity-smelling breath. Her mother mentions that she omitted her evening insulin dose yesterday because she was feeling unwell. Vital signs show temperature 37.8°C, heart rate 110 bpm, respiratory rate 24/min, blood pressure 95/60 mmHg. Laboratory results reveal blood glucose 450 mg/dL, pH 7.28, bicarbonate 14 mEq/L, and positive serum ketones. What is the most important initial intervention?

options.label: A
options.text: Admin intravenous normal saline bolus 20 mL/kg

options.label: B
options.text: Start intravenous insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour

options.label: C
options.text: Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate for acidosis

options.label: E
options.text: Obtain head CT to rule out cerebral edema

questions.initialExplanation: Acidosis with ketones: the most important initial intervention is a 20 mL/kg NS bolus.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This patient presents with Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA) characterized by hyperglycemia, metabolic acidosis
(pH 7.28, bicarbonate 14 mEq/L), and ketonuria. The most critical initial step in DKA management is fluid
resuscitation with intravenous normal saline to restore circulating volume, improve tissue perfusion, and help
lower blood glucose. A fluid bolus of 20 mL/kg is the standard initial treatment. While insulin therapy is
essential, fluid resuscitation should precede or accompany insulin initiation to prevent rapid fluid shifts and
reduce the risk of cerebral edema. Bicarbonate therapy is generally not recommended as it may worsen
cerebral edema and hypokalemia. Potassium replacement is important but should follow the initial fluid bolus
and after confirming serum potassium levels. Head CT would only be indicated if cerebral edema is suspected
(altered mental status, neurological signs), which is not present here.

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl presents with a 3-week history of increased thirst, frequent urination, and 4 kg weight loss. She wakes 2-3 times nightly to void and has daytime accidents despite being toilet-trained. Random capillary glucose is 280 mg/dL. Her paternal grandmother has type 2 diabetes. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.label: D
options.text: Secondary diabetes due to cystic fibrosis \*

options.label: E
options.text: \ Transient neonatal diabetes Drug-induced diabetes mellitus

questions.initialExplanation: Thirst and polyuria with glucose 280 in a 7-year-old girl with a grandmother with diabetes: most likely T1DM.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This patient presents with the classic symptoms of type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM), including polyuria, polydipsia, and
significant weight loss over a relatively short period. The acute onset of symptoms over 3 weeks, the age of presentation
(7 years falls within one of the peak incidence periods of 5-7 years), and the severity of hyperglycemia (280 mg/dL) are
‘      highly suggestive of T1DM. The family history of type 2 diabetes in a grandparent does not change the likelihood, as
T1DM has different genetic associations primarily with HLA haplotypes rather than family history of type 2 diabetes.
- Option A (Type 2 diabetes mellitus) is incorrect because T2DM is extremely rare in young, non-obese children, and
typically presents more insidiously over months rather than weeks. Option B (MODY) is incorrect because MODY typically
presents in adolescence or young adulthood with a strong family history in multiple generations, which is not present
here. Option D (Transient neonatal diabetes) is incorrect as it presents in the neonatal period, not at 7 years of age.
Option E (Drug-induced diabetes) is incorrect as there is no history of any medications known to cause diabetes.

---

questions.stem: A 9-year-old girl is brought to the pediatric clinic for evaluation of recurrent urinary tract infections. Urinalysis reveals glycosuria but no evidence of infection. Her mother reports that she has been drinking more fluids than usual and has gained weight over the past month. Random blood glucose is 145 mg/dL. Her weight is at the 75th percentile and height at the 50th percentile. What is the most appropriate next step to confirm the diagnosis of diabetes mellitus?
questions.initialExplanation: To confirm diabetes, fasting plasma glucose (>=126 mg/dL) or another criterion is enough.
questions.detailedExplanation:
According to the American Diabetes Association criteria, the diagnosis of diabetes mellitus can be established by any of
the following: fasting plasma glucose 2126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L), 2-hour plasma glucose 2200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) during
an oral glucose tolerance test, hemoglobin A1C 26.5%, or random plasma glucose 2200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) in a patient
with classic symptoms of hyperglycemia. In this patient with glycosuria and random glucose of 145 mg/dL, a fasting
plasma glucose is the most appropriate next step to confirm or rule out diabetes mellitus.

- Option A (Oral glucose tolerance test) is more commonly used for diagnosing gestational diabetes or impaired glucose
tolerance but is less practical and not first-line for pediatric diagnosis. Option B (Hemoglobin A1C) can be used but may
be less reliable in certain conditions and the fasting glucose is more readily available. Option D (C-peptide) would be
useful to distinguish type 1 from type 2 diabetes but is not the initial diagnostic test. Option E (Anti-islet cell antibodies)
confirm the autoimmune etiology but are not required for initial diagnosis.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy is diagnosed with type 1 diabetes mellitus. His parents ask about the typical age distribution of T1DM onset. They are concerned because their son is young and want to know if this affects prognosis. Which statement regarding the epidemiology of type 1 diabetes mellitus in children is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Peak incidence occurs only during adolescence

options.label: B
options.text: Incidence is higher in girls than boys

options.label: C
options.text: Socioeconomic status is a major risk factor

options.label: E
options.text: Incidence has two peaks: at 5-7 years and during puberty

questions.initialExplanation: Type 1 diabetes has two incidence peaks, at 5-7 years and at puberty.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The epidemiological pattern of type 1 diabetes mellitus demonstrates a characteristic bimodal age distribution with two
distinct incidence peaks. The first peak occurs between 5-7 years of age, which may correspond to the period of increased
exposure to infectious agents coinciding with school entry and socialization. The second peak occurs during puberty, which
‘    is mediated by the growth spurt induced by gonadal steroid secretion and increased pubertal growth hormone production,
both of which antagonize insulin action and may precipitate clinical diabetes in genetically susceptible individuals. Notably,
a growing proportion of cases are now presenting between 1-2 years of age, reflecting either enhanced surveillance or true
changes in disease epidemiology.
- The statement that peak incidence occurs only during adolescence is incorrect, as the 5-7 year peak is equally important.
Boys and girls are almost equally affected, with no significant gender predilection. The incidence of type 1 diabetes is
actually increasing in many regions globally, particularly in younger age groups, rather than declining. Socioeconomic
status does not appear to correlate with type 1 diabetes risk, in contrast to type 2 diabetes where lower socioeconomic
status is associated with higher prevalence.

---
