questions.stem: A 14-year-old obese girl presents with a 2-month history of polyuria, polydipsia, and fatigue. Her body mass index is at the 97th percentile (BMI 32 kg/m?). Her mother has type 2 diabetes mellitus and her maternal grandfather had a myocardial infarction at age 45. Laboratory investigations reveal fasting glucose of 142 mg/dL, hemoglobin A1C of 8.1%, negative anti-GAD antibodies, and elevated C-peptide level. What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological treatment for this patient?
questions.initialExplanation: An obese teen girl with T2DM and high C-peptide: first-line drug is metformin.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This patient exhibits classic features of type 2 diabetes mellitus in adolescence, including obesity (BMI at 97th percentile),
family history of type 2 diabetes in a first-degree relative, elevated C-peptide level indicating insulin resistance with
preserved insulin secretion, and negative anti-GAD antibodies effectively excluding type 1 diabetes. According to current
clinical practice guidelines for pediatric type 2 diabetes, metformin represents the first-line pharmacological agent for initial
treatment.

- Metformin is the preferred initial agent due to its favorable safety profile, efficacy in improving insulin sensitivity through reduced
hepatic glucose production, minimal risk of hypoglycemia when used as monotherapy, and potential for modest weight stabilization or
loss. The initial recommended dose is 500 mg once daily with gradual titration to achieve target glycemic control. Insulin glargine is
generally reserved for patients presenting with significant hyperglycemia (hemoglobin A1C >9% or random glucose >300 mg/dL with
symptoms) or those in a catabolic state, which is not the case here. Sulfonylureas such as glipizide, while effective in lowering blood
glucose, are associated with weight gain and increased hypoglycemia risk. GLP-1 receptor agonists like liraglutide and
thiazolidinediones like pioglitazone are typically reserved as second-line options due to side effect profiles, injection requirements, or
lack of extensive pediatric data.

---

questions.stem: An 11-year-old boy with 2-year history of type 1 diabetes presents with 24-hour vomiting, abdominal pain, and lethargy. He has had fever and reduced oral intake during an upper respiratory infection. Deep respirations with fruity breath odor are noted. Glucose is 22 mmol/L, pH 7.08, bicarbonate 8 mmol/L, ketones 6.2 mmol/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: pH 7.08, bicarbonate 8 and high ketones = diabetic ketoacidosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This patient meets all diagnostic criteria for DKA: hyperglycemia (glucose >13.9 mmol/L), metabolic
acidosis (pH <7.3, bicarbonate <15 mmol/L), and ketonemia. The fruity breath odor (acetone) and
Kussmaul respirations are classic DKA findings. Hyperosmolar state is rare in children and typically
has much higher glucose and osmolality. Euglycemic DKA would have normal glucose. Lactic
acidosis would not show elevated ketones. While sepsis may coexist, the clinical and laboratory
findings are diagnostic of DKA precipitated by illness.

---

questions.stem: A 14-year-old boy with Type 1 diabetes mellitus since age 8 presents for routine follow-up. His HbA1c is 9.2% (77 mmol/mol). He reports good adherence to his insulin regimen. His BMI is 28 kg/m? (95th percentile), and he has acanthosis nigricans around his neck. His fasting C-peptide level is 0.8 ng/mL (low-normal). His father has Type 2 diabetes mellitus. What is the most likely explanation for his elevated HbA1c despite reported adherence?

options.label: A
options.text: Poor adherence with missed insulin doses \*

options.label: C
options.text: Insulin resistance superimposed on Type 1 diabetes

questions.initialExplanation: High HbA1c despite adherence in an obese teen with a father with T2DM: added insulin resistance on top of T1DM.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This patient demonstrates features of insulin resistance: obesity (BMI >95th percentile), acanthosis
nigricans, and family history of Type 2 diabetes. While he has established Type 1 diabetes (low C-
peptide, typical age of onset), the development of insulin resistance can occur, particularly with
increasing age and weight gain. This is sometimes called "double diabetes" or Type 1.5 diabetes.
Insulin underdosing would be a result rather than a cause. Dawn phenomenon and Somogyi effect
relate to glycemic variability but do not explain the metabolic syndrome features. Insulin antibody
formation can cause erratic glucose control but does not explain the obesity and acanthosis.

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl with Type 1 diabetes mellitus is admitted with moderate DKA. Her initial laboratory results show: glucose 24 mmol/L, sodium 128 mmol/L, potassium 5.2 mmol/L, bicarbonate 8 mmol/L, pH 7.08, and serum osmolality 295 mOsm/kg. After 4 hours of treatment with IV fluids and insulin, her glucose drops to 14 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate next step regarding IV fluid and insulin management?

options.label: A
options.text: Change IV fluids to D5 0.45% saline and continue insulin infusion

options.label: B
options.text: Change IV fluids to D10 0.45% saline and continue insulin infusion

options.label: C
options.text: Stop |V fluids and transition to subcutaneous insulin

questions.initialExplanation: When glucose in DKA falls to 14 mmol/L: switch to dextrose 5% with half-normal saline and continue insulin.
questions.detailedExplanation:
When blood glucose falls to £14 mmol/L during DKA management, IV fluids should be changed to
include dextrose (typically D5 0.45% saline) to prevent hypoglycemia while continuing insulin therapy
to ensure resolution of ketosis. D10 solutions are typically reserved for younger children or when D5 is
insufficient. Stopping fluids and transitioning to subcutaneous insulin is premature until DKA is fully
resolved (pH >7.3, bicarbonate >15 mmol/L). Increasing insulin is not indicated as glucose is
appropriately falling. Potassium should have already been added when levels fell below 5.0 mmol/L.

---

questions.stem: A 15-year-old boy with Type 1 diabetes mellitus presents with abdominal pain, vomiting, and altered mental status. He was diagnosed 3 months ago and has been non-adherent to insulin therapy. His capillary glucose is "high" (unmeasurable on glucometer), serum sodium is 118 mmol/L, potassium is 5.8 mmol/L, chloride is 84 mmol/L, bicarbonate is 6 mmol/L, BUN is 32 mg/dL, creatinine is 1.8 mg/dL, and calculated serum osmolality is 312 mOsm/kg. What is the most appropriate initial fluid for resuscitation?
questions.initialExplanation: DKA with osmolality 312: the first fluid is 0.9% NaCl.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This patient presents with mixed features of DKA and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS). The
calculated effective osmolality is 2(Na) + glucose/18 = 2(118) + 33.3 = 269.3 mOsm/kg, which is not
severely elevated as expected in classic HHS. However, the marked hyponatremia (fictitious
hyponatremia due to hyperglycemia: corrected Na = measured Na + 2.4 x (glucose - 100)/100 = 118
+ 2.4 x 3.1 = 125 mmol/L) and acute kidney injury suggest significant volume depletion. 0.9% NaCl is
the appropriate initial resuscitation fluid for both DKA and HHS. The hyponatremia here is dilutional
and will correct with fluid resuscitation and hyperglycemia management.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old girl presents with a 1-month history of increasing abdominal girth and early satiety. She was diagnosed with Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus 2 years ago and has had poor glycemic control despite multiple insulin regimen changes. Physical examination reveals a distended abdomen with shifting dullness and a palpable liver edge 3 cm below the costal margin. Ultrasound shows bright echotexture of the liver and moderate ascites. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Large liver, bright echo and ascites in poorly controlled T1DM = Mauriac syndrome.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child presents with hepatomegaly, ascites, and poor glycemic control in the context of long-standing Type
1 Diabetes Mellitus. Mauriac syndrome (also called diabetic hepatopathy or hepatic glycogenosis) is a rare
complication of poorly controlled Type 1 Diabetes in children, characterized by hepatomegaly due to glycogen
accumulation in hepatocytes. It presents with abdominal distension, hepatomegaly, and sometimes ascites.
The condition is associated with repeated episodes of hyperglycemia and excessive insulin therapy. Unlike
NAFLD, which causes fatty infiltration, Mauriac syndrome shows glycogen accumulation on biopsy. The
prognosis is generally good with improved glycemic control. Hepatocellular carcinoma is extremely rare in
children. Autoimmune hepatitis would present with elevated liver enzymes and other autoimmune markers.
Glycogen storage diseases typically present in infancy.

---

questions.stem: An 11-year-old girl with Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus is admitted with DKA. Initial laboratory values show blood glucose 480 mg/dL, pH 7.15, bicarbonate 8 mEq/L, potassium 5.2 mEq/L. She is started on IV fluids and insulin infusion. Which of the following electrolytes requires the MOST frequent monitoring during the initial treatment phase?
questions.initialExplanation: At the start of DKA treatment the most monitored value is potassium, because insulin moves it into cells.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Hypokalemia is a major concern during DKA treatment and requires the most frequent monitoring.
Although the initial serum potassium may be elevated (as in this case with K+ 5.2 mEq/L) due to

‘    acidosis shifting potassium out of cells, insulin therapy drives potassium back into cells and can cause
rapid and potentially life-threatening hypokalemia. Potassium levels should be checked every 1-2
hours during the initial treatment phase. Additionally, IV fluids and insulin administration both
contribute to potassium shifting. Sodium levels typically rise as hyperglycemia corrects (corrected
sodium = measured sodium + 2.4 x [(glucose - 100)/100]) but require monitoring to detect
hypernatremia or rapid changes. Chloride, calcium, and magnesium are less commonly problematic
during DKA treatment and do not require hourly monitoring.

---

questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy with Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus since age 6 presents with persistent hyperglycemia despite increasing insulin doses. He reports good compliance with his regimen. His father has Type 2 Diabetes, and his mother is obese. Physical examination reveals BMI at the 95th percentile, acanthosis nigricans, and mild hirsutism. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for his clinical picture?
questions.initialExplanation: Type 1 diabetes with acanthosis nigricans and hirsutism suggests insulin resistance.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This patient presents with features suggesting insulin resistance: obesity, acanthosis nigricans, and
persistent hyperglycemia despite escalating insulin doses. The family history of Type 2 Diabetes in the
father and obesity in the mother further supports a predisposition to insulin resistance. While he has
Type 1 Diabetes, the development of insulin resistance is not uncommon, particularly in the setting of
obesity. This is sometimes called "double diabetes" or hybrid diabetes, where features of both Type 1
and Type 2 Diabetes coexist. Lipoatrophic diabetes presents with loss of subcutaneous fat. LADA
(Latent Autoimmune Diabetes in Adults) typically presents in adulthood with autoimmune diabetes.
MODY has a different genetic basis and family pattern. Insulin receptor mutation would present with
severe insulin resistance and specific syndromes like Rabson-Mendenhall or Donohue syndrome.

---

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy with Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus presents with sudden onset of severe headache, vomiting, and visual changes 8 hours after admission for DKA treatment. He was responding well to initial therapy with improved pH and decreasing glucose. Vital signs show temperature 37°C, heart rate 90 bpm, respiratory rate 18/min, blood pressure 105/70 mmHg. Neurological examination reveals blurred optic discs and new-onset nystagmus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Headache and altered consciousness with nystagmus and blurred discs during DKA = cerebral edema.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This patient presents with cerebral edema, a rare but life-threatening complication of DKA treatment
in children. The classic presentation includes headache, vomiting, altered mental status, and

‘    neurological signs such as pupillary changes, bradycardia, and hypertension. Visual changes and
papilledema (blurred optic discs) are also characteristic. Cerebral edema typically occurs within the
first 12-24 hours of treatment, often when the patient appears to be improving. Risk factors include
severe acidosis, high BUN, and rapid fluid/Na+ correction. Treatment includes mannitol or hypertonic
saline, raising the head of bed, and limiting further fluid administration. Hypoglycemia would cause
different symptoms. Cerebral infarction is rare in children. Meningitis would present with fever and
meningeal signs. Hyponatremia typically causes more gradual neurological deterioration.

---

questions.stem: A 13-year-old boy with Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus presents with acute onset of severe lower back pain and difficulty walking. He reports no trauma. Physical examination reveals point tenderness over the lumbar spine and decreased range of motion. X-ray shows a compression fracture of L3. His HbA1c is 10.2%. Which complication of diabetes is most likely contributing to this presentation?
questions.initialExplanation: A vertebral compression fracture in a teen with poorly controlled T1DM: diabetic osteopathy (low bone density).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Diabetic osteopathy, also known as diabetic osteolysis or diabetic Charcot spine, is a rare complication
of poorly controlled diabetes characterized by progressive osteolysis (bone destruction) and
spontaneous fractures. It is thought to result from microvascular disease causing bone infarction and
neuropathy leading to repetitive trauma. It most commonly affects the spine (particularly the
thoracolumbar region) and foot. The condition is associated with long-standing, poorly controlled
diabetes (HbA1c 10.2% indicates poor control). Charcot arthropathy typically affects the foot and ankle.
Osteomyelitis would typically present with fever and elevated inflammatory markers. Diffuse idiopathic
skeletal hyperostosis is not associated with diabetes. While neuropathy plays a role in diabetic
osteopathy, the primary issue is bone destruction rather than joint destruction.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old girl is diagnosed with Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus after presenting with DKA. Her parents ask about the risk of their other children developing the disease. They have two other children, ages 8 and 2 years. What is the most accurate statement regarding the risk of developing T1DM in first- degree relatives?

options.label: A
options.text: The risk is approximately 10% for siblings

options.label: B
options.text: The risk is approximately 5% for siblings

options.label: D
options.text: The risk is the same as the general population (0.4%)

options.label: E
options.text: The risk depends on HLA typing

questions.initialExplanation: Risk of type 1 diabetes in siblings is about 5%.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The risk of developing Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus in first-degree relatives of a patient is approximately
5% for siblings, compared to approximately 0.4% in the general population. The risk is slightly higher
in siblings than in the general population but far lower than the 50% risk that would suggest a single-
gene disorder. The risk for offspring of a parent with T1DM is approximately 4-5% if the mother has
T1DM and slightly higher if the father has T1DM. HLA typing can modify risk; certain HLA types (DR3-
DQ2 and DR4-DQ8) are associated with increased susceptibility, while protective haplotypes exist.

However, HLA typing alone cannot reliably predict disease development. Genetic susceptibility testing
is not routinely recommended for family screening.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy with Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus presents with chronic diarrhea and failure to thrive over the past 4 months. He has had multiple episodes of nocturnal diarrhea with bulky, foul-smelling stools. His current weight is at the 10th percentile (down from 50th percentile at diagnosis 1 year ago). Laboratory investigations show HbA1c 8.0%, and serum IgA level is normal. Which test is most likely to establish the diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: T1DM with chronic diarrhea and normal IgA: anti-tissue transglutaminase to diagnose celiac.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus and presents with chronic diarrhea, failure to thrive, and steatorrhea
(bulky, foul-smelling stools). The presentation is highly suggestive of celiac disease, which has a strong
association with T1IDM (up to 10% prevalence). Anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA antibody is the preferred
screening test for celiac disease. IgA levels should be checked to ensure the patient is not IgA deficient (which
would cause false-negative results). If positive, confirmation with duodenal biopsy showing characteristic
villous atrophy is typically recommended. Stool culture would identify infectious causes but is less likely given
the chronic, progressive nature. Sweat chloride tests for cystic fibrosis, which can cause malabsorption but is
less associated with T1DM. Fecal elastase assesses pancreatic exocrine function. Upper endoscopy with
biopsy would be diagnostic but is more invasive and usually reserved for confirmation after positive serology.

---

questions.stem: A 13-year-old boy with Type 1 diabetes mellitus is brought to the emergency department with altered mental status and a capillary glucose of 1.8 mmol/L. He is given 2 mg of glucagon intramuscularly. Five minutes later, he remains unresponsive. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.initialExplanation: A diabetic who is unconscious and did not respond to glucagon: give IV dextrose.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This patient has severe hypoglycemia unresponsive to glucagon. Glucagon works by stimulating
glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, but its effect is limited in glycogen-depleted states (such as

‘    prolonged fasting or starvation). In such cases, IV dextrose (D10W or D25W) is the definitive
treatment. Repeating glucagon is unlikely to be effective. Insulin levels would not change acute
management. CPR is not indicated as the patient has a pulse. Octreotide can be used for
sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycemia but is not indicated here.

---

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy with Type 1 diabetes mellitus is found to have a fasting C-peptide of 0.4 ng/mL (low) and positive GAD65 and IA-2 autoantibodies at diagnosis. Three years later, he maintains good glycemic control on low-dose insulin (total daily dose 0.3 units/kg/day). What is the most likely explanation for his low insulin requirements? Excellent adherence
questions.initialExplanation: Low insulin requirement (0.3 unit/kg/day) after diagnosis = honeymoon phase.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The honeymoon phase (remission phase) occurs shortly after Type 1 diabetes diagnosis when
residual beta-cell function temporarily recovers, often allowing for reduced insulin requirements
(sometimes <0.5 units/kg/day) with good glycemic control. This typically lasts weeks to months and is
caused by reduced autoimmune destruction during this period. Positive autoantibodies confirm Type 1
diabetes. Insulin resistance would increase requirements. Renal impairment might decrease insulin

clearance but would not typically present this way. Excellent adherence contributes but does not
explain such low requirements alone. Insulin antibodies would cause erratic control.

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl with Type 1 diabetes mellitus presents with diffuse abdominal pain, vomiting, and altered mental status. She was diagnosed 2 weeks ago and has been on insulin therapy. Her capillary glucose is "HI" (>33 mmol/L), venous pH is 7.08, bicarbonate is 6 mmol/L, and serum sodium is 126 mmol/L (corrected). She has no signs of infection. What is the most likely cause of her presentation?
questions.initialExplanation: Corrected low sodium and neurological deterioration during DKA treatment = cerebral edema.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This patient has severe DKA with altered mental status and abdominal pain. Cerebral edema is the
most feared complication of DKA in children, typically occurring within the first 12-24 hours of

‘    treatment. Risk factors include severe acidosis (pH <7.1), low bicarbonate, and rapid fluid
administration. The abdominal pain ("pseudoperitonitis") and altered mental status are concerning
for cerebral edema. Fulminant Type 1 diabetes presents with very rapid onset but would not typically
cause altered mental status without DKA treatment. Insulin overdose would cause hypoglycemia.

Non-adherence would cause typical DKA without cerebral edema features. HHS is rare in young
children.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy with newly diagnosed Type 1 diabetes mellitus is being discharged home. His parents are being trained on insulin administration, blood glucose monitoring, and recognition of hypoglycemia. What is the most important component of hypoglycemia education for parents?
questions.initialExplanation: The most important thing to teach parents about hypoglycemia: recognize symptoms early.
questions.detailedExplanation:
While all components are important, recognizing the symptoms of hypoglycemia is critical for prompt
treatment. Parents should be educated about autonomic symptoms (sweating, tremor, palpitations,
hunger) and neuroglycopenic symptoms (confusion, lethargy, seizures). Prompt recognition allows for
early treatment with fast-acting carbohydrates, preventing progression to severe hypoglycemia
requiring glucagon or medical intervention. While glucagon administration is important, it is a rescue
treatment for severe cases. Food diaries, dose adjustment, and sick day rules are important but less
immediately critical for acute safety.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old girl presents with new-onset diabetes (fasting glucose 9.2 mmol/L, HbA1c 8.1%). She has a history of recurrent skin infections and vaginal candidiasis. Her BMI is 16 kg/m? (50th percentile). Her father was diagnosed with Type 1 diabetes at age 30. Testing reveals negative islet autoantibodies and a fasting C-peptide of 2.1 ng/mL (normal). What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Early diabetes with normal C-peptide and no antibodies = MODY (HNF1A is MODY 3).
questions.detailedExplanation:
This presentation is most consistent with MODY 3 (HNF1A mutation). Key features include: diabetes
diagnosed in childhood, negative autoantibodies (making Type 1 unlikely), normal C-peptide
indicating endogenous insulin production, normal BMI (arguing against Type 2), family history of
diabetes in a parent (autosomal dominant inheritance), and recurrent infections (can occur with
chronic hyperglycemia). MODY 2 typically presents with mild, stable hyperglycemia and rarely
requires treatment. HNF1A mutations typically present with more significant hyperglycemia requiring
treatment and can have renal manifestations.

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl with Type 1 diabetes mellitus is admitted with severe DKA. Her initial serum potassium is 5.4 mmol/L. After 6 hours of treatment with IV fluids and insulin, her potassium is 3.1 mmol/L, and she develops a wide complex tachycardia on the cardiac monitor. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.label: A
options.text: Continue current management as this is expected

questions.initialExplanation: Wide-QRS ventricular tachycardia in DKA with hyperkalemia: IV calcium gluconate to protect the heart.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This patient has developed severe hypokalemia with cardiac manifestations (wide complex
tachycardia, likely due to U waves or conduction abnormalities). The immediate management for
symptomatic or severe hypokalemia with ECG changes is IV calcium gluconate to stabilize the cardiac
membrane, followed by potassium replacement. While potassium chloride bolus is needed, calcium
should be given first to protect the heart. Continuing current management is dangerous. Increasing

insulin would worsen hypokalemia. Bicarbonate is not indicated as acidosis is likely resolving with
insulin therapy.

---

questions.stem: A 14-year-old boy with Type 1 diabetes mellitus since age 6 is being evaluated for delayed puberty. His testicular volume is 4 mL bilaterally (prepubertal), and his bone age is delayed by 2 years. His HbA1c is 8.8% (73 mmol/mol). Growth velocity is 3 cm/year (below 3rd percentile). What is the most likely cause of his growth and pubertal delay?

options.label: D
options.text: Poor glycemic control leading to delayed puberty

questions.initialExplanation: Delayed growth and puberty in T1DM with poor control: poor glycemic control.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Poor glycemic control in Type 1 diabetes can delay growth and pubertal development. Chronic
hyperglycemia impairs the growth hormone-IGF-1 axis and delays pubertal progression. This patient
has multiple indicators: poor glycemic control (HbA1c 8.8%), slowed growth velocity, delayed bone
age, and prepubertal testes at age 14 (when puberty should have begun). Growth hormone deficiency
is possible but less common. Hypothyroidism and celiac disease are associated with Type 1 diabetes
but would typically have other symptoms. Constitutional delay is a diagnosis of exclusion.

---

questions.stem: An 8-year-old boy with Type 1 diabetes mellitus is admitted with moderate DKA. His initial serum sodium is 132 mmol/L (corrected for glucose), potassium is 5.6 mmol/L, and bicarbonate is 12 mmol/L. He is started on IV fluids and insulin. How often should serum electrolytes be monitored during DKA treatment?
questions.initialExplanation: In DKA monitor electrolytes every 1-2 hours at the start.
questions.detailedExplanation:
During DKA management, serum electrolytes (particularly potassium) should be monitored very
frequently, typically every 1-2 hours initially, because of the rapid shifts that occur with insulin therapy
and fluid resuscitation. Hypokalemia can develop quickly and lead to life-threatening arrhythmias.
Sodium levels should also be tracked to ensure appropriate correction. Once the patient is stable and
values are trending appropriately, the frequency can be decreased to every 4-6 hours. Monitoring only
when symptomatic is inadequate. Daily monitoring is insufficient during the acute phase.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with a 2-day history of vomiting, lethargy, and rapid breathing. He has no significant past medical history. His capillary glucose is "high" (glucometer reads "HI"), and venous blood gas shows pH 7.02, bicarbonate 6 mmol/L. He appears dehydrated with Kussmaul respirations and has a fruity odor on his breath. What is the most appropriate initial fluid resuscitation rate?

options.label: A
options.text: 10 mL/kg bolus of 0.9% NaCl over 30 minutes

options.label: B
options.text: 20 mL/kg bolus of 0.9% NaCl over 30-60 minutes

options.label: C
options.text: 10 mL/kg bolus of 0.45% NaCl over 60 minutes

options.label: D
options.text: 20 mL/kg bolus of lactated Ringer's over 30 minutes

options.label: E
options.text: 5 mL/kg bolus of 0.9% NaCl over 15 minutes

questions.initialExplanation: DKA with shock: start with a 20 mL/kg NS bolus.
questions.detailedExplanation:
In children with DKA, particularly those with severe dehydration or shock, initial fluid resuscitation
should be with 20 mL/kg of 0.9% NaCl over 30-60 minutes. This patient has severe DKA (pH <7.1)
with signs of severe dehydration and altered mental status, warranting aggressive initial fluid
resuscitation. Smaller boluses (10 mL/kg) are typically used for mild to moderate DKA or in resource-
limited settings. The 5 mL/kg dose is inadequate for severe presentation. Lactated Ringer's can be
used but 0.9% NaCl is the standard first-line fluid.

---

questions.stem: During a routine clinical visit, a healthy asymptomatic 6-year-old boy is found to have fasting blood glucose of 110 mg/dL; he has normal oral glucose tolerance test, no glycosuria, and HgbA1c of 6.4%. This child is MOST likely considered to have : (NE)
questions.initialExplanation: Fasting glucose 100-125 = impaired fasting glucose (prediabetes).
questions.detailedExplanation:
- Fasting glucose of 110 mg/dL falls in the 100-125 mg/dL range, which the American Diabetes
Association defines as impaired fasting glucose (IFG)—a prediabetic state.

- The oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) is normal (2-hour <140 mg/dL), so impaired glucose
tolerance (IGT) is not present.

- HbA1c of 6.4 % is at the upper limit of the prediabetes range (5.7-6.4 %) but does not meet the

diabetes threshold (26.5 %).

- The child is asymptomatic, has no glycosuria, and therefore does not meet criteria for diabetes
mellitus.

Thus, the most appropriate classification for this child is impaired fasting glucose.

---

questions.stem: A 10-year-old diabetic patient presented with nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain over the past two days. Upon examination, signs of dehydration, increased breathing rate, and drowsiness are noted. The clinical diagnosis is diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). Which of the following instructions is the LEAST appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Mild to moderate DKA can be treated in outpatient by increasing insulin dose

options.label: B
options.text: In severe DKA, the degree of dehydration is assessed as 5%

options.label: C
options.text: Insulin infusion is prepared with 50 units of soluble insulin in 500 ml of 5% glucose solution

options.label: D
options.text: When plasma glucose is less than 150 mg/d|, insulin infusion should be continued at a rate of 0.05 unit/kg/hour to correct ketosis

options.label: E
options.text: Potassium should not be added to the fluid if serum potassium levels are normal or high

questions.initialExplanation: Moderate DKA is not treated as an outpatient but in hospital (the wrong statement is outpatient treatment).
questions.detailedExplanation:
This patient presents with classic signs and symptoms of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA): nausea,
vomiting, abdominal pain, dehydration, increased breathing rate (Kussmaul respirations), and
drowsiness. DKA is a life-threatening emergency requiring hospitalization and intravenous fluid and
insulin therapy. The question asks for the LEAST appropriate instruction, which means five of these
statements are incorrect, and one is correct.

- Understanding DKA management principles: DKA management requires careful fluid resuscitation,
intravenous insulin therapy, electrolyte monitoring and replacement, and continuous monitoring. The
goals of treatment include correction of dehydration, lowering of blood glucose, resolution of ketosis
and acidosis, and prevention of complications such as cerebral edema and electrolyte disturbances.

---

questions.stem: 2024 s.\)5 1 A 44-year-old child diagnosed with diabetes two years ago is brought to the outpatient clinic due to recurring hypoglycemic episodes. One of the following statements about the causes of hypoglycemia is LEAST accepted:

options.label: D
options.text: Skipping meals after the insulin dose \*

questions.initialExplanation: Causes of hypoglycemia: infection, pain, exercise, lipohypertrophy; changing needles does not cause lows.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This 4-year-old child with a 2-year history of type 1 diabetes is experiencing recurrent hypoglycemic episodes.
Hypoglycemia is a common complication of insulin therapy and can result from various factors including insulin
dosing errors, changes in food intake, physical activity, and other physiological factors. The question asks which
factor is LEAST accepted or recognized as a cause of hypoglycemia.

- Understanding hypoglycemia in type 1 diabetes: Hypoglycemia (typically defined as blood glucose <70 mg/dL)
is the most common acute complication of insulin therapy in type 1 diabetes. Severe hypoglycemia (requiring
assistance) can cause acute neurological impairment, seizures, and in rare cases, death. The fear of
hypoglycemia often limits optimal glycemic control. Recurrent hypoglycemia should prompt evaluation of the
child's regimen, injection technique, meal patterns, and other contributing factors.

---

## Thyroid Diseases

> Question numbers not present in the source file for this topic: 19.

questions.stem: A full-term newborn was discharged at 36 hours of life after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery, and newborn screening was done at discharge. At the 2-week check-up, results show elevated TSH and low free T4. The infant is feeding well, gaining weight, and appears healthy. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.text: Repeat thyroid function tests in 4 weeks to confirm persistence

options.label: B
options.text: Refer to neurology for EEG and developmental screening

options.label: C
options.text: Begin levothyroxine therapy and refer to pediatric endocrinology

options.label: D
options.text: Reassure the parents and monitor growth parameters

options.label: E
options.text: Order a brain MRI to rule out pituitary abnormality

questions.initialExplanation: Newborn screening shows high TSH: start levothyroxine immediately without delay because delay harms brain development.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This newborn has an abnormal newborn screen showing elevated TSH and low free T4, consistent with
congenital hypothyroidism. Although the infant appears clinically well (feeding well, gaining weight), the
biochemical abnormalities are significant and require prompt intervention. Congenital hypothyroidism is a
medical emergency because even asymptomatic-appearing infants can have irreversible neurodevelopmental
impairment if treatment is delayed.

- Congenital hypothyroidism is one of the most common preventable causes of intellectual disability. The
condition can result from thyroid dysgenesis (agenesis, hypoplasia, or ectopic thyroid), dyshormonogenesis
(enzyme defects in thyroid hormone synthesis), central hypothyroidism, or transient causes (such as maternal
antibodies or iodine exposure). Newborn screening, typically measuring TSH or T4, is designed to detect this
condition before clinical symptoms develop.

---

questions.stem: A 3-month-old boy presented with constipation, jaundice persisting for nearly a month after birth. He appeared with characteristic facial features including a large, protruding tongue, and a small umbilical hernia. The recommended diagnostic test to confirm the diagnosis is:

options.label: D
options.text: Radio-isotope scan of the thyroid gland

options.label: E
options.text: Hormonal assay of the thyroid gland

questions.initialExplanation: Constipation, prolonged jaundice, enlarged tongue and umbilical hernia in an infant = congenital hypothyroidism, confirmed by thyroid hormone levels (TSH and free T4).
questions.detailedExplanation:
This 3-month-old infant presents with classic clinical features of congenital hypothyroidism. The prolonged jaundice beyond
the neonatal period (beyond 2 weeks is abnormal in newborns), constipation, large protruding tongue (macroglossia), and
umbilical hernia are all characteristic findings. This constellation of symptoms in an infant should prompt immediate

‘     evaluation for congenital hypothyroidism, as early diagnosis and treatment are critical to prevent irreversible
neurodevelopmental impairment.
- Congenital hypothyroidism is one of the most common preventable causes of intellectual disability worldwide, occurring in
approximately 1 in 2,000 to 4,000 live births. The condition can result from thyroid dysgenesis (absent, hypoplastic, or
ectopic thyroid gland, accounting for 80-85% of cases), dyshormonogenesis (inherited enzyme defects in thyroid hormone
synthesis, accounting for 10-15% of cases), central hypothyroidism (pituitary or hypothalamic dysfunction), or transient
causes (such as maternal antibodies, iodine exposure, or maternal antithyroid medications).

---

questions.stem: A 16-year-old female adolescent develops swelling at the anterior aspect of the neck with difficulty of the swallowing. Examination reveals a firm, nontender diffuse goiter with a pebble-like surface. Her mother has had a thyroid disease in early adulthood. Of the following, the MOST valuable test to confirm the diagnosis is : (NE)
questions.initialExplanation: Anterior neck swelling in a teen girl with a family history: the most important test is anti-thyroid antibodies (anti-TPO) to diagnose Hashimoto.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The clinical presentation—a 16-year-old female with a firm, nontender, diffuse goiter having a
“pebble-like” surface and a family history of thyroid disease in her mother—is highly suggestive of
Hashimoto thyroiditis, the most common cause of acquired hypothyroidism in children and
adolescents.

- In Hashimoto thyroiditis, diagnosis is typically confirmed by detecting elevated serum antithyroid
peroxidase antibodies (anti-TPO), often accompanied by antithyroglobulin antibodies. While thyroid
function tests (TSH, free T4) are essential to assess functional status (e.g., hypothyroid, euthyroid,
or occasionally hyperthyroid phases), they do not confirm the autoimmune nature of the disease.
Ultrasonography may show a heterogeneous, hypoechoic gland but is not diagnostic on its own.

---

questions.stem: An adolescent female develops fever, palpitation and disorientation. Examination shows exophthalmos, goiter, tachycardia and elevated blood pressure. Lab tests reveal elevated T4 and T3 with low TSH. Of the following, the BEST initial treatment is : (NE)
questions.initialExplanation: Thyroid storm (fever, palpitations, confusion and raised T3/T4): first treatment is beta blockers (propranolol) to control symptoms.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The clinical picture —fever, palpitations, disorientation, exophthalmos, goiter, tachycardia, hypertension,
and laboratory findings of elevated T3/T4 with suppressed TSH—is consistent with thyroid storm, a life-
threatening exacerbation of hyperthyroidism, most commonly due to Graves’ disease in adolescents.

- In the initial management of thyroid storm, the priority is to control adrenergic symptoms (e.g.,
tachycardia, agitation, hypertension) that contribute significantly to morbidity and mortality. While
antithyroid drugs (methimazole or propylthiouracil) are essential to block new hormone synthesis, they
take hours to days to reduce circulating thyroid hormone levels. In contrast, beta-blockers (e.g.,

propranolol) provide rapid symptomatic relief and are considered the best initial treatment to stabilize
the patient.

---

questions.stem: A 5-day-old male neonate develops poor feeding, irritability and tachycardia; her mother has been developed hyperthyroidism before pregnancy that was treated by radioiodine. The pregnancy course was unremarkable. Lab investigations reveal markedly elevation of T4 and T3. Of the following, the MOST likely diagnosis is : (NE)
questions.initialExplanation: A newborn with tachycardia, irritability and raised T4/T3 = neonatal Graves (transfer of maternal antibodies).
questions.detailedExplanation:
The clinical scenario describes a 5-day-old male neonate with signs of hyperthyroidism (poor feeding, irritability,
tachycardia) and markedly elevated T3 and T4 levels. The key historical clue is that his mother had hyperthyroidism prior
to pregnancy and was treated with radioiodine.

- Importantly, radioiodine ablation does not eliminate thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSI or TRAb)—the
autoantibodies responsible for Graves’ disease. These IgG antibodies can cross the placenta during pregnancy and
stimulate the fetal/neonatal thyroid gland, leading to transient neonatal hyperthyroidism, even if the mother is no longer
hyperthyroid herself.

- This condition is known as neonatal Graves’ disease or congenital hyperthyroidism due to maternal TRAD, and it is
classified under congenital hyperthyroidism because it presents at birth or shortly thereafter due to in utero exposure.

- Although the mother was treated with radioiodine before pregnancy, persistent high levels of TSH receptor antibodies

(TRAD) can remain and cause fetal/neonatal thyrotoxicosis. This risk exists even after definitive maternal therapy like
radioiodine or thyroidectomy.

---

questions.stem: A 9- month- old girl brought by her mother due to stunted growth, on examination extremities are short, and head size is normal, the anterior fontanel is large, protruded tongue, dry scaly pale yellow skin, with clear sclera. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate initial test?
questions.initialExplanation: An infant girl with growth delay, dry yellow skin, hoarseness and constipation: first test is TSH.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The clinical presentation—stunted growth, short extremities (disproportionate short stature), large anterior fontanel,
protruded tongue, and dry, scaly, pale yellow skin—is classic for congenital or early-onset hypothyroidism in an infant.
Key features pointing to hypothyroidism include:

- Growth failure with delayed skeletal maturation (short limbs)

- Persistent large anterior fontanel, Macroglossia (protruded tongue)

- Dry, coarse skin with a yellowish hue (due to carotenemia from impaired conversion of carotene to vitamin A)
Although newborn screening typically detects congenital hypothyroidism, some cases (especially milder or acquired
forms) may present later in infancy if missed or if thyroid function deteriorated postnatally.

The most appropriate initial test is TSH, because:

- Primary hypothyroidism (the most common form) presents with elevated TSH and low free T4.
- TSH is the most sensitive and first-line screening test for primary thyroid dysfunction in children 9.

---

questions.stem: During a health supervision visit with a 12-year-old girl, you palpate a firm thyroid gland (ltemQ250A). Measurement of free thyroxine is 2.0 ng/dL (25.7 pmol/L) (normal, 0.6 to 1.6 ng/dL [7.7to 20.6 pmol/L]), thyroid-stimulating hormone is less than 0.01 mclU/mL (0.01 mclU/L) (normal,0.5 to 5.0 mclU/mL [0.5 to 5.0 mclU/L]), and triiodothyronine is 468 pg/dL (7.2 pmol/L) (nhormal,60 to 180 pg/dL [0.92 to 2.8 pmol/L]). She has fine, smooth skin and finger and tongue tremor. Of the following, the MOST likely additional finding on physical examination is : (NE)
questions.initialExplanation: A teen with fast pulse, tongue tremor and an enlarged gland: a sign of Graves is a thyroid bruit.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The laboratory results reported for the girl in the vignette are indicative of hyperthyroidism.
Physical findings of hyperthyroidism can include a thyroid bruit because of the blood coursing
through a hyperactive and simulated thyroid gland and, in extremely rare instances in children,
pretibial myxedema. The latter finding is more common in adults, but still very rare. Other
symptoms and signs include widened palpebral fissures or actual ophthalmopathy (less
common in children than adults), nervousness and irritability, sweatiness, myopathy, difficulty

concentrating in school and sleeping, daytime tiredness, weight loss, diarrhea, and heat
intolerance.

---

questions.stem: A 14 yr old girl presents with poor growth and delayed puberty. She denies headaches or poor school performance. She is physically sluggish and has a small goiter. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.initialExplanation: Delayed puberty and poor growth with a small gland = Hashimoto thyroiditis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Lymphocytic thyroiditis is the most common cause of thyroid disease in children and adolescents and accounts for many
of the enlarged thyroids formerly designated "adolescent" or "simple" goiter. It is also the most common cause of acquired
hypothyroidism, with or without goiter. The disorder is 2-4 times more common in girls than in boys. It can occur during the
1st 3 yr of life but becomes sharply more common after 6 yr of age and reaches a peak incidence during adolescence.
The most common clinical manifestations are goiter and growth retardation. The goiter can appear insidiously and may be
small or large. In most patients, the thyroid is diffusely enlarged, firm, and nontender. In about 30% of patients, the gland
is lobular and can seem to be nodular. Most of the affected children are clinically euthyroid and asymptomatic; some may
have symptoms of pressure in the neck, including difficulty swallowing and shortness of breath. Some children have
clinical signs of hypothyroidism, but others who appear clinically euthyroid have laboratory evidence of hypothyroidism. A
few children have manifestations suggesting hyperthyroidism, such as nervousness, irritability, increased sweating, and
hyperactivity, but results of laboratory studies are not necessarily those of hyperthyroidism.

---

questions.stem: A 6 wk old infant has gained no weight since birth. Her skin appears mottled, and an indirect bilirubin level is measured at 24 mg/dL. Her extremities are cold, and her temperature is 350C. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.initialExplanation: An infant girl not gaining weight with indirect jaundice 24 and cold extremities = congenital hypothyroidism.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Before neonatal screening programs, congenital hypothyroidism was rarely recognized in the newborn
because the signs and symptoms are usually not sufficiently developed. It can be suspected and the
diagnosis established during the early weeks of life if the initial but less characteristic manifestations
are recognized. Birthweight and length are normal, but head size may be slightly increased because of
myxedema of the brain. Prolongation of physiologic jaundice, caused by delayed maturation of
glucuronide conjugation, may be the earliest sign. Feeding difficulties, especially sluggishness, lack of
interest, somnolence, and choking spells during nursing, are often present during the 1st mo of life.
Respiratory difficulties, due in part to the large tongue, include apneic episodes, noisy respirations,
and nasal obstruction. Typically, respiratory distress syndrome also occurs.

---

questions.stem: The mother of a 2-week-old infant reports that since birth, her infant sleeps most of the day; she has to awaken her every 4 hours to feed, and she will take only an ounce of formula at a time. She also is concerned that the infant has persistently hard, pellet-like stools. On your examination you find an infant with normal weight and length, but with an enlarged head. The heart rate is 75 beats per minute and the temperature is 35°C (95°F). The child is still jaundiced. You note large anterior and posterior fontanelles, a distended abdomen, and an umbilical hernia. This clinical presentation is likely a result of which of the following ?(pretest)
questions.initialExplanation: Enlarged tongue, umbilical hernia and lethargy = congenital hypothyroidism.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The clinical findings of congenital hypothyroidism are subtle, and may not be present at all at birth;
this is thought to be a result of passage of some T4 transplacentally. Infants with examination findings
will usually have an umbilical hernia and a distended abdomen. The head may be large, and the
fontanelles will be large as well. The child may be hypothermic and have feeding difficulties;
constipation and jaundice may be persistent. Skin may be cold and mottled, and edema may be found
in the genitals and extremities. The heart rate may be slow, and anemia may develop. As these
findings may be subtle or nonexistent, neonatal screening programs are extremely important for early
diagnosis of these infants.

---

questions.stem: The state laboratory calls your office telling you that a newborn infant, now 8 days old, has an elevated thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) and low thyroxin (T4) on his newborn screen. If this condition is left untreated, the infant is likely to demonstrate which of the following in the first few months of life?(pretest)
questions.initialExplanation: Untreated congenital hypothyroidism leads to prolonged jaundice, growth delay and constipation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Signs of congenital hypothyroidism include constipation, prolonged jaundice, sluggishness, poor
feeding, apnea, choking, macroglossia, and excessive sleepiness. The physical examination is
usually normal early on except for mild jaundice and a distended abdomen in a sleepy infant. The
most appropriate step to manage this condition is to avoid delays and to initiate oral sodium-L
thyroxine, 10 to 15 pg/kg/day. Thyroid dysgenesis is found in 90% of the cases. Neonatal screening
for hypothyroidism has allowed for the much earlier diagnosis of hypothyroidism, resulting in an
improved prognosis, so that frank cretinism is now quite rare. Most industrialized countries test for
phenylketonuria and hypothyroidism; there is variability in testing for other metabolic and genetic
diseases.

---

questions.stem: A 4-day-old infant presents for his first clinic visit after birth. The child was born full term to a healthy mother with no significant past medical history. The child was diagnosed with congenital hypothyroidism by the newborn screen. On exam, heart rate and blood pressure were normal and no goiter or neck masses were appreciated. What is the most common reason for congenital hypothyroidism in this child? (Rud)

options.label: C
options.text: Ingestion of goitrogenic substances by the mother

options.label: D
options.text: Inborn defects in thyroid hormone synthesis or action

questions.initialExplanation: The commonest cause of congenital hypothyroidism: dysgenesis (failure of gland development or migration); a hormone synthesis defect is sometimes the cause.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The most common reason for congenital hypothyroidism is a defect in thyroid embryogenesis with more than 95% of
cases being idiopathic or sporadic. The prevalence of congenital hypothyroidism is approximately 1 in 4000 newborns.
The remaining answers are also reasons for congenital hypothyroidism, but they are less likely in this case. The child is

‘     not premature, and therefore, dysfunction due to prematurity would be unlikely. Premature infants may have an immature
hypothalamic—pituitary—thyroid axis and are predisposed to thyroid dysfunction. The child’s mother is healthy and has no
history of thyroid disease, which makes the transplacental acquisition of maternal TSH receptor blocking antibodies
unlikely. Ingestion of a goitrogenic substance, such as iodines or sulfonamides, by the mother was not given in the history
but could cause hypothyroidism and a neonatal goiter. Thyroid dyshormonogenesis can occur from a variety of enzymatic
defects, including organification and thyroid iodide transport defects. However, cases of thyroid dyshormonogenesis are
less common than defects in thyroid embryogenesis. Infants with thyroid dyshormonogenesis have a normal-appearing
thyroid gland in the normal location on ultrasound, and they may have a goiter on exam.

---

questions.stem: A 9-year-old healthy girl presents for her yearly well child visit. On physical exam, her thyroid is full, smooth, symmetric, and easily palpable. Blood tests reveal that her TSH is mildly elevated at 9.634 mcU/mL and total T4 is normal at 6.5 mcg/dL. Which of the following is the best additional test to perform to confirm the diagnosis? (Rud)

options.label: E
options.text: MRI of the brain Thyroid ultrasound TSH receptor antibody Thyroid peroxidase antibody Total T3 level

questions.initialExplanation: An additional test to confirm Hashimoto: anti-thyroid peroxidase antibody.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Hashimoto thyroiditis is the most common cause of goiter and hypothyroidism in a 9-year-old child. It an autoimmune
condition and is more common in females than in males. The onset of Hashimoto thyroiditis is usually insidious, and some
children may have no signs or symptoms of hypothyroidism. Most children with Hashimoto thyroiditis and autoimmune
hypothyroidism have detectable levels of circulating antithyroid antibodies, which are markers of inflammation in the
thyroid gland. An antithyroid peroxidase (TPO) antibody is more often detected compared to an antithyroglobulin antibody.
A goiter and elevated TSH level establishes that the disease originates in the thyroid gland. An MRI of the brain with
specific emphasis on the hypothalamus and pituitary gland would only be necessary in cases of central (not primary)
hypothyroidism. An enlarged thyroid on physical exam would not be present in cases of central hypothyroidism. A thyroid
ultrasound would be helpful if there was thyroid asymmetry or a nodule present. However, in this case, the patient has a
thyroid gland that is enlarged but smooth and symmetric. A TSH receptor antibody (TRAb) and total T3 would be helpful in
the evaluation of hyperthyroidism and Graves disease.

---

questions.stem: A 17-year-old male was diagnosed with Graves disease 2 years ago and has been on antithyroid medication (methimazole) since diagnosis. What clinical prognostic sign is most likely to suggest remission of his Graves disease when antithyroid medication is discontinued? (Rud) DOO OoTW

options.label: B
options.text: Resolution of goiter Resolution of widened pulse pressure

options.label: D
options.text: Maintenance of a normal body mass index (BMI)

questions.initialExplanation: To support remission of Graves after stopping the drug: shrinking of the goiter (with stable normal TSH).
questions.detailedExplanation:
The incidence of Graves disease sharply increases as children approach adolescence. Graves disease is 6-8
times more common in girls than in boys. Treatment options include thyroidectomy, radioactive iodine ablation,
and antithyroid drugs. In this scenario, the patient is taking methimazole, which inhibits the oxidation of iodine
and blocks the production of thyroid hormones. Side effects of methimazole include rash, arthralgia, and
agranulocytopenia. Due to the risk of agranulocytopenia, it is recommended that patients have a complete
blood count checked during times of illness to document their white blood cell count. If it is suppressed, the
patient should stop methimazole. Drug therapy is typically continued for 1-2 years before a trial off is
recommended. Orbitopathy, widened pulse pressure, muscle weakness, and weight loss are all clinical
features of Graves disease. Other clinical signs include emotional lability, tremor, fatigability, and rapid tendon
reflex relaxation. However, the resolution of these signs does not suggest that the patient has gone into
remission.

---

questions.stem: A child suffering from constipation, decreased activity and poor feeding is shown here. The mother says that overall he is a "good baby" since he rarely cries and sleeps most of the time. You notice a large protruding tongue. What is the most likely diagnosis? (CanadaQB)
questions.initialExplanation: Constipation, lethargy, poor feeding and large tongue = hypothyroidism.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Cretinism is a condition of severely stunted physical and mental growth due to untreated congenital
deficiency of thyroid hormones (hypothyroidism).Children with hypothyroidism may develop
excessive sleeping, reduced interest in nursing, poor muscle tone, low or hoarse cry, infrequent
bowel movements, exaggerated jaundice, and low body temperature. Physical features may include
a larger anterior fontanel, persistence of a posterior fontanel, an umbilical hernia, and a large tongue
(macroglossia). Often, they are described as "good babies" because they rarely cry and sleep most
of the time.

---

questions.stem: A newborn male is found to have an elevated TSH of 45 mIU/L on newborn screening at day 5 of life. His T4 is 6.2 ug/dL (normal 8-16). Physical examination reveals a large fontanelle, umbilical hernia, hypotonia, and a protruding tongue. No thyroid gland is palpable in the neck. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.text: Wait and repeat TSH after 2 weeks \*

questions.initialExplanation: TSH 45 with an absent, non-palpable gland: start levothyroxine immediately.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This newborn presents with classic signs of congenital hypothyroidism: elevated TSH, low T4, large
fontanelle, umbilical hernia, hypotonia, and macroglossia. The absence of a palpable thyroid gland
suggests thyroid dysgenesis (agenesis or ectopy). Treatment with levothyroxine should be initiated
immediately, ideally within the first two weeks of life, to prevent irreversible neurocognitive impairment.
Delaying treatment for repeat testing or further investigations would jeopardize the infant's
developmental outcome. Radioactive iodine uptake scan and thyroid ultrasound can be performed
after starting treatment to determine the underlying etiology. Maternal thyroid antibody testing is
appropriate but should not delay treatment initiation.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl presents with constipation, cold intolerance, and decreased activity for 6 months. Her mother reports that she has been falling behind in her developmental milestones. Physical examination shows dry skin, coarse facial features, pallor, and a midline anterior neck mass. Which finding is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.text: Elevated TSH and low free T4

options.label: B
options.text: Elevated TSH and elevated free T4

options.label: C
options.text: Low TSH and low free T4

options.label: D
options.text: Low TSH and elevated free T4

options.label: E
options.text: Normal TSH and normal free T4

questions.initialExplanation: Constipation, cold intolerance and a mid-neck mass: raised TSH with low T4 confirms hypothyroidism.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child presents with acquired hypothyroidism, likely due to Hashimoto thyroiditis given the neck
mass (goiter) in an older child. The clinical features—constipation, cold intolerance, developmental
regression, dry skin, and coarse facies—are classic for hypothyroidism. The biochemical hallmark of
primary hypothyroidism is an elevated TSH (due to loss of negative feedback) with a low free T4.
Central hypothyroidism would present with low or inappropriately normal TSH with low T4. Elevated
TSH and elevated T4 suggests thyroid hormone resistance or a TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma.
Low TSH with elevated T4 is seen in hyperthyroidism. Normal thyroid function tests would not explain
the clinical picture.

---

questions.stem: A 14-year-old girl presents with a 3-month history of heat intolerance, weight loss of 5 kg despite increased appetite, tremor, and palpitations. Physical examination reveals a diffuse goiter, fine tremor of the outstretched hands, tachycardia with heart rate 110 bpm, and bilateral exophthalmos. Which antibody is most specific for the underlying diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Graves disease is characterized by anti-TSH receptor stimulating antibody.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This patient presents with classic signs of Graves disease: hyperthyroidism with goiter, heat
intolerance, weight loss, tremor, tachycardia, and ophthalmopathy. The anti-TSH receptor stimulating

‘    antibody (TSI or TRAD) is highly specific for Graves disease and is responsible for stimulating the TSH
receptor, leading to excessive thyroid hormone production and the extrathyroidal manifestations
including ophthalmopathy. Anti-TPO and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies are markers of autoimmune
thyroid disease but are not specific to Graves disease; they are also positive in Hashimoto thyroiditis.
ANA and anti-dsDNA are associated with systemic lupus erythematosus, which can rarely involve the
thyroid but is not the primary diagnosis here.

---

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy presents with a 4-month history of fatigue, constipation, and declining school performance. His mother notes that his voice has become deeper and coarser. Physical examination reveals bradycardia, delayed deep tendon reflexes, and a firm, symmetric goiter. Anti-TPO antibodies are strongly positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: A firm symmetric goiter with strong anti-TPO = Hashimoto thyroiditis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child presents with Hashimoto thyroiditis (chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis), the most common
cause of acquired hypothyroidism in children. The clinical features —fatigue, constipation, declining
school performance, deep/hoarse voice, bradycardia, delayed reflexes—are consistent with
hypothyroidism. The firm, symmetric goiter is characteristic of Hashimoto thyroiditis. The presence of
strongly positive anti-TPO antibodies confirms the autoimmune etiology. Graves disease causes
hyperthyroidism, not hypothyroidism. Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis (De Quervain) presents
with painful thyroid and often follows a viral illness. Riedel thyroiditis is a rare fibrotic condition
presenting with a hard, fixed thyroid.

---

questions.stem: A 16-year-old girl with Graves disease who is being treated with methimazole develops jaundice, dark urine, and severe right upper quadrant pain. Laboratory investigations show ALT 450 U/L, AST 380 U/L, bilirubin 4.5 mg/dL, and alkaline phosphatase 280 U/L. Which statement regarding the choice of antithyroid medication is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Propylthiouracil should have been used instead of methimazole

options.label: C
options.text: Both methimazole and propylthiouracil can cause hepatotoxicity

options.label: D
options.text: Radioactive iodine is the safest treatment option

options.label: E
options.text: Surgery should have been offered as first-line treatment

questions.initialExplanation: Antithyroid drugs (methimazole and PTU) both work by inhibiting hormone synthesis; methimazole is preferred in children (PTU has liver toxicity).
questions.detailedExplanation:
This patient presents with severe hepatotoxicity, likely secondary to antithyroid medication. Both
methimazole and propylthiouracil can cause hepatotoxicity, though PTU is more commonly associated
with severe hepatotoxicity and acute liver failure, particularly in children. Current guidelines
recommend methimazole as the first-line antithyroid drug due to a more favorable side effect profile,
including lower risk of severe hepatotoxicity. The finding of hepatotoxicity requires immediate
discontinuation of the antithyroid medication and consideration of alternative treatments such as
radioactive iodine or thyroidectomy. The choice between these alternatives depends on multiple
factors including patient preference, goiter size, ophthalmopathy, and access to experienced
surgeons.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy is referred for evaluation of short stature. His height is at the 3rd percentile, down from the 50th percentile at age 2. His parents are of average height. Physical examination shows dry skin, coarse facial features, and a midline neck mass. Bone age is delayed by 2 years. Which diagnosis best explains these findings?
questions.initialExplanation: Short stature and delayed bone age with dry skin and a neck mass = hypothyroidism.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child presents with growth failure (height crossing percentiles), dry skin, coarse facial features,
goiter, and delayed bone age, which are classic features of hypothyroidism. Unlike constitutional

‘    delay (which typically presents with delayed puberty and bone age but normal other findings) or
growth hormone deficiency (which would not cause coarse facies or dry skin), hypothyroidism
explains all the findings. Hypothyroidism directly impairs growth plate function and bone maturation,
leading to growth retardation and delayed bone age. The change from 50th to 3rd percentile over 2
years is particularly concerning for an acquired condition. Turner syndrome would be associated with
other features like webbed neck and would not cause the described skin changes.

---

questions.stem: A newborn male has a positive newborn screen for congenital hypothyroidism. Confirmatory venous testing shows TSH >100 mIU/L and free T4 3.2 pg/dL (low). Thyroid ultrasound shows an absent thyroid gland in the normal position. What is the most likely etiology?
questions.initialExplanation: A newborn with an absent gland in its normal place = thyroid dysgenesis (commonest cause).
questions.detailedExplanation:
This newborn has severe primary hypothyroidism with an absent thyroid gland on ultrasound. Thyroid
dysgenesis (agenesis, hypoplasia, or ectopy) accounts for approximately 80-85% of cases of
permanent congenital hypothyroidism. The combination of very high TSH, low T4, and absent thyroid
on ultrasound confirms thyroid dysgenesis. Dyshormonogenesis (defects in thyroid hormone
synthesis) would typically show an enlarged or eutopic thyroid on ultrasound. Central hypothyroidism
would show low or inappropriately normal TSH with low T4. Thyroid hormone resistance would show
elevated T4 with inappropriately normal or elevated TSH. Transient hypothyroidism can be caused by
maternal factors or prematurity but would not typically show an absent thyroid.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy is referred for evaluation of a neck mass. On examination, there is a firm, non-tender, 2 cm nodule in the right lobe of the thyroid. He has no history of radiation exposure and no family history of thyroid cancer. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Observation with repeat examination in 1 year \*

questions.initialExplanation: A neck mass in a child: the first step is thyroid ultrasound to evaluate the nodule.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has a solitary thyroid nodule, which requires evaluation to rule out malignancy. The initial
imaging study of choice is thyroid ultrasound, which can characterize the nodule's size, echotexture,
margins, calcifications, and vascularity. Features concerning for malignancy include hypoechogenicity,
irregular margins, microcalcifications, and taller-than-wide shape. Based on ultrasound findings, the
decision can be made to proceed with fine needle aspiration (FNA) if indicated. Observation alone is
not appropriate for a palpable nodule. Levothyroxine suppressive therapy is not recommended for
pediatric thyroid nodules. Radioactive iodine scan can help determine if a nodule is functioning (hot) or
non-functioning (cold), but ultrasound is the initial test of choice.

---

questions.stem: A 16-year-old boy presents with a 6-month history of anxiety, difficulty concentrating, and irritability. His teachers have noted declining academic performance. Physical examination reveals a fine tremor, tachycardia (HR 105 bpm), and a small, non-tender goiter. Laboratory results show TSH 0.1 mIU/L, free T4 2.8 ng/dL (elevated), and anti-TSI antibody positive. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
questions.initialExplanation: Graves in a teen: first-line is methimazole.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This patient has Graves disease with hyperthyroidism. Methimazole is the first-line antithyroid
medication for children and adolescents with Graves disease. It inhibits thyroid hormone synthesis by
blocking the organification of iodine. Propylthiouracil also inhibits thyroid hormone synthesis and
blocks the peripheral conversion of T4 to T3, but it has a higher risk of severe hepatotoxicity and is
generally reserved for pregnant patients in the first trimester or those who cannot tolerate
methimazole. Beta-blockers (like propranolol) can be used for symptom control but do not treat the

underlying hyperthyroidism. Radioactive iodine and thyroidectomy are definitive treatments but are
typically considered if medical therapy fails or is not desired.

---

questions.stem: A 10-year-old girl presents with a 1-month history of a painless neck mass. Physical examination reveals a firm, non-tender 3 cm left thyroid nodule with no cervical lymphadenopathy. Ultrasound shows a solid, hypoechoic nodule with microcalcifications measuring 2.5 cm. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Observation and repeat ultrasound in 6 months \*

questions.initialExplanation: A solid hypoechoic nodule with microcalcifications: FNA biopsy to confirm malignancy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has a thyroid nodule with suspicious ultrasound features: solid, hypoechoic, with
microcalcifications, and >1 cm in size. According to pediatric thyroid nodule guidelines, FNA is
indicated for nodules >1 cm with suspicious ultrasound features or clinical risk factors. The presence
of microcalcifications increases concern for papillary thyroid carcinoma. Observation alone is not
appropriate given the suspicious features. Levothyroxine suppressive therapy is not recommended for
pediatric thyroid nodules. Thyroidectomy may be performed based on FNA results but requires
cytological confirmation first. Radioactive iodine scan would help determine if the nodule is
hyperfunctioning but does not replace the need for cytological evaluation.

---

## Short Stature

> Question numbers not present in the source file for this topic: 23.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl has a height that is 2.5 SD below the mean and a height velocity that is 0.5 SD below the mean. Her birth history is unremarkable. Bone age is equivalent for 4.5 yr with normal body proportions and no dysmorphic features. Growth hormone assay and IGF-1 are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.text: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty

questions.initialExplanation: Short stature with normal GH and IGF-1 and no malformations = constitutional delay of growth (or familial) as the commonest causes.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child demonstrates classic features of constitutional delay of growth and puberty (CDGP): short stature for
chronological age with significantly delayed bone age (4.5 years vs. 7 years), normal growth velocity for bone
age, normal body proportions, and normal GH/IGF-1 levels. The delayed bone age indicates the child is
growing at a rate appropriate for a younger age, predicting eventual catch-up growth and spontaneous puberty.
Hypothyroidism typically causes more severe growth velocity reduction and systemic symptoms. Idiopathic
short stature presents with normal or minimally delayed bone age, not a 2.5-year discrepancy. Russell-Silver
syndrome requires intrauterine growth restriction and characteristic dysmorphic features absent here. Turner
syndrome often shows normal bone age and dysmorphic stigmata, requiring karyotype for diagnosis. CDGP is
a diagnosis of exclusion with excellent prognosis; these "late bloomers" achieve normal adult height without
intervention.

---

questions.stem: The parents of an 8-year-old boy are concerned about his short stature. They noticed that over the past 18 months, he has grown only 4 cm, and he attends school regularly. His father's height is 165 cm, and the mother is 150 cm tall. On physical exam, his height is below the 3rd percentile and weight is at the 25th percentile. He has normal body proportions, no dysmorphic features, and prepubertal genitalia. Growth chart review confirms a downward crossing of percentiles over the last 2 years. What is the most appropriate next step in evaluating this child's growth problem?

options.label: A
options.text: Reassure the family based on mid-parental height

options.label: B
options.text: Order growth hormone stimulation test and serum IGF-1

options.label: D
options.text: Obtain a bone age and assess growth velocity

options.label: E
options.text: Begin empiric treatment with recombinant growth hormone

questions.initialExplanation: Short stature with delayed milestones: the next step is bone age to define the pattern.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This 8-year-old boy presents with significant short stature (height below 3rd percentile), recent growth
deceleration (only 4 cm growth over 18 months, which is below the expected 5-6 cm per year), and a
downward crossing of percentiles over 2 years. The parents have short stature (father 165 cm, mother 150
cm), but the child has crossed percentiles, suggesting a pathologic process rather than genetic short stature.

- Genetic (familial) short stature typically presents with height below the expected range based on mid-parental
height but with a growth velocity that is parallel to the growth curve (maintaining the same percentile channel).
In contrast, pathologic short stature often presents with downward crossing of percentiles, indicating that the
child is growing more slowly than expected. This patient has crossed percentiles over 2 years, which is
concerning for an underlying disorder.

---

questions.stem: A 13-year-old boy presents for evaluation of short stature, his height below 3rd percentile. His growth velocity was normal until the past year, when it slowed significantly. His parents have normal height, and his developmental milestones are normal. Physical examination reveals no dysmorphic features, no systemic abnormalities with no signs of puberty. What is the MOST likely cause of this child's short stature? 2025 s,s
questions.initialExplanation: A 13-year-old with no pubertal signs and short stature = constitutional delay of growth and puberty.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This adolescent presents with classic features of constitutional delay of growth and puberty (CDGP): short
stature (<3rd percentile), recent slowing of growth velocity, and absent pubertal signs at age 13. CDGP
represents a normal variant where children follow a delayed growth trajectory with postponed puberty but
ultimately achieve normal adult height. The recent deceleration in growth velocity often precedes the delayed
pubertal growth spurt. Normal parental heights do not exclude CDGP, as it can occur sporadically or reflect a
familial pattern of late maturation not evident in parents who may have had similar histories. Growth hormone
deficiency typically causes persistent, not recent, growth velocity reduction with characteristic immature facies.
Hypothyroidism produces more severe growth failure with systemic symptoms. Klinefelter syndrome usually
presents with tall stature and hypogonadism, not short stature. Cushing's syndrome causes growth arrest with

weight gain and characteristic physical stigmata. Bone age assessment would confirm delayed skeletal
maturation in CDGP.

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy is referred for evaluation of short stature. His height is at the 2nd percentile, and his father is 162 cm and mother is 155 cm. Both parents were short as children but reached normal adult height. Physical examination reveals a healthy-appearing boy with normal proportions. Which of the following is most likely to confirm the diagnosis? Elevated IGF-1 levels
questions.initialExplanation: To confirm short stature with a delay pattern: bone age assessment (usually delayed).
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child presents with features consistent with familial short stature, the most common cause of
proportionate short stature. Both parents are short with a history of eventual normal adult height, and
the child has a normal appearance. In familial short stature, bone age is typically normal for
chronological age, not advanced. Growth hormone levels are normal. IGF-1 levels are typically
normal. Karyotype is not indicated unless there are dysmorphic features or other concerns. The key
feature distinguishing familial short stature from constitutional delay is that bone age is not delayed in
familial short stature. Children with familial short stature grow at a normal rate and maintain their
position on the growth curve, eventually reaching a height consistent with their genetic potential.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old girl presents with growth failure over the past year. Her height has crossed from the 25th to below the 3rd percentile. She has chronic diarrhea and appears pale. Physical examination shows abdominal distension and digital clubbing. Which test is most likely to establish the diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Failure to thrive with abdominal distension and clubbing = cystic fibrosis; the test is sweat chloride.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child presents with growth failure, chronic diarrhea, pallor, and clubbing, which are classic
features of cystic fibrosis. The chronic respiratory and gastrointestinal manifestations lead to poor
growth. Cystic fibrosis is associated with malabsorption due to pancreatic insufficiency, recurrent
infections, increased work of breathing, and reduced appetite —all contributing to short stature. The
sweat chloride test is the gold standard diagnostic test for cystic fibrosis. Anti-tissue transglutaminase
antibodies would be appropriate for celiac disease, which can also cause growth failure but typically
presents with different features. Serum IgA would screen for IgA deficiency. Urine organic acids
would be relevant for metabolic disorders. Echocardiogram might show cardiac involvement but
would not establish the primary diagnosis.

---

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy is evaluated for short stature. His height is below the 3rd percentile, and he has a history of premature birth at 28 weeks gestation with birth weight 900 grams. He has not shown adequate catch-up growth despite appropriate nutrition. Which statement regarding his condition is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: About 90% of children born SGA show complete catch-up growth

options.label: B
options.text: Growth hormone therapy is not indicated in this scenario

options.label: C
options.text: Growth hormone therapy may be indicated if catch-up growth is insufficient by age 4

options.label: D
options.text: He is not at increased risk for metabolic complications

options.label: E
options.text: Prematurity alone does not affect final adult height

questions.initialExplanation: Failure to catch up despite good nutrition: may relate to GH deficiency per the given option.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child was born small for gestational age (SGA) with extreme prematurity. Approximately 10% of
children born SGA or extremely premature remain short into childhood and adulthood. Current

‘    guidelines indicate that growth hormone therapy may be indicated if there is insufficient catch-up
growth by 4 years of age, regardless of growth hormone levels. This is one of the approved indications
for growth hormone therapy in children. About 90% of SGA infants do show catch-up growth, but the
remaining 10% may require intervention. Prematurity and SGA are associated with increased risk for
metabolic complications including insulin resistance. Prematurity can affect final adult height,
particularly in the most extreme cases.

---

questions.stem: A 15-year-old boy comes to your office for a health supervision visit. He expresses concern that he is only 5 ft, 2 in tall and is not competitive in track. On physical examination, he appears healthy, has a height of 62 in, and weighs 96 Ib.
