His testes are 8 mL in volume bilaterally, there is slight pubertal phallic enlargement, and he has Sexual Maturity Rating 3 pubic hair. He has a small amount of subareolar breast tissue. His last health supervision visit was 2 years ago. He did not have pubic hair at the last visit, and his testes were described as "prepubertal" in size. Of the following, the MOST likely cause of his short stature is :
questions.initialExplanation: A teen with short stature and small prepubertal testes: constitutional delay (will grow later).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Unless other features are present on physical examination or history, it is very difficult to separate
boys who have delayed puberty clinically from those who have true hypogonadotropic hypogonadism
until failure of pubertal progression persists for several years. After puberty commences, adult
testicular size usually is achieved by 3.2+1.8 years.

The boy described in the vignette is of normal height for age and is progressing into puberty, based
on review of his previous visit and his present appearance. Most likely, he has only mild constitutional
delayed puberty. Most boys who have constitutional delayed puberty are underweight and do not
have other signs of chronic illness.

---

questions.stem: A 12-year-old girl is evaluated for short stature. Her height is below the 3rd percentile. She has a history of recurrent otitis media and mild edema of the hands and feet. Physical examination shows a webbed neck, widely spaced nipples, and a systolic murmur. What is the most appropriate initial diagnostic test?
questions.initialExplanation: A girl with short stature, webbed neck and widely spaced nipples = Turner syndrome; the test is karyotype.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This presentation is classic for Turner syndrome. The key features include short stature, webbed neck,
widely spaced nipples (shield chest), and cardiac murmur (commonly bicuspid aortic valve or

‘    coarctation). Recurrent otitis media is also common due to Eustachian tube dysfunction. Turner
syndrome should be considered in ALL short females, even with minimal features. Karyotype analysis
(typically 46,XX or mosaic variants) is the diagnostic test of choice. Growth hormone stimulation
testing is not indicated initially. Thyroid function should be checked as autoimmune thyroiditis is
common in Turner syndrome but is not the initial diagnostic test. Cardiac echo is important for
evaluating the murmur but does not establish the underlying diagnosis.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy is referred for short stature. His height and weight are both below the 3rd percentile. He has chronic loose stools and failure to thrive. Anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA antibodies are positive. What is the most appropriate management?
questions.initialExplanation: Short stature and growth failure with positive anti-tTG IgA = celiac disease, treated with a gluten-free diet.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child presents with celiac disease, confirmed by positive anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies.
Celiac disease can present with growth failure, chronic diarrhea, and failure to thrive. It may present
without classic gastrointestinal symptoms. The treatment for celiac disease is a strict, lifelong gluten-
free diet, which should lead to catch-up growth and resolution of symptoms. Growth hormone therapy
is not indicated as the short stature is secondary to malabsorption. Thyroid hormone replacement
would be appropriate for hypothyroidism, which is not suggested by the presentation. Pancreatic
enzyme replacement is used for cystic fibrosis or pancreatic insufficiency, not celiac disease. Surgical
evaluation is not indicated for uncomplicated celiac disease.

---

questions.stem: An 8-year-old boy presents with short stature. His height is at the 1st percentile, and he has gained weight disproportionately, with weight at the 25th percentile. Physical examination shows a moon facies, buffalo hump, and purple striae on the abdomen. Which finding is most likely on laboratory investigation?
questions.initialExplanation: Short stature with central obesity, purple striae and moon face = Cushing, with high cortisol.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child presents with Cushing syndrome, characterized by growth failure with disproportionate
weight gain, moon facies, buffalo hump, and striae. The most common cause in children is iatrogenic
from exogenous corticosteroid use. Non-iatrogenic Cushing syndrome is unusual in childhood and
may be caused by pituitary or adrenal pathology. Laboratory findings would show elevated cortisol
levels (with loss of diurnal variation), elevated urinary free cortisol, and failure to suppress cortisol on
low-dose dexamethasone testing. Low cortisol would suggest adrenal insufficiency. Low IGF-1 can be
seen in growth hormone deficiency. Elevated TSH would suggest hypothyroidism. The combination of
short stature with excess weight gain is characteristic of endocrine causes of growth failure.

---

questions.stem: A 14-year-old boy is evaluated for short stature. His height is at the 2nd percentile, and he has not started puberty. His father reports starting puberty at age 16 and reaching his final height at age 20. Physical examination shows Tanner stage 1 genital development. Bone age is delayed by 2 years. What is the most appropriate treatment if puberty is delayed beyond 16 years?
questions.initialExplanation: Delayed puberty after age 16 with delayed bone age: a short course of testosterone induces puberty.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has constitutional delay of growth and puberty (CDGP), a common variant of normal growth.
The family history of delayed puberty in the father with eventual normal height is classic. Bone age is
typically delayed 1-2 years, as seen here. IGF-1 levels are low for chronological age but within normal
range for bone age. Growth hormone responses to provocative testing may be lower than in children
with typical timing of puberty. The prognosis for normal adult height is good. Current guidelines
suggest that boys with more than 2 years of pubertal delay (beyond age 14) may benefit from a short
course of testosterone therapy to hasten puberty. This can improve self-esteem and allow for the
pubertal growth spurt. Growth hormone therapy is NOT indicated for constitutional delay. LH-RH
agonists would delay puberty further. Aromatase inhibitors are experimental in this setting.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy is referred for short stature. His height is below the 3rd percentile. His parents report that he has been increasingly withdrawn and has abnormal eating patterns, including voracious appetite at times. Physical examination shows severe wasting and emotional withdrawal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Severe wasting and emotional withdrawal = psychosocial dwarfism (emotional deprivation).
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child presents with psychosocial dwarfism (also called maternal deprivation dwarfism or functional
hypopituitarism). The key features include short stature with severe wasting, abnormal eating patterns
(voracious appetite or food refusal), and emotional/behavioral disturbances. Psychosocial deprivation
causes functional hypopituitarism with low IGF-1 levels and inadequate responses to GH stimulation
testing. Puberty may be normal or premature. The condition is difficult to diagnose because parents
often hide family circumstances, and children may not verbalize their experiences. Affected children
show rapid catch-up growth when placed in a nurturing environment. Celiac disease, cystic fibrosis,
and GH deficiency can cause similar growth failure but would not explain the behavioral and eating
pattern abnormalities.

---

questions.stem: A 10-year-old girl is evaluated for short stature. Her height is below the 3rd percentile. She has characteristic facial features including a broad forehead, short nose, full lips, and stellate iris pattern. She has a systolic murmur. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Short stature, elfin face (short nose, full lips, stellate irides) and a murmur = Williams syndrome.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This presentation is classic for Williams syndrome. The characteristic features include elfin facies
(broad forehead, short nose, full lips, stellate iris pattern), supravalvular aortic stenosis (systolic
murmur), and short stature. Williams syndrome is caused by a microdeletion on chromosome 7
(7q11.23) involving the ELN gene. Turner syndrome presents with webbed neck and shield chest but
different facial features. Noonan syndrome includes webbed neck and pulmonary stenosis but
different facial features. Down syndrome presents with upslanting palpebral fissures, flat nasal bridge,

and simian crease. Russell-Silver syndrome presents with triangular face, limb asymmetry, and
growth failure.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy presents with growth failure. His height has crossed from the 50th to below the 3rd percentile over 18 months. Physical examination shows dry skin, coarse facial features, and a midline neck mass. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Growth arrest with dry skin and a neck mass = hypothyroidism.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child presents with classic features of hypothyroidism. The crossing of centiles over a relatively
short period, combined with dry skin, coarse facial features, and goiter, is highly suggestive of
autoimmune thyroiditis causing acquired hypothyroidism. Hypothyroidism is one of the endocrine
causes of short stature and is characterized by children being relatively overweight (weight centile
higher than height centile). Growth failure in hypothyroidism is disproportionate. When treated, catch-
up growth rapidly occurs but often with rapid entry into puberty that can limit final height. Growth
hormone deficiency would not cause coarse facial features or goiter. Celiac disease might cause
growth failure but not this specific pattern of findings.

---

questions.stem: An 8-year-old girl is referred for short stature. Her height is at the 1st percentile. She was born at 32 weeks gestation with birth weight 1.2 kg. She has had good catch-up growth and is now at the 25th percentile for weight. What is the most appropriate management?
questions.initialExplanation: After catch-up growth and weight gain, no further intervention is needed.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child was born premature and small for gestational age but has demonstrated excellent catch-up
growth, reaching the 25th percentile for weight. Most infants born SGA or premature show catch-up
growth within the first 2-3 years of life. Approximately 90% of children born SGA show complete
catch-up growth. Growth hormone therapy is only considered if there is insufficient catch-up growth
by age 4 years. Since this child has demonstrated adequate catch-up growth and is now thriving, no
further intervention is needed. Continued monitoring of growth is appropriate, but active treatment or
extensive evaluation is not indicated at this time.

---

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy with asthma on long-term inhaled corticosteroids presents with short stature. His height is at the 2nd percentile, down from the 25th percentile 2 years ago. Weight is at the 50th percentile. Physical examination shows cushingoid features. What is the most likely mechanism of his growth failure?
questions.initialExplanation: Long-term inhaled corticosteroid with Cushingoid features: growth is directly affected by the steroid.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has growth failure due to corticosteroid excess, most likely from his inhaled corticosteroid
therapy. Inhaled corticosteroids can cause systemic effects including growth suppression, even at
relatively low doses. Corticosteroids impair growth through multiple mechanisms, including direct
effects on the growth plate cartilage by inhibiting chondrocyte proliferation and inducing apoptosis.
They also suppress GH secretion, decrease IGF-1 production, and have effects on collagen
synthesis. Alternate-day therapy may reduce but not eliminate growth suppression. This case
illustrates that growth failure with disproportionate weight gain (weight centile higher than height
centile) is characteristic of endocrine causes of short stature, including corticosteroid excess.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old girl is evaluated for short stature. Her height is below the 3rd percentile. She has asymmetric limb length discrepancy with one leg 2 cm shorter than the other. Physical examination shows triangular facies and limb asymmetry. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Short stature, limb asymmetry and triangular face = Russell-Silver syndrome.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This presentation is characteristic of Russell-Silver syndrome. Key features include short stature with
prenatal onset (disproportionate short stature), limb asymmetry (one side longer than the other), and
characteristic triangular facies (broad forehead, narrow chin, downturned mouth). Russell-Silver
syndrome is a genetic disorder that can be caused by abnormalities on chromosome 7 (maternal
uniparental disomy) or chromosome 11. Turner syndrome may cause short stature but not limb
asymmetry. Noonan syndrome includes webbed neck and pulmonary stenosis. Achondroplasia
causes rhizomelic limb shortening with normal trunk length but not asymmetry.

---

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy presents with short stature. His height is at the 1st percentile. He has a history of neonatal hypoglycemia and micropenis. Physical examination shows midline defects and sparse hair. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Short stature, micropenis and midline defects = septo-optic dysplasia (pituitary hormone deficiency).
questions.detailedExplanation:
This presentation suggests septo-optic dysplasia or another midline defect involving the hypothalamic-
pituitary axis. The key features include short stature (possibly due to GH deficiency), neonatal
hypoglycemia (suggesting cortisol deficiency), micropenis (suggesting gonadotropin deficiency), and
midline defects (sparse hair, possible optic nerve hypoplasia). Septo-optic dysplasia is characterized
by the triad of optic nerve hypoplasia, pituitary hormone deficiencies, and midline brain abnormalities.
Growth hormone deficiency can be isolated or part of combined pituitary hormone deficiency. Prader-
Willi syndrome presents with hypotonia in infancy, hyperphagia, obesity, and hypogonadism. Kallmann
syndrome presents with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and anosmia.

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl presents with short stature. Her height is below the 3rd percentile. She has dysmorphic features including low-set ears, hypertelorism, and a webbed neck. She has a systolic murmur consistent with pulmonary stenosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Short stature with webbed neck and pulmonary stenosis = Noonan syndrome (may resemble Turner but with a different genetic basis).
questions.detailedExplanation:
This presentation is classic for Noonan syndrome. Key features include short stature, characteristic
facial features (low-set ears, hypertelorism), webbed neck, and congenital heart disease (pulmonary
stenosis is the most common cardiac lesion). Noonan syndrome is caused by mutations in the
PTPN11 gene (and other RAS-MAPK pathway genes) and is inherited in an autosomal dominant
pattern. Turner syndrome also causes short stature and webbed neck but typically does not include
pulmonary stenosis; Turner syndrome features include shield chest and widely spaced nipples.
Williams syndrome includes elfin facies and supravalvular aortic stenosis. Down syndrome includes
upslanting palpebral fissures and congenital heart disease (AV canal).

---

questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy with constitutional delay of growth and puberty is being evaluated. His bone age is delayed by 2 years. His IGF-1 level is low for chronological age but within the normal range for bone age. What is the most accurate statement regarding his condition?

options.label: B
options.text: He will likely reach a normal adult height

options.label: D
options.text: His bone age will advance before puberty

questions.initialExplanation: Constitutional delay: bone age catches up later and the child often reaches normal height.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has constitutional delay of growth and puberty (CDGP), a common variant of normal growth.
The key features include delayed bone age (1-2 years), low IGF-1 for chronological age but normal for
bone age, and family history of delayed puberty with eventual normal adult height. The prognosis for
normal adult height is good in CDGP. Growth hormone therapy is NOT indicated for CDGP as these
children reach normal adult height without treatment. The bone age delay allows for a prolonged
growth period, and the pubertal growth spurt, though delayed, contributes to final height. Treatment
with testosterone may be offered to boys with significant pubertal delay after age 14 to induce puberty,
but this is not for growth promotion per se.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy presents with short stature. His height is below the 3rd percentile. He has chronic diarrhea and recurrent respiratory infections. Sweat chloride test is positive at 80 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate intervention for his growth failure?

options.label: B
options.text: Optimize cystic fibrosis management including nutrition

questions.initialExplanation: CF with growth failure: optimizing nutrition and respiratory care (optimize CF care) treats growth.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has cystic fibrosis, confirmed by the positive sweat chloride test. Growth failure in cystic
fibrosis is multifactorial, resulting from malabsorption (due to pancreatic insufficiency), recurrent
infections, increased work of breathing, and reduced appetite. The most appropriate approach to
improving growth is to optimize the overall management of cystic fibrosis, including aggressive
nutritional support (high-calorie diet, pancreatic enzyme replacement with meals), treatment of
pulmonary exacerbations, and airway clearance therapies. Growth hormone therapy may be
considered in some cases of CF with persistent growth failure despite optimal management, but it is

not first-line treatment. The primary focus should be on addressing the underlying causes of growth
failure through comprehensive CF care.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy presents with short stature. His height is below the 3rd percentile. His parents are concerned about the psychosocial impact of his short stature. Which statement is most accurate regarding the psychological effects of short stature?

options.label: B
options.text: Short stature has no impact on self-esteem

options.label: C
options.text: Children with short stature are never teased

options.label: D
options.text: Short stature affects only athletic performance

questions.initialExplanation: Most short children do not have major psychological problems.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Most children with short stature are psychologically well-adjusted to their size. However, there may
be problems including teasing or bullying at school, poor self-esteem, and disadvantage in

‘    competitive sports. Short children are often assumed by adults to be younger than their true age and
may be treated inappropriately. Growth hormone treatment may improve self-esteem and quality of
life in some children, but it does not always improve psychological outcomes and should not be used
solely for psychosocial reasons. The psychological impact varies among individuals and depends on
multiple factors including family support, peer relationships, and the child's coping mechanisms.

---

questions.stem: A 10-year-old girl presents with short stature. Her height is below the 3rd percentile. She has a history of polydipsia, polyuria, and weight loss. Laboratory investigations show blood glucose 250 mg/dL and HbA1c 9.5%. She is diagnosed with Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus. What is the most appropriate management of her growth failure?
questions.initialExplanation: Growth failure in T1DM: improve glycemic control to reach normal growth.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus presenting with growth failure. Poorly controlled diabetes can
cause growth failure through multiple mechanisms including the catabolic effects of insulin deficiency,
chronic illness, and associated complications. The most appropriate initial approach to managing her
growth failure is to optimize glycemic control with adequate insulin therapy, proper nutrition, and
regular monitoring. When diabetes is well-controlled, growth typically normalizes. Growth hormone
therapy is not indicated as the growth failure is secondary to poor diabetes control. Addressing the
underlying cause (poor glycemic control) is the priority. Once diabetes is optimally controlled, if growth
failure persists, further evaluation for other causes may be warranted.

---

questions.stem: 2024 s.')5 1 A 4-year-old boy presents with pallor and jaundice associated with passing dark urine over the last 2 days following an upper respiratory tract infection. Laboratory findings: hemoglobin 5 g/dl, WBC 8,000/cmm, platelet count 255,000/cmm. What is the most likely underlying cause?
questions.initialExplanation: Pallor, jaundice and dark urine after an upper respiratory infection in a male with Hb 5 and normal platelets and WBC = acute hemolysis; the likely cause is G6PD deficiency.
questions.detailedExplanation:
(Nelson & AAP Guidelines): This presentation is classic for G6PD deficiency, the most common enzymatic disorder of red blood cells globally. According to Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics, G6PD deficiency typically presents in males (X-linked inheritance) with acute hemolysis triggered by infections, certain medications, or fava beans. The temporal relationship with an upper respiratory tract infection, dark urine (hemoglobinuria), and acute hemolytic anemia are pathognomonic. The AAP emphasizes that G6PD deficiency should be considered in any male infant or child with unexplained hemolytic anemia. Laboratory confirmation requires G6PD enzyme assay, though levels may be normal during acute hemolysis due to selective destruction of deficient cells .

---

questions.stem: An 18-month-old girl presents with severe anemia. Hemoglobin is 4.6 g/dl. Dietary history reveals consumption of 36 ounces of cow's milk daily. No family history of blood disorders. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: An infant drinking 36 oz of cow's milk daily with severe anemia = iron deficiency anemia (milk is iron-poor and causes occult GI blood loss).
questions.detailedExplanation:
(Nelson & AAP Guidelines): This case exemplifies classic iron deficiency anemia in infancy, the most common nutritional deficiency worldwide. According to Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics and AAP guidelines, excessive cow's milk consumption (>24 oz/day) is a major risk factor as it replaces iron-rich foods and can cause occult gastrointestinal blood loss. The AAP recommends limiting cow's milk to no more than 16-24 ounces daily in children over 12 months. Iron deficiency anemia typically presents with microcytic, hypochromic anemia (though severe cases may not show microcytosis initially). The AAP emphasizes screening for iron deficiency at 12 months and providing dietary counseling to prevent this preventable condition .

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old child diagnosed with iron-deficiency anemia was started on oral iron therapy. The family is asking about some instructions of this treatment. Which of the following statements is INCORRECT regarding iron therapy in this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Iron should be taken between meals or with vitamin C to enhance absorption

options.label: B
options.text: A dark green or black stool is a normal finding during iron therapy

options.label: C
options.text: Dairy products should not be given around the time of iron administration

options.label: D
options.text: Iron should be temporarily withheld during acute febrile infections

options.label: E
options.text: Oral iron therapy is stopped after 1 month once hemoglobin improves

questions.initialExplanation: The incorrect statement is stopping iron after one month; the correct approach is to continue about 2-3 months after Hb normalizes to replenish stores.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This statement is incorrect because iron therapy must continue for 2-3 months after hemoglobin normalizes to fully replenish depleted iron stores, not stopped after 1 month when hemoglobin merely begins to improve. Premature discontinuation risks rapid recurrence of anemia due to inadequate ferritin repletion. Iron is best absorbed on an empty stomach or with vitamin C, which enhances reduction to the ferrous form. Dark green or black stools are expected from unabsorbed iron excretion and are harmless. Dairy products contain calcium that competitively inhibits iron absorption and should be separated by 1-2 hours. Withholding iron during acute febrile infections is reasonable because elevated hepcidin reduces absorption and may theoretically limit pathogen access to iron.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy presents with 2 days of pallor and tea-colored urine following a recent flu. He is now active, eating well, and hemodynamically stable. Exam shows mild jaundice without hepatosplenomegaly. Labs reveal Hb 7.5 g/dL, normal WBC and platelets, and elevated indirect bilirubin. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.text: Immediate packed red blood cell transfusion

options.label: B
options.text: Administer corticosteroids and order a direct Coombs test

options.label: C
options.text: Start empirical antibiotics for possible infection

options.label: D
options.text: Observe with supportive care and monitor hemoglobin

options.label: E
options.text: Refer for abdominal ultrasound to rule out obstructive jaundice

questions.initialExplanation: A stable G6PD child after influenza with Hb 7.5: observe without transfusion or steroids, since hemolysis is self-limited.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child presents with acute hemolytic anemia likely due to G6PD deficiency triggered by a viral infection, evidenced by pallor, tea-colored urine (hemoglobinuria), jaundice, elevated indirect bilirubin, and preserved stability. Since he is hemodynamically stable, active, and eating well with a hemoglobin of 7.5 g/dL, immediate transfusion is unnecessary and reserved for severe symptomatic anemia or Hb <5-6 g/dL. Corticosteroids and Coombs testing target autoimmune hemolysis, which is less likely given the infection trigger and typical G6PD presentation. Empirical antibiotics are unwarranted without signs of active bacterial infection. Abdominal ultrasound is not indicated as indirect hyperbilirubinemia reflects hemolysis, not biliary obstruction. Supportive care with hydration, avoidance of oxidative triggers, and serial hemoglobin monitoring allows the self-limited hemolytic episode to resolve spontaneously. Confirmatory G6PD testing should be performed after recovery to avoid false-negative results from reticulocytosis.

---

questions.stem: An African-American mother brings her previously healthy 2-year-old son to the emergency department because he looked pale when he woke up this morning. She also reports fever and decreased activity over the last few days. He was diagnosed with a urinary tract infection and given trimethoprim- sulfamethoxazole 3 days ago. On physical examination, he is markedly pale and appears jaundiced. His heart rate is 170 beats/min, and his respiratory rate is 30 breaths/min. The rest of his physical examination findings are unremarkable. Laboratory evaluation reveals a hemoglobin concentration of 5 g/dL (50 g/L). Of the following, the MOST likely cause of this boy's anemia is:
questions.initialExplanation: A 2-year-old Black boy given trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole then pallor, jaundice and Hb 5 = G6PD deficiency.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The sudden onset of pallor and jaundice in a healthy child is suggestive of acute hemolytic anemia, and the history of recent use of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, as reported for the boy in the vignette, should raise the suspicion of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency. G6PD is an enzyme used for glucose metabolism. Deficiency of the enzyme results in a decrease in reduced glutathione, which is important for the removal of oxygen radicals. When oxidant drugs are administered to those who have G6PD deficiency, the oxygen radicals cannot be removed adequately, and the red cell membrane is damaged. Trimethoprim sulfamethoxazole is an oxidant drug commonly prescribed for children. Other oxidant drugs include chloramphenicol, nitrofurantoin, primaquine, and acetylsalicylic acid. Moderate-to-severe illness may be another cause of oxidant stress without medication use and may be an inciting factor for acute hemolysis in those who have G6PD deficiency.

questions.stem: An 11-month-old African American boy has a hematocrit of 24% on a screening laboratory done at his well-child checkup. Further testing demonstrates: hemoglobin 7.8 g/dL; hematocrit 22.9%; leukocyte count 12,200/uL with 39% neutrophils, 6% bands, 55% lymphocytes; hypochromia on smear; free erythrocyte protoporphyrin (FEP) 114 ug/dL; lead level 6 pg/dL whole blood; platelet count 175,000/uL; reticulocyte count 0.2%; sickle-cell preparation negative; stool guaiac-negative; and mean corpuscular volume (MCV) 64 fL. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?
questions.initialExplanation: An 11-month-old with low Hb, MCV 64, high FEP and low retics (hypochromia): iron deficiency; treat with oral ferrous sulfate.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Response to a therapeutic trial of iron is an appropriate and cost-effective method of diagnosing iron- deficiency anemia. A prompt reticulocytosis and rise in hemoglobin and hematocrit follow the administration of an oral preparation of ferrous sulfate. Intramuscular iron dextran should be reserved for situations in which compliance cannot be achieved, since this treatment is expensive, painful, and no more effective than oral iron. Dietary modifications, such as limiting the intake of cow’s milk and including iron-fortified cereals along with a mixed diet, are appropriate long-term measures, but they will not make enough iron available to replenish iron stores. The gradual onset of iron deficiency anemia enables a child to adapt to surprisingly low hemoglobin concentrations. Transfusion is rarely indicated unless a child becomes symptomatic or is further compromised by a superimposed infection.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old previously well African American boy is brought to the office by his aunt. She reports that he developed pallor, dark urine, and jaundice over the past few days. He stays with her, has not traveled, and has not been exposed to a jaundiced person, but he is taking trimethoprim sulfamethoxazole for otitis media. The CBC in the office shows a low hemoglobin and hematocrit, while his “stat” serum electrolytes, blood urea nitrogen (BUN), and chemistries are remarkable only for an elevation of his bilirubin levels. His aunt seems to recall his 8-year-old brother having had an “allergic reaction” to aspirin, which also caused a short-lived period of anemia and jaundice. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s symptoms?
questions.initialExplanation: After TMP-SMX, with a brother who had hemolysis after aspirin: G6PD deficiency (X-linked inheritance).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Synthesis of the RBC enzyme glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) is determined by genes on the X chromosome, and the pattern of inheritance is X-linked recessive. The enzyme found in most populations is termed G6PDB1. There are more than 380 deficient variants of the enzyme, affecting over 100 million people worldwide. Among them is variant G6PDA1, a mutant enzyme affecting about 13% of African American males and 2% of African American females. The disease occurs, though less commonly, in other ethnic groups, including Middle Eastern, African, and Asian groups. Deficiency of G6PD compromises the generation of reduced glutathione and upon exposure to oxidant agents such as sulfa drugs, antimalarials, nitrofurans, naphthalene mothballs, or infection, a hemolytic episode usually occurs. The degree of hemolysis depends on the nature of the oxidant and severity of the enzyme deficiency. In African Americans, the older, more G6PD-deficient cells are destroyed, but since young cells have sufficient enzyme to prevent further RBC destruction even if the inciting factor is still present, the hemolytic crisis is usually self-limited. Blood transfusion may be unnecessary.

---

questions.stem: You are counseling a family about iron supplementation after their son was found to have iron-deficiency anemia on routine screening at his 1-year well child visit. Which of the following is true about supplementation for iron deficiency?

options.label: A
options.text: All iron supplementation, regardless of formulation, should be taken with milk.

options.label: B
options.text: Proton pump inhibitors can improve the absorption of iron supplementation.

options.label: C
options.text: To avoid gastrointestinal pain, iron should always be taken with food.

options.label: D
options.text: The hemoglobin begins to rise within 1 week of starting iron supplementation.

options.label: E
options.text: Taking iron supplementation with orange juice can improve absorption.

questions.initialExplanation: Iron absorption improves with orange juice (vitamin C); milk and proton pump inhibitors reduce it.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Iron deficiency is the most common global nutritional deficiency, and iron-deficiency anemia is the most common hematologic disease of infancy and childhood. Nonheme dietary iron comes primarily

’    in the ferric state (Fe 3+) and is reduced to the ferrous state (Fe 2+) in an acidic environment. Ascorbic acid can therefore improve the absorption of iron. Iron supplementation should never be taken with milk, food, or proton pump inhibitors as these all inhibit the absorption of iron. Hemoglobin is one of the last indices to improve, although reticulocytosis can be seen within 1 week of starting iron supplementation.

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy presents to your office with pallor and fatigue. His mother tells you that he is a picky eater who drinks at least 32 oz of milk each day. His laboratory studies reveal a hemoglobin of 4.8 g/dL and a MCV of 51 fL. You suspect iron-deficiency anemia. In counseling the mother, you tell her that:

options.label: A
options.text: The patient should drink milk when taking the iron you are prescribing.

options.label: B
options.text: The patient should continue to drink milk as it is a good source of iron.

options.label: C
options.text: Milk should be avoided because it contains phytates that chelate iron.

options.label: D
options.text: Milk proteins can irritate the GI tract and lead to microscopic blood loss.

options.label: E
options.text: The patient will require iron therapy for 1 month.

questions.initialExplanation: Cow's milk may irritate the gut and cause microscopic blood loss that leads to iron deficiency.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Milk can contribute to the development of iron deficiency in multiple ways. It is a poor source of iron, so toddlers who rely primarily on milk for nutrition have insufficient iron intake. Milk contains proteins that can irritate the gastrointestinal tract of some patients and lead to microscopic blood loss, and milk inhibits the absorption of iron. Phytates are compounds found in plants; they can chelate iron and inhibit its absorption. Typical therapy for iron-deficiency anemia continues for several months after the anemia is corrected in order to replenish iron stores.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old African American boy with HIV is taking dapsone for PCP prophylaxis due to a sulfa allergy. He presents with tachypnea and fatigue, and appears cyanotic, but his oxygen saturation does not improve with supplemental oxygen. You suspect pseudocyanosis from methemoglobinemia as a complication of dapsone therapy. Before you treat him with methylene blue, you ask about the family history or personal history of which of the following disorders?
questions.initialExplanation: A child on dapsone with false cyanosis and methemoglobinemia: before methylene blue ask about G6PD deficiency, as it may cause severe hemolysis in G6PD deficiency.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Methemoglobin is created when the iron component of hemoglobin is in the ferric state (Fe 3+), which cannot bind oxygen. This occurs throughout the RBC life cycle, but is typically reduced through an intracellular cytochrome b5 reductase enzyme. There are congenital and acquired causes of methemoglobinemia, which occurs when the intracellular reductase pathways are overwhelmed or dysfunctional. In acquired methemoglobinemia, methylene blue is the treatment of choice. Methylene blue reduces methemoglobin via an alternative NADPH-flavin pathway. Importantly, the NADPH flavin pathway requires G6PD to generate glutathione. In patients with G6PD deficiency, methylene blue is ineffective, and may cause hemolysis.

---

questions.stem: A healthy 1-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of pallor for 2 weeks. Her immunizations are up-to-date. She was fed commercial formula until the age of 6 months and has been fed 2% cow's milk and table food since then. Development has been normal. She is at the 50th percentile for height and the 90th percentile for weight. Hematocrit is 26%. A blood smear with Wright stain is shown. Supplementation with which of the following is most likely to have prevented this condition?
questions.initialExplanation: Anemia at 12 months due to cow's milk and a poor diet: prevention with iron.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Iron deficiency anemia (IDA) presents with microcytic, hypochromic anemia with otherwise normal shape of red blood cells. IDA is extremely prevalent worldwide, especially in developing countries, in pregnant women, and in children. Infants and children are particularly vulnerable to IDA as a result of rapid growth and dietary deficiencies. The patient has been fed primarily cow's milk for the past 6 months, along with table food, while formula was stopped at 6 months of age. This places the infant at risk for iron deficiency given the insufficient amount of iron in cow's milk. Many types of formulas and foods are fortified with iron to ensure appropriate supplementation. Iron is required for the synthesis of heme, which is a necessary component of the hemoglobin molecule, and thus, of erythrocytes. It functions to shuttle oxygen to and from peripheral tissues. Erythrocytes on the peripheral blood smear are hypochromic as a result of deficient hemoglobin concentration. It is hypothesized that erythrocytes are microcytic as a result of continuing erythrocyte division in order to reach an adequate hemoglobin concentration. Because hemoglobin stores are inadequate, cell division continues beyond what would normally occur and causes the cells to be smaller than normal. Treatment in the case of poor dietary intake is with oral iron supplementation. If severe, parenteral iron can be administered.

questions.stem: A 14-month-old toddler consumes 1200 mL cow's milk daily and refuses iron-rich foods. Examination shows marked pallor, smooth shiny tongue, and angular stomatitis. Labs: Hb 7.2 g/dL, MCV 64 fL, MCH 18 pg, MCHC 28 g/dL. Peripheral smear shows microcytic hypochromic cells with target cells. What is the most appropriate initial therapeutic intervention?

options.label: A
options.text: Immediate blood transfusion with packed red cells

options.label: B
options.text: Oral ferrous sulfate 6 mg/kg/day of elemental iron in three divided doses

options.label: D
options.text: Dietary modification with iron-fortified cereal introduction

questions.initialExplanation: An infant with severe iron deficiency (Hb 7.2, MCV 64): initial treatment is oral iron (ferrous sulfate 6 mg/kg/day elemental in three doses), not transfusion.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child presents with classic iron deficiency anemia (IDA) characterized by microcytic hypochromic anemia (MCV 64 fL, MCH 18 pg, MCHC 28 g/dL), glossitis (smooth shiny tongue), and angular stomatitis. The history of excessive cow's milk consumption (>1000 mL/day) and refusal of iron-rich foods is a classic cause of IDA in toddlers. The peripheral smear showing microcytic hypochromic cells with target cells confirms the diagnosis. Oral iron therapy at the standard pediatric dose of 6 mg/kg/day elemental iron in three divided doses is the first-line treatment for stable IDA in children.

---

questions.stem: A 9-month-old exclusively breastfed infant is evaluated for pale complexion and poor weight gain. The child was born at 32 weeks gestation weighing 1.8 kg. Current weight is 6.2 kg. Examination reveals generalized pallor and hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory results show Hb 8.5 g/dL with microcytic hypochromic indices. What is the most likely underlying cause of this anemia?

options.label: A
options.text: Iron deficiency due to low birth weight and rapid growth

questions.initialExplanation: An exclusively breastfed late-preterm of 9 months with hypochromic anemia: the cause is iron deficiency from low birth stores and rapid growth.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This infant was born prematurely at 32 weeks with low birth weight (1.8 kg) and is now showing signs of iron deficiency anemia. Premature infants have inadequate iron stores and require supplementation due to rapid postnatal growth and developmental demands. The exclusive breastfeeding without iron supplementation, combined with rapid weight gain from 1.8 kg to 6.2 kg, places the infant at high risk for iron deficiency.

The microcytic hypochromic indices on laboratory testing confirm the diagnosis of iron deficiency anemia rather than other hereditary anemias. The child is not old enough for thalassemia to present, and the absence of hemolysis rules out sickle cell anemia. Hereditary spherocytosis typically presents with spherocytes and positive family history, while autoimmune hemolysis would show a positive Coombs test.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy presents with progressive pallor and fatigue over 2 months. He has a history of recurrent abdominal pain and occasional melena. His mother reports he drinks tea with meals daily. Examination shows pale conjunctiva and a firm, non-tender liver edge 2 cm below costal margin. What diagnostic test would be most valuable to determine the underlying cause?
questions.initialExplanation: Iron deficiency with abdominal pain and black stools (melena): upper GI endoscopy to find the bleeding source.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child's presentation with melena (black stools), recurrent abdominal pain, and iron deficiency anemia suggests gastrointestinal bleeding, which is a common cause of iron deficiency in older children. The history of drinking tea with meals is particularly significant because tea contains tannins that reduce iron absorption, contributing to the anemia. Upper Gl endoscopy is the most valuable diagnostic test as it can directly visualize the upper gastrointestinal tract to identify potential bleeding sources such as peptic ulcers, gastritis, or varices.

Stool occult blood testing would confirm bleeding but not identify its source. Hemoglobin electrophoresis is unnecessary without evidence of hemolysis. Bone marrow aspiration is invasive and rarely needed for uncomplicated iron deficiency. Abdominal ultrasound may show organomegaly but won't identify the bleeding source.

---

questions.stem: A 6-month-old infant with failure to thrive and iron deficiency anemia shows no improvement after 4 weeks of oral iron therapy at 6 mg/kg/day elemental iron. The child is taking the medication as prescribed and has no vomiting or diarrhea. Repeat labs show Hb 7.0 g/dL (unchanged). What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.text: Check for underlying bleeding with Meckel's scan

options.label: D
options.text: Increase the oral iron dose to 12 mg/kg/day

questions.initialExplanation: Iron deficiency anemia not improving after 4 weeks of iron: the source's answer is celiac screening (malabsorption), alongside checking adherence and bleeding.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This infant has failed to respond to oral iron therapy despite adequate dosing and compliance, suggesting an underlying malabsorptive condition rather than simple iron deficiency. Celiac disease is a common cause of treatment-resistant iron deficiency anemia in infants, particularly those with chronic diarrhea and failure to thrive. The chronic diarrhea and poor weight gain in this case are classic red flags for malabsorption.

Screening for celiac disease with anti-transglutaminase antibodies is non-invasive and has high sensitivity and specificity for celiac disease. Double iron dosing could be dangerous, and parenteral iron is not indicated without evidence of malabsorption. Meckel's scan would be considered if there was evidence of Gl bleeding.

---

questions.stem: A 16-month-old toddler with iron deficiency anemia presents with behavioral changes including irritability, poor concentration, and developmental regression. The mother reports the child was previously meeting all developmental milestones but has shown recent decline in cognitive abilities and motor skills. Which iron study parameter is most sensitive for detecting early iron deficiency before anemia develops?
questions.initialExplanation: The earliest indicator of iron deficiency before anemia develops is serum ferritin.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Serum ferritin is the most sensitive indicator of iron deficiency because it reflects total body iron stores and is the first parameter to decrease before any changes in hemoglobin or red cell indices occur. In ‘    iron deficiency states, ferritin levels decline rapidly as iron stores are depleted, making it the most valuable screening tool for early iron deficiency. The behavioral changes described - irritability, poor concentration, and developmental regression - are classic neurological manifestations of iron deficiency that occur before frank anemia develops. Serum iron and transferrin saturation fluctuate with diurnal variation and acute phase responses. Total iron binding capacity increases in iron deficiency but is less specific. Red cell distribution width becomes elevated later in the progression of iron deficiency.

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old child is found to have Hb 11.0 g/dL with MCV 65 fL during routine screening. The child appears well with normal growth and development. The mother reports the child consumes approximately 800 mL of cow's milk daily and eats minimal solid foods. What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.label: B
options.text: Counsel on dietary modification and retest in 3 months

questions.initialExplanation: Hb 11 and MCV 65 in a well child with poor nutrition: advise dietary changes and recheck in 3 months.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has borderline anemia (Hb 11.0 g/dL with MCV 65 fL) and represents a common scenario in toddlers consuming excessive cow's milk (>500 mL/day) with minimal ironrich solid foods. The child appears well with normal growth and development, indicating this is early iron deficiency rather than established disease. Dietary counseling should focus on reducing cow's milk to less than 500 mL/day and introducing iron-fortified cereals and other iron-rich foods.

Starting iron therapy immediately would be appropriate for symptomatic anemia or severely low hemoglobin levels. Hemoglobin electrophoresis is indicated only if there is evidence of hemolysis or family history of hemoglobinopathies. A referral to hematology Is unnecessary for this mild presentation, and bone marrow biopsy is far too invasive for this scenario.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy with iron deficiency anemia shows excellent response to oral iron therapy. His Hb increases from 7.8 g/dL to 10.2 g/dL over 4 weeks. However, his mother asks when to stop the iron supplementation. For how long should iron therapy be continued after normal hemoglobin levels are achieved?
questions.initialExplanation: After Hb is corrected, continue iron for 2 months to refill body stores.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Iron therapy should be continued for 2 months after hemoglobin levels normalize to replenish depleted iron stores completely. While hemoglobin levels may rise within 1-2 weeks of starting iron therapy,

’    complete restoration of iron stores requires continued treatment for a total of 3-4 months from the start of therapy. Stopping iron supplementation immediately after hemoglobin normalization often leads to recurrence of iron deficiency anemia because stores remain depleted.

Shorter durations (2 weeks to 1 month) are insufficient to restore iron stores. Longer durations (3-6 months) are typically unnecessary if the underlying cause has been addressed and adequate dietary intake is established. The 2-month duration after hemoglobin normalization is evidence-based and allows for adequate repletion of iron stores.

---

questions.stem: A 15-month-old infant presents with pica behavior, eating dirt and paint chips from the walls. Physical examination shows marked pallor, spoon-shaped nails (koilonychia), and a beefy red tongue. Laboratory findings include Hb 6.8 g/dL with microcytic hypochromic indices. Which additional laboratory finding would most strongly support the diagnosis?

options.label: E
options.text: Low serum ferritin and elevated total iron binding capacity

questions.initialExplanation: Pica, koilonychia, red tongue and hypochromic anemia: iron deficiency; supported by low ferritin and high TIBC.
questions.detailedExplanation:
These laboratory findings are classic for iron deficiency anemia and help differentiate it from other causes of microcytic hypochromic anemia. Low serum ferritin indicates depleted iron stores, while elevated total iron binding capacity reflects increased ironbinding capacity of transferrin as the body attempts to maximize iron uptake. This combination is pathognomonic for iron deficiency.

Elevated serum folate and vitamin B12 levels would suggest megaloblastic anemia rather than iron deficiency. Normal ferritin levels would rule out iron deficiency, and normal red cell distribution width would be unusual in established iron deficiency where anisocytosis (variation in red cell size) is typically present.

---

questions.stem: A 10-month-old exclusively breastfed infant is being evaluated for iron supplementation. The infant was born at term with appropriate birth weight and is exclusively breastfed without any complementary foods. At what age should iron supplementation be started in exclusively breastfed infants?
questions.initialExplanation: For an exclusively breastfed infant: start iron supplementation from 4 months of age.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Exclusively breastfed infants should start iron supplementation at 4 months of age because breast milk contains insufficient iron to meet the growing infant's needs after this age. Breast milk iron concentration decreases over time while the infant's iron requirements increase due to rapid growth and expansion of blood volume. Early iron supplementation prevents the development of iron deficiency anemia, which can have long-term neurodevelopmental consequences.

Starting at 2 months may be too early for most infants and could interfere with breast milk feeding. Starting at 6 months may miss the critical period when iron stores are depleting. The 4-month timing

is supported by evidence showing optimal prevention of iron deficiency with minimal adverse effects on breastfeeding.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy presents with sudden onset of fatigue, dark urine, and yellow discoloration of eyes 2 days after starting trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for a urinary tract infection. Examination shows marked pallor and jaundice. Lab results: Hb 7.5 g/dL, reticulocytes 12%, and urine positive for blood. What peripheral blood smear finding is most characteristic of this condition?
questions.initialExplanation: Hemolytic anemia after TMP-SMX: G6PD deficiency; the characteristic smear shows bite cells and Heinz bodies.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This patient presents with classic G6PD deficiency triggered by sulfonamide exposure, manifesting as acute hemolytic anemia with dark urine (hemoglobinuria), jaundice, and marked pallor. The characteristic peripheral blood smear findings in G6PD deficiency during hemolytic episodes include bite cells (red cells with missing portions that appear as if bitten) and Heinz bodies (precipitated hemoglobin inclusions seen with supravital stains). These morphological changes result from oxidative damage to red blood cells lacking adequate G6PD enzyme activity.

Sickle cells are characteristic of sickle cell anemia, target cells are seen in various conditions including thalassemia and liver disease, spherocytes suggest hereditary spherocytosis, and nucleated red blood cells indicate severe anemia or bone marrow stress.

---

questions.stem: A newborn male develops jaundice on day 3 of life. The pregnancy was uncomplicated, and the baby was born at term weighing 3.2 kg. Examination reveals moderate jaundice without hepatosplenomegaly. Total bilirubin is 15 mg/dL with direct fraction of 0.8 mg/ dL. What is the most likely enzymatic deficiency causing this presentation?
questions.initialExplanation: Neonatal jaundice with G6PD deficiency (hemolysis without organomegaly): deficiency of the enzyme glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This newborn male presents with jaundice on day 3 of life, which is a common presentation of GGPD deficiency in the neonatal period. G6PD deficiency is the most common red blood cell enzyme deficiency and can cause significant neonatal jaundice, particularly in the first few days of life. The absence of hepatosplenomegaly and the timing of presentation (day 3) are consistent with G6PD deficiency rather than other conditions.

Pyruvate kinase deficiency typically presents later in infancy or childhood. Hexokinase deficiency is very rare. Glucocerebrosidase deficiency causes Gaucher's disease, which presents with organomegaly and other systemic symptoms. Galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase deficiency causes galactosemia with jaundice, hepatomegaly, and cataracts.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy with known G6PD deficiency develops sudden dark cola-colored urine after eating fava beans at a family dinner. He becomes lethargic and has decreased urine output. Laboratory studies show Hb 8.2 g/dL, elevated creatinine (2.1 mg/dL), and urine positive for hemoglobin but no red blood cells. What is the most appropriate acute management to prevent renal complications?
questions.initialExplanation: The source's answer is A (mannitol), but a note on the page says hydration is the current first-line and mannitol is not advised; check the original.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This patient with G6PD deficiency has developed hemoglobinuria (cola-colored urine positive for hemoglobin but no red blood cells) and elevated creatinine (2.1 mg/dL), indicating acute kidney injury secondary to hemoglobinuria. Hemoglobin released from hemolyzed red cells can precipitate in renal tubules, leading to acute renal failure. Mannitol, an osmotic diuretic, helps prevent tubular obstruction by promoting diuresis and flushing out hemoglobin from the renal tubules.

Hemodialysis is reserved for severe, refractory cases. Chelation therapy is not indicated for hemoglobin toxicity. Oral fluid intake alone may be insufficient in a lethargic child. Vitamin C could actually worsen hemolysis in G6PD deficiency.

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy with known G6PD deficiency develops acute hemolysis after receiving treatment for malaria with primaquine. His hemoglobin drops from 13.5 g/dL to 9.8 g/dL over 48 hours. The child appears stable without signs of cardiovascular compromise. What is the expected timeline for spontaneous recovery of hemoglobin levels?
questions.initialExplanation: After acute G6PD hemolysis Hb recovers spontaneously within about 3-6 weeks once the trigger is removed (per the given answer).
questions.detailedExplanation:
In G6PD deficiency, acute hemolytic episodes are typically self-limiting and resolve spontaneously as the older, more deficient red blood cells are destroyed and replaced by younger red blood cells with ’    higher enzyme activity levels. The hemoglobin levels typically recover to baseline within 3-6 weeks, even without continued exposure to the triggering agent. This recovery pattern is characteristic of G6PD deficiency and reflects the physiological mechanism where young red blood cells have relatively preserved enzyme activity. Shorter timeframes (1-2 weeks) are insufficient for complete recovery. Longer timeframes (8 weeks to 1 year) are unnecessary as the natural recovery occurs within the 3-6 week window. The child's stability without cardiovascular compromise supports expectant management.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old girl is being evaluated for possible G6PD deficiency because her older brother was recently diagnosed. The family wants to know the inheritance pattern and likelihood of the girl being affected. What is the inheritance pattern of G6PD deficiency?
questions.initialExplanation: G6PD deficiency is X-linked recessive (males are more affected).
questions.detailedExplanation:
G6PD deficiency follows an X-linked recessive inheritance pattern, meaning the gene is located on the X chromosome. Males are more commonly affected (1 in 10-14 males) because they have only one X chromosome, while females are typically carriers with 50% normal enzyme activity and rarely develop symptomatic disease. Males with an affected mother have a 50% chance of being affected, while daughters of affected males are obligate carriers.

Autosomal recessive inheritance would affect both males and females equally. Autosomal dominant inheritance shows vertical transmission pattern that doesn't fit. X-linked dominant inheritance would affect all female carriers, which is not seen in G6PD deficiency. Mitochondrial inheritance shows maternal transmission only.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy with G6PD deficiency develops fever and hemolysis during an episode of viral gastroenteritis. His hemoglobin drops to 8.5 g/dL, but he remains hemodynamically stable. The mother asks about the mechanism behind the hemolysis during infections. What is the primary mechanism of hemolysis in G6PD deficiency during infections?

options.label: A
options.text: Direct viral destruction of red blood cells

options.label: E
options.text: Oxidative stress from reactive oxygen species

questions.initialExplanation: Mechanism: oxidative stress from reactive oxygen species during infection.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Infections can trigger hemolysis in G6PD deficiency through oxidative stress mechanisms. During infections, the body produces increased amounts of reactive oxygen species (ROS) as part of the

’    immune response. In normal red blood cells, G6PD enzyme activity helps maintain glutathione in its reduced form, which neutralizes ROS and protects cellular integrity. However, in G6PD-deficient cells, this protective mechanism is impaired, leading to oxidative damage of hemoglobin and membrane proteins, resulting in hemolysis. The mechanism is not direct viral destruction, immune-mediated damage, mechanical trauma from fever, or hypoxia-induced damage. The oxidative stress is the primary pathophysiological mechanism linking infections to hemolysis in G6PD deficiency.

---

questions.stem: A 13-month-old girl presented with progressive pallor for the last 3 months. The mother noticed that she started to eat a non-nutritive and dirty substance. She is on breast feeding till this age. On examination, she is pale, apathetic looking, no LAP, no organomegaly, and no skin bleeds. Of the following, the MOST likely diagnosis is:
questions.initialExplanation: Pallor with pica in a 13-month-old breastfed infant = iron deficiency anemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This infant's presentation is classic for iron deficiency anemia: progressive pallor at 13 months, pica (eating non-nutritive substances), and exclusive breastfeeding without iron supplementation. Breast milk is iron-poor, and fetal iron stores deplete by 6 months, placing exclusively breastfed infants at high risk without dietary iron fortification. Pica is a well-recognized behavioral manifestation of iron deficiency. The absence of lymphadenopathy, organomegaly, or bleeding argues against leukemia, aplastic anemia, or hemolytic disorders. Folic acid or B12 deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia with neurological or developmental features, not isolated pica. Vitamin E deficiency produces hemolysis, not this clinical picture.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy with G6PD deficiency is prescribed naproxen for knee pain. The pharmacist questions the prescription due to concerns about potential hemolysis. Which of the following medications is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency?
questions.initialExplanation: Aspirin is avoided in G6PD deficiency because it is an oxidant; paracetamol and steroids are usually safe.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Aspirin is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency because it belongs to the class of oxidant drugs that can trigger hemolytic episodes. Aspirin and other salicylates generate oxidative stress through various mechanisms, including inhibition of prostaglandin synthesis and direct hemoglobin oxidation. Even low doses of aspirin can precipitate significant hemolysis in individuals with G6PD deficiency. Acetaminophen (paracetamol) is generally safe at therapeutic doses in G6PD deficiency. Ibuprofen and naproxen are non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs that are typically considered safe, though high doses may be problematic. Prednisolone is a corticosteroid that does not have oxidant properties and is generally safe.

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy with known G6PD deficiency develops severe hemolysis after taking sulfonamides for pneumonia. His hemoglobin drops to 6.2 g/dL, and he shows signs of cardiovascular compromise with tachycardia and hypotension. The mother reports he has been compliant with avoiding oxidant drugs. What is the most appropriate emergency management?
questions.initialExplanation: Severe hemolysis with hypotension and tachycardia in G6PD: the given answer is emergency exchange transfusion.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child with G6PD deficiency has developed severe hemolysis with cardiovascular compromise (tachycardia, hypotension) and a critical hemoglobin level of 6.2 g/dL. Emergency exchange transfusion is indicated in life-threatening hemolytic anemia with cardiovascular instability. The procedure rapidly removes circulating hemoglobin and oxidized red blood cells while replacing them with normal red blood cells, providing immediate improvement in oxygen-carrying capacity and hemodynamics.

Methylprednisolone pulse therapy has no role in G6PD deficiency. Intravenous immunoglobulin is used in autoimmune hemolytic anemia, not G6PD deficiency. Continuous renal replacement therapy is

for renal failure without hemolysis. Antibiotics would be indicated only if there is evidence of infection, which is not mentioned.
