questions.stem: A 18-month-old toddler presents with failure to thrive and microcytic hypochromic anemia. Laboratory studies show: Hb 8.0 g/dL, MCV 62 fL, serum iron 25 ug/dL (normal 60-170), TIBC 450 pg/dL (normal 250-370), ferritin 8 ng/mL (normal 15-150). The child has a history of chronic diarrhea and poor weight gain. Which additional test would be most helpful to determine the underlying cause?
questions.initialExplanation: Hypochromic anemia with iron deficiency, chronic diarrhea and poor growth: suspect celiac disease, so request anti-transglutaminase antibodies.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This toddler presents with classic features of celiac disease causing refractory iron deficiency anemia: microcytic hypochromic anemia with extremely low ferritin (8 ng/mL), chronic diarrhea, failure to thrive, ’    and iron studies consistent with iron deficiency. Celiac disease is a common cause of treatment- resistant iron deficiency anemia in children due to malabsorption of iron in the damaged small intestinal mucosa. Anti-transglutaminase IgA antibodies are highly sensitive and specific for celiac disease and are the preferred screening test. Hemoglobin electrophoresis would be indicated if there was evidence of hemolysis. G6PD enzyme activity is not relevant to iron deficiency. Bone marrow biopsy is invasive and unnecessary for this presentation. Abdominal CT scan would expose the child to unnecessary radiation.

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old child with dark urine and pallor after a viral illness has the following laboratory results: Hb 8.2 g/dL, reticulocytes 8%, serum haptoglobin <25 mg/dL, and positive direct Coombs test. The child has no previous history of similar episodes. What is the most appropriate diagnostic approach to distinguish between G6PD deficiency and autoimmune hemolytic anemia?

options.label: A
options.text: Check for bite cells and Heinz bodies on peripheral smear

options.label: C
options.text: Order flow cytometry for CD55/CD59 expression

questions.initialExplanation: To differentiate G6PD from AIHA: the blood smear (bite cells and Heinz bodies) supports G6PD, and the direct Coombs is positive in AIHA.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child presents with acute hemolytic anemia and a positive direct Coombs test, which can occur in both autoimmune hemolytic anemia and G6PD deficiency. The presence of bite cells and Heinz bodies on peripheral smear is highly specific for G6PD deficiency during hemolytic episodes and can help differentiate it from autoimmune hemolytic anemia. G6PD deficiency can sometimes be associated with secondary autoimmune phenomena.

G6PD enzyme assay immediately may give misleading results during acute hemolysis. Flow cytometry for CD55/CD59 deficiency is for paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria. Complement levels are not specific for G6PD deficiency. Bone marrow biopsy is unnecessary.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy presents with two separate episodes of hemolytic anemia occurring 8 months apart. Both episodes were triggered by infections and resolved spontaneously within 3-4 weeks. Between episodes, the child appears completely healthy with normal hemoglobin levels. Examination during an asymptomatic period shows no organomegaly. What is the most cost-effective diagnostic test to confirm the suspected diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.text: Genetic testing for known G6PD mutations

questions.initialExplanation: Recurrent hemolytic episodes with infections and good health between episodes: the most suitable and cheapest test is G6PD enzyme activity.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child presents with recurrent episodes of hemolytic anemia triggered by infections that resolve spontaneously, consistent with G6PD deficiency. Between episodes, the child appears healthy with ’    normal hemoglobin levels, which is typical of G6PD deficiency. The history strongly suggests G6PD deficiency rather than other causes of hemolytic anemia. G6PD enzyme activity measurement is the most cost-effective and specific diagnostic test for G6PD deficiency, with good sensitivity and specificity. Genetic testing for known mutations is expensive and unnecessary for initial diagnosis. Flow cytometry for CD55/CD59 deficiency is for paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria. Hemoglobin electrophoresis is for hemoglobinopathies. Osmotic fragility test is for hereditary spherocytosis.

---


## Thalassemia | Hereditary Spherocytosis

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy presents with pallor, jaundice, and ill health. Laboratory findings: hemoglobin 8 g/dl, MCV 69 fl, MCHC 36%. Family history reveals an uncle underwent splenectomy. What is the most likely etiology of his anemia?
questions.initialExplanation: Jaundice and pallor with high MCHC (36%) and a relative who had splenectomy = a red cell membrane disorder (hereditary spherocytosis).
questions.detailedExplanation:
(Nelson & AAP Guidelines): The elevated MCHC (36%) is pathognomonic for hereditary spherocytosis, a red cell membrane disorder. According to Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics, hereditary spherocytosis typically presents in early childhood with hemolytic anemia, jaundice, and splenomegaly. The microcytic anemia (MCV 69 fl) results from membrane loss leading to spherocyte formation. Family history of splenectomy is common in severe cases. The AAP emphasizes that MCHC >36% is a key diagnostic criterion, differentiating it from other hemolytic anemias like thalassemia or G6PD deficiency

---

questions.stem: A 9-month-old infant presents with pallor and hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory findings: hemoglobin 6.2 g/dl, hypochromic microcytic anemia with many target cells on blood smear. Hemoglobin electrophoresis shows: Hb F 90%, Hb A 6%, Hb A2 4%. What is the most appropriate curative treatment?
questions.initialExplanation: Very high HbF with hepatosplenomegaly in an infant (beta-thalassemia major): the curative treatment is matched allogeneic bone marrow transplant.
questions.detailedExplanation:
(Nelson & AAP Guidelines): The hemoglobin electrophoresis pattern (Hb F 90%, Hb A 6%, Hb A2 4%) is diagnostic for B-thalassemia major. Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics and AAP guidelines consistently identify allogenic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation as the only curative therapy for B-thalassemia major. This replaces the defective hematopoietic stem cells with healthy donor cells. While regular transfusions and iron chelation are essential for management, they are supportive rather than curative. Splenectomy may reduce transfusion requirements but does not address the underlying genetic defect. Early transplantation (ideally before age 2) provides the best outcomes .

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy with sickle cell disease develops increasing pallor over a few hours, with significant splenomegaly on examination. Laboratory findings: hemoglobin 3.2 g/dl, WBC 8, 400/cmm, platelets 167,000/cmm, reticulocyte count 8%. Select the most likely complication that explains his condition:
questions.initialExplanation: A sickle cell child with sudden pallor, massive splenomegaly, Hb 3.2 and high retics = splenic sequestration crisis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
(Nelson & AAP Guidelines): This presentation is classic for splenic sequestration crisis in a young child with sickle cell disease. According to Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics, splenic sequestration occurs most commonly in children aged 5 months to 5 years (before splenic autoinfarction). The AAP emphasizes that sudden enlargement of the spleen with rapid decrease in hemoglobin (>2 g/dl drop) is diagnostic. The elevated reticulocyte count (8%) indicates active bone marrow compensation. Unlike aplastic crisis (which shows low reticulocytes) or hyperhemolytic crisis (which typically shows jaundice and elevated bilirubin), splenic sequestration is characterized by splenomegaly and rapid blood pooling in the spleen

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child is found to have mild pallor during a routine exam. Labs show Hb 10.5 g/dL with microcytic, hypochromic anemia, and hemoglobin electrophoresis confirms B-thalassemia trait. What is the most appropriate management for this child?

options.label: B
options.text: Avoid sports as it will affect the general health

options.label: C
options.text: Administer folic acid supplementation to support red blood cell production

options.label: D
options.text: Monitor the child regularly and no specific treatment is necessary

options.label: E
options.text: Start chelation therapy to prevent iron overload

questions.initialExplanation: Beta-thalassemia trait in an asymptomatic child: periodic follow-up only; no treatment and no chelation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Beta-thalassemia trait is a benign carrier state characterized by mild microcytic hypochromic anemia without clinical symptoms or complications. No specific treatment is required, as these children have normal growth, development, and life expectancy. Routine monitoring during well-child visits suffices to ensure stable hemoglobin and address any parental concerns. Iron supplementation should be avoided unless iron deficiency is confirmed by low ferritin, as unnecessary iron can accumulate over time. Folic acid supplementation is reserved for thalassemia intermedia or major with increased erythropoiesis, not for the trait. Dietary iron restriction, activity limitation, and chelation therapy are inappropriate and potentially harmful. Genetic counseling should be offered to discuss inheritance patterns and implications for future family planning.

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy presents with fatigue, pallor, and jaundice. His parents note similar episodes since infancy, often triggered by infections. Examination reveals splenomegaly. Labs show Hb 9.5 g/dL, MCV 85 fL, MCHC 38 pg, reticulocyte count 15%, and bilirubin 3.5 mg/dL. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Hemolytic episodes triggered by infection, splenomegaly, high MCHC and retics 15% = hereditary spherocytosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child presents with chronic hemolytic anemia (jaundice, reticulocytosis, elevated bilirubin), splenomegaly, and a notably elevated MCHC (38 g/dL). The high MCHC is a hallmark finding in Hereditary Spherocytosis (HS) caused by red cell membrane dehydration and loss of surface area. The history of episodes since infancy supports a congenital etiology rather than acquired autoimmune hemolytic anemia. G6PD deficiency typically presents with episodic hemolysis triggered by oxidants but lacks splenomegaly and elevated MCHC. Thalassemias and iron deficiency cause microcytosis with low MCHC. Confirmatory tests include eosin-5- maleimide (EMA) binding or osmotic fragility testing, and management involves folate supplementation and potential splenectomy for severe cases.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy is evaluated for chronic anemia. He has had recurrent episodes of fever and painful hand and foot swelling but has never needed a transfusion. Exam shows pallor and mild splenomegaly. Growth and facial features are normal. Which finding best distinguishes his condition from other chronic hemolytic anemias?

options.label: E
options.text: History of hand and foot swelling

questions.initialExplanation: Hand-foot syndrome (dactylitis) distinguishes sickle cell disease from other chronic hemolytic anemias.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The history of painful hand and foot swelling (dactylitis or "hand-foot syndrome") is pathognomonic for sickle cell disease in young children and best distinguishes it from other chronic hemolytic anemias. Dactylitis results from vaso-occlusion of the small bones of the hands and feet by sickled erythrocytes, typically presenting between 6 months and 2 years of age. Mild pallor (A) and splenomegaly (B) are non-specific findings common to many hemolytic anemias including hereditary spherocytosis and thalassemia. Normal growth pattern (C) and facial features (D) help exclude severe thalassemia major (which causes growth failure and characteristic facies) but are not positive diagnostic indicators.

---

questions.stem: On a routine-screening CBC, a 1-year-old is noted to have a microcytic anemia. A follow-up hemoglobin electrophoresis demonstrates an increased concentration of hemoglobin A2. The child is most likely to have which of the following?
questions.initialExplanation: Microcytic anemia with raised HbA2 = beta-thalassemia trait.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The concentration of hemoglobin A2 is increased in p-thalassemia trait (also called B-thalassemia minor). Patients have a single abnormal gene for the -globin component of hemoglobin; they do not typically have problems aside from a mild microcytic anemia. It is important to distinguish between 3- thalassemia trait and the more common iron deficiency anemia, as iron is not useful to patients with B-thalassemia trait. In severe iron deficiency, hemoglobin A2 may be decreased. In mild to moderate iron deficiency, the level of hemoglobin A2 is normal. The level is also normal in sickle-cell anemia, chronic systemic illness, and lead poisoning.

---

questions.stem: A neonate’s blood differs from that of older children and adults in many respects. Which of the following correctly describes a characteristic that is particular to the neonate?

options.label: A
options.text: The RBC of the neonate has a low MCV that increases as the patient ages.

options.label: B
options.text: Newborns have a high hemoglobin concentration that declines over the first 2 days of life.

options.label: C
options.text: Neonatal RBCs contain primarily embryonic hemoglobin.

options.label: D
options.text: Newborn blood has higher oxygen affinity than that of a 1-year-old.

options.label: E
options.text: The neonate has higher levels of protein C than a 1- year- old.

questions.initialExplanation: Newborn blood has HbF, which has higher oxygen affinity than the blood of a one-year-old.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Fetal hemoglobin has higher oxygen affinity than hemoglobin A. Newborn RBCs have high levels of fetal hemoglobin (a2y2) —approaching 70%. After birth, the percentage of fetal hemoglobin decreases after synthesis of y-globin is replaced by -globin synthesis. At 4 months of age fetal hemoglobin accounts for 40% of the total hemoglobin, and by 1 year of age, hemoglobin A (0232) is predominant—98%. The higher oxygen affinity of fetal hemoglobin is due to its relative decrease in affinity for 2,3-bisphosphogylcerate (2,3-BPG) compared with HbA. The RBC of the neonate has a high MCV (on average 107 fL) that decreases in the first year of life, and then rises with age. Newborns have a high hemoglobin level that then rises in the first 2 days of life as plasma volume initially decreases postnatally. Protein C levels are low at birth and rise with age, reaching adult levels by adolescence.

---

questions.stem: You are evaluating a 4-year-old child with B-thalassemia major; he is on chronic transfusion therapy since the age of 1 year; you suspect transfusion-induced hemosiderosis. Of the following, the organ that is LEAST likely to be affected by iron deposition at this time is :
questions.initialExplanation: In beta-thalassemia major on early transfusions: the liver, pancreas and endocrine glands are affected by iron deposition; the heart is the least affected at this early stage (per the source).
questions.detailedExplanation:
In transfusion-induced hemosiderosis, iron deposition follows a specific temporal sequence. The liver is invariably the first organ affected, serving as the primary storage site. Endocrine glands (pituitary, thyroid, pancreas) are highly susceptible to oxidative stress from iron, and dysfunction (such as growth failure or hypothyroidism) can manifest in childhood. In contrast, significant cardiac iron deposition typically accumulates later in the disease course, often becoming clinically evident in adolescence or young adulthood rather than early childhood. While cardiac siderosis is the leading cause of mortality, a 4-year-old with ~3 years of transfusions is least likely to have significant cardiac involvement compared to the liver and endocrine organs. Regular monitoring with ferritin and MRI T2* guides chelation therapy to prevent eventual cardiac toxicity.

---

questions.stem: Although sickle hemoglobin is present only in red blood cells, patients with sickle cell anemia are at risk of having multiple organs damaged as a consequence of either hemolysis or vaso-occlusion arising from sickled RBCs. Which of the following studies is routinely performed to assess the likelihood of damage to a target organ?

options.label: A
options.text: Audiology examination to assess the risk of hearing loss

options.label: B
options.text: Renal ultrasound to assess the risk of hyposthenuria

options.label: C
options.text: Bone density scan to assess bone damage from vasoocclusive crises

options.label: D
options.text: Chest radiograph to assess the risk of pulmonary hypertension

options.label: E
options.text: Transcranial Doppler ultrasound to assess the risk of stroke

questions.initialExplanation: To assess stroke risk in sickle cell patients, transcranial Doppler ultrasound is done routinely.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Hemolysis and vaso-occlusion are the 2 main causes of complications from sickle cell disease (SCD). Transcranial Doppler ultrasounds are used to screen for sickle cell patients who are at increased risk of stroke. Clinical strokes occur in 11% of patients with SCD by the age of 18 years if they do not receive primary stroke prophylaxis and of those patients who have a clinically overt stroke, 50% to 90% have an additional stroke. Transcranial Dopplers are used to detect stenosis in the major cerebral arteries. Children with stenosis begin chronic transfusions to maintain their HbS concentration at less than 30% to decrease their stroke risk.

---

questions.stem: You are counseling a father about the treatment options for his child with B-thalassemia major. In addition to the increased risk of infection, splenectomized patients are at an increased risk of which of the following?
questions.initialExplanation: After splenectomy in beta-thalassemia the risk of thrombosis rises (besides infection).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Splenomegaly can be a complication of chronic transfusions, which is the mainstay of treatment for thalassemia major. Chronic transfusions can decrease extramedullary hematopoiesis and prolong and improve quality of life. However, patients who develop splenomegaly have an increased transfusion requirement due to the associated hypersplenism and increased RBC clearance. As a result, splenectomy can be recommended. It is well known that asplenic patients are at higher risk of infection from encapsulated organisms, and should be immunized prior to splenectomy. However, these patients are also at higher risk for thrombosis and pulmonary hypertension. There is no known association between splenectomy and renal failure, malignancy, aplastic anemia, or increased bleeding.

---

questions.stem: A 6-month-old infant who was normal at birth begins to develop progressive pallor, poor feeding, and failure to thrive. Physical examination reveals hepatosplenomegaly and frontal bossing. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin 4 g/dL with microcytic hypochromic anemia and elevated HbF levels. Which form of thalassemia is most likely in this presentation?
questions.initialExplanation: An infant with pallor, hepatosplenomegaly, frontal bossing and Hb 4 with high HbF = beta-thalassemia major.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Beta-thalassemia major (Cooley's anemia) presents between 3-6 months of age when fetal hemoglobin (HbF) production naturally declines, exposing the deficiency in beta-globin chain synthesis. At birth, infants appear normal because HbF does not contain beta chains. The presentation includes severe anemia (Hb 2-8 g/dL), hepatosplenomegaly, and characteristic facial changes (frontal bossing, maxillary hyperplasia) due to bone marrow expansion. The pathophysiology involves ineffective erythropoiesis in the bone marrow combined with peripheral hemolysis, leading to the need for regular blood transfusions. This distinguishes it from beta- thalassemia intermedia, which presents later with milder symptoms and may not require regular transfusions.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child presents with microcytic anemia, and hemoglobin electrophoresis shows HbA2 6.5% and HbF 15%. The child is asymptomatic with no hepatosplenomegaly. Both parents have mild microcytic anemia on screening. What is the most appropriate diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: HbA2 6.5% in an asymptomatic child with parents who have mild anemia = beta-thalassemia minor (trait).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Beta-thalassemia minor (trait) is characterized by heterozygous mutations in one beta-globin gene, resulting in mild microcytic anemia (Hb typically 10-12 g/dL) without significant symptoms or organ involvement. The diagnostic feature is elevated HbA2 levels >4% (typically 4-7% in >90% of cases), which distinguishes it from iron deficiency anemia where HbA2 remains normal. The family screening showing microcytic anemia in both parents supports the autosomal recessive inheritance pattern. The elevated HbF (up to 10%) is also common in beta-thalassemia trait but is less specific than HbA2 elevation. This condition requires differentiation from iron deficiency using iron studies (which are normal in thalassemia trait), and hemoglobin electrophoresis remains the definitive diagnostic test.

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old child with beta-thalassemia major has been receiving regular transfusions. The medical team decides to initiate iron chelation therapy. The child has received 12 units of packed red blood cells. When is iron chelation therapy typically initiated in thalassemia patients?

options.label: B
options.text: At diagnosis regardless of transfusion history

options.label: D
options.text: Only when iron overload symptoms appear

questions.initialExplanation: Iron chelation usually starts after 10-15 transfusions (or when ferritin is high).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Iron chelation therapy should be initiated after 10-15 transfusions or when serum ferritin levels consistently exceed 1000 ng/mL to prevent iron accumulation and subsequent organ damage. Early

’    initiation is crucial because iron-mediated organ damage is largely irreversible once established. Waiting for symptoms of iron overload to appear is inappropriate as cardiac and endocrine damage may already be present. The 10-15 transfusion threshold represents approximately 2-3 years of regular transfusion therapy in most patients, providing adequate time for iron stores to accumulate significantly. Current guidelines emphasize that ferritin monitoring every 3 months is essential, and chelation should be started before iron overload becomes clinically apparent.

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old child presents with progressive pallor and failure to thrive. He was normal at birth but developed symptoms around 6 months of age. Examination reveals marked pallor, hepatosplenomegaly, and facial bone changes. Laboratory results show Hb 6.8 g/ dL, MCV 45 fL, MCH 18 pg, and peripheral smear with nucleated RBCs, target cells, and basophilic stippling. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Severe anemia, hepatosplenomegaly, facial bone changes, target cells and nucleated RBCs = beta-thalassemia major.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child presents with the classic presentation of beta-thalassemia major, which typically becomes apparent between 3-6 months when fetal hemoglobin (HbF) production declines and adult hemoglobin (HbA) production should begin. The findings of severe microcytic hypochromic anemia (MCV 45fL), hepatosplenomegaly, and bone changes are characteristic. The peripheral smear showing nucleated RBCs, target cells, and basophilic stippling is also typical. Beta-thalassemia minor would present with mild anemia and be essentially asymptomatic. Iron deficiency would show elevated iron-binding capacity and low ferritin. Sickle cell anemia presents with vaso-occlusive episodes and sickle-shaped cells. Hereditary spherocytosis shows spherocytes with normal MCV and elevated MCHC.

---

questions.stem: A 6-month-old infant with known beta-thalassemia major has been receiving regular blood transfusions every 4 weeks. His parents ask about iron chelation therapy. He has received 12 transfusions so far. Current Hb is 11.2 g/dL on transfusion. What is the appropriate timing and choice for iron chelation therapy?

options.label: A
options.text: Start deferasirox immediately, as he has received >10 transfusions

options.label: B
options.text: Continue monitoring until he reaches 10 years of age

options.label: D
options.text: Chelation is not needed if transfusions are regular

options.label: E
options.text: Start oral deferasirox after 5 years of age

questions.initialExplanation: The source's answer: start deferasirox early after more than 10 transfusions, per its criteria (taking age and dose into account).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Iron chelation therapy should be initiated after 10-15 units of blood have been transfused to prevent iron overload complications. This infant has received 12 transfusions, making him eligible for

’    chelation. Deferasirox (Exjade) is preferred over deferoxamine in children as it's oral, has fewer side effects, and improves compliance compared to subcutaneous deferoxamine infusions. Starting at 10 years or 5 years is too late and risks iron overload complications. Waiting until 15-20 transfusions delays necessary therapy. Chelation is essential regardless of transfusion frequency to prevent iron-mediated organ damage.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child with beta-thalassemia major shows radiographic changes described as "hair-on-end appearance" on skull X-ray. His mother is concerned about bone changes and asks about the mechanism. What is the primary mechanism responsible for these bone changes?

options.label: A
options.text: Bone marrow infiltration by malignant cells

options.label: D
options.text: Chronic hypoxia leading to compensatory bone marrow expansion

questions.initialExplanation: "Hair-on-end" changes result from compensatory marrow expansion due to chronic hypoxia and increased erythropoiesis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
In beta-thalassemia major, the combination of ineffective erythropoiesis and chronic hemolytic anemia leads to severe hypoxia. This stimulates compensatory expansion of bone marrow in the skull and other bones, causing cortical thinning, bossing, and the characteristic "hair-on-end" appearance on X-ray. This is the body's attempt to increase red blood cell production despite the underlying defect.

The changes are not due to direct invasion, iron deposition (which affects other organs more), steroid therapy, or direct genetic effects on bone.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child with beta-thalassemia major develops worsening hepatomegaly, cardiac arrhythmias, and delayed growth despite regular transfusions and chelation therapy. Family asks about curative treatment options. What is the most successful curative treatment option for beta-thalassemia major?

options.label: A
options.text: Repeated blood transfusions with irradiated blood products

options.label: C
options.text: Bone marrow transplantation from matched sibling donor

questions.initialExplanation: The most successful cure in beta-thalassemia major is bone marrow transplant from a matched sibling.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is the only established curative treatment for beta- thalassemia major. With matched sibling donors, survival rates exceed 90%, and many patients achieve complete cure. However, this requires an HLA-matched donor and carries transplant-related risks.

Gene therapy is still experimental. Continued transfusions and chelation are supportive but not curative. Splenectomy helps reduce transfusion requirements but doesn't cure the underlying disorder. Folic acid supplementation is supportive but not curative.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child is found to have microcytic hypochromic anemia on routine screening. Hb is 10.2 g/dL, MCV 68 fL, with normal iron studies and normal hemoglobin electrophoresis. Both parents are carriers of beta-thalassemia trait. What hemoglobin electrophoresis pattern would be expected?
questions.initialExplanation: Beta-thalassemia trait: raised HbA2 (about 8%), predominant HbA and normal or mildly raised HbF.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This pattern is characteristic of beta-thalassemia minor (trait), where there is mild elevation of HbA2 (usually >4%) with normal or slightly reduced HbA and normal HbF levels. The mild anemia and microcytosis with normal iron studies confirm beta-thalassemia trait rather than iron deficiency. High HbF levels suggest beta-thalassemia major. Normal HbA2 would suggest alphathalassemia or other causes. The pattern with very high HbA2 and normal HbA suggests different variants.

---

questions.stem: A 9-month-old infant presents with severe anemia, jaundice, and hepatosplenomegaly. Hemoglobin electrophoresis shows HbF 85%, HbA 10%, HbA2 5%. The parents report the child was normal at birth but deteriorated around 6 months. What additional laboratory finding would be most confirmatory for the diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.text: Elevated serum iron and ferritin levels

options.label: C
options.text: Family history of beta-thalassemia in both parents

questions.initialExplanation: An infant with HbF 85% and onset around 6 months: beta-thalassemia major; recessive inheritance with carrier parents supports it.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The clinical presentation and hemoglobin electrophoresis pattern are highly suggestive of beta4 / 17 Thalassemia major. Confirmation comes from genetic testing showing mutations in both beta-globin genes, which would be confirmed by family studies showing both parents are carriers (beta- thalassemia trait).

Elevated iron studies suggest iron overload but don't confirm the diagnosis. Osmotic fragility test is for hereditary spherocytosis. High reticulocyte count might suggest hemolysis but isn't specific. Coombs test would suggest autoimmune hemolysis.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child presents with jaundice and splenomegaly. Laboratory results show Hb 9.8 g/dL, MCV 88 fL, MCHC 38 g/dL (elevated), and peripheral smear shows numerous spherocytes. Reticulocyte count is 12%. What is the inheritance pattern of this condition?
questions.initialExplanation: Hereditary spherocytosis is autosomal dominant in most cases.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Hereditary spherocytosis is most commonly inherited as an autosomal dominant disorder, though approximately 25% of cases result from new mutations. The condition affects membrane proteins (spectrin or ankyrin) responsible for red blood cell shape and deformability, leading to premature destruction in the spleen.

X-linked patterns don't apply to this condition. Autosomal recessive inheritance is less common. Mitochondrial inheritance shows maternal transmission only. The family history and inheritance pattern are important for genetic counseling.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old child with hereditary spherocytosis develops sudden severe pallor, lethargy, and decreased urine output following a viral illness. Laboratory results show Hb 5.2 g/dL with reticulocyte count of 0.5% (markedly decreased). What is the most likely diagnosis and immediate management?

options.label: B
options.text: Iron deficiency due to chronic hemolysis; start iron therapy

options.label: D
options.text: Aplastic crisis due to parvovirus B19; supportive care and transfusion if needed

options.label: E
options.text: DIC due to infection; start heparin

questions.initialExplanation: An HS patient with severe pallor and very low retics after a viral infection: aplastic crisis from parvovirus B19; supportive care and transfusion if needed.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Parvovirus B19 infection causes temporary cessation of erythropoiesis in patients with chronic hemolytic anemias, leading to severe anemia with reticulocytopenia. The history of viral illness followed by severe anemia with low reticulocytes is classic. Supportive care with transfusion if hemodynamically unstable is the treatment of choice.

Splenic sequestration causes increased splenic pooling with high reticulocytes. Autoimmune

hemolysis would show positive Coombs test. Iron deficiency would show Low iron studies. DIC doesn't fit the clinical picture.

---

questions.stem: A 10-year-old child with hereditary spherocytosis has persistent severe hemolysis (Hb 8.5 g/dL, reticulocytes 18%) despite folic acid supplementation. The spleen is enlarged 6 cm below costal margin. The child has had two previous aplastic crises. What is the most appropriate management option?

options.label: C
options.text: Increase folic acid dose to 5 mg daily

questions.initialExplanation: Severe HS with ongoing hemolysis, aplastic crises and a large spleen: splenectomy is the most suitable option.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Splenectomy is indicated in hereditary spherocytosis when there is severe hemolysis (Hb <10 g/dL), evidence of hypersplenism, recurrent aplastic crises, poor growth, or when other complications are present. This child meets multiple criteria for splenectomy. The procedure is usually recommended after 6 years of age.

Conservative management isn't appropriate given the severity. Higher-dose folic acid won't address the underlying splenic destruction. Iron chelation is for iron overload, not indicated here. Regular transfusions aren't first-line therapy.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy presents with intermittent jaundice, fatigue, and a history of gallstones identified on ultrasound. His mother reports that he has required hospital admission twice for “very low blood” following viral illnesses. On exam, he has mild splenomegaly. CBC reveals Hb 9.8 g/dL, normal MCV, and elevated MCHC (37 g/dL). Reticulocyte count is 12%. Peripheral smear shows small, dense RBCs lacking central pallor. Osmotic fragility testing is positive. What is the underlying defect?

options.label: A
options.text: Glutamic acid — valine substitution in 3-globin chain

options.label: B
options.text: Deficiency of spectrin or ankyrin in RBC cytoskeleton

questions.initialExplanation: HS: a defect in cytoskeletal proteins (spectrin or ankyrin) causes spherocytes and osmotic fragility.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Hereditary spherocytosis (HS) is an autosomal dominant RBC membrane disorder caused by mutations in spectrin, ankyrin, band 3, or protein 4.2, leading to loss of membrane surface area and

’     formation of non-deformable spherocytes that are trapped and destroyed in the spleen. Key findings include normocytic anemia, high MCHC, reticulocytosis, spherocytes on smear, gallstones, and aplastic crises triggered by Parvovirus B19. Option A describes sickle cell disease; C is a- thalassemia; D is G6PD deficiency (causes episodic hemolysis after oxidant stress); E is warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia. Osmotic fragility is classically increased in HS, though not highly specific

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old child with sickle cell anemia presents with sudden abdominal pain, vomiting, and marked pallor. Examination reveals a rapidly enlarging spleen and hypotension. Laboratory results show Hb 5.8 g/dL (drop of 3.2 g/dL from baseline). What is the most likely diagnosis and emergency management?

options.label: A
options.text: Aplastic crisis; supportive care and observation

options.label: B
options.text: Acute chest syndrome; oxygen and antibiotics

options.label: C
options.text: Vaso-occlusive crisis; hydration and pain control

options.label: D
options.text: Splenic sequestration; urgent transfusion and stabilization

questions.initialExplanation: Sickle cell anemia with a rapidly enlarging spleen, hypotension and falling Hb: splenic sequestration; urgent transfusion and stabilization.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Splenic sequestration is a life-threatening complication characterized by rapid trapping of blood in the spleen, causing acute splenomegaly, sudden drop in hemoglobin (>2 g/dL from baseline), and potential cardiovascular collapse. Emergency transfusion and hemodynamic stabilization are required.

Aplastic crisis shows low reticulocytes, not high. Vaso-occlusive crisis wouldn't cause such rapid

spleen enlargement. Acute chest syndrome involves respiratory symptoms. Gallstone colic doesn't cause splenomegaly.
