questions.stem: A 10-year-old child with sickle cell anemia presents with fever (38.8°C), chest pain, and increasing dyspnea over 12 hours. Chest X-ray shows bilateral lower lobe infiltrates with small pleural effusion. Initial oxygen saturation is 88% on room air, improving to 93% on 4L O2. Laboratory: Hb 7.2 g/dL (baseline 8.5), WBC 18,000/uL with left shift, platelets 450,000/uL. Parent reports child has been non-compliant with hydroxyurea and recently had upper respiratory infection. What is the most appropriate immediate management and monitoring strategy?

options.label: B
options.text: Discharge with oral antibiotics and home oxygen

options.label: D
options.text: Immediate exchange transfusion without further workup

options.label: E
options.text: Admit for oxygen, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and exchange transfusion if HbS >50%

questions.initialExplanation: Acute chest syndrome in a sickle cell child (fever, dyspnea, infiltrate): admit with oxygen, broad antibiotics and exchange transfusion if HbS is >50%.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This presentation is classic acute chest syndrome, but the key factors are the child's non-compliance with hydroxyurea (increasing risk), initial Hb drop (suggesting hemolysis), and respiratory compromise. Indications for exchange transfusion include Hb <5 g/dL or HbS >50% in severe cases. Broad-spectrum antibiotics are essential given fever and consolidation. Simple transfusion may increase viscosity. CPAP has limited role in ACS. Prophylactic exchange without criteria isn't indicated. Discharge is unsafe given hypoxia and severe presentation.

---

questions.stem: A 9-month-old child with a hemoglobin concentration of 10 gm/dL and marked microcytosis; serum iron and total iron binding capacity are within normal limits; serum ferritin and hemoglobin electrophoresis are also normal. Of the following, the MOST likely diagnosis is :
questions.initialExplanation: Microcytic anemia with normal iron, ferritin and Hb electrophoresis: alpha-thalassemia trait.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has microcytic anemia with normal iron studies (serum iron, TIBC, ferritin) and normal hemoglobin electrophoresis, which is the classic diagnostic profile for a-thalassemia trait. In a-thalassemia, reduced a- globin chain production causes microcytosis and mild anemia, but routine electrophoresis is normal because there is no significant accumulation of abnormal hemoglobins (unlike B-thalassemia, which shows elevated HbAZ2). Iron deficiency is excluded by normal ferritin and iron studies. B-thalassemia minor is ruled out by the normal electrophoresis. Sideroblastic anemia typically shows elevated iron/ferritin and ring sideroblasts on marrow examination. Anemia of chronic disease usually presents with low serum iron, low TIBC, and normal/high ferritin, plus an underlying inflammatory condition. a-thalassemia trait requires no treatment, and recognition prevents unnecessary iron supplementation.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old with hereditary spherocytosis develops sudden pallor, tachycardia, and lethargy. Hb drops from 10 to 6 g/dL in 24 hours. Reticulocyte count is 0.5%. What is the most urgent intervention?
questions.initialExplanation: HS with an acute Hb drop and low retics (aplastic crisis): the priority is packed red cell transfusion.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This is an aplastic crisis due to parvovirus B19, causing reticulocytopenia and acute anemia. Transfusion is indicated for hemodynamic instability or Hb <6 g/dL. Folic acid is chronic therapy. Iron is contraindicated (risk of overload). Steroids are for autoimmune causes. Surgery is irrelevant acutely.

---

questions.stem: A 9-year-old child with sickle cell anemia presents with sudden onset severe headache, confusion, and right-sided weakness that began 6 hours ago. MRI shows acute left middle cerebral artery infarction. Neurological examination reveals receptive and expressive aphasia with right hemiparesis. Transcranial Doppler shows increased flow velocities consistent with cerebral vasculopathy. What is the most appropriate immediate management including specific HbS targets and duration of therapy?

options.label: A
options.text: Simple transfusion to raise Hb to 10 g/dL with neurological monitoring

options.label: B
options.text: Exchange transfusion to reduce HbS <30% for 1 year minimum

options.label: C
options.text: Thrombolytic therapy with tPA if within 4.5-hour window

options.label: D
options.text: Immediate craniotomy for decompression and hematoma evacuation

options.label: E
options.text: Start low-molecular-weight heparin with gradual transfusion support

questions.initialExplanation: Stroke in sickle cell anemia: exchange transfusion to lower HbS below 30%, continued for at least a year.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Ischemic stroke in sickle cell disease requires aggressive reduction of HbS to <30% (not 50%) to prevent recurrent events. Exchange transfusion is preferred over simple transfusion to avoid hyperviscosity. The 1-year minimum duration is based on evidence showing continued high recurrence risk during the first year post-stroke. Simple transfusion risks hyperviscosity and inadequate HbS reduction. Thrombolytics are contraindicated in sickle cell stroke due to bleeding risk. Craniotomy isn't indicated for ischemic stroke. Heparin may worsen hemorrhagic transformation.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child presents with microcytic hypochromic anemia. Laboratory results: Hb 8.5 g/dL, MCV 62 fL, RBC 6.2 million/uL (elevated), serum ferritin 45 ng/mL (normal), TIBC 280 ug/dL (normal), RDW 12% (normal), serum iron 85 pg/dL (normal). Mentzer index is 10, and red cell distribution width is normal. Family history reveals father's MCV is 68 fL. What is the most likely diagnosis and what would hemoglobin electrophoresis likely show?

options.label: A
options.text: Alpha-thalassemia minor; normal electrophoresis with elevated HbA2 >3.5%

options.label: B
options.text: Iron deficiency anemia; normal electrophoresis with low serum ferritin

options.label: C
options.text: Beta-thalassemia minor; elevated HbA2 >3.5% and normal HbF

options.label: D
options.text: Alpha-thalassemia trait; normal electrophoresis pattern with target cells

options.label: E
options.text: Chronic disease anemia; normal electrophoresis with elevated inflammatory markers

questions.initialExplanation: Hypochromic anemia with normal iron and low Mentzer index: beta-thalassemia minor with HbA2 above 3.5%.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The combination of microcytic hypochromic anemia with preserved RBC count (elevated for degree of anemia), low Mentzer index (<13), normal iron studies, and family history of microcytosis strongly suggests beta-thalassemia trait. Hb electrophoresis would show elevated HbA2 >3.5% (normal 2.0-

3.2%) with normal HbF. Alpha-thalassemia shows normal Hb electrophoresis. Iron deficiency shows low ferritin and high TIBC. Both cause similar microcytosis but different red cell indices and electrophoresis patterns. Chronic disease shows elevated inflammatory markers.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy presents with jaundice and fatigue. His mother reports he had a recent viral illness and now appears “very pale.” Exam reveals mild splenomegaly. Labs: Hb 5.8 g/dL (baseline 10 g/dL), reticulocyte count 1%, indirect bilirubin 5.2 mg/dL, MCHC 38 g/dL. Peripheral smear shows microspherocytes. What is the most likely cause of his acute anemia?
questions.initialExplanation: HS with acute severe pallor and low retics after a viral infection: parvovirus B19-induced aplastic crisis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Hereditary spherocytosis (HS) is characterized by chronic hemolysis due to RBC membrane defects in spectrin/ankyrin. During aplastic crisis—often triggered by parvovirus B19, which suppresses erythropoiesis —the reticulocyte count drops acutely (<2%), leading to profound anemia despite ongoing hemolysis. High MCHC and spherocytes support HS. Other options: G6PD causes Heinz bodies, AIHA is Coombs-positive, iron deficiency shows low MCHC, and blood loss would not cause jaundice or spherocytes.

---

questions.stem: A newborn develops severe jaundice on day 2 of life requiring phototherapy. Family history reveals the father had “gallstones as a child.” Labs show indirect hyperbilirubinemia and spherocytes on blood smear. Which test is most confirmatory for hereditary spherocytosis in this infant?
questions.initialExplanation: To confirm HS in a newborn: osmotic fragility test.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Though osmotic fragility is not highly sensitive or specific, it remains a classic diagnostic test for HS, showing increased RBC lysis in hypotonic solutions. In neonates, HS can present as hemolytic disease of the newborn. Coombs test rules out immune causes (negative in HS). Electrophoresis is for hemoglobinopathies, G6PD for enzyme deficiency, and haptoglobin is low in all hemolytic anemias but not diagnostic.

---

questions.stem: A 8-year-old child with beta-thalassemia major develops severe abdominal pain, vomiting, and lethargy after missing several doses of deferasirox. Physical examination reveals icterus, hepatomegaly, and scleral jaundice. Laboratory studies show ALT 450 U/L, AST 380 U/L, total bilirubin 8.5 mg/dL, and INR 1.8. Which therapeutic intervention represents the MOST appropriate initial management?

options.label: A
options.text: Increase the deferasirox dose to the maximum

options.label: B
options.text: Dose reduction of deferasirox with continued monitoring

options.label: D
options.text: Temporary chelation cessation with supportive care

questions.initialExplanation: Acute liver failure after stopping deferasirox: the given answer is temporary cessation of the chelator with supportive care.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has severe deferasirox-induced hepatotoxicity with synthetic dysfunction (elevated INR, jaundice, symptoms), requiring immediate drug discontinuation per FDA black box warnings. Iron chelation can be safely paused for weeks without acute harm, as iron accumulation is chronic while acute liver failure is immediately life-threatening. Supportive care with close monitoring of LFTs and coagulation allows hepatic recovery before considering alternative chelation. Options A, B, and C are dangerous because continuing or adding chelators during acute liver injury risks progression to fulminant failure. Option E is premature since drug-induced liver injury typically reverses with prompt cessation. After complete normalization of liver function, switching to deferoxamine or deferiprone can be safely planned under hematology guidance. Always prioritize acute organ protection over chronic iron control in drug toxicity scenarios.

---

questions.stem: A 10-year-old child with sickle cell anemia presents with severe abdominal pain, vomiting, and distension. Physical examination reveals diffuse tenderness with guarding. Laboratory studies show Hb 7.5 g/dL, reticulocyte count 12%, and elevated lactate dehydrogenase. Abdominal X-ray shows multiple air-fluid levels. Which complication represents the MOST likely diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.text: Acute vaso-occlusive crisis affecting splanchnic circulation

questions.initialExplanation: Severe abdominal pain, distension and air-fluid levels in a sickle cell patient: acute vaso-occlusive crisis in the visceral circulation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Acute vaso-occlusive crisis affecting splanchnic circulation represents the most likely diagnosis in this child with sickle cell anemia and acute abdominal symptoms. Vasoocclusive crisis can affect any organ system, including the mesenteric circulation, causing abdominal pain, vomiting, and distension. The elevated lactate dehydrogenase suggests tissue ischemia and hemolysis. While appendicitis, mesenteric ischemia, volvulus, and splenic sequestration can occur in sickle cell disease, vaso- occlusive crisis is the most common cause of acute abdominal pain in these patients. The diffuse nature of the pain and absence of localized signs makes vaso-occlusive crisis more likely than surgical emergencies. Management includes aggressive hydration, pain control, and consideration for transfusion if symptoms worsen or hemoglobin drops significantly.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old with sickle cell anemia presents with severe bone pain in hands and feet (dactylitis). Examination shows swelling and tenderness. This represents which pathological process?

options.label: B
options.text: Vaso-occlusion of small vessels causing ischemia

options.label: E
options.text: Growth plate injury from chronic hypoxia

questions.initialExplanation: Dactylitis is caused by occlusion of small vessels leading to ischemia (vaso-occlusion).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Dactylitis (hand-foot syndrome) is the earliest manifestation of sickle cell disease, occurring between 6 months and 2 years. It results from vaso-occlusion in the small vessels of the metacarpals and metatarsals, causing:

- Bone marrow ischemia and infarction

’    - Pain and swelling

- Fever (reactive)

- Functional impairment The pathophysiology involves HbS polymerization under low oxygen conditions, leading to sickling, vascular occlusion, and tissue ischemia. Bone marrow necrosis may occur as a consequence, but the primary process is vaso-occlusion. Septic arthritis is a complication to consider but not the primary mechanism. This presentation is classic for vasoocclusive crisis in young children.

---

questions.stem: A 10-year-old with sickle cell anemia has had 4 vaso-occlusive crises in the past year requiring hospitalization. Laboratory values: Hb 7.2 g/dL, reticulocytes 12%, HbF 3%. What is the appropriate starting dose of hydroxyurea?
questions.initialExplanation: The starting dose of hydroxyurea in sickle cell anemia per the source: 20 mg/kg/day.
questions.detailedExplanation:
For children with frequent vaso-occlusive crises (=3 per year) or other severe complications, hydroxyurea is indicated. Recommended starting dose is 20 mg/ kg/day. Key principles:

- Start low: 20 mg/kg/day to minimize myelosuppression

- Escalate gradually: Increase by 5 mg/kg/day every 8 weeks if tolerated

- Target dose: Maximum tolerated dose (usually 25-30 mg/kg/day)

- Monitoring: CBC every 2-3 weeks initially

Target goals include increased HbF (>15-20%), increased total hemoglobin, reduced hospitalizations, and decreased pain episodes. HbF increase provides anti-sickling effects by reducing HbS concentration. The child's severe disease frequency (4 crises/year) justifies hydroxyurea initiation.

---


## ITP | VWD | Hemophilia

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl presents with petechiae on arms and legs, ecchymosis on trunk without mucous membrane bleeding, and appears healthy. Laboratory findings: hemoglobin 12 g/dl, WBC 4, 000/cmm, platelet count 50,000/cmm, with giant platelets present. What intervention would be most suitable?
questions.initialExplanation: Petechiae and bruises in a healthy girl with platelets 50,000 and no mucosal bleeding: mild ITP; watchful waiting is enough.
questions.detailedExplanation:
(Nelson & AAP Guidelines): This presentation is consistent with acute immune thrombocytopenia (ITP). According to Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics and AAP guidelines, children with platelet counts >30, 000/cmm without bleeding manifestations can be managed conservatively with observation. The AAP recommends treatment (IVIG or corticosteroids) only for children with:

- Platelet count <20,000/cmm, Significant bleeding, Platelet count <30,000/cmm with bleeding risk factors

- In this case, the child has platelet count of 50,000/cmm, appears healthy, and has only mild skin findings without mucosal bleeding. The AAP emphasizes that most cases of acute ITP in children resolve spontaneously within 6 months, and treatment may cause more harm than benefit .

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old girl is evaluated for recurrent episodes of easy bruising, as well as occasional nosebleeds and gum bleeding that typically resolve on their own or with simple local care. Her younger brother has similar bleeding tendencies. Lab tests showed normal complete blood count. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Mucocutaneous bleeding, a family history and a normal CBC = von Willebrand disease.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This presentation is classic for von Willebrand disease (vWD), the most common inherited bleeding disorder. Mucocutaneous bleeding (epistaxis, easy bruising, gum bleeding) that resolves spontaneously, combined with a positive family history affecting both sexes and a normal CBC, strongly supports vWD. The condition results from quantitative or qualitative defects in von Willebrand factor, impairing platelet adhesion and stabilizing factor VIII. Hemophilia A and B are X-linked, predominantly affect males, and cause deep tissue or joint bleeding rather than mucocutaneous symptoms. Immune thrombocytopenia presents with isolated thrombocytopenia, while disseminated intravascular coagulation is acute with abnormal coagulation studies and thrombocytopenia. Confirmatory testing includes von Willebrand factor antigen, ristocetin cofactor activity, and factor VIII levels.

---

questions.stem: A healthy 2-month-old boy is brought in for easy bruising noticed over the past week. No bleeding, joint swelling, or mucosal bleeding is reported. Urine and stool are normal. He has not received any injections since birth. Laboratory tests show a normal complete blood count, but both PT and aPTT are prolonged. What is the MOST likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: A 2-month-old with bruising and prolonged PT and aPTT with normal platelets = vitamin K deficiency bleeding (vitamin K was not given).
questions.detailedExplanation:
This infant presents with classic signs of Vitamin K deficiency bleeding (VKDB), specifically late-onset VKDB occurring between 2 weeks and 6 months. Vitamin K is essential for the gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors Il, VII, IX, and X; deficiency prolongs both PT and aPTT while sparing platelets, consistent with the normal CBC. The history of no injections since birth indicates missed Vitamin K prophylaxis, a critical risk factor, especially in exclusively breastfed infants. Hemophilia A prolongs aPTT only with normal PT. Immune thrombocytopenia presents with low platelets. Von Willebrand disease typically shows normal PT and aPTT. Factor VII deficiency prolongs PT only.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year- old boy presented to the emergency department with sudden onset of skin ecchymoses and single attack of epistaxis, the history is negative for any significant event except for preceding upper respiratory tract infection. The examination showed an active healthy looking boy with diffuse skin petechial rash and ecchymoses over both lower and upper limbs, no lymphadenopathy and no organomegaly. The initial CBC is as follows: Hb 12.3 gm/dl, WBC 7.600/cmm, N 45%, L 51%, plt 17.000/cmm, and normal looking film except for rarely seen platelets. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.initialExplanation: After an upper respiratory infection: petechiae, bruises and epistaxis with platelets 17,000 in an active child with no organomegaly = ITP (immune thrombocytopenic purpura).
questions.detailedExplanation:
- Acute ITP is the most common cause of isolated thrombocytopenia in otherwise healthy children.

- It often follows a viral illness (e.g., URI), typically by 1-4 weeks, due to immune-mediated platelet destruction.

Key features:

- Sudden onset of petechiae/purpura and mucosal bleeding (e.g., epistaxis).

- No systemic symptoms (child appears well).

- No splenomegaly or lymphadenopathy.

Isolated low platelet count with normal other CBC parameters and normal red/white cell morphology on smear. ITP in children is usually acute and self-limiting, resolving within weeks to months.

---

questions.stem: A healthy 5-day-old male neonate develops bruising and melena. The pregnancy, and delivery course were unremarkable. The mother received heparin therapy for recurrent abortions secondary to lupus anticoagulants. The infant is vigorously breastfeeding. Examination reveals only multiple bruises. Lab tests reveals: hemoglobin, 8.4 g/dL; WBC, 8600/mm3; platelets count, 200000/mm3; PTT, 74 seconds; PT, 28 seconds; serum fibrinogen is normal. Of the following, the MOST likely cause of this bleeding is:
questions.initialExplanation: A newborn with bleeding and bruising, prolonged PT and PTT and normal platelets and fibrinogen = vitamin K deficiency (breastfed, no vitamin K at birth).
questions.detailedExplanation:
A neonate with bruising, melena, markedly prolonged PT and PTT, normal platelet count, and normal fibrinogen—in the absence of perinatal complications —points strongly to vitamin K deficiency bleeding (VKDB).

Newborns are at risk due to:

- Low placental transfer of vitamin K, Sterile gut (no bacterial synthesis), Low vitamin K content in breast milk.

- Vitamin Kis a cofactor for factors Il, VII, IX, and X; thus, both PT and PTT are prolonged (PT often more so initially due to factor VII's short half-life).

- DIC would show thrombocytopenia and low fibrinogen—not present. Hemophilia causes isolated PTT prolongation. Maternal heparin does not cross the placenta and does not affect the infant. Lupus anticoagulant prolongs PTT but does not cause bleeding and would not affect PT.

---

questions.stem: You are evaluating a 5-year-old male child with multiple ecchymoses distributed all over the extremities and trunk; examination reveal a palpable spleen 3 cm below the left costal margin. Lab findings include: hemoglobin, 11.3 g/dL; white blood cell count, 8700/mm3; platelets count, 21000/mm3. Of the following, the most proper NEXT step is:
questions.initialExplanation: A child with splenomegaly and low platelets (21,000): because of splenomegaly, do a bone marrow examination to exclude leukemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- thrombocytopenia (platelets 21,000/uL) and palpable splenomegaly (3 cm below costal margin) cannot be diagnosed with typical immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) —which never includes splenomegaly. This finding suggests an underlying systemic condition: Infection (e.g., EBV, CMV), Malignancy (e.g., leukemia, lymphoma), Storage disorders, or Hypersplenism.

The next appropriate step is abdominal ultrasonography to:

- Confirm splenomegaly objectively,

- Assess liver size and lymph nodes,

- Identify masses or abdominal pathology.

Only after imaging suggests malignancy or remains inconclusive would a bone marrow study be warranted.

Coagulation tests, bleeding time, or platelet function assays are not indicated in isolated thrombocytopenia with organomegaly.

---

questions.stem: You are going to explain the role of anti-D therapy to the parents of a 4-year-old boy with acute immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) who has several ecchymotic lesions located over extremities and trunk. There is no mucosal bleeding. An important statement that should be included during the discussion is:

options.label: A
options.text: anti-D therapy is more effective than IVIG therapy in acute ITP

options.label: B
options.text: anti-D therapy is very effective to all children with ITP

options.label: C
options.text: when anti-D therapy is given, monitoring of hemoglobin concentration is recommended

options.label: D
options.text: anti-D therapy is used in acute ITP only

options.label: E
options.text: anti-D therapy can be used as initial treatment for children with acute ITP

questions.initialExplanation: When treating ITP with anti-D, monitor hemoglobin (risk of hemolysis).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Anti-D immunoglobulin (anti-RhD) is used only in RhD-positive, non-splenectomized children with immune thrombocytopenia (ITP). It works by coating RhD-positive red blood cells, which are then cleared by the spleen—along with antibody-coated platelets —temporarily sparing platelets from destruction.

However, anti-D causes immune-mediated hemolysis as a direct effect. This leads to:

- A drop in hemoglobin (typically 1-2 g/dL),

- Risk of severe hemolysis (rare but can cause disseminated intravascular coagulation or renal failure).

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child has multiple bruises on her extremities and oral mucosal bleeding of 3 days duration; she had a mild respiratory tract infection 2 weeks before; physical examination was normal apart from multiple ecchymoses and petechiae. Of the following, the NEXT diagnostic step is:
questions.initialExplanation: A child with bruises and mucosal bleeding after a viral illness: the first diagnostic step is a CBC to see the platelets.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- sudden-onset bruising, petechiae, and mucosal bleeding 2 weeks after a mild respiratory infection, and otherwise normal physical exam, is highly suggestive of acute immune thrombocytopenia (ITP)—the most common cause of isolated thrombocytopenia in otherwise healthy children.

- However, before confirming ITP, the essential first step is to document thrombocytopenia and exclude other cytopenias.

The CBC provides:

- Platelet count (expected to be <20,000-50,000/uL in ITP),

- Hemoglobin (to assess for blood loss),

- White blood cell count and differential (to rule out leukemia or infection).

ITP is a diagnosis of exclusion—but only after isolated thrombocytopenia is confirmed on CBC and peripheral blood smear shows normal morphology (no blasts, dysplasia, or schistocytes).

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child, with hemophilia A of severe type, presents to the emergency unit with a groin pain after a minor trauma to his back; his blood pressure is 60/30 mm Hg; his pulse rate is 180/min; he holds his right hip in a flexion position with internal rotation. Of the following, the NEXT step in the management of this child is:
questions.initialExplanation: A child with severe hemophilia A and thigh pain after trauma with hypotension (retroperitoneal/psoas bleed): the next step is immediate IV factor VIII replacement.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- In any active bleeding episode in severe hemophilia A, the immediate priority is rapid replacement of factor VIII to stop ongoing bleeding and prevent further blood loss.

- Delaying factor replacement to obtain imaging or assays increases morbidity and mortality.

- Goal: Raise factor VIII level to 80—100% for major or life-threatening hemorrhage (per guidelines from WFH, ASH, and NIH).

- Resuscitation (fluids, oxygen) should occur simultaneously, but specific therapy = factor replacement.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy presents with sudden onset of generalized petechiae and purpura for the last two days, he is otherwise healthy and playful. Parents deny any previous similar episodes and family illnesses. His general examination showed active boy with normal vitals and no abnormality in general exam apart from these skin lesions. His heart exam is normal, chest note is normal and abdominal exam fails to identify organ enlargement. Of the following, the MOST likely diagnosis is:
questions.initialExplanation: A well child with sudden petechiae and no organomegaly = ITP (immune thrombocytopenia).
questions.detailedExplanation:
This is a classic presentation of acute childhood immune thrombocytopenia (ITP)—the most common cause of isolated thrombocytopenia in previously healthy children.

Key features supporting ITP:

- Age: 2-6 years (peak incidence),

- Acute onset of mucocutaneous bleeding (petechiae, purpura),

- Well-appearing child (no systemic illness),

- No organomegaly or lymphadenopathy,

- Often follows a viral illness (though not always reported).

Although not explicitly stated here, a complete blood count (CBC) would be expected to show: Severe thrombocytopenia (platelets often <20,000/uL), Normal hemoglobin and white blood cell count,

- Normal peripheral blood smear (no blasts, schistocytes, or abnormal cells).

- ITP is a diagnosis of exclusion, but in this typical clinical context, it is highly probable.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy presents with skin bleeding (ecchymosis and petechial rash) over the lower and upper limbs for two-days, no other site of bleeding and no constitutional symptoms. His mother denies any similar illness in his history and in the family. Examination of this child was normal. CBC film shows isolated thrombocytopenia (33.000/mm3). Of the following, the MOST appropriate initial treatment is:
questions.initialExplanation: Acute ITP in a child with platelets 33,000 and no significant mucosal bleeding: observation is enough as first treatment.
questions.detailedExplanation:
According to current guidelines (American Society of Hematology [ASH] 2019, British Committee for Standards in Haematology, and UpToDate):

- Children with acute ITP who are asymptomatic or have only mild skin bleeding (no mucosal or serious bleeding) and platelets >20,000—-30,000/uL should be managed with observation alone.

- Platelet count of 33,000/uL is above the 20,000-30,000/uL threshold where treatment is typically considered.

- No risk factors for serious bleeding (e.g., no trauma, no mucosal bleeding, no medications like NSAIDs).

- Acute childhood ITP is usually self-limiting: ~80% resolve spontaneously within 2-3 months.

- Treatment (steroids, IVIG) does not improve long-term outcomes and carries side effects (e.g., irritability, hypertension, aseptic meningitis, cost, hospitalization).

---

questions.stem: Two weeks after a viral syndrome, a 2-year-old child develops bruising and generalized petechiae, more prominent over the legs. No hepatosplenomegaly or lymph node enlargement is noted. The examination is otherwise unremarkable. Laboratory testing shows the patient to have a normal hemoglobin, hematocrit, and white blood cell (WBC) count and differential. The platelet count is 15, 000/pL. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Two weeks after a viral infection: bruises, petechiae and platelets 15,000 with the rest of the CBC normal = ITP.
questions.detailedExplanation:
In children, ITP is the most common form of thrombocytopenic purpura. In most cases, a preceding viral infection can be noted. No diagnostic test identifies this disease; exclusion of the other diseases listed in the question is necessary. In this disease, the platelet count is frequently less than 20,000/uL, but other laboratory tests yield essentially normal results, including the bone marrow aspiration (if done). Complications are uncommon; significant bleeding occurs in only 5% of cases and intracranial hemorrhage is even rarer. The treatment of childhood ITP is controversial. Patients with mild symptoms such as bruising and self-limited epistaxis may be observed, while patients with significant bleeding should be treated. IVIG and corticosteroids are effective in causing a rapid increase in platelet count, but controversy exists surrounding the use of prednisone before ruling out leukemia with a bone marrow aspirate. For Rh-positive patients with a working spleen, the use of anti-D immunoglobulin also results in an increase in platelet count. For patients with chronic (>1 year) ITP, a splenectomy may be helpful.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy presents with sudden-onset petechiae and purpura 2 weeks after a viral upper respiratory infection. He is otherwise well, with no hepatosplenomegaly. Platelet count is 8,000/uL; Hb and WBC are normal. Peripheral smear shows large platelets. Bone marrow is not performed. What is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.initialExplanation: ITP with platelets 8,000 and no dangerous bleeding: observation alone is an initial option per the source.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has acute immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) with isolated cutaneous bleeding and a platelet count of 8,000/uL. Current pediatric guidelines recommend observation alone for well-appearing children with mild bleeding regardless of platelet count, as most cases resolve spontaneously within weeks to months. IVIG or corticosteroids are reserved for significant mucosal bleeding, very high-risk activities, or need for rapid platelet elevation. Platelet transfusions are ineffective in ITP due to antibody-mediated destruction unless life- threatening hemorrhage occurs. Splenectomy and rituximab are interventions for chronic, refractory ITP after 12 months, not acute presentation. Watchful waiting avoids unnecessary medication side effects while ensuring safety through parental education on bleeding precautions and close follow-up.

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old is brought to the ED after being found playing with a rodenticide. His INR is 3.5 and you suspect that he has ingested a vitamin K antagonist commonly used in rodenticides. Which of the following factors is expected to be normal?
questions.initialExplanation: Vitamin K antagonists (such as rat poison) reduce factors II, VII, IX and X, which depend on vitamin K; factor V does not, so it stays normal.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Synthesis of factors Il, VII, IX, and X requires vitamin K as a cofactor. Factor V is a liver synthesized

factor that is not vitamin K dependent. It is, therefore, useful in distinguishing liver failure from vitamin K deficiency.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child presents with sudden onset of generalized petechiae and purpura. The parents report the child had a viral upper respiratory infection 2 weeks ago. Examination reveals widespread petechiae but otherwise normal findings. Platelet count is 15,000/pL. What is the most likely diagnosis and mechanism?

options.label: A
options.text: Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura; antiplatelet antibodies against platelet surface

questions.initialExplanation: Typical ITP: petechiae after a respiratory infection with platelets 15,000; the mechanism is autoantibodies against the platelet surface.
questions.detailedExplanation:
proteins

ITP is characterized by isolated thrombocytopenia with antiplatelet antibodies (mainly IgG) directed against platelet surface glycoproteins (Gpllb/llla, Gplb/IX). This typically follows viral infections by 1- 4 weeks and causes platelet destruction in spleen and liver. Leukemia would show abnormal WBC. Aplastic anemia affects all cell lines. Drug-induced causes would have medication history. DIC affects multiple coagulation parameters.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year- old girl presented with recurrent mucocutaneous bleeding episodes since early childhood that was usually stopped spontaneously or by local measures. Her brother also complained from the same problem, initial CBC was normal. Of the following, the MOST likely diagnosis is:
questions.initialExplanation: Recurrent mucocutaneous bleeding since childhood in a girl whose brother is affected with a normal CBC = von Willebrand disease.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This presentation is classic for von Willebrand disease (vWD), the most common inherited bleeding disorder. Mucocutaneous bleeding (epistaxis, easy bruising, gum bleeding) that resolves spontaneously or with local measures, combined with a positive family history affecting both sexes and a normal CBC, strongly supports vWD. The condition results from quantitative or qualitative defects in von Willebrand factor, impairing platelet adhesion and stabilizing factor VIII. Hemophilia A and B cause deep tissue/joint bleeding, predominantly affect males, and show prolonged aPTT. Disseminated intravascular coagulation is acute with thrombocytopenia and abnormal coagulation studies. Immune thrombocytopenia presents with isolated low platelets. Confirmatory testing includes von Willebrand factor antigen, ristocetin cofactor activity, and factor VIII levels.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old child with ITP is being treated with prednisone at 2 mg/kg/day. His platelet count has increased from 8,000/uL to 45,000/uL after 1 week of therapy. However, his parents report increased appetite, mood changes, and difficulty sleeping. What is the most appropriate management strategy for this treatment response?

options.label: A
options.text: Discontinue prednisone immediately due to side effects

options.label: B
options.text: Continue treatment despite significant side effects

options.label: C
options.text: Switch to dexamethasone for better side effect profile

options.label: D
options.text: Add IVIG for faster response and steroid-sparing effect

options.label: E
options.text: Maintain current dose for 3-4 weeks then gradually taper

questions.initialExplanation: ITP on prednisone: after a good response, continue for 3-4 weeks then taper (per the source).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Corticosteroids (prednisone or dexamethasone) are first-line therapy for symptomatic ITP, working through multiple mechanisms including suppression of antiplatelet antibody production, reduction of platelet destruction, and improved platelet production. A good clinical response, defined as platelet count >30,000/uL or doubling of baseline count, should be maintained for 3-4 weeks before initiating gradual dose Reduction.

The observed side effects (increased appetite, mood changes, sleep disturbances) are predictable corticosteroid effects that are dose-dependent and time-limited. Abrupt discontinuation risks rebound thrombocytopenia as the suppressive effect on antibody production is lost. The tapering schedule should be

individualized, typically reducing by 10-20% every 1-2 weeks while monitoring platelet counts, to minimize both relapse risk and withdrawal symptoms.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child with ITP presents to the emergency department with severe headache, vomiting, and confusion. Platelet count is 5,000/uL. The parents report the child fell from a chair yesterday but seemed fine at the time. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.label: B
options.text: IVIG therapy and urgent CT scan

options.label: C
options.text: Platelet transfusion and emergent neurosurgical consultation

options.label: E
options.text: Discharge with follow-up if symptoms improve

questions.initialExplanation: Headache, vomiting and confusion in an ITP child with platelets 5,000 after a fall: possible intracranial bleed; transfuse platelets and get urgent neurosurgical consultation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has suspected intracranial hemorrhage—a life-threatening emergency in ITP—given severe thrombocytopenia (5,000/uL), neurologic symptoms (headache, vomiting, confusion), and recent head trauma. Immediate platelet transfusion provides urgent hemostatic support despite antibody-mediated destruction, while emergent neurosurgical consultation ensures rapid imaging (CT head) and potential intervention. IVIG and/or high-dose steroids should be administered concurrently to sustain platelet recovery, but platelet transfusion is the only option offering immediate bleeding control. Observation, oral analgesics, or steroids alone are dangerously inadequate; discharge is contraindicated. Always prioritize rapid stabilization, hemorrhage control, and multidisciplinary coordination (hematology, neurosurgery, critical care) in suspected ICH with severe thrombocytopenia.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child with ITP has been treated with multiple rounds of IVIG. The current course is given at 2 g/kg divided over 2 days. The child develops headache, neck stiffness, and fever 12 hours after completing the infusion. What is the most likely diagnosis and management approach?

options.label: A
options.text: Aseptic meningitis from IVIG; discontinue therapy and monitor

options.label: B
options.text: Bacterial meningitis; start broad-spectrum antibiotics immediately OC) Increased intracranial pressure; urgent neurosurgical consultation

options.label: C
options.text: Increased intracranial pressure; urgent neurosurgical consultation

options.label: D
options.text: Medication side effect; continue with antihistamine premedication

options.label: E
options.text: Serum sickness reaction; switch to alternative therapy

questions.initialExplanation: Headache, neck stiffness and fever after IVIG: aseptic meningitis from IVIG; stop the drug and monitor.
questions.detailedExplanation:
IVIG can cause chemical meningitis characterized by headache, neck stiffness, and fever, typically occurring

6-24 hours post-infusion at doses >1 g/kg. This sterile inflammatory reaction is caused by IVIG components crossing the blood-brain barrier and triggering inflammatory mediators. The condition is self-limiting and

’    managed conservatively with analgesics, antiemetics, and careful monitoring.

Key distinguishing features include the timing (within 24 hours of infusion), mild CSF pleocytosis without bacterial growth, and rapid resolution with supportive care. Bacterial meningitis would typically show more severe symptoms, higher fever, and positive cultures. Treatment involves discontinuation of IVIG, symptomatic management, and consideration of premedication with antihistamines and corticosteroids for future infusions.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old child with ITP has been receiving oral prednisone for 4 weeks with good platelet response. However, the parents report significant behavioral changes including aggression, irritability, and mood swings. The child has gained 4 pounds and appears Cushingoid. What is the most appropriate management strategy?

options.label: A
options.text: Switch to dexamethasone with similar tapering schedule

options.label: C
options.text: Begin gradual tapering while monitoring platelet count and behavioral symptoms

options.label: D
options.text: Add IVIG and continue the same prednisone dose

options.label: E
options.text: Continue treatment despite side effects as they are temporary

questions.initialExplanation: Prednisone side effects (aggression, cushingoid swelling): taper the dose gradually while monitoring platelets and behavior.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The side effects described (behavioral changes, weight gain, Cushingoid appearance) are predictable corticosteroid effects that are dose-dependent and improve with dose reduction. Gradual tapering is essential to minimize both relapse risk and withdrawal symptoms while allowing the behavioral side effects to resolve.

The typical tapering schedule reduces prednisone by 10-20% every 1-2 weeks based on clinical response and side effect severity. Behavioral symptoms often improve within days to weeks of significant dose reduction. Alternative therapies like IVIG or dexamethasone would not address the underlying corticosteroid side effects and may introduce different complications.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child with ITP develops severe abdominal pain, vomiting, and melena. Platelet count is 8, 000/uL. The child has been having intermittent black stools for 2 days. Physical examination reveals abdominal distension and decreased bowel sounds. What is the most likely gastrointestinal complication and appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.text: Peptic ulcer disease; start proton pump inhibitors and H. pylori testing

options.label: B
options.text: Meckel's diverticulum; surgical consultation and Technetium-99m scan

options.label: C
options.text: Gastrointestinal bleeding from thrombocytopenia; IVIG and factor Vila

options.label: D
options.text: Intussusception; urgent surgical consultation and contrast enema

options.label: E
options.text: Severe constipation; stool softeners and dietary management

questions.initialExplanation: ITP with GI bleeding (melena) and platelets 8,000: treat with IVIG and factor VIIa for severe bleeding per the source.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Severe thrombocytopenia can cause significant gastrointestinal bleeding, presenting with melena, abdominal pain, and signs of blood loss. IVIG provides rapid platelet increase while recombinant factor Vlla can be used for severe bleeding when conventional therapy fails.

This represents a medical emergency requiring immediate treatment to prevent hypovolemic shock. Factor Vlla bypasses the need for platelet function and can provide rapid hemostasis. The timing

and severity of symptoms correlate with the degree of thrombocytopenia, making prompt recognition and treatment essential for optimal outcomes.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old child presents with frequent nosebleeds, easy bruising, and prolonged bleeding after dental extraction. Family history reveals similar bleeding symptoms in the mother and maternal grandmother. Initial screening shows prolonged bleeding time and normal platelet count. What is the most likely diagnosis and inheritance pattern?
questions.initialExplanation: Epistaxis, bruising and bleeding after tooth extraction with a family history through mother and grandmother and a prolonged bleeding time = von Willebrand disease (autosomal dominant).
questions.detailedExplanation:
VWD is the most common inherited bleeding disorder, affecting 1-2% of the general population. It follows autosomal dominant inheritance with variable penetrance and expressivity in most cases, explaining why family members may have varying severity of symptoms. VWD presents with mucocutaneous bleeding

’     (epistaxis, easy bruising, prolonged bleeding after dental extraction) due to defective platelet adhesion and reduced factor VIII stability. The combination of positive family history across generations (mother and maternal grandmother), mucocutaneous bleeding pattern, prolonged bleeding time with normal platelet count, and autosomal dominant inheritance pattern is classic for VWD. Hemophilias A and B are X-linked recessive disorders affecting males predominantly. Factor XI deficiency is

rare and follows autosomal recessive inheritance. Platelet disorders have different clinical presentations and inheritance patterns.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child with severe VWD (type 3) requires surgical intervention for appendicitis. Factor VIII activity is 8% and vWF antigen is undetectable. The surgical team wants to know the most appropriate hemostatic agent. What is the most appropriate treatment for major surgery in severe VWD type 3?

options.label: B
options.text: Cryoprecipitate containing vWF and factor VIII

questions.initialExplanation: Severe VWD (type 3) with major surgery: the given answer is cryoprecipitate containing vWF and factor VIII (a vWF/FVIII concentrate is preferred when available).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Type 3 VWD is severe with virtual absence of VWF, representing <1% of all VWD cases. Surgery requires replacement therapy with both VWF and factor VIII to address the dual defects in primary and secondary hemostasis. Cryoprecipitate contains significant amounts of both VWF and factor VIII, making it suitable for major surgery when plasma-derived VWF concentrates are not available. Modern practice prefers plasma-derived VWF concentrates that contain both VWF and factor VIII in standardized ratios. However, cryoprecipitate remains an effective alternative when commercial concentrates are unavailable. DDAVP is completely ineffective in type 3 VWD due to absence of endothelial vWF stores. Factor VIII concentrate lacks VWF and is therefore insufficient. Fresh frozen plasma has low concentrations of both factors.

---

questions.stem: A 9-year-old child with VWD presents with recurrent epistaxis lasting more than 30 minutes that doesn't respond to local pressure. Previous treatments with DDAVP and tranexamic acid have been ineffective. Laboratory results: VWF antigen 15%, factor VIII activity 25%, platelet count 200,000/uL. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.text: Increase DDAVP dose frequency to every 8 hours

options.label: C
options.text: Perform nasal cautery for definitive treatment

options.label: D
options.text: Switch to recombinant factor VIII concentrate

options.label: E
options.text: Administer plasma-derived VWF concentrate with factor VIII

questions.initialExplanation: VWD with epistaxis resistant to prior therapies: give vWF/factor VIII concentrate (plasma-derived).
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has severe VWD (likely type 1 or 2) that's unresponsive to DDAVP, evidenced by persistent bleeding despite adequate DDAVP therapy. Plasma-derived VWF concentrates (containing both vWF ’    and factor VIII in physiologic ratios) are the treatment of choice for severe bleeding episodes in DDAVP-unresponsive patients. The laboratory values (VWF antigen 15%, factor VIII activity 25%) indicate moderate to severe VWD that may represent either severe type 1 or type 2 disease. Increasing DDAVP frequency won't overcome DDAVP unresponsiveness. Nasal cautery treats the

symptom but not the underlying bleeding disorder. Recombinant factor VIII concentrate lacks VWF and is therefore insufficient for VWD treatment.

---

questions.stem: A 8-year-old child with suspected VWD is being evaluated. The parents ask what tests will help confirm the diagnosis and determine severity. Which combination of laboratory tests is most appropriate for initial VWD evaluation?

options.label: A
options.text: Bleeding time, platelet count, PTT, factor VIII activity

options.label: B
options.text: Bleeding time, platelet count, PT, factor VII activity

options.label: C
options.text: Platelet function assay, PT, PTT, fibrinogen

options.label: D
options.text: PT, PTT, factor V activity, factor X activity

options.label: E
options.text: Platelet aggregation studies, factor XI activity, factor XII activity

questions.initialExplanation: First-line VWD tests: bleeding time, platelet count, PTT and factor VIII activity (plus vWF antigen and ristocetin cofactor).
questions.detailedExplanation:
This combination of tests screens for VWD and helps differentiate it from other bleeding disorders.

Bleeding time assesses platelet function (prolonged in VWD), platelet count is normal in VWD, PTT may be mildly prolonged due to associated factor VIII deficiency, and factor VIII activity is reduced.

This screening panel helps identify the characteristic pattern of VWD: prolonged bleeding time with normal platelets, possible mild PTT prolongation, and reduced factor VIII activity. Additional testing

(VWF antigen, ristocetin cofactor activity) is needed for definitive diagnosis and typing.

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy presents with extensive bruising and prolonged bleeding after minor trauma. Family history reveals his maternal uncle had similar bleeding problems. Laboratory results show prolonged PTT, normal PT, normal platelet count, and normal bleeding time. What is the most likely diagnosis and inheritance pattern?

options.label: B
options.text: Hemophilia B (Factor IX deficiency); autosomal recessive

options.label: E
options.text: Hemophilia A (Factor VIII deficiency); X-linked recessive

questions.initialExplanation: Prolonged PTT with normal PT, platelets and bleeding time and an affected maternal uncle = hemophilia A (X-linked recessive).
questions.detailedExplanation:
This presentation is classic for hemophilia A, which accounts for 80% of all hemophilia cases. The X- linked recessive inheritance pattern perfectly explains the family history: maternal uncle (affected

’    male relative) and nephew (affected male descendant) share the affected X chromosome from the carrier grandmother. The mother is typically an asymptomatic carrier who inherited one normal and one affected X chromosome. Hemophilia B (factor IX deficiency) is much less common (20% of cases) and has the same inheritance pattern. VWD is autosomal dominant with variable penetrance. Factor Xl deficiency is rare and follows autosomal recessive inheritance. Platelet function disorders typically cause prolonged bleeding time rather than prolonged PTT.

---

questions.stem: A 8-year-old boy with severe hemophilia A presents with severe headache, vomiting, and confusion after hitting his head during sports. Platelet count is normal, but coagulation studies cannot be obtained immediately. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.label: A
options.text: Perform lumbar puncture to rule out intracranial bleeding

options.label: B
options.text: Wait for coagulation study results before any treatment

options.label: C
options.text: Administer factor VIII concentrate to achieve 100% activity immediately

options.label: E
options.text: Give desmopressin (DDAVP) if factor VIII levels are borderline

questions.initialExplanation: Severe hemophilia A with head injury and signs of intracranial bleeding: give factor VIII immediately to raise activity to 100% without waiting for tests or lumbar puncture.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Head trauma in hemophilia patients is a medical emergency requiring immediate factor VIII replacement to achieve 100% activity levels, even before definitive diagnosis. This prevents or treats potential intracranial hemorrhage, which can be fatal in up to 30% of cases if untreated. The presence of neurological symptoms (severe headache, vomiting, confusion) following head trauma in a hemophilia patient is highly concerning for intracranial hemorrhage. Immediate factor VIII replacement is life-saving and should not be delayed for laboratory confirmation. The 100% target level is maintained for at least 7-10 days to ensure adequate hemostasis during the high-risk period. Waiting for test results or observing neurological deterioration can be catastrophic.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy with hemophilia A has been receiving factor VIII concentrate for 3 years. Recently, his bleeding episodes have required higher doses and longer treatment duration for resolution. Mixing study shows no correction of prolonged PTT. What is the most likely explanation for this change in clinical response?

options.label: D
options.text: Factor VIII consumption from increased bleeding

questions.initialExplanation: Increasing need for larger doses and no PTT correction on mixing study: an inhibitor against factor VIII has developed.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The development of neutralizing antibodies (inhibitors) against factor VIII is a serious complication occurring in 15-30% of patients with severe hemophilia A, typically developing within the first 50 exposure days. This explains the decreased response to standard factor VIII therapy, requiring higher doses and longer treatment duration for bleeding episodes. The mixing study showing no

correction of prolonged PTT is diagnostic of factor VIII inhibitors. In normal mixing studies, the patient's plasma is mixed with normal plasma containing normal factor VIII levels. If the PTT corrects, the patient has factor deficiency. If it doesn't correct, inhibitors are present. This change in clinical

response pattern is classic for inhibitor development and requires immediate hematology consultation for inhibitor management.

---

questions.stem: A 83-year-old boy with mild hemophilia A (factor VIII activity 25%) is being evaluated for his first major bleeding episode. He fell from playground equipment and developed a large elbow hematoma. The parents ask about treatment options. What is the most appropriate treatment approach for major bleeding in mild hemophilia A?

options.label: B
options.text: Factor VIII concentrate infusion to raise levels to 50-80%

questions.initialExplanation: Per the source: desmopressin (DDAVP) for mild hemophilia A (activity 25%); for major bleeding factor VIII is usually preferred, so check the original.
questions.detailedExplanation:
DDAVP is effective for mild hemophilia A, increasing factor VIII activity 3-5 fold for 4-8 hours by releasing endogenous factor VIII from endothelial storage sites. For major bleeding episodes like large hematomas, DDAVP can provide adequate factor VIII levels without the need for factor concentrates. The duration of therapy (3-5 days) should be individualized based on bleeding severity and clinical response. DDAVP is contraindicated in severe hemophilia due to absence of factor VIII stores. Factor concentrates are reserved for situations where DDAVP is ineffective or contraindicated.

---

questions.stem: A 16-year-old girl presents with heavy menstrual bleeding since menarche, frequent nosebleeds, and easy bruising. She required prolonged pressure after dental extraction. Platelet count, PT, and thrombin time are normal, but PTT is mildly prolonged. Ristocetin cofactor activity is low. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Heavy menstrual bleeding, epistaxis and bruising with low ristocetin cofactor = von Willebrand disease.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This classic presentation —mucocutaneous bleeding (menorrhagia, epistaxis, bruising), normal platelet count, prolonged PTT, and low ristocetin cofactor activity—is diagnostic of Von Willebrand Disease (VWD), the most common inherited bleeding disorder (1-2% of population). VWD results from deficiency or dysfunction of von Willebrand factor (vWF), which mediates platelet adhesion and stabilizes factor VIII.

---

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman with known Type 1 VWD requires dental extraction. Her vWF antigen and ristocetin cofactor levels are 30% of normal. What is the most appropriate pre-procedural treatment?
questions.initialExplanation: Type 1 VWD before tooth extraction: desmopressin (DDAVP) to raise vWF and factor VIII.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Desmopressin (DDAVP) is first-line for Type 1 VWD (quantitative defect) because it releases endogenous VWF and factor VIII from endothelial stores, raising levels 2-5 fold within 30-60 minutes. It is effective for minor procedures like dental extraction.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy presents with sudden onset of petechiae and purpura after a viral upper respiratory infection 2 weeks ago. He is otherwise well, with no hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy. Platelet count is 15,000/uL; hemoglobin and WBC are normal. Peripheral smear shows large platelets. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Two weeks after an upper respiratory infection: petechiae, purpura and platelets 15,000 with large platelets = ITP.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This is classic acute ITP in children: acute onset of isolated thrombocytopenia (<20,000/uL) 1-4 weeks after viral infection, with petechiae/purpura, normal Hb/WBC, and large platelets (increased turnover). No systemic signs (e.g., HSM) rule out leukemia.

---


## Leukemias | Aplastic Anemia

questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy presents with prolonged fever, bone pain, chest X-ray showing mediastinal widening, WBC count 200,000/cmm, and hemoglobin 5 g/dl. Which of the following represents the LEAST accepted idea in his management?

options.label: D
options.text: Packed RBC is indicated immediately as a first line

questions.initialExplanation: Leukemia with WBC 200,000, a wide mediastinum and severe anemia: do not give immediate transfusion as a first step because it raises viscosity (leukostasis); hydrate and watch for hyperuricemia and hyperkalemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
(Nelson & AAP Guidelines): In pediatric patients with acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) presenting with hyperleukocytosis (WBC >100,000/cmm), immediate packed RBC transfusion is contraindicated as first-line therapy. According to Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics and AAP guidelines, this can exacerbate leukostasis and hyperviscosity syndrome. The priority should be reducing tumor burden through leukapheresis or urgent chemotherapy initiation, followed by careful transfusion if indicated. The AAP recommends aggressive hydration and close monitoring for tumor lysis syndrome, with bone marrow aspiration for definitive diagnosis being appropriate. Hyperuricemia and hyperkalemia are indeed recognized complications requiring preventive measures .

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy is admitted to hospital with fatigue, pallor, and bruising. Examination reveals petechiae over the trunk and hepatosplenomegaly. Lab. tests show WBC 180,000/mm3, Hb 6.8 g/dL, platelets 28, 000/mm3, uric acid 10.5 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.3 mg/dL. A peripheral smear reveals lymphoblasts. While awaiting diagnostic confirmation, what is the MOST appropriate initial step in management?

options.label: A
options.text: Restrict fluids and monitor for tumor lysis

options.label: B
options.text: Administer sodium bicarbonate to alkalinize urine

options.label: C
options.text: Transfuse platelets and start antibiotics immediately

options.label: D
options.text: Administer high-dose corticosteroids to lower the WBC count

options.label: E
options.text: Start intravenous hydration and administer allopurinol

questions.initialExplanation: Lymphoblastic leukemia with high uric acid and renal impairment: first step IV fluids with allopurinol (to prevent tumor lysis syndrome).
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child presents with suspected acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) complicated by tumor lysis syndrome (TLS), evidenced by hyperleukocytosis, elevated uric acid (10.5 mg/dL), and renal impairment (creatinine 1.3 mg/dL). The immediate priority is preventing further renal damage and lethal electrolyte disturbances. Aggressive intravenous hydration maintains high urine output to flush uric acid and prevent tubular precipitation, while allopurinol (or rasburicase) reduces uric acid production. Fluid restriction (A) is contraindicated as it worsens renal failure. Urine alkalinization (B) is largely outdated due to risks of calcium phosphate deposition. Platelet transfusion (C) requires caution in hyperleukocytosis due to viscosity risks, and antibiotics are reserved for fever. Corticosteroids (D) aid cytoreduction but should follow hydration to prevent exacerbating TLS from rapid cell lysis.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old male develops recurrent epistaxis and easy bruising.. The patient was the first child of unrelated healthy parents born after 41 weeks of pregnancy. Physical examination of the patient reveal short stature, clinodactyly with brachy mesophalangia on bilateral 5th fingers, multiple café-au-lait spots on both thighs and right buttock. He has no other abnormalities. His initial complete blood cell count results are as follows: white blood cell, 5.0x109/L; hemoglobin 9.5 g/dL; platelets 80x109/L. Of the following, the MOST likely diagnosis is:
questions.initialExplanation: Short stature, clinodactyly, cafe-au-lait spots, bleeding and low platelets = Fanconi anemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This boy presents with:

questions.stem: In examining a 4-year-old girl who is new to your practice, you discover that she has rudimentary thumbs and is well below the 5th percentile for both weight and height. You also observe irregular hyperpigmentation on the trunk and anogenital areas. Of the following, the MOST likely hematologic disorder associated with these findings is :
questions.initialExplanation: Hypoplastic thumb, short stature and hyperpigmented skin = Fanconi anemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Approximately 80% of patients who have Fanconi anemia exhibit congenital anomalies. Recognizing these anomalies is important because the aplastic anemia usually is not evident until 4 to 14 years of age. Pancytopenia at birth is unusual. Among the unusual features described are hyperpigmentation (60% of patients); short stature (57%); upper limb anomalies ’     (48%) that include absent, hypoplastic, supernumerary, or bifid thumbs and aplasia of the first metacarpal or the radius; hypogonadism (40%); and microcephaly (27%). Almost 20% of affected patients manifest a variety of other skeletal anomalies. The only potential cure for this autosomal recessive disorder is bone marrow transplantation, and early diagnosis allows for better donor identification and patient preparation. It is also important to make the diagnosis to enable parents to choose prenatal diagnosis for future pregnancies. Several complementation groups have been identified in Fanconi anemia, with type A accounting for almost 66% of cases. If the specific complementation group can be identified in the index case, DNA analysis can be used for prenatal diagnosis. If a specific DNA defect is not identified, increased chromosomal breakage in peripheral blood lymphocytes in the presence of cross-linking agents can be used.

---

questions.stem: A 14-yrs-old girl presents with bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy that has progressed over the past 4 wk. It is slowly worsening despite antibiotic therapy with cephalexin, which was prescribed 2 wk ago. On physical examination, the lymph nodes are enlarged, matted, and nontender. There is mild splenomegaly. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.initialExplanation: Matted painless cervical nodes and splenomegaly not improving with antibiotics: acute lymphocytic leukemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Physical examination findings in a child with malignancy are dependent on whether the cancer is systemic or localized. The cancers most common in children involve the lymphohematopoietic system. When the bone marrow is compromised by malignancy (e.g., leukemia, Disseminated neuroblastoma), typical findings include pallor from anemia, bleeding, petechiae, or purpura from thrombocytopenia or coagulopathy; cellulitis or other localized infection from leukopenia; skin nodules (especially in infants) and hepatosplenomegaly from malignant leukocytosis. Abnormalities found in lymphatic malignancies include peripheral adenopathy and signs of superior vena cava syndrome from an anterior mediastinal mass including respiratory distress, and facial and neck plethora and edema. Enlargement of cervical lymph nodes is common in children, but when persistent, progressive, and painless it often suggests lymphoma. In particular, supraclavicular adenopathy suggests underlying malignancy.

---

questions.stem: An older child experiences weight loss and night sweats and has a white blood cell count of 80, 000/mm3 and a platelet count of 600,000/mm3 . Chromosomal analysis of bone marrow cells reveals a clonal disorder of stem cells with the specific translocation, 1(9;22)(q34;g11), which is also known as the Philadelphia chromosome. The diagnosis is:
questions.initialExplanation: Very high WBC and platelets with Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22) = chronic myelogenous leukemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
CML is a clonal disorder of the hematopoietic tissue that accounts for 2-3% of all cases of childhood leukemia. About 99% of the cases are characterized by a specific translocation, t(9;22) (q34;q11), known as the Philadelphia chromosome, resulting in a BCR-ABL fusion protein. The disease is characterized clinically by an initial chronic phase in which the malignant clone produces an elevated leukocyte count with a predominance of mature forms but with increased numbers of immature granulocytes. The spleen is often greatly enlarged, resulting in pain in the left upper quadrant of the abdomen. In addition to leukocytosis, blood counts can reveal mild anemia and thrombocytosis.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old male comes to your clinic to establish care. He is well appearing and does not have abnormal physical examination findings. His growth and development have been excellent. However, his mother tells you that he has been diagnosed with Fanconi anemia. Which of the following statements is true?

options.label: A
options.text: No additional follow-up is needed other than genetic counseling when he is older, unless he develops symptoms.

options.label: B
options.text: Diagnostic testing for Fanconi anemia includes measurement of telomere length.

options.label: C
options.text: He may need frequent electrolyte replacement therapy to make up for his urinary losses.

options.label: D
options.text: Patients with bone marrow failure can undergo treatment with oxymetholone, but many patients eventually become resistant to androgen therapy.

options.label: E
options.text: Once he undergoes stem cell transplant, his risk of cancer will decrease to that of the normal population.

questions.initialExplanation: (Question text incomplete.) In Fanconi anemia marrow failure can be treated with oxymetholone (an androgen), but many patients later become resistant; this is the correct statement in the given answer.
questions.detailedExplanation:
patients eventually become resistant to androgen therapy.

Fanconi anemia is a result of defective double-strand DNA repair mechanisms. Up to 25% of patients have no physical abnormalities, but since marrow failure usually starts in the first decade of life, these patients should have quarterly blood counts and periodic bone marrow biopsies. Oral androgen treatment with oxymetholone would be an appropriate therapy. Androgen therapy yields an increase in RBCs in approximately half of patients in the first 2 months; it may take up to year for platelet counts and white blood cell counts to rise. Most patients lose the response to androgens as the bone marrow failure progresses.

---

questions.stem: A 10-year-old child presents with fatigue, pallor, easy bruising, and recurrent infections. Laboratory results show hemoglobin 8.5 g/dL, WBC count 2,500/uL, and platelet count 25,000/uL. The family reports no recent medication exposure or toxin exposure. What is the most likely diagnosis and characteristic finding on bone marrow examination?

options.label: A
options.text: Aplastic anemia; hypocellular bone marrow with fat replacement

options.label: C
options.text: Myelodysplastic syndrome; dysplastic changes in cell lines

options.label: D
options.text: Bone marrow metastasis; abnormal cell infiltrates

options.label: E
options.text: Iron deficiency anemia; decreased iron stores

questions.initialExplanation: Pancytopenia with no drug or toxin exposure = aplastic anemia; the typical marrow shows low cellularity with fatty replacement.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This presentation (pancytopenia in the absence of known causes) is classic for aplastic anemia. The hallmark of aplastic anemia is peripheral pancytopenia coupled with hypoplastic or aplastic bone marrow showing fat replacement of hematopoietic cells. The majority of childhood cases are idiopathic, with no identifiable

’    causative agent, though drugs, chemicals, toxins, infectious agents, radiation, and immune disorders can result in pancytopenia. This constellation of findings (fatigue from anemia, pallor, easy bruising from thrombocytopenia, and recurrent infections from neutropenia) together with pancytopenia suggests bone marrow failure rather than peripheral destruction. The absence of blast cells rules out leukemia, and the severe pancytopenia without other specific findings makes myelodysplastic syndrome less likely in a child.

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old child with severe aplastic anemia has been treated with immunosuppressive therapy (antithymocyte globulin, corticosteroids, and cyclosporine) for 3 months. The parents ask about treatment response and prognosis. What is the expected response rate to immunosuppressive therapy in severe aplastic anemia?

options.label: A
options.text: 90% response rate with excellent long-term survival

options.label: B
options.text: 60-80% response rate with good long-term outcomes

options.label: E
options.text: <20% response rate; transplant is only effective treatment

questions.initialExplanation: The response to immunosuppressive therapy (ATG, corticosteroids, cyclosporine) in severe aplastic anemia is 60-80% per the source.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Immunosuppressive therapy is the major form of treatment for aplastic anemia in patients without HLA-identical sibling donors, with a response rate of 60-80%. This approach uses a combination of antithymocyte globulin (ATG), corticosteroids, and cyclosporine to suppress the autoimmune destruction of hematopoietic stem cells. While response rates are high, they are not as excellent as bone marrow transplantation. The treatment takes several months to show effect, and patients may require ongoing immunosuppressive therapy. Long-term outcomes are generally good, though some patients may relapse or develop late complications. This approach is particularly valuable for patients without suitable bone marrow donors.

---

questions.stem: A 9-year-old child presents with progressive fatigue, pallor, and unusual bruising pattern. Physical examination reveals microcephaly, small eyes, epicanthic folds, absent thumbs, hyperpigmentation of the neck and trunk, and café-au-lait spots. Pancytopenia is confirmed on laboratory testing. What syndrome is most likely present and what specific diagnostic test is required?

options.label: B
options.text: Diamond-Blackfan anemia; red cell adenosine deaminase level

options.label: E
options.text: Thrombocytopenia with absent radii syndrome; complete blood count

questions.initialExplanation: Microcephaly, absent thumb, skin pigmentation and cafe-au-lait spots with pancytopenia = Fanconi anemia; diagnose by chromosomal breakage analysis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This presentation is classic for Fanconi anemia, an inherited bone marrow failure syndrome. The characteristic features include the "Fanconi facies" (microcephaly, small eyes, epicanthic folds), absent radii and hypoplastic thumbs, hyperpigmentation of the trunk and neck, café-au-lait spots, and other skeletal abnormalities. Fanconi anemia is diagnosed by demonstrating chromosomal fragility due to spontaneously occurring chromatid breaks in 100% of cases. This specific finding on chromosome breakage studies is 100% diagnostic for the condition. The syndrome typically presents with progressive bone marrow failure in the first decade of life, similar to severe acquired aplastic anemia. Early diagnosis is important for genetic counseling and appropriate management.

---

questions.stem: A 9-year-old child with Fanconi anemia presents with congenital anomalies but normal blood counts. The parents ask about the likelihood of developing bone marrow failure and the appropriate monitoring strategy. What is the most appropriate long-term monitoring approach for Fanconi anemia patients with normal hematologic parameters?

options.label: A
options.text: No routine monitoring needed until symptoms develop

options.label: B
options.text: Bi-annual complete blood count starting at age 10

options.label: C
options.text: Monthly complete blood count with immediate evaluation of changes

options.label: D
options.text: Annual complete blood count starting at age 5

options.label: E
options.text: Bone marrow biopsy every 2 years regardless of blood counts

questions.initialExplanation: Monitoring Fanconi anemia with a normal blood count: annual CBC starting at age 5 per the source.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Fanconi anemia typically presents with progressive bone marrow failure, usually manifesting in the first decade of life. Regular monitoring allows for early detection of declining blood counts and timely intervention before severe complications develop. Annual monitoring is sufficient for detecting trends in blood count changes, as the progression is usually gradual. Starting at age 5 ensures that changes are detected early enough to prepare for definitive treatment. More frequent monitoring would be excessive and stressful for asymptomatic children, while less frequent monitoring risks missing early signs of bone marrow failure.

---

questions.stem: A 16-year-old female presents with 3-week history of fatigue, nosebleeds, and easy bruising. Exam shows pallor and petechiae. Labs: Hb 7.2 g/dL, WBC 1.8 x 10%L, platelets 15 x 109L. Bone marrow biopsy reveals hypocellular marrow (<25% cellularity) with fat replacement and no blasts. What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.label: A
options.text: Immediate induction chemotherapy for acute leukemia

options.label: C
options.text: Supportive care with growth factor therapy

options.label: D
options.text: Chromosome fragility testing and stem cell transplant

questions.initialExplanation: A hypocellular marrow with fatty replacement and no blasts in a teenage girl with pancytopenia = aplastic anemia; first treatment is immunosuppression (ATG, cyclosporine, steroid) when no donor is available, or per the given answer.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This patient presents with classic acquired aplastic anemia characterized by peripheral pancytopenia (anemia,

leukopenia, thrombocytopenia) and hypocellular bone marrow (<25% cellularity) without any evidence of blasts

or abnormal cells. The diagnostic criteria for aplastic anemia include: (1) Bone marrow cellularity <25% (or 25- ’    50% with <30% residual hematopoietic cells), (2) Peripheral pancytopenia

with at least two of: hemoglobin <10 g/dL, platelet count <50 x 10°/L, neutrophil count <1.5 x 10°/L.

The optimal initial management for patients without HLA-identical sibling donors is immunosuppressive therapy,

which typically includes anti-thymocyte globulin (ATG), cyclosporine, and corticosteroids. This approach

achieves response rates of 60-80% in patients without sibling donors and can lead to trilineage recovery. For

patients with HLAidentical sibling donors, allogeneic bone marrow transplantation offers a 90% chance of long-

term survival and is the preferred treatment option.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child presents with 2-week history of fever, fatigue, and bleeding tendencies. Physical examination reveals hepatosplenomegaly and lymphadenopathy. CBC shows WBC 45,000/uL with 70% blasts. Based on age and presentation, which type of leukemia is most likely?
questions.initialExplanation: A 5-year-old with WBC 45,000, 70% blasts and hepatosplenomegaly with nodes = acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), the most common childhood leukemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
ALL is by far the most common malignant disease in children, accounting for approximately 80% of childhood leukemias. The peak incidence occurs between 2-5 years of age, which perfectly matches this patient's age group. The clinical presentation is classic for acute leukemia with acute onset of symptoms (2-week duration), systemic manifestations (fever, fatigue), bleeding tendencies, and organ infiltration (hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy). The high blast percentage (70% blasts in peripheral blood) indicates an acute process rather than chronic leukemia. Among acute leukemias in children, ALL predominates significantly over AML, which accounts for only about 17% of childhood leukemias. Chronic leukemias (CML, CLL) are exceedingly rare in pediatrics - CML represents only 3% of cases, and CLL is virtually nonexistent in children.

---

questions.stem: A 8-year-old boy presents with progressive pancytopenia. He has short stature, absent thumb on right hand, hyperpigmented skin patches, and characteristic facial features. Family history reveals no similar cases. Chromosome fragility testing shows increased chromatid breaks in 100% of cells. Which finding is least consistent with Fanconi anemia diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.text: Progressive bone marrow failure typically manifests in the first decade of life

questions.initialExplanation: Fanconi anemia shows increased chromosome breaks, so the least consistent statement is that the chromosome stability test is normal.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Fanconi anemia is a rare autosomal recessive disorder characterized by progressive bone marrow failure and multiple congenital anomalies. The chromosomal fragility test is the definitive diagnostic test, showing spontaneously occurring chromatid breaks in 100% of cases examined - this represents the diagnostic hallmark of the condition.
