Therefore, finding "normal chromosome stability testing" would be inconsistent with Fanconi anemia diagnosis.

The clinical presentation is classic: (A) Progressive bone marrow failure typically manifests in the first decade of life as pancytopenia develops, (B) Absent or hypoplastic thumbs occur in about 50% of patients and are among the most characteristic congenital anomalies, (C) Short stature with growth failure is common and may be associated with abnormal growth hormone secretion or hypothyroidism, (D) Mental retardation occurs in approximately 10% of patients and may be related to associated microcephaly.

---

questions.stem: A 15-year-old presents with pancytopenia and bone marrow showing 18% blasts. Physical examination is remarkable for lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly. Blood smear shows circulating blast cells. What is the most likely diagnosis and appropriate management?

options.label: B
options.text: Myelodysplastic syndrome - supportive care LC) Acute leukemia - immediate induction chemotherapy

questions.initialExplanation: Pancytopenia with peripheral blasts (18%) and hepatosplenomegaly and adenopathy: acute leukemia; start induction chemotherapy promptly.
questions.detailedExplanation:
While the conventional diagnostic threshold for acute leukemia is >20% blasts in bone marrow, this case presents with 18% blasts along with compelling clinical evidence that strongly favors acute leukemia over aplastic anemia. The key distinguishing features are: (1) Organ infiltration with lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly, which is not typical of aplastic anemia, (2) Circulating blast cells in peripheral blood smear, (3) The clinical presentation with bone marrow failure symptoms. In cases with 18-19% blasts, clinical judgment is crucial. The presence of organ infiltration and circulating blasts indicates that this represents an evolving acute leukemia rather than aplastic anemia. The bone marrow is likely hypercellular (not hypocellular as in aplastic anemia) with increased blast percentage.

---

questions.stem: A 10-year-old with suspected leukemia has the following laboratory results: WBC 8,000/uL (normal), hemoglobin 8.5 g/dL (low), platelets 45,000/uL (low), and peripheral smear shows no circulating blasts. What additional test is most important to establish the diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.text: Repeat complete blood count in one week

questions.initialExplanation: Suspected leukemia with no peripheral blasts: the most diagnostic test is bone marrow aspiration and biopsy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
A normal white blood cell count does not exclude leukemia, as approximately 20% of leukemia patients present with normal or low WBC counts at diagnosis. The presence of anemia and thrombocytopenia suggests bone marrow dysfunction, which mandates bone marrow evaluation for definitive diagnosis. Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy is the gold standard test for establishing leukemia diagnosis.

The bone marrow examination provides crucial information: (1) Blast percentage (diagnostic threshold >20% for acute leukemia), (2) Cell lineage determination (myeloid vs lymphoid), (3) Morphological assessment and dysplasia, (4) Immunophenotyping by flow cytometry, (5) Cytogenetic analysis for prognostic information, (6) Molecular studies for targeted therapies.

---

questions.stem: An infant can lift his head from a prone position 45° off the examining table, smiles when encouraged, and makes cooing sounds. He cannot maintain a seated position. The MOST likely age of the infant is:
questions.initialExplanation: Lifting the head 45° when prone with a social smile, cooing and not yet sitting = about 3 months.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This infant demonstrates a specific pattern of developmental milestones that corresponds to the 3-month age range. The key is to correlate each
milestone with the expected age of achievement and determine which option best fits the entire clinical picture.

Analyzing the developmental milestones described:

- Head lift in prone position: At birth, infants have no head control in prone position. By 1 month, they may briefly lift the head. By 2 months, they can lift
the head to the level of the body. By 3 months, infants can lift the head and chest off the surface, typically at a 45-90 degree angle, and sustain this
position briefly. The description of lifting the head 45° off the examining table is consistent with 3 months of age.

- Social smiling: The true social smile (in response to social stimuli such as a caregiver's face or voice) typically emerges between 6-8 weeks
(approximately 2 months) and becomes more consistent and responsive by 3 months. Smiling "when encouraged" suggests this is a true social smile,
not a reflex smile.
- Cooing: Cooing (producing vowel-like sounds such as "00," "ah") typically begins around 2 months and becomes more elaborate by 3-4 months. Cooing
is a precursor to babbling and represents emerging language development.

- Inability to maintain seated position: This is an important negative finding. Independent sitting typically develops between 4-7 months. By 3 months,

infants have not yet achieved independent sitting and may only have minimal head lag when pulled to sit. The inability to sit is appropriate for a 3-month-

---

questions.stem: A healthy boy can sustain his head in the plane of his body on ventral suspension, follows a moving object 180 degrees, and smiles on social contact. His probable age will be:
questions.initialExplanation: Raising the head to body level, tracking objects through 180° and a social smile = 2 months.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The described developmental milestones align closely with those expected at 2 months of age:

- Head control in ventral suspension: By 2 months, an infant can briefly hold the head in line with the
trunk when suspended prone (though full head control develops by 3—4 months).

- Visual tracking 180 degrees: At 2 months, infants typically track objects past the midline, up to 180
degrees horizontally.

- Social smile: A responsive, social smile (as opposed to reflexive neonatal smiling) reliably emerges
around 6-8 weeks, i.e., by 2 months.

---

questions.stem: A 12-month-old girl has a head circumference of 47 cm, a weight of 9.5 kg, and a length of 75 cm. She was born full term with a birth weight of 2.5 kg. What is the MOST accurate interpretation of her growth?

options.label: B
options.text: All parameters are within expected normal limits

options.label: C
options.text: Weight is too low for age

options.label: E
options.text: Evidence of chronic malnutrition based on weight-for-age

questions.initialExplanation: Head circumference 47, weight 9.5 and length 75 at 12 months (birth weight 2.5): all measurements are within normal limits.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This 12-month-old girl was born at term with a birth weight of 2.5 kg (which is at the lower end of normal for a term infant, typically 2.5-4.0
kg). At 12 months, her measurements are: head circumference 47 cm, weight 9.5 kg, and length 75 cm. To interpret these growth
parameters correctly, we need to compare them to standard growth charts and consider her birth parameters.

- Head circumference: Normal head circumference at 12 months is approximately 44-47 cm. The 50th percentile is approximately 45-46
cm, so 47 cm is at or slightly above the 95th percentile but is still within normal limits. Macrocephaly is typically defined as head
circumference >2 standard deviations above the mean, which would be approximately >48 cm at 12 months.

- Weight: Average weight at 12 months is approximately 9.6 kg (range 7.5-11.5 kg is typical). A weight of 9.5 kg is at approximately the
50th percentile and is perfectly normal.

- Length: Average length at 12 months is approximately 75 cm (range 70-80 cm is typical). A length of 75 cm is at the 50th percentile and
is perfectly normal.

---

questions.stem: An 11-month-old infant in routine check-up can roll over both ways, babble "bye-bye" and " mama" and "baba," and is able to transfer objects between hands and use pincer grasp. However, he has not yet started sitting independently or attempting to crawl. Which developmental domain is most likely delayed in this child?
questions.initialExplanation: An 11-month-old who rolls but does not sit or crawl: delay in the gross motor domain.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This 11-month-old infant demonstrates good development in several areas—social engagement (babbling specific words),

fine motor skills (transferring objects, pincer grasp), and emerging language —but has not achieved sitting independently or
crawling, which are gross motor milestones.

- Sitting independently: Most infants achieve independent sitting between 4-7 months of age. By 8-9 months, sitting
independently is well established, and the infant can sit and reach for objects without falling. By 11 months, sitting
independently for extended periods is expected, and the infant should be able to move in and out of sitting position.

- Crawling: There is significant variation in crawling. Some infants never crawl, preferring to "scoot" or go directly to walking.
However, most infants show some form of mobility between 6-10 months. By 11 months, most infants are either crawling or
showing clear precursors to mobility.

- Rolling: Rolling both ways (back to front and front to back) typically develops around 4-6 months, which this infant has
achieved.

---

questions.stem: An 18-month-old boy is brought in for a routine check-up. His parents report that he only started walking independently in the past two weeks. He speaks 10-15 words, follows simple instructions, drinks from a cup, scribbles, points to objects, and shows stranger anxiety. Growth and neurological exams are normal. Which of the following best describes his developmental status?
questions.initialExplanation: An 18-month-old with normal development and neurological exam and stranger anxiety: normal development.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This 18-month-old boy presents with a spectrum of developmental skills that are appropriate for his age. The key to this question is
understanding normal developmental milestones at 18 months and recognizing that each developmental domain should be evaluated
independently. While the parents expressed concern about late walking, all other developmental skills are within normal limits.

normal developmental milestones at 18 months:

- Gross motor: Walking independently typically begins between 9-17 months, with a mean of 12-13 months.

- While 18 months is on the later end of normal, it is still within the range of typical development. Walking independently by 18 months is
considered normal, even if later than average.

- Language: By 18 months, children typically have 10-50 words and understand simple commands. Having 10-15 words is at the lower
end of normal but within acceptable limits.

- Social/emotional: Stranger anxiety typically emerges between 6-12 months and persists through the second year. Pointing to objects
and showing items to others (joint attention) are developing skills at this age.

- Fine motor: Drinking from a cup (with help) and scribbling with crayons are appropriate fine motor skills for 18 months.

---

questions.stem: Mohammed rides tricycle; stands momentarily on 1 foot; makes tower of 10 cubes; copies circle; knows age and sex; helps in dressing; and washes hands. What is the expected age of Mohammed?
questions.initialExplanation: Rides a tricycle, stands on one foot briefly and copies a circle = 3 years (36 months).
questions.detailedExplanation:
- Riding a tricycle and standing momentarily on one foot are gross motor milestones typically achieved by 36
months.

- Making a tower of 10 cubes and copying a circle are fine motor skills expected around 3 years (36 months).
- Knowing age and sex, helping in dressing, and washing hands independently reflect cognitive and self-care
abilities consistent with a 3-year-old.

Other options:

- 30 months: Children may build a tower of 8-9 cubes and begin to copy circles, but tricycle riding and
consistent one-foot balance are usually not yet mastered.

- 24 months or younger: Far too early for these combined milestones—e.g., 24-month-olds typically build
towers of only 6-7 cubes and cannot ride a tricycle.

Thus, 36 months best fits Mohammed’s developmental profile.

---

questions.stem: Ali can hop on 1 foot; throws ball overhand; uses scissors to cut out pictures; copies cross and square; draws man with 2-4 parts besides head; tells story; plays with several children; and goes to toilet alone. What is the expected age of Ali?
questions.initialExplanation: Hopping on one foot, cutting pictures and copying a cross and a square = 4 years (48 months).
questions.detailedExplanation:
- Hopping on one foot, throwing a ball overhand, and using scissors to cut out pictures are fine and gross motor milestones
typically achieved by 48 months (4 years).

- Copying a cross and square, as well as drawing a person with 2-4 body parts besides the head, are visual-motor skills
characteristic of a 4-year-old.

- Telling a story, playing cooperatively with several children, and going to the toilet independently reflect language, social,
and self-care development consistent with 48 months.
Why not other options?

- 36—42 months: Children may hop briefly or snip with scissors but usually cannot yet cut out pictures cleanly or draw a
person with multiple body parts. Storytelling and cooperative play are less developed.

- 60 months (5 years): Exceeds the described abilities—by then, children can typically copy triangles, print some letters,
skip, and dress completely independently.

Thus, 48 months best matches Ali's constellation of developmental milestones.

---

questions.stem: Salma can skip; draws triangle from copy; names heavier of 2 weights; names 4 colors; counts 10 pennies correctly; dresses and undresses; and asks questions about meaning of words. What is the expected age of Salma?
questions.initialExplanation: Alternate hopping, drawing a triangle, counting 10 objects and naming 4 colors = 5 years (60 months).
questions.detailedExplanation:
- Skipping is a gross motor milestone typically achieved by 5 years (60 months).

- Drawing a triangle from copy, naming four colors, and identifying the heavier of two weights reflect fine motor and
cognitive development consistent with a 5-year-old.

- Counting 10 pennies correctly (demonstrating one-to-one correspondence and number understanding) and asking
questions about word meanings are language and numeracy skills expected around 60 months.

- Independent dressing and undressing is well-established by this age.

Why not other options?

- 48 months (4 years): Children can usually draw a person with 2—4 body parts, copy a cross or square, and may know 2-3
colors—but not typically a triangle, nor reliably count 10 objects or compare weights. Skipping is also uncommon before 5
years.

- 72 months (6 years): Exceeds the described abilities; by then, children can usually copy more complex shapes (e.g.,
diamond), read simple words, and understand basic arithmetic concepts beyond counting.

---

questions.stem: A normal height mother brought her 2-year-old son whose height is 90 cm asking you about the expected adult height of her son, you answer that the approximate adult height is :
questions.initialExplanation: A child's height at 2 years is about half the expected adult height: 90 cm x 2 = 180 cm.
questions.detailedExplanation:
A commonly used clinical rule of thumb is that a child’s adult height can be roughly estimated by doubling their
height at age 2 years.

The child’s current height = 90 cm

Estimated adult height =90 cm x 2 = 180 cm

This method provides a reasonable approximation for boys at age 2, as they are typically close to half their
eventual adult height at this age.

- Although mid-parental height would refine this estimate further, the question states the mother is of normal
height and does not provide the father’s height. In the absence of additional data, the doubling method is
appropriate and points clearly to 180 cm.

---

questions.stem: A 1-year-old child presents with repetitive, stereotyped, and rhythmic movements in the form of head banging and body rocking. These behaviors typically occur with the transition to sleep at bedtime, but also at nap times and after nighttime arousals. Of the following, the MOST important aspect in management is :
questions.initialExplanation: Repetitive rhythmic movements at bedtime in a 1-year-old (rhythmic movement disorder) is a benign condition, and the key is reassuring the family.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Repetitive, stereotyped, and rhythmic movements such as head banging and body rocking that occur around sleep
transitions in a 1-year-old are characteristic of benign sleep-related rhythmic movement disorder, which is common in
infancy and typically resolves by school age. These behaviors are often self-soothing mechanisms used to help the child
relax and fall asleep, and they are not indicative of epilepsy or neurological pathology when occurring in an otherwise
developmentally normal child.

EEG (A), MRI brain (B), neurology referral (C), and antiepileptic drugs (E) are not indicated unless there are additional red
flags, such as: Daytime seizures, Developmental regression, Asynchronous or asymmetric movements, Movements
occurring outside of sleep-wake transitions

In the absence of such concerns, parental reassurance—along with safety measures like padding the crib or moving it
away from the wall—is the cornerstone of management.

---

questions.stem: An infant can regard his parent’s face, follow to the midline, lift his head from the examining table, smile spontaneously, and respond to a bell. He does not yet regard his own hand, follow past the midline, nor lift his head to a 45° angle off the examining table. Which of the following is the most likely age of the infant? (pretest)
questions.initialExplanation: Follows a face to the midline and lifts the head 45° = about 1 month of age.
questions.detailedExplanation:
At one month infants typically regard face, follow items to the midline, begin to vocalize, respond to a
bell,and lift their head from the examining table. An 8-week-old child normally should be able to smile
and coo when smiled at or talked to. Not until about 3 months of age would an infant be expected to
follow a moving toy from side to side and also in the vertical plane. Such skills as maintaining a seated
position are developed at about 6 to 8 months of age.

---

questions.stem: A child is brought to your clinic for a routine examination. She can put ona T-shirt but requires a bit of help dressing otherwise. She can copy a circle wellbut has difficulty in copying a square. Her speech is understandable and she knows four colors. She balances proudly on each foot for 2 seconds but is unable to hold the stance for 5 seconds. Which of the following is the most likely age of this child? (pretest)
questions.initialExplanation: Standing on one foot for 5 seconds: mastered at about 4 years.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Four- and five-year-old children begin to be able to copy a square; children younger than this age have
difficulty with this task. By 4 years of age the language should be fully understandable and children
begin to be able to name four colors, define five words, and know three adjectives. A 4-year-old can
stand on each leg for 2 seconds, and by 5 years of age that skill can be maintained for at least 5
seconds. A 4-year-old may require some help with some clothing, but by 5 years of age they are able
to dress themselves independently.

---

questions.stem: Third-year medical students are rotating in the normal newborn nursery. The students learn that most neonates actually lose weight after birth. One student asks what the average rate of weight gain is following the initial period of weight loss. After 2 weeks of age, a term neonate will gain an average of which of the following increments of weight? (Lange)
questions.initialExplanation: After the first two weeks, a newborn gains about 30 g per day.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Newborns may lose up to 10% of their birth weight in the first few days of life, but with normal nutrition
birth weight is regained in approximately 10 days. The infant subsequently gains approximately 30
g/day for the first several months.

---

questions.stem: A mother brings her 6-month-old son in for a checkup. She is concerned that when she is playing with him and puts a toy behind her back, he does not try to find it. Object permanence, the understanding that objects continue to exist even when not seen, is a major milestone that occurs closest to which of the following ages? (Lange)
questions.initialExplanation: Object permanence develops at 9-12 months.
questions.detailedExplanation:
At 9-12 months, infants gradually develop the concept of object permanence, or the under standing
that objects exist even when they are not seen. Around the time this milestone is achieved, infants
develop frontal activity on the electroencephalogram. Infants first apply this concept of object
permanence to the image of their mother because of her emotional importance; this realization is a
critical part of attachment behavior.

---

questions.stem: A worried mother brings her 2-year-old to the pediatrician for a well-child check. She is concerned because the child still has only 50 words in his vocabulary. Which of the following best describes the characteristic age of a toddler who speaks 50 words? (Lange)
questions.initialExplanation: The child says about 50 words at 24 months.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Following the realization that words can stand for things, the child’s vocabulary balloons from about
10-15 words at 18 months to 100 or more at 3 years. After 18 months, there is a dramatic increase in
expressive and receptive vocabulary and by the end of the second year, a quantum leap occurs in

language development, such that most children presenting for their 2-year-old checkup are reported
to say at least 50 words

---

questions.stem: The mother of a 3-year-old boy reports that he is “on the go” all the time. Typically, children stop taking daytime naps at which of the following ages? (Lange)
questions.initialExplanation: A child usually stops daytime naps at about 4 years (48 months).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Even during the neonatal period, up to 10 of an infant’s average of 16 hours of sleep per day are
concentrated at night. This is reflective of an adaptation process which began in the third trimester of
pregnancy. Daytime sleep progressively declines in infancy; the 12-month-old typically takes two 1-

hour naps during the day. By the age of 3, most toddlers sleep 1 hour during the day, and the majority
of 4-year-olds do not take a daytime nap.

---

questions.stem: A 1-week-old infant male presents to his primary care provider’s office for his first visit. His mother is concerned because he sleeps a lot. Which of the following is the average amount of sleep per day experienced by infants in the first month of life? (Lange)
questions.initialExplanation: An infant needs about 16 hours of sleep daily in the first month.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The majority of a newborn’s early days are spent sleeping. Total requirements for sleep are 16 hr/24
hr in the first month of life, with most of the sleeping hours concentrated at night. Sleep requirements

decline slowly over the first year. By the age of 9 months, the average infant sleeps 14 hr/day and by
3 years of age, most toddlers sleep 12 hr/day.

---

questions.stem: First-time parents of a 1-month-old are anxious to hear what they can expect in the next few months. Which of the following best describes the usual sequence for attainment of gross motor milestones in a young infant? (Lange)

options.label: A
options.text: head control, rolling over, hands together in midline, sits without support

options.label: B
options.text: head control, hands together in midline, rolling over, pulls to stand

options.label: C
options.text: rolls over, sits without support, hands together in midline, pulls to stand

options.label: D
options.text: sits without support, hands together in midline, pulls to stand, walks along

options.label: E
options.text: pulls to stand, walks along table, sits without support, hands together at midline

questions.initialExplanation: Gross motor sequence: head control, hands at midline, rolling, then pulling to stand.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The attainment of gross motor milestones begins at approximately 2 months of age with steady head
control. This allows better visual interaction between infants and parents. The child is then able to be
pulled to sit without head lag at around 3 months of age. Putting hands together in the midline at
around 3 months of age allows the infant to examine objects in the midline and manipulate them with
both hands. Once the asymmetric Tonic neck reflex is gone, at around 4 months of age, infants are
able to begin to roll over, first from stomach to back and finally around 6 months of age from back to
stomach. Infants will sit without support at approximately 6 months of age and will pull to stand and
cruise around furniture by 9 months of age. The average age of beginning to walk alone is 12 months.

---

questions.stem: The parents of a 15 month old are concerned that their daughter does not seem to be able to stack cubes into a tower like their son could at the same age. Her pediatrician reviews the child’s prior fine motor development with the parents. Which of the following best describes the correct sequence of fine motor development one should see in a healthy infant/toddler? (Lange)

options.label: A
options.text: thumb—finger grasp, grasps rattle, transfers objects from hand to hand

options.label: B
options.text: grasps rattle, thumb—finger grasp, reaches for objects, transfers objects from hand to hand

options.label: C
options.text: grasps rattle, transfers objects from hand to hand, builds tower of two cubes, thumb—finger grasp

options.label: D
options.text: reaches for objects, transfers objects from hand to hand, turns pages of book, builds tower of two cubes

options.label: E
options.text: grasps rattle, transfers objects from hand to hand, thumb—finger grasp, builds tower of two cubes

questions.initialExplanation: Fine motor sequence: grasps a rattle, transfers hand to hand, then pincer grasp, then builds a block tower.
questions.detailedExplanation:
two cubes

Around the same time as the infant is able to put hands together in the midline, he is able to grasp
objects and examine them. This occurs at an average of 3.5 months of age. He can transfer objects
from hand to hand at approximately 5.5 months of age, allowing him to compare objects. He attains
thumb—finger grasp at approximately 8 months of age, at which time he begins to feed himself finger
foods. At around 1 year of age he is able to turn pages in a book, and by 13 months of age he has
attained sufficient visual-motor coordination to scribble. By 15 months of age he can build a tower of
two cubes, using objects in combination, and by 22 months of age he can build his tower up to six
cubes, which requires visual, gross, and fine motor coordination.

---

questions.stem: A 7-month-old infant presents for well-child care and the physician notes a well-developed Moro reflex, palmar grasp reflex, and tonic neck reflexes on examination. The persistence of neonatal reflexes is an indicator of develop mental delay, he tells the mother of the infant. At which age should the Moro reflex typically disappear?
questions.initialExplanation: The Moro reflex disappears at 3-6 months in most references, and the given answer is 6-8 months; persistence beyond that is a sign of delay.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Reflex movement begins in fetal development as early as 9 weeks gestation. However, most of the
reflexes associated with the newborn develop between 20 and 38 weeks gestation. The Moro reflex

‘    disappears by 7 months of age. Palmar grasp usually disappears by 6 months of age, facilitating
release of objects. The Tonic neck reflex, which is elicited by turning the infant’s head, resulting in
extension of the arm and leg on the side toward which the head is turned and flexion of the opposite
side, disappears by 8 months of age, unless myelinization or brain development is pathologic. The
Babinski (upgoing toes) sign, which develops in an infant just prior to term, does not disappear until
16 months of age, when adequate myelinization has occurred.

---

questions.stem: A 6-month-old infant is being evaluated during a well-child visit. Head circumference is 44 cm. What is the approximate expected head circumference at 1 year of age?
questions.initialExplanation: Head circumference at 6 months is 44 cm, reaching about 47 cm by one year.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Brain growth occurs almost exclusively during the early years of life. Head circumference (OFC) is
approximately 35 cm at birth, increases to about 47 cm by 1 year of age, and reaches approximately
55 cm in adulthood. At birth, the brain is 25% of adult size and reaches 75% of adult size by 1 year.
Full brain development is not achieved until adolescence. Rapid head growth in the first year reflects
the critical period of brain development and myelination. Abnormal head circumference (microcephaly
or macrocephaly) may indicate underlying neurological pathology.

---

questions.stem: A mother brings her 5-month-old infant for routine evaluation. She reports that her baby has been growing well. The infant's birth weight was 3.5 kg. What is the expected current weight?
questions.initialExplanation: Birth weight doubles by 5 months: 3.5 x 2 = 7 kg.
questions.detailedExplanation:
During infancy, growth follows a rapid but decelerating pattern. The average infant's birth weight
doubles within 5 months and triples by 1 year. A birth weight of 3.5 kg would be expected to double to
approximately 7 kg by 5 months of age. Length increases by approximately 30% at 5 months and
reaches 50% above birth length at 1 year. By age 2-3 years, the child's stature reflects their own
genetic endowment rather than maternal size and health. Growth velocity slows after the first year,
with childhood growth occurring at a rate of 5-6 cm per year.

---

questions.stem: A 6-month-old infant has not yet developed head control. When pulled to sitting position, the head lags significantly. Which developmental field is most delayed?
questions.initialExplanation: Poor head control (head lag) at 6 months = gross motor delay.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Head control is a gross motor milestone. By 4-6 months, infants should have good head control when
pulled to sitting, with minimal or no head lag. Gross motor development involves the development of
locomotion and large muscle control. Delay in head control may indicate neurological disorders such
as cerebral palsy, hypotonia, or developmental delay. The other developmental fields (fine motor,
language, social) are assessed separately. Gross motor milestones typically develop in a predictable
sequence: head control precedes rolling, sitting, crawling, standing, and walking.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old preschooler can dress partially but needs help with buttons and laces. She can use scissors to cut paper. These skills reflect development in which domain?
questions.initialExplanation: Partial dressing and cutting paper = fine motor skills.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Dressing skills, using scissors, and button manipulation are fine motor skills requiring eye-hand
coordination anddexterity. By 4 years, children can dress partially with help for difficult tasks. By 5-6
years, they can dress independently. Fine motor development progresses from grasp patterns in
infancy to precise manipulation in the preschool years. Gross motor involves large muscle groups
and locomotion. Language involves verbal communication. Social-emotional involves interactions
and emotional regulation. Understanding developmental domains helps identify specific areas of
delay.

---

questions.stem: A concerned mother brings her 10-month-old son for evaluation. She reports that he was born prematurely at 28 weeks gestation and has been followed in the neonatal intensive care unit for 3 months before discharge. At his current corrected age of 7 months, he can roll from supine to prone but cannot yet sit independently. His paternal grandmother mentions that she observed the parachute reflex when the baby was suspended face down. Which of the following statements regarding the parachute reflex is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: The parachute reflex persists throughout life \*

options.label: B
options.text: The parachute reflex typically appears at 8-9 months of age and never disappears

options.label: C
options.text: The parachute reflex appears at 3-4 months and is absent in cerebral palsy

options.label: D
options.text: The parachute reflex is a primitive reflex that indicates upper motor neuron lesion if absent

options.label: E
options.text: The parachute reflex appears before the lateral propping reflex in normal development

questions.initialExplanation: The parachute reflex appears at 8-9 months and does not disappear.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The parachute reflex is a postural (secondary) reflex that normally appears at 8-9 months of age and
persists throughout life. It is tested by suspending the infant face down and observing for symmetric
arm extension as though to save themselves from falling. This reflex never disappears and its
absence after 9 months is abnormal. The infant's corrected age of 7 months is slightly early for this
reflex to be present, but its presence is reassuring.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old girl is brought for preschool evaluation. Her parents report that she can draw a circle, can name four colors, and knows her first name. She can hop on one foot, rides a tricycle well, and can dress herself except for tying shoelaces. She engages in cooperative play with other children and can take turns. Which of the following developmental tasks would be most challenging for her at this age?

options.label: B
options.text: Drawing a person with at least 6 body parts

options.label: C
options.text: Using a spoon and fork independently

options.label: E
options.text: Walking up and down stairs alternating feet

questions.initialExplanation: The concept of conservation (constancy of quantity) is hard for a 5-year-old because it appears in middle childhood (about 6-7 years).
questions.detailedExplanation:
The child demonstrates age-appropriate development across all four developmental domains. However, the
concept of conservation, which is the understanding that quantity remains the same despite changes in shape
or appearance, is typically achieved during the concrete operational stage of cognitive development according
to Piaget's theory. This concept is usually not fully understood until 7-11 years of age, making it the most
challenging task among the options for a 5-year-old.

- Option A is incorrect because building a tower of 9-10 blocks is a typical fine motor skill for a 5-year-old.
Option B is incorrect because drawing a person with multiple body parts is expected by age 5. Option C is
incorrect because using utensils independently is typically achieved by 4-5 years of age. Option E is incorrect
because walking up and down stairs alternating feet is a gross motor milestone usually achieved by 4-5 years

---

questions.stem: A 2-month-old infant is brought for well-child visit. The infant was born at 38 weeks gestation with birth weight 3.0 kg. The mother reports that the baby feeds well and sleeps for 4-5 hour stretches at night. On examination, the infant weighs 5.2 kg (50th percentile), length is 58 cm (50th percentile), and head circumference is 40 cm (50th percentile). The parents ask about expected weight gain. Which of the following is the most accurate statement?

options.label: A
options.text: Birth weight should double by 3 months and triple by 6 months

options.label: B
options.text: Birth weight should double by 5 months and triple by 12 months

options.label: C
options.text: Birth weight should increase by 200-250 grams per week during the first 3 months

options.label: D
options.text: Birth weight should increase by 100 grams per week \*

options.label: E
options.text: Birth weight should increase by 150-200 grams per week during the first 3 months Birth weight should triple by 6 months of age

questions.initialExplanation: Birth weight doubles by 5 months and triples by one year.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The expected weight gain pattern in infancy is that birth weight doubles by approximately 5 months of
age and triples by 1 year of age. This represents the rapid but decelerating growth velocity

‘    characteristic of the infantile growth phase. The infant described is tracking appropriately at the 50th
percentile for weight.
- Option A is incorrect because birth weight doubles by 5 months, not 3 months. Option C is incorrect
because the expected weight gain during the first 3 months is 150-200 grams per week (about 600-
800 grams per month), not 200-250 grams per week. Option D is incorrect because while 150-200
grams per week is the typical gain, this option is incomplete as it doesn't address the longer-term
milestones. Option E is incorrect because birth weight triples by 12 months, not 6 months.

---

questions.stem: A 3-month-old infant does not smile socially, track objects past midline, or coo. He lifts his head briefly during tummy time but has persistent fisting. Birth history is uncomplicated. What is the most concerning finding?
questions.initialExplanation: The more worrying finding: absence of a social smile at 3 months.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Social smile should be robust by 2-3 months; its absence is a major red flag for neurodevelopmental
disorders like autism or cerebral injury. Visual tracking and cooing also emerge by 2-3 months but
show more variability. Persistent fisting and head lag may reflect mild motor delay but are less
specific. Lack of social engagement is the strongest predictor of later impairment. Immediate referral
for developmental assessment and vision/hearing screening is warranted.

---

questions.stem: A 10-month-old infant is brought for developmental evaluation. The infant was born at 36 weeks gestation with birth weight 2.4 kg. The infant is now at a corrected age of 8.5 months. The parents report that the baby can sit independently, can pull to stand, and has begun to cruise. The infant says "mama" and "dada" nonspecifically and uses a crude pincer grasp. On examination, the lateral propping reflex is present and symmetric. Which of the following developmental assessments is most appropriate based on corrected age?

options.label: A
options.text: All milestones are appropriate for corrected age

options.label: B
options.text: Language development is delayed for corrected age

options.label: C
options.text: Gross motor development is delayed for corrected age

options.label: D
options.text: Fine motor development is delayed for corrected age

options.label: E
options.text: The infant demonstrates advanced development for corrected age

questions.initialExplanation: In a premature infant development is assessed by corrected age.
questions.detailedExplanation:
When using corrected age (chronological age minus weeks of prematurity), this infant's corrected age
is 8.5 months. At 8-9 months corrected age, the expected milestones include sitting independently,
pulling to stand, beginning to cruise, nonspecific babbling ("mama"/'dada"), and crude pincer grasp.
The lateral propping reflex should also be present at this age. All of the described milestones are
appropriate for the corrected age.

- Option B is incorrect because nonspecific use of "mama" and "dada" is appropriate for 8-9 months.
Option C is incorrect because sitting independently, pulling to stand, and cruising are appropriate
gross motor milestones. Option D is incorrect because crude pincer grasp is appropriate for this age.
Option E is incorrect because the development is appropriate, not advanced.

---

questions.stem: A 2-month-old infant is examined in the pediatric clinic. The infant was born at 41 weeks gestation with birth weight 3.6 kg. On examination, the infant demonstrates the rooting reflex, palmar grasp, Moro reflex, and stepping reflex. The infant has good head control when prone and when pulled to sit shows minimal head lag. Which of the following statements is most accurate regarding primitive reflex development?

options.label: A
options.text: All primitive reflexes should be present at this age

options.label: B
options.text: The stepping reflex typically disappears by 2 months

options.label: C
options.text: The Moro reflex should have disappeared by 2 months

options.label: D
options.text: The palmar grasp reflex typically disappears by 2 months

options.label: E
options.text: All primitive reflexes persist throughout infancy

questions.initialExplanation: The stepping reflex disappears at about 2 months.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The stepping reflex (walking or dance reflex) is a primitive reflex that is present at birth but typically
disappears by 2 months of age. It involves stepping movements when the infant is held vertically with
the feet touching a surface. The other primitive reflexes described (rooting, palmar grasp, Moro) are
still expected to be present at 2 months of age.

- Option A is incorrect because not all primitive reflexes are present at this age; the stepping reflex is
about to disappear. Option C is incorrect because the Moro reflex typically disappears between 2-4
months, so it may still be present at 2 months. Option D is incorrect because the palmar grasp

persists until 5-6 months. Option E is incorrect because primitive reflexes gradually disappear as the
nervous system matures.

---

questions.stem: A mother to a 4-year-old child who has pauses and repetitions of initial sounds visited outpatients department. Of the following, the MOST appropriate advice is : (NE)

options.label: A
options.text: this is a normal phenomenon affecting about 5% of preschool children

options.label: B
options.text: there is no need for action as 80% of affected children recover by their own

options.label: C
options.text: tries to reduce pressures associated with speaking

options.label: D
options.text: I'll refer him to ENT specialist for further evaluation

options.label: E
options.text: I'll refer him to speech therapist

questions.initialExplanation: Developmental stuttering in a 4-year-old is managed by reducing speech-related pressure and encouraging the child without punishment.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The 4-year-old child exhibits pauses and repetitions of initial sounds, which are classic features of developmental
stuttering—a common speech disfluency in preschool-aged children.

C. "Tries to reduce pressures associated with speaking"

— This is the cornerstone of initial management in developmental stuttering. Parents should be advised to:
Avoid interrupting or correcting the child

Speak slowly and calmly

Create a relaxed communication environment

Not pressure the child to “speak properly” or perform verbally

This evidence-based, first-line strategy reduces anxiety and prevents worsening of disfluency.

---

questions.stem: Ali can sit on small chair; walks up stairs with 1 hand held; makes tower of 4 cubes; and can name pictures. What is the expected age of Ali?
questions.initialExplanation: Sits on a small chair, climbs stairs with one hand held and builds a tower of 4 blocks = 18 months.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- Sitting on a small chair, walking up stairs with one hand held, building a tower of 4 cubes, and naming pictures
are all developmental milestones typically achieved around 18 months of age.

- At 12 months, children usually walk with support or independently but cannot yet climb stairs with assistance
or build a 4-cube tower.

- By 15 months, some may walk up stairs with two-hand support and stack 2-3 cubes, but naming pictures is
less consistent.

- At 24 months, children can typically build towers of 6-7 cubes, walk up stairs with alternating feet (with
support), and use 2-word phrases—surpassing the described abilities.

- 30 months is too advanced, as children at that age can copy circles, kick a ball, and speak in short sentences.
Thus, 18 months best fits the constellation of milestones described.

---

questions.stem: Salem runs well, opens doors; climbs on furniture; makes tower of 7 cubes, puts 3 words together; handles spoon well; and helps to undress. What is the expected age of Salem?
questions.initialExplanation: Runs, opens doors, builds a tower of 7 blocks and combines three words = 24 months.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- Running well, climbing on furniture, and opening doors are typical gross motor skills seen by 24
months.

- A tower of 7 cubes aligns with fine motor development at 24 months (typically 6-7 cubes; 18-month-
olds usually manage only 3—4).

- Putting 3 words together reflects language development consistent with a 2-year-old (24 months); 18-
month-olds typically use single words or 2-word phrases.

- Handling a spoon well and helping to undress are self-care milestones generally achieved around 24
months.

---

## Down & Turner

> Question numbers not present in the source file for this topic: 16, 22.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy is evaluated for progressive muscle weakness. He had delayed walking and now has trouble climbing stairs and rising from the floor, using his hands to push upon his thighs (Gower's sign). His serum creatine kinase level is markedly elevated. A maternal uncle had a similar condition and was wheelchair-bound by adolescence. Which inheritance pattern best describes this condition?
questions.initialExplanation: Progressive muscle weakness in a boy with loss of walking in adolescence = Duchenne muscular dystrophy, X-linked recessive inheritance.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This 6-year-old boy presents with classic features of Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD): progressive proximal muscle
weakness, delayed motor milestones (delayed walking), difficulty with activities requiring leg strength (climbing stairs, rising
from floor), Gower's sign (using hands to "walk" up the legs to stand), markedly elevated creatine kinase (CK) levels, and a
positive family history affecting a maternal uncle. The inheritance pattern of X-linked recessive perfectly explains the clinical
presentation and family history.

- Duchenne muscular dystrophy is the most common and severe form of muscular dystrophy, affecting approximately 1 in
3,500-5,000 male births. It is caused by mutations in the DMD gene located on the short arm of the X chromosome (Xp21),
which encodes the protein dystrophin. Dystrophin is essential for maintaining muscle cell membrane integrity during muscle
contractions. Without functional dystrophin, muscle fibers are damaged with use, leading to progressive weakness and
replacement of muscle with fat and connective tissue.

---

questions.stem: A couple has a child with Down syndrome due to a chromosome 21 translocation. They are now planning another pregnancy and ask about the risk of recurrence. What is the MOST appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Reassure that the recurrence risk equals that of the general population \*

options.label: B
options.text: Offer an early ultrasound in the next pregnancy

options.label: C
options.text: Recommend chromosomal testing (karyotype) for both parents

options.label: D
options.text: Advise that all future children will likely be affected

options.label: E
options.text: Refer for in vitro fertilization with preimplantation genetic testing

questions.initialExplanation: Down syndrome due to a chromosome 21 translocation: karyotyping of the parents is advised because one may be a carrier, which raises recurrence risk.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This couple has a child with Down syndrome caused by a chromosome 21 translocation. The key clinical
question is determining the recurrence risk for future pregnancies and providing appropriate genetic counseling.
The most critical first step is to determine whether one of the parents is a balanced translocation carrier, as this
significantly impacts recurrence risk.

- Down syndrome is typically caused by trisomy 21 (nondisjunction), which accounts for approximately 95% of
cases and has a recurrence risk of approximately 1% (or the age-related risk, whichever is higher). However,
approximately 3-4% of Down syndrome cases are due to Robertsonian translocations involving chromosome
21. In these cases, the extra genetic material from chromosome 21 is attached to another acrocentric
chromosome (most commonly chromosome 14).

---

questions.stem: A 5-month-old female is admitted for surgical treatment of preductal coarctation of the aorta. During evaluation, the patient is found to have a horseshoe kidney as well as lymphedema affecting the hands and feet. The patient has low-set ears. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: A heart defect with hand and foot lymphedema and low-set ears in a girl = Turner syndrome.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This 5-month-old female infant presents with multiple congenital anomalies: preductal coarctation of
the aorta, horseshoe kidney, lymphedema of hands and feet, and low-set ears. The constellation of
cardiovascular, renal, and lymphatic abnormalities in a female infant is highly suggestive of Turner
syndrome, which results from complete or partial absence of the second X chromosome.

- Turner syndrome (45,X) is a chromosomal disorder affecting females, with an incidence of
approximately 1 in 2,500 live female births. It results from complete or partial monosomy X, with the
classic karyotype being 45,X (approximately 45-50% of cases). Other variants include mosaicism (45,
X/46,XX) and structural abnormalities of the X chromosome (isochromosome Xq, deletions, rings).

---

questions.stem: A newborn infant is brought due to dysmorphic features. Upon examination, there is upward slanting of the eyes, hypotonia, a flat facial profile, a flattened occiput, epicanthal folds, and abdominal distension. Which of the following conditions is the MOST likely cause of the infant's dysmorphic features?
questions.initialExplanation: Typical features (epicanthal folds and a flat occiput) and a distended abdomen (duodenal atresia) = trisomy 21.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This newborn presents with classic dysmorphic features highly suggestive of Down syndrome
(Trisomy 21). The constellation of facial features, hypotonia, and abdominal distension is
characteristic and should prompt immediate chromosomal testing and evaluation for associated
medical conditions.

- Down syndrome is the most common chromosomal disorder, with an incidence of approximately 1
in 700-1,000 live births. It results from the presence of a third copy of chromosome 21 (either
complete trisomy, Robertsonian translocation, or mosaicism). The phenotype results from
overexpression of genes on chromosome 21 and the resulting effects on development.

---

questions.stem: An affected father transmits status to all his daughters but none of his sons. Which disorder follows the same rule of inheritance?
questions.initialExplanation: An affected father passes the disease to all daughters and no sons: X-linked dominant (e.g., hypophosphatemic rickets).
questions.detailedExplanation:
This question addresses the fundamental principles of X-linked inheritance patterns. The scenario
describes an affected father who transmits his condition to all his daughters but none of his sons.
Understanding the pattern of transmission is essential for genetic counseling and diagnosis.

- In humans, females have two X chromosomes (XX), and males have one X and one Y
chromosome (XY). The sex chromosomes are inherited as follows: males inherit their X
chromosome from their mother and their Y chromosome from their father; females inherit one X
chromosome from each parent.

---

questions.stem: A couple of 38-year-old husband and a 23-year-old wife with Down syndrome consult you because the husband is planning to have a baby, he asks you about the chance of having a baby with Down syndrome, if his wife becomes pregnant. Your proper answer, the chance of having Down syndrome is : (NE)
questions.initialExplanation: A mother with Down syndrome (non-mosaic trisomy 21) passes the extra chromosome to about half her children: 50% risk.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Down syndrome is most commonly caused by trisomy 21 (95% of cases), which typically arises from maternal
meiotic nondisjunction and is not inherited. However, when a person with Down syndrome has children, the
reproductive implications differ by sex.

- Women with Down syndrome are generally fertile, and studies show they have approximately a 50% chance
of conceiving a child with Down syndrome or another chromosomal abnormality. This is because during
oogenesis, a woman with trisomy 21 can produce eggs with either one or two copies of chromosome 21 due to
irregular segregation; roughly half the viable gametes carry an extra chromosome 21.

- In contrast, men with Down syndrome are usually infertile, but this question involves a female with Down
syndrome (the 23-year-old wife) who is capable of pregnancy. Therefore, the risk that her child will have Down

syndrome is about 50%, though some pregnancies may end in miscarriage due to severe chromosomal
imbalances.

---

questions.stem: A 3-week-old small for gestational age newborn presents with webbing of the neck, protruding ears, and non-pitting swellings of the hands and feet. Echo shows bicuspid aortic valve with coarctation of the aorta. Of the following, the MOST likely diagnosis is : (NE)
questions.initialExplanation: Neck webbing, coarctation and a bicuspid aortic valve in a young girl = Turner syndrome.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This neonate presents with a classic constellation of findings highly suggestive of Turner syndrome (45,X):

- Webbed neck (due to fetal lymphedema)

- Peripheral lymphedema causing non-pitting swelling of hands and feet (a hallmark in newborns with Turner syndrome)
- Small for gestational age (prenatal growth restriction is common)

- Cardiac anomalies, specifically bicuspid aortic valve and coarctation of the aorta—both are strongly associated with
Turner syndrome

- Protruding or low-set ears may also be seen, though less specific

Turner syndrome occurs exclusively in females due to complete or partial absence of one X chromosome. While the
question doesn’t explicitly state the infant’s sex, the clinical features are so characteristic that Turner syndrome remains
the most likely diagnosis, and in practice, this presentation would prompt karyotype testing confirming 45,X or variant.

---

questions.stem: A newborn infant is noted to have dysmorphic features. The pregnancy was complicated by breech presentation, decreased fetal movements, and polyhydramnios. The child demonstrates hypotonia, a flat face, flattened occiput, epicanthal folds, and abdominal distention. The most likely cause of this child's dysmorphology is: (NE)
questions.initialExplanation: Characteristic features and a distended abdomen (duodenal atresia) in a newborn = Down syndrome (trisomy 21).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Although there is variability in the clinical features, the constellation of phenotypic features is fairly
consistent and permits clinical recognition of trisomy 21

---

questions.stem: Friends are considering adopting a “special needs” child from another country. The family has few details, but the information they have received so far suggests the 4-year-old child has had surgery for an endocardial cushion defect, is short for his age, and had a history of what sounds like surgically repaired duodenal atresia at birth. You are suspicious this child may have which of the following syndromes? (pretest)
questions.initialExplanation: Duodenal atresia at birth = Down syndrome.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Down syndrome has many diagnostic features, including short stature, microcephaly, centrally placed
hair whorl, small ears, redundant skin on the nape of the neck, upslanting palpebral fissures,
epicanthal folds, flat nasal bridge, Brushfield spots, protruding tongue, short and broad hands, simian
creases, widely spaced first and second toe, and hypotonia. Cardiac lesions are found in 30% to 50%
of children with Down syndrome, including endocardial cushion defect (30%), VSD (30%), and
tetralogy of Fallot (about 30%). At birth, duodenal atresia is a common finding. It causes bilious
vomiting and a characteristic KUB radiographic findings of a double bubble (dilatation of the stomach
and the proximal duodenum).

---

questions.stem: A 4-month-old female infant has generalized hypotonia, small ears, inner epicanthal folds, clinodactyly, and wide-spaced first and second toes. For which of the following problems is she most at risk?(Lange)
questions.initialExplanation: An infant girl with hypotonia, small ears, clinodactyly and a gap between the first two toes: most at risk of hearing loss.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The described patient has classical signs and symptoms of trisomy 21. The occurrence of trisomy 21
or Down syndrome increases with advancing maternal age. There is no single physical finding that
makes a diagnosis of Down syndrome; rather, the combination of minor and major anomalies often
leads to a diagnosis. All the listed anomalies are more common in Down syndrome, however, hearing
loss affecting more than 60% of patients is the most common. About 40% of patients have cardiac
abnormalities with endocardial cushion defect being the most common.

---

questions.stem: What is the most important test to obtain a diagnosis in a 14-year-old girl with primary amenorrhea, and short stature, who has a history of repaired coarctation of the aorta in infancy?

options.label: C
options.text: fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) of chromosome 22q11

questions.initialExplanation: A girl with primary amenorrhea, short stature and a history of coarctation: the test needed is karyotype (Turner).
questions.detailedExplanation:
The patient has classical findings of Turner syndrome. Patients with this syndrome have an XO
karyotype. Short stature is the cardinal finding in all girls with Turner syndrome. Ovarian dysgenesis
is present and sexual maturation usually fails to occur, although a small percent age of girls may
have spontaneous breast development and menstrual periods. Other clinical features that may be
present are webbed neck,low hairline, and wide-spaced nipples. Cardiac defects occur in about half
of the patients and bicuspid aortic valves are the most commonly found abnormality. Renal
abnormalities, such as horseshoe kidney, occur in a majority of patients.

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old girl is brought to the pediatric clinic for a routine well-child visit. On examination, you notice upward-slanting palpebral fissures, epicanthal folds, and a flat nasal bridge. Her mother mentions that she has a protruding tongue that she constantly keeps sticking out. The child has global developmental delay with an estimated developmental age of 12 months. Which of the following is the most common chromosomal abnormality associated with this child's condition?
questions.initialExplanation: The commonest cause of Down syndrome is trisomy 21 from meiotic nondisjunction.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child presents with classic clinical features of Down syndrome (trisomy 21), including characteristic facial
features (upward-slanting palpebral fissures, epicanthal folds, flat nasal bridge, macroglossia) and
developmental delay. Full trisomy 21 due to meiotic nondisjunction accounts for approximately 95% of all Down
syndrome cases. This occurs when there is failure of chromosome 21 to separate during meiosis, resulting in
an extra copy of chromosome 21 in all cells. The risk of nondisjunction increases with maternal age, and
approximately 70% of cases result from maternal nondisjunction during meiosis |, 20% during meiosis Il, and
5% from paternal nondisjunction during meiosis Il.

- Robertsonian translocation accounts for only 3-4% of cases, while mosaicism accounts for 1-2% of cases.
Monosomy X is Turner syndrome, and Klinefelter syndrome is 47,XXY.

---

questions.stem: A 35-year-old pregnant woman undergoes routine prenatal screening at 12 weeks of gestation. The combined first-trimester test shows increased nuchal translucency on ultrasound and abnormal serum markers (low PAPP-A, elevated free B-hCG). Which confirmatory diagnostic test is most appropriate for definitive diagnosis at this gestational age? 2999720997920099220992°0°099°°0992°0092°00927907°
questions.initialExplanation: For definitive early diagnosis in pregnancy: chorionic villus sampling (CVS) at 10-13 weeks.
questions.detailedExplanation:
At 12 weeks of gestation, chorionic villus sampling (CVS) is the most appropriate confirmatory
diagnostic test for Down syndrome. CVS is performed between 9-14 weeks of gestation and involves
obtaining a sample of placental tissue (chorionic villi) for genetic analysis. It has the advantage of
earlier diagnosis compared to amniocentesis, allowing for earlier decision-making regarding
pregnancy management.

- Amniocentesis is performed at 15-22 weeks and involves sampling of amniotic fluid. Percutaneous
umbilical cord blood sampling (cordocentesis) is performed at 18-22 weeks and is primarily used
when rapid karyotyping is needed or when other methods have failed. Cell-free DNA testing is a
screening test, not a diagnostic test. The quad screen is a second-trimester screening test performed
at 15-18 weeks.

---

questions.stem: A newborn male infant is examined shortly after birth. The obstetrician notes excessive skin at the nape of the neck and a single transverse palmar crease. On physical examination, you observe hypotonia, a small oral cavity with a protruding tongue, and low-set ears. The infant is also noted to have a heart murmur. Which cardiac malformation is most commonly associated with this condition?
questions.initialExplanation: The commonest heart defect with Down syndrome: atrioventricular septal defect.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This newborn has classic features of Down syndrome. Congenital heart defects occur in approximately
50% of individuals with Down syndrome. The most common cardiac malformation is atrioventricular

‘    septal defect (AVSD), also known as endocardial cushion defect, which accounts for approximately
40-50% of all congenital heart defects in Down syndrome patients. AVSD involves a defect in the atrial
septum, ventricular septum, and atrioventricular valves, resulting in a common AV valve.
- Other common cardiac defects include ventricular septal defect (VSD), atrial septal defect (ASD),
tetralogy of Fallot (TOF), and patent ductus arteriosus (PDA). While all of these can occur in Down
syndrome, AVSD is the most characteristic and common presentation.

---

questions.stem: A 6-month-old infant with Down syndrome is found to have a heart murmur on routine examination. Echocardiogram reveals a ventricular septal defect with left-to-right shunting. The parents ask about the prognosis and life expectancy for their child. What is the average life expectancy for individuals with Down syndrome in the modern era?
questions.initialExplanation: Modern life expectancy in Down syndrome is about 60 years.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Life expectancy for individuals with Down syndrome has significantly improved over the past several
decades due to advances in medical care, particularly in the management of congenital heart defects
and infections. The average life expectancy is now approximately 60 years, compared to just 25 years
in 1983. Common causes of death in individuals with Down syndrome, in decreasing order of
incidence, include infections (particularly pneumonia), congenital malformations (particularly
congenital heart diseases), circulatory diseases (e.g., coronary artery disease), and dementia.

- While life expectancy has improved dramatically, individuals with Down syndrome still have a shorter
life expectancy than the general population due to increased susceptibility to various medical
conditions, including respiratory infections, congenital heart disease, and early-onset Alzheimer
disease.

---

questions.stem: A 12-year-old girl presents to the pediatric endocrinology clinic for evaluation of short stature. Her height is at the 5th percentile, which is significantly below her mid-parental height. She also has a broad chest with widely spaced nipples and mild webbing of the neck. On physical examination, you note a heart murmur. Which of the following karyotypes is most commonly associated with this clinical presentation?
questions.initialExplanation: A girl with short stature, delayed puberty and a heart murmur: the best-known karyotype is 45,X (Turner).
questions.detailedExplanation:
This clinical presentation is classic for Turner syndrome. The classic karyotype is 45,XO (monosomy
X), which accounts for approximately 50% of cases and typically presents with the full phenotype of
Turner syndrome, including short stature, shield chest, webbed neck, and cardiovascular
abnormalities.

- The other karyotypes listed represent variants of Turner syndrome. Mosaicism (45,X0/46,XX or 45,
X0/46,XY) typically presents with a milder phenotype because of the presence of a normal cell line.
The 45,X0 karyotype results from complete loss of one X chromosome and is associated with the
most severe manifestations. Unlike Klinefelter syndrome, Turner syndrome is not associated with
advanced maternal age.

---

questions.stem: A newborn female infant is noted to have lymphedema of the hands and feet at birth. The obstetrician also noted excessive nuchal skin on prenatal ultrasound. On physical examination, you observe a webbed neck and low-set posterior hairline. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: A newborn girl with lymphedema, webbed neck and low hairline = Turner syndrome.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This newborn presents with classic features of Turner syndrome, including fetal or neonatal
lymphedema (affecting the hands and feet), cystic hygroma (which can present as excessive nuchal
skin or folds on prenatal ultrasound), webbed neck (pterygium colli), and low-set posterior hairline.
These features result from abnormal lymphatic development during fetal life.

- While Noonan syndrome can also present with webbed neck and short stature, the combination of
lymphedema in the newborn period and the specific pattern of anomalies is more characteristic of
Turner syndrome. Down syndrome has different characteristic features, Klippel-Feil syndrome
involves fusion of cervical vertebrae, and Marfan syndrome has distinct skeletal and cardiovascular
features.

---

questions.stem: A 10-year-old girl with Turner syndrome is found to have hypertension on routine examination. Blood pressure measurements in both arms are elevated compared to leg pressures. Which of the following is the most likely cause of hypertension in this patient?
questions.initialExplanation: Turner with higher blood pressure in the arm than the leg: coarctation of the aorta.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child with Turner syndrome presents with upper extremity hypertension and likely diminished lower
extremity pulses, suggesting coarctation of the aorta. Coarctation of the aorta is a known cardiovascular
abnormality associated with Turner syndrome, occurring in approximately 10-20% of patients. It typically
presents as a discrete narrowing of the descending aorta, often just distal to the origin of the left subclavian
artery.

- The clinical presentation includes hypertension in the upper extremities with weak or delayed femoral pulses
(brachial-femoral delay). Coarctation can present in childhood or adolescence and requires surgical or
catheter-based intervention. Cardiovascular evaluation with echocardiogram or MRI should be performed in all
individuals with Turner syndrome to assess for this and other structural heart defects.

---

questions.stem: A 1-week-old female infant presents with bilious vomiting and abdominal distension. Prenatal ultrasound showed a “double bubble” sign. She has hypotonia, a single palmar crease, and Brushfield spots on ophthalmologic exam. An abdominal X-ray confirms duodenal atresia. Which genetic condition is most strongly associated with this presentation?
questions.initialExplanation: Bilious vomiting and abdominal distension with confirmed duodenal atresia: strongly associated with Down syndrome.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Duodenal atresia is strongly associated with Down syndrome, occurring in 1-5% of cases. The “double
bubble” sign on prenatal ultrasound is pathognomonic for duodenal obstruction. Brushfield spots (iris
speckling), single palmar crease, and hypotonia further support Down syndrome. Trisomy 18/13
present with more severe malformations (e.g., rocker-bottom feet, polydactyly) and rarely duodenal
atresia. Turner syndrome (D) may have Gl issues but not duodenal atresia as a hallmark.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy with Down syndrome is brought for developmental delay. He walked at 28 months and uses only 10 words. His mother asks about his expected cognitive trajectory. Which statement best characterizes intellectual disability in Down syndrome?

options.label: B
options.text: IQ typically ranges from 30-70, with an average of 50

options.label: D
options.text: Cognitive function is normal in mosaic cases

questions.initialExplanation: Intelligence in Down syndrome is usually between 30 and 70 with a mean of about 50 (mild to moderate intellectual disability).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Intellectual disability in Down syndrome is variable but typically moderate, with an average 1Q of ~50.
Developmental milestones are achieved at ~twice the typical age. Mosaic cases (E) may have milder

impairment but not normal cognition. 1Q does not progressively decline in childhood (E); early-onset
Alzheimer’s causes decline in adulthood.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old female with confirmed Turner syndrome is undergoing comprehensive evaluation. Renal ultrasound reveals a horseshoe kidney configuration. The pediatric urologist discusses the implications of this finding with the parents. Which statement regarding renal abnormalities in Turner syndrome is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: Horseshoe kidney occurs in approximately 15-30% of individuals with Turner syndrome

options.label: B
options.text: Renal anomalies significantly increase the risk of renal malignancy

options.label: C
options.text: No specific precautions are necessary during surgical procedures

options.label: D
options.text: Horseshoe kidney is not associated with increased morbidity or mortality

options.label: E
options.text: Individuals with Turner syndrome and renal anomalies should undergo lifelong annual renal ultrasound surveillance

questions.initialExplanation: In Turner syndrome a horseshoe kidney occurs in about 15-30% (kidney ultrasound is done).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Renal abnormalities are common in Turner syndrome, occurring in approximately 30-40% of affected
individuals. Horseshoe kidney (fusion of the kidneys at the lower poles) is the most common renal
malformation, with an incidence of approximately 10-30% in Turner syndrome. Other renal anomalies
include malrotation, duplicated collecting systems, and ureteropelvic junction obstruction.

- The statement that horseshoe kidney occurs in approximately 30% is accurate and clinically
important. While horseshoe kidney itself is not associated with significant renal dysfunction, awareness

of this anomaly is important for surgical planning and during procedures involving the abdomen or
retroperitoneum.

---

questions.stem: A 42-year-old pregnant woman presents for prenatal counseling. She iscurrently 8 weeks pregnant with her first child. Her sister has a child with Down syndrome, and she is concerned about her risk of having an affected pregnancy. What is the most appropriate genetic risk assessment and counseling approach?

options.label: A
options.text: Advise that her risk is significantly elevated only if paternal age is advanced

options.label: B
options.text: Assure her that her risk is similar to the general population of 1:700

options.label: C
options.text: 0) Recommend chorionic villus sampling immediately as her risk is 1:30

options.label: D
options.text: Explain that family history of Down syndrome increases her risk to 1:350

options.label: E
options.text: Inform that maternal age is the primary risk factor, with risk at her age being approximately 1:100

questions.initialExplanation: Maternal age 42: the main risk is maternal age, estimated per the given answer at about 1 in 100.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Maternal age is the most significant risk factor for Down syndrome. At age 40, the risk of having a pregnancy

with trisomy 21 is approximately 1:100, and by age 45, the risk increases to approximately 1:30. This is due to

increased likelihood of meiotic nondisjunction in older oocytes. While a family history of Down syndrome in a
‘    sibling increases risk slightly, the maternal age effect is much more significant. The patient should be offered

first-trimester screening with combined test or diagnostic testing via chorionic villus sampling (9-14 weeks) or
amniocentesis (15-22 weeks).

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old child with Down syndrome presents for routine follow-up. The parents report that the child seems more tired than usual, has gained weight despite unchanged diet, and seems less interested in activities. On examination, you note dry skin and bradycardia. What is the most likely endocrine disorder and appropriate screening test?

options.label: A
options.text: Type 1 diabetes; check fasting blood glucose and HbA1c

options.label: B
options.text: Type 2 diabetes; check oral glucose tolerance test

options.label: C
options.text: Hypothyroidism; check TSH and free T4 levels

options.label: D
options.text: Growth hormone deficiency; check IGF-1 levels

questions.initialExplanation: Down syndrome with dry skin and slow heart rate = hypothyroidism; TSH and free T4 are checked yearly.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Hypothyroidism is one of the most common endocrine disorders associated with Down syndrome,
with both congenital and acquired forms occurring at increased frequency. The symptoms described
(fatigue, weight gain, decreased interest in activities, dry skin, bradycardia) are classic for
hypothyroidism. Annual thyroid function testing (TSH and free T4) is recommended for all individuals
with Down syndrome starting in infancy. Early detection and treatment with levothyroxine is important
for optimal development and quality of life.

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl is referred for evaluation of short stature. On examination, you note a webbed neck, low-set posterior hairline, and high-arched palate. You also observe that her fourth fingers appear shortened. What additional finding would further support the diagnosis of Turner syndrome?

options.label: B
options.text: Short fourth metacarpals and nail dysplasia

questions.initialExplanation: Turner with short stature: supported by short fourth metacarpals and nail dysplasia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Short fourth metacarpals and nail dysplasia are characteristic skeletal findings in Turner syndrome.
The high-arched palate is also commonly seen. Other classic features include cubitus valgus
(increased carrying angle of the elbow), shield chest (broad chest with widely spaced nipples), and
the lymphatic abnormalities including webbed neck and lymphedema. These features help distinguish
Turner syndrome from other genetic conditions. Down syndrome, for example, has features like
clinodactyly of the fifth finger and sandal gap, which are not typical of Turner syndrome.

---

questions.stem: A 12-year-old girl with Down syndrome presents to the emergency department with fever, neck pain, and progressive weakness in her arms over the past 3 days. Her mother reports she fell while playing soccer last week but seemed fine initially. On examination, she has limited neck flexion, hyperreflexia in upper extremities, and decreased grip strength bilaterally. Neurological examination shows positive Babinski sign bilaterally. What is the most likely underlying anatomical abnormality predisposing to this presentation?
questions.initialExplanation: Down syndrome with neurological neck signs: atlantoaxial instability (instability between the first and second vertebrae).
questions.detailedExplanation:
This patient with Down syndrome presents with acute cervical myelopathy following minor trauma. Atlantoaxial instability
is a well-recognized skeletal complication in Down syndrome, occurring due to connective tissue deficiency and
ligamentous laxity, particularly affecting the transverse ligament of the atlas. Approximately 10-20% of individuals with
Down syndrome have atlantoaxial instability, though most are asymptomatic. The minor trauma from the soccer fall likely
caused subluxation or increased instability, leading to spinal cord compression. Clinical features of cord compression
include neck pain, limited neck movement, upper motor neuron signs (hyperreflexia, Babinski sign), and motor weakness.
This is a medical emergency requiring immediate cervical spine imaging (lateral cervical X-ray in flexion and extension, or
CT/MRI) and neurosurgical consultation. Children with Down syndrome should be screened for atlantoaxial instability
before participating in contact sports or activities requiring neck manipulation. Syringomyelia and Chiari malformation are
not associated with Down syndrome. Spinal muscular atrophy would present with lower motor neuron signs (hyporeflexia,
fasciculations). Cervical stenosis is unlikely in a 12-year-old.

---

questions.stem: A 15-day-old baby with Down syndrome, during routine blood testing found to have high leukocyte count (34,000), the baby otherwise is asymptomatic. Of the following, the MOST appropriate advice /action is :

options.label: A
options.text: to refer the baby to a hematologist as it may be the prodrome of leukemia

options.label: B
options.text: collect blood culture and treat the baby with empiric antibiotic therapy

options.label: C
options.text: do septic screen and wait for the results

options.label: D
options.text: reassure the parents and advice for follow-up

questions.initialExplanation: High white count in a Down infant without symptoms: usually transient abnormal myelopoiesis, so reassure the family and follow up.
questions.detailedExplanation:
In newborns with Down syndrome, a transient leukemoid reaction or transient abnormal myelopoiesis
(TAM) —formerly called transient myeloproliferative disorder —is relatively common, occurring in up to

‘    10% of cases. This condition is driven by somatic GATA1 mutations and typically presents with
elevated white blood cell counts (often >20,000-30,000/uL), circulating blasts, and sometimes
hepatosplenomegaly or effusions. However, many infants are asymptomatic, and TAM usually
