options.text: They contain weakened bacteria that can still replicate but have lost their virulence factors

options.label: B
options.text: They contain inactivated bacterial toxins that have been modified to be non-toxic while retaining immunogenicity

options.label: C
options.text: They contain only the polysaccharide capsule of bacteria conjugated to a carrier protein

options.label: D
options.text: They contain messenger RNA that encodes the bacterial toxin protein

options.label: E
options.text: They contain killed whole bacteria with intact cell walls and membrane proteins

questions.initialExplanation: A toxoid vaccine contains an inactivated bacterial toxin that cannot cause disease but still stimulates immunity.
questions.detailedExplanation:
immunogenicity

Toxoid vaccines contain bacterial toxins that have been chemically modified (usually with formaldehyde) to
eliminate their toxic properties while preserving their ability to stimulate an immune response. The resulting "
toxoid" is non-toxic but immunogenic, meaning it can stimulate the production of neutralizing antibodies against
the toxin.

The tetanus and diphtheria components of DTaP are classic examples of toxoid vaccines. The tetanus toxoid
stimulates production of antibodies that neutralize tetanus toxin, preventing the toxin from binding to neural
tissue and causing the muscle spasms and rigidity characteristic of tetanus. Similarly, the diphtheria toxoid
stimulates antibodies that neutralize diphtheria toxin, preventing the systemic effects of the toxin.

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl is receiving the Japanese encephalitis vaccine before international travel to an endemic area. The physician explains that two types of Japanese encephalitis vaccine are available: an inactivated vaccine derived from mouse brain tissue and a live attenuated vaccine. The child's parents ask about the advantages of the inactivated vaccine. Which statement is true regarding inactivated/killed vaccines compared to live attenuated vaccines?

options.label: A
options.text: nactivated vaccines require fewer doses and provide longer-lasting immunity

options.label: B
options.text: nactivated vaccines are safer in immunocompromised patients

options.label: C
options.text: nactivated vaccines stimulate stronger cell-mediated immune responses

options.label: D
options.text: nactivated vaccines provide better mucosal immunity

options.label: E
options.text: nactivated vaccines can revert to virulent forms

questions.initialExplanation: Inactivated vaccines are safer for those with immunodeficiency because they do not replicate.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Inactivated/killed vaccines contain non-replicating organisms that cannot cause disease, even in
immunocompromised hosts. This makes them safer than live attenuated vaccines, which can replicate
uncontrollously in individuals with impaired immune function.

Patients with immunodeficiencies, those receiving immunosuppressive therapy, or those with certain
medical conditions can safely receive inactivated vaccines, whereas live vaccines are contraindicated
or require careful consideration. This is the primary safety advantage of inactivated vaccines.

---

questions.stem: An 18-month-old boy receives his first dose of the MMR vaccine. Two weeks later, his parents notice that he has developed a mild fever, transient rash, and swelling of the parotid glands. They are concerned about these symptoms and request evaluation. On examination, the child is playful and interactive with no respiratory distress. His temperature is 38.0°C, and he has bilateral parotid enlargement that is nontender. Which statement best explains the timing and nature of these symptoms?

options.label: A
options.text: This represents a serious infection requiring hospital admission \*

options.label: B
options.text: This is a severe adverse reaction requiring immediate antiviral therapy

options.label: C
options.text: These are common, self-limited side effects of the MMR vaccine occurring 1-2 weeks after vaccination

options.label: D
options.text: This represents an allergic reaction to the gelatin stabilizer in the vaccine

options.label: E
options.text: This indicates vaccine failure requiring immediate revaccination

questions.initialExplanation: Rash or parotid swelling 2 weeks after MMR are mild, self-limited and expected 1-2 weeks later.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The symptoms described —Ilow-grade fever, transient rash, and parotid gland swelling occurring approximately 2 weeks

after MMR vaccination—are wellrecognized, benign side effects of the vaccine.

The mumps component of the MMR vaccine can cause mild parotitis (parotid gland swelling) in some vaccine recipients.
‘     This occurs because the vaccine virus replicates in the salivary glands, causing a mild inflammatory response. The parotid

swelling is typically unilateral or bilateral, non-tender or minimally tender, and resolves spontaneously.

The rash and fever are also common vaccine-associated reactions that occur as the vaccine virus replicates and

stimulates an immune response. These symptoms are selflimited and resolve spontaneously within 1-3 days.

The timing (approximately 2 weeks post-vaccination) is characteristic of vaccine reactions, as it corresponds to the peak

of viral replication and immune response. This is consistent with the typical timing of mumps vaccine-associated parotitis,

which usually occurs 2-3 weeks after vaccination.

---

questions.stem: A 10-year-old girl receives the Tdap vaccine as part of her routine immunization. Six hours later, she develops pain, redness, and swelling at the injection site, along with generalized fatigue and low-grade fever (37.8°C). Her mother calls the pediatrician's office to report these symptoms. Which statement best describes the expected timeline and characteristics of common side effects from the Tdap vaccine?

options.label: A
options.text: Side effects typically begin within minutes of vaccination and indicate anaphylaxis

options.label: B
options.text: Side effects usually occur within 24-48 hours and are self-limited, resolving within 1-3 days

options.label: C
options.text: Side effects begin 2-3 weeks after vaccination and indicate delayed hypersensitivity

options.label: D
options.text: Side effects occur 1-2 months after vaccination and indicate autoimmune reaction

options.label: E
options.text: Side effects are expected to persist for 2-3 weeks before resolving

questions.initialExplanation: Tdap symptoms (local pain and fever) appear within 24-48 hours and resolve in 1-3 days.
questions.detailedExplanation:
days

Common side effects of the Tdap vaccine, including local reactions (pain, redness, swelling at the
injection site) and systemic reactions (fatigue, low-grade fever), typically begin within 24-48 hours of
vaccination and resolve spontaneously within 1-3 days.

These reactions result from the immune response to vaccine antigens and are not Indications of
adverse reactions requiring intervention. The inflammatory response to vaccine components attracts

immune cells to the injection site, causing local symptoms, while systemic cytokine release causes
fatigue and low-grade fever.

---

questions.stem: A previously healthy 7-year-old boy presents for a school-required immunization update. His vaccination record shows completion of all primary series by age 4, but no boosters. He has no chronic illnesses, takes no medications, and has no known allergies. His mother reports he developed a mild fever and soreness at the injection site after his 4-year-old MMR vaccine but no anaphylaxis or severe reactions. What is the most appropriate next step in his immunization plan?

options.label: A
options.text: Administer Tdap, IPV, MMR, and varicella vaccines today

options.label: B
options.text: Administer only Tdap and IPV; defer MMR and varicella due to prior reaction

options.label: C
options.text: Administer Tdap, IPV, and inactivated influenza vaccine; defer MMR and varicella

options.label: D
options.text: Defer all vaccines until age 11 per school policy

options.label: E
options.text: Administer DTaP instead of Tdap because he is under 10 years old

questions.initialExplanation: A healthy 7-year-old without contraindications: give Tdap, IPV, MMR and varicella together at the same visit (catch-up).
questions.detailedExplanation:
At age 7, this child is due for booster doses of Tdap (not DTaP, which is for children <7 years), IPV,
and second doses of MMR and varicella if not already given—per the CDC catch-up schedule. Mild

‘    local reactions (fever, soreness) after MMR are common and not contraindications to re-vaccination;
only severe allergic reactions (e.g., anaphylaxis) or immunocompromise would warrant deferral.
Option B incorrectly withholds live vaccines based on a benign prior reaction. Option C unnecessarily
defers indicated live vaccines. Option D contradicts standard school-entry requirements (boosters are
needed at 4—6 years; if missed, give as soon as possible). Option E is incorrect because DTaP is not
recommended after age 6; Tdap is the appropriate formulation for children 27 years.

---

questions.stem: A 9-year-old girl with a history of egg allergy (hives after eating scrambled eggs) presents for routine vaccination. She has never received an influenza vaccine. Her immunization record is up to date except for annual flu shots. She is otherwise healthy, on no medications, and has no history of asthma or anaphylaxis. Her parents are concerned about vaccine safety due to her egg allergy. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.text: Administer live attenuated influenza vaccine (LAIV) intranasally

options.label: B
options.text: Administer inactivated influenza vaccine (lV) in the clinic without special precautions

options.label: C
options.text: Refer to an allergist for skin testing before any influenza vaccination

options.label: D
options.text: E Avoid influenza vaccination entirely due to egg allergy

options.label: E
options.text: Administer IV only after premedication with antihistamines

questions.initialExplanation: Egg allergy (hives) does not prevent inactivated influenza vaccine, which is given without special precautions.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Current CDC and AAP guidelines state that any influenza vaccine (11V or LAIV) can be safely
administered to individuals with any severity of egg allergy, including anaphylaxis, without special
precautions. This is because modern influenza vaccines contain only trace amounts of ovalbumin (<1
pg/dose), which is insufficient to trigger allergic reactions. Premedication (Option E) or allergist
referral (Option C) is unnecessary. Option A (LAIV) is also acceptable in this patient, but IIV is
preferred in many settings and equally safe; however, B is the best answer because it directly
addresses the most common and universally recommended approach. Option D is incorrect—egg
allergy is not a contraindication to flu vaccination. Avoiding vaccination puts the child at preventable
risk of influenza complications.

---

questions.stem: An 8-year-old boy is brought to the clinic for a pre-camp physical. His mother states he has never received the varicella vaccine because “chickenpox is just a childhood illness.” He has no history of varicella infection and no immunocompromising conditions. He is otherwise healthy, takes no medications, and has no allergies. His other vaccines are up to date through age 4. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.text: Reassure the mother that natural infection is preferable to vaccination

options.label: B
options.text: Administer one dose of varicella vaccine today

options.label: C
options.text: Administer two doses of varicella vaccine today, spaced 4 weeks apart

options.label: D
options.text: Administer one dose of varicella vaccine today and schedule a second dose in 3 months

options.label: E
options.text: Check varicella IgG serology before proceeding with vaccination

questions.initialExplanation: Child with missing vaccination history: per the given answer, give a varicella dose today and the second dose after 3 months (age 8 years).
questions.detailedExplanation:
For children 27 years who lack evidence of immunity to varicella (no prior infection, no vaccination),
the CDC recommends two doses of varicella vaccine. The first dose can be given at any time, and the

‘    second dose should be administered at least 3 months later (minimum interval is 4 weeks, but for
catch-up in this age group, 3 months is standard and aligns with school requirements). Option A is
incorrect—natural infection carries risks of complications (e.g., pneumonia, encephalitis, secondary
bacterial infections), whereas the vaccine is safe and effective. Option B provides only partial
protection; two doses are required for full immunity. Option C is wrong because the two doses cannot
be given on the same day. Option E (serologic testing) is not routinely recommended before
vaccination in healthy children—it adds cost and delays without improving outcomes, as vaccination is
safe even in previously immune individuals.

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy with a history of well-controlled HIV infection (CD4 count 650 cells/uL, undetectable viral load) presents for vaccination update. He is on antiretroviral therapy and has received all primary vaccines except MMR and varicella. His parents report he missed these due to concerns about live vaccines. He has no fever or acute illness today. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.text: Defer all live vaccines indefinitely due to HIV status

options.label: B
options.text: Administer MMR and varicella vaccines today

options.label: C
options.text: Administer MMR today but defer varicella

options.label: D
options.text: Check CD4 percentage before administering live vaccines

options.label: E
options.text: Administer only inactivated vaccines; avoid MMR and varicella permanently

questions.initialExplanation: Well-controlled HIV (CD4 >= 15%): MMR and varicella (live vaccines) can be given safely.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Children with HIV who are not severely immunocompromised (i.e., CD4 count 215% for age or, in
children 26 years, CD4 =200 cells/uL) can safely receive live vaccines, including MMR and varicella.
This 7-year-old has a CD4 count of 650 cells/uL and undetectable viral load—indicating good immune
reconstitution on antiretroviral therapy. Per CDC and AAP guidelines, both MMR and varicella are
recommended in such patients. Option A is incorrect because live vaccines are not contraindicated in
non-severely immunocompromised HIV patients. Option C arbitrarily defers varicella without
justification. Option D is unnecessary —the absolute CD4 count and clinical status are sufficient; CD4

percentage is more relevant in younger children. Option E is outdated and harmful, as it leaves the
child vulnerable to preventable diseases.

---

questions.stem: A 9-year-old girl is brought to the clinic for a routine check-up. Her mother reports she received her first dose of HPV vaccine at age 10, but they missed the follow-up due to insurance issues. She has no chronic illnesses, takes no medications, and has no allergies. She has not yet started menstruation. Her other vaccines are up to date. What is the most appropriate next step regarding HPV vaccination?

options.label: A
options.text: Restart the series with three doses because more than 6 months have passed

options.label: B
options.text: Administer the second dose now and schedule the third dose 6 months later

options.label: C
options.text: Administer the second dose now; no further doses are needed

options.label: D
options.text: Defer HPV vaccination until age 11 per school policy

options.label: E
options.text: Check HPV serology to determine need for further doses

questions.initialExplanation: After the first HPV dose at age 10 years: two doses are enough if started before age 15.
questions.detailedExplanation:
For individuals who initiate the HPV vaccine series at age 9-14 years, only two doses are required,
given 6-12 months apart. Since this girl received her first dose at age 10 (within the 9-14 window),

‘    she needs just one more dose, regardless of the interval since the first—there is no need to restart
the series, even after long delays. Option A is incorrect because a three-dose schedule is only for
those starting at age 215 or immunocompromised individuals. Option B wrongly adds a third dose.
Option D is false—HPV vaccination can and should begin as early as age 9. Option E is not
recommended; serologic testing is not used to guide HPV vaccination decisions.

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the clinic after his school flagged missing immunizations. His records show he received 4 doses of DTaP (at 2, 4, 6, and 15 months) but no booster since. He has a history of a generalized seizure 8 days after his 4-month DTaP dose, which was diagnosed as a simple febrile seizure. He is otherwise neurologically normal and on no medications. What is the most appropriate next step in vaccination?

options.label: A
options.text: Delay all vaccinations until neurological evaluation \*

options.label: E
options.text: Avoid all pertussis-containing vaccines due to seizure history Administer Tdap today Administer DTaP today Administer Td today and avoid pertussis component permanently Defer vaccination until age 11

questions.initialExplanation: Missing vaccines with a stable neurological condition: give Tdap today.
questions.detailedExplanation:
A febrile seizure occurring after DTaP is not a contraindication to future pertussis-containing vaccines.
Current guidelines (CDC, AAP) state that febrile seizures—even if temporally associated —are not
linked to long-term neurological harm and do not preclude further vaccination. At age 7, the child
should receive Tdap (not DTaP), as DTaP is only licensed for children under 7 years. Option C
(DTaP) is therefore incorrect due to age-inappropriate formulation. Option A and D are overly cautious
and not evidence-based; pertussis protection remains important. Option E delays necessary school-
required immunization without justification. Tdap provides appropriate booster coverage against
tetanus, diphtheria, and acellular pertussis in this age group.

---

questions.stem: A 9-year-old girl with a history of anaphylaxis to gelatin presents for routine vaccination. Her immunization record shows she is missing MMR and varicella vaccines. She has no other allergies, is otherwise healthy, and takes no medications. Her parents are concerned about vaccine safety. What is the most appropriate next step in management? Ne

options.label: A
options.text: Administer MMR and varicella vaccines in the clinic with extended observation

options.label: B
options.text: Avoid MMR and varicella vaccines permanently

options.label: C
options.text: Refer to an allergist for evaluation before vaccination

options.label: D
options.text: Administer only MMR; varicella is contraindicated

options.label: E
options.text: Administer both vaccines after premedication with antihistamines and corticosteroids

questions.initialExplanation: Anaphylaxis to gelatin: refer to an allergist before vaccines containing it.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Gelatin is a stabilizer used in MMR and varicella vaccines, and a history of anaphylaxis to gelatin is a
precaution (and potentially a contraindication) to these vaccines. While not all gelatin-allergic
individuals react to vaccine-derived gelatin, the risk warrants allergist evaluation—which may include
skin testing or graded challenge —to determine if vaccination can be safely administered. Option A is
unsafe without prior assessment. Option B is overly restrictive; many patients can still be vaccinated
under supervision. Option D is incorrect because both vaccines contain gelatin. Option E
(premedication) does not prevent anaphylaxis and is not recommended as a substitute for proper
allergy evaluation.

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy presents for a routine check-up. His mother reports he received all primary vaccines but missed his 4-6 year booster doses. He has a history of progressive encephalopathy of unknown etiology diagnosed at age 3, with ongoing developmental delay. He is otherwise stable, on no medications, and has no acute illness. What is the most appropriate next step regarding vaccination?

options.label: A
options.text: Administer Tdap, IPV, MMR, and varicella today

options.label: B
options.text: Administer Td and IPV only; defer live vaccines

options.label: C
options.text: Defer all vaccines due to encephalopathy

options.label: D
options.text: Administer all indicated vaccines except pertussis-containing ones

options.label: E
options.text: Check EEG before proceeding with any vaccination

questions.initialExplanation: After a neurological event related to pertussis: give all vaccines except those containing pertussis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
A history of progressive encephalopathy of unknown etiology is a precaution (and often considered a
contraindication) to pertussis-containing vaccines (DTaP/Tdap), per CDC guidelines, due to theoretical
concern for exacerbation—though evidence is limited. However, all other vaccines (IPV, MMR, varicella) are
safe and recommended in this child. Option A is incorrect because it includes Tdap, which should be avoided.
Option B unnecessarily defers live vaccines (MMR/varicella are safe in non-immunocompromised children
with stable neurologic conditions). Option C is overly restrictive and leaves the child unprotected against
preventable diseases. Option E (EEG) is not required for vaccination decisions. Thus, giving Td (instead of
Tdap), IPV, MMR, and varicella is appropriate—but since Td isn't listed as an option, the best choice is D,
which correctly excludes pertussis-containing vaccines while implying others may proceed.

---

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy with a history of nephrotic syndrome (currently in remission, off inmunosuppressants for 6 months) presents for vaccination. He missed his MMR and varicella vaccines due to prior steroid use. He is otherwise healthy, with no fever or acute illness. His last prednisone dose was 7 months ago. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.text: Defer live vaccines for another 6 months

options.label: B
options.text: Administer MMR and varicella vaccines today

options.label: D
options.text: Check lymphocyte count before administering live vaccines

options.label: E
options.text: Avoid live vaccines permanently due to prior immunosuppression

questions.initialExplanation: Nephrotic syndrome in remission with steroids stopped 7 months ago: MMR and varicella are given safely.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Live vaccines (MMR and varicella) are contraindicated during active immunosuppression, but can be
safely given at least 1 month after discontinuation of short-course corticosteroids (e.g., <2 weeks of

‘    high-dose steroids) or 3 months after long-term immunosuppressive therapy. This child has been off
prednisone for 7 months and is in remission—well beyond the required waiting period. No additional
testing (e.g., lymphocyte count, Option D) is needed in a clinically stable, immunocompetent-
appearing child. Option A unnecessarily delays protection. Option C lacks rationale —both vaccines
are indicated. Option E is incorrect; prior immunosuppression does not contraindicate future live
vaccines once immune function has recovered.

---

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman receives the rubella vaccine and becomes pregnant one month later, despite counseling to avoid conception for 28 days post-vaccination. She is anxious about potential fetal consequences. Which of the following best describes the expected outcome of this pregnancy?

options.label: A
options.text: High risk of spontaneous abortion directly attributable to the rubella vaccine

options.label: B
options.text: Significant likelihood of congenital malformations, particularly cardiac and ocular defects

options.label: C
options.text: Development of a clinical syndrome consistent with congenital rubella syndrome (CRS)

options.label: D
options.text: Requirement for detailed fetal monitoring due to proven teratogenicity of the vaccine strain

options.label: E
options.text: No increased risk of adverse outcomes; pregnancy is unlikely to be affected - F) moowy»

questions.initialExplanation: Rubella vaccine then pregnancy a month later: no confirmed fetal risk (CRS is almost nonexistent).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Although live attenuated rubella vaccine is contraindicated during pregnancy as a precautionary
measure, decades of surveillance data—including from the CDC and international registries —have
not identified a single confirmed case of congenital rubella syndrome (CRS) caused by the vaccine
strain. The Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) and other major health bodies
emphasize that inadvertent rubella vaccination before or during early pregnancy is not a reason to
terminate the pregnancy, as the vaccine is not considered teratogenic. While the theoretical risk
exists because the virus can cross the placenta, real-world evidence consistently shows no
increased risk of fetal harm, miscarriage, or congenital anomalies.

---

questions.stem: A 1.2-kg preterm infant is born to a mother who is confirmed hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) negative during pregnancy. The neonatal nurse consults you regarding the appropriate timing for initiating the hepatitis B vaccination series. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.text: Administer the first dose when the infant reaches a weight of 1.8 kg

options.label: B
options.text: Administer the first dose at the time of hospital discharge, provided the infant is clinically stable

options.label: C
options.text: NC. Delay the first dose until the infant is 2 months of chronological age

options.label: D
options.text: Administer a reduced (half) dose of the vaccine immediately

options.label: E
options.text: Withhold hepatitis B vaccination entirely due to prematurity and low birth weight

questions.initialExplanation: A 1.2 kg premature infant to an HBsAg-positive mother: HBIG plus the first vaccine dose within 12 hours is the usual rule; the given option states a different timing (per the given answer).
questions.detailedExplanation:
For preterm infants with birth weight <2000 g born to HBsAg-negative mothers, the hepatitis B birth dose is not
recommended because immune response is suboptimal in this population. Instead, the first dose should be given at
hospital discharge or by 1 month of chronological age, whichever occurs first, as long as the infant is medically stable and
feeding well.

- Option A is incorrect: While older guidance sometimes referenced a 2000-g threshold, current recommendations do not
require waiting for a specific weight (e.g., 1.8 kg); stability and discharge timing are key.

- Option C unnecessarily delays immunization; the first dose should be given earlier—at discharge or around 1

month —not deferred to 2 months. Option D is inappropriate: Hepatitis B vaccine is always administered as a full standard
dose (0.5 mL intramuscularly); half-dosing is not supported and may impair immunogenicity. Option E is incorrect:

Prematurity alone is not a contraindication; vaccination is essential and should be initiated per schedule once the infant is
stable.

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old child presents for routine immunizations. His older brother has a known but incompletely characterized primary immunodeficiency, and a full immunologic evaluation is pending. Which of the following vaccines should be deferred in the healthy sibling until the brother’s immune status is clarified?

options.label: B
options.text: Haemophilus influenzae type b conjugate vaccine (Hib)

options.label: C
options.text: Diphtheria, tetanus, and acellular pertussis vaccine (DTaP)

questions.initialExplanation: A sibling with immunodeficiency: defer varicella vaccine (or follow the exception guidance) until the sibling's immunity is clarified.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Varicella vaccine is a live attenuated viral vaccine. While live vaccines are generally safe in healthy children,
they may pose a theoretical risk of transmission to severely immunocompromised household

contacts —particularly those with T-cell deficiencies (e.g., severe combined immunodeficiency, Wiskott-Aldrich
syndrome). Although documented transmission of vaccine-strain varicella is extremely rare, current CDC and
AAP guidelines recommend caution: if the nature or severity of the immunodeficiency is unknown, it is prudent
to defer live vaccines (such as varicella and MMR) in the healthy sibling until the immunologic workup is
complete.

- Options A (IPV), B (Hib), C (DTaP), and E (PCV13) are all inactivated or subunit vaccines, which pose no risk
to immunocompromised contacts and should be administered on schedule.

Option D (Varicella) is the only live vaccine listed and is the only one that warrants temporary deferral in this
specific context.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child presents for scheduled immunizations. He was diagnosed with an upper respiratory tract infection (URTI) four days ago and has been on antibiotics since then. Today, he is afebrile but has persistent cervical lymphadenopathy and pharyngeal congestion. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step regarding vaccination?

options.label: B
options.text: Wait until the antibiotic course is completed before administering vaccines

options.label: C
options.text: Administer the scheduled vaccines as planned

options.label: D
options.text: Defer vaccination until lymphadenopathy resolves completely

options.label: E
options.text: Seek additional specialist opinion before proceeding - F) moow

questions.initialExplanation: Mild illness (mild fever or congestion) is not a contraindication to vaccination; give as planned.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Mild acute illnesses—such as URTI, with or without low-grade fever, pharyngeal congestion, or reactive
lymphadenopathy —are not contraindications to vaccination. The CDC and AAP clearly state that vaccines
should be given on schedule even in the presence of minor illnesses, including during antibiotic therapy.
Enlarged lymph nodes and throat congestion are common reactive findings in viral or bacterial URTIs and do
not indicate a moderate-to-severe systemic illness that would warrant deferral.

Option A is incorrect: There is no evidence-based reason to delay vaccines for a full month in this scenario.
Option B is unnecessary: Antibiotics do not interfere with vaccine efficacy (except for live oral typhoid vaccine,
which is not relevant here), and completion of treatment is not required before immunization.

Option D is overly cautious: Reactive lymphadenopathy is benign and does not contraindicate vaccination.
Option E is not indicated: This is a straightforward clinical situation that does not require specialist input.

---

questions.stem: A baby born at 35 weeks’ gestation is brought by his mother for routine immunizations. Which of the following statements regarding vaccination is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Administer vaccines at the same chronological age as recommended for term infants

options.label: B
options.text: Delay all vaccinations by 2 months based on corrected gestational age

options.label: C
options.text: Administer vaccines on schedule but reduce the dose to half

options.label: D
options.text: Defer vaccination and consult an infectious disease specialist

options.label: E
options.text: Withhold live vaccines until the infant reaches 40 weeks’ postmenstrual age

questions.initialExplanation: A premature infant is vaccinated by chronological age, not corrected age.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Preterm infants, including those born as early as 35 weeks’ gestation, should receive all routine vaccines according to the
standard chronological age schedule, regardless of birth weight or gestational age — provided they are clinically stable.
Immune responses to most vaccines (including DTaP, Hib, PCV, IPV, and hepatitis B) are generally adequate even in
preterm infants, and delaying vaccination increases their vulnerability to vaccine-preventable diseases during a high-risk
period.

- Option B is incorrect: Vaccination is not delayed based on corrected age; only the hepatitis B birth dose may be deferred
in infants <2000 g if the mother is HBsAg-negative—but this does not apply to other vaccines or to a 35-week infant who is
likely >2000 g.Option C is false: Full standard doses (e.g., 0.5 mL) must be used; reduced doses compromise
immunogenicity and are never recommended.

- Option D and E are unnecessary: No specialist consultation is required, and live vaccines (e.g., rotavirus, MMR) are

given on schedule unless the infant has a specific contraindication (e.g., severe immunodeficiency) —not prematurity
alone.

---

questions.stem: A mother brings her 5-year-old child for routine immunizations, including the fifth dose of the diphtheria, tetanus, and acellular pertussis (DTaP) vaccine. She asks how long the protection from this vaccine is expected to last. Which of the following best reflects the duration of immunity conferred by the DTaP series? Approximately 7 years Approximately 10 years
questions.initialExplanation: DTaP immunity lasts about 10 years.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The DTaP vaccine provides protection against diphtheria, tetanus, and pertussis. While acellular
pertussis immunity wanes after 4-6 years, the diphtheria and tetanus toxoid components confer

‘     protection for approximately 10 years. Because vaccination schedules and booster timing (e.g., Tdap
at age 11) are based on this 10-year window, and because exam questions often refer to the vaccine
as a whole, 10 years is the accepted standard answer for the duration of DTaP-induced immunity in
clinical practice and postgraduate assessments.
- Option A (5 years) reflects pertussis-specific waning but is not the best answer when the question

refers to the entire DTaP vaccine. Options B, D, and E do not align with established booster intervals
or serologic data.

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy presents with fever, malaise, and a diffuse maculopapular rash 10 days after receiving his first dose of MMR vaccine. His temperature is 38.5°C (101.3°F), and the rash is non-pruritic and fading. He has no respiratory distress, neck stiffness, or petechiae. His mother is concerned this is an allergic reaction. What is the most likely explanation for these symptoms?

options.label: A
options.text: Anaphylaxis to gelatin in the vaccine

options.label: E
options.text: Normal attenuated viral replication from MMR vaccine

questions.initialExplanation: Rash and fever 7-12 days after MMR = replication of the attenuated vaccine virus, which is expected.
questions.detailedExplanation:
A mild febrile illness with maculopapular rash 7-10 days after MMR vaccination is a well-documented,
benign reaction caused by replication of the attenuated measles component of the vaccine. It is not
contagious, self-limited, and does not require treatment. Option C (varicella reactivation) is incorrect
because this child has not received varicella vaccine yet (per prior questions), and the rash timing
aligns with MMR, not VZV. Option A (anaphylaxis) typically occurs within minutes to hours, not days,
and would include urticaria, angioedema, or hypotension—not a delayed rash. Option B is misleading;
while it is due to the vaccine-strain virus, it is not a true "infection" in the pathologic sense and is
expected. Option D (ITP) can occur post-MMR but presents with petechiae/purpura and
thrombocytopenia, not a maculopapular rash.

---

questions.stem: An 8-year-old girl is brought to the clinic for a school immunization audit. Her records show she received 3 doses of hepatitis B vaccine as an infant, but serologic testing at age 2 showed anti-HBs <10 mIU/mL. She has no chronic illnesses and is not immunocompromised. Her parents never followed up on revaccination. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.text: Administer one additional dose of hepatitis B vaccine and check anti-HBs in 1-2 months

options.label: B
options.text: < B. Restart the entire 3-dose hepatitis B series

options.label: C
options.text: No further action is needed; primary series confers lifelong protection

options.label: D
options.text: Check current anti-HBs level before deciding on revaccination

options.label: E
options.text: Administer two doses of hepatitis B vaccine 1 month apart

questions.initialExplanation: Previous nonresponse to HepB: give an extra dose and check anti-HBs after 1-2 months.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Children who completed the primary hepatitis B series but are non-responders (anti-HBs <10 mIU/mL)
should receive one additional dose, followed by anti-HBs testing 1-2 months later. If the titer remains

‘    low, they complete a second full 3-dose series (not a restart from zero immediately). Option B is
incorrect because you do not restart the entire series upfront—a single booster is tried first. Option C
is false; non-responders lack protective immunity. Option D (checking current titer first) is unnecessary
since we already know she was a non-responder and has not been revaccinated—guidelines support
giving a booster without retesting. Option E (two doses) does not follow standard protocol; the
approach is 1 booster — test — if still negative, give 3-dose series.

---

questions.stem: An 8-year-old boy presents for a catch-up vaccination visit. His records show he received 3 doses of DTaP in infancy but no booster. He has a history of stable, well-controlled epilepsy with no seizures in the past 2 years. He is on levetiracetam and has no other medical issues. What is the most appropriate next step in vaccination?

options.label: C
options.text: Avoid all pertussis-containing vaccines due to seizure disorder

options.label: E
options.text: Administer Td only, omitting pertussis component

questions.initialExplanation: An 8-year-old with an incomplete record: give Tdap today (with other missing vaccines).
questions.detailedExplanation:
A history of stable, well-controlled epilepsy with no recent seizures is not a contraindication to
pertussis-containing vaccines. The outdated concern about DTaP/Tdap triggering seizures applies
only to progressive neurologic disorders or uncontrolled encephalopathy —not stable epilepsy. At age
8, the child should receive Tdap (not DTaP, which is for children <7 years) as part of routine catch-up
immunization. Option D (deferring until age 11) unnecessarily leaves him unprotected against
pertussis, tetanus, and diphtheria. Option C is incorrect and reflects obsolete guidance. Option E (Td
only) omits pertussis protection without justification. Option B uses an age-inappropriate formulation
(DTaP).

---

questions.stem: A 9-year-old girl presents for a routine check-up. Her mother reports she received all primary vaccines but missed her 4—6 year boosters. She has a history of idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) diagnosed 3 months ago, now resolved with normal platelet counts. She is otherwise healthy and on no medications. What is the most appropriate next step regarding MMR vaccination?

options.label: B
options.text: Defer MMR indefinitely due to prior ITP

options.label: C
options.text: Check platelet count before administering MMR

options.label: D
options.text: Avoid MMR; use serologic testing instead

options.label: E
options.text: Administer MMR only if platelets remain normal for 6 more months

questions.initialExplanation: A 9-year-old girl who has not received an MMR dose: give it today.
questions.detailedExplanation:
A history of resolved idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) is not a contraindication to MMR
vaccination. Although MMR can rarely cause ITP (estimated risk: 1 in 30,000-40,000 doses), this
‘    risk is much lower than the risk of thrombocytopenia from natural measles infection. Current
guidelines (CDC, AAP) state that MMR may be given to children with a history of ITP if they are
otherwise immunocompetent and currently have normal platelet counts—which this patient does.
Option B is overly cautious and not evidence-based. Option C (checking platelets) is unnecessary

since the history confirms resolution and normal counts. Options D and E delay needed protection
without justification.

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy presents for a school-required immunization update. His mother reports he received all primary vaccines by age 2 but no boosters. He has a history of anaphylaxis to eggs (wheezing and hypotension after eating cake containing egg). He is otherwise healthy and takes no medications. Which of the following vaccines can be safely administered today without special precautions?
questions.initialExplanation: A vaccine safe without special precautions in a patient with a certain immune condition: MMR (per the given answer).
questions.detailedExplanation:
The MMR vaccine can be safely administered to individuals with any severity of egg allergy, including
anaphylaxis. This is because the vaccine is grown in chick embryo fibroblast cultures and contains negligible
or no egg protein. Current CDC, AAP, and ACIP guidelines state that no special precautions (e.g., skin testing,
prolonged observation) are needed for MMR in egg-allergic patients. In contrast, yellow fever vaccine (Option
B) is produced in whole eggs and can trigger reactions in egg-allergic individuals—it requires allergist
evaluation or testing. LAIV (Option A) is also safe in egg allergy per current guidelines, but MMR is the best
answer here because it is universally accepted without caveats, whereas LAIV may be avoided in some
settings due to historical caution (though evidence supports its safety). Rabies (Option D) and oral typhoid
(Option E) are not relevant to routine childhood vaccination at this age and are not contraindicated by egg
allergy—but MMR is the most appropriate and directly indicated vaccine in this context.

---

questions.stem: An 8-year-old boy presents for catch-up immunizations. His records show he received 4 doses of DTaP, 3 doses of IPV, and 1 dose each of MMR and varicella by age 2. He has no chronic illnesses, allergies, or prior vaccine reactions. His family recently moved from a region with low vaccination rates. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.text: Administer Tdap, IPV, MMR, and varicella today

options.label: B
options.text: Administer only Tdap and IPV; MMR and varicella require 3-month intervals

options.label: C
options.text: Administer Tdap and second doses of MMR and varicella; IPV is complete

options.label: D
options.text: Administer DTaP, IPV, MMR, and varicella today

questions.initialExplanation: Catch-up for an 8-year-old from a low-coverage region: Tdap, IPV, MMR and varicella today.
questions.detailedExplanation:
At age 8, this child is due for catch-up boosters:
- Tdap (not DTaP, which is only for children <7 years)
- IPV (4th dose; he only received 3)

‘     - Second dose of MMR (required for full immunity)
- Second dose of varicella (also required)
All these vaccines can be administered safely on the same day at different injection sites. Option E (deferring
until age 11) is incorrect—delaying leaves the child vulnerable to preventable diseases and violates school
immunization requirements. Option B is wrong because MMR and varicella do not require a 3-month interval
when given as second doses in catch-up; they can be given simultaneously. Option C incorrectly assumes IPV
is complete (he needs a 4th dose). Option D uses DTaP, which is not approved for children 27 years.

---

questions.stem: A 9-year-old girl presents for a pre-summer camp physical. Her mother states she received all routine vaccines except hepatitis A. She has no chronic illnesses, takes no medications, and has no allergies. She will be attending a 2-week outdoor camp in the western United States. What is the most appropriate next step regarding hepatitis A vaccination?

options.label: A
options.text: Administer one dose of hepatitis A vaccine today

options.label: B
options.text: Administer two doses of hepatitis A vaccine today

options.label: C
options.text: Defer hepatitis A vaccination until after camp

options.label: D
options.text: No hepatitis A vaccine is needed for camp attendance

options.label: E
options.text: Administer immune globulin instead of vaccine

questions.initialExplanation: Travel to camp: one dose of hepatitis A vaccine today.
questions.detailedExplanation:
For children 212 months, one dose of hepatitis A vaccine provides rapid and effective protection, with
seroconversion occurring in >95% within 4 weeks. Since the child is attending camp in 2 weeks, a
single dose is sufficient for short-term protection and fulfills the first part of the routine 2-dose series
(second dose given 6—18 months later). Immune globulin (Option E) is not preferred for healthy
individuals 212 months; it is reserved for those <12 months, immunocompromised patients, or when
vaccine is contraindicated. Option B is incorrect—doses must be spaced at least 6 months apart.
Option C delays needed protection. Option D is false; while not always required for camp, hepatitis A
vaccination is recommended for all children in the U.S. as part of routine immunization.

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy presents for a routine visit. His mother reports he received all primary vaccines but missed his 4—6 year boosters. He has a history of Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) 8 weeks after an influenza infection at age 5. He has fully recovered and is otherwise healthy. What is the most appropriate next step regarding vaccination?

options.label: A
options.text: Avoid all future vaccinations due to GBS history

options.label: B
options.text: Administer Tdap, IPV, MMR, and varicella today

options.label: C
options.text: Defer only influenza vaccine; administer all other indicated vaccines

options.label: D
options.text: Administer all vaccines except Tdap due to GBS risk

options.label: E
options.text: Check nerve conduction studies before vaccinating

questions.initialExplanation: Catch-up: Tdap, IPV, MMR and varicella today.
questions.detailedExplanation:
A history of Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) following influenza infection—not vaccination—is not a
contraindication to any routine childhood vaccine. Even if GBS occurred after a vaccine, current

‘    guidelines (CDC) state that it is only a precaution for future doses of that specific vaccine, not an
absolute contraindication, and does not affect other vaccines. Since this child’s GBS followed natural
influenza infection, there is no increased risk with Tdap, IPV, MMR, or varicella. Option A is incorrect
and would leave the child dangerously under-immunized. Option C unnecessarily restricts influenza
vaccine in the future (though not relevant here, as flu vaccine isn’t part of this visit). Option D lacks
rationale —Tdap is safe. Option E (nerve studies) is not indicated for vaccination decisions.

---

questions.stem: An 8-year-old boy presents for catch-up immunizations. His records show he received 3 doses of hepatitis B vaccine as an infant, but no other vaccines since age 2. He has no chronic illnesses, takes no medications, and has no allergies. His mother is concerned about "too many shots at once." What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.text: Administer only one vaccine per visit to reduce stress

options.label: B
options.text: Administer all indicated catch-up vaccines today

options.label: C
options.text: Defer live vaccines until after inactivated vaccines are complete

options.label: D
options.text: Administer Tdap and IPV today; schedule MMR and varicella in 4 weeks

options.label: E
options.text: Check titers for all diseases before vaccinating

questions.initialExplanation: "Too many shots" is not a barrier: give all needed catch-up vaccines at the same visit.
questions.detailedExplanation:
There is no immunologic or safety reason to separate live and inactivated vaccines or limit the number
of vaccines given at one visit. The CDC catch-up schedule explicitly allows all indicated
vaccines—including Tdap, IPV, MMR, and varicella—to be administered simultaneously at different
injection sites. This approach ensures timely protection and reduces missed opportunities. Option C is
a common misconception; live and inactivated vaccines can be given together without interference.
Option A prolongs vulnerability and increases clinic visits. Option D unnecessarily delays live
vaccines. Option E (checking titers) is not recommended for routine catch-up —it is costly, delays
protection, and vaccination is safe even in previously immune individuals.

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy presents for immunization update. His records show he received 4 doses of DTaP, 3 doses of IPV, and 1 dose each of MMR and varicella by age 2. He has a history of functional asplenia due to sickle cell disease, diagnosed at birth. He is on penicillin prophylaxis and has received all recommended vaccines for asplenia up to age 5. What is the most appropriate next step in vaccination?

options.label: A
options.text: Administer Tdap, IPV, MMR, varicella, and MenACWY today

options.label: B
options.text: Administer Tdap, IPV, MMR, varicella, and PCV20 today

options.label: C
options.text: Administer Tdap, IPV, MMR, varicella, MenACWY, and a booster dose of PCV15 or PCV20

options.label: D
options.text: Defer all vaccines until age 11 due to asplenia

options.label: E
options.text: Administer only MenACWY and Hib today

questions.initialExplanation: Asplenia or previously vaccinated: Tdap, IPV, MMR, varicella, MenACWY and a PCV dose.
questions.detailedExplanation:
PCV20

Children with functional asplenia (e.qg., sickle cell disease) are at high risk for encapsulated bacterial
‘    infections and require enhanced vaccination schedules. By age 7, they should receive:

- Routine catch-up vaccines: Tdap, IPV, second doses of MMR and varicella

- MenACWY booster (first dose typically given at age 2, then boosters every 5 years)

- A booster dose of pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV15 or PCV20) at age 26 if the primary

series was completed before age 5—per CDC guidelines for high-risk groups.

---

questions.stem: An 8-year-old girl is brought to the clinic 10 days after receiving Tdap and inactivated influenza vaccines. Her mother reports she developed fever, headache, and progressive leg weakness over the past 48 hours. On exam, she has flaccid paralysis of both lower extremities and absent deep tendon reflexes. Sensation is intact. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Flaccid leg weakness and absent reflexes 10 days after Tdap = Guillain-Barré syndrome.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) is a rare but recognized complication following certain vaccines, including
influenza vaccine (both inactivated and live). It typically presents 1-6 weeks post-vaccination with ascending
symmetric flaccid paralysis, areflexia, and intact sensation—classic findings in this case. Although the
association is strongest with influenza vaccine, Tdap has also been rarely implicated. Option D is incorrect
because inactivated influenza and Tdap vaccines do not contain live viruses and cannot cause poliomyelitis;
polio vaccine—derived disease only occurs with oral polio vaccine (OPV), which is not used in the U.S. Option A
(ADEM) usually involves encephalopathy and multifocal CNS deficits. Option C (transverse myelitis) would
present with a sensory level and bladder dysfunction. Option E lacks supporting evidence.

Note: While GBS is a precaution for future influenza vaccination, it is not an absolute contraindication,
especially if benefits outweigh risks.

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy receives his first dose of the varicella vaccine. Two weeks later, his parents notice a few vesicular lesions on his trunk. They bring him for evaluation concerned that he has developed chickenpox from the vaccine. On examination, there are approximately five vesicles in various stages of healing, and the child is otherwise well Which statement is correct regarding this presentation?

options.label: A
options.text: This represents a severe adverse reaction requiring antiviral therapy

options.label: B
options.text: This represents an allergic reaction to vaccine components

options.label: C
options.text: The child should be isolated from other children to prevent transmission

options.label: D
options.text: This indicates vaccine failure requiring revaccination

options.label: E
options.text: This is a common, mild side effect of the varicella vaccine

questions.initialExplanation: A mild rash two weeks after the varicella vaccine is a common mild side effect.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The development of a few vesicular lesions 1-4 weeks after varicella vaccination is a well-recognized,

benign side effect of the vaccine. This "varicella-like" rash occurs in approximately 3-5% of vaccine
‘    recipients and represents a mild infection with the vaccine strain of varicella-zoster virus (Oka strain).

The lesions are typically fewer in number and milder than wild-type varicella, and the child is usually

otherwise well. No antiviral therapy is indicated, and the child does not need to be isolated, as

transmission is extremely rare.

The vaccine strain can occasionally be transmitted to contacts, but this is rare and typically results in

mild disease. The benefits of varicella vaccination in preventing severe chickenpox and its
complications far outweigh this small risk.

---

questions.stem: A 2-month-old infant presents for her first well-child visit. Her parents are recently separated and share custody. The infant's birth weight was 3.2 kg, and she has been exclusively breastfed. On examination, she weighs 5.0 kg and is in the 50th percentile for weight. Which vaccines are recommended for administration at this visit according to the current CDC immunization schedule?

options.label: A
options.text: DTaP, IPV, Hib, PCV13, and rotavirus vaccines

options.label: B
options.text: DTaP, IPV, Hib, PCV13, rotavirus, and MMR vaccines

options.label: C
options.text: DTaP, IPV, Hib, PCV13, rotavirus, and hepatitis B vaccines

options.label: D
options.text: DTaP, IPV, Hib, PCV13, rotavirus, and varicella vaccines

options.label: E
options.text: DTaP, IPV, Hib, PCV13, rotavirus, and meningococcal vaccines

questions.initialExplanation: At 2 months: DTaP, IPV, Hib, PCV and rotavirus (with HepB per the record).
questions.detailedExplanation:
At the 2-month well-child visit, the recommended vaccines include DTaP (diphtheria, tetanus, acellular
pertussis), IPV (inactivated poliovirus), Hib (Haemophilus influenzae type b), PCV13 (pneumococcal
conjugate), and rotavirus vaccines. These vaccines protect against serious bacterial and viral
diseases that can affect young Infants. The rotavirus vaccine is given orally, while the others are given
by injection. MMR and varicella vaccines are not administered at 2 months; they are recommended at
12-15 months of age. Hepatitis B vaccine is typically started at birth, not at 2 months (though it can be

given if not previously administered). Meningococcal vaccine is not routinely recommended at this

---

questions.stem: A 6-month-old infant presents for her routine well-child visit. Her immunization record shows she received the following vaccines: hepatitis B at birth and 2 months, DTaP, IPV, Hib, PCV13, and rotavirus at 2 and 4 months. Which vaccines are recommended for administration at this 6-month visit? DTaP, IPV, Hib, PCV13, rotavirus, and MMR vaccines DTaP, IPV, Hib, PCV13, rotavirus, and varicella vaccines

options.label: A
options.text: DTaP, IPV, Hib, PCV13, rotavirus, and MMR vaccines \*

options.label: B
options.text: DTaP, IPV, Hib, PCV13, rotavirus, and varicella vaccines \*

options.label: C
options.text: DTaP, IPV, Hib, PCV183, rotavirus, and influenza vaccines (if during flu season)

options.label: D
options.text: DTaP, IPV, Hib, PCV13, rotavirus, and hepatitis B vaccines

options.label: E
options.text: DTaP, IPV, Hib, PCV183, rotavirus, and HPV vaccines

questions.initialExplanation: At 6 months: DTaP, IPV, Hib, PCV and rotavirus, with influenza during its season.
questions.detailedExplanation:
At the 6-month visit, infants typically receive their third doses of DTaP, IPV, Hib, PCV13, and rotavirus
(depending on the specific vaccine brand and schedule). The rotavirus vaccine series is completed by 8
months of age, and the third dose can be given at 6 months. Additionally, annual influenza vaccination is

‘    recommended for all children 6 months and older during flu season. The influenza vaccine is particularly
important for young children, who are at increased risk of complications from influenza. The third dose of
hepatitis B is typically given at 6-18 months, but if the infant received doses at birth and 2 months, the third
dose can be given now or at any subsequent visit. MMR and varicella vaccines are not given at 6 months;
they are recommended at 12-15 months. HPV vaccine is not recommended at this age. The correct answer
includes the routine vaccines at 6 months plus influenza vaccine when indicated.

---

questions.stem: A 6-month-old infant is being evaluated during flu season. His parents report that he has not yet received the influenza vaccine. The infant is generally healthy with no significant medical history. Which statement is correct regarding influenza vaccination in infants?

options.label: A
options.text: The influenza vaccine is not recommended for infants younger than 6 months

options.label: B
options.text: The influenza vaccine is contraindicated in breastfed infants

options.label: C
options.text: The influenza vaccine should only be given to infants with chronic medical conditions

options.label: D
options.text: The influenza vaccine is recommended annually for all children 6 months and older

options.label: E
options.text: The influenza vaccine requires two doses in the first year of administration

questions.initialExplanation: Influenza vaccine is recommended yearly for all children 6 months and older.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Annual influenza vaccination is recommended for all individuals 6 months of age and older who do not
have contraindications. This includes healthy infants and children, not just those with chronic medical
conditions.

Infants younger than 6 months cannot receive the influenza vaccine, which is why it is particularly
important for household contacts and caregivers to be vaccinated to protect these vulnerable infants.
For infants receiving the influenza vaccine for the first time, two doses are required, separated by at

least 4 weeks, to provide adequate protection. However, this recommendation applies only to the first
year of vaccination, not to all years.

---

questions.stem: A 15-month-old boy is brought to the pediatric clinic for routine immunization. His mother reports that he has been generally healthy with no significant medical history. He was born at term via normal vaginal delivery and has met all developmental milestones appropriately. On physical examination, his vital signs are stable, and he appears well-nourished and active. The physician prepares to administer the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine. Which of the following best describes the classification of this vaccine?
questions.initialExplanation: MMR is a live attenuated vaccine.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The MMR vaccine is a live attenuated vaccine containing weakened strains of the measles, mumps,
and rubella viruses. These viruses have been modified through serial passage in cell culture to
reduce their virulence while maintaining their ability to replicate in the host. When administered, live
attenuated vaccines mimic natural infection and stimulate a robust immune response involving both
humoral and cell-mediated immunity. This type of vaccine provides long-lasting immunity, often after
a single dose or limited number of doses. Live attenuated vaccines like MMR replicate in the host,
leading to prolonged antigen exposure and strong immunological memory. The immune system is
exposed to the viral antigens over an extended period, allowing for better development of
immunological memory and stronger protection against future exposures.

---

questions.stem: A 6-week-old infant presents for her first well-child visit. She was born prematurely at 32 weeks gestation and currently weighs 4.2 kg. Her mother is concerned about which vaccines are appropriate for her daughter's age. The pediatrician discusses the rotavirus vaccine, which will be administered orally. This vaccine works by inducing mucosal immunity in the gastrointestinal tract. Which characteristic is most specific to the mechanism of action of this type of vaccine?

options.label: A
options.text: < A) Contains inactivated whole organisms that cannot replicate but retain antigenic properties

options.label: B
options.text: Contains weakened organisms capable of limited replication without causing disease

options.label: C
options.text: Contains only specific protein antigens purified from the pathogen

options.label: D
options.text: Contains viral RNA that instructs host cells to produce viral antigens

options.label: E
options.text: Contains modified viral vectors that deliver genetic material encoding antigens

questions.initialExplanation: An oral vaccine (e.g., rotavirus/OPV) contains weakened organisms that replicate in a limited way without causing disease.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The rotavirus vaccine is a live attenuated vaccine that contains weakened strains of rotavirus capable of limited

replication in the gastrointestinal tract after oral administration. This limited replication mimics natural infection

and stimulates both systemic and mucosal immunity, particularly IgA production in the gut, which is crucial for
‘    protection against rotavirus disease.

The oral route of administration is particularly important for rotavirus vaccine because it allows the vaccine virus

to replicate in the intestinal mucosa, the same site where wildtype rotavirus causes disease. This localized

replication stimulates a strong mucosal immune response that can neutralize wild-type rotavirus before it can
establish infection.

Live attenuated vaccines are characterized by their ability to replicate in the host without causing disease. The
weakened strains have lost their virulence factors through serial passage in cell culture but retain the ability to
enter cells, replicate, and present antigens to the immune system.

---

questions.stem: A 10-year-old girl is receiving the human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine as part of the routine adolescent immunization schedule. She completed the two-dose series with the second dose administered 6 months after the first. The nurse explains that this vaccine is a recombinant vaccine that uses virus-like particles (VLPs) to stimulate immunity. Which statement best explains the immunological basis for the efficacy of this vaccine?

options.label: A
options.text: The vaccine contains live attenuated virus that replicates in the host \*

options.label: B
options.text: The vaccine contains inactivated whole virus particles that cannot replicate

options.label: C
options.text: The vaccine contains purified viral proteins that self-assemble into non-infectious particles

options.label: D
options.text: The vaccine contains mRNA that is translated into viral proteins within host cells

options.label: E
options.text: The vaccine contains viral vectors that infect cells and produce viral antigens

questions.initialExplanation: The HPV vaccine relies on purified viral proteins that assemble into non-infectious particles (VLPs).
questions.detailedExplanation:
The HPV vaccine is a recombinant vaccine that contains virus-like particles (VLPs) formed by the self-assembly
of the L1 major capsid protein of HPV. These VLPs resemble the outer structure of the HPV virus but contain no
viral DNA, making them noninfectious and non-oncogenic.

The VLPs are produced by recombinant DNA technology, where the gene encoding the L1 protein is inserted
into a vector (typically yeast or insect cells), which then produces large quantities of the L1 protein. When
purified, these proteins spontaneously assemble into VLPs that are structurally identical to the outer shell of the
HPV virus.

When administered, these VLPs stimulate the immune system to produce neutralizing antibodies against HPV.
The antibodies recognize and bind to the L1 protein, preventing HPV from infecting cells and thus protecting
against HPV infection and its complications, including cervical cancer and genital warts.

---

## Pediatric Emergencies

> Question numbers not present in the source file for this topic: 19.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl is found lying on the ground. She is unresponsive to voice and touch. If you open the airway and find no signs of breathing and you check the carotid pulse for 10 seconds and do not detect a pulse. What should you do next?

options.label: A
options.text: Give two rescue breaths and then reassess \*

options.label: D
options.text: Wait for emergency medical services to arrive

options.label: E
options.text: Recheck the pulse for another 10 seconds

questions.initialExplanation: A girl unresponsive with no breathing and no pulse after 10 seconds: start chest compressions immediately (C-A-B) without delay.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This 3-year-old child is unresponsive, not breathing, and has no detectable pulse. This represents cardiac arrest requiring
immediate cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR).

- In children, cardiac arrest is most commonly caused by respiratory failure progressing to cardiac arrest (asphyxial arrest),
unlike adults where primary cardiac causes predominate. However, once the child is pulseless, the resuscitation sequence
is the same regardless of the cause.

Pediatric BLS algorithm: The sequence for pediatric cardiac arrest is:

1. Verify scene safety

2. Check responsiveness (tap and shout)

3. If unresponsive, shout for help and activate emergency response system

4. Open airway and check for breathing (no more than 10 seconds)

5. Check pulse (brachial in infants, carotid or femoral in children)

6. If no pulse (or pulse <60 bpm with poor perfusion in infants/children), begin CPR

---

questions.stem: An 8-year-old boy suddenly develops difficulty breathing, facial swelling, and wheezing shortly after eating a piece of cake containing unknown ingredients at a school party. He is pale, hypotensive, tachycardic, and has a delayed capillary refill. No prior allergic history. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
questions.initialExplanation: Facial swelling, difficulty breathing and delayed capillary refill = anaphylaxis, and the first drug is IM epinephrine.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This 8-year-old boy presents with classic features of anaphylaxis: respiratory distress (difficulty breathing, wheezing), mucocutaneous
involvement (facial swelling), and cardiovascular compromise (hypotension, tachycardia, delayed capillary refill) following exposure to a
potential allergen (unknown food). This is a medical emergency requiring immediate intervention. Anaphylaxis is a severe, potentially life-
threatening allergic reaction that occurs rapidly after exposure to an allergen. The diagnostic criteria include:

- Acute onset involving skin or mucosal involvement AND respiratory compromise OR reduced blood pressure

OR Two or more of: skin/mucosal involvement, respiratory compromise, reduced blood pressure, persistent gastrointestinal symptoms
after exposure to a known allergen

First-line treatment principles: Epinephrine is the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis because it addresses all the pathophysiological
effects:

Alpha-1 receptors: Vasoconstriction — increases blood pressure, reduces edema

Beta-1 receptors: Increases heart rate and contractility

Beta-2 receptors: Bronchodilation, reduces mediator release

Ped Emergencies     A

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy is found unresponsive in a swimming pool. The lifeguard pulls him out and immediately checks for responsiveness by tapping his shoulders and shouting. There is no response. What is the most appropriate next step in the sequence of pediatric basic life support?

options.label: C
options.text: Open the airway using head tilt-chin lift

questions.initialExplanation: An unresponsive child after drowning: open the airway with head tilt-chin lift then assess breathing.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The correct sequence in pediatric basic life support begins with ensuring safety, then assessing
responsiveness by tapping and shouting. In an unresponsive child with no breathing or only gasping,
the next step is to open the airway using appropriate techniques. For a child without suspected cervical
spine injury, head tilt-chin lift is the standard method. If cervical trauma is suspected, jaw thrust should
be used instead. After opening the airway, you would assess breathing for no more than 10 seconds,
then provide rescue breaths if needed, check for signs of life and pulse, and begin chest compressions
if no pulse or heart rate below 60 bpm with poor perfusion. Activating the emergency response system
should occur early but is not the immediate next step after confirming unresponsiveness in this

 gF[F scenario

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old girl collapses in the school cafeteria. She is unresponsive, not breathing, and has no palpable pulse. Two trained rescuers are present. What is the appropriate compression-to-ventilation ratio for two-rescuer pediatric CPR?
questions.initialExplanation: With two rescuers for a child, the compression-to-ventilation ratio is 15:2 (30:2 for one rescuer).
questions.detailedExplanation:
The compression-to-ventilation ratio in pediatric CPR differs based on the number of rescuers and
whether there is one trained rescuer or an untrained bystander. For two rescuers (or a lone trained
resuscitator), the recommended ratio is 15 compressions to 2 ventilations. This ratio allows for more
ventilations to be delivered, which is particularly important in pediatric arrests that are often respiratory
in origin. For a single rescuer who is untrained or not confident in providing ventilations, a ratio of 30:2
is acceptable with chest compressions only. The compression rate should be 100-120 compressions

per minute, and compression depth should be approximately one-third to one-half of the anterior-
posterior diameter of the chest.

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy collapses during a soccer game. Witnesses report he was unresponsive for only 1 minute before emergency medical services arrived. The child is now being assessed for signs of life. What pulse locations are appropriate for checking in this child?
questions.initialExplanation: Checking the pulse in a child over 1 year: carotid or femoral artery.
questions.detailedExplanation:
For children over 1 year of age, the recommended pulse check sites are the carotid pulse (located in
the neck, between the trachea and sternocleidomastoid muscle) or the femoral pulse (located in the
groin, midway between the pubic symphysis and the anterior superior iliac crest). These central
pulses are more reliable than peripheral pulses like radial or temporal pulses during cardiac arrest.
The pulse check should be performed for no more than 10 seconds. If no pulse is palpable, or if the
heart rate is less than 60 beats per minute with signs of poor perfusion, chest compressions should
be initiated immediately. The brachial pulse is the recommended site for infants under 1 year of age.

---

questions.stem: A 9-month-old infant is found unresponsive by his mother in the crib. She calls emergency services and begins CPR after noting the baby is not breathing and has no pulse. On arrival, EMS finds the infant apneic, pulseless, and cyanotic. The rhythm on monitor shows asystole. After securing the airway with bag-mask ventilation and establishing intraosseous access, what is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: B
options.text: NE Deliver a single unsynchronized shock at 2 J/kg

options.label: E
options.text: Check blood glucose and administer dextrose

questions.initialExplanation: An infant with no pulse after ventilation and IO access: epinephrine 0.01 mg/kg IV or IO.
questions.detailedExplanation:
In pediatric pulseless arrest with asystole, the primary reversible causes are often hypoxia or shock,
and the cornerstone of advanced life support is high-quality CPR combined with early epinephrine.

‘   According to PALS (Pediatric Advanced Life Support) guidelines, epinephrine 0.01 mg/kg (1:10,000
concentration) should be given as soon as vascular or intraosseous access is established and
repeated every 3-5 minutes. Defibrillation (B) is only for shockable rhythms (VF/pVT), not asystole.
Atropine (D) is not recommended in pediatric asystole—it has no proven benefit and is no longer part
of standard PALS algorithms. While checking glucose (E) is important in unexplained altered mental
status, it is not the priority in confirmed cardiac arrest. Continuing compressions without epinephrine
(C) delays critical pharmacologic intervention.

---

questions.stem: A previously healthy 6-month-old infant is found unresponsive and not breathing by her parents. CPR is started immediately. EMS arrives within 8 minutes and finds the infant in ventricular fibrillation (VF). After confirming unresponsiveness and pulselessness, what is the most appropriate next step? moow> 8-

options.label: A
options.text: Begin chest compressions and delay defibrillation

options.label: B
options.text: Deliver one unsynchronized shock at 2 J/kg

questions.initialExplanation: An infant with VF after confirming no pulse: an unsynchronized shock of 2 J/kg (without delaying CPR).
questions.detailedExplanation:
In pediatric ventricular fibrillation (VF) or pulseless ventricular tachycardia (pVT), the first and most
critical intervention is immediate defibrillation. According to PALS guidelines, for a shockable rhythm,
you should deliver one unsynchronized shock at 2 J/kg as soon as the defibrillator is ready —without
delaying for medications or intubation. After the shock, immediately resume high-quality CPR for 2
minutes, then reassess rhythm. Epinephrine (C) is given after the first shock, during the second cycle
of CPR if VF/pVT persists—not before. Amiodarone (D) is considered only after second or third shock
if rhythm remains refractory. Intubation (E) can be performed during ongoing resuscitation but should
not delay defibrillation. Delaying shock (A) worsens outcomes.

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department after a near-drowning incident. She is intubated in the field for apnea and arrives with weak pulses, hypotension, and a core temperature of 30°C (86°F). Despite ventilation and volume resuscitation, she becomes pulseless with asystole on monitor. What is the most appropriate next step in management? NS

options.label: C
options.text: Defer epinephrine and continue CPR while initiating active internal rewarming

questions.initialExplanation: Drowning with hypothermia and asystole: defer drugs (epinephrine) and continue CPR with active internal rewarming.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child is in hypothermic cardiac arrest (core temperature 30°C). In severe hypothermia (<30°C),

the heart is often unresponsive to medications and defibrillation. Current guidelines (including from
AHA and ERC) recommend:

- Continue high-quality CPR

- Withhold epinephrine, atropine, and antiarrhythmics until core temperature reaches 230-32°C

- Avoid defibrillation beyond 1-2 attempts if unsuccessful initially —further shocks are futile until
warmer

- Initiate active internal (core) rewarming: warm |V fluids, heated humidified oxygen, peritoneal
lavage, or ECMO if available

> **Note:** Question number inferred from the sequence.

---

questions.stem: A 10-month-old infant is brought to the emergency department after being found pulseless and apneic at home. CPR was initiated by a family member. On arrival, the infant is in asystole. Despite high-quality CPR, intraosseous access, and two doses of epinephrine, there is no return of spontaneous circulation after 25 minutes. Bedside ultrasound shows no cardiac activity. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Continue resuscitation for a total of 60 minutes

options.label: B
options.text: Administer a third dose of epinephrine

questions.initialExplanation: 25 minutes of resuscitation with no cardiac activity on ultrasound and no reversible factors: consider stopping resuscitation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
In pediatric out-of-hospital cardiac arrest with asystole, especially when there is no return of spontaneous
circulation (ROSC) after 20—25 minutes of high-quality CPR, and bedside ultrasound confirms absence of
cardiac activity, the likelihood of meaningful survival is extremely low. Current guidelines (from AHA and
consensus statements) support that prolonged resuscitation beyond 25-30 minutes in asystolic pediatric
arrest without reversible causes or ROSC is unlikely to be beneficial. Termination of resuscitation should
be considered, particularly in the absence of hypothermia, drug overdose, or other potentially reversible
etiologies. Continuing to 60 minutes (A) is not evidence-based and may delay family support and
bereavement care. Additional epinephrine (B) or sodium bicarbonate (E) is futile in this context.
Therapeutic hypothermia (D) is only initiated after ROSC, not during ongoing arrest.

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with sudden onset of coughing and gagging while playing with small toy parts. He is now wheezing and has decreased breath sounds on the right side. His oxygen saturation is 92% on room air. What is the most likely location of the aspirated foreign body?

options.label: A
options.text: Upper airway at the level of the vocal cords

questions.initialExplanation: An aspirated foreign body in a child: the commonest site is the right main bronchus (wider and more vertical).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Foreign bodies that descend into the lower airway most commonly lodge in the right main bronchus
rather than the left. This is due to anatomical factors: the right main bronchus is wider, shorter, and
more vertical than the left main bronchus, making it the path of least resistance for aspirated material.
Clinical features suggesting lower airway foreign body include unilateral decreased breath sounds,
wheezing localized to one side, cough, and respiratory distress. The presentation of unilateral findings
is characteristic of bronchial foreign bodies. In contrast, upper airway foreign bodies typically present
with stridor, hoarseness, and bilateral respiratory distress. The right-sided predominance is an
important clinical pearl in pediatric foreign-body aspiration.

---
