questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl is choking on a grape. She is conscious, cannot cough effectively, and is making no sounds. What is the most appropriate initial management for this child with severe airway obstruction?

options.label: B
options.text: Perform back blows followed by chest thrusts

options.label: C
options.text: Perform blind finger sweep of the mouth

options.label: D
options.text: Lay the child flat and perform CPR

options.label: E
options.text: Administer rescue breaths to push the object lower

questions.initialExplanation: Severe choking (a conscious child who cannot cough or make sounds): abdominal thrusts for those over 1 year.
questions.detailedExplanation:
For children over 1 year of age with severe airway obstruction (cannot cough, cannot make any
sound), the Heimlich maneuver (abdominal thrusts) is the recommended initial treatment. In a
standing position, the rescuer should stand behind the child, wrap their arms around the child's
waist, and place the heel of one hand just above the umbilicus and below the rib cage. Quick,
upward abdominal thrusts are performed to create pressure that may expel the foreign body. For
an unconscious child, the child should be lowered to the ground and CPR begun with chest
compressions. Blind finger sweeps are not recommended as they may push the foreign body
deeper or cause trauma. In infants, back blows and chest thrusts are used instead of abdominal
thrusts due to the risk of liver injury.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy has a witnessed aspiration of a peanut. He initially had severe coughing and respiratory distress but now has mild persistent cough and mild wheezing. What is the most important next step in evaluation?
questions.initialExplanation: Peanut aspiration with mild stable symptoms: the first step is a chest X-ray to locate it.
questions.detailedExplanation:
In children with suspected foreign-body aspiration, chest radiography is an important initial diagnostic
study. While many aspirated foreign bodies are radiolucent (like peanuts, vegetables, or plastic),
radiographic findings may include atelectasis, hyperinflation (due to ball-valve effect), mediastinal shift,
or direct visualization of a radiopaque foreign body. A normal chest X-ray does not rule out foreign-
body aspiration, and clinical suspicion should guide further evaluation. In this child with persistent
symptoms despite initial improvement, bronchoscopy may be indicated if suspicion remains high. The
chest X-ray is a non-invasive initial study that can provide valuable information and should be
performed early in the evaluation of suspected foreign-body aspiration.

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy is playing with small toy parts when he suddenly begins coughing, becomes hoarse, and develops inspiratory stridor. He is able to speak in short phrases but appears anxious and has increased work of breathing. On examination, there is decreased air entry on the right side of the chest. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: B
options.text: Perform immediate laryngoscopy and Magill forceps removal

questions.initialExplanation: A foreign body with decreased air entry on one side: needs rigid bronchoscopy for removal.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child presents with acute onset of cough, stridor, hoarseness, and asymmetric breath sounds after playing
with small objects —classic signs of foreign body (FB) inhalation, likely lodged in the right mainstem bronchus
(anatomically more vertical). In a partially obstructed airway with respiratory distress but maintained air
exchange, the diagnosis is clinical, and imaging (C)—such as lateral neck X-ray or chest X-ray—may support
the diagnosis (e.g., air trapping, atelectasis), but should not delay definitive management. Nebulized
epinephrine (A) is used for croup, not FB. Abdominal thrusts (D) are for complete airway obstruction with
inability to speak or breathe —not applicable here. Direct laryngoscopy with Magill forceps (B) is only useful for
supraglottic or laryngeal FBs, not tracheobronchial ones. Rigid bronchoscopy (E) is the gold standard for both

diagnosis and removal of lower airway foreign bodies in children and should be performed urgently by an
experienced operator.

---

questions.stem: A 14-month-old girl suddenly develops paroxysmal coughing and wheezing while eating peanuts. She becomes cyanotic for a few seconds but then recovers, though she continues to have persistent wheezing localized to the right lung. She is afebrile and has no history of asthma. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Sudden cough and wheeze in one lung without fever or asthma = foreign body aspiration.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has a classic presentation of foreign body (FB) aspiration:

- Acute onset during eating (peanuts —a common culprit)

- Paroxysmal coughing and transient cyanosis (indicating partial airway obstruction)

- Persistent unilateral wheezing (suggesting a ball-valve effect in a bronchus, typically the right mainstem due to anatomy)
- No fever or prior respiratory illness, making infection (A, D) unlikely

- No history of asthma (B), and wheezing is localized, not diffuse

- Tracheomalacia (E) causes expiratory stridor or noisy breathing from infancy, not acute focal wheezing after choking
Foreign body aspiration should be suspected in any toddler with sudden choking followed by persistent respiratory

symptoms, even if they appear to recover initially. Chest X-ray may show air trapping or atelectasis, but rigid bronchoscopy
remains diagnostic and therapeutic.

---

questions.stem: An 18-month-old boy is eating grapes when he suddenly becomes unable to cry, turns blue, and clutches his throat. He is conscious but has no audible breath sounds and marked retractions. A bystander begins back blows and chest thrusts without success. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.text: Perform direct laryngoscopy and attempt removal with Magill forceps

options.label: C
options.text: Perform a blind finger sweep of the mouth \*

options.label: D
options.text: Give rescue breaths and transport without further intervention \*

options.label: E
options.text: Perform direct laryngoscopy and attempt removal with Magill forceps Administer nebulized epinephrine Proceed immediately to rigid bronchoscopy in the operating room Begin bag-mask ventilation Perform emergency needle cricothyrotomy

questions.initialExplanation: Choking with failed back blows and chest thrusts and loss of consciousness: direct laryngoscopy and removal with Magill forceps.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has acute, complete upper airway obstruction by a foreign body (grapes), evidenced by inability to
vocalize, cyanosis, choking, and absent breath sounds—a true emergency. In a conscious child with complete
obstruction, initial maneuvers are back blows and chest thrusts (as attempted). If these fail and the child
remains conscious, direct laryngoscopy should be performed immediately to visualize and remove a
supraglottic or laryngeal foreign body using Magill forceps. This is a life-saving bedside procedure that can be
done in the emergency department without delay.

- Rigid bronchoscopy (C) is definitive for tracheobronchial foreign bodies but requires transfer to the OR and is
not appropriate when immediate airway access is needed. Bag-mask ventilation (D) will likely fail if the
obstruction is complete and may push the object deeper. Nebulized epinephrine (B) is for croup. Needle
cricothyrotomy (E) is a last resort if the child becomes apneic and cannot be intubated or oxygenated —but he
is still conscious.

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department after a witnessed choking episode while eating popcorn. She initially coughed violently but now appears well, with normal vital signs and clear lung sounds. Chest X-ray is unremarkable. What is the most appropriate next step in management? “c
questions.initialExplanation: A normal chest X-ray with suspected foreign body: do an expiratory-phase chest X-ray (shows air trapping).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Although this child appears well now, she had a withessed choking episode with popcorn—a common cause of
foreign body (FB) aspiration in toddlers. Normal lung sounds and a standard (inspiratory) chest X-ray do not
rule out an aspirated FB, especially if it is radiolucent (like food). In such cases, additional imaging is warranted:
- Expiratory-phase chest X-ray (or decubitus views in non-cooperative children) can reveal air trapping due to a
ball-valve effect, even when the inspiratory film is normal.

- If the expiratory film shows air trapping or other signs of obstruction, rigid bronchoscopy is indicated.

- Discharge (A) is premature without further evaluation. Observation alone (B) without imaging risks missing a
retained FB, which can lead to complications like pneumonia or bronchiectasis. Bronchoscopy (C) is not
performed empirically in asymptomatic children with normal imaging. Corticosteroids (E) have no role here.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with suspected septic shock. His vital signs show heart rate 160 bpm, blood pressure 65/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 35/min, and capillary refill 5 seconds. He has cool, mottled extremities and altered mental status. What stage of shock is this patient experiencing?
questions.initialExplanation: Cold mottled extremities and altered mental status = decompensated shock (low blood pressure).
questions.detailedExplanation:
This patient is exhibiting signs of decompensated shock, characterized by hypotension (systolic blood
pressure below the 5th percentile for age), declining mental status, and signs of poor perfusion
(prolonged capillary refill, cool extremities). In decompensated shock, the body's compensatory
mechanisms have failed, and hypotension develops as a late sign. The child has tachycardia, which is
an early and universal sign of shock, but the presence of hypotension distinguishes decompensated
from compensated shock. Compensated shock would show normal blood pressure despite poor
perfusion. Immediate intervention is required, including fluid resuscitation, vasopressor support, and
treatment of the underlying cause (antibiotics and source control for septic shock).

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl with severe gastroenteritis and dehydration presents with tachycardia, delayed capillary refill of 4 seconds, cool extremities, and normal blood pressure. Her mental status is appropriate. What is the most appropriate initial fluid resuscitation?

options.label: B
options.text: N B) 20 mL/kg normal saline bolus over 5-10 minutes

questions.initialExplanation: Severe dehydration with shock: bolus of NS 20 mL/kg over 5-10 minutes.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child is in compensated shock with signs of poor perfusion (tachycardia, delayed capillary refill,
cool extremities) but normal blood pressure. The initial management of shock, regardless of type,

‘    includes rapid fluid resuscitation with isotonic crystalloids (normal saline or Ringer's lactate) at a dose
of 20 mL/kg bolus over 5-10 minutes. This volume is designed to rapidly restore intravascular volume
and improve perfusion. The bolus may be repeated based on clinical response, with reassessment
after each bolus. For hypovolemic shock from gastroenteritis, this aggressive fluid resuscitation is
critical. Oral rehydration is appropriate for mild dehydration but not for shock states. Maintenance
fluids alone are insufficient in shock.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy with suspected tension pneumothorax presents with hypotension, distended neck veins, absent breath sounds on the left side, and tracheal deviation to the right. What is the most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.label: A
options.text: Needle decompression followed by chest tube insertion

questions.initialExplanation: Tension pneumothorax: start with needle decompression then chest tube.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child presents with classic signs of tension pneumothorax, a form of obstructive shock caused by
accumulation of air in the pleural space under pressure, leading to mediastinal shift and impaired
venous return. The signs include hypotension, distended neck veins, absent breath sounds, and
tracheal deviation. Tension pneumothorax is a medical emergency requiring immediate
decompression to prevent cardiac arrest. The initial treatment is needle decompression at the second
intercostal space in the midclavicular line, followed by definitive management with chest tube
insertion. Delaying treatment for imaging or other interventions can be fatal. This is one of the few
situations where immediate intervention without imaging is indicated.

---

questions.stem: A 6-month-old infant is brought to the emergency department with a 2-day history of vomiting, poor feeding, and decreased urine output. On examination, he is lethargic, tachycardic (HR 180 bpm), and has delayed capillary refill (>4 seconds). His extremities are cool, and pulses are weak. He weighs 7 kg, and his current weight is 8% less than at his last well-child visit. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.text: Administer 10 mL/kg of normal saline bolus

options.label: B
options.text: Administer 20 mL/kg of normal saline bolus

options.label: E
options.text: Obtain serum lactate before fluid administration

questions.initialExplanation: An infant with dehydration and 8% weight loss after diarrhea: NS bolus 20 mL/kg.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This infant has signs of hypovolemic shock due to gastroenteritis and dehydration:

- Lethargy, tachycardia, delayed capillary refill (>3 sec), cool extremities, weak pulses, and 8% weight
loss (indicating severe dehydration)

- In pediatric shock, the first and most critical intervention is rapid volume resuscitation with isotonic
crystalloid (normal saline or lactated Ringer’s). Guidelines (from PALS and WHO) recommend an

initial bolus of 20 mL/kg over 5-10 minutes in children with compensated or hypotensive shock. This
can be repeated up to 60 mL/kg if needed.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with high fever, rash, and lethargy. On examination, he is hypotensive (BP 70/40 mmHg), tachycardic (HR 160 bpm), and has warm extremities with brisk capillary refill. He has a diffuse erythematous rash and neck stiffness. Laboratory studies show WBC 22,000/uL, platelets 80,000/uL, and elevated CRP. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: E
options.text: Administer 10 mL/kg normal saline followed by dopamine

questions.initialExplanation: High fever, low platelets and high CRP with signs of sepsis: start NS 20 mL/kg then antibiotics.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child presents with signs of distributive (septic) shock:

- Hypotension, tachycardia, warm extremities, brisk capillary refill, fever, rash, and meningeal signs

- Lab findings suggest bacterial infection (leukocytosis, thrombocytopenia, elevated CRP)—concerning
for meningococcemia or other invasive bacterial disease

- In pediatric septic shock, the first step is always rapid fluid resuscitation with 20 mL/kg isotonic
crystalloid bolus, even in “warm” shock. Unlike adults, children often have a hypovolemic component
due to third-spacing and poor intake, and fluids frequently reverse early shock. Vasopressors like
norepinephrine (B) are reserved for fluid-refractory shock —not first-line.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old girl with a history of congenital heart disease (single ventricle physiology, post-Fontan) presents with increasing fatigue, tachycardia (HR 140 bpm), and cool extremities. Blood pressure is 80/50 mmHg, capillary refill is 3 seconds, and she has mild hepatomegaly. She is not febrile and has no signs of infection. What is the most likely type of shock, and what is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Hypovolemic shock; administer 20 mL/kg normal saline bolus

options.label: B
options.text: Cardiogenic shock; administer 10 mL/kg normal saline cautiously

questions.initialExplanation: A congenital heart disease patient in shock: often cardiogenic shock, so give fluid cautiously (10 mL/kg) with monitoring.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has single ventricle physiology post-Fontan, a high-risk condition for cardiogenic shock due
to limited cardiac reserve. Her presentation —fatigue, tachycardia, cool extremities, borderline
hypotension, and hepatomegaly (sign of congestion) —suggests low cardiac output with possible mild
systemic venous congestion, not hypovolemia or infection.

- In cardiogenic shock, aggressive fluid boluses (e.g., 20 mL/kg) can worsen heart failure by
increasing preload in a non-compliant circulation. Instead, small, cautious fluid challenges (5-10
mL/kg) may be used if there is evidence of some hypovolemia, but often inotropic support (e.g.,
milrinone or epinephrine) and afterload reduction are needed. However, among the given options, B is
the most appropriate: it correctly identifies cardiogenic shock and recommends cautious fluid
administration.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy develops sudden onset of facial swelling, generalized urticaria, and wheezing 10 minutes after eating a peanut butter sandwich. He is anxious, tachycardic (HR 140 bpm), and has mild respiratory distress with oxygen saturation of 94% on room air. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.initialExplanation: Facial swelling, wheeze and difficulty breathing after exposure = anaphylaxis: IM epinephrine 0.01 mg/kg (max 0.3 mg).
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child meets criteria for anaphylaxis: acute onset of skin/mucosal involvement (facial swelling, urticaria) plus

respiratory compromise (wheezing, distress) after exposure to a known allergen (peanut). According to

international anaphylaxis guidelines (e.g., WAO, AAAAI, Resuscitation Council), intramuscular epinephrine is
‘    the first-line and life-saving treatment, regardless of severity or oxygen saturation.

Epinephrine acts rapidly to:

- Reverse bronchospasm and upper airway edema
- Stabilize mast cells and basophils

- Increase vascular tone and cardiac output

---

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy develops sudden onset of urticaria, angioedema, wheezing, and hypotension 5 minutes after receiving an intravenous antibiotic. What is the most appropriate initial treatment for this patient?
questions.initialExplanation: Urticaria, swelling, wheeze and hypotension after an IV drug: IM epinephrine first.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Epinephrine is the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis and should be administered immediately when
the diagnosis is suspected. The recommended dose is 0.01 mg/kg intramuscularly (maximum 0.3-0.5
mg per dose), preferably in the anterolateral thigh. Epinephrine works through alpha-1 adrenergic
effects (vasoconstriction, reduced mucosal edema), beta-1 effects (increased heart rate and
contractility), and beta-2 effects (bronchodilation, reduced mediator release). Intramuscular
administration provides rapid onset of action. Antihistamines (H1 and H2 blockers), corticosteroids,
and bronchodilators are important adjunctive therapies but should NOT delay or replace epinephrine
administration. Epinephrine should be repeated every 5-15 minutes as needed for persistent or
recurrent symptoms.

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl with anaphylaxis has received epinephrine IM and is now being prepared for discharge after symptom resolution. Her parents ask how long she should continue antihistamine therapy. What is the recommended duration?
questions.initialExplanation: Antihistamines after anaphylaxis are given for 24-48 hours after symptoms resolve (per the given answer).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Patients with anaphylaxis should continue on H1 and H2 blockers for 24-48 hours after resolution of
symptoms to prevent biphasic reactions, which can occur in a significant percentage of cases. A short
course of oral steroids (3-5 days) may also be warranted to reduce the risk of recurrent or protracted
anaphylaxis. The observation period should be at least 4-6 hours, and some guidelines recommend 24
hours of observation given that late-phase or biphasic reactions can occur 8-12 hours after the initial
attack. Patients should be discharged with an epinephrine auto-injector and education on its use, as
well as follow-up with an allergy/immunology specialist for further evaluation and prevention strategies.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old girl with anaphylaxis has received epinephrine and is now hemodynamically stable but has persistent respiratory distress with wheezing. What additional pharmacologic therapy is most appropriate for her respiratory symptoms?
questions.initialExplanation: Persistent wheeze after epinephrine: nebulized epinephrine or albuterol, per the specific answer.
questions.detailedExplanation:
For persistent respiratory symptoms (wheezing, upper airway edema) despite intramuscular
epinephrine, nebulized epinephrine (racemic epinephrine) is an appropriate adjunctive therapy.
Nebulized epinephrine acts directly on the airway receptors to cause vasoconstriction and reduce
mucosal edema, particularly useful for upper airway obstruction from angioedema. Inhaled beta-
agonists like albuterol are also useful for bronchospasm. Nebulized epinephrine provides rapid relief
of upper airway edema and may prevent the need for intubation in severe cases. The effects are
temporary, and patients need close monitoring. Systemic therapies (antihistamines, corticosteroids)
have slower onset and are not as effective for immediate relief of airway obstruction.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old girl with known peanut allergy accidentally ingests peanut-containing candy. She develops urticaria, facial angioedema, and mild wheezing. Her blood pressure is normal. What is the most appropriate dose of epinephrine for this patient?
questions.initialExplanation: A 5-year-old girl (about 18 kg): the IM epinephrine dose is 0.15 mg.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The recommended dose of epinephrine for anaphylaxis is 0.01 mg/kg intramuscularly, with a
maximum single dose of 0.3 mg for children. For a 5-year-old girl, assuming a weight of
approximately 18-20 kg, the dose would be 0.18-0.2 mg. However, the available auto-injector
formulations include 0.15 mg (for 15-30 kg) and 0.3 mg (for 30 kg and above). The 0.15 mg auto-
injector would be appropriate for this patient. The dose is rounded to the nearest available auto-
injector strength. If the child weighs more than 30 kg, the 0.3 mg dose would be used. Epinephrine
auto-injectors are available in fixed doses to simplify administration in emergency situations.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old girl with a known allergy to bee venom is stung while playing outside. Within minutes, she develops hoarseness, stridor, and generalized hives. She is tachycardic (HR 130 bpm) and anxious but has normal oxygen saturation (98% on room air). Her parents administer an epinephrine auto-injector (0.3 mg) intramuscularly. Ten minutes later, her stridor persists, and she appears more fatigued. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Administer a second dose of intramuscular epinephrine

questions.initialExplanation: Persistent stridor after the first dose: a second epinephrine dose after 5-15 minutes.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child is experiencing progressive upper airway obstruction due to anaphylaxis, evidenced by
persistent stridor and increasing fatigue after an initial dose of epinephrine. Fatigue in this context is a
dangerous sign—it may indicate impending respiratory failure as the work of breathing exhausts
respiratory muscles.

- Guidelines (from WAO, AAAAI, and PALS) state that if symptoms persist or worsen 5-15 minutes
after the first dose, a second dose of intramuscular epinephrine should be given immediately. Delaying
epinephrine increases the risk of airway loss or cardiovascular collapse.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy develops sudden onset of generalized hives, vomiting, and respiratory distress after eating scrambled eggs. He is given intramuscular epinephrine (0.15 mg) by his parents and improves within minutes. On arrival to the emergency department 30 minutes later, he is asymptomatic with normal vital signs. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.text: Discharge home with an epinephrine auto-injector and allergist referral

options.label: B
options.text: Observe for at least 4—6 hours due to risk of biphasic reaction

options.label: C
options.text: Administer oral prednisolone and diphenhydramine, then discharge

options.label: E
options.text: Perform skin prick testing in the emergency department

questions.initialExplanation: After symptoms resolve: observe 4-6 hours because of the risk of a biphasic reaction.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child experienced anaphylaxis (hives, vomiting, respiratory distress) after egg ingestion and
responded well to epinephrine. However, biphasic anaphylaxis—a recurrence of symptoms without re-
‘    exposure—occurs in up to 20% of pediatric cases, typically within 1-72 hours, with most recurrences
within 8 hours. Therefore, observation for at least 4—6 hours post-epinephrine is standard of care,
even if the child appears fully recovered.
- Discharge immediately (A or C) is unsafe without observation. Admission for 24 hours (D) is
unnecessary in a completely asymptomatic child after the observation period. Skin prick testing (E)
should never be performed in the acute setting—it is done later by an allergist during follow-up.

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after ingesting an unknown amount of liquid from an unmarked container. His mother suspects it was kerosene used for lighting lamps. He is asymptomatic, with normal vital signs and clear breath sounds. Chest X-ray is normal. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: D
options.text: Observe in hospital for at least 6 hours

questions.initialExplanation: After suspected exposure with no symptoms: hospital observation for at least 6 hours.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Kerosene is a hydrocarbon with low systemic toxicity but high risk of chemical pneumonitis due to
aspiration during ingestion or vomiting. Symptoms (cough, tachypnea, hypoxia) may be delayed up to
6 hours. Gastric decontamination (A, B) is contraindicated —it increases aspiration risk 9. Activated
charcoal does not adsorb hydrocarbons. NAC (E) is for paracetamol. Even if asymptomatic,
observation for 6-8 hours is standard to monitor for respiratory deterioration.

---

questions.stem: An 18-month-old girl is found playing with a remote control. One hour later, she develops drooling and refuses to eat. A chest X-ray reveals a disc-shaped object in the upper esophagus. What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.initialExplanation: A disc battery in the esophagus with a drooling girl: urgent endoscopic removal within hours to avoid burns.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Button batteries lodged in the esophagus cause alkaline tissue injury via electrolysis, leading to
ulceration, perforation, tracheoesophageal fistula, or aortoesophageal fistula within 2—6 hours. Urgent
endoscopic removal is mandatory. Honey (A) may be given only if <12 hours post-ingestion and >1
year old as a temporizing measure to reduce injury, but does not replace endoscopy. Observation (D)
is dangerous. Charcoal (B) and PPIs (E) are irrelevant.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy ingests an unknown quantity of drain cleaner containing sodium hydroxide. On arrival, he has oral burns, drooling, and stridor. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: C
options.text: Give milk or water to dilute

options.label: D
options.text: Secure airway and avoid oral intake

questions.initialExplanation: Alkaline cleaner ingestion with stridor: secure the airway and keep the child nil by mouth.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Corrosive (alkali) ingestions cause liquefactive necrosis, with risk of progressive airway edema and
esophageal perforation. The priority is airway protection—early intubation may be needed before
swelling worsens. Do not give anything by mouth (C)—it may worsen injury. Activated charcoal (A)

and lavage (B) are contraindicated. Steroids (E) do not prevent stricture formation and may increase
infection risk.

---

questions.stem: A 22-month-old toddler is found with an open bottle of laundry detergent pods. He has profuse vomiting and respiratory distress. On examination, he has wheezing and oxygen saturation of 90%. What is the most likely mechanism of toxicity?
questions.initialExplanation: Laundry detergent with stridor and hypoxia: the mechanism is chemical pneumonitis (aspiration).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Detergent pods contain concentrated surfactants that cause severe mucosal irritation. Vomiting often
leads to aspiration, resulting in chemical pneumonitis, bronchospasm, and hypoxia—the most common
cause of morbidity. Systemic toxicity is rare. Esophageal perforation (C) is possible but less acute.
Methemoglobinemia (D) occurs with nitrates/anilines, not detergents.

---

## Poisoning

> Question numbers not present in the source file for this topic: 2.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department after being found near an open container of insecticide. Within an hour, he developed drooling, vomiting, diarrhea, and progressive drowsiness. On examination, he is noted to have pinpoint pupils, muscle fasciculations, bradycardia, wheezing, and copious respiratory secretions. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
questions.initialExplanation: Drooling, bradycardia and copious respiratory secretions = organophosphate poisoning, and the antidote is atropine.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This 3-year-old boy presents with classic signs of organophosphate insecticide poisoning following
exposure to an unknown insecticide. The clinical features (drooling, vomiting, diarrhea, pinpoint pupils,
muscle fasciculations, bradycardia, bronchorrhea, wheezing, drowsiness) constitute the cholinergic
toxidrome, which results from inhibition of acetylcholinesterase.

- Organophosphates are acetylcholinesterase inhibitors found in many insecticides, nerve agents, and
some pesticides. They irreversibly bind to acetylcholinesterase, preventing the breakdown of
acetylcholine. This leads to accumulation of acetylcholine at muscarinic and nicotinic receptors,
causing the cholinergic crisis.

---

questions.stem: When considering the treatment of a patient with acetaminophen poisoning, and after assessment of the ABCs, it is helpful to place the patient into one of 4 stages. Of the following, stage 1 is characterize by :

options.label: D
options.text: E right upper quadrant abdominal pain

questions.initialExplanation: Stage I of paracetamol poisoning (0-24 hours): nausea, vomiting and sweating.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Acetaminophen (paracetamol) toxicity progresses through four clinical stages. Stage 1 occurs within
the first 24 hours after ingestion and is characterized primarily by gastrointestinal symptoms such as
nausea, vomiting, anorexia, and malaise. At this point, liver enzyme levels (ALT, AST), coagulation
parameters (INR), and abdominal pain are typically normal or not yet prominent—these develop later
in Stage 2 (24-72 hours) and peak in Stage 3 (72-96 hours) when hepatotoxicity becomes evident.
Therefore, among the options listed, only nausea and vomiting correctly describe Stage 1. The other
choices reflect signs of hepatic injury or synthetic dysfunction that occur in later stages.

---

questions.stem: In acetaminophen poisoning, when the initiation of N-Acetylcysteine therapy is delayed, there is the greater the risk of acute liver failure. N-Acetylcysteine should be instituted no later than :
questions.initialExplanation: N-acetylcysteine is best started within 8 hours of poisoning to prevent liver failure.
questions.detailedExplanation:
N-Acetylcysteine (NAC) is most effective when administered within 8 hours of acute acetaminophen
ingestion. This is because NAC works primarily by replenishing hepatic glutathione stores, which
detoxify the toxic metabolite N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI). If NAC is given within 8 hours,
the risk of hepatotoxicity is dramatically reduced, and liver injury is often prevented entirely. While
NAC still provides benefit even when started later (e.g., 24—48 hours post-ingestion), its efficacy
declines significantly with delay, and the risk of acute liver failure rises. Therefore, 8 hours is the
widely accepted critical window for optimal protection, making option D the best choice. Options A-C
are unnecessarily restrictive and not supported by guidelines, while E exceeds the ideal therapeutic
window.

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the ED after being found near an open kerosene container. His mother reports brief coughing and vomiting at home but no loss of consciousness. On exam, he is alert with a respiratory rate of 36/min, oxygen saturation 93% on room air, and diffuse wheezes on auscultation. Chest X-ray reveals bilateral interstitial infiltrates. What is the most appropriate next step in management? 6-

options.label: D
options.text: Provide supplemental oxygen and supportive care

options.label: E
options.text: Administer ipecac syrup to induce emesis

questions.initialExplanation: Hydrocarbon (e.g., kerosene) inhalation with lung infiltrates: supportive care and oxygen, and do not induce vomiting.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Kerosene poisoning in children primarily causes chemical pneumonitis due to aspiration rather than
systemic toxicity from ingestion. Gastric lavage (B) is contraindicated because it increases the risk of
further aspiration and does not improve outcomes. Activated charcoal (A) is ineffective for
hydrocarbons like kerosene and may itself cause aspiration pneumonia. Ipecac (E) is obsolete and
dangerous in this context. N-acetylcysteine (C) is used for paracetamol overdose, not hydrocarbon
exposure. Management focuses on supportive care: oxygen supplementation, monitoring for
respiratory deterioration, and avoiding interventions that provoke vomiting or airway manipulation.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after ingesting an unknown quantity of liquid drain cleaner. She is drooling, refusing to swallow, and crying inconsolably. On examination, she has stridor, erythema of the lips and oropharynx, and appears anxious with a respiratory rate of 40 breaths per minute. Her oxygen saturation is 94% on room air. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: D
options.text: Give oral neutralizing agents (e.g., vinegar or milk) \*

questions.initialExplanation: Alkaline cleaner ingestion with dangerous airway signs: secure the airway with immediate intubation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child shows signs of significant corrosive ingestion (stridor, drooling, respiratory distress),
indicating upper airway edema and impending obstruction. In such cases, the priority is securing
the airway before it becomes completely obstructed —hence, immediate endotracheal intubation is
critical. Administering oral neutralizing agents (D) is dangerous: acid-base reactions can generate
heat and worsen tissue injury. Activated charcoal (A) does not bind corrosives and is not useful.
EGD (C) is important for assessing mucosal injury but must be delayed until the airway is secure.
Observation alone (E) risks fatal airway compromise. Thus, airway protection takes precedence
over all other interventions.

> **Note:** Question number inferred from the sequence.

---

questions.stem: An 18-month-old boy is brought to the ED by his parents after they found him playing with a discarded remote control. He has been irritable for the past 2 hours and now refuses to eat, complaining of throat pain. On examination, he has mild tachycardia, drooling, and tenderness over the suprasternal notch. A plain X-ray of the neck shows a round, radiopaque object lodged in the upper esophagus. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: D
options.text: Observe at home with a soft diet \*

questions.initialExplanation: A round object stuck in the esophagus (often a battery): urgent endoscopic removal.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has ingested a button battery, which is a true emergency when lodged in the esophagus.
Button batteries can cause severe tissue necrosis within 2 hours due to electrical current and alkali
leakage, leading to perforation, fistula formation, or fatal hemorrhage. Inducing vomiting (A) is
dangerous —it may cause re-aspiration or further injury. Honey (C) may be considered only in children
>1 year if endoscopy will be delayed >12 hours, but it is not definitive management and does not
replace urgent removal. Observation (D) risks catastrophic complications. Corticosteroids (E) do not
prevent battery-induced injury. Urgent endoscopic removal (<2 hours) is the standard of care to
prevent life-threatening complications.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department 3 hours after ingesting an unknown number of his grandmother’s “heart pills,” later identified as aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid). He is tachypneic with a respiratory rate of 42 breaths per minute, has a temperature of 38.5°C, and appears flushed and diaphoretic. Arterial blood gas shows pH 7.48, PaCO2 22 mmHg, and HCOs™ 16 mEq/L. Serum salicylate level is 45 mg/dL. What is the most appropriate next step in management?.

options.label: E
options.text: Observe and repeat the salicylate level in 6 hours \*

questions.initialExplanation: Aspirin poisoning with obvious acidosis and level 45 mg/dL: IV sodium bicarbonate to alkalinize urine and speed excretion.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has moderate to severe salicylate (aspirin) poisoning, evidenced by a serum level of 45 mg/dL (>
30-40 mg/dL in acute ingestion is concerning), respiratory alkalosis with compensatory metabolic acidosis,
and signs of toxicity (tachypnea, fever, diaphoresis). The mainstay of treatment is urinary alkalinization with IV
sodium bicarbonate, which enhances renal excretion of salicylate by trapping the ionized form in the urine.
Activated charcoal (A) may be beneficial if given within 1 hour of ingestion, but it is not the most appropriate
next step now —3 hours have passed, and the priority is correcting acid-base disturbances and enhancing
elimination. Hemodialysis (B) is reserved for severe cases (e.g., levels >90-100 mg/dL, cerebral edema, renal
failure, or refractory acidosis). Gastric lavage (D) is rarely used and not recommended beyond 1 hour.
Observation alone (E) is inadequate given the toxic level and symptoms.

---

questions.stem: A 22-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department by her parents 4 hours after they noticed she had access to a bottle of liquid paracetamol (acetaminophen). They estimate she may have ingested up to 150 mg/kg. She is currently asymptomatic, with normal vital signs and a benign abdominal exam. A serum acetaminophen level drawn 4 hours post-ingestion is 220 pg/mL. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: D
options.text: E Repeat acetaminophen level in 4 hours

questions.initialExplanation: Paracetamol level 220 at 4 hours (above the treatment line): IV N-acetylcysteine.
questions.detailedExplanation:
In acetaminophen (paracetamol) overdose, the 4-hour serum level is interpreted using the Rumack-
Matthew nomogram. A level of 220 ug/mL at 4 hours falls above the treatment line (which starts at
150 pg/mL at 4 hours), indicating significant risk of hepatotoxicity. Therefore, N-acetylcysteine (NAC)
should be initiated immediately, even if the child is asymptomatic—early treatment is highly effective
in preventing liver injury. Activated charcoal (A) may be considered if given within 1-2 hours of
ingestion, but it is not a substitute for NAC when the level is toxic. Discharge (C) is unsafe given the
supratherapeutic level. Repeating the level (D) is unnecessary —the 4-hour level is definitive for
treatment decisions. Gastric lavage (E) is not recommended beyond 1 hour and offers no benefit
here.

---

questions.stem: A 83-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department 90 minutes after ingesting a small amount of kerosene from a lantern. He has mild coughing but no respiratory distress, and his oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. Chest auscultation is clear, and he is playful and interactive. A chest X-ray is unremarkable. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.initialExplanation: A child after ingestion with no symptoms and a normal exam: discharge home with parental education.
questions.detailedExplanation:
In asymptomatic children with suspected kerosene (hydrocarbon) ingestion and a normal chest X-ray
at 2 hours post-exposure, the risk of developing delayed pneumonitis is very low. Current guidelines

‘    (including from AAP and poison control centers) support discharge with clear return precautions if the
child remains asymptomatic after a 4-6 hour observation period. Since this child is already 90 minutes
post-ingestion, playful, with no respiratory signs and a normal X-ray, he can be safely discharged after
a short period of monitoring (often completed in ED). Admission (C) is unnecessary in truly
asymptomatic cases. Activated charcoal (A) and gastric lavage (B) are not recommended for
hydrocarbons due to aspiration risk and lack of benefit. Antibiotics (E) are not indicated
prophylactically.

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department after her mother witnessed her swallowing a small amount of toilet bowl cleaner. On arrival, she is crying, with visible burns on her lips and tongue, and refuses to drink water. She has no stridor or respiratory distress. Her vital signs are stable. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: D
options.text: Give oral milk to dilute the ingestion \*

questions.initialExplanation: Caustic ingestion with no airway symptoms: early EGD to assess the burn.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has evidence of oropharyngeal injury from a corrosive ingestion (toilet bowl cleaner, typically
a strong acid). The presence of visible burns on lips and tongue indicates significant exposure, and
such patients are at high risk for esophageal and gastric injury, even in the absence of respiratory
symptoms. EGD within 12-24 hours (ideally within 12) is indicated to assess the extent of mucosal
damage, guide management, and predict complications like stricture formation. Activated charcoal (A)
is ineffective for corrosives and may obscure endoscopic views. Oral neutralizing agents like milk (B)
are not recommended —they can cause exothermic reactions or vomiting, worsening injury.
Corticosteroids (D) do not prevent strictures and may increase infection risk. Observation alone (E) is
inadequate when mucosal injury is already evident.

---

questions.stem: An 18-month-old boy is brought to the ED after his parents found him with a partially chewed lithium coin cell from a key fob. He has no respiratory distress but complains of neck pain and has mild drooling. Lateral neck X-ray confirms a radiopaque disc-shaped object in the proximal esophagus. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: E
options.text: Observe with a repeat X-ray in 24 hours \*

questions.initialExplanation: Ingested disc-shaped object in the esophagus: urgent endoscopic removal.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Button (coin) battery ingestion with esophageal impaction is a medical emergency, especially in
children under 5 years. Even if asymptomatic initially, necrosis can occur within 2 hours due to
electrical current generating hydroxide ions at the tissue—battery interface, leading to esophageal
perforation, tracheoesophageal fistula, or fatal vascular erosion (e.g., aortoesophageal fistula). **
Urgent endoscopic removal (<2 hours from identification)** is the standard of care. Honey (A) may be
given *only* if the child is >1 year old and endoscopy will be delayed beyond 2 hours—it is adjunctive,
not definitive. Observation (B) risks catastrophic complications. Activated charcoal (D) does not bind
metals and is useless here. PPIs (E) do not mitigate battery-induced injury.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy weighing 18 kg is brought to the emergency department 4 hours after ingesting an unknown number of acetaminophen tablets from his grandmother's purse. He is awake, alert, and complains of nausea. His physical examination is otherwise unremarkable. Serum acetaminophen level drawn now is 180 ug/mL (1,190 pmol/L). What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.initialExplanation: Paracetamol level 180 at 4 hours: start NAC by mouth.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has ingested a potentially toxic amount of acetaminophen, as evidenced by the serum level
of 180 pg/mL obtained 4 hours post-ingestion. According to the Rumack-Matthew nomogram, levels
above the treatment line at 4 hours indicate the need for antidote therapy. The threshold for possible
risk is 900 pmol/L, and this child's level of 1,190 pmol/L exceeds this threshold. Oral N-acetylcysteine
is the preferred initial treatment, given as a loading dose of 140 mg/kg followed by 70 mg/kg every 4
hours for 17 doses. Activated charcoal may be considered if within 1-2 hours of ingestion, but NAC

should not be delayed. Gastric lavage is generally not recommended in children due to risk of
aspiration and limited benefit beyond the first hour.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department 2 hours after ingesting approximately 10 adult aspirin tablets (325 mg each). He is alert but tachypneic with a respiratory rate of 38 breaths per minute. Arterial blood gas reveals pH 7.52, PaCO: 24 mmHg, and HCOs~ 19 mEq/L. Serum salicylate level is 35 mg/dL. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: E
options.text: Observe with repeat salicylate levels in 2 hours

questions.initialExplanation: Aspirin poisoning with acidosis: correct with sodium bicarbonate.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has acute salicylate (aspirin) toxicity with a serum level of 35 mg/dL at 2 hours, which is above the
treatment threshold (=30 mg/dL in acute pediatric ingestion). The ABG shows respiratory alkalosis with
compensatory metabolic acidosis, a classic finding in salicylism. IV sodium bicarbonate serves two critical

‘    roles: (1) it alkalinizes the urine, enhancing renal excretion of salicylate by ion trapping, and (2) it helps correct
acidemia, which, if unchecked, drives salicylate into the central nervous system and worsens toxicity.
Activated charcoal (A) may be considered if given within 1 hour, but it is not the priority now. Hemodialysis (C)
is reserved for severe cases (e.g., levels >90-100 mg/dL, altered mental status, pulmonary edema, or

refractory acidosis). N-acetylcysteine (D) is for paracetamol overdose. Observation alone (E) is unsafe given
the toxic level and symptoms.

---

questions.stem: A 83-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department 3 hours after ingesting an unknown quantity of liquid paracetamol. She is asymptomatic with normal vital signs. A serum acetaminophen level drawn at 3 hours post-ingestion is 180 pyg/mL. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: D
options.text: Repeat level in 4 hours and plot on nomogram

questions.initialExplanation: Paracetamol 180 at 3 hours (above the treatment line): IV NAC.
questions.detailedExplanation:
While the Rumack-Matthew nomogram is typically used with a 4-hour post-ingestion acetaminophen
level, levels drawn earlier than 4 hours can still be interpreted cautiously. A level of 180 pg/mL at 3
hours is highly concerning—extrapolation suggests it will likely exceed the treatment line (150 pg/mL)
at 4 hours. In clinical practice, if an early level is above 100-120 pg/mL at 2-3 hours, especially with a
known significant ingestion, treatment with N-acetylcysteine (NAC) should not be delayed. Waiting to
repeat the level (D) risks missing the window for optimal hepatoprotection. NAC is most effective when
started within 8 hours and has an excellent safety profile. Activated charcoal (B) may be considered if

given within 1-2 hours, but it’s now 3 hours post-ingestion and not a substitute for NAC. Discharge (A)
or gastric lavage (E) are inappropriate.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after ingesting a small amount of concentrated sodium hydroxide drain opener. On examination, he has hoarseness, drooling, and refuses to swallow. There is no stridor or respiratory distress. Oropharyngeal exam reveals white, leathery mucosal lesions. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: B
options.text: Give oral vinegar to neutralize the alkali

questions.initialExplanation: Caustic ingestion with white leathery oral lesions: urgent EGD to assess burns.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has evidence of significant corrosive injury (hoarseness, drooling, refusal to swallow, and visible
oropharyngeal burns) following alkali ingestion (sodium hydroxide). While airway compromise is a concern, he
currently has no stridor or respiratory distress, so immediate intubation (C) is not yet indicated—but the airway
must be closely monitored. The priority now is urgent EGD within 12-24 hours (ideally <12—24 h) to assess the
depth and extent of esophageal injury, which guides prognosis and management (e.g., risk of stricture).
Activated charcoal (A) is ineffective for corrosives. Oral neutralizing agents like vinegar (B) are

dangerous —they cause exothermic reactions that worsen tissue damage. Discharge (E) is unsafe given clear
signs of mucosal injury.

Note: If the child develops stridor, increased work of breathing, or voice changes, then immediate intubation
becomes critical —but not preemptively in a stable airway.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy is evaluated in the emergency department 2 hours after ingesting an unknown quantity of acetaminophen tablets. The mother is uncertain of the exact time of ingestion but believes it was approximately 2-3 hours ago. Which of the following statements regarding serum acetaminophen level interpretation is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: A single level at any time after ingestion is always sufficient \*

options.label: B
options.text: The nomogram can be used regardless of when the ingestion occurred

options.label: C
options.text: Levels obtained less than 4 hours after ingestion are unreliable for predicting toxicity

options.label: D
options.text: Sustained-release preparations do not require nomogram interpretation

options.label: E
options.text: A nondetectable level rules out toxicity

questions.initialExplanation: A paracetamol level taken before 4 hours after ingestion is unreliable, so wait until 4 hours to interpret it.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Serum acetaminophen levels must be obtained at least 4 hours after ingestion to accurately interpret
toxicity risk using the Rumack-Matthew nomogram. Levels drawn before 4 hours may not reflect peak
absorption and can be falsely low, potentially leading to underestimation of toxicity risk. The
nomogram is only applicable for immediate-release preparations; it may not be reliable for sustained-
release formulations due to prolonged absorption. A nondetectable level obtained more than 4 hours
after ingestion suggests no significant toxicity, but levels obtained before 4 hours, unless truly
nondetectable, cannot be used to estimate potential for toxicity and should be repeated if clinical
suspicion remains high.

---

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl presents with nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain 48 hours after ingesting approximately 150 mg/kg of acetaminophen in a suicide attempt. Her laboratory results show ALT 450 IU/L, AST 520 IU/L, bilirubin 1.8 mg/dL, and INR 1.3. What is the most likely explanation for this clinical presentation?
questions.initialExplanation: Mild AST rise and INR 1.3 at 24-48 hours: Stage II (liver injury).
questions.detailedExplanation:
This patient is presenting 48 hours post-ingestion with evidence of hepatic injury manifesting as
elevated transaminases (ALT and AST in the hundreds) and mild coagulopathy. This corresponds to

‘    Stage Il of acetaminophen toxicity (24-48 hours), during which patients develop right upper quadrant
pain and tenderness with laboratory abnormalities including elevated bilirubin, transaminases, and
prothrombin time. Stage | (0-24 hours) would show gastrointestinal symptoms without liver enzyme
elevation. Stage Ill (3-5 days) typically shows peak transaminase elevations often exceeding 1,000
IU/L with more pronounced coagulopathy. The moderate elevation of transaminases and timing are
most consistent with Stage II hepatic involvement.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy weighing 16 kg ingested an unknown amount of acetaminophen approximately 8 hours ago. He now complains of nausea and appears mildly lethargic. Serum acetaminophen level is 95 pg/mL (630 umol/L). His liver function tests are currently normal. What is the most appropriate management for this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Discharge home with no further treatment \*

options.label: E
options.text: Observe for 24 hours with repeat levels

questions.initialExplanation: Paracetamol with normal LFTs but a level above the line: start oral NAC.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child's serum acetaminophen level of 95 ug/mL (630 pmol/L) obtained at 8 hours post-ingestion
exceeds the treatment threshold. According to the Rumack-Matthew nomogram, levels above the
treatment line at any time point indicate the need for N-acetylcysteine therapy. The threshold of 900
pmol/L is specifically mentioned for possible risk at 4 hours, but the nomogram accounts for declining
levels over time. Since this level exceeds the treatment line, N-acetylcysteine should be initiated
immediately. Oral N-acetylcysteine is given as a loading dose of 140 mg/kg followed by 70 mg/kg
every 4 hours for 17 doses. Waiting or observation alone would be inappropriate given the elevated
level and potential for severe hepatotoxicity.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old girl is admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit with suspected organophosphate poisoning following exposure to pesticides in her family's garden. She has profuse secretions, respiratory distress, and altered mental status. Her blood cholinesterase level is reported as 35% of normal. What is the significance of this cholinesterase level?

options.label: A
options.text: It confirms the diagnosis of organophosphate poisoning

options.label: B
options.text: It indicates severe poisoning requiring aggressive treatment

options.label: C
options.text: It represents a level consistent with mild toxicity

options.label: D
options.text: It is within normal limits and rules out poisoning

options.label: E
options.text: It cannot be interpreted without baseline values

questions.initialExplanation: A low cholinesterase level of 35% = severe poisoning needing aggressive treatment.
questions.detailedExplanation:
A blood cholinesterase level less than 50% of normal is diagnostic for organophosphate poisoning and
indicates significant toxicity requiring aggressive treatment. Levels between 20-50% typically indicate

‘    moderate poisoning, while levels below 20% suggest severe poisoning. This patient's level of 35% falls
within the moderate to severe range, confirming significant organophosphate exposure. While baseline
values can be helpful for comparison, a level below 50% of the normal reference range is sufficient to
confirm poisoning in the appropriate clinical context. The clinical presentation with profuse secretions,
respiratory distress, and altered mental status further supports severe poisoning requiring immediate
intervention with atropine and pralidoxime.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy with organophosphate poisoning is being treated with atropine sulfate. Despite multiple doses, he remains tachycardic with persistent bronchorrhea and miosis. What is the appropriate dosing strategy for atropine in organophosphate poisoning?

options.label: A
options.text: Atropine 0.02 mg/kg every 15-20 minutes until symptoms resolve

options.label: B
options.text: Atropine 0.02 mg/kg every 1-2 hours until pupils normalize

options.label: C
options.text: Atropine 0.02 mg/kg as a single loading dose

options.label: D
options.text: Atropine 0.02 mg/kg continuously until secretions dry

options.label: E
options.text: Atropine 0.02 mg/kg as needed for bradycardia only

questions.initialExplanation: Atropine 0.02 mg/kg every 15-20 minutes until bronchial secretions resolve.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The appropriate dosing of atropine in organophosphate poisoning involves repeated dosing of 0.02
mg/kg intravenously every 15-20 minutes until the target endpoints are achieved. These endpoints
include drying of respiratory secretions, normalization of heart rate and blood pressure, and
resolution of bronchospasm. Unlike typical atropine dosing for bradycardia, organophosphate
poisoning requires much larger cumulative doses over an extended period. The dose should be
titrated to effect rather than given as a fixed schedule or single dose. Therapy may continue for hours
to days depending on the severity of poisoning and the specific organophosphate involved. The goal
is not just to normalize pupils but to control the life-threatening muscarinic effects, particularly
respiratory secretions and bronchospasm.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department after ingesting an unknown amount of kerosene from a container stored in the garage. He is coughing and has decreased breath sounds on the right side of his chest. What is the most serious complication of hydrocarbon ingestion in children?
questions.initialExplanation: The most dangerous complication of hydrocarbon ingestion: aspiration pneumonitis (chemical pneumonia).
questions.detailedExplanation:
The most serious and characteristic complication of hydrocarbon ingestion is aspiration pneumonitis,
which occurs when hydrocarbon liquids enter the lungs, either during ingestion or with subsequent
vomiting. Hydrocarbons cause direct damage to pulmonary tissue through inactivation of type Il
pneumocytes and resultant surfactant deficiency, leading to alveolar collapse, pneumonitis, and
respiratory failure. This can progress rapidly to acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS).
Kerosene, gasoline, and other low-viscosity hydrocarbons have the highest risk of aspiration
pneumonitis because they spread rapidly across lung surfaces. Even small quantities (less than 1
mL) of these agents can cause significant pulmonary injury. While CNS depression and cardiac
arrhythmias can occur, they are less common than the characteristic pulmonary complications.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy is being evaluated in the emergency department 6 hours after ingesting kerosene. He is currently asymptomatic with normal vital signs and lung examination. What is the appropriate management for this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Discharge home after observation for 2 hours

questions.initialExplanation: Kerosene and an asymptomatic child at 6 hours: admit for observation (per the given answer).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Even asymptomatic patients with hydrocarbon ingestion should be admitted for observation and
monitoring because respiratory deterioration can occur rapidly and unpredictably. Pulmonary infiltrates
and clinical signs of pneumonitis may not appear immediately after ingestion; patients can remain
asymptomatic for several hours before developing respiratory distress. The classic teaching is that
chest X-ray findings may not be evident for 6-24 hours after aspiration, though infiltrates are often
visible on CXR performed more than 6 hours later. Admission allows for serial monitoring of vital signs,
oxygen saturation, and respiratory status, with prompt intervention if deterioration occurs. Discharge is
inappropriate due to risk of delayed respiratory failure. Gastric lavage and activated charcoal are
generally contraindicated due to risk of aspiration and limited benefit.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy ingested gasoline from a portable fuel container approximately 1 hour ago. He is alert, coughing occasionally, and has normal oxygen saturation on room air. What is the most appropriate initial management for this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Induce vomiting to remove unabsorbed gasoline

options.label: E
options.text: Give mineral oil to bind the gasoline

questions.initialExplanation: Gasoline with normal oxygenation: observe without intervention.
questions.detailedExplanation:
For hydrocarbon ingestions, the most appropriate management in an asymptomatic patient within the
first hour is observation without specific decontamination measures. Gastric lavage and induced

‘    vomiting are contraindicated because of the high risk of aspiration, which could convert a primarily
gastrointestinal exposure into a severe pulmonary injury. Activated charcoal is generally ineffective for
hydrocarbons and may complicate airway management if vomiting occurs. There is no role for mineral
oil or other binding agents. The patient should be observed for development of respiratory symptoms,
with chest X-ray performed after 6 hours if symptoms develop or as a screening tool. Most
importantly, the airway should be protected, and the patient should be kept calm to reduce the risk of
aspiration from crying or gagging.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy ingested a household cleaner containing hydrochloric acid. He has oral pain and is refusing to drink. His father asks about the expected pattern of injury. Which statement accurately describes acid-induced tissue injury?

options.label: B
options.text: Acids cause coagulative necrosis that limits further injury

options.label: C
options.text: Acids cause liquefactive necrosis allowing deep penetration

options.label: D
options.text: Acids primarily affect the esophagus with sparing of the stomach

options.label: E
options.text: Acids do not cause significant tissue damage

questions.initialExplanation: Acid causes coagulative necrosis, which limits depth, unlike alkalis (liquefactive).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Acid ingestion produces coagulative necrosis, which involves the denaturation of proteins and
formation of an eschar or coagulum on the surface of the tissue. This coagulum may limit the further
penetration of the acid into deeper tissues, potentially limiting the extent of injury compared to alkali
ingestion. Common acids involved in caustic ingestions include hydrochloric acid, phosphoric acid, and
sulfuric acid, found in drain cleaners, rust removers, toilet bowl cleaners, and tile cleaners. While
perforation can still occur with acid ingestion, the coagulative necrosis may create a barrier that slows
the progression of injury. However, the stomach may be more severely affected than the esophagus
due to acid pooling, and the full extent of injury may not be apparent immediately.

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department after ingesting a small amount of undiluted bleach. On examination, she has mild erythema of the lips but no drooling, stridor, or respiratory distress. She is drinking water without difficulty. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: B
options.text: N B. Give oral milk to neutralize the agent

options.label: D
options.text: Observe for 6 hours and discharge if asymptomatic

questions.initialExplanation: Ingestion of a harmful substance with no symptoms: observe 6 hours and discharge if no symptoms appear.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child has mild corrosive exposure (lip erythema only) after ingesting household bleach, which is a
dilute sodium hypochlorite solution (typically <6%). Unlike strong acids or alkalis (e.g., drain cleaners),
‘    dilute bleach rarely causes significant esophageal injury. In the absence of oral burns, drooling,
vomiting, or swallowing difficulty, the risk of serious injury is very low. Current guidelines recommend
observation for 4-6 hours; if the child remains asymptomatic and tolerates oral fluids, discharge is
safe. Endoscopy (C) is not indicated in mild or asymptomatic cases—it is reserved for patients with
signs of moderate to severe injury (e.g., oropharyngeal burns, stridor, hematemesis). Activated
charcoal (A) is ineffective for corrosives. Neutralizing agents like milk (B) are unnecessary and not
recommended. Corticosteroids (E) do not prevent strictures and are not used prophylactically.

---

## Autism

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the pediatric clinic due to concerns about unusual behavior. He has limited verbal communication, avoided eye contact, and showed little interest in social play. He frequently lines up toys and becomes distressed when the order is changed. On examination, the child exhibits repetitive behaviors and limited social interaction. Which of the following features is MOST indicative of autism spectrum disorder?

options.label: C
options.text: Preference for structured routines over free play

questions.initialExplanation: A key DSM-5 criterion: repetitive behaviors and restricted interests (in addition to impaired social communication).
questions.detailedExplanation:
According to the DSM-5, a diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) requires the presence of two core
domains of symptoms:

- Persistent deficits in social communication and social interaction across multiple contexts.

- Restricted, repetitive patterns of behavior, interests, or activities.

The case describes a 3-year-old with:

- Limited verbal communication, Avoidance of eye contact, Lack of interest in social play, Repetitive behaviors
(lining up toys), Distress when routines are disrupted

These features align closely with DSM-5 criteria. While social communication deficits are also essential, among
the answer choices provided, option D directly reflects one of the two defining diagnostic pillars of

ASD —restricted, repetitive behaviors and interests—which is highly specific to ASD compared to other
developmental disorders.

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy is brought by his parents; they feel he is not interactive with them. The boy usually plays by himself and does not appear to be interested in joining group activities. He becomes very frustrated when he does not get his way. He typically makes poor eye contact. What is the MOST APPROPRIATE intervention at this time to perform? 2024 Js

options.label: D
options.text: Modified checklist for autism in toddlers(M-CHAT)

questions.initialExplanation: The initial autism screen in a young child: M-CHAT.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child displays red flags for autism spectrum disorder: poor eye contact, solitary play, lack of social
engagement, and rigidity with frustration. The M-CHAT is a validated, parent-completed screening tool
specifically designed for toddlers 16-30 months to identify ASD risk before formal diagnostic referral. It is
recommended by the AAP as part of routine developmental surveillance at 18 and 24 months. EEG, genetic
testing, lead levels, and thyroid studies are not first-line interventions without specific indications (seizures,
dysmorphic features, exposure history, or systemic symptoms). Screening with M-CHAT efficiently stratifies
risk, guides appropriate referral to developmental specialists, and avoids unnecessary testing.

---

questions.stem: You are meeting parents of a 3-year-old boy who has normal developmental milestone and social interaction; they have older child with autism; they have a concern about having this young kid with autism as well. You state that most children with autism have clinical manifestations by the age of :

options.label: A
options.text: second or third year of life

questions.initialExplanation: Most symptoms appear during the second or third year of life.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Most children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) display clinical manifestations by the second or
third year of life, often becoming evident between 12 and 24 months of age. Early signs may include
delayed language development, lack of joint attention, reduced eye contact, and limited social
reciprocity. While some children may appear to develop typically in the first year, regression or
stagnation in skills commonly occurs during the second year. Although milder cases might not be
recognized until preschool or later, the majority of core symptoms are present by age 3. Options B-D
reflect ages when diagnosis may sometimes occur—especially in high-functioning individuals —but
not when manifestations typically begin. Option E is incorrect because ASD has a well-established
early onset pattern.

---

questions.stem: Comorbidities are commonly encountered in children with autism, especially other psychiatric disorders. Of the following, the MOST commonly associated disease with autism is :
questions.initialExplanation: The commonest condition associated with autism: intellectual disability (mental retardation).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Intellectual disability (ID) is the most common comorbidity in children with autism spectrum disorder
(ASD), occurring in approximately 30-50% of cases, depending on the population studied. While
psychiatric comorbidities such as ADHD (E), anxiety disorders (C), and OCD (D) are also frequent,
they are generally less prevalent than ID. Seizure disorders (B) occur in about 20-30% of individuals
with ASD, particularly in those with comorbid ID or motor deficits, but still less commonly than ID
itself. It's important to note that diagnostic criteria for ASD (per DSM-5) allow for co-diagnosis with ID,
and the two often coexist, especially in nonverbal or minimally verbal children. Thus, A is the best
answer based on epidemiological data.

---

questions.stem: The earliest studies of autism suggested a relatively poor prognosis, with only a small number of individuals being able to function independently as adults. Of the following, the factor that carry POOR outcome is :
questions.initialExplanation: Per the given answer, the factor linked to prognosis is early onset; better to check the reference since language and IQ are the strongest predictors.
questions.detailedExplanation:
In autism spectrum disorder (ASD), early onset of symptoms —particularly before 12—18 months of
age—is associated with a poorer long-term prognosis. This is because very early and severe
manifestations often reflect more significant underlying neurodevelopmental disruption, frequently
accompanied by intellectual disability, minimal language development, and greater functional
impairment. In contrast, higher IQ (B), better language skills (C), good communication abilities (D),
and average nonverbal cognitive skills (E) are all well-established positive prognostic indicators,
correlating with greater independence, adaptive functioning, and social integration in adulthood.
Thus, among the listed options, only early onset is linked to a poorer outcome, making A the correct
choice.

---

questions.stem: A 3-yr-old boy is noted to have stereotypical body movements and poor verbal and nonverbal communication, with absence of empathy. At daycare, he has not made any friends. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.initialExplanation: Stereotyped movements, impaired verbal and nonverbal communication and lack of empathy = autism.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This 3-year-old boy exhibits core features of autism spectrum disorder (ASD): persistent deficits in social communication
and interaction (e.g., poor verbal and nonverbal communication, absence of empathy, inability to form peer relationships)
along with restricted, repetitive behaviors (stereotypical body movements). According to the DSM-5, a diagnosis of ASD
requires symptoms to be present in early childhood and to cause functional impairment—both of which are evident here.
- Option A (ADHD) is incorrect because ADHD primarily involves inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity —not social
communication deficits or stereotypies. Option B (Dysthymic syndrome) refers to chronic low-grade depression, which is
extremely rare in 3-year-olds and does not explain stereotyped movements or absent empathy. Option C (Deaf-mutism)
might mimic language delay but would not account for lack of nonverbal communication, social disinterest, or repetitive
movements. Option E (Cerebral palsy) is a motor disorder due to brain injury; while it may coexist with developmental
delays, it does not typically cause the specific social and behavioral profile described.

---

questions.stem: You are seeing a 2-year-old girl in your office for a well-child visit. Her mother is concerned that she is not talking much. She only says 5 words, but she knows her body parts and follows simple directions. According to the mother, she doesn’t seem interested in playing with other children. You are aware that a language delay and atypical social development may be early signs of autism. Among the following, which question, if answered negatively by the mother, would be the most revealing about a possible diagnosis of an autistic spectrum disorder (ASD)?

options.label: A
options.text: If you point to a toy in a room, does your child look at it and then look at you?

options.label: B
options.text: Does your child enjoy playing peek-a-boo? Does your child understand what people say to her?

options.label: C
options.text: Does your child have sensitivities to particular foods or fabrics?

options.label: D
options.text: Does your child often seem to worry when in new situations? POO OoTW

questions.initialExplanation: The most revealing question: when you point to a toy, does your child look at it and then at you? (joint attention).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Children with ASD have a deficit in 3 core areas of development: a delay in communication (delayed language
milestones or awkward use of language in social situations), atypical social skills, and interests characterized as
rigid and inflexible (often with repetitive or stereotypic movements). One of the most revealing developmental
milestones that is absent in toddlers with ASD is joint attention—when an infant shares his or her gaze between
an object or event and another person by looking back and forth between the 2. Joint attention can be seen just
after the first birthday; it should be established by 18 months. Limited joy when playing peek-a-boo, delayed
receptive language, and sensory hypersensitivities are seen in many children with ASD, but they are not
consistently present. Excessive worry in a toddler is usually an expression of a shy, slow-to-warm-up
temperament; it may or may not be an early clue to anxiety.

---

questions.stem: The parents of a 21-month-old boy are concerned because he used to say a few words and more recently, he is just babbling with no recognizable words. They are worried these may be features of autism. Which of the following is a feature that characterizes autistic spectrum disorders?

options.label: B
options.text: Use of 2 word phrases by 18 months

options.label: E
options.text: Lack of sensitivity to textures or sounds

questions.initialExplanation: Loss of previously acquired language with decreased eye contact = a sign of autism.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Autism is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by impaired socialization, impaired verbal
and nonverbal communication, and restricted, repetitive patterns of behavior. Early recognition of

‘    autism, preferably before the second year of life, is critical. Referral criteria in the second year of life
include no pointing or waving by 18 months, a preference for solitary play, diminished eye contact,
and an oversensitivity to textures and noises. Nystagmus is more likely to be associated with an
ocular disorder. Lack of use of two-word phrases is a concern after the age of 2 years.

---

questions.stem: A young couple bring their 30-month-old infant son to their pediatrician because he has not learned to speak, does not interact or play with other children, does not display eye contact and repeatedly flaps his hands. Physical examination is normal. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Hand flapping and speech delay in a 30-month-old = pervasive developmental disorder (autism).
questions.detailedExplanation:
Autism is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by impaired social interaction and
communication, repetitive and stereotyped patterns of behavior, and uneven intellectual
development often with mental retardation.

Symptoms begin in early childhood. The cause in most children is unknown, although evidence
supports a genetic component; in some, autism may be caused by a medical condition. Diagnosis is
based on developmental history and observation. Treatment consists of behavioral management and
sometimes drug therapy.

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the pediatric clinic because he is not speaking any words. His mother reports that he rarely makes eye contact and prefers to play alone. He lines up his toys instead of playing with them in an imaginative way and becomes very upset if his daily routine is changed. There is no regression of previously acquired skills. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Speech delay and insistence on routine without regression of skills = autism spectrum disorder.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This child exhibits classic features of autism spectrum disorder including impaired social interaction
(poor eye contact, preference for solitary play), impaired communication (delayed speech), and
restricted repetitive behaviors (lining up toys, distress with routine changes). The onset is before 3
years of age. Autism is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by persistent deficits in social
communication and social interaction accompanied by restricted, repetitive patterns of behavior,
interests, or activities. The male-to-female ratio is approximately 4:1.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old girl has been diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder. Her parents ask about the cause of her condition. Which of the following is the most appropriate statement regarding the etiology of autism?

options.label: A
options.text: Autism is caused by poor parenting

options.label: B
options.text: There is a strong genetic influence with multiple genes involved

options.label: C
options.text: Autism is caused by the MMR vaccine

options.label: D
options.text: Autism has a single identifiable cause

options.label: E
options.text: Autism is caused exclusively by environmental factors

questions.initialExplanation: Autism has a strong genetic influence with multiple genes (not vaccines).
questions.detailedExplanation:
The etiology of autism spectrum disorder is complex and multifactorial, with strong genetic influence.
