Many genes have been associated with autism, and there is a notably higher prevalence in
monozygotic twins compared to dizygotic twins and siblings. Environmental factors such as prenatal
infections and toxin exposure may increase risk, but no specific single cause has been identified.
Numerous large studies have conclusively shown no link between vaccines (including MMR) and
autism. The vaccine controversy has been thoroughly debunked.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy with autism spectrum disorder is being evaluated. His parents report that he had normal development until 18 months of age, when he started losing language skills and social engagement. He now has minimal verbal communication and engages in repetitive hand-flapping movements. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial diagnostic step?
questions.initialExplanation: First assessment in a child with language delay and a distinctive behavior: a hearing test to make sure there is no hearing loss.
questions.detailedExplanation:
When evaluating a child with language delay or regression, hearing impairment must be ruled out as
an underlying cause. Even in children with autism, hearing should be tested to ensure that language
delays are not due to hearing loss. After hearing is confirmed to be normal, further investigations may
include chromosomal analysis if dysmorphic features are present, EEG if seizures are suspected, and
other tests as indicated.

---

questions.stem: A 18-month-old boy is brought for routine well-child visit. The pediatrician uses a screening tool for autism called the Checklist for Autism in Toddlers (CHAT). At what age is the CHAT screening tool designed to be used?
questions.initialExplanation: The CHAT screen is done at 18 months.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The Checklist for Autism in Toddlers (CHAT) is a screening tool designed for use with 18-month-old
children. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends screening for ASD at 18 months and 24
months of age. Early screening is crucial because early intervention leads to better outcomes. The
screening includes questions about social interaction, communication, and symbolic play.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy with autism spectrum disorder has difficulty with social interactions. He does not understand other people's emotions and rarely shares his enjoyment or interests with others. He has limited facial expressions and does not use gestures appropriately. Which domain of the DSM-5 criteria for ASD is most impaired in this child?
questions.initialExplanation: In DSM-5 the domain most affected here: deficits in social-emotional reciprocity.
questions.detailedExplanation:
The DSM-5 criteria for ASD include three subcategories under social communication deficits: (1)
deficits in social-emotional reciprocity, (2) deficits in nonverbal communicative behaviors, and (3)
deficits in developing, maintaining, and understanding relationships. This child's difficulty sharing
enjoyment and understanding others' emotions represents deficits in social-emotional reciprocity.

Treatment should address these core social communication deficits through behavioral and
educational interventions.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old girl with autism spectrum disorder engages in repetitive hand-flapping when excited and becomes extremely distressed when there are unexpected changes to her daily routine. She has intense interest in spinning objects and becomes upset when anyone touches her toys. Which of the following best describes the DSM-5 criteria met by this presentation?
questions.initialExplanation: Attachment to toys and anger when they are touched represents a restricted, repetitive pattern of behavior.
questions.detailedExplanation:
This presentation illustrates the second major domain of ASD criteria: restricted, repetitive patterns of
behavior, interests, or activities. The manifestations include stereotyped or repetitive motor movements
(hand-flapping), insistence on sameness and inflexible adherence to routines, highly restricted fixated
interests (spinning objects), and hyper- or hyporeactivity to sensory input (distress with touching toys).
These behaviors must be present currently or by history.

---

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy with autism spectrum disorder has been receiving behavioral therapy for 2 years. His parents ask about the prognosis. Which of the following is the most accurate statement regarding the prognosis of autism spectrum disorder?

options.label: A
options.text: Most children outgrow autism by adolescence

options.label: B
options.text: Autism is a lifelong condition with variable outcomes

options.label: C
options.text: All individuals with autism require institutional care as adults

options.label: E
options.text: Autism always leads to severe intellectual disability

questions.initialExplanation: Autism is a lifelong condition with variable outcomes.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Autism spectrum disorder is a lifelong neurodevelopmental condition. Although a minority of individuals
respond so well to therapy that they no longer meet criteria for the diagnosis, most will make progress
but continue to have some impairment in social and behavioral function as adults. Outcome depends
on cognitive and language skills at diagnosis, severity of symptoms, and early initiation of intensive
treatment. Many individuals can achieve functional independence with appropriate support.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy with autism spectrum disorder has been evaluated for associated medical conditions. His parents want to know what other conditions are commonly associated with autism. Which of the following is the most common psychiatric comorbidity in autism spectrum disorder?
questions.initialExplanation: The commonest psychiatric comorbidity in autism: anxiety disorder.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Anxiety disorders affect approximately 40% of individuals with autism spectrum disorder and represent
one of the most common psychiatric comorbidities. Other common comorbidities include depression
(12-70%), obsessive-compulsive disorder (7-24%), ADHD, and various behavioral disorders. Medical
comorbidities include epilepsy (8-35%), sleep disorders (50-80%), and intellectual disability
(approximately 45%). Comprehensive evaluation should screen for these associated conditions.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy with autism spectrum disorder has a history of seizures. His parents ask about the relationship between autism and seizures. What is the prevalence of epilepsy in individuals with autism spectrum disorder? Less than 1% 50-75%
questions.initialExplanation: About 8-35% of people with autism have epilepsy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Epilepsy occurs in approximately 8-35% of individuals with autism spectrum disorder, representing a
significant comorbidity. The risk is higher in individuals with intellectual disability and those with
regression. Seizures may present at any age but often emerge during adolescence. EEG
abnormalities are even more common, though not all require treatment.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy with autism spectrum disorder has sleep difficulties. His parents report he takes a long time to fall asleep and wakes frequently during the night. What is the most common sleep disorder in children with autism spectrum disorder?
questions.initialExplanation: The commonest sleep problem in autism: insomnia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Sleep disorders affect 50-80% of children with autism spectrum disorder, with insomnia being the most
common manifestation. Insomnia includes difficulty falling asleep, frequent nighttime awakenings, and
early morning waking. Contributing factors may include sensory sensitivities, anxiety, irregular sleep-
wake patterns, and co-occurring medical conditions. Melatonin is often used to address sleep onset
difficulties.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy with autism spectrum disorder is being evaluated for his treatment options. His parents want to know what is the most effective intervention. Which of the following has the strongest evidence for effectiveness in treating autism spectrum disorder?
questions.initialExplanation: The strongest evidence for treatment: intensive behavioral therapy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Intensive behavioral therapies, particularly Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA), have the strongest
evidence for effectiveness in treating autism spectrum disorder. Earlier age at initiation of treatment
and higher intensity of treatment are associated with better outcomes. Programming must be
individualized, and no single approach is successful for all children. There is no scientific evidence to
support special diets, vitamin supplements, chelation therapy, or hyperbaric oxygen for treating
autism.

---

questions.stem: A 2-year-old girl is being evaluated for possible autism. She makes good eye contact and has some pretend play but does not point to share interests with others. Which of the following is a red flag for autism in toddlers?

options.label: C
options.text: Lack of pointing to share interest

questions.initialExplanation: Lack of pointing to share interest is an early sign of autism.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Lack of pointing to share interest with others is one of the early red flags for autism spectrum disorder.
Other concerning signs include absence of babbling by 12 months, no single words by 16 months, no
two-word phrases by 24 months, loss of previously acquired language or social skills, and lack of eye

contact. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends autism-specific screening at 18 and 24
months.

---

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy with autism spectrum disorder engages in pica (eating non-food items). His parents report this behavior is frequent. What is the prevalence of pica in children with autism spectrum disorder?
questions.initialExplanation: About 36% of children with autism have pica.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Pica occurs in approximately 36% of individuals with autism spectrum disorder. Behavioral disorders
are common comorbidities, with aggressive behaviors occurring in up to 68% and self-injurious
behaviors in up to 50% of individuals. These behaviors should be addressed through behavioral
interventions and may require medication if severe.

---

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy with autism spectrum disorder does not respond when his name is called. He also has poor eye contact and does not point to indicate what he wants. Which of the following is the most common differential diagnosis that should be excluded?
questions.initialExplanation: Language delay and not responding to name: hearing loss must be excluded before diagnosing autism.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Hearing impairment must be ruled out in any child presenting with language delay, poor response to
name, or communication difficulties. Even when the clinical picture strongly suggests autism, a
hearing test is essential to exclude hearing loss as a cause. Once hearing is confirmed to be normal,
the diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder can be made based on the pattern of deficits in social
communication and restricted repetitive behaviors.

---

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy with autism spectrum disorder has been in behavioral therapy for 2 years. His parents ask about the role of family support. Which of the following is an important component of family support in autism management?

options.label: A
options.text: Parents should avoid accepting the child's behavior

options.label: B
options.text: Parental education on interaction with the child

options.label: C
options.text: Parents should limit time with the child

options.label: D
options.text: Parents should not be involved in therapy

options.label: E
options.text: Parents should focus only on academic skills

questions.initialExplanation: Family support includes educating the family on how to interact with the child.
questions.detailedExplanation:
Family support and counseling, including parental education on interaction with the child and
acceptance of their behavior, is an important component of autism management. This often benefits
the relationship between parents and the affected child and may significantly improve quality of life.
Early intervention programs typically include parent training as a core component.
